potentiating ferroptosis jointly. This ferroptosis-inducing activity yielded 
potent in vivo antitumor efficacy in Huh-7 tumor-bearing nude mice, with a tumor 
inhibition rate of 74.23% and minimal systemic toxicity. Collectively, the 
organelle-specific targeting combined with co-delivery of synergistic drug pairs 
represents a promising strategy for combating malignancies and provides a 
blueprint for the rational design of multifunctional nanosystems.

Multi-resonance thermally activated delayed fluorescence (MR-TADF) has 
established a new approach for narrowband blue organic light emitting diodes

high doping concentrations while preserving the intrinsic narrowband emission 
remains a formidable challenge. Herein, a novel designing paradigm is proposed

Proteomic Profiling of Xenobiotic and Nutrient Transporters in Human Placenta of 
Different Gestational Ages.

Weaver EM(1)(2), Topletz-Erickson A(1), Kelly EJ(1)(2)(3), Wang J(1)(2), 
Isoherranen N(1), Unadkat JD(1)(2), Arnold SLM(1)(2).

(2)University of Washington Transporter Elucidation Network, University of

The placenta serves a critical role in nutrient uptake and waste elimination for 
the developing fetus. The placenta is also responsible for the uptake and/or 
exchange of xenobiotics, including medications, between the maternal and fetal 
bloodstreams. An estimated 40-80% of women take medications or drugs during 
pregnancy. Very little is understood about fetal drug and nutrient exposure 
during pregnancy and how it may change over the course of fetal development. 
This study aimed to characterize the abundance of transport proteins in 
placental tissue, which are important in modulating fetal nutrient and drug 
exposure, over the duration of pregnancy. Using a mass spectrometry-based global 
proteomic approach, the relative abundance of proteins in placental tissue 
samples was profiled from first trimester, second trimester, and term placenta 
samples. Our analysis detected a total of 6331 proteins which included a total 
of 139 solute carrier and ATP-binding cassette transport proteins that were 
detected across the dataset, and 80 that were quantified in every sample. In 
general, membrane-associated proteins, including solute carrier and ATP-binding 
cassette transport proteins, were significantly enriched in placental tissue 
collected during early gestation compared to term placental tissue. Overall, 
this study presents a comprehensive profiling of membrane-associated proteomic 
changes during gestation and identifies significant gestational age associated 
abundance changes at the protein level in several transport protein families. 
These data provide critical information to support future studies into the 
understanding of fetal exposure to xenobiotics and nutrients circulating in the 
maternal bloodstream.

point-prevalence surveys (PPS) were conducted using rectal and throat swabs.
RESULTS: In August 2023, two LOGBS cases (bacteremia and meningitis) triggered 
the investigation. Two more LOGBS bacteremias occurred pending WGS results.

cluster 1, serotype Ia). The fourth was 1 SNV different from a conjunctivitis 
case detected a week later (cluster 2, serotype V). PPS revealed 5 asymptomatic 
cases genomically unrelated to either cluster. In February 2024, two further 
LOGBS cases (bacteremia; asymptomatic bacteruria) emerged. The first matched the

infections occurred through October 2025.
CONCLUSIONS: This prolonged NICU outbreak involved multiple serotypes. WGS was

Patient Participation as Expectation or Exception? Negotiating Responsibility 
Among Patients, Families and Nurses in Chronic Illness Care: A Focused 
Ethnography.

Wang Y(1)(2)(3), Zhu L(3)(4), Liu Y(1), Zhang Y(1), Fan X(1)(5), Avilés L(3), 
Chandler C(3), Hong J(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)School of Nursing, Anhui Medical University, Hefei, China.
(2)School of Public Health, Anhui Medical University, Hefei, China.
(3)School of Health in Social Science, The University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, 
UK.
(4)Department of Nursing, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai, China.
(5)Department of Critical Care Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital of USTC, 
Division of Life Science and Medicine, University of Science and Technology of 
China, Hefei, China.

AIM: To examine how responsibilities for patient participation are understood, 
distributed and negotiated among chronically ill patients, family members and 
nurses in everyday nursing care.
DESIGN: Focused ethnography.
METHODS: The study was conducted in a public hospital in China. Data comprised 
90 h of participant observation and 30 semi-structured interviews with nurses, 
patients and family members. Data were analysed using inductive and abductive 
reflexive thematic analysis.
RESULTS: Participation was enacted through role-based and relational 
expectations. Patients were expected to cooperate with treatment, report 
symptoms and contribute to recovery; family members provided practical and 
emotional support; and nurses educated, coordinated, monitored and safeguarded 
care. However, responsibilities were often assumed rather than explicitly 
clarified, making participation dependent on adjustment, mediation and 
workarounds. Responsibility enabled participation, but also made it conditional 
and uneven when transferred without supervision, when protection constrained 
patient voice, or when responsibilities became burdensome.
CONCLUSION: Responsibility is not merely an individual duty or policy demand, 
but a relational and culturally situated practice shaping when, how and for whom 
participation becomes possible.
IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: Nurses should move beyond 
broad calls for shared responsibility by clarifying expectations, supporting 
patients and families to take on responsibilities safely, and negotiating 
responsibilities when routines, family involvement or patient preferences create 
uncertainty.
IMPACT: This study addresses the overlooked role of responsibility in patient 
participation. Participation depends on how responsibilities are distributed, 
assumed, transferred and negotiated among patients, family members and nurses. 
The findings may inform chronic illness and family-involved nursing care.
REPORTING METHOD: COREQ.
PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: Patients and family members contributed to data 
generation through participation in observations and interviews. They were not 
involved as research partners in the study design, data analysis or 
interpretation or manuscript preparation.

Eosinophilic Oesophagitis and Incidence of Gastrointestinal Cancer: A 
Population-Based Cohort Study.

Kurt G(1)(2), Farkas DK(1), Dellon ES(3), Jensen ET(3)(4), Sørensen HT(1)(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Clinical Epidemiology, Center for Population Medicine, Aarhus 
University and Aarhus University Hospital, Aarhus, Denmark.
(2)Department of Surgery, Randers Regional Hospital, Randers, Denmark.
(3)Center for Esophageal Diseases and Swallowing, Division of Gastroenterology 
and Hepatology, Department of Medicine, University of North Carolina School of 
Medicine, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA.
(4)Department of Epidemiology and Prevention, Wake Forest School of Medicine, 
Winston-Salem, North Carolina, USA.

BACKGROUND: Evidence concerning gastrointestinal cancer risk after eosinophilic 
oesophagitis (EoE) diagnosis is limited.
AIMS: To examine the association between EoE and incident gastrointestinal 
cancer in a population-based cohort.
METHODS: Using nationwide Danish health registries, we identified all patients 
diagnosed with EoE between 1997 and 2024, using a validated algorithm. We 
computed standardised incidence ratios (SIRs) for gastrointestinal cancers 
overall and site-specific cancers compared with the general population. To 
distinguish short-term diagnostic activity from longer-term risk, we stratified 
analyses by < 1 and ≥ 1 year after EoE diagnosis. Secondary analyses examined 
oesophageal cancer incidence among EoE patients with coexisting Barrett's 
oesophagus (BE).
RESULTS: Among 9115 EoE patients, 170 developed gastrointestinal cancers. During 
the first year after EoE diagnosis, the SIR was 2.83 (95% confidence interval: 
2.10-3.74). Beyond 1 year, the overall SIR attenuated (1.03 [0.85-1.23]) but 
remained elevated for oesophageal cancer (2.40 [1.42-3.79]) and hepatocellular 
carcinoma (2.05 [0.98-3.77]). Among patients who developed oesophageal cancer 
≥ 1 year after EoE diagnosis (n = 18), most had prior BE. The SIR for 
oesophageal cancer was 5.44 (2.90-9.31) among patients with both EoE and BE and 
4.84 (4.36-5.37) among patients with BE alone. SIR for patients with EoE alone 
could not be reported due to the low number of cancer cases.
CONCLUSIONS: One year after EoE diagnosis, oesophageal cancer and hepatocellular 
carcinoma rates remained elevated. Most oesophageal cancers occurred in patients 
with prior BE, suggesting that the association between EoE and oesophageal 
cancer may be mediated largely through BE.

Maternal Factors Modifying the Link Between Genetic Risk for Autism and 
Developmental Milestones.

D'Alesio L(1)(2), Patel VN(3), Walsh M(4), Messias E(1)(2), Lin PI(1)(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience, Saint Louis University 
School of Medicine, St. Louis, Missouri, USA.
(2)School of Medicine, Saint Louis University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA.
(3)College of Public Health and Social Justice, Saint Louis University, St. 
Louis, Missouri, USA.
(4)Department of Family and Community Medicine, Saint Louis University, St. 
Louis, Missouri, USA.
(5)Discipline of Psychiatry and Mental Health, School of Clinical Medicine, 
University of New South Wales, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia.

Although common genetic liability-quantified through polygenic risk scores 
(PRS)-accounts for substantial variance in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) 
liability, how prenatal environmental exposures interact with genetic 
predisposition to shape developmental outcomes remains poorly understood. Using 
the data from Autism Genetic Resource Exchange (AGRE), we examined whether 
maternal prenatal factors moderate the association between ASD PRS and 
developmental outcomes, including language delay, motor delay, and core ASD 
traits. In exploratory gene-environment interaction analyses, amniocentesis was 
a candidate positive moderator of the association between PRS and both language 
and motor delay, such that higher polygenic liability was associated with a 
greater likelihood of these delays among prenatally exposed children. 
First-trimester vaginal bleeding showed a similar positive interaction estimate 
for motor delay. Maternal use of over-the-counter (OTC) medications during 
pregnancy-predominantly acetaminophen, reported by 59.9% of OTC users-was 
associated with an inverse interaction estimate, corresponding to a decreased 
association between polygenic liability and language delay among exposed 
children. These observations suggest that several prenatal factors may modify 
the association between common genetic liability and developmental outcomes 
among autistic children and should be considered hypothesis-generating until 
replicated in larger, population-based cohorts. Replication in independent 
samples, together with analyses that address selection and confounding, will be 
required before these candidate gene-environment interactions can be interpreted 
as reflecting specific developmental mechanisms.

Long-term outcomes and factors associated with revision after medial open-wedge 
high tibial osteotomy in 274 knees: a Kellgren-Lawrence grade-stratified 
analysis.

Gomi N(1), Chikaishi N(2), Isozaki R(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Joint Surgery Center, Sakaide Kaisei Hospital, Sakaide, Japan. 
maseratthigransports@yahoo.co.jp.
(2)Department of Joint Surgery Center, Sakaide Kaisei Hospital, Sakaide, Japan.
(3)Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Kagawa University, Miki, Japan.

PURPOSE: We aimed to investigate long-term outcomes and factors associated with 
revision after medial open-wedge high tibial osteotomy (OWHTO) according to 
Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grade.
METHODS: This retrospective study included 274 knees (158 KL grade 4 [KL4] knees 
and 116 KL grades 2-3 [KL2-3] knees; mean age 64.7 ± 7.2 years) with a minimum 
follow-up of 10 years (mean follow-up, 12.5 ± 2.6 years) after OWHTO. Revision 
surgery (conversion to total knee arthroplasty [TKA] or unicompartmental knee 
arthroplasty [UKA]) was defined as the endpoint. Clinical and radiographic 
outcomes were evaluated. Multivariate logistic regression analyses were 
performed separately for KL4 and KL2-3 knees to identify factors associated with 
revision.
RESULTS: The mean Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score improved from 
60.6 preoperatively to 91.0 at plate removal, followed by gradual deterioration 
during long-term follow-up. Final JOA scores were significantly lower in KL4 
knees than in KL2-3 knees (71.6 versus 83.1; p < 0.001). Revision surgery was 
performed in 43 knees (15.7%) and was significantly more frequent in KL4 than in 
KL2-3 knees (22.2% versus 6.9%; p < 0.01). Ten-year joint preservation rates 
were 90.5% in KL4 knees and 96.5% in KL2-3 knees (log-rank p = 0.006). In KL4 
knees, postoperative percentage mechanical axis (%MA) at the time of plate 
removal was independently associated with revision risk (odds ratio [OR] 0.94, 
95% confidence interval [CI] 0.91-0.98; p = 0.004). In KL2-3 knees, an 
exploratory multivariate analysis suggested an association between progression 
of joint line convergence angle during follow-up (ΔJLCA) and revision (OR 3.31, 
95% CI 1.52-7.21; p = 0.003), whereas postoperative %MA showed no significant 
association.
CONCLUSIONS: Long-term outcomes after OWHTO differed according to KL grade. KL4 
knees demonstrated higher revision rates and inferior joint preservation 
survival, and postoperative weight-bearing line position was associated with 
revision risk. In contrast, revision was uncommon in KL2-3 knees, and 
exploratory analysis suggested a possible association with longitudinal changes 
in joint line convergence rather than postoperative alignment. These findings 
suggest that factors associated with revision may differ according to disease 
severity.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: This was a level IV, retrospective cohort study.

Perioperative management of acute type A aortic dissection using extended 
half-life factor IX (Alprolix) in a patient with severe hemophilia B: a case 
report.

Kitamura T(1), Ryu Y(2), Nakaji S(2), Taniguchi S(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Cardiovascular Surgery, Sasebo Chuo Hospital, 15 Yamato, Sasebo 
City, Nagasaki, 857-1195, Japan. kitamura-t@nagasaki-u.ac.jp.
(2)Department of Cardiovascular Surgery, Sasebo Chuo Hospital, 15 Yamato, Sasebo

BACKGROUND: Emergency surgery for acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) in 
patients with severe hemophilia B is extremely rare, and perioperative 
coagulation management is a major challenge.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 63-year-old man with severe hemophilia B (factor IX 
activity < 1%) was diagnosed with ATAAD and underwent emergency surgery. 
Replacement therapy with an extended half-life factor IX product (eftrenonacog 
alfa; Alprolix) was administered targeting a factor IX activity of 80-100%, and 
total arch replacement was performed. Cardiopulmonary bypass was performed under 
standard heparinization conditions. Since rapid measurement of factor IX 
activity was not possible, postoperative replacement therapy was based primarily 
on the clinical assessment of hemostasis, with serial activated partial 
thromboplastin time measurements providing supportive information, whereas 
intraoperative anticoagulation was managed using standard activated clotting 
time monitoring. Intra- and postoperative bleeding volumes were within ranges 
comparable to those observed in standard complex aortic surgery, and the 
postoperative course was uneventful.
CONCLUSIONS: The use of an extended half-life factor IX product may be a 
practical option for perioperative coagulation management during emergency 
aortic surgery in patients with severe hemophilia B.

Racial Disparities in Severe Maternal Morbidity: The Role of Maternal 
Comorbidities.

Milazzo A(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)University of Rome Unitelma Sapienza, Rome, Italy.
(2)University of Houston, Houston, Texas, USA.

The U.S. maternal health crisis disproportionately affects Black women, who face 
nearly twice the risk of severe maternal morbidity (SMM) compared with White 
women. Using 2016-2022 Texas hospital discharge data and a validated obstetric 
comorbidity score, the analysis first documents that the prevalence of SMM 
increased by 18% between 2016 and 2022, whereas maternal comorbidity burden 
increased by 42% over the same period. To better assess the role of 
comorbidities, the comorbidity score is disaggregated into underlying health and 
pregnancy-specific conditions. Oaxaca-Blinder decompositions indicate that the 
former accounts for the largest share-49 to 53%-of the Black-White SMM gap, 
while the latter accounts for an additional third of the disparity. After 
accounting for these factors, a residual Black-White SMM gap of 17%-20% persists 
across and within hospitals, including among women treated by the same 
physician. Overall, the findings underscore the critical need to improve women's 
health well before childbirth hospitalization and throughout the reproductive 
life course, while also strengthening prenatal care to prevent and effectively 
manage conditions that arise during pregnancy.

Capsaicin suppresses microglial inflammation through TRPV1-SSR4 interaction.

Hou Y(#)(1)(2)(3), Wang S(#)(1)(2), Yang Y(1)(2), Zhao Z(1)(2), Xie Y(1)(2), 
Ouyang X(1)(2), Zhang K(4)(5), Chen H(6)(7), Xu J(8)(9).

jianrong.xu@shutcm.edu.cn.
(9)Shuguang Lab of Future Health, Shanghai Frontiers Science Center of TCM

BACKGROUND: Transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) is increasingly 
recognized as an important regulator of microglial response during 
neuroinflammation, a key pathological feature of various neurodegenerative 
diseases such as Alzheimer's disease. Capsaicin, the primary pungent component 
in chili peppers, executes its anti-inflammatory properties as a TRPV1 agonist. 
Although the mechanism of TRPV1 channel activation and signal transduction by 
capsaicin has been extensively studied, the protein-protein interaction-based 
mechanisms by which TRPV1 modulates microglial inflammatory responses in the 
context of neurodegeneration remains unclear.
METHODS: We used a lipopolysaccharide-induced acute neuroinflammation model to 
examine the effects of TRPV1 activation and pharmacological blockade of TRPV1 
channel gating on microglial inflammatory responses. Proximity labeling-based 
proteomics, bioluminescence resonance energy transfer, and NanoLuc Binary 
Technology were used to identify and characterize TRPV1-interacting proteins. 
Signal sequence receptor subunit 4 (SSR4) knockdown and forced interaction 
between TRPV1 and SSR4 were performed to assess the functional contribution of 
the TRPV1-SSR4 interaction. Structural modeling, BRET-based domain mapping, and 
colocalization analyses were further used to examine the molecular and 
subcellular features of SSR4 recruitment by TRPV1.
RESULTS: In the neuroinflammatory model, the TRPV1 agonist capsaicin attenuated 
pro-inflammatory cytokine production, neuronal apoptosis, microgliosis, and 
microglial soma enlargement in a TRPV1-dependent manner. Notably, 
pharmacological blockade of TRPV1 channel gating by capsazepine did not abolish 
the anti-inflammatory action of capsaicin, suggesting an alternative mechanism 
of action beyond the canonical ligand-gated Ca2⁺ influx. Screening of TRPV1 prey 
proteins and validation strategy identified SSR4 as a capsaicin-responsive, 
TRPV1-associated protein. SSR4 knockdown in microglia significantly diminished 
the suppression of inflammatory responses caused by TRPV1 activation. 
Conversely, forced interaction between TRPV1 and SSR4 partially mimicked the 
anti-inflammatory effects of TRPV1 activation. Further structural and cellular 
analyses suggested that the transmembrane region of TRPV1 supports SSR4 
recruitment.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that capsaicin suppresses microglial 
inflammation mediated by the TRPV1-SSR4 interaction, providing new insights into 
the chemical biology basis of TRPV1 interoceptive signaling and potential 
applications of natural TRPV1 agonists for modifying therapy of 
neuroinflammation-associated neurodegeneration.

Occupational injury patterns in a hospital-based cross-sectional study in 
Türkiye: sectoral characteristics, injury profiles, and determinants of multiple 
injuries (2019-2023).

Aydogan HC(1), Unat Öztürk Z(2), Yaşar Teke H(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Forensic Medicine, Ordu University Training and Research 
Hospital, Ordu, Türkiye. drcanberkaydogan@gmail.com.
(2)Department of Forensic Medicine, Ordu University Training and Research 
Hospital, Ordu, Türkiye.

BACKGROUND: Occupational accidents remain a major public health and economic 
burden, particularly in middle-income countries. While healthcare workers and 
high-energy industrial sectors are often examined separately, hospital-based 
injury data derived from forensic medical records provide a structured 
opportunity to compare sector-specific injury patterns within a unified 
analytical framework.
METHODS: This retrospective hospital-based cross-sectional study included all 
occupational injury cases presenting to a tertiary emergency department and 
systematically documented through forensic medical records between 2019 and 2023 
(n = 402). Sociodemographic characteristics, sector, accident mechanism, injury 
location, and injury count were analysed. Associations were assessed using chi 
square tests and Cramérs V. Independent predictors of multiple injuries were 
examined using binary logistic regression, and sector- and mechanism-specific 
within-sample relative risks were calculated.
RESULTS: The study population was predominantly male (66.9%) and young (45.5% 
aged 18-29 years). Construction, healthcare, and logistics were the most 
represented sectors. Physical trauma accounted for 95.3% of cases, while 
infectious exposure risk was identified in 21.4%, mainly from needlestick 
injuries and body-fluid splashes in healthcare. Multiple injuries occurred in 
35.8% of cases and were disproportionately concentrated in high-energy sectors, 
including electrical-mechanical work (OR = 44.43; 95% CI = 3.72-531.12), 
manufacturing (OR = 12.82; 95% CI = 2.91-56.50), construction (OR = 4.64; 95% 
CI = 1.58-13.62), and logistics. Traffic incidents and falls were the strongest 
contributors to multi-region trauma. Upper-extremity injuries, particularly hand 
and finger trauma, predominated in healthcare workers, mainly nurses and 
healthcare technicians, and were more frequent among females.
CONCLUSIONS: Among workers presenting to a single tertiary hospital, injury 
patterns differed by sector, with infectious exposure predominating in 
healthcare and high-energy mechanisms in industrial sectors. These within-sample 
patterns identify potential targets for sector-specific prevention; however, 
without workforce denominators, they do not establish which sectors or age 
groups carry the highest injury risk, and broader prioritization requires 
population-level evidence.

Activation of the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes 
(cGAS-STING) pathway is a mechanistically compelling strategy for cancer 
immunotherapy, but first-generation STING agonists have shown limited clinical 
activity despite clear pharmacodynamic induction of interferon-related signals. 
This translational gap suggests that therapeutic benefit depends not only on 
pathway engagement but also on where, in which cells, at what amplitude, and for 
how long STING is activated. In this review, we summarize the cellular context 
of cGAS-STING signaling, the pharmacological evolution and clinical experience 
of STING agonists, and the major barriers imposed by route, species differences, 
biological heterogeneity, and systemic inflammatory toxicity. We then examine 
how nanoengineering may improve agonist protection, cytosolic access, tissue and 
cell-type selectivity, and temporal exposure. Importantly, we distinguish 
improved delivery or tumor accumulation from direct evidence of altered 
signaling kinetics or a wider therapeutic window. Representative lipid, 
polymeric, inorganic, biogenic, biomimetic, antibody-directed, and prodrug-based 
platforms are evaluated together with mechanism-based combination sequencing, 
hematologic malignancy-specific considerations, biomarker-guided patient 
selection, repeated-dose safety, and manufacturability. Overall, nano-STING 
therapy should be developed toward immunodynamic control rather than simple 
delivery enhancement, with benefit judged by the relationship among delivery, 
cell-resolved pharmacodynamics, antitumor efficacy, and toxicity.

Herpesviruses show consistency in their nuclear egress-associated induction of 
lamina-depleted areas as measured in an autofluorescent reporter cell model.

Dhotre K(1), Weghorn L(1), Schütz M(1)(2), Marschall M(3).

Author information:
(1)Harald zur Hausen Institute of Virology, Friedrich-Alexander University of 
Erlangen- Nürnberg (FAU), Erlangen, Germany.
(2)La Jolla Institute for Immunology, San Diego, CA, USA.
(3)Harald zur Hausen Institute of Virology, Friedrich-Alexander University of 
Erlangen- Nürnberg (FAU), Erlangen, Germany. manfred.marschall@fau.de.

Human herpesvirus infections span a wide variety of pathogenic outcomes, with 
individual representatives comprising a huge clinical relevance on human health. 
Translational research efforts are directed towards the improvement of broadly 
applicable preventive measures and detailed understanding of viral pathogenesis. 
Here, we studied rate-limiting steps in viral replication that show high 
mechanistic conservation among the Herpesviridae family members, in particular 
concerning the viral nucleocytoplasmic capsid egress. As characterized for 
several herpesviruses, viral nuclear egress is facilitated by the virus-induced 
local nuclear lamina rearrangements of infected cells. Hereby, the 
virus-mediated site-specific phosphorylation at lamin A/C Ser22, followed by 
cis/trans isomerization of the structural conformation, leads to the induction 
of lamina-depleted areas (LDAs). We have generated an LDA reporter system in 
primary human fibroblasts (HFFs), which conditionally express the 
autofluorescent lamin A/C-RFP fusion construct, for quantifying viral nuclear 
egress activity. This system was successfully applied for human and animal 
cytomegaloviruses as well as a selection of α-, β-, and γ-herpesviruses shown 
here. Our results illustrate that (i) the reporter system was effective in a 
quantitative way for all viruses analyzed; (ii) the process of LDA formation 
showed consistency among herpesviruses; (iii) the impairment of viral kinase 
activity, responsible for lamin A/C Ser22 phosphorylation, significantly reduced 
LDA formation; and (iv) inhibitory small molecules, directed either to the viral 
nuclear egress complex or the cellular isomerase activity, likewise provide an 
LDA-blocking effect leading to strong antiviral efficacy. Thus, the 
autofluorescent reporter cell model provides manifold options to study 
herpesviral productive replication, nuclear host interaction, and the 
pathogenesis-related impact of regulatory factors.

BACKGROUND: The exact disease-causing mechanisms in ALS remain incompletely 
understood. A possible cause is inflammation of neurons. Compared to other 
neurodegenerative diseases, neuroinflammation is pronounced in ALS, presumably 
leading to disease progression and neuronal death. Patients with ALS can have 
neuronal autoantibodies and most notably antibody-producing cells in the 
cerebrospinal fluid. The CD20-binding therapeutic antibody rituximab targets 
these antibody-producing B-cells. Rituximab is a medication commonly used in 
neurology. Single patients with ALS have already been treated with rituximab, 
which was well tolerated. We therefore want to evaluate safety and efficacy of a 
treatment with rituximab in ALS patients in a double-blind placebo-controlled 
trial. With this trial we aim for slower disease progression and unveiling 
disease-causing mechanisms in ALS.
METHODS: A total of 52 male and female patients older than 18 years with active 
sporadic ALS and disease duration of less than 24 months who are on a stable 
dose of riluzole (50 mg BID) should be included. Patients requiring assisted 
ventilation of any kind or have a known intolerance to the study medication 
rituximab are excluded. The study medication rituximab or placebo should be 
administered over a period of 52 weeks at 4 distinct time points, followed by a 
follow-up period of 79 weeks with 4 visits. Treatment efficacy should be 
evaluated using the ALS functioning scale ALSFRS-R-SE at every study visit 
(except safety visits). Safety will be assessed through regular laboratory 
analyses, adverse event (AE) and serious adverse event (SAE) monitoring, and 
CD20+ B-cell kinetics. The primary endpoint is the change in the ALS Functional 
Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R-SE) from baseline to week 79. Trial sites will be 
at Charité/DZNE Berlin and DZNE Bonn.
DISCUSSION: ALS is a rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disease with limited 
treatment options. Recent preclinical in vivo studies suggest that 
B-cell-mediated autoimmunity contributes to disease progression. This trial will 
evaluate whether rituximab, which specifically depletes CD20+ B-cells, can slow 
ALS progression and provide insights into disease mechanisms.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: The trial was registered in the German WHO-recognized 
primary register Deutsches Register Klinische Studien DRKS (German Clinical 
Trials Register) on 3/07/2023 under registration number DRKS00030948.

Massive enlargement of a previously unrecognized bronchogenic cyst over 8 years 
with intracystic hemorrhage and complex surgical resection: a case report.

Kobayashi S(1), Fukui E(2), Nagata H(1), Kimura K(1), Kimura T(1), Kanou T(1), 
Ose N(1), Shintani Y(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of General Thoracic Surgery, Graduate School of Medicine, The 
University of Osaka, 2-2-L5 Yamadaoka, Suita, Osaka, 565-0871, Japan.
(2)Department of General Thoracic Surgery, Graduate School of Medicine, The 
University of Osaka, 2-2-L5 Yamadaoka, Suita, Osaka, 565-0871, Japan. 
fukui@thoracic.med.osaka-u.ac.jp.

BACKGROUND: Bronchogenic cysts are usually asymptomatic and are often detected 
incidentally; however, they may become symptomatic due to infection, hemorrhage, 
or enlargement. We report a case of a previously unrecognized bronchogenic cyst 
that showed substantial enlargement from 4.8 to 13 cm over an 8-year interval, 
with intracystic hemorrhage, ultimately requiring partial resection of the 
esophageal muscularis.
CASE PRESENTATION: A man in his 20s presented with upper abdominal pain and 
nausea. Computed tomography revealed a 13-cm mass extending from below the 
tracheal bifurcation to the level of the gastric cardia. A CT scan obtained 
eight years earlier during the evaluation of abdominal pain had shown a 4.8-cm 
cystic lesion below the tracheal bifurcation, demonstrating substantial 
enlargement over the intervening period. Although conservative treatment was 
attempted, compressive symptoms persisted; therefore, surgical resection was 
performed for definitive diagnosis and symptom relief. Severe inflammatory 
adhesions necessitated right open thoracotomy with partial resection of the 
esophageal muscularis. The cyst contained a large hematoma, and 
histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of a bronchogenic cyst 
with intracystic hemorrhage.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates substantial enlargement of a previously 
unrecognized bronchogenic cyst from 4.8 to 13 cm over an 8-year interval, with 
intracystic hemorrhage, symptomatic progression, and technically demanding 
surgical resection. The potential for substantial enlargement and increasing 
surgical complexity should be considered when determining the timing of 
resection for bronchogenic cysts.

BACKGROUND: Norovirus (NoV) is a major pathogen responsible for acute 
gastroenteritis and outbreaks of diarrhea in humans. Children, due to their 
underdeveloped immune systems and higher risk of exposure, constitute a 
population with a relatively concentrated incidence of infection and disease 
burden. In recent years, research on NoV infections in children has been growing 
globally; however, there remains a lack of systematic quantitative analysis 
regarding the evolution of research themes, models of international 
collaboration, and future development directions in this field. Therefore, this 
study employs bibliometric methods to conduct a visual analysis of the knowledge 
structure, research hotspots, and development trends in the global field of NoV 
infection research in children, providing a reference for future scientific 
research and the formulation of prevention and control strategies.
METHODS: This study retrieved literature on pediatric NoV infections published 
between January 1998 and December 2025 from the Web of Science Core Collection 
(WoSCC) database. Using CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and Bibliometrix software, we 
conducted a visual analysis of annual publication trends, countries/regions, 
institutions, authors, journals, keywords, and references to reveal the research 
trajectory, knowledge base, and cutting-edge directions in this field.
RESULTS: This study included a total of 2,161 relevant publications. The results 
show that research on NoV infections in children worldwide has generally 
followed a steady upward trend, with activity remaining high in recent years. 
The United States, China, and Japan are the leading contributors to research in 
this field, with the United States exerting significant influence through 
international collaboration. The University of Tokyo, Emory University, and 
Chiang Mai University are the research institutions with the highest number of 
publications. Vinje, Jan; Ushijima, Hiroshi; and Khamrin, Pattara were the most 
prolific core authors, while Atmar, Robert L.; Lindesmith, Lisa C.; and Patel, 
Manish M. demonstrated strong academic influence. Keyword analysis revealed that 
research in this field primarily focuses on viral molecular characteristics, 
epidemiological features, and clinical manifestations in children, and is 
gradually expanding toward disease burden assessment, global prevention and 
control strategies, and vaccine development.
CONCLUSION: Global research on NoV infections in children has evolved into a 
Multi-Disciplinary research framework driven by virology, epidemiology, clinical 
medicine, and public health. Current research focuses primarily on molecular 
epidemiology and genetic diversity, as well as epidemiological characteristics 
and outbreak transmission mechanisms, while the assessment of disease burden and 
the optimization of global prevention and control strategies are gradually 
emerging as key future research directions. In the future, international 
collaboration, multicenter surveillance, and interdisciplinary research should 
be further strengthened to advance research on pediatric NoV infection from 
describing disease characteristics toward precision surveillance, proactive 
prevention, and comprehensive control and prevention measures.

Prognostic factors associated with outcomes after knee cartilage repair across 
different procedure types: a systematic review.

Han JH(1)(2), Jung M(1)(2), Chung K(1)(3), Moon HS(1)(4), Jung SH(1)(2), Baik 
SH(1)(2), Koo J(1)(2), Kim SH(5)(6).

Author information:
(1)Arthroscopy and Joint Research Institute, Yonsei University College of 
Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea.
(2)Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Severance Hospital, Yonsei University 
College of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea.
(3)Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Yongin Severance Hospital, Yonsei 
University College of Medicine, Yongin-si, Republic of Korea.
(4)Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Gangnam Severance Hospital, Yonsei 
University College of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea.
(5)Arthroscopy and Joint Research Institute, Yonsei University College of 
Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea. orthohwan@gmail.com.
(6)Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Severance Hospital, Yonsei University 
College of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea. orthohwan@gmail.com.

PURPOSE: To identify and describe the prognostic factors associated with 
outcomes after knee cartilage repair within distinct procedure and disease 
contexts.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar were searched 
from inception to 29 August 2026; backward and forward citation searching was 
also performed. Eligible reports quantitatively evaluated baseline 
factor-postoperative outcome associations after knee cartilage repair. Two 
reviewers independently selected reports, extracted association-level data, and 
applied the quality in prognosis studies tool. Because effect measures could not 
be harmonized, findings were synthesized without meta-analysis by disease 
context, procedure, factor, outcome, and follow-up.
RESULTS: Thirty-one reports were included, with report-level sample sizes 
totaling 13,022; cohort overlap prevented determination of the number of unique 
participants. Of 37 study-analysis units, 29 were at high risk-of-bias and 8 at 
moderate risk; none were at low risk. In isolated marrow stimulation, increasing 
age was associated with less favorable short- and long-term outcomes in two 
multivariable analyses at high overall risk-of-bias, whereas lesion-size 
findings varied across outcomes and follow-up. Autologous chondrocyte 
implantation (ACI)/matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation (MACI) 
studies reported outcome-specific associations involving age, sex, body mass 
index, baseline status, defect characteristics, previous surgery, and 
manufacturing variables. Adjusted osteochondral-allograft failure analyses 
identified age, body mass index, diagnosis, graft area, and bony realignment as 
candidate factors; clinical-threshold and machine-learning findings remained 
context dependent. In osteoarthritis-associated cell-based cohorts, older age 
and bipolar lesions were associated with long-term failure in one adjusted 
analysis, while other findings were imprecise or derived from overlapping 
cohorts. No factor was consistently established across procedures or outcomes. A 
formal certainty-of-evidence framework was not applied because of marked 
heterogeneity, sparse context-specific evidence, and generally high 
risk-of-bias; definitive between-procedure comparisons were not possible.
CONCLUSIONS: Available evidence identifies candidate prognostic associations 
within specific disease, procedure, outcome, and follow-up contexts. However, 
substantial clinical heterogeneity, potential confounding, cohort overlap, and 
sparse context-specific evidence limit the certainty and generalizability of the 
findings. The evidence does not support universal clinical cutoffs or 
conclusions that prognostic effects differ between procedures.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: level IV, systematic review of level I-IV studies.

Ensuring equitable emergency, critical and operative care.

Baker T(1)(2), Schell CO(3), Convocar P(4), Kifle F(5), Kissoon N(6), Roy N(7),

Author information:

Conditions requiring emergency, critical and operative (ECO) care account for a 
substantial proportion of preventable mortality and disability worldwide, yet 
ECO systems remain fragmented and underdeveloped in many settings. Recent global 
policy advances, including the adoption of the World Health Organization (WHO) 
Global Strategy and Action Plan for Integrated ECO Care by the World Health 
Assembly, provide an important opportunity to strengthen these systems. However, 
implementation must prioritise equity. ECO care spans a wide spectrum of 
complexity and cost, from basic triage, oxygen therapy and essential operations 
to advanced intensive care and specialised surgery. Given finite resources, 
health systems should first ensure universal access to foundational ECO care: 
early recognition of illness, basic airway and oxygen support, essential 
medications, monitoring, infection prevention, and timely referral. Approaches 
such as Essential Emergency and Critical Care (EECC) offer a feasible, highly 
cost-effective minimum standard of care, and prioritising such foundational ECO 
care is both an ethical imperative and the most effective pathway to achieving 
equitable population-level health gains.

Stroke-associated pneumonia: from immunodepression to bedside management and 
future research directions.

Benkendorff A(1)(2), Meisel A(3)(4).

Author information:
(1)Department of Neurology with Experimental Neurology, Charité - University 
Medical Center Berlin, corporate member of Freie Universität Berlin and 
Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Charitéplatz 1, Berlin, 10117, Germany. 
alexander.benkendorff@charite.de.
(2)Center for Stroke Research Berlin, Charité - University Medical Center 
Berlin, corporate member of Freie Universität Berlin and Humboldt-Universität zu 
Berlin, Charitéplatz 1, Berlin, 10117, Germany. 
alexander.benkendorff@charite.de.
(3)Department of Neurology with Experimental Neurology, Charité - University 
Medical Center Berlin, corporate member of Freie Universität Berlin and 
Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Charitéplatz 1, Berlin, 10117, Germany. 
andreas.meisel@charite.de.
(4)Center for Stroke Research Berlin, Charité - University Medical Center 
Berlin, corporate member of Freie Universität Berlin and Humboldt-Universität zu 
Berlin, Charitéplatz 1, Berlin, 10117, Germany. andreas.meisel@charite.de.

Stroke-associated pneumonia (SAP) is one of the most frequent complications 
after acute stroke, affecting approximately one in eight stroke patients. 
Besides prolonged hospitalisation and increased healthcare costs, it is also a 
major risk factor for mortality and poor functional recovery. The 
pathophysiology of SAP is driven by two converging processes: impaired local 
airway defence due to dysphagia as well as reduced airway clearance reflexes, 
and systemic stroke-induced immunodepression driven by dysfunction of the 
autonomic nervous system. While post-stroke immunodepression is a major risk 
factor for SAP, it might limit unwanted autoimmune responses within the brain. 
Conversely, SAP itself may drive neuroinflammation and contribute to post-stroke 
cognitive impairment. Despite its clinical importance, high-quality evidence to 
guide practice on prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of SAP remains scarce and 
guideline recommendations are mostly based on expert consensus. Diagnosis of SAP 
is suggested to be based on standardised clinical criteria supported by chest 
radiography and C-reactive protein as an adjunct where uncertainty persists. 
After diagnosis, guidelines suggest prompt empirical antibiotic therapy 
according to local protocols. In contrast, preventive antibiotics, even for 
high-risk patients, neither improve clinical outcome nor reduce SAP frequency. 
Currently recommended preventive strategies for SAP therefore mostly focus on 
dysphagia management and early mobilisation. This review integrates the 
pathophysiology, long-term consequences of SAP and further research directions 
based on the current knowledge on post-stroke immunology with prevention, 
diagnosis and treatment of SAP as set out in the recent European Stroke 
Organisation guideline and related guidelines.

Exercise for Older People with Heart Failure and Frailty: Should We Even Try?

Krishnan S(1), Goddard ACN(2)(3), Annals M(2)(3), Squire IB(1), Sze S(1)(4)(5).

Author information:

The benefits of exercise in older patients with heart failure (HF) and frailty 
are twofold: (i) improvement in cardiopulmonary capacity, thus reducing 
HF-related sequelae; (ii) attenuation of decline in physical function, thus 
improving frailty status. Despite the clear benefits, exercise training (ET) 
remains underutilised as a treatment modality in this patient population. 
Guidelines on the specific type of exercise intervention best suited for this 
population are still lacking. In this review, we discuss (i) pathophysiology 
underlying exercise intolerance in patients with HF; (ii) impact of frailty on 
HF and exercise capacity; (iii) benefits and safety of ET; (iv) recommended ET 
programme for this population; (v) mode of delivery and (vi) potential barriers 
in the uptake of ET and strategies to overcome them. An effective ET 
intervention in this population warrants individualisation to patient's physical

Cost-effectiveness of iStent-based trabecular micro-bypass stenting combined 
with cataract surgery in mild-to-moderate open-angle glaucoma: a systematic 
review of analytic perspectives and time horizons.

Drobin D(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, 
Sweden. dan.drobin@ki.se.

BACKGROUND: Glaucoma remains a major cause of irreversible blindness and was 
estimated to affect 64.3 million people worldwide in 2013. Despite growing 
clinical use of minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS), reimbursement and 
uptake remain constrained by uncertainty about long-term cost-effectiveness. 
iStent-based trabecular micro-bypass implantation is commonly performed at the 
time of cataract surgery in patients with mild-to-moderate open-angle glaucoma, 
yet its economic value has not been synthesised systematically across healthcare 
systems.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of iStent trabecular micro-bypass 
implantation performed concurrently with cataract surgery for mild-to-moderate 
open-angle glaucoma, and to examine how the analytic perspective and time 
horizon adopted in the underlying models relate to the decision the evidence is 
intended to inform.
METHODS: A systematic review was performed of published model-based economic 
evaluations. Eligible studies used a formal decision-analytic model, reported 
quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), and evaluated an iStent device implanted 
concurrently with cataract surgery. PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library and Web 
of Science were searched on 27 July 2026 without date, language or 
publication-type restriction. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs), 
QALYs, analytic perspectives, time horizons, discount rates and probabilistic 
results were extracted with a page reference for each value. Reporting was 
appraised item-by-item against CHEERS 2022. Findings were synthesised 
narratively; no quantitative pooling was attempted. Reporting followed PRISMA 
2020.
RESULTS: Of 418 records identified and 293 after de-duplication, eight economic 
evaluations from eight countries met the eligibility criteria. All eight 
compared the device added to cataract surgery against cataract surgery alone; 
seven used a cohort Markov model and one an individual-patient microsimulation. 
Six adopted a payer or health-system perspective and two a societal perspective; 
five used a lifetime horizon, one 35 years and two 15 years. No evaluation 
adopted a provider perspective or a base-case horizon shorter than 15 years. All 
eight reported a favourable base-case result in the mild-to-moderate target 
population: reported ratios included €1,154 per QALY in France, €12,676 in 
Spain, €13,037 in Italy, €10,955 to €15,673 in Germany, JPY 1,430,647 in Japan 
and A$2,430 in Australia, together with two instances of dominance. Six of the 
eight were funded by the device manufacturer. Incremental QALY gains were small 
throughout, between approximately 0.005 and 0.17, so the reported ratios are 
highly sensitive to small changes in the denominator. One study did not report a 
price year and for a second it could not be verified; no study reported a 
pre-specified health economic analysis plan, and none modelled long-term 
structural change in medication prices, prescribing practice or competing 
alternatives.
CONCLUSIONS: The included peer-reviewed models generally project that adding an 
iStent-family device to cataract surgery can be cost-effective over long 
horizons. That projection depends on sustained medication reduction, on 
extrapolated glaucoma progression and on local device and treatment costs. 
Direct evidence that the modelled long-term clinical benefit is realised in 
practice and offsets the acquisition cost remains limited: the evidence base is 
small, concentrated in industry-funded analyses of a single device family 
drawing largely on the same two-year pivotal trial, and built on incremental 
QALY gains close to zero. All included evaluations adopt a payer, health-system 
or societal perspective over 15 years or longer, and none addresses whether the 
marginal cost of adding a stent to an already-scheduled cataract procedure is 
justified within an annual operating budget. This is a gap in the included 
QALY-based cost-utility literature; the review was not designed to identify 
provider-perspective budget-impact analyses outside these eligibility criteria.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable. This study is a systematic review of 
published economicevaluations; no clinical trial registration was required. The 
review was not registeredprospectively in PROSPERO.

BACKGROUND: High-income countries globally are becoming increasingly diverse. 
People from ethnically diverse communities experience inequities in accessing 
bereavement support, but evidence to inform equitable provision remains limited. 
We aimed to determine how formal bereavement support services can better serve 
ethnically diverse communities by identifying barriers to and facilitators of 
equitable access, defining key components of culturally safe and appropriate 
bereavement care, and developing a logic model and recommendations for equitable 
bereavement support.
METHODS: Multi-phase national qualitative study, drawing on experience-based 
co-design principles. We conducted interviews (n = 53) and focus groups (n = 9) 
with 121 bereaved people from 13 ethnically diverse backgrounds, interviews with 
23 bereavement support providers across 12 services, four online co-design 
workshops with bereaved people and stakeholders (n = 53), and a hybrid workshop 
to refine recommendations (n = 29 stakeholders). Recruitment and data collection 
prioritised cultural safety and an asset-based approach. Directed thematic 
analysis was informed by Levesque et al.'s access to healthcare framework.
RESULTS: Barriers to equitable bereavement support arose across the access 
pathway but were concentrated mainly within bereavement support organisations 
and the wider bereavement support system. Racism and intersectionality were 
cross-cutting themes, influencing whether bereaved people could identify, trust, 
reach and engage with support. Key barriers included poor signposting and 
referral, long waiting lists, limited staff diversity, language barriers, weak 
organisational commitment to equity, precarious funding, and white-centred, 
individualised models of grief support. Participants identified culturally safe 
and equitable care as requiring anti-racist practice, sustained community 
partnership, provision of support in trusted settings and community languages, 
holistic and flexible provision, and greater investment in grassroots services 
designed and delivered by ethnically diverse communities. The logic model and 
recommendations identify system-wide actions needed to address barriers and 
support equitable access.
CONCLUSIONS: Inequitable access to bereavement support for ethnically diverse 
communities is rooted primarily in the design, organisation and cultural 
orientation of services and the wider bereavement support system. Improving 
equity will require sustained investment in community-led provision, 
accountability mechanisms, and genuine partnership with ethnically diverse 
communities. Findings from this robust multi-perspective study provide 
actionable recommendations to reform bereavement support across high- and 
middle-income settings.

Blocking IL-6 trans-signaling mitigates benzalkonium chloride-induced 
inflammation, oxidative imbalance, ER stress, and barrier disruption in human 
corneal epithelial cells.

Lax K(#)(1), Glass J(#)(1), Aliste A(1), Sharma A(1)(2), Sharma S(3)(4).

Author information:
(1)Center for Biotechnology and Genomic Medicine, Medical College of Georgia, 
Augusta University, 1120 15th Street, Augusta, GA, 30912, USA.
(2)Department of Ophthalmology, Augusta University, Augusta, GA, USA.
(3)Center for Biotechnology and Genomic Medicine, Medical College of Georgia, 
Augusta University, 1120 15th Street, Augusta, GA, 30912, USA. 
shsharma@augusta.edu.
(4)Department of Ophthalmology, Augusta University, Augusta, GA, USA. 
shsharma@augusta.edu.
(#)Contributed equally

BACKGROUND: Benzalkonium chloride (BAC), a commonly used preservative in 
ophthalmic formulations, elicits a pro-inflammatory cytokine response and 
cytotoxic effects in corneal epithelial cells, contributing to ocular surface 
injuries associated with dry eye disease (DED). Interleukin-6 (IL-6) 
trans-signaling is a well-established pro-inflammatory pathway that contributes 
to endothelial and epithelial barrier dysfunction. Thus, this study investigated 
whether targeted inhibition of IL-6 trans-signaling with sgp130Fc could 
attenuate BAC-induced cytotoxic injury in corneal epithelial cells.
METHODS: Human telomerase-immortalized corneal epithelial (hTCEpi) cells were 
exposed to 0.001% BAC for 30 min in the presence or absence of 10 μg/mL 
sgp130Fc. Markers of inflammation, oxidative imbalance, endoplasmic reticulum 
(ER) stress, and epithelial barrier disruption were assessed using enzyme-linked 
immunosorbent assay, reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction, and 
western blot analyses. Reactive oxygen species (ROS), antioxidant capacity, and 
intracellular calcium flux were quantified using colorimetric, 
fluorescence-based, and luminescence-based assays. Epithelial barrier function 
was assessed using electric cell-substrate impedance sensing. Statistical 
analyses were performed using one-way analysis of variance followed by Tukey's 
or Holm-Šídák multiple-comparison tests, with P < 0.05 considered statistically 
significant.
RESULTS: BAC exposure activated IL-6 trans-signaling as indicated by an 
increased sIL-6R/sgp130 ratio, reduced mIL-6R levels, and unchanged gp130 
levels. BAC also increased secreted IL6 levels, IL6RA expression, and downstream 
inflammatory mediators MCP1 and ICAM1, all of which were attenuated by sgp130Fc. 
BAC-induced oxidative imbalance was characterized by increased ROS and hydrogen 
peroxide production, reduced antioxidant enzymes, and diminished total 
antioxidant capacity, whereas sgp130Fc mitigated these effects. In addition, BAC 
increased intracellular calcium levels and ER stress markers, including HSP72, 
BiP, PERK, and Ero1α, and impaired epithelial barrier function as observed by 
reduced trans-epithelial electrical resistance and decreased β-catenin, 
occludin, and claudin-1 levels. sgp130Fc mitigated increases in intracellular 
calcium, partially alleviated ER stress responses, and preserved epithelial 
barrier integrity and junctional protein levels.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate that IL-6 trans-signaling contributes to 
BAC-induced corneal epithelial injury, suggesting that targeting this pathway 
may have therapeutic potential for DED and related ocular surface inflammatory 
disorders.

Cobimetinib impairs tumor survival and immune escape by altering my-CAFs in

Udinotti M(1), Ramm N(2), Hamdan TAAA(1), Khan MSA(1), Siebolts U(1)(3), Bauer 
M(1), Lorenz K(4), Dierks C(5)(6), Wickenhauser C(1), Seliger B(7)(8)(9).

Author information:
(1)Institute of Pathology, Section Immunopathology, Martin Luther University 
Halle-Wittenberg, Halle, Germany.
(2)Institute of Tumor Immunology, Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg, 
Halle, Germany.
(3)Institute of Pathology, University Hospital, Cologne, Germany.
(4)Department of Visceral, Vascular and Endocrine Surgery, Martin Luther

(5)Department of Hematology/Oncology and Stem Cell Transplantation, KIM IV, 
Martin-Luther University Halle-Wittenberg, Halle, Germany.
(6)Department of Hematology and Oncology, Freiburg University Medical Center, 
Albert-Ludwigs-University of Freiburg, Breisgau, Germany.
(7)Institute of Pathology, Section Immunopathology, Martin Luther University 
Halle-Wittenberg, Halle, Germany. barbara.seliger@uk-halle.de.
(8)Institute of Translational Immunology, Center for Translational Medicine, 
Faculty of Health Sciences Brandenburg, Brandenburg Medical School Theodor

(9)Fraunhofer Institute for Cell Therapy and Immunology (IZI), Leipzig, Germany. 
barbara.seliger@uk-halle.de.

Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is one of the most aggressive thyroid cancers 
characterized by rapid progression and high resistance to conventional 
therapies. Although mutations in the BRAF gene are common in thyroid cancer, 
targeted therapies against this mutation show limited clinical benefit. This 
study investigated whether inhibition of downstream signaling pathways using the 
selected MEK inhibitor cobimetinib provides advantages over direct BRAF 
inhibition. Genomic and expression analyses of thyroid cancer datasets confirmed 
frequent BRAF alterations and activation of MAPK-pathway-associated signaling. 
Functional studies using thyroid cancer cell lines demonstrated that cobimetinib 
more effectively reduced MAPK pathway activity specifically reducing ERK1/2 
phosphorylation compared to direct BRAF inhibition. This pathway suppression was 
associated with decreased tumor cell invasion, migration, and expression of 
epithelial-mesenchymal transition markers, alongside increased induction of late 
apoptosis. Furthermore, cobimetinib altered immune-related features of tumor 
cells by reducing expression of immune inhibitory molecules and cytokine 
secretion, while simultaneously enhancing expression of molecules involved in 
antigen presentation, such as HLA-ABC. Co-culture experiments with human 
fibroblasts showed that cobimetinib modulates tumor-fibroblast communication and 
fibroblast phenotype composition. Cobimetinib reduced the formation of specific 
immune-suppressive fibroblast subtypes, whereas exposure to interleukin-8 
promoted their development and increased tumor cell migration. Secretome 
profiling confirmed that cobimetinib markedly depleted pro-tumorigenic 
cytokines, particularly reducing IL-8 secretion. While data provide preclinical 
evidence that downstream MEK inhibition alters tumor cell signaling and 
IL-8-associated tumor-fibroblast communication in ATC-centered models, they do 
not establish cobimetinib monotherapy as a replacement for clinically 
established BRAF/MEK combination therapies. Instead, these data support the 
broader therapeutic potential of MEK inhibitors as a strategy to target both 
tumor progression and immune evasion in aggressive endocrine malignancies.

Multidomain Autonomic Dysfunction assessed with COMPASS-31 among patients with 
type 2 diabetes in Zanzibar: prevalence and associated factors.

Haji HT(1)(2), Ali RM(3), Khamis AG(4), Ramaiya K(5), Munseri P(6), Mashili 
FL(7)(8).

Author information:

(3)School of Nursing and Midwifery, Aga Khan University, Dar-es-Salaam,

(4)Zanzibar Agricultural and Livestock Research Institute, Zanzibar, Tanzania.
(5)Department of Internal Medicine, Shree Hindu Mandal Hospital, Dar-es- Salaam,

BACKGROUND: Autonomic dysfunction is an important but frequently 
under-recognized complication of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), particularly 
in settings where objective autonomic testing is not routinely available. The 
Composite Autonomic Symptom Score-31 (COMPASS-31) provides a practical 
symptom-based approach for assessing autonomic dysfunction across multiple 
domains. This study compared socioeconomic, lifestyle, and clinical 
characteristics among adults with T2DM in Zanzibar according to 
COMPASS-31-defined autonomic dysfunction and examined factors associated with 
its presence.
METHODS: This hospital-based cross-sectional study included 665 adults with T2DM 
attending the diabetes clinic at Mnazi Mmoja Hospital, Zanzibar. Autonomic 
symptoms were assessed using COMPASS-31, including the orthostatic intolerance, 
gastrointestinal, and bladder domains. Participants were classified as having 
autonomic dysfunction when they met the prespecified threshold for dysfunction 
in at least one assessed domain. Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (CAN) was 
assessed separately using standardized cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests 
performed with an automated CAN Analyzer and was not included in the COMPASS-31 
composite outcome. Modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimation 
was used to calculate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% confidence 
intervals (CIs).
RESULTS: Overall, 309 participants (46.5%) had COMPASS-31-defined autonomic 
dysfunction. Orthostatic intolerance was the most common domain, affecting 271 
participants (40.8%), followed by gastrointestinal dysfunction in 177 (26.6%) 
and urinary dysfunction in 123 (18.5%). Separately, 305 participants (45.9%) met 
the analyzer-based criteria for CAN. In the multivariable analysis, autonomic 
dysfunction was more prevalent among participants without a family history of 
diabetes (aPR = 1.37, 95% CI: 1.16-1.61; p < 0.001), those with diabetes 
duration of ≥ 10 years (aPR = 1.45, 95% CI: 1.14-1.75; p < 0.001), those not 
using oral hypoglycemic agents (aPR = 1.66, 95% CI: 1.39-1.97; p < 0.001), and 
those who rarely consumed vegetables or consumed one portion per day 
(aPR = 1.79, 95% CI: 1.37-2.34; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Approximately half of the adults with T2DM in this tertiary-care 
population had COMPASS-31-defined autonomic dysfunction. Higher prevalence was 
associated with no family history of diabetes, longer diabetes duration, non-use 
of oral hypoglycemic agents, and lower vegetable intake. These findings 
highlight the potential value of symptom-based autonomic assessment and support 
further prospective research to better understand the clinical and lifestyle 
factors associated with autonomic dysfunction among adults with T2DM in 
Zanzibar.

Cancer metastasis: biological mechanisms, therapeutic bottlenecks, and emerging 
interventions.

Ye H(1), Wei Y(1), He X(2), Wei X(3).

Author information:
(1)Laboratory of Aging Research and Immunology, State Key Laboratory of 
Biotherapy and Cancer Center, National Clinical Research Center for Geriatrics, 
West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, Sichuan, China.
(2)Laboratory of Aging Research and Immunology, State Key Laboratory of 
Biotherapy and Cancer Center, National Clinical Research Center for Geriatrics, 
West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, Sichuan, China. 
hexuemei1116@126.com.
(3)Laboratory of Aging Research and Immunology, State Key Laboratory of 
Biotherapy and Cancer Center, National Clinical Research Center for Geriatrics, 
West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, Sichuan, China. 
xiaweiwei@scu.edu.cn.

Metastatic cancer remains a major clinical challenge, which is driven by the 
continuous adaptation of disseminated tumor cells to diverse tissue environments 
and therapeutic pressures. Although current treatments, including conventional 
therapies, small-molecule drugs, antibody-drug conjugates, and immunotherapies, 
have improved clinical outcomes in selected patients, they rarely achieve 
durable disease control, largely because each stage of the metastatic cascade 
presents distinct therapeutic bottlenecks. This review examines these 
bottlenecks and identifies therapeutic vulnerabilities that can be targeted at 
each metastatic stage. Cross-stage adaptive programs, encompassing genetic, 
epigenetic, metabolic, immune, and microenvironmental alterations, are linked to 
the specific modes of therapeutic failure they drive, thereby connecting 
underlying mechanisms with their corresponding clinical consequences. Emerging 
therapeutic strategies are discussed in the context of the metastatic stage, and 
general design principles for combination regimens are proposed. We also 
highlight the potential of liquid biopsy-guided dynamic treatment adjustment and 
advanced preclinical models to inform patient selection, treatment timing, and 
the design of therapies aimed at overcoming resistance. By integrating 
metastatic biology, mechanisms of therapeutic failure, and emerging 
interventions, this review provides a framework for understanding and targeting 
the bottlenecks that limit durable disease control in metastatic cancer.

BACKGROUND: Trifocal intraocular lenses differ in how their optical architecture 
apportions incident light between foci, but comparative evidence combining 
acuity, defocus testing, contrast sensitivity and patient-reported outcomes in 
large routine-care cohorts is limited. We compared 12-month visual, refractive 
and patient-reported outcomes after implantation of two trifocal intraocular 
lens designs.
METHODS: This retrospective comparative cohort screened 432 patients and 
analysed one right eye from each of 340 patients (170 per group) implanted with 
a sinusoidal pupil-adaptive or a conventional diffractive trifocal lens. 
Allocation was non-randomised and individual selection reasons were unavailable. 
Primary outcomes, selected a priori before access to the study records, were 
12-month uncorrected intermediate acuity at 65 cm and uncorrected near acuity at 
40 cm. Assessment covered distance acuity, refractive accuracy, defocus curves, 
contrast sensitivity, dysphotopsia, spectacle independence and the National Eye 
Institute Visual Function Questionnaire-25. Models adjusted for baseline and 
operative-period differences, with propensity-score sensitivity analyses.
RESULTS: At 12 months the sinusoidal design showed better intermediate acuity 
(0.09 (0.05) vs. 0.12 (0.05) logMAR; adjusted difference - 0.025, 95% CI - 0.037 
to - 0.013) and near acuity (0.10 (0.06) vs. 0.16 (0.05) logMAR; -0.066, 95% 
CI - 0.080 to - 0.053; both P < 0.001). Propensity-weighted and doubly robust 
estimates were almost identical (near-acuity E-value 5.4). Refractive 
predictability was equivalent (83.5% vs. 84.7% within ± 0.50 D; P = 0.88); all 
eyes were within ± 1.00 D. In exploratory unadjusted analyses, defocus 
area-under-the-curve, contrast sensitivity at most tested spatial frequencies, 
halo, glare and questionnaire outcomes also favoured the sinusoidal design; 
distance-acuity differences were clinically negligible.
CONCLUSIONS: Both designs achieved excellent distance vision and refractive 
predictability. The sinusoidal design was associated with better intermediate 
and near function across several independent measures, and the estimates were 
robust to propensity-score weighting. Because allocation was not randomised and 
the groups differed at baseline, residual confounding cannot be excluded and 
prospective confirmation is required.

Outcome measures and monitoring framework in juvenile systemic sclerosis: 
bridging routine care and clinical trials.

Foeldvari I(1), Marrani E(2).

Author information:
(1)Hamburger Zentrum Für Kinder- Und Jugendrheumatologie, Am Schön Klinik 
Eilbek, Dehnhaide 120, 22081, Hamburg, Germany. 
Sprechstunde@kinderrheumatologie.de.
(2)Pediatric Rheumatology, Meyer Children's Hospital IRCCS, Firenze, Italy.

INTRODUCTION: Juvenile systemic sclerosis (jSSc) is an orphan multisystem 
autoimmune disease that can cause significant morbidity during childhood and can 
lead to significant worsening of quality of life. The pathophysiological 
features are identical with adult-onset systemic sclerosis (SSc), jSSc exhibits 
a distinct clinical phenotype characterized by a significantly higher prevalence 
of diffuse cutaneous involvement, frequent overlap syndromes, distinct 
autoantibody profiles, and different long-term survival trajectories. 
Historically, the evaluation of jSSc has relied heavily on the extrapolation of 
adult outcome measures, which fail to account for developmental physiology, 
somatic growth, and pediatric-specific feasibility constraints.
AREAS COVERED: This review provides a comprehensive overview of indicators of 
disease activity and severity which might be used in daily clinical practice and 
adapted as outcome measures in future clinical trials. It includes global 
outcome measures, organ-specific outcomes (including skin, pulmonary, cardiac, 
gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, renal, and vascular involvement), 
patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), and clinician-reported outcomes 
(ClinROs). The performance of adult indices within pediatric cohorts are 
evaluated, if applicable. Additionally, we analyze severity scores like the 
Juvenile Systemic Sclerosis Severity Score (J4S) alongside modern consensus 
metrics derived from the international Hamburg symposia. We emphasize the 
integration of pediatric-adapted clinical assessments, quantitative imaging, and 
patient and physician related outcomes.
EXPERT OPINION: The development of outcome measure in jSSc requires a paradigm 
shift from static severity scores to dynamic, multi-dimensional indicators 
capable of differentiating reversible inflammatory activity from potential 
permanent damage accrual. Validating pediatric-specific thresholds for 
physiological and cutaneous change remains an urgent priority. Over the next 
decade, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven quantitative 
imaging, decentralized home-based digital health tools, and molecular biomarkers 
probably will gain an essential role to optimize clinical trial readiness and 
personalize therapeutic strategies for children with systemic sclerosis.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

Gender-transformative action as a strategy for health system strengthening: a 
framework for advancing equity, accountability, and resilience.

Vandi M(1)(2), Osborne A(3).

Author information:
(1)Ministry of Health, Freetown, Sierra Leone. moriebartvandi@gmail.com.
(2)Medical University of South Carolina, Charleston, USA. 
moriebartvandi@gmail.com.
(3)Institute for Development, Western Area, Freetown, Sierra Leone.

Gender inequity is embedded in the organisation, financing, leadership, and 
everyday practice of health systems. It shapes who receives care, who provides 
it, who advances into decision-making roles, whose labour is undervalued, and 
whose safety is treated as negotiable. While health systems are often presented 
as neutral institutions, they frequently reproduce the gendered hierarchies of 
the societies in which they operate. This viewpoint argues that 
gender-transformative action should be treated as a core strategy for health 
system strengthening rather than as a peripheral equity concern. It proposes a 
three-domain framework for understanding and addressing gender inequity in 
health systems: capacity, institutional structures, and contextual barriers. 
Capacity refers to the ability of health workers, managers, educators, and 
policymakers to recognise and respond to gender bias in policy and practice. 
Institutional structures refer to the formal and informal rules that shape 
leadership, pay, career progression, workplace safety, budgeting, and 
accountability. Contextual barriers refer to the wider social conditions that 
influence whether people can access services and whether workers can participate 
equitably in institutional life, including restrictive gender norms, unpaid care 
burdens, violence, insecurity, and economic dependence. Drawing on purposively 
selected evidence from diverse settings, the paper examines how inequity is 
reproduced across these domains and outlines four practical areas for action: 
gender-sensitive training and mentorship, equitable governance and workforce 
reform, community engagement and norm change, and strengthened digital gender 
data systems. It argues that isolated or symbolic interventions are unlikely to 
produce durable change unless they alter the distribution of power, resources, 
and institutional recognition. Gender-transformative action is therefore not an 
optional addition to health policy, but a practical requirement for building 
health systems that are more equitable, accountable, resilient, and capable of 
advancing universal health coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals. As a 
viewpoint, the framework is offered as an analytic and planning aid rather than 
as an empirically validated model. Evidence on how gender-transformative reforms 
interact across domains remains limited, and the claims made here about what 
such reform can achieve should be read as arguments for a direction of travel 
rather than as established effect estimates.

BACKGROUND: Head, face, and neck injuries impose a substantial burden for 
emergency departments (ED); the mechanisms driving them across the life course 
however remain poorly understood at the population level. Large-scale, 
integrated analysis spanning anatomical regions, injury mechanisms, age groups, 
settings, and associated products or environmental surfaces offers an 
opportunity to identify the patterns and vulnerable populations that smaller or 
shorter-term studies cannot resolve.
METHODS: We queried National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) 
records from 2006 to 2025 for injuries to the head, face, eyes, mouth, neck, or 
ears. Demographics, anatomical region, injury setting, associated products or 
environmental surfaces, and ED disposition were extracted, and a rule-based 
narrative classifier assigned 1 of 17 injury mechanisms from free-text 
descriptions. Non-routine ED disposition was defined as admission, transfer, 
observation, or fatality. Analyses were descriptive and based on unweighted 
NEISS case records.
RESULTS: Among 2,345,287 ED presentations, representing 31.8% of all NEISS-coded 
visits, the head was most often injured (51.2%), followed by the face (28.2%). 
Annual volume rose 35.2% (105,727 in 2006 to 142,918 in 2025), driven mainly by 
head injuries (+ 83.4%). Median age was 14 years and 56.4% of patients were 
male, but among older adults (≥ 65 years), females predominated (60.6%). Falls 
were the leading mechanism (53.0% across subcategories). Most patients were 
treated and discharged (89.4%) and admission rate rose roughly 18-fold from 
toddlers (1.3%) to older adults (23.3%). Non-routine ED disposition increased 
with age, and syncope- or medical-related falls had the highest non-routine ED 
disposition rate (33.9%). The home was the most common injury setting (63.1%). 
Injury exposures varied by age group, with beds most common in infants, tables 
in toddlers, sports equipment in children and adolescents, and floors in older 
adults.
CONCLUSIONS: Head, face, and neck injuries represent a large and growing share 
of NEISS-coded ED presentations, with distinct patterns by age, sex, injury 
mechanism, setting, and clinical outcome. These findings may assist in the 
planning of targeted prevention strategies and future research on risk 
stratification for vulnerable age groups and injury mechanisms.
