OBJECTIVE: To examine whether the Risk Analysis Index (RAI), last calibrated in 
2010-2014, requires scoring system changes to remain an effective measure of 
surgical frailty.
SUMMARY BACKGROUND DATA: The RAI is among the most validated and widely used 
measures of surgical frailty. However, like any clinical prediction model, the 
RAI's scoring system might be prone to algorithmic drift that could invalidate 
continued use.
METHODS: Retrospective cohort study of patients evaluated in outpatient surgery 
clinics at Veterans Health Administration (VHA) or University of Pittsburgh 
Medical Center (UPMC). All-cause mortality was measured 180 days after frailty 
assessment using the RAI-clinical questionnaire (RAI-C).
RESULTS: In 410,715 patients from UPMC and 190,044 patients from VHA, the 
existing RAI-C scoring system demonstrated strong discrimination (c = 0.868 95% 
CI [0.864-0.872] for UPMC, 0.827 [0.822-0.832] for VHA) which improved modestly 
after recalibrating parameter weights (c = 0.872 95% CI [0.868-0.876], for UPMC, 
0.839 [0.834-0.845] for VHA). Calibration improved slightly, especially at the 
extremes where the model tends to underpredict mortality, but little change was 
observed in the range around the threshold of frailty. Of note, the scoring 
weights associated with a cancer diagnosis demonstrated some 
multicollinearity-driven instability, but cancer remained the largest 
contributor to total score. Decision curve analysis demonstrated that 
reclassification of just a single additional patient as frail would require 
screening 1400-6000 patients with the recalibrated system, depending on the 
threshold score defining frailty, and after accounting for the harms of 
false-positive classification, weighted proportional to the odds at each 
threshold probability.
CONCLUSIONS: The RAI scoring system remains robust after a decade of widespread 
use without evidence of meaningful algorithmic drift. The minimal incremental 
improvement associated with recalibration does not justify the resources 
required to disseminate and implement a revised scoring system.

To assess temporal trends of urinary heavy metal(loid)s burden and lipid levels, 
and explore the single and joint associations of heavy metal(loid)s exposure 
with lipid profiles among children in Guiyu, a typical e-waste dismantling area 
in China. Based on 2016 and 2024 surveys in Guiyu, 197 children (aged 3-7) were 
enrolled. Urinary concentrations of 13 heavy metal(loid)s were determined using 
inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Serum lipid parameters 
including total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), low-density lipoprotein 
cholesterol (LDL-C), and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) were 
measured, and non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (non-HDL-C) was 
calculated. To investigate the independent and combined associations between 
metals and blood lipid profiles, multiple linear regression and Bayesian kernel 
machine regression (BKMR) models were employed. Urinary concentrations of 
Chromium (Cr), Nickel (Ni), Copper (Cu), Cadmium (Cd), and Lead (Pb) in 2024 
were significantly lower than those in 2016 (all P < 0.05). In adjusted models, 
Manganese (Mn), Cobalt (Co), Cd, and Pb were positively associated with TC and 
non-HDL-C, while Cd and Pb were negatively associated with HDL-C (all P < 0.05). 
BKMR confirmed a significant joint positive effect of a 12-metal mixture on TC 
and non-HDL-C, and a negative effect on HDL-C. Despite decreased individual 
metal levels over the eight-year interval, the biological risk from co‑exposure 
to these metals remains a critical concern These findings highlight the need for 
vigilance regarding the synergistic cardiovascular toxicity of heavy metals on 
pediatric lipid homeostasis.

Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are a significant public health concern 
globally. Among the most prevalent NCDs the study aims to explore the 
association of some elements with the the likelihood of cardiovascular diseases 
(CVDs) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) development. In this cross-sectional 
case control study, 300 individuals with CVDs (n = 110), T2D (n = 70), and a 
control group (n = 120) from the Ravansar Non-Communicable Disease (RaNCD) 
cohort in western Iran were examined. The RaNCD cohort is part of the PERSIAN 
cohort study, consisting of 10,000 adults. Participants aged 35-65 were 
stratified into three clusters based on their health status. Various elements, 
including aluminum (Al), calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg), phosphorus (P), manganese 
(Mn), potassium (K), cobalt (Co), lithium (Li), boron (B), molybdenum (Mo), and 
vanadium (V) in the blood serum was performed using the ICP-MS method, and data 
were analyzed using multivariable techniques, including logistic regression and 
clustering analysis. Our analysis revealed a notable association between most 
elements and the risks of CVD and T2D in the logistic regression model after 
adjusting for age and gender. Specifically, increased odds ratios of CVD and T2D 
were identified for higher Ca, Mn, Mg, Li, V, Al, P, and Mo levels. In the T2D 
group, four clusters were identified: Al-B, Mn-Co-Mo, K-P, and V-Li-Ca-Mg. In 
the CVD group, five clusters were observed: K, B-Co-Mo, Li-Mg, Ca-P, and 
Mn-Al-V. The study provides valuable insights into the role of some essential 
elements in the development of CVDs and T2D. The key elements that are most 
linked to the elevated risk of CVDs and T2D include calcium, manganese, 
molybdenum, vanadium, lithium, aluminum, phosphorus, and magnesium. Further 
exploration of the intricate relationships between elements and disease risk 
could enhance our understanding of preventive strategies and personalized 
interventions for individuals at risk of CVDs and T2D.

Although microRNAs are essential regulators of development in complex 
eukaryotes, little is known about their functions in fungi. With its clear

mechanism of milRNAs in P. ostreatus, and lays the foundation for further

Chitin valorisation through enzymatic bioconversion offers a sustainable route 
for converting biowastes into value-added bioactive products. In this study, the 
chitinolytic strain Ssg, showing close phylogenetic affinity with Streptomyces 
mutabilis, was evaluated for chitinase production in a waste-integrated 
submerged fermentation system based on crustacean-derived colloidal chitin and 
supplemented with date seed and orange-peel powders as low-cost co-substrates. 
The isolate showed a high chitinolytic index of 17.20 ± 0.70. Plackett-Burman 
screening identified substrate composition and incubation time as key 
determinants of chitinase production, while Box-Behnken optimisation revealed 
significant interaction effects and identified the best-performing combination. 
At 10 g/L date seed powder, 4.08 g/L orange peel powder, and 72 h of incubation, 
chitinase activity reached 3196 ± 1.73 U/mL, closely matching the predicted 
value of 3198.01 U/mL. Optimisation increased enzyme production 7.6-fold and 
reduced fermentation time from 6 days to 72 h. Specific activity also increased 
from 4870 ± 170 to 13,620 ± 105 U/mg, reflecting stronger chitinolytic 
performance of the optimised preparation. Both the Optimised Cell-Free 
Supernatant and the crude chitin hydrolysate exhibited comparable antifungal 
activity against Aspergillus brasiliensis and Fusarium sp., with a slight 
advantage for the hydrolysate. The strongest response was observed against 
Fusarium sp. with the crude chitin hydrolysate, showing an inhibition zone of 
24.00 ± 1.00 mm and mycelial growth inhibition of 38.75%. Microscopic 
observations revealed hyphal deformation and structural disorganisation. 
Overall, this study establishes a waste-integrated strategy for high-level 
chitinase production and supports the potential of the Ssg system for chitin 
bioconversion and biocontrol-oriented applications.

Hospital Burden and Care Pathways of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis in Italy: A 
Focus on Clinical, Economic, and Geographic Dimensions.

Banks H(1), Fattore G(2), Jommi C(3)(4), Soro M(5), Alberici F(#)(6)(7), 
Quartuccio L(#)(8).

Author information:
(1)Centre for Research on Health and Social Care Management (CERGAS), SDA 
Bocconi School of Management, Bocconi University, Milan, Italy. 
helen.banks@unibocconi.it.
(2)Department of Social and Political Sciences, CERGAS-SDA Bocconi, and Carlo F. 
Dondena, Bocconi University, Milan, Italy.
(3)Centre for Research on Health and Social Care Management (CERGAS), SDA 
Bocconi School of Management, Bocconi University, Milan, Italy.
(4)Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Università del Piemonte Orientale, 
Novara, Italy.
(5)CSL Vifor, Global Value, Access, and Policy, Rome, Italy.
(6)Department of Medical and Surgical Specialties, Radiological Sciences, and 
Public Health, University of Brescia, Brescia, Italy.
(7)Nephrology Unit, ASST Spedali Civili di Brescia, Brescia, Italy.
(8)Division of Rheumatology, Department of Medicine, University of Udine, 
Azienda Sanitaria Universitaria Friuli Centrale (ASUFC), Udine, Italy.
(#)Contributed equally

BACKGROUND: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitides 
(AAVs) are rare autoimmune diseases characterized by heterogeneous clinical 
presentation and substantial morbidity. Evidence suggests high healthcare 
utilization and economic burden of ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV), 
particularly owing to hospitalization as well as geographic variation in the 
organization of specialized care. However, national-level analyses examining 
outcomes, resource use, and geographic differences in care pathways remain 
limited.
OBJECTIVE: The study aimed to identify hospitalized patients with granulomatosis 
with polyangiitis (GPA) and microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) using administrative 
data, characterize their hospital burden and geographic care pathways in Italy, 
and investigate determinants of hospital costs and in-hospital mortality.
METHODS: Nationwide Italian hospital discharge records (2010-2019) were used to 
identify patients with GPA and MPA using International Classification of 
Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM)-based algorithms. 
Hospital resource use, costs, in-hospital mortality, inter-regional mobility, 
and continuity of specialized care were estimated. Determinants of hospital 
costs were analyzed using generalized linear models (gamma distribution and log 
link), and in-hospital mortality was analyzed using the Cox proportional hazards 
model.
RESULTS: We identified 3763 patients with GPA and 1206 patients with MPA, with a 
mean of 6.9 and 8.6 admissions per patient, respectively, over 10 years. 
In-hospital mortality was 20.3% (GPA) and 21.4% (MPA), with over 70% of deaths 
occurring within 2 years of the first observed key diagnosis in hospital 
records. Mean cumulative observed hospital costs during 2010-2019 were 
substantial (€28,275 for GPA and €36,462 for MPA per patient), with around 60% 
of costs concentrated in the year of the first observed key diagnosis and 
adjacent years. Marked regional variation in care pathways was observed, with 
patients residing in southern regions frequently receiving AAV-related care in 
northern hospitals. Lower hospital loyalty (seeking AAV-related care in numerous 
hospitals) was more commonly observed in several southern regions. In regression 
analyses, infections were the strongest predictors of both higher costs and 
in-hospital mortality, while lower hospital loyalty was associated with 
substantially higher costs but not in-hospital mortality.
CONCLUSIONS: Our analysis showed that hospitalized patients with AAV in Italy 
experienced substantial inpatient burden, frequent admissions, and high 
in-hospital mortality. Infections and renal involvement were strongly associated 
with both costs and in-hospital mortality. The observed regional differences in 
mobility patterns and continuity of specialized care suggest important 
geographic variation in AAV care pathways within the Italian hospital system. 
These findings may help inform efforts to improve the coordination and 
continuity of specialized AAV care.

Cardioplegia.

Ghanem FK(1).

Author information:
(1)Gilbert and Rose-Marie Chagoury School of Medicine, Lebanese American 
University, Byblos, Lebanon. firas.ghanem@lau.edu.

"Cardioplegia" is a poem situated at the intersection of medicine, mortality, 
and human attachment. Drawing on the clinical language of cardiac surgery, the 
poem considers the paradox of deliberately arresting the heart in order to 
preserve life. Cardioplegia becomes both a physiological intervention and a 
metaphor for the ways human beings confront vulnerability, loss, and emotional 
suspension. By placing the technical vocabulary of medicine alongside the 
symbolic and intimate meanings attributed to the heart, the poem explores the 
tension between the heart as an organ and the heart as a site of memory, love, 
and grief. "Cardioplegia" seeks to illuminate how medical language can carry 
meanings beyond its clinical function and how poetic attention may create space 
for reflection on the lived and emotional dimensions of medicine.

Age-specific survival after breast conservation versus mastectomy for ductal 
carcinoma in situ of the breast.

de Boniface J(1)(2), Szulkin R(3), Karlsson P(4), Johansson ALV(3)(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Medical Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Karolinska Institutet, 
Stockholm, SE- 17177, Sweden. jana.de-boniface@ki.se.
(2)Department of Surgery, Capio St. Göran's Hospital, Stockholm, Sweden. 
jana.de-boniface@ki.se.
(3)Department of Medical Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Karolinska Institutet, 
Stockholm, SE- 17177, Sweden.
(4)Department of Oncology, Institute of Clinical Sciences, Sahlgrenska Academy, 
University of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden.
(5)Cancer Registry of Norway, Norwegian Institute of Public Health, Oslo, 
Norway.

PURPOSE: Breast conservation for invasive breast cancer is associated with 
better survival and fewer complications than mastectomy, which is especially 
relevant for older patients. It is unclear whether this can be extrapolated to 
ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS).
METHODS: This population-based cohort study used data from the Breast Cancer 
Database Sweden (BCBaSe 3.0) to compare overall survival (OS), breast 
cancer-specific survival (BCSS) and local recurrence (LR) probabilities in three 
different age groups (< 60, 60-69, 70 + years) of women with primary DCIS 
undergoing breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy (BCS + RT), mastectomy 
without radiotherapy (Mx-RT), or breast-conserving surgery without radiotherapy 
(BCS-RT) during 2008-2019. Complete cases (CC) and multiple imputation (MI) 
analyses were applied.
RESULTS: In 7165 women, treatment was BCS + RT (53.3%), BCS-RT (13.4%), or Mx-RT 
(33.2%). Estimated 10-year OS was 90.4% (95% CI 89.3-91.5) and BCSS 98.8% 
(98.3-99.2). After adjustments for patient and tumour factors, including 
socioeconomic status and comorbidity, Mx-RT was associated with a higher overall 
mortality than BCS + RT in CC (HR 2.10; 95% CI 1.20-3.67) but not in MI analyses 
(HR 1.29; 0.95-1.76). In age 70 + years, however, the overall mortality was 
consistently increased (CC: HR 2.48; 1.09-5.62, MI: HR 1.89; 1.23-2.90). Also 
BCS-RT was associated with a higher overall mortality than BCS + RT (CC: HR 
2.68; 1.34-5.34, and MI: HR 1.72; 1.23-2.39). The 10-year LR probability was low 
(7.2%, 95% CI 6.3-8.0). Compared to BCS + RT, Mx-RT was associated with a lower 
(HR 0.18, 95% CI 0.11-0.28) and BCS-RT with a higher LR risk (HR 1.79; 
1.31-2.46), especially among ages 70+.
CONCLUSION: BCS + RT in DCIS appears safe. Acknowledging potential selection 
bias, BCS + RT may be associated with favourable overall survival outcomes in 
older women despite a higher risk of local recurrence.

Operationalizing cattle-environment interactions in a traditional silvopastoral 
system: CEII (Cattle Environment Interaction Index) and SWAI (Silvopastoral 
Water Accessibility Index) for assessing vegetation and topographic controls in 
Türkiye.

Karaca O(1), Yilmaz O(2), Eren Ö(3), Ata N(1), Cemal İ(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Animal Science, Faculty of Agriculture, Aydın Adnan Menderes 
University, Aydın, Türkiye.
(2)Department of Animal Science, Faculty of Agriculture, Aydın Adnan Menderes 
University, Aydın, Türkiye. oyilmaz@adu.edu.tr.
(3)Department of Biology, Faculty of Science, Aydın Adnan Menderes University, 
Aydın, Türkiye.

This study characterizes a traditional silvopastoral cattle production system in 
the Beşparmak Mountains of southwestern Türkiye and examines patterns of cattle 
use of heterogeneous vegetation and grazing resources, water accessibility, and 
producer-reported ecosystem-service benefits and environmental pressures. Field 
observations, semi-structured interviews with 104 cattle-producing households, 
and secondary data were integrated to describe herd structure, grazing-resource 
use, seasonal management practices, cattle use of vegetation types, and water 
provision. Two field-based composite indicators were developed to summarize 
selected dimensions of the system: the Cattle Environment Interaction Index 
(CEII), which represents the relative balance between producer-reported 
ecosystem-service benefits and environmental pressures, and the Silvopastoral 
Water Accessibility Index (SWAI), which integrates water-source composition and 
dependence on tractor-assisted water transportation. The production system was 
characterized by relatively small- to medium-sized cattle herds, extensive 
outdoor grazing, seasonal use of olive groves, limited housing, selective 
supplementary feeding, and reliance on multiple natural and managed water 
sources. Patterns of cattle use differed among vegetation types. During field 
visits, grazing was recorded in grasslands, maquis, phrygana, and 
ruderal-segetal areas; resting was recorded in forested areas; and water 
consumption was recorded in hygrophilous habitats. Among the producer-reported 
categories, fire-risk reduction and natural fertilization were the most 
frequently reported benefits, whereas environmental pressures were reported less 
frequently and were mainly associated with olive groves. CEII values revealed 
spatial variation in the reported benefit-pressure balance among districts, 
while sensitivity analysis showed stable rankings under ± 10% and ± 20% 
perturbations of the benefit component. SWAI further demonstrated spatial 
differences in water accessibility, with tractor dependency representing an 
important structural constraint in settlements relying on transported water. 
Overall, the findings indicate that traditional silvopastoral cattle production 
in the Beşparmak Mountains is embedded within a heterogeneous agro-silvopastoral 
landscape in which grazing resources, vegetation use, water provision, and local 
management practices are interconnected. The CEII and SWAI provide complementary 
comparative measures of producer-reported benefit-pressure balance and 
water-accessibility conditions, respectively. The observed cattle-vegetation use 
patterns further highlight the importance of heterogeneous grazing resources and 
water availability for understanding how cattle use the landscape.

Safety and efficacy of neoadjuvant S-1 and oxaliplatin therapy for gastric 
cancer in the elderly: combined phase II trials of KSCC1601 and KSCC1801.

Ryujin K(1), Shirabe K(1), Sato S(1), Otake A(1), Shin Y(1), Natsugoe K(1), 
Kawazoe T(1), Nambara S(1), Tsuda Y(1), Nakanoko T(1), Ando K(1), Ota M(2), 
Iwatsuki M(3), Saeki H(4), Yoshizumi T(1), Oki E(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Surgery and Science, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, 
Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan.
(2)Department of Gastroenterological Surgery, National Hospital Organization 
Kyushu Medical Center, Fukuoka, Japan.
(3)Department of Gastroenterological Surgery, Kumamoto University, Kumamoto, 
Japan.
(4)Department of General Surgical Science, Gastroenterological Surgery, Gunma 
University, Gunma, Japan.
(5)Department of Advanced Medicine and Innovative Technology, Kyushu University, 
3-1-1 Maidashi, Higashi-Ku Fukuoka-City, Fukuoka, 812-8582, Japan. 
oki.eiji.857@m.kyushu-u.ac.jp.

BACKGROUND: The efficacy of neoadjuvant chemotherapy in elderly patients with 
locally advanced gastric cancer remains unclear. We evaluated neoadjuvant S-1 
plus oxaliplatin (SOX) therapy in elderly patients using patient data from two 
phase II trials.
METHODS: Patient data from KSCC1601 and KSCC1801 phase II trials were 
integrated. Patients were divided into an elderly group (age ≥75 years) and a 
non-elderly group (age <75 years). Adverse events, postoperative complications, 
and outcomes were compared. Overall survival (OS) and recurrence-free survival 
(RFS) were calculated from treatment initiation.
RESULTS: Among the 73 patients enrolled in trials, 66 (90.4%) underwent surgery 
and 65 (89.0%) achieved R0 resection. Neoadjuvant SOX therapy was administered 
to 69 patients (94.5%). Among those with R0 resection, 22 were aged ≥75 years 
and 43 were aged <75 years. PS 1 was significantly more common in the elderly 
group, with no other baseline differences. Postoperative complications developed 
in 11 patients (16.9%), including 1 (4.5%) in the elderly group and 10 (23.3%) 
in the non-elderly group (p = 0.12). Grade III or higher complications occurred 
only in the non-elderly group. OS and RFS did not differ significantly between 
the age groups (OS: Hazard ratio (HR) = 0.78, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 
0.27-2.21, p = 0.64; RFS: HR = 1.12, 95% CI 0.51-2.44, p = 0.79). 
Undifferentiated histology, stage III disease, and poor pathological response 
were associated with worse survival.
CONCLUSIONS: Neoadjuvant SOX therapy is feasible in selected elderly patients 
with locally advanced gastric cancer and yields survival comparable to those of 
younger patients.

Measurement of thermodiffusion in liquid Ag60Cu40.

Krüger AT(1), Sondermann E(2), Meyer A(1).

Author information:
(1)Institute for Frontier Materials on Earth and in Space, German Aerospace 
Center (DLR), Linder Höhe, 51147, Cologne, Germany.
(2)Institute for Frontier Materials on Earth and in Space, German Aerospace 
Center (DLR), Linder Höhe, 51147, Cologne, Germany. elke.sondermann@dlr.de.

Thermodiffusion, or the Soret effect, designates a diffusive motion of particles 
driven by a temperature gradient, leading to a build-up of a concentration 
gradient. This effect is here measured in the liquid state on the eutectic alloy 
Ag60Cu40 , which shows negligible excess volume. No significant thermodiffusion 
was observed using both in situ X-ray radiography or ex situ energy-dispersive 
X-ray spectroscopy on separately solidified parts of the sample. This is in 
contrast to the significant Soret coefficients observed in molten Ag-Al and 
Al-Ni. Molecular dynamics simulations of thermodiffusion in liquid Ag-Cu [Sarder 
et al., Philos. Mag. 99, 468-491 (2019)] report significantly stronger 
thermodiffusion. However, the trend that thermodiffusion in liquid Ag-Cu is 
weaker than in other liquid alloys like Al-Ni is supported by our experiment.

Clinical outcomes and feasibility of a fast-track protocol after total ankle 
replacement: a prospective study.

Vena LM(1), Moggio L(2), Cofano E(3), Longo UG(4), van Dijk P(5), van Dijk 
CN(6), Gasparini G(3), Mercurio M(3).

Author information:
(1)Scarnati Clinic, Cosenza, Italy.
(2)Rehabilitation Unit, Ospedale degli Infermi, Biella, Italy. 
lucrezia.moggio@gmail.com.
(3)Department of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery, Magna Graecia University, 
Catanzaro, Italy.
(4)Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Campus Bio-Medico, Roma, Italy.
(5)Department of Orthopedic Surgery and Sports Medicine, Amsterdam UMC, 
Amsterdam Movement Sciences, University of Amsterdam, Amsterdam, Netherlands.
(6)Professor Em. University of Amsterdam, Department of Orthopedic Surgery, 
University of Amsterdam, Amsterdam, Netherlands.

PURPOSE: Postoperative recovery after total ankle replacement remains 
challenging, and evidence supporting the use of fast-track protocols in this 
setting is limited. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the short-term 
clinical outcomes and safety of a fast-track protocol following total ankle 
replacement.
METHODS: A prospective observational study was conducted on consecutive adult 
patients undergoing primary total ankle replacement through an anterior approach 
between January 2023 and June 2024. All procedures were performed by a single 
experienced surgeon using the same implant. The fast-track protocol included 
early postoperative mobilization, multimodal pain management, bleeding control, 
and structured physiotherapy with standardized discharge criteria. Ankle 
function was assessed using the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society's 
(AOFAS) Ankle Hindfoot Scale preoperatively and at hospital discharge. Secondary 
outcomes included time to active ankle mobilization, time to assisted ambulation 
with crutches, length of hospital stay, and wound healing evaluated using the 
ASEPSIS wound score.
RESULTS: Twenty-two patients were included. Median AOFAS Ankle Hindfoot Scale 
scores improved significantly from 29.0 preoperatively to 68.0 at discharge. 
Active ankle mobilization was achieved after a median of two days, assisted 
ambulation after three days, and the median hospital stay was five days. Wound 
healing outcomes were favourable, with low ASEPSIS scores and only one minor 
wound complication managed conservatively. No major wound complications, 
infections, or prosthesis-related adverse events were observed.
CONCLUSION: In this prospective single-arm study, a fast-track protocol 
following total ankle replacement was feasible and was associated with early 
functional recovery and favourable short-term safety outcomes. These findings 
should be interpreted as preliminary and descriptive, given the absence of a 
control group. Larger comparative studies with longer follow-up are needed to 
determine its effectiveness relative to conventional postoperative care.

Hantaviruses as Emerging Zoonotic Pathogens: Molecular Biology, Epidemiology, 
Therapeutics, vaccine, and Pathogenesis.

Akbarin MM(1)(2), Farjami Z(1)(3), Álvarez HR(4)(5).

Author information:
(1)Virology, Genetics, and Molecular Biology Laboratory, Faculty of Higher 
Studies Cuautitlan, Veterinary Medicine, National Autonomous University of 
Mexico, Campus 4, Cuautitlan Izcalli, Mexico.
(2)Mashhad Medical Sciences-Medical School- Mashhad, Islamic Azad University, 
Mashhad, Iran.
(3)Department of Biology, Damghan Branch, Islamic Azad University, Mashhad, 
Iran.
(4)Virology, Genetics, and Molecular Biology Laboratory, Faculty of Higher 
Studies Cuautitlan, Veterinary Medicine, National Autonomous University of 
Mexico, Campus 4, Cuautitlan Izcalli, Mexico. ramiralh@unam.mx.
(5)Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México. FES-Cuautitlán, Estado de México, 
Carretera Cuautitlán-Teoloyucan Km. 2.5, San Sebastián Xhala, Estado de México, 
54714, Cuautitlán Izcalli, México. ramiralh@unam.mx.

Hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens belonging to the family 
Hantaviridae and are responsible for two major human diseases, hemorrhagic fever 
with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). 
Despite substantial progress in hantavirus research, important challenges remain 
in understanding the interactions among viral evolution, reservoir ecology, 
environmental change, transmission dynamics, and host immunopathology. This 
review provides an integrated One Health perspective that connects molecular 
virology and host-virus interactions with transmission ecology, global 
epidemiology, and the mechanisms underlying vascular leakage and severe disease. 
In addition to summarizing established knowledge, we highlight recent advances 
in hantavirus taxonomy, genomic and molecular surveillance, ecological and 
transmission modeling, and the identification of hantavirus circulation in 
previously underrecognized regions. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of 
reservoir host dynamics, climate and environmental change, habitat disturbance, 
and human-wildlife interactions in shaping spillover risk, as well as on 
endothelial dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and coagulation abnormalities as 
interconnected mechanisms of disease severity. We also identify persistent 
knowledge gaps concerning host susceptibility, viral persistence, determinants 
of differential virulence and tissue tropism, interspecies transmission, and the 
development of effective antiviral therapies and vaccines. By integrating these 
complementary perspectives, this review provides a framework for understanding 
hantavirus emergence and pathogenesis while identifying priorities for future 
surveillance, prevention, and therapeutic research.

In silico guided design and in vivo evaluation of Diacerein loaded SLNs embedded 
in situ gels for sustained intra-articular osteoarthritis therapy.

Ayesha BT(1)(2), Erum A(3), Shahid N(4), Tulain UR(1)(5).

Author information:
(1)Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Sargodha, Sargodha, Pakistan.
(2)Riphah Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Riphah International University, 
Lahore, Pakistan.
(3)Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Sargodha, Sargodha, Pakistan. 
alia.erum@uos.edu.pk.
(4)Faculty of Pharmacy, The University of Lahore, Lahore, Pakistan.
(5)Interdisciplinary Research Centre for One Health, University of Sargodha,

BACKGROUND: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a multifactorial joint disorder characterized 
by inflammation, oxidative stress, and progressive cartilage degeneration, for 
which conventional therapeutic agents remain limited by low bioavailability and 
systemic side effects.
OBJECTIVES: This study aims to integrate in silico guided and experimental 
nanoparticle-based drug formulations and in vivo analysis targeting the 
inflammatory genes, proteins, and oxidative markers in OA therapy.
METHODS: In silico screening was conducted on ligands based on SwissSimilarity 
and led to the identification of TNF-α inhibitors. High binding affinity and 
stability of the complex were verified by Docking studies (AutoDock Vina) and 
molecular dynamics simulations (Desmond), 100 ns. THA was produced. SLNs with 
Diacerein (DC-SLNs) were prepared and entrapped into thermosensitive in situ 
gels (ISG) that were made of THA, poloxamer 407 and poloxamer 188. The 
formulations were assessed physically and in vitro release dynamics. The 
efficacy of in vivo drug formulation was determined by osteoarthritis rat model 
with knee diameter, oxidative and inflammatory markers.
RESULTS: Swiss-similarity screening with Rhein as a reference ligand identified 
eight structurally similar compounds in the DrugBank database, including 
Diacerein, Rheinanthrone, Salsalate, and others, with high similarity scores (> 
0.7); DC showed the strongest TNF-α binding (- 10.7 kJ/mol). The complex 
stability was proved by MD simulations (RMSD 2.6 A). In both gels, gelation was 
appropriate, injectability was excellent, and non-Fickian release occurred.

structure. Both formulations yielded significant reductions in joint swelling, 
pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, NF-κB), improved antioxidant activity, 
and reduced inflammatory and oxidative mediators associated with cartilage 
degradation, while the DC-SLN@THA-ISG has better therapeutic efficacy than 
DC@THA-ISG.
CONCLUSION: In silico in vivo studies prove the efficacy of DC-SLN@THA-ISG as a 
biocompatible and sustained intra-articular formulation in managing 
osteoarthritis.

Murrah buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) bull semen.

Kumar Y(1), Singh AK(2), Singh N(3), Ratta NS(3), Singh P(4), Mavi GK(3),

Author information:
(1)Department of Veterinary Gynaecology and Obstetrics, Guru Angad Dev

This study was designed to evaluate the effect of glycine supplementation (0.0, 
5.0, 10.0, 15.0, 20.0 and 25.0 mM) in freezing media on post-thaw quality of 
buffalo bull spermatozoa. Thirty-six semen ejaculates from six breeding Murrah

INTRODUCTION: Patients with heart failure (HF) with reduced ejection fraction 
(HFrEF) remain at high risk of cardiovascular (CV) death and hospitalization 
following a worsening heart-failure event. Data on vericiguat, a prescription 
oral medication used to treat symptomatic chronic HF, in adult Indian patients 
are limited.
METHODS: Adults with chronic HFrEF and a worsening heart-failure event were 
enrolled in a prospective, multicenter, open-label, single-arm phase IV study 
design. Participants received vericiguat in addition to foundational medical 
therapy (FMT) and were followed for approximately 48 weeks. The primary endpoint 
was CV death or first hospitalization for HF. Secondary endpoints included CV 
death, first hospitalization for HF, all-cause death or first hospitalization 
for HF, all-cause death and safety outcomes.
RESULTS: Of 231 patients who underwent screening, 205 received vericiguat and 
comprised the safety analysis set; of these, 203 patients constituted the full 
analysis set. The mean age of participants was 58 years. Baseline use of 
angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 
inhibitors was 52.7% and 75.6%, respectively. At week 48, Kaplan-Meier (KM) 
estimates were 10.1% for the primary endpoint, 3.3% for CV death, 9.1% for first 
hospitalization for HF, 11.5% for all-cause death or first hospitalization for 
HF, and 5.9% for all-cause death. Attainment of the target dose was 91.6%, with 
69.5% of participants reaching and maintaining 10 mg by week 4. Study 
drug-related adverse events (AEs) were reported in 3.4% of participants, and 
treatment-emergent AEs requiring discontinuation in 2.0% of participants.
CONCLUSION: In Indian patients with worsening HFrEF, high target-dose attainment 
and no new safety signals were observed during 48 weeks of vericiguat treatment.

Environmental variability versus extrinsic mortality as correlates of mammalian 
lifespan: a pre-specified comparative analysis with phylogenetic and deep-time 
evidence.

Li D(1).

Author information:
(1)Independent Researcher, Wuhan, China. 745075416@qq.com.

What explains the large variation in lifespan across species? I examine an 
information-turnover proposition-that ancestral environmental variability should 
shorten captive lifespan after controlling for body mass, temperature and 
extrinsic mortality (P1), with a possible lineage-fate interaction (P2)-against 
the classical extrinsic-mortality prediction that safer niches permit longer 
life. I state the decision rules in advance rather than register a third-party 
protocol. Integrating AnAge (4,219 records), PanTHERIA, WorldClim/CHELSA climate 
and a 4,100-species mammal phylogeny with Pagel's-λ phylogenetic generalized 
least squares (PGLS), together with Paleobiology Database fossils across two 
mass extinctions, the lifespan-mass scaling reproduces (slopes 0.158 mammals, 
0.212 birds; P < 10⁻140). P1 is not supported under the most conservative 
specifications: weak proxy signals attenuate or reverse at λ = 1 and under 
family fixed effects, and the set of analyses is best read as overlapping 
sensitivity and robustness checks rather than independent falsifications; 
equivalence intervals for the climate coefficients exclude large 
(arboreality-sized) effects but not small ones. A basal-metabolic-rate correlate 
likewise dissolves at λ = 1. Turning the same pipeline to niche safety, flight, 
arboreality, aquatic life and hibernation carry positive mass-corrected 
coefficients in raw and maximum-likelihood-λ contrasts; at λ = 1 in a joint 
model (n = 652) only multiply-origin arboreality is significant 
(b = + 0.106 dex, 95% CI 0.065-0.147, P = 5.8 × 10-7), whereas flight and 
aquatic life are inconclusive with wide confidence intervals. Ancestral 
reconstruction recovers dozens of independent arboreal gains (42 by parsimony; 
45-50 by maximum-likelihood; stochastic-mapping median 70-81, 95% range ≈ 57-94) 
versus one to a few for flight or aquatic life. Bivalve geographic breadth is 
associated with survival across the K-Pg and end-Permian extinctions, although 
the effect weakens after controlling for sampling completeness and is a 
genus-level extinction phenomenon rather than an individual-lifespan mechanism. 
Turtles live ≈ 1.8 × longer than same-mass squamates (turtle-squamate comparison 
n = 179, P = 8 × 10-8). Human lifespan is an extreme outlier on the scaling 
plane. The comparative evidence is therefore most consistent with a strong 
association between extrinsic-mortality regime (niche safety) and lifespan, and 
with no detectable independent role for environmental fluctuation rate at the 
effect sizes this study could resolve; I report where inference is inconclusive 
rather than claim a null effect or a decisive causal setting. The focal analyses 
comprise 977 mammals and 1,063 birds for the scaling law, 798 species with 
climate data, 878 species with trait contrasts, 652 species in the joint 
phylogenetic model, and 349 species with basal metabolic rate (298 in the 
tree-matched model); each result reports its own sample size.

Metagenomic analysis of oral microbiota in Chinese children with obesity.

Wang W(#)(1)(2), Feng Y(#)(3), Wang Y(4), Wang G(5), Wang X(6).

Author information:
(1)Department of Stomatology, Xianyang Central Hospital, Xianyang, 712000,

(2)School of Stomatology, Lanzhou University, Lanzhou, 730000, China. 
wangwei18003@163.com.
(3)Department of Dermatology, Nuclear Industry 215 Hospital of Shaanxi Province,

(4)Second Department of Intensive Care Medicine(NICU), Xianyang Central

(5)Department of Stomatology, Xianyang Central Hospital, Xianyang, 712000,

(6)Department of Stomatology, Xianyang Central Hospital, Xianyang, 712000,

(#)Contributed equally

Childhood obesity represents an increasingly severe global public‑health 
concern, whose precise etiology remains incompletely elucidated and is likely 
multifactorial. In addition to genetic and lifestyle factors, mounting evidence 
indicates that the microbes in the digestive tract play a crucial role in the 
development and progression of obesity. Among them, the oral microbiota may 
contribute to obesity through mechanisms such as inducing systemic chronic 
inflammation and promoting gut microbiota dysbiosis. In the present study, 
saliva samples were collected from 9 obese children and 9 normal-weight 
children. Using metagenomic sequencing, we aimed to analyze the structural 
characteristics and functional profiles of the oral microbiota in Chinese 
school‑age children with obesity, so as to comprehensively dissect the oral 
microbiome ecology of this population from structural and functional 
perspectives. The results revealed that the microbiota diversity was similar 
between the two groups. At the species level, Dialister invisus, Treponema 
porcinum, Moraxella sp., Moraxella sp. VT 16 12, Moraxella lacunata, and 
Moraxella caprae were significantly enriched in the normal-weight group. 
Conversely, Campylobacter concisus, Veillonella sp. oral taxon 158, Veillonella 
rogosae, Veillonella sp. S13053 19, Streptococcus ilei, and Streptococcus 
australis were significantly enriched in the obese group. Functional annotation 
analysis demonstrated significant enrichment of functional genes associated with 
the hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) signaling pathway, peroxisome 
proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) signaling pathway, beta-alanine 
metabolism, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling pathway, and apoptosis 
in the normal-weight group. In contrast, functional genes related to biofilm 
formation-Vibrio cholerae, selenocompound metabolism, RNA polymerase, xylene 
degradation, and dioxin degradation were significantly enriched in the obese 
group. Correlation analysis further revealed strong positive correlations 
between Veillonella sp. oral taxon 158, Veillonella sp. S13053 19, Streptococcus 
ilei, Streptococcus australis and the functional pathways of biofilm 
formation-Vibrio cholerae, selenocompound metabolism, xylene degradation, and 
dioxin degradation. These observations suggest that the oral microbiome 
undergoes compositional and functional alterations in children with obesity, 
implying a potential role of oral microbiota in the etiology of childhood 
obesity.

Fungal infections have emerged as a significant concern in healthcare, due to 
the development of antifungal resistance and the limited availability of 
diagnostic and therapeutic options. The Candida species represent a category of 
particular importance with regard to fungi. Therefore, the implementation of 
infection prevention and control measures, such as hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) 
disinfection, is imperative in healthcare settings. In consideration of the 
existing literature, which demonstrates that repeated exposure to H2O2 does not 
compromise microbial tolerance to the disinfectant, the expression of virulence 
attributes may be altered under the influence of external selective pressure.The 
present study aims to evaluate the effect of repeated exposure to H2O2 on 
antifungal susceptibility profiles, catalase production, and biofilm formation 
on Candida strains in a phenotypic assessment of the microbial behaviour.In 
previous studies, strains of C. albicans, C. parapsilosis, and C. auris were

susceptibility to the disinfectant over 30 days. The present study demonstrated

antifungal susceptibility of C. albicans and C. parapsilosis, but not of C. 
auris. Repeated exposure to H₂O₂ demonstrated no variation in catalase 
production or alteration in biofilm formation for the evaluated species.In 
conclusion, repeated exposure to H₂O₂ resulted in only minor fluctuations in 
antifungal susceptibility in C. albicans and C. parapsilosis strains, 
demonstrating that utilization of H2O2 as a daily disinfectant is safe in 
relation to microbial adaptation. However, environmental surveillance is advised 
to prevent the inadvertent development of antifungal resistance.

The Key Role of Perceived Attractiveness of Walking Route.

Lourenço AC(1), Nogueira HG(2)(3), Rodrigues D(2)(4), Gama A(2)(5),

BACKGROUND: Walking to school contributes to children's health and development, 
yet its prevalence has declined in recent decades. Identifying factors 
associated with walking to school is essential for developing effective 
interventions. This study aimed to determine a context-specific feasible walking 
distance for children aged 6-10 years in Porto, Portugal, and to examine factors 
associated with walking to school among children living within this distance.
METHOD: This cross-sectional study included 596 children. Home-to-school walking 
distances were calculated using OpenRouteService. Four perceived neighborhood 
environmental attributes were assessed. Complex samples logistic regression 
models accounting for clustering within schools were estimated.
RESULTS: A context-specific feasible walking distance of 1400 m was identified. 
Among children living within this distance, those whose mothers had a medium 
educational attainment were more likely to walk to school than those whose 
mothers had a high educational attainment (OR = 2.66, 95% CI = 1.56-4.55). 
Children living in households without access to a motorized vehicle were also 
more likely to walk (OR = 5.48, 95% CI = 2.49-12.06). The likelihood of walking 
decreased with increasing home-to-school distance (OR = 0.32, 95% CI = 0.22-0.47 
per 350-m increase). Among the neighborhood environmental attributes, only the 
presence of interesting to look at while walking was independently associated 
with walking to school (OR = 6.55, 95% CI = 3.78-11.36).
CONCLUSION: Beyond home-to-school distance and household socioeconomic 
circumstances, perceived attractiveness of the walking route was independently 
associated with walking to school. Enhancing school route attractiveness may 
complement existing strategies to promote walking to school.

BACKGROUND: To compare late toxicities, cosmetic outcomes, and reconstruction 
failure in patients undergoing immediate autologous reconstruction (AR) versus 
implant-based reconstruction (IBR) followed by postmastectomy radiotherapy 
(PMRT).
METHODS: A multi-institutional retrospective cohort study (2013-2024) assessed 
patients undergoing mastectomy with immediate reconstruction and PMRT. Primary 
endpoints were reconstruction failure (loss or replacement of the index implant 
reconstruction, or total flap loss) and late toxicities, including contracture, 
fat necrosis, and cosmesis (Kroll scale).
RESULTS: 113 patients were included (68 AR, 45 IBR). AR utilised deep inferior 
epigastric perforator flaps; IBR cohort consisted of 41 direct-to-implant 
procedures and four latissimus dorsi flaps combined with implants. Among 
available baseline variables, cohorts were broadly similar except that AR 
patients were slightly older. Reconstruction failure was analysed in all IBR 
patients; four IBR patients were not evaluable for subsequent capsular 
contracture and cosmetic assessment because of implant removal before late 
assessment. Reconstruction failure occurred exclusively in IBR (28.9% [13 of 45] 
vs. 0% [0/68] in AR; P < 0.001). Clinically significant firmness was observed in 
46.3% (19/41) of IBR versus 14.7% (10/68) of AR patients (P < 0.001). Fat 
necrosis occurred in 16.2% of AR patients without flap loss. Good/Excellent 
physician-assessed cosmesis was more frequent after AR (83.8% vs. 36.6%; 
P < 0.001). Recurrence rates were comparable between cohorts.
CONCLUSIONS: AR was associated with higher reconstruction survival and more 
favourable physician-assessed cosmetic outcomes compared with predominantly 
direct-to-implant, subpectoral IBR after PMRT. For patients with a high 
probability of requiring PMRT, AR should be discussed early and strongly

Geoelectric and vulnerability assessment of aquifers in recharge, discharge and 
intermediate zones of Southwestern Nigeria.

Ale TO(1), Faseki OE(2), Aminu MB(3), Ololade IA(4), Daramola SO(5), Ayeniyo 
OO(6), Olotu EJ(7).

Author information:
(1)Department of Earth Sciences, Adekunle Ajasin University, Akungba-Akoko, Ondo 
State, Nigeria. ale.temitayo@aaua.edu.ng.
(2)Geotechnics and Foundation Engineering Unit, Department of Civil and

(3)Department of Earth Sciences, Adekunle Ajasin University, Akungba-Akoko, Ondo

(4)Environmental Monitoring Unit, Department of Chemical Sciences, Adekunle

(5)Department of Applied Geology, Federal University of Technology, Akure, Ondo

(6)School of Earth, Environment and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Lowa

(7)Department of Microbiology, Adekunle Ajasin University, Akungba-Akoko, Ondo

Eighteen Schlumberger Vertical Electrical Soundings were conducted to evaluate 
groundwater potential and aquifer vulnerability across recharge, discharge, and 
intermediate zones in the basement terrain of Akungba-Akoko, southwestern 
Nigeria. Geoelectric parameters were integrated with published data of 
groundwater samples and index-based models including transmissivity, hydraulic 
conductivity, longitudinal conductance, GLSI, GOD, and DRASTIC. Vulnerability 
maps were validated quantitatively against published soil and groundwater 
quality data. Four geoelectric layers with HA, AA, AK, and HK curve types were 
identified. Aquifer depth ranges 3.5-9.0 m and thickness 4.1-9.8 m. Topsoil 
resistivity of 87.9-405.2 Ωm indicates low corrosivity. Transmissivity ranges 
from 0.71-3.48 m2/day and hydraulic conductivity from 
1.27 × 10-6-1.53 × 10-5 m/s, indicating low yield potential, with better 
prospects in intermediate zones. Longitudinal conductance < 0.1 mhos over 89% of 
the VES points indicates poor protective capacity. GOD classifies 56% of the VES 
points as highly vulnerable, while DRASTIC classifies the whole area as moderate 
vulnerability. Single-parameter sensitivity analysis identified impact of vadose 
zone, depth to groundwater, and net recharge as parameters contributing most 
strongly to the calculated DRASTIC index. Validation showed significant 
correlation between the DRASTIC Index and hydrochemical validation dataset 
(Total dissolved solid) with Pearson r = 0.771, p = 0.009. The thin, clayey sand 
overburden provides limited natural protection, making the aquifer susceptible 
to surface contaminants. This study advances methodology by combining 
zonation-based VES with effective recharge estimates and quantitative validation 
and provides a practical framework for groundwater resource management, land-use 
planning, and targeted monitoring in rapidly urbanizing basement terrains.

Extreme temperatures and the epithelial barrier theory.

Ogulur I(1), Babayev H(1), Zeyneloglu C(1), Zhao B(1), Bicer C(1), Liu X(1), 
Zhang Y(1), D'Avino P(1), Li M(1), Maldonado A(1)(2), Hotie J(1), Ardicli 
S(1)(3), Pat Y(1)(4), Akdis M(1), Nadeau KC(4), Akdis CA(5).

Author information:
(1)Swiss Institute of Allergy and Asthma Research (SIAF), University of Zurich, 
Herman Burchard Str. 9, Davos, CH-7265 , Switzerland.
(2)Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, School of Chemistry, 
Complutense University of Madrid, Madrid, Spain.
(3)Department of Genetics, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Bursa Uludag 
University, Bursa, Turkey.
(4)Department of Environmental Health, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public 
Health, Boston, MA, USA.
(5)Swiss Institute of Allergy and Asthma Research (SIAF), University of Zurich, 
Herman Burchard Str. 9, Davos, CH-7265 , Switzerland. akdisac@siaf.uzh.ch.

Extreme temperatures are now recognized as significant global health threats, 
driving morbidity and mortality across diverse diseases by compromising 
epithelial barrier integrity and causing periepithelial inflammation. The 
epithelial barrier theory posits that environmentally induced barrier 
dysfunction, driven by modern industrial and urban exposures, leads to 
compromised surfaces of the exposed tissues accompanied by epithelial activation 
and barrier dysfunction, microbial dysbiosis, loss of commensal bacteria, 
opportunistic pathogen colonization, bacterial translocation, inflammation and 
immune dysregulation. While toxic chemical exposures have been the primary focus 
of barrier research, temperature extremes-now intensified by anthropogenic 
warming, altered weather patterns and regional climatic variability-may 
similarly disrupt epithelial structure and function. Heat and cold can alter 
tight-junction regulation, induce mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum 
stress, oxidative stress, apoptosis and modify cytokine and chemokine profiles, 
thereby weakening barrier defenses and enhancing susceptibility to pollutants, 
allergens and pathogens. These effects may be amplified by co-exposures such as 
humidity fluctuations, UV radiation, wildfire smoke and increased pollutant 
loads associated with floods, droughts and other environmental catastrophes. 
Shifts in the exposome, including contamination of water systems and food 
chains, further link temperature-related barrier injury to rising rates of 
noncommunicable diseases (NCDs). Clinical and epidemiological evidence supports 
associations between heat waves and disease exacerbations, between cold exposure 
and infectious or allergic responses, and between altered weather patterns and 
growing prevalence of NCDs. This review synthesizes mechanistic, environmental 
and epidemiological data to highlight extreme temperatures as critical drivers 
of epithelial barrier dysfunction and global disease burden.

M4DTrack: A DICOM-Based Imaging Informatics Workflow for User-Supervised 4DCT 
Lung Tumor Motion Reporting.

Lee TK(1).

Author information:
(1)Indiana University Health Arnett, Lafayette, IN, USA. physcein@hotmail.com.

Four-dimensional computed tomography (4DCT) is routinely used in radiotherapy 
simulation to evaluate respiration-induced tumor motion, but the motion 
information is often reviewed visually rather than captured as structured, 
phase-resolved data. We developed and evaluated M4DTrack, a DICOM-based 
imaging-informatics workflow for user-supervised 4DCT lung tumor motion analysis 
and structured, exportable three-dimensional center-of-mass (CoM) motion 
reporting. M4DTrack imports phase-resolved DICOM CT images, groups images by 
respiratory phase, displays linked axial/coronal/sagittal views, supports 
crosshair-based tumor localization and HU inspection, and applies seed or linked 
3D-box initialization with sequential phase-to-phase HU-volume propagation. An 
8-case lower-lobe lung 4DCT dataset (80 respiratory phases) was analyzed. 
Directional amplitudes, 3D vector amplitude, maximum phase-wise displacement, 
and agreement with independent ITV-GTV reference amplitudes were quantified. 
HU-weighted CoM amplitudes were 2.44 ± 1.44 mm, 2.64 ± 1.37 mm, and 6.04 ± 2.48 
mm in X, Y, and Z patient-coordinate directions, respectively. Mean 3D vector 
amplitude was 7.26 ± 2.50 mm, and mean maximum phase-wise 3D displacement was 
6.20 ± 2.10 mm. Biases versus ITV-GTV reference amplitudes were 0.01, - 0.84, 
and 0.23 mm for X, Y, and Z, respectively, with a 3D vector amplitude bias 
of - 0.29 mm. M4DTrack provides a user-supervised imaging-informatics bridge 
between qualitative 4DCT cine review and structured quantitative motion 
documentation. The pilot results support feasibility for generating exportable, 
phase-resolved tumor-motion metrics while preserving user-supervised review of 
4DCT artifacts, HU-capture uncertainty, adjacent anatomy, and differences 
between CoM-based and extent-based measurements.

3D-DDN Faster R-CNN: Pulmonary Nodule Detection Through Cross-Slice Feature 
Fusion and Dynamic Displacement Modeling.

Guan C(#)(1), Yang D(#)(2)(3)(4), Leng Z(1), Liu S(1), Zu A(1), Luo D(5), Chen 
H(6), Wang J(7).

Author information:
(1)School of Microelectronics and Data Science, Anhui University of Technology, 
Ma'anshan, Anhui, China.
(2)The Second Department of Thoracic Surgery, Anhui Chest Hospital, Hefei, 
Anhui, China.
(3)Department of Geriatric Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, The First 
Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University, Hefei, Anhui, China.
(4)Anhui Geriatric Institute, Hefei, Anhui, China.
(5)School of Microelectronics and Data Science, Anhui University of Technology, 
Ma'anshan, Anhui, China. luodmahut@126.com.
(6)The Second Department of Thoracic Surgery, Anhui Chest Hospital, Hefei, 
Anhui, China. chanhai@aliyun.com.
(7)School of Microelectronics and Data Science, Anhui University of Technology, 
Ma'anshan, Anhui, China. wangjm@ahut.edu.cn.
(#)Contributed equally

Accurate pulmonary nodule detection in computed tomography (CT) remains 
challenging because small- and low-contrast nodules may resemble vessels and 
other anatomical structures on individual axial slices. We propose 3D-DDN Faster 
R-CNN, a multi-slice detection framework that incorporates structured local 
axial context into a two-stage detector. The five-slice interactive blending 
(5-SIB) strategy organizes five consecutive CT slices as an ordered contextual 
group and preserves slice-specific feature streams extracted by a shared 
two-dimensional backbone. The cross-slice feature fusion (CSFF) module applies 
slice-wise spatial self-attention at shallow feature levels and learnable 
cross-slice aggregation at deep feature and region-of-interest levels. The 
dynamic displacement constraint (DDC) models proposal displacement across 
adjacent slices using a positive-sample regression loss and a margin-based 
negative-sample contrastive loss, while a class-weighted focal loss alleviates 
foreground-background imbalance. The model was evaluated on a private hospital 
dataset, LIDC-IDRI, and LNDb using patient-level data partitions. On the private 
hospital dataset, 3D-DDN achieved an average precision at an IoU threshold of 
0.5 (AP0.5) of 75.80% ± 1.05%, a sensitivity of 89.33% ± 1.91%, and a 
competition performance metric (CPM) of 91.20% ± 1.50%. The corresponding 
AP0.5 values on LIDC-IDRI and LNDb were 66.27% ± 0.45% and 48.20% ± 0.30%, 
respectively. Ablation experiments showed that direct five-slice stacking 
degraded performance, whereas structured feature fusion and displacement 
supervision recovered the performance loss and improved the overall detection 
profile. These results indicate that ordered cross-slice representation, 
hierarchical feature fusion, and proposal-displacement supervision provide 
complementary mechanisms for incorporating local three-dimensional context.

Operational Ontology for Radiology: A Framework for Profiling and Characterizing 
CT Imaging Data.

Alsaihati N(1)(2)(3), Cai Y(4), Wells J(4)(5)(6), Solomon J(4)(5)(6), Frush 
DP(5), Samei E(4)(5)(6).

Author information:
(1)Center for Virtual Imaging Trials, Carl E. Ravin Advanced Imaging 
Laboratories, Department of Radiology, Duke University Medical Center, Durham, 
NC, USA. Njood.alsaihati@duke.edu.
(2)Department of Radiology, Duke University Medical Center, Durham, NC, USA. 
Njood.alsaihati@duke.edu.
(3)Clinical Imaging Physics Group, Duke University Health System, Durham, NC, 
USA. Njood.alsaihati@duke.edu.
(4)Center for Virtual Imaging Trials, Carl E. Ravin Advanced Imaging 
Laboratories, Department of Radiology, Duke University Medical Center, Durham, 
NC, USA.
(5)Department of Radiology, Duke University Medical Center, Durham, NC, USA.
(6)Clinical Imaging Physics Group, Duke University Health System, Durham, NC,

Medical imaging data are increasingly used for benchmarking, quality 
improvement, research, and artificial intelligence applications. However, the 
lack of consistent metadata characterization limits the reliability and 
scalability of such analyses. Existing standards provide syntactic 
interoperability but often fail to capture the semantic clinical context and 
workflow details necessary for secondary uses such as AI development and 
radiation safety assessment, affecting the utility for reproducible profiling of 
imaging examinations across institutions. In this work, we describe key gaps in 
current approaches to imaging data standardization. These include syntactic 
interoperability without semantic equivalence, limited representation of 
clinically relevant context, inconsistent definitions of radiology procedures 
across institutions, and the absence of mechanisms to systematically profile 
imaging examinations for analysis. These limitations make it difficult to 
compare imaging practices, aggregate datasets, and interpret results across 
sites. To address these challenges, we have devised an ontology framework, the 
Operational Ontology for Radiology (OOR), that models the radiology study 
workflow from ordering through interpretation using explicitly defined entities, 
relationships, and annotated data properties. A CT-focused implementation of the 
framework was then formed, including 34 classes, 15 object properties, and 156 
data properties in this present formation. The framework was deployed in a 
demonstrative use case scenario to illustrate the utility of OOR in drawing more 
clinically relevant radiation dose aggregates from clinical CT data. The work 
demonstrates that OOR provides both a structured representation of imaging data 
and a foundation for more transparent data aggregation, scalable secondary 
analysis, and reproducible characterization of imaging practices across 
institutions.

TurkRadLLM: A Compact MedGemma-Based Model for Structuring Turkish Lumbar and 
Cervical Spine MRI Reports-A Multi-reader Validation Study.

Turgan AH(1), Çolakoğlu H(2), Demir A(2), Sakcı Z(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Radiology, Ümraniye Training and Research Hospital, University 
of Health Sciences, Istanbul, Turkey. ahmetharunturgan@gmail.com.
(2)Department of Radiology, Ümraniye Training and Research Hospital, University 
of Health Sciences, Istanbul, Turkey.

To develop and validate a compact, locally deployable MedGemma-based model 
converting unstructured Turkish spine MRI reports into structured six-field 
output. In this retrospective single-institution study, 5210 lumbar and 5017 
cervical Turkish spine MRI reports were used to fine-tune MedGemma 4B IT with 
QLoRA. Silver-standard labels from a proprietary large language model served as 
training targets and as the reference for automated fidelity analyses, but not 
as the clinical reference standard. Evaluation comprised multi-reader validation 
of 180 authentic reports interleaved with 20 adversarial cases, a second round 
in which the readers scored the silver labels themselves, and comparison on the 
full held-out set against a rule-based baseline, the non-fine-tuned base model, 
and a much larger model. Every output was valid, schema-conformant JSON, and the 
grouped acceptance rate was 100% (95% CI 97.9-100), though one reader judged 
negative-finding lists incomplete in 57.8% of reports. On the full held-out set 
(1025 reports), fine-tuning increased agreement with the silver-label impression 
from 17.7% to 67.1% and urgent-flag sensitivity against the silver 
reference from 18.8% to 62.5% (both p < .001); the larger non-fine-tuned model 
reached 27.5% and 50.0%, and a rule-based baseline 99.0% on body region. When 
the readers scored the silver labels themselves, the model was rated higher on 
negative findings and lower on the impression. Deployment required 14.75 GB of 
GPU memory on a consumer card. Fine-tuning a compact medical language model 
produced structured output rated acceptable by clinicians, though 
negative-finding completeness remained reader-dependent. The gain lay in 
content-level fidelity rather than output validity.

Stepwise accumulation of SecA mutations enables high-stringency azide-based 
selection in Escherichia coli.

Nakagami M(1), Abe A(2)(3).

Author information:
(1)Graduate School of Infection Control Sciences, Kitasato University, 
Minato-Ku, Tokyo, Japan.
(2)Graduate School of Infection Control Sciences, Kitasato University, 
Minato-Ku, Tokyo, Japan. abe@lisci.kitasato-u.ac.jp.
(3)Ōmura Satoshi Memorial Institute, Kitasato University, Minato-Ku, Tokyo, 
Japan. abe@lisci.kitasato-u.ac.jp.

The global spread of multidrug-resistant bacteria has reduced the effectiveness 
of many conventional antibiotics and complicated genetic analyses that rely on 
antibiotic resistance genes as selection markers. Genetic selection systems that 
do not rely on antibiotic-resistance genes are therefore increasingly important, 
particularly for multidrug-resistant strains. Sodium azide (Az) inhibits the 
essential ATPase SecA, but previously reported secA mutations confer only 
limited resistance and have not been developed into practical plasmid-based 
markers; plasmid-borne secA (F598L) confers only marginal resistance in an 
Az-sensitive background. Here, we show that this limited resistance results from 
coexistence of plasmid-derived mutant SecA with chromosomal wild-type SecA, 
which attenuates the resistant phenotype. The combination of F598L with a newly 
identified G516C mutation markedly enhanced Az resistance. Chromosomal 
replacement with secA (G516C/F598L) confirmed that wild-type SecA suppresses the 
resistant phenotype when coexpressed. Using error-prone PCR, we further 
generated cumulative SecA mutants and identified a variant harboring five amino 
acid substitutions (G516C, F598L, L279P, S678I, and A867G) that supported 
substantially improved, though progressively reduced, growth in liquid culture 
at Az concentrations up to 200 µg ml-1. Collectively, these results demonstrate 
that cumulative SecA mutations can overcome Az-mediated inhibition and provide a 
plasmid-borne marker that does not itself encode antibiotic resistance. In the 
present prototype, stable recovery of transformants still required co-selection 
with tetracycline, and selection by Az alone remains to be achieved. The system 
nonetheless represents a proof of concept in E. coli that, given the conserved 
essentiality of SecA, is conceptually extendable to other bacteria, including 
multidrug-resistant strains.

Dietary supplementation with methionine and/or turmeric oil enhances carcass 
cuts, economics, meat quality, and antioxidant status in broilers: insights into 
DNA methyltransferase transcripts.

Khalifa OA(1), Shehata SF(2), Abdel-Haleem MI(3), Mamdouh M(4), Baloza SH(5).

Author information:
(1)Genetics and Genetic Engineering, Department of Animal Wealth Development, 
Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Benha University, Benha, 13736, Egypt. 
olla.khalifa@fvtm.bu.edu.eg.
(2)Veterinary Economics and Farm Management, Department of Animal Wealth 
Development, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Benha University, Benha, 13736, 
Egypt.
(3)Department of Avian and Rabbit Diseases, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, 
Benha University, Benha, 13736, Egypt.
(4)Physiology Department, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Benha University, 
Benha, 13736, Egypt.
(5)Genetics and Genetic Engineering, Department of Animal Wealth Development,

Dietary methionine (Met) and turmeric oil (TO) may influence downstream gene 
transcription via DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs), which are fundamentally 
associated with DNA methylation pathways. This study evaluated their individual 
and interactive effects on carcass traits, meat quality, antioxidant status, 
gene expression, and economic outcomes in broiler chickens. Two hundred 
one-day-old male broilers were assigned to four dietary treatments, with five 
replicate pens of 10 birds each, for 35 days: control (Con),1.0 g 
DL-methionine/kg (Met), 200 mg turmeric oil/kg (TO), or their combination 
(Met + TO). Data were analyzed using a 2 × 2 factorial model.The relative mRNA 
expression profiles of the DNMT gene family (DNMT1, DNMT3A, and DNMT3B) and 
antioxidant genes (CAT, SOD, and GPX) were analyzed using quantitative real-time 
PCR RESULTS: Dietary Met increased breast weight, breast return, return from 
broiler cuts, total return, and net return. TO increased full and empty gizzard 
weights (P = 0.023 and 0.041, respectively) but reduced ultimate pH and meat 
redness (P = 0.033 and 0.017, respectively). In contrast, combined Met and TO 
supplementation increased production costs without improving net return or 
economic-efficiency indices. Regarding antioxidant status, a significant Met × 
TO interaction was observed for both CAT and SOD enzyme activities, with 
supplemented groups enhancing overall SOD activity, while dietary TO 
independently up-regulated CAT and GPX expression. Within the DNMTs family, 
dietary Met up-regulated all members, whereas TO down-regulated DNMT1 and 3A, 
with a significant interaction stabilizing DNMT3A transcripts close to control 
levels. In conclusion, targeted Met and TO interventions distinctly modulate 
DNMT and antioxidant transcripts, supporting metabolic homeostasis, poultry 
health, and economic returns.

Hearing relies on the lifelong stability of the actin core within hair cell 
stereocilia, yet the molecular mechanisms ensuring this stability are largely 
unknown. Here, we identify the transcription factor Sox3 as a key regulator of 
this core structure in mice. In the absence of Sox3, the stereocilia core 
progressively disassembles, leading to hearing loss and impaired 
mechanotransduction. Sox3-deficient stereocilia are also more susceptible to 
acoustic trauma and fail to repair structural gaps, whereas Sox3 overexpression 
confers resilience against noise-induced damage. Mechanistically, Sox3 deletion 
downregulates β-thymosin genes in hair cells, most prominently Tmsb10, an 
essential regulator of actin monomer availability. Depleting Tmsb10 
recapitulates the core degeneration observed in Sox3-deficient hair cells, 
establishing the Sox3-Tmsb10 axis as a novel molecular mechanism governing the 
lifelong preservation of the stereocilia actin core. This regulatory pathway 
also represents a promising target for therapeutic intervention in noise-induced 
hearing loss.

Gαi2 promotes microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments to stabilise 
nascent axons in vivo.

Higgs VE(1), Anwas D(1), Astapenka A(1), Toro-Tapia G(1), Das RM(2).

Author information:
(1)Division of Molecular and Cellular Function, School of Biological Sciences, 
Faculty of Biology Medicine and Health, Manchester Academic Health Science

(2)Division of Molecular and Cellular Function, School of Biological Sciences, 
Faculty of Biology Medicine and Health, Manchester Academic Health Science

raman.das@manchester.ac.uk.

Axon initiation is a critical step in the establishment of neuronal morphology. 
However, the mechanisms regulating stable axon initiation during embryonic 
development remain poorly understood. Here, using fixed-tissue super-resolution 
and high-resolution live-tissue imaging in the developing chick spinal cord, we 
reveal that stable axon initiation is characterised by microtubule-directed 
neurofilament accumulation in the emerging axon, and identify the 
multifunctional G-protein Gαi2 as a regulator of this process. Before axon 
initiation, microtubule network orientation shifts towards the site of the 
future axon where coiled Gαi2-associated neurofilaments accumulate 
asymmetrically before unfurling into the initiating axon behind microtubules. 
Crucially, Gαi2 is associated with neurofilaments and microtubules at their 
points of contact. Gαi2 depletion reduces engagement between these cytoskeletal 
networks and leads to impaired passage of neurofilaments into initiating axons 
and disrupted axon outgrowth, supporting a role for Gαi2 in regulating 
microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments in nascent axons. These 
findings advance mechanistic understanding of polarity establishment and provide 
insight into cytoskeletal regulation during axon formation.

A Web-Based Registry Framework Linking Transfusion Practice to Long-Term Patient 
Outcomes: Design and Single-Center Feasibility Study.

Nürenberg-Goloub E(1), Friedrichson B(1), Nordine M(1), Storf H(2), Zacharowski 
K(1), Kloka JA(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Anaesthesiology, Intensive Care Medicine and Pain Therapy, 
Goethe University, University Hospital Frankfurt, Frankfurt, Hessen, Germany.
(2)University Medicine, Institute of Medical Informatics, Goethe University, 
Frankfurt, Germany.
(3)Department of Anaesthesiology, Intensive Care Medicine and Pain Therapy, 
Goethe University, University Hospital Frankfurt, Frankfurt, Hessen, Germany. 
Kloka@med.uni-frankfurt.de.

Blood transfusions are among the most common medical interventions performed 
worldwide. Several comprehensive databases link transfusions to routinely 
collected health data but do not include the indication and the decision-making 
basis for a particular administration, nor patient-reported long-term outcomes. 
We developed a web-based registry for the standardized assessment of transfusion 
practice and patient outcomes, designed for an observation period of up to 30 
years. The framework combines clinical data captured at the point of care with 
patient-reported outcome measures collected through automated digital follow-up, 
ensures privacy by design through physical separation of identifying and medical 
data, and codes diagnoses and procedures in SNOMED CT. We evaluated feasibility 
in a single-center pilot at Goethe University Hospital Frankfurt (11 September 
2024-15 January 2026), with patient-reported follow-up collected through 13 
August 2026. A total of 408 patients were enrolled, yielding 1,298 
administrations across nine treatment categories in a predominantly cardiac 
surgical cohort. The pilot demonstrated that the registry integrates into 
routine clinical workflows, captures the parameters required for 
guideline-adherence monitoring, and supports sex-disaggregated, descriptive 
analyses of transfusion practice. Follow-up was completed by 12.5% of patients 
at 3 months and 15.2% of patients at 1 year; paired baseline-follow-up 
assessments of physical capacity and frailty demonstrate the data structure for 
capturing functional recovery. Risk-adjusted benchmarking, network-wide 
analyses, and donor outcomes are designed capabilities of the framework that 
were not evaluated in this pilot. The platform is available in 16 languages and 
participation is open to further institutions.

PFAS:VDR interactions and immunotoxicity through disruption of monocyte 
differentiation.

Barnes M(1)(2)(3), Lewis J(1), Banegas E(1)(2), Ekins S(3), Kullman S(4)(5)(6).

Author information:
(1)Department of Biological Sciences, North Carolina State University, Raleigh,

(2)Toxicology Program, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA.
(3)Collaborations Pharmaceuticals Inc, Raleigh, NC, USA.
(4)Department of Biological Sciences, North Carolina State University, Raleigh,

(5)Toxicology Program, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA.

(6)Center for Human Health and the Environment. North Carolina State University,

Accumulating evidence indicates that per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) 
have the capacity to modulate vitamin D receptor (VDR) signaling however, the 
underlying mechanisms governing these interactions remain poorly understood. In 
the present study, we investigated direct interactions between PFAS and VDR 
signaling, as well as a novel, putative mechanism by which PFAS may induce 
immunotoxicity through disruption of VDR molecular functionalities. VDR is 
widely expressed across both the innate and adaptive branches of the immune 
system, where it plays critical roles in regulating immune cell activation, 
differentiation, and function. While PFAS exposure has been consistently 
associated with immune dysregulation and reduced vaccine responsiveness in both 
human and animal studies, the molecular basis of PFAS-induced immunotoxicity is 
only partially defined. To address these knowledge gaps, we examined a panel of 
PFAS compounds previously identified through computational modeling to possess 
measurable binding affinities for the VDR. We employed a suite of complementary, 
orthogonal bioassays to characterize the functional interactions between PFAS 
and the vitamin D receptor. These included a transient transactivation assay to 
assess global receptor agonist and antagonist activity, a Mammalian two-Hybrid 
(M2H) assay to evaluate PFAS effects on VDR interactions with its obligate 
heterodimerization partner (RXR), coactivator (SRC-1), and corepressor (NCoR1), 
and a THP-1 cell differentiation/transcription assay to probe the 
transcriptional consequences of PFAS exposure on vitamin D-facilitated monocyte 
cell differentiation. Collectively, our findings reveal that select PFAS engage 
in complex molecular interactions with the VDR and act as potent antagonists, 
effectively inhibiting vitamin D-mediated receptor function and downstream THP-1 
cell signaling.

Long-read sequencing enables accurate analysis of complex and repetitive genomic 
regions but has distinct error profiles compared to short-read sequencing. 
Consequently, the tools for calling small variants - the predominant source of 
human genetic diversity - have shifted towards deep learning-based methods. This 
transition has reshaped variant calling across biological contexts, including 
germline, de novo, somatic and mosaic variants, and sequencing modalities for 
capturing both DNA and RNA at different resolutions. These deep learning 
frameworks are being developed in combination with alignment-based, 
assembly-based and pangenome-based strategies for small variant detection. In 
this Review, we chart the trajectory towards complete telomere-to-telomere 
profiling of small variants and consider the computational innovations needed to 
benchmark newly accessible repetitive regions and complex variants.

Mehra S(1)(2), Hong J(1)(3), Yeh C(1), Su J(1)(2), Stone K(1)(2), Wapnir

PURPOSE: Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis (IGM) is a benign inflammatory breast 
condition that can resemble mastitis or malignancy clinically and 
radiographically. We aimed to develop a quantitative scoring system, based off 
the Komen Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC) scoring system [1], evaluating 
clinical and radiologic features to distinguish IGM from benign and malignant 
breast conditions.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective chart review of biopsy-proven IGM patients 
diagnosed from 2014 to 2025 via institutional electronic medical records. 
Clinical symptom onset, features, and diagnostic imaging were analyzed. A 
continuous scoring scale (1-50) was created, encompassing three categories: 
symptom onset, clinical features, and radiographic findings. Scores of IGM 
patients were compared with those of patients diagnosed with IBC, mastitis 
(lactational and non-lactational), and locally advanced breast cancer (LABC). 
Welch's two-sample t-test assessed statistical differences, and Youden index 
identified the optimal score threshold for predicting IGM.
RESULTS: Among 148 IGM patients, predominantly Hispanic (56.8%) and Asian 
(26.7%), the mean age was 37.2 years, older than mastitis patients and younger 
than IBC patients. Key clinical features included pain or painful breast mass 
(100%), fistula or draining wound (77.7%), erythema (94.6%), and phlegmon 
(87.8%). Imaging revealed mass with collection in 84.6% and multiple 
masses/collections in 38.9%. The mean IGM score (35.5) was significantly higher 
than scores for IBC, mastitis, and LABC groups (14.4, 18, and 15.2, 
respectively; p ≤ 0.05). A score ≥ 24.5 predicted IGM with 93% sensitivity and 
95% specificity.
CONCLUSIONS: This novel scoring system provides an objective framework to 
differentiate IGM from similar breast conditions, facilitating early diagnosis 
and guiding appropriate management.

Microorganisms have the potential to deliver growth-promoting benefits to plants 
and crops; however, to be useful in a field setting, their gene expression 
should be programmable and restricted to specific plant hosts and conditions. 
Here, using O-methyl-L-tyrosine (OMY) as a model compound, we establish

This study investigated South African consumers', farmers', and industry 
stakeholders' perceptions of ostrich welfare using a questionnaire distributed 
nationwide between September 2018 and September 2019. The survey included
