Tissue macrophages are highly versatile immune cells whose morphologies shift 
dramatically depending on their activation state and tissue environment. This 
morphological plasticity reflects their diverse origins and functions but also 
poses significant challenges for both manual and automated image analysis. In 
the skin, macrophages display particularly intricate shapes, ranging from 
rounded to highly elongated, irregular, and non-convex forms. We developed a 
deep learning-based approach for the automated identification, 3D segmentation, 
and quantitative morphological profiling of dermal tissue macrophages in mice, 
facilitating large-scale analysis of cellular volume and elongation. This 
allowed us to build a dataset of 3D-segmented dermal tissue macrophages, 
comprising 947 single cells. To ensure accuracy, automatically generated 
segmentations were refined using a custom-designed Napari plugin. To illustrate 
technical validity and potential reuse, we quantified macrophage volume and 
elongation in adult steady-state and five-day post-Staphylococcus aureus 
infection samples, showing that the dataset captures biologically interpretable 
morphological variation.

Aqueous extract of Ormocarpum cochinchinense promotes fracture healing through 
coordinated angiogenic, osteogenic, and cytoprotective mechanisms.

Vincent P(1), Pugazhendi A(1), Dhanakaran V(2), Mani KP(3).

Author information:
(1)Vascular Science and Angiogenesis Lab, SASTRA Deemed to Be University, 
Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, 613401, India.
(2)Department of Veterinary Surgery and Radiology, Veterinary College and 
Research Institute, Tamil Nadu Veterinary and Animal Sciences University, 
Orathanadu, Tamil Nadu, 614625, India.
(3)Vascular Science and Angiogenesis Lab, SASTRA Deemed to Be University, 
Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, 613401, India. krishnapriya@scbt.sastra.ac.in.

Ormocarpum cochinchinense has long been used in traditional medicine for the 
management of bone fractures. Despite its widespread ethnomedicinal use, 
scientific evidence supporting its efficacy and underlying mechanisms in 
fracture healing remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the safety and 
fracture-healing potential of the aqueous extract of O. cochinchinense (OCE) 
with emphasis on angiogenesis and osteogenesis, and to elucidate its role in 
modulating endothelial cell inflammation. The biological activity of OCE was 
assessed using a combination of in vitro and in vivo approaches. The 
phytochemical characterization of the extract was performed using GC-MS 
analysis. The safety profile of OCE was assessed through in vivo toxicity 
evaluation and the fracture-healing efficacy was investigated through 
radiographic and histological analyses. Molecular mechanisms were examined by 
assessing the expression of angiogenic and osteogenic marker genes. 
Additionally, endothelial protective effects were evaluated under 
lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammatory conditions by measuring oxidative 
stress markers and pro-inflammatory mediators. GC-MS analysis identified a total 
of 25 phytocompounds in OCE. OCE exhibited no observable toxicity in rats. It 
accelerated fracture healing by promoting advanced callus formation, enhancing 
collagen-rich matrix deposition, and improving mineralization. OCE significantly 
upregulated angiogenic (VEGFA, VEGFR2) and osteogenic (BMP2, SP7, RUNX2, ALP, 
Col1A1, OPN, OCN) gene expression, indicating coordinated activation of bone 
regeneration pathways. Furthermore, OCE protected endothelial cells from 
LPS-induced cytotoxicity by reducing reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide 
levels and downregulating inflammatory mediators including NOX1, NOX2, NOX4, 
iNOS, IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. OCE promoted fracture healing through a 
multifaceted mechanism involving enhanced angiogenesis and osteogenesis. It also 
confers endothelial protection by mitigating inflammation and oxidative stress 
that might aid in improved endothelial function and thereby fracture healing. 
These findings validate its traditional use and highlight its potential as a 
safe and effective natural therapeutic agent for bone regeneration.

Microbial constituents in the gastrointestinal tract, the urine and prostate 
tissue are being linked with clinical differences in prostate cancer, and a 
recent meta-analysis has linked periodontal disease to this cancer. Several 
hypotheses exist regarding how specific bacteria can contribute towards the 
development of prostate cancer. Recovering microbial genomes, and their genomic 
features, from clinical samples and investigating fine-scale taxonomy is a 
critical first step in investigating causality. Here, we describe the microbial 
diversity of samples associated with prostate cancer. Metagenomic assembly of 
non-human reads from the PanProstate Cancer Group, derived from blood, saliva 
samples and prostate tissue whole-genome data (N = 247), successfully 
reconstructed 249 highly complete bacterial genomes, predominantly from oral 
samples. Our data, reveals eighteen bacterial species from the oral cavity 
without species level classification, while demonstrating a wide range of known 
species. This approach enables us to gain additional insights of the microbes in 
cancer patients at no additional sequencing cost and has the potential to reveal 
new links that could improve our understanding of cancer initiation and 
development.

Mechanism of M18BP1-mediated activation of condensin II for mitotic DNA 
compaction.

Borsellini A(1), Chamera S(2), Cecatiello V(2), Andrecka J(2), Vannini A(3).

Author information:
(1)Human Technopole, Milan, Italy. Alessandro.Borsellini@fht.org.
(2)Human Technopole, Milan, Italy.
(3)Human Technopole, Milan, Italy. Alessandro.Vannini@fht.org.

DNA compaction by human condensin II is crucial for the correct organization of 
mitotic chromosomes. Mitotic activation of condensin II is a multilayered 
process, controlled mainly by the opposing activity of the MCPH1 and M18BP1 
proteins, acting as an interphase inhibitor and a mitotic activator, 
respectively. Mitotic phosphorylation favors M18BP1 binding to condensin II, 
resulting in effective and timely chromosome compaction. However, the molecular 
mechanisms underlying condensin II activation in driving DNA compaction remain 
uncharacterized. Here, combining cryo-electron microscopy with single-molecule 
imaging, we unravel the mechanism of condensin II activation by M18BP1 and 
elucidate their role in DNA compaction. The specific interaction with 
phosphorylated M18BP1 induces conformational changes in the condensin II 
complex, relieving an autoinhibitory conformation and allowing stable DNA 
binding and DNA compaction. Beyond the activity of isolated condensin II 
complexes on DNA, we observe the emergence of multimeric species that withstand 
the forces applied by optical tweezers, suggesting that condensin II 
multimerization might contribute to the mechanical reinforcement of mitotic 
chromosomes.

Macrophages orchestrate immunity via transcriptional reprogramming, largely 
controlled by the master regulator NF-κB. However, mechanisms of promoter 
selection remain enigmatic. Here, we reveal that DNA secondary structures called 
G-quadruplexes (G4s) modulate the macrophage transcriptome during inflammation. 
By investigating the G4 ligand pyridostatin (PDS) in 
lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophages, we establish that G4 stabilization 
significantly decreases the inflammatory response without affecting 
mitochondrial metabolism or pathogen clearance. Instead, NF-κB-dependent 
transcription of activation markers and proinflammatory cytokines is selectively 
repressed. Using chromatin accessibility profiling, NF-κB ChIP, and in silico 
predictions, we demonstrate that G4 stabilization sterically hinders NF-κB 
promoter occupancy. Furthermore, PDS stabilizes transient, transcription-induced 
G4s, prematurely shutting down transcription and reverting local chromatin to a 
dormant state. Thus, G4 formation represents a potential strategy to modulate 
dysregulated macrophage activation.

Studying the neural circuits that mediate context-induced fear memory retrieval 
is of importance to develop new therapeutic approaches to prevent post-traumatic 
stress disorder relapse. The basolateral amygdala (BLA) is crucial for 
context-induced retrieval of fear memory. Previous studies indicate that 
projection neurons from the ventral hippocampus CA1 (vCA1) to the BLA (vCA1-BLA 
neurons) mediate context-induced retrieval of fear memory. However, it remains 
unclear whether other projection neurons to the BLA are involved in 
context-induced retrieval of fear memory and how they interact with vCA1-BLA 
neurons. Our findings indicate that the postrhinal cortex (POR) to the BLA 
(POR-BLA) neurons are also involved in context-induced retrieval of fear memory. 
These neurons innervate the same BLA neurons as vCA1-BLA neurons and participate 
in fear memory retrieval. These results suggest that two different projection 
neurons of POR-BLA and vCA1-BLA innervate on the same BLA neurons and POR-BLA 
neurons and vCA1-BLA neuron contribute to fear memory retrieval. These findings 
provide new insights into the neural mechanisms underlying fear memory 
retrieval.

Adeno-associated virus (AAV) is widely used for liver-directed gene therapy, 
with AAV serotype 3B (AAV3B) showing particularly high tropism for human 
hepatocytes. However, pre-existing neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) against AAV 
represent a major barrier to efficient gene transfer and patient eligibility. We 
have recently demonstrated that subjects with intermediate NAb levels 
(1:5-1:45), that would be excluded from clinical trials, can be converted in 
eligible patients by the administration of IgG-cleaving enzymes. It is thus 
crucial to assess not only the seroprevalence but also titer distribution. Here, 
we analyzed anti-AAV3B NAb titers, using a validated cell-based transduction 
inhibition assay, in healthy adults and patients with Wilson's disease, a 
hepatic metabolic disorder amenable to AAV3B-mediated gene therapy. Two 
independent cohorts of healthy adults (n = 200 and n = 580) were analyzed; 
33-36% of individuals were NAb positive, and prevalence increased with age. 
Differences were observed across ethnicities. Importantly, a substantial 
proportion of seropositive individuals (19%) exhibited intermediate NAb titers. 
In contrast, only 17.4% of Wilson's disease patients (n = 23) were positive, all 
with high NAb titers. These findings provide insights into target population 
eligibility, and titer distribution data support the potential of NAb-reduction 
approaches to expand access to systemic AAV3B-based gene therapies.

The use of medical real-world data is constrained by fragmented data 
infrastructures and the absence of tools integrating longitudinal clinical with 
molecular data at scale. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), 
the most common monogenic cause of kidney failure, exemplifies this gap given 
its phenotypic complexity and the need for individualized treatment decisions. 
We present MEDA-PKD (MEdical DAta translation service of Polycystic Kidney 
Disease), an interactive, near-real-time analytics platform that integrates 
clinical routine with research data from the German AD(H)PKD Tolvaptan Registry 
(NCT02497521, DRKS00008910) into a harmonized database ( 
https://doi.org/10.18716/adpkd_registry ). MEDA-PKD provides automated 
near-real-time analysis and dynamic visualization, replacing traditional static 
approaches to clinical cohorts. As of March 2026, MEDA-PKD visualized data from 
1735 patients (mean follow-up 796 days). eGFR slope analysis of data from 
patients initiating tolvaptan therapy (332 patients) demonstrates the platform's 
capacity to evaluate real-world therapeutic impact in real-time. Other tabs 
include family history, medication, lifestyle, quality of life and a wide array 
of lab values (20,894 entries). Besides, MEDA-PKD integrates proteomics data and 
allows for secure individual patient-level data access. MEDA-PKD represents a 
paradigm shift by transforming static cohort data into a living, actionable 
knowledge resource in ADPKD and will serve as a template for other diseases.

Inflammation resolution depends on coordinated communication between tissue 
compartments, yet how the intestinal epithelium shapes its immune 
microenvironment remains poorly understood. Here, using colonic biopsies from 
patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and mouse models enabling tissue-wide 
visualization of NF-κB activity, we combine single-cell RNA sequencing and 
secretome analysis to define epithelial communication during colitis. We show 
that, paradoxically, the NF-κB-driven pro-inflammatory secretome of intestinal 
epithelial cells (IECs) is essential for recovery and prevents unrestrained 
inflammation. Mechanistically, epithelial NF-κB promotes CCL22-dependent 
regulatory T cell (Treg cell) recruitment and promotes a tolerogenic, pro-repair 
cell state, accompanied by induction of the lipid-metabolism-associated GDPD3 
and CCR4. In UC, epithelial NF-κB is not uniformly activated but instead induces 
a selective pro-inflammatory transcriptional program while repressing targets 
regulating T cell recruitment. Thus, we identify dynamic epithelial-immune 
communication and demonstrate a protective IEC NF-κB-Treg cell axis important 
for resolution of intestinal inflammation.

Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome characterized by dysregulated immune 
responses and metabolic dysfunction, and remains a major cause of global 
mortality. While nanomedicine offers new opportunities for sepsis therapy, 
current strategies rarely achieve comprehensive modulation of macrophage 
immunometabolism and microenvironmental signaling. Here, we develop a 
glutathione-responsive nanotherapeutic platform (EONPs) by conjugating the 
stimulator of interferon genes (STING) inhibitor 4-octyl itaconate to 
polyethylene glycol, followed by encapsulation of the dihydroorotate 
dehydrogenase (DHODH) inhibitor EA6. Integrated transcriptomic, metabolomic, and 
metagenomic analyses combined with pharmacological assessments reveal that EONPs 
suppress systemic hyperinflammation, reprogram macrophages toward an 
anti-inflammatory phenotype, restore gut microbial homeostasis, and protect 
against multi-organ injury in septic models. Notably, EONPs enhance the 
production of the microbiota-derived metabolite 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid 
(5-HIAA), which is functionally linked to the anti-inflammatory response and may 
further support macrophage reprogramming. Our findings establish a previously 
unrecognized strategy for precise metabolic and microbiota-driven modulation of 
macrophages, offering a conceptual framework for further investigation of 
macrophage-targeted nanotherapeutics in sepsis.

Yu Y(#)(1)(2)(3), Yin R(#)(1)(2), Anderson I(4), Wang Y(4), Kramer J(1)(4),

Optomechanical transduction harnesses the interaction between optical fields and 
mechanical motion to achieve sensitive measurement of weak mechanical quantities 
with inherently low noise. Lithium niobate combines low optical loss, strong 
piezoelectricity, a high intrinsic f × Qm factor, and low thermal conductivity, 
making it promising for exploring optomechanical platforms targeting thermal 
sensing applications. Here, we demonstrate an integrated optomechanical platform 
on thin-film lithium niobate with precisely engineered optical, mechanical, and 
thermal fields within a compact 40 μm-diameter footprint. The platform 
integrates suspended microring resonators with ultrathin central membranes, 
reducing effective mass and thermal capacitance while maintaining a high 
intrinsic optical quality factor Qo of 106 and a mechanical quality factor Qm of 
1117, which increases to 5.1 × 104 upon optomechanical oscillation. The two-step 
etching suppresses thermal dissipation into the silicon substrate and enhances 
thermal sensitivity, achieving a temperature coefficient of frequency of 
-124 ppm K-1, a measurable loaded thermal response time of 7.2 μs, and a 
noise-equivalent power of 6.2 nW Hz-1/2 at 10 kHz and room temperature. This 
compact and scalable platform opens new opportunities for high-sensitivity 
thermal sensing and power detection and supports heterogeneous integration with 
infrared absorbers for uncooled infrared detection, thereby paving the way 
toward large-format infrared sensing arrays with low-noise, all-optical readout. 
Through co-design of the thermal, mechanical, and optical domains, we 
demonstrate low-noise sensing with a microsecond-scale response time at room 
temperature in air.

Effect of chemical surface pretreatments on microtensile bond strength of resin 
composite to dentin when using universal adhesives: a systematic review of 
laboratory studies.

Isaac E(1), Abd-Elhakim SH(1), Hamama HH(2)(3), Riad M(4).

Author information:
(1)Conservative Dentistry Department, Faculty of Dentistry, Minia University, 
Minia, Egypt.
(2)Conservative Dentistry Department, Faculty of Dentistry, Mansoura University, 
Mansoura, Egypt. hamdy@connect.hku.hk.
(3)Conservative Dentistry Department, Faculty of Oral and Dental Medicine, Delta 
University for Science and Technology, Gamasa, Egypt. hamdy@connect.hku.hk.
(4)Conservative Dentistry Department, Faculty of Dentistry, Cairo University, 
Cairo, Egypt.

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effect of different chemical pretreatments of sound 
dentin on the microtensile bond strength (µTBS) of resin composite to dentin.
METHODS: A comprehensive online search was performed across four electronic 
databases: PubMed (Medline), Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane libraries 
to identify relevant studies, followed by screening based on established 
eligibility criteria. In vitro studies examining the effect of chemical 
pretreatment on the microtensile bond strength of sound dentin to resin 
composite were included. Only English studies published from 2013 until February 
10, 2026 were considered. Studies that used animal teeth, focused on carious, 
sclerotic, or desensitized dentin, or assessed mechanical or laser pretreatments 
were excluded. The protocol followed PRISMA guidelines and was registered with 
PROSPERO (CRD420261299181). Selected studies underwent a risk-of-bias analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 17 studies met the inclusion criteria. Across the included 
studies, microtensile bond strength results revealed that certain chemical 
pretreatments can significantly enhance immediate bond strength as well as 
maintain long-term bond durability. Pretreatment with 50% Dimethyl Sulfoxide 
(DMSO), acetone wet-bonding, glutaraldehyde desensitizers, and copper-based 
(Cu-P) pretreatments significantly increased µTBS of the majority of dental 
adhesives and preserved their long-term stability. Selective dentin etching 
(SDE) for 3 seconds, along with glycolic acid and zirconium oxynitrate (ZON) 
etchants, yielded significantly higher immediate bond strengths than traditional 
15-second phosphoric acid etching. In cases of blood contamination, grape seed 
extract and hesperidin collagen cross-linkers restored bond strength to nearly 
uncontaminated control levels. Conversely, silver-based solutions significantly 
reduced µTBS, and limonene had no significant effect on bond strength.
CONCLUSION: Several chemical pretreatments, including selective dentin etching, 
solvent-based pretreatments, copper-based (Cu-P) pretreatments, glutaraldehyde 
desensitizers, and collagen cross-linkers, enhanced the bond strength of 
universal adhesives to sound dentin.

Radiation-induced lung injury (RILI) is a common dose-limiting toxicity after 
radiotherapy for lung cancer, but the immunological mechanisms contributing to 
RILI pathogenesis remain poorly understood. Here we analyze a RILI mouse model 
using high-dose, restricted-field irradiation to the left lung. Flow cytometry 
and cytokine profiling analysis of innate lymphoid cells (ILC) reveals a 
radiation-induced shift from lung-resident type 2 ILCs (ILC2) toward

Swallowing Outcomes Following Early Treatment of Head and Neck Cancer-Related 
Lymphedema.

Gregor JW(1), Charney SA(2), Zacharias SC(1), Skrove A(1), Miller M(1), Lott 
DG(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, Mayo Clinic, Phoenix, 
Arizona, USA.
(2)Department of Otorhinolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, Hospital of the

OBJECTIVE(S): Head and neck cancer-related lymphedema (HNCRL) is a common, 
chronic consequence of head and neck cancer (HNC) treatment that contributes to 
progressive fibrosis, functional impairment, and reduced quality of life. 
Although early intervention is advocated, its association with longitudinal 
swallow outcomes remains poorly understood. This study evaluated whether early 
HNCRL treatment was associated with improved objective and patient-reported 
swallowing outcomes following radiation treatment (RT) and/or chemoradiation 
(CRT).
METHODS: Medical records from 110 patients enrolled in a standardized HNC care 
pathway were retrospectively reviewed. Internal HNCRL was identified in all 
participants at 3-months post-RT/CRT, when lymphedema treatment was recommended. 
Seventy-two patients completed treatment with an advanced pneumatic compression 
device (APCD) or manual lymphatic drainage (MLD), while 38 did not. Swallowing 
physiology, patient-reported outcomes, and maximum interincisal opening (MIO) 
were evaluated at baseline, 3-months, and 15-months post-RT/CRT. Longitudinal 
within- and between-group comparisons were performed.
RESULTS: Treated patients demonstrated significantly more favorable longitudinal 
DIGEST outcomes for overall severity, swallowing safety, and swallowing 
efficiency (all p < 0.001), greater improvement in EAT-10 (-3.63 vs. +1.13,

and RSI remained significant after multivariable adjustment.
CONCLUSIONS: Early HNCRL treatment was associated with greater improvements in 
swallowing physiology and patient-reported swallowing outcomes. These findings 
support routine HNCRL surveillance and timely intervention within 
multidisciplinary HNC care pathways.

Does bespoke metabolic investigation reduce urinary stone recurrence? A 
narrative review.

Wiseman OJ(1), Turney BW(2)(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Urology, Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, 
Cambridge, UK.
(2)Nuffield Department of Surgical Sciences, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK.
(3)Department of Urology, Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, 
Oxford, UK.

OBJECTIVE: To examine whether individualised ('bespoke') metabolic investigation 
and targeted dietary and medical therapy reduces urinary stone recurrence, and 
whether the approach also improves health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and 
lowers financial and environmental cost.
METHODS: In this narrative review we searched PubMed/Medical Literature Analysis 
and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE), the Cochrane Library and Europe PubMed 
Central (PMC) (January 1980 to March 2026) for randomised trials, controlled 
cohorts and systematic reviews on metabolic assessment and stone recurrence 
prevention in adults, supplemented by European Association of Urology (EAU), 
American Urological Association (AUA), National Institute for Health and Care 
Excellence (NICE) and American College of Physicians (ACP) guidance and by 
hand-searching of reference lists.
RESULTS: Interventions that correct a defined urinary abnormality each reduce 
stone recurrence. Increased fluid intake approximately halves it (relative risk 
[RR] 0.45-0.55); a normal calcium, reduced sodium, reduced animal protein diet 
achieves a similar reduction in hypercalciuric calcium-oxalate formers (RR 
0.49); and targeted pharmacotherapy lowers it further (potassium citrate RR 
approximately 0.25, thiazides 0.52, allopurinol 0.59), although the rigorous 
NOSTONE trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03057431) found no significant 
thiazide benefit. After shockwave lithotripsy and percutaneous nephrolithotomy, 
medical therapy reduces stone formation and residual-fragment regrowth. Evidence 
that 24-h-urine-directed therapy outperforms empirical therapy is confined to 
high-risk patients, in whom selective treatment yields significantly fewer 
stone-related events. Stone disease impairs disease-specific quality of life and 
is costly, so preventing stone recurrence is cost-saving.
CONCLUSIONS: The case for bespoke prevention is strongest in recurrent, 
high-risk and post-procedural stone formers. Identifying the abnormality, 
correcting it, ensuring adherence and confirming the response by repeat testing 
offers the best chance to reduce stone recurrence and residual-stone growth, 
improve HRQOL, and lower financial cost.

Boers JRM(1)(2)(3), Terry G(1)(4)(5), Rodrigues L(6), Surita F(6), Doshi 
J(#)(7), Mehta B(#)(7)(8).

Author information:
(1)Weill Medical College of Cornell University New York US.

OBJECTIVE: Our objective was to evaluate the ability of different large language 
models (LLMs) to translate and analyze qualitative interviews describing 
pregnancy experiences among women with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). An 
additional objective was to compare themes identified by LLMs with those 
identified by human researchers.
METHODS: We analyzed 26 semi-structured interviews originally conducted in 
Portuguese by Rodrigues et al. among women with SLE exploring their perinatal 
care experiences. Three prompting strategies (zero-shot, few-shot, and 
chain-of-thought) were used on the transcripts across four state-of-the-art LLMs 
(GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and DeepSeek R) to generate key 
themes. Model outputs were evaluated using an LLM-as-a-judge framework assessing 
thematic coverage, thematic unity, and semantic similarity.
RESULTS: Across models and prompting strategies, LLMs generated similar themes 
that closely aligned with those identified by human researchers. LLM-as-a-judge 
evaluations demonstrated high thematic unity and semantic similarity. Claude 
Sonnet 4.5 showed the most consistent performance. Few-shot prompting 
consistently outperformed zero-shot and chain-of-thought approaches.
CONCLUSION: LLMs show promise as supportive tools for analyzing qualitative 
research by preserving thematic coherence and capturing the complexity of 
pregnancy experiences in women with SLE. Although zero-shot prompting is widely 
used, it produced lower thematic results in our study, whereas few-shot 
prompting achieved the most comprehensive and coherent theme extraction. 
LLM-assisted qualitative analysis may complement human interpretation and has 
the potential to support the inclusion of non-English language data and diverse 
patient perspectives in lupus research.

Hospital nurses are exposed to various occupational hazards, some of which are 
dangerous or even fatal. This systematic review aimed to synthesize evidence 
regarding occupational hazards and nurses' protective behaviors in hospital 
settings. Following PRISMA guidelines and the PICO framework, a comprehensive

Sustained Inhibition of Structural Damage Progression and Improvements in

Erosive Psoriatic Arthritis: Results Through Week 48 of the Phase 3b Randomized, 
Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled APEX Study.

Ritchlin CT(1), Mease PJ(2)(3), Coates LC(4), Kollmeier AP(5), Zhou B(6), Jiang 
Y(6), Bensley K(6), Im K(7), Batra R(8), Lozenski K(9), Chakravarty SD(9)(10), 
Rahman P(11), van der Heijde D(12).

(1)Department of Medicine, Allergy/Immunology and Rheumatology, University of

OBJECTIVE: In APEX, guselkumab, which binds to the IL-23p19 subunit and CD64 on 
IL-23-producing cells, demonstrated significant joint efficacy and inhibition of 
structural damage progression in participants with active and erosive PsA 
through Week (W)24; W48 findings are reported herein.
METHODS: The APEX modified full analysis set included 1020 biologic-naïve adults 
with active PsA (≥3 tender joints; ≥3 swollen joints; CRP ≥0.3mg/dL; ≥2 erosive 
joints) randomized to guselkumab every (Q)4W (N=273), guselkumab at W0,4 then 
Q8W (N=371), or placebo followed by guselkumab Q4W beginning at W24 (N=376). 
Outcomes through W48 included ACR20/50/70 response rates (using 
multiple/nonresponder imputation); least squares mean (LSM) change in 
PsA-modified van der Heijde-Sharp score (vdH-S); achievement of clinically 
meaningful improvement (CMI; ≥0.35-point) in HAQ-DI, ≥90% improvement in 
Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI90), and minimal disease activity (MDA).
RESULTS: Through W48, 93% (950/1020) of participants completed study 
intervention. Guselkumab Q4W and Q8W through W48 demonstrated durable 
ACR20/50/70 response rates (71-74%/51-56%/31-35%), and low rates of structural 
damage progression (vdH-S LSM change: 0.60-0.78); 60-64% of participants 
reported HAQ-DI CMI, 74-80% achieved PASI90, 36-41% achieved MDA. Following 
transition to guselkumab, structural damage progression among placebo-randomized 
participants diminished (vdH-S LSM change W0-24: 0.96; W24-48: 0.41) and 
clinical response rates increased through W48. Adverse event rates were 
consistent with placebo and guselkumab through W24 and stable through W48 of 
guselkumab.
CONCLUSION: APEX W48 findings further support guselkumab use for durable and 
comprehensive treatment of diverse PsA manifestations. Inhibition of cumulative 
joint damage with guselkumab may optimize outcomes.

Metabolic traits and adaptations of mice lacking Slc12a5 in insulin-secreting 
β-cells.

Rathod YD(1), Di Fulvio M(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Wright State University, School of 
Medicine Dayton, OH, USA.

Pancreatic β-cells integrate metabolic and electrical signals to couple nutrient 
sensing with insulin secretion, yet the physiological contribution of the 
neuronal K+Cl- cotransporter-2, Kcc2 (Slc12a5) to β-cell function and whole-body 
metabolic regulation remains incompletely understood. To define its role in 
vivo, we generated mice lacking Kcc2 selectively in insulin-secreting β-cells 
(Kcc2βKO) and evaluated growth, body composition, feeding behavior, glucose 
homeostasis and islet function from weaning through early adulthood. Kcc2βKO 
mice developed sex- and age-dependent metabolic phenotypes. Females exhibited 
lower body weight at weaning and increased lean mass during adulthood, whereas 
males displayed reduced body-weight gain despite increased food intake. Feeding 
microstructure analyses identified age-dependent alterations in meal patterning 
in male Kcc2βKO mice. Morphometric analysis demonstrated increased mean islet 
area without changes in endocrine cell composition, and isolated islets 
exhibited enhanced glucose-stimulated insulin secretion at younger ages. Male, 
but not female, Kcc2βKO mice showed improved glucose tolerance and age-dependent 
differences in glycemic responses to exogenous insulin, whereas both sexes 
exhibited attenuated glycemic responses to alanine challenge. Fasting blood 
glucose remained largely preserved across genotypes, although fasting plasma 
insulin concentrations varied according to sex, age and fasting duration. These 
findings identify β-cell Kcc2 as a physiological contributor to 
nutrient-stimulated insulin secretion and demonstrate that disruption of β-cell 
chloride homeostasis is accompanied by integrated, age- and sex-dependent 
adaptations in body-weight regulation, feeding behavior and glucose homeostasis.

Neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive processes in sequential 
decision-making.

Nanjo Y(1)(2)(3), Aguilar-Lleyda D(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of System Neuroscience, Division of Cerebral Integration, National 
Institute for Physiological Sciences, 38 Nishigonaka, Okazaki, Aichi, 444-8585, 
Japan.
(2)Department of Physiological Sciences, School of Life Science, SOKENDAI (The 
Graduate University for Advanced Studies), Shonan Village, Hayama, Kanagawa, 
240-0193, Japan.
(3)RIKEN CBS-TOYOTA Collaboration Center (BTCC), RIKEN Center for Brain Science, 
2-1 Hirosawa, Wako, Saitama, 351-0198, Japan.

Self-monitoring in decision-making is a hallmark of self-improvement in 
cognitive processes. To enhance outcomes in future decisions, individuals must 
accurately assess the correctness of prior choices and apply the information to 
control subsequent decisions. Although metacognition encompasses monitoring and 
control functions, the neural mechanisms underlying these processes and their 
relationships remain unclear. Furthermore, while the prefrontal cortex (PFC) is 
implicated in both functions, their distinct neural substrates and 
interrelations require further elucidation. In this study, we employed a 
sequential perceptual decision-making task with confidence ratings to examine 
how initial confidence influences subsequent decisions while recording neural 
activity using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Subjects (female 
and male) performed a visual discrimination of two different-sized stimuli and 
subsequently rated their decision confidence. Behavioral results showed that 
subjects were more likely to change their choices between initial and subsequent 
decisions according to confidence levels. A signature of confidence (confidence 
magnitude) in initial decisions was observed primarily in the anterior medial 
PFC (amPFC). In contrast, the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) exhibited 
higher neural activity related to changes of their initial choice at subsequent 
decisions. Furthermore, the pregenual ACC (pgACC) was associated with both 
processes, and it exhibited effective connectivity with the amPFC and dACC. 
These findings suggest that the medial PFC plays a role in integrating 
metacognitive monitoring and subsequent control in the sequential 
decision-making processes.Significance Statement Metacognition, encompassing 
monitoring and control, is fundamental to self-regulation and sequential 
decision-making. Despite their distinct roles, the neural mechanisms of how 
monitoring connects to subsequent control remain unclear. Using functional 
magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), we reveal distinct yet interconnected medial 
prefrontal regions that support metacognitive processes. Specifically, the 
anterior medial prefrontal cortex encodes confidence in initial decisions, while 
the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex supports changes of mind. Effective 
connectivity analysis indicates that the pregenual anterior cingulate cortex 
integrates these processes. These findings advance our understanding of medial 
prefrontal mechanisms underlying adaptive self-regulation, with implications for 
addressing disorders characterized by impaired behavioral control.

The association of gout flare resolution with physical activity and sleep: a 
prospective remote-monitoring study.

Stewart S(1)(2), Girven B(1), Clarke M(1), Zeng I(3), Gaffo A(4), Stamp 
LK(5)(6), Edwards NL(7), Rice D(1)(8), Ka'ai T(9), Rudolph K(1), Collis J(10), 
Kayes N(11), Dalbeth N(2)(12).

Author information:
(1)School of Allied Health, Faculty of Environmental Sciences, Auckland 
University of Technology, Auckland, New Zealand.
(2)Department of Medicine, Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences, University of 
Auckland, Auckland, New Zealand.
(3)Clinical Sciences Management, Faculty of Health and Environmental Sciences, 
Auckland University of Technology, Auckland, New Zealand.
(4)The University of Alabama at Birmingham and the Birmingham VA Medical Center, 
Alabama, United States.
(5)Department of Medicine, University of Otago, Christchurch, Christchurch, New 
Zealand.
(6)Health New Zealand, Te Whatu Ora Waitaha, New Zealand.
(7)University of Florida, Florida, United States.
(8)Department of Anaesthesiology and Perioperative Medicine, Health New Zealand 
Te Whatu Ora Waitematā, Auckland, New Zealand.
(9)Te Ipukarea Research Institute, Auckland University of Technology, Auckland,

(10)Department of Allied Health, School of Health Sciences, Swinburne

(11)Centre for Person Centred Research, Auckland University of Technology, 
Auckland, New Zealand.
(12)Health New Zealand, Te Whatu Ora Te Toka Tumai, New Zealand.

OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to determine whether gout flare resolution is 
associated with physical activity and sleep. These findings were intended to 
inform the future development of a definition for flare resolution.
METHODS: Data from 81 participants with gout who experienced >1 flare during a 
6-month prospective observational study were included. Daily activity (step 
count) and sleep (total sleep time and deep sleep percentage) were collected 
remotely using wrist-worn trackers. Daily flare occurrence was captured using 
smartphone diaries. Activity/sleep outcomes during each flare episode were 
compared to those during three resolution timeframes: T1: the first day 
following the flare; T2: the consecutive window immediately following the flare 
and equal in length to the flare; and T3: the consecutive window equal in length 
to the flare and immediately following a washout window (equal in length to the 
flare). Adjusted differences in medians between flare and resolution timeframes 
were estimated using linear quantile mixed models.
RESULTS: Daily step count was lower during flares compared with all resolution 
timeframes (all P<0.033). T3 provided the best overall model fit, suggesting 
that resolution is most clearly distinguished from the flare when using this 
timeframe. No significant differences between flare and resolution were observed 
for the sleep outcomes for any resolution timeframe.
CONCLUSIONS: Physical activity improves soon after flare cessation, with the 
clearest distinction between flare and resolution observed over a longer 
post-flare recovery period, whereas sleep metrics do not differentiate flare 
from resolution states. These findings support physical activity as a useful 
objective domain for gout flare resolution.

An artificial intelligence model combining MRI and ultrasound images (MRUSuNet) 
for prostate cancer detection outperforms radiologist MRI interpretation.

Jahanandish H(1)(2), Sang S(2), Li CX(3), Vesal S(1)(2), Bhattacharya I(1), Lee 
JH(2), Venkataraman R(4), Fan RE(1), Sonn GA(1)(2), Rusu M(1)(2)(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Urology, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA.
(2)Department of Radiology, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA.
(3)Institute of Computational and Mathematical Engineering, Stanford University, 
Stanford, CA, USA.
(4)Eigen Health Services LLC, Grass Valley, CA, USA.
(5)Department of Biomedical Data Science, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, 
USA.

OBJECTIVES: To develop the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-UltraSound UNet 
(MRUSuNet), a model that uses both MRI and transrectal ultrasonography (TRUS) as 
input to detect and localise the three-dimensional spatial volume of clinically 
significant prostate cancer on TRUS images to allow better visualisation of 
cancer in the TRUS space.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Pre-biopsy MRI is increasingly used to target suspicious 
prostate lesions. The lesions identified by radiologists are mapped onto TRUS 
images to enable real-time targeting during the biopsy. Yet, the misalignment of 
MRI and TRUS results in sampling errors, and in some cases even missing the 
clinically significant cancers. This study included two MRI-TRUS fusion biopsy 
cohorts (3000 patients) for model development, and one radical prostatectomy 
cohort (110 patients) used for independent validation and for the comparison 
with radiologist interpretation. A total of 1700 independent cases were reserved 
to compare the MRUSuNet with single-modality MRI-only and TRUS-only models. 
Sensitivity and lesion-level Dice similarity scores were computed using targeted 
biopsy pathology as the reference standard in the biopsy cohorts and whole-mount 
prostatectomy pathology in the radical prostatectomy cohort.
RESULT: The MRUSuNet achieved significantly superior sensitivity (0.80) and 
lesion Dice score (0.42) across all test cohorts compared to the MRI-only model 
(sensitivity: 0.73, P = 0.033; Dice score: 0.30, P < 0.001) and the TRUS-only 
model (sensitivity: 0.49, P < 0.001; Dice score: 0.27, P < 0.001). Compared to 
radiologists in the prostatectomy cohort, the MRUSuNet showed significantly 
higher specificity (0.88 vs 0.78; P = 0.004) and lesion Dice score (0.32 vs 
0.27; P = 0.048), with no observed statistical difference in sensitivity (0.79; 
P = 1.000).
CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrate the potential of combining MRI and TRUS in 
a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) model to improve localisation of 
clinically significant prostate cancer on TRUS images relative to 
single-modality models. These findings support further study of such multimodal 
AI models as an adjunct to MRI-TRUS fusion workflows.

Modulation of apoptotic genes and microRNAs by Shilajit in cryopreserved rooster 
sperm.

Semen Z(1), Nizam MY(2), Selçuk M(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Veterinary and Animal Sciences, University of Copenhagen, 
Frederiksberg, DK-1870, Denmark; Department of Biochemistry, Faculty of 
Veterinary Medicine, Dokuz Eylul University, Izmir, 35400, Turkey. Electronic 
address: zeynep.semen@sund.ku.dk.
(2)Department of Reproduction and Artificial Insemination, Faculty of Veterinary 
Medicine, Dokuz Eylul University, Izmir, 35400, Turkey. Electronic address: 
mustafayigit.nizam@deu.edu.tr.
(3)Department of Reproduction and Artificial Insemination, Faculty of Veterinary 
Medicine, Ondokuz Mayis University, Samsun, 55200, Turkey. Electronic address: 
mselcuk@omu.edu.tr.

Cryopreservation imposes severe oxidative stress on avian spermatozoa, 
triggering apoptotic cascades that compromise fertility. Shilajit, a natural 
phytocomplex rich in fulvic acid, is known for its bioenergizing and antioxidant 
properties. However, its molecular mechanism of action in regulating the 
apoptotic machinery of rooster sperm remains unexplored. This study evaluated 
the effects of Shilajit supplementation on post-thaw rooster sperm kinematics 
and the relative abundance of selected apoptosis-associated mRNAs and 
stress-related miRNAs. Materials and methods: Pooled semen collected from 
Plymouth Rock roosters was diluted with Beltsville Poultry Semen Extender (BPSE) 
containing 5% glycerol and supplemented with Shilajit at final concentrations of 
0 (Control), 5, 15, and 25 μg/mL. Following cryopreservation and thawing, sperm 
kinematic parameters were assessed using a Computer-Assisted Sperm Analysis 
(CASA) system. The relative expression levels of apoptotic genes (p53, Bax, 
Bcl-2) and a panel of stress-related miRNAs (gga-miR-34a, -155, -146b, -26a, 
-215, -122) were quantified via qPCR. Shilajit supplementation did not 
significantly alter total or progressive motility, vitality, morphology, or the 
major CASA velocity and trajectory parameters compared with the Control 
(p > 0.05). Beat Cross Frequency (BCF) was higher at 15 μg/mL than at 25 μg/mL 
(p = 0.043), although neither group differed from the Control. Shilajit was also 
associated with distinct changes in the post-thaw sperm RNA profile. p53 mRNA 
was highest at 5 μg/mL, whereas Bax was lower at 15 and 25 μg/mL and Bcl-2 was 
lower across all Shilajit-treated groups. Five of the six examined miRNAs, 
including gga-miR-34a and gga-miR-155, were lower than the Control across all 
Shilajit concentrations, while gga-miR-146b showed a concentration-specific 
response. Shilajit supplementation produced limited effects on conventional 
post-thaw sperm-quality parameters but was associated with marked changes in 
apoptosis- and stress-associated sperm RNAs. The divergent mRNA response 
together with the broader reduction across the selected miRNAs indicates 
modulation of the post-thaw molecular profile in mature rooster spermatozoa. 
These findings support further investigation of the relationship between 
Shilajit-associated RNA changes and apoptosis, mitochondrial function, and 
reproductive competence.

Effect of electrical impedance tomography-guided positive end-expiratory

BACKGROUND: Pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg positioning during 
laparoscopic colorectal surgery promote atelectasis and increase the risk of 
postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs). Electrical impedance tomography 
(EIT) enables individualised PEEP titration by visualising regional lung 
collapse, facilitating lung-protective ventilation. However, evidence of its 
effect on clinical PPCs remains limited.
METHODS: In this single-centre, parallel-group RCT, adults with intermediate to 
high risk for PPCs (ARISCAT score ≥26) who underwent laparoscopic colorectal 
surgery were randomly assigned to receive intraoperative PEEP titration guided 
by EIT or a conventional fixed PEEP of 5 cm H2O. The primary outcome was PPCs 
incidence within 30 days, as determined by a multidisciplinary adjudication team 
using standardised criteria.
RESULTS: Among the 117 randomised participants (mean [range] age: 62 [37-80] yr; 
37% female), EIT-guided PEEP (n=59) resulted in lower driving pressure (16 
[15-18] cm H2O) compared with fixed PEEP (n=58; 19 [17-22] cm H2O; P<0.0001). 
The incidence of 30 day PPCs was lower among participants randomised to 
EIT-guided PEEP (29/59 [49.2%]) than those in the fixed-PEEP group (42/58

Age and disease status as negative prognostic factors for 5-year survival in 
chondrosarcoma: A single-institution analysis.

Chao SC(1), Lin WH(2), Liu SH(3), Yang RS(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Traumatology, National Taiwan University Hospital, Taipei,

characteristics, and metastasis as key prognostic factors for chondrosarcoma 
survival, data specifically focusing on the Taiwanese population remain sparse.
METHODS: This retrospective study included patients who were pathologically

The heat is on for plant nitrogen nutrition.

Martin GT(1), Fiorucci AS(2).

Author information:
(1)Institute for Integrative Biology of the Cell (I2BC), Université 
Paris-Saclay, CEA, CNRS, 91198 Gif-sur-Yvette, France.
(2)Institute for Integrative Biology of the Cell (I2BC), Université 
Paris-Saclay, CEA, CNRS, 91198 Gif-sur-Yvette, France. Electronic address: 
anne-sophie.fiorucci@i2bc.paris-saclay.fr.

Global warming leads to increased average atmospheric temperatures, which will 
inevitably have an impact on plant growth and crop yields. It is essential to 
understand how plant nutrition will be affected by elevated temperatures. 
Nitrogen is one of the major mineral nutrients, and its uptake is enhanced 
during the light period, peaking at the day/night transition, whereas its 
storage, especially in the form of nitrate (NO3-), is favoured in the dark. 
Given the overlap between light and temperature responses, we review the 
interaction between nitrogen nutrition and light responses and place this in the 
context of new findings on temperature sensing. We also suggest new hypotheses 
on the potential links between temperature and NO3- homeostasis.

Association between ECAP signal artifacts and electrical components from a 
cochlear implant impedance model.

Veloso de Oliveira J(1), Weiss NM(1), Wollenberg B(1), Wimmer W(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Otorhinolaryngology, TUM University Hospital, Technical 
University of Munich, Munich, Germany.
(2)Department of Otorhinolaryngology, TUM University Hospital, Technical 
University of Munich, Munich, Germany. Electronic address: 
wilhelm.wimmer@tum.de.

electrically evoked compound action potentials (ECAPs) are among the few 
objective measures of auditory nerve activity available in clinical practice and 
provide valuable insight into a patient's neural status. ECAP recordings are 
typically performed using different electrodes for stimulation and recording to 
avoid amplifier saturation caused by electrode polarization. However, 
same-electrode recording could reduce the spatial separation between the site of 
neural activation and the recording site, potentially providing a more localized 
assessment of neural activity and improving the sensitivity of ECAP-based 
biomarkers. Here, we introduce a method to characterize stimulation artifacts 
and estimate their parameters using a previously published impedance model. The 
artifact waveform was described by a shared double exponential function, while 
electrical components of an equivalent circuit were estimated from impedance 
measurements acquired with multiple pulse durations. Artifact recordings 
exhibited clear polarity-dependent behavior. Nevertheless, the amplitude of the 
fast exponential component showed a significant association with its 
impedance-based estimate (fixed-effect coefficient β=0.37 and β=0.44 for 
anodic-cathodic and cathodic-anodic stimulation, respectively; p<0.001). 
Furthermore, longitudinal changes in the fast exponential component were similar 
to changes in near-field impedance subcomponent, suggesting that the ECAP 
artifact could be partially influenced by postoperative changes at the 
electrode-electrolyte interface.

Effectiveness of three preparation methods on pulmonary function test 
performance and procedure-related fear in children: A three-arm randomized 
controlled trial.

Gunes SN(1), Kucukoglu S(2).

Author information:
(1)Selcuk University, Institute of Health Sciences, Turkey.
(2)Selcuk University, Faculty of Nursing, Konya, Turkey. Electronic address: 
sibel.kucukoglu@selcuk.edu.tr.

BACKGROUND: Successful spirometry in children requires adequate cooperation and 
correct respiratory maneuvers. This study compared routine verbal instruction, 
verbal instruction with demonstration, and animation-assisted preparation for 
pediatric spirometry.
METHODS: This three-arm randomized controlled trial included 96 children aged 
6-12 years referred to a tertiary pediatric pulmonary function test unit. 
Children were stratified-randomized to verbal instruction, verbal instruction 
with demonstration, or animation-assisted preparation (n = 32 each). Data were 
collected using the Descriptive Characteristics Form, Pulmonary Function Test 
Parameters Form, and Children's Fear Scale. Pulmonary function was assessed 
during the first three acceptable maneuvers, and fear before and after testing.
RESULTS: Baseline characteristics and pulmonary function were similar across 
groups (p > 0.05). Forced inspiratory vital capacity was higher in the 
animation-assisted group at the second measurement (mean difference = 0.50, 95% 
CI 0.11-0.89) and in the verbal instruction group at the third measurement (mean 
difference = 0.63, 95% CI 0.22-1.04), both compared with demonstration. Peak 
expiratory flow was higher in the animation-assisted group than in the 
demonstration group at the third measurement (mean difference = 0.66, 95% CI 
0.13-1.19; p < 0.05). No significant group×time interactions were observed for 
pulmonary function (all p > 0.05) or fear (F = 0.03, p = 0.973, η2 = 0.001), 
although fear decreased in all groups.
CONCLUSION: Animation improved selected spirometry parameters without consistent 
superiority. Fear decreased similarly across all groups, suggesting that 
animation may be a useful alternative for preparing children for spirometry.
IMPLICATIONS TO PRACTICE: Selective differences in pulmonary function did not 
demonstrate overall superiority of any preparation method, supporting flexible 
selection based on clinical context and resources.

Amino acid sequences in peptides and proteins can be used to store data with the 
advantages of high capacity and stability, offering a solution for storing 
ever-increasing amounts of data. Compared with peptides, proteins have longer 
sequences and can be produced at a much lower cost, enabling more efficient data 
storage and allowing specific functions to be incorporated using established 
protein techniques. Although data storage using peptides and proteins has been 
demonstrated, challenges related to cost, throughput, error rates, data density, 
and scalability remain to be addressed. Emerging technologies to overcome these 
challenges are under active development, and their successful commercialization 
could drive a paradigm shift, enabling high-density and very long-term data 
storage.

Engineering large genomic segments is rapidly expanding the scope of plant 
genome manipulation from individual genes to chromosome-scale redesign. Recent 
advances in double-strand break-, prime-editing-, recombinase-, and 
transposase-based technologies now enable programmable deletion, insertion, 
replacement, duplication, inversion, and translocation of DNA fragments ranging 
from kilobases to megabases. In this review, we summarize the major strategies 
for large-fragment genome engineering in plants, compare their strengths and 
limitations, and discuss their applications in both fundamental plant biology 
and crop breeding. We further highlight that the integration of artificial 
intelligence is catalyzing the rapid optimization of large-fragment genome 
engineering. The ongoing transition from genome editing to chromosome 
engineering promises to revolutionize crop breeding and plant synthetic biology, 
ultimately enabling rational design of plant genomes.

Biological carbon fixation is currently limited to seven naturally occurring 
pathways. Synthetic carbon fixation pathways have the potential to surpass 
natural aerobic pathways in efficiency, but none have been realized in living 
cells. Here, we present the reductive methylaspartate cycles, a family of four 
energy-efficient aerobic CO2 fixation pathway variants. These cycles have the 
potential to outperform the yields and/or rates of the Calvin cycle and 
previously proposed synthetic CO2 fixation cycles. To realize these designs, we 
adopted a modular engineering approach in Escherichia coli. Several pathway 
modules, up to a cascade of 11 enzymes, were realized via engineering and 
evolution. We demonstrate crotonyl- coenzyme A carboxylase-dependent growth 
under both elevated and ambient CO2 conditions, and we show in vitro activity of 
the other CO2-fixing 2-oxoglutarate carboxylase, which requires further activity 
optimization for mesophilic temperatures. This article demonstrates important 
steps toward realizing efficient synthetic carbon fixation pathways in living 
organisms.

BACKGROUND: Clinical T1 micropapillary urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is an 
aggressive variant histology for which early radical cystectomy (RC) is commonly 
recommended. However, there remain conflicting data on whether conditions in 
carefully selected patients may be managed with initial bladder-sparing 
approaches without compromising oncologic outcomes.
OBJECTIVE: The objective is to systematically review and synthesize the 
available literature comparing bladder-sparing approaches, such as Bacillus 
Calmette-Guerin (BCG) therapy, and early RC outcomes in clinical stage 1 primary 
tumor (cT1) micropapillary carcinoma of the bladder.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: A systematic search was performed according 
to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 
statement and Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions.
OUTCOME MEASUREMENT AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS: The primary end points were 
overall survival (OS) and cancer-specific survival (CSS). The included articles 
were descriptively assessed and time-to-event analysis was performed for select 
endpoints.
RESULTS AND LIMITATIONS: Among 461 identified reports, nine retrospective 
studies met the criteria for quantitative analysis, encompassing 9402 patients 
of whom 9287 (99%) had non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) and 1033 (11%) 
had a micropapillary subtype. A total of 625 patients (62%) underwent 
bladder-sparing approaches, whereas 392 (39%) underwent early RC. Of the 
bladder-sparing approaches, 88% of patients received intravesical BCG therapy. 
For a bladder-sparing approach for cT1 disease with a micropapillary component, 
pooled unadjusted hazard ratios were not statistically significant for CSS 
(hazard ratio [HR] 1.32, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.60-2.88, p = 0.5) and OS 
(HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.68-1.07, p = 0.16) compared with early RC. Data evaluating 
bladder-sparing strategies beyond BCG were limited.
CONCLUSIONS: NMIBC with micropapillary features is an aggressive disease 
conventionally managed with early RC. In retrospective cohorts of selected 
patients with micropapillary cT1, available unadjusted data did not provide 
clear evidence of statistically significant differences in CSS or OS between 
initial bladder-sparing approaches and early RC.

The deregulated utilization of nutrients by tumors, first observed over a 
century ago, is recognized as a hallmark of cancer and continues to be exploited 
clinically to image neoplastic disease. Despite this historic focus on cancer 
cells and, more recently, their neighbors, metabolic reprogramming is not 
limited to the tumor microenvironment. Tumors also have the capacity to rewire 
the metabolism of cells throughout the body, including those at distant sites, 
often referred to as the tumor macroenvironment. Alterations in the metabolism 
of noncancerous tissues outside the local tumor ecosystem are gaining attention, 
but their origins and consequences remain incompletely defined. A deeper 
understanding of these changes may reveal previously unrecognized signatures of 
disease and unexplored opportunities for therapeutic intervention.

BACKGROUND: Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is an established biomarker for 
amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, it remains unclear whether 
biomarkers reflecting amyloid-β metabolism (Aβ), tau (phosphorylated tau, pTau), 
and astrogliosis (glial fibrillary acidic protein, GFAP) can complement NfL in 
clinical applications. It is also unclear how Alzheimer's disease (AD) 
co-pathology affects disease progression in ALS.
METHODS: We studied 264 patients with ALS and 164 disease-control participants, 
analysing baseline cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) NfL, Aβ peptides, pTau181, pTau217, 
and GFAP. A two-step diagnostic strategy was examined in individuals with 
intermediate NfL values, using machine-learning models. Prognostic associations 
were evaluated using linear mixed-effects and Cox models adjusted for 
established predictors; survival was additionally examined in pooled analyses 
including an external ALS cohort (n = 153).
FINDINGS: Patients with ALS exhibited higher CSF NfL, Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42, pTau181, 
and pTau217 than controls, even within Aβ-negative subgroups. NfL discriminated 
ALS from controls with an AUC of 0.85 (0.82-0.88), which increased to 0.90 
(0.88-0.92) in machine-learning models incorporating additional biomarkers. The 
machine-learning models maintained a high positive predictive value (0.90) for 
classifying cases with intermediate NfL values. Significant Aβ × NfL 
interactions were observed for longitudinal functional decline, and pooled 
survival analyses showed stronger associations between NfL and survival in the 
Aβ-positive ALS subgroup (14%) than in the Aβ-negative ALS subgroup (HR 4.02 
[2.17-7.45] vs 1.62 [1.36-1.92]).
INTERPRETATION: Multiple biomarker assessments can reduce misclassification of 
individuals with intermediate NfL values. CSF Aβ positivity modified the 
association between baseline NfL and disease progression. Personalised diagnosis 
and prognosis based on fine-grained co-pathology evaluation may enhance clinical 
management of ALS.

complete list of funding organisations is provided in Acknowledgements.

BACKGROUND: While life expectancy for people with intellectual disabilities (ID) 
has improved, health inequalities, premature ageing and elevated mortality 
persist. Oral health is rarely considered as a determinant of survival, despite 
evidence in general populations linking tooth loss to increased mortality.
OBJECTIVE/HYPOTHESIS: To determine whether tooth loss predicts all-cause and 
respiratory mortality in older adults with ID.
METHODS: A 13-year longitudinal analysis of 752 adults with ID aged ≥40 years at 
Wave 1 (2009/2010) of the Intellectual Disability Supplement to The Irish 
Longitudinal Study on Ageing. Dentition was categorised as dentate, edentulous 
with dentures, or edentulous without dentures. Fully adjusted models used 
complete cases (n = 742). Mortality was determined through death-certificate 
linkage to March 2023 using Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards analyses.
RESULTS: Over follow-up, 225 participants with baseline dentition data died 
(29.9%), including 114 (15.2%) from respiratory causes. Mortality was highest 
among those edentulous without dentures (54.4%), compared with dentate 
participants (24.3%) and those edentulous with dentures (29.9%). After 
adjustment, edentulism without dentures remained associated with all-cause 
mortality (HR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.21-2.35; p = .002) and respiratory mortality 
(HR = 1.92, 95% CI: 1.22-3.01; p = .005); edentulism with dentures was not 
significantly associated with either outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: Complete tooth loss, particularly without denture replacement, was

Tumor innervation in non-central nervous system tumors: origins, mechanisms, and 
phenotypic plasticity.

Zhang Y(1), Ye Z(2), Wang Y(2), Tang S(2), Chen G(3).

Author information:
(1)Basic Medical Research Center, Medical School of Nantong University, 
Co-Innovation Center of Neuroregeneration, Nantong, Jiangsu Province 226001,

(2)Basic Medical Research Center, Medical School of Nantong University,

(3)Basic Medical Research Center, Medical School of Nantong University, 
Co-Innovation Center of Neuroregeneration, Nantong, Jiangsu Province 226001, 
China; Key Laboratory of Neuroregeneration of Jiangsu and the Ministry of 
Education, Nantong University, Nantong, Jiangsu Province 226001, China; 
Department of Anesthesiology, Affiliated Hospital of Nantong University, 
Nantong, Jiangsu Province 226001, China. Electronic address:

The peripheral nervous system has emerged as an important regulator of solid 
tumor biology. We synthesize recent advances in cancer neuroscience, focusing on 
three interconnected themes: the cellular origins of tumor-associated nerves, 
the molecular mechanisms that govern neural recruitment and remodeling, and the 
resulting phenotypic plasticity within the tumor microenvironment. Tumor 
innervation arises through axon extension from pre-existing nerves, recruitment 
of neural precursors, and neuron-like transdifferentiation of non-neuronal 
cells. These processes are driven by neurotrophic factors, axon guidance cues, 
extracellular vesicles, and stress-associated pathways. The functional 
consequences of innervation are context-dependent, with sympathetic, 
parasympathetic, and sensory inputs exerting distinct effects across tumor types 
and stages. We conclude by outlining key challenges and future directions for 
therapeutic translation.

403. Physiother Theory Pract. 2026 Oct 20:1-10. doi: 10.1080/09593985.2026.2751571. 
Online ahead of print.

Cardiopulmonary exercise testing in children with cerebral palsy: Feasibility 
and the relationship between aerobic capacity and gross motor function: A pilot 
study.

Özdemir Tekeş SE(1), Turan BK(1), Kutlay Ş(1), Sonel Tur B(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, Ankara University Faculty 
of Medicine, Ankara, Turkey.

INTRODUCTION: Children with cerebral palsy (CP) may exhibit reduced aerobic 
capacity. While the cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) is the gold standard 
for determining aerobic capacity, motor disorders and accompanying disturbances 
make its application challenging. The 6-minute walk test (6-MWT) may offer a 
practical alternative.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the feasibility of CPET, explore its relationship with 
the 6-MWT, and investigate the association between aerobic capacity and gross 
motor function in children with CP.
METHODS: Children aged 6-13 years with unilateral/bilateral spastic CP 
classified as Gross Motor Function Classification System Level II, who could 
follow instructions and walk on a treadmill without physical assistance, were 
included. The Gross Motor Function Measure-88 (GMFM-88), 6-MWT, and 
treadmill-based CPET were performed. CPET feasibility was evaluated by maximal 
exertion and termination reasons.
RESULTS: Eight participants (four males, four females; four spastic unilateral, 
four spastic bilateral) with a median age of 8.5 years were enrolled. The median 
(minimum-maximum) peak oxygen consumption (VO2peak), respiratory exchange ratio 
(RER), and maximum heart rate (HRmax) in CPET were 21 (17.1-30.6) mL/kg/min, 
0.87 (0.81-1.00), and 145.5 (97-174) bpm, respectively. One participant achieved 
near-maximal exertion during CPET, while the others demonstrated submaximal 
effort. Reasons for CPET termination included lower limb fatigue (n = 5) and 
poor compliance (n = 3). The 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) was not significantly 
correlated with VO2peak (r = 0.000, p > .999). 6MWD was strongly correlated with 
the GMFM-88 total score (r = 0.790, p = .020). Moderate correlations, which were 
not statistically significant, were found between 6MWD and the GMFM-88 
Dimensions D (r = 0.672, p = .068) and E (r = 0.695, p = .056). No significant 
correlations were observed between the GMFM-88 scores and VO2peak, RER, or 
HRmax.
CONCLUSION: Treadmill-based CPET demonstrated limitations in reaching maximal 
aerobic capacity in this pilot sample of children with CP. The 6-MWT may offer a 
practical approach for evaluating functional performance, given its association 
with gross motor function.

PMID: 42901802

Single-cell analysis reveals CXCL16(+) dendritic cells and clonally expanded

Mullins BJ(#)(1), Shwetar J(#)(2), Herrera A(#)(3), Cheng AY(4), Yang KL(1),

(1)Department of Pathology, NYU Grossman School of Medicine, New York, NY, USA.
(2)Division of Precision Medicine, Department of Medicine, NYU Grossman School

of Medical Sciences, New York, NY, 10065.

(9)Department of Cell Biology, New York University Grossman School of Medicine, 
New York, NY, 10016, USA.
(10)Division of Rheumatology, Department of Medicine, NYU Grossman School of 
Medicine, New York, NY, USA.
(11)NYU Colton Center for Autoimmunity, Department of Medicine, NYU Langone 
Health, New York, NY, USA.

OBJECTIVE: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a chronic immune-mediated arthritis 
affecting approximately 30% of individuals with psoriasis. The mechanisms 
driving PsA joint inflammation remain incompletely defined.
METHODS: To address this gap, we performed multimodal single-cell sequencing of 
immune cells from matched peripheral blood and synovial fluid (SF) from 6 PsA 
patients, with comparisons to a rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patient and 6 healthy 
controls (HC).
RESULTS: SF CD4 and CD8 T cells displayed elevated expression of TOX, PDCD1, 
CTLA4, GZMK, CXCR3, and CXCR6, reflecting a tissue-specific activation state. 
CD4 T cell sub-clustering revealed clonally expanded populations enriched for 
GZMK and cytotoxic gene programs, suggesting antigen-driven activation. In 
contrast, CD8 T cell clonality showed a significant correlation with GZMK 
expression, however GZMK+ CD8 T cells in the joint exhibited a transcriptional 
signature consistent with functional exhaustion. Concurrently, SF was enriched 
for CD141+, CD1c+, CCR7+, and SIGLEC6+ dendritic cells (DCs), characterized by 
increased CXCL16 expression and antigen presentation pathways. Flow cytometry 
and ELISA in an additional 25 PsA patients and 16 HCs confirmed protein-level 
enrichment of key chemokines and GZMK+ T cells. Cell-cell communication analysis 
highlighted CXCR6-CXCL16 and CXCR3-CXCL10 chemokine axes as mediators of immune 
cell recruitment and retention, while in vitro assays showed enhanced migration 
of PsA SF T cells toward a CXCL16 gradient relative to paired blood.
CONCLUSION: Together, these findings suggest that clonally expanded GZMK+ CD4 T 
cells in PsA are cytotoxic and antigen-responsive, contributing to joint 
inflammation following recruitment by CXCL16-producing dendritic cells.

SIRT5 Attenuates Traumatic Brain Injury by Preserving OPA1-Mediated 
Mitochondrial Fusion and Limiting Oxidative Stress.

Wang L(1), Li W(2), Sun B(1), Ouyang Q(1), Wu X(3), Luo J(1), Cui Y(4), Jiang 
L(1), Song M(1), Cheng J(1), Ma Y(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Neurosurgery, The General Hospital of Western Theater Command, 
Chengdu, China.
(2)Department of Neurology, The General Hospital of Western Theater Command, 
Chengdu, China.
(3)Department of Neurosurgery, Tangdu Hospital, Fourth Military Medical 
University, Xi'an, Shaanxi, China.
(4)Department of Clinical Lab, The 945th Army Hospital of the Chinese People's 
Liberation Army, Yaan, Sichuan Province, China.

AIMS: Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central pathological 
drivers of disease progression following traumatic brain injury (TBI). Sirtuin 5 
(SIRT5), a predominantly mitochondrial NAD+-dependent deacylase, plays critical 
roles in mitochondrial quality control, redox homeostasis, and metabolic 
regulation. This study aims to define the upstream regulatory machinery 
controlling SIRT5 stability and to identify the downstream pathway linking SIRT5 
to mitochondrial remodeling after TBI.
RESULTS: In this study, we demonstrated that TBI promotes neuronal SIRT5 protein 
degradation via a synergistic regulatory mechanism involving USP7 and TRIM21. 
Using neuron-specific Sirt5 conditional knockout mice, we found that SIRT5 
deficiency exacerbates TBI-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative damage, 
cerebral edema, and neurological deficits. SIRT5 regulates OPA1 expression 
through a MEF2A-dependent mechanism, thereby preserving mitochondrial structure 
and function and alleviating oxidative injury. The protective effects of 
neuronal SIRT5 overexpression were abolished in mice lacking Opa1 specifically 
in neurons, confirming that OPA1 is a critical downstream effector of 
SIRT5-mediated neuroprotection. Finally, rabies virus glycoprotein 
(RVG)-conjugated extracellular vesicles loaded with SIRT5 mRNA demonstrated both 
efficacy and safety in preclinical TBI models.
INNOVATION: This study identifies the USP7/TRIM21-SIRT5-MEF2A-OPA1 axis as a 
novel regulatory cascade that governs the transition between adaptive and 
maladaptive mitochondrial remodeling after TBI, a concept with broad 
implications for acute brain injury and neurodegeneration.
CONCLUSION: This study defines the USP7/TRIM21-SIRT5-MEF2A-OPA1 axis as a novel 
regulatory cascade that controls mitochondrial remodeling after TBI. SIRT5 acts 
through a MEF2A-dependent mechanism to maintain OPA1 expression and 
mitochondrial fusion, and its transient restoration via RVG-EV delivery of SIRT5 
mRNA is a promising therapeutic strategy. Antioxid. Redox Signal. 00, 000-000.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of multi-health behavior interventions to 
reduce common mental health symptoms in people living with and beyond cancer.

Tavares VDO(1)(2), Schuch FB(3)(4)(5)(6)(7), Skinner G(6), Baker T(6), 
France-Ratcliffe M(8), Menezes de Sousa G(2), Quan ML(9), Cuthbert C(1), 
Teychenne M(6).

Author information:
(1)Faculty of Nursing, University of Calgary, Calgary, AB, Canada.
(2)Laboratory of Hormone Measurement, Department of Physiology and Behavior, 
Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte, Natal, Brazil.
(3)Department of Sports Methods and Techniques, Federal University of Santa 
Maria, Santa Maria, RS, Brazil.
(4)Institute of Psychiatry, Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, Rio de 
Janeiro, RJ, Brazil.
(5)Faculty of Health Sciences, Universidad Autónoma de Chile, Providencia, 
Chile.
(6)Institute for Physical Activity and Nutrition (IPAN), School of Exercise and 
Nutrition Sciences, Deakin University, Geelong, Australia.
(7)Food and Mood Centre, Institute for Mental and Physical Health and Clinical 
Translation (IMPACT), Deakin University, Geelong, Australia.
(8)Department of Sport and Exercise Science, Manchester Metropolitan University, 
Institute of Sport, Manchester, UK.
(9)Department of Surgery and Oncology, University of Calgary, Calgary, Canada.

BACKGROUND: People living with and beyond cancer often report lower levels of 
physical activity, poorer sleep, and poorer diet quality, all of which may 
contribute to an increased risk of common mental health symptoms. This 
systematic review aimed to investigate the effects of multi-health behavior 
interventions designed to reduce common mental health symptoms in people living 
with and beyond cancer.
METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analyses followed PRISMA guidelines. 
The search, conducted up to July 2, 2025, included PubMed, Embase, Web of 
Science, PsycInfo, and PsyAPA, and grey literature. Multi-health behavior 
interventions (randomized and non-randomized trials) for people living with and 
beyond cancer, that targeted at least two behaviors (physical activity, diet, 
sleep, mindfulness) and assessed effects on common mental health outcomes 
(depression, anxiety, stress) were included.
RESULTS: A total of 22 studies (n = 2,191 participants, 77.5% female; mean age 
55 years) were included. Multi-health behavior interventions demonstrated small 
but significant improvements in depression (g = 0.40, 95% CI [0.26,0.55], 
p < 0.001), anxiety (g = 0.33, 95% CI [0.22,0.45], p < 0.001), and stress 
(g = 0.26, 95% CI [0.09,0.43], p = 0.003). Effects were consistent across 
treatment phases, cancer types, intervention type (flexible interventions and 
structured programs), number of intervention components, and intervention 
duration, with all subgroups showing significant improvements in at least one 
mental health outcome.
CONCLUSION: Multi-health behavior interventions are associated with small but 
significant improvements in common mental health symptoms among people living 
with and beyond cancer. However, given the limitations and variable certainty of 
the available evidence, further high-quality RCTs are needed to confirm these 
findings.

Generative AI in clinical practice: how should rheumatologists evaluate and 
monitor emerging tools?

Kouranloo K(1)(2)(3), MBBChir MD(3)(4), Yazdany J(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)University of California San Francisco (UCSF), San Francisco, California, 
USA.
(2)Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital, 1001 Potrero Ave, San Francisco, 
California, USA.
(3)Centre for Rheumatic Diseases, Weston Education Centre (WEC), Cutcombe Road, 
London, UK, SE5 9RJ.
(4)Department of Rheumatology, King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, 
Denmark Hill, London, UK, SE5 9RS.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in 
rheumatology practice, to assist with tasks such as documentation, record 
summarization, and clinical decision support. Rheumatologists need a practical 
approach to determining what evidence and oversight each application requires. 
This narrative review proposes a framework based on two dimensions: contextual 
complexity and influence on patient care. Greater contextual complexity can make 
errors harder to detect, whereas greater influence on care increases the 
potential consequences of an undetected error. We examine evidence for workflow 
benefits and clinical effectiveness within this framework and consider safety, 
equity, privacy, governance, and implementation. Existing evidence on the 
benefits, accuracy and reliability of AI applications remains mixed. For 
example, studies of ambient AI scribes suggest reduced documentation burden, but 
evidence of improved patient outcomes from applications supporting clinical 
decisions is more limited. For applications with limited clinical influence, 
evaluation has initially focused on workflow, usability, and documentation 
quality. Tools that synthesize longitudinal information require additional 
assessment of completeness and source traceability. Those influencing diagnosis 
or treatment require prospective evaluation of clinical benefit and safety. 
Relevant vendor evidence should be assessed alongside proportionate local 
testing and ongoing monitoring. Safeguards should address risks such as 
hallucinations, automation bias, and propagating documentation errors, with 
attention to performance across patient groups. Changes in functionality or 
clinical use should prompt reassessment. The framework provides a structured 
basis for adoption decisions and identifies priorities for research on patient 
outcomes and feasible oversight in routine rheumatology care.
