The content and reporting completeness of physical therapist-led interventions 
for glenohumeral osteoarthritis: a systematic review.

Muhammad DG(1), Foster NE(1)(2), Pelaez M(3), O'Leary K(1), Ackerman IN(4), 
Quicke JG(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Surgical Treatment and Rehabilitation Service (STARS) Education and Research 
Alliance, The University of Queensland and Metro North Health, Brisbane, 
Australia.
(2)Centre for Innovation in Pain and Health Research, School of Health and 
Rehabilitation Sciences, The University of Queensland, Queensland, Australia.
(3)Independent researcher, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada.
(4)School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, Monash University, 
Melbourne, Australia.

OBJECTIVES: This study synthesised the content and reporting completeness of 
published physical therapist-led interventions for glenohumeral osteoarthritis 
(GHOA).
METHODS: This systematic review undertook electronic database searches in 
PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane, CINAHL and PEDro (until June 2025) for any 
peer-reviewed articles/studies describing physical therapist-led interventions 
across non-surgical and perioperative settings for adults aged 45 years and over 
with GHOA. The content and reporting completeness were synthesized using the 
22-item Template for Intervention Description and Replication for rehabilitation 
interventions (TIDIeR_Rehab).
RESULTS: Overall, 134 articles/studies describing 156 physical therapist-led 
interventions were included, comprising mostly case series designs (n=47, 35.1%) 
or narrative reviews (n=38, 28.4%). Of the remaining 49 articles/studies, only 
11 were studies reporting RCT results and three were protocols of RCTs in 
progress. Intervention content varied considerably, and the overall completeness 
of intervention item reporting was poor (only 18%). Interventions in 
non-surgical contexts commonly included strengthening exercises (n=33, 53.2%), 
range of motion (ROM) exercises (n=23, 37.1%), and electrotherapy modalities 
(n=16, 25.8%). Sling immobilisation was most reported in postoperative 
interventions (n=64, 72.7%). Many different proposed mechanisms of action were 
reported (n=49, 31.4%); but all were biomechanically orientated.
CONCLUSION: Very few high-quality empirical studies evaluating physical 
therapist-led interventions for GHOA have been published. We found substantial 
heterogeneity in the content of published physical therapist-led interventions, 
and the reporting completeness was generally poor. This suggests considerable 
uncertainty regarding best practice physical therapy for GHOA in terms of 
intervention content. Future high-quality empirical research is needed, 
preferably using RCT designs that include clear descriptions of interventions.

BACKGROUND: Extent of uveitis risk in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is 
based on clinical factors. We aim to compare the trajectories of tear-based 
biomarker levels of patients with JIA with and without uveitis.
METHODS: This prospective multicenter study included children with JIA at risk 
for uveitis (JIA-no-U), and with JIA-associated uveitis (JIA-U). Serial tear 
samples were collected from each eye by Schirmer strips at enrollment (E) and 
follow-up (FU1, FU2). S100 proteins, cytokines, and chemokines were assayed by 
Luminex or ELISA and compared between groups.
FINDINGS: Fifty patients (37 JIA-no-U, 13 JIA-U) contributed 222 samples (150 
JIA-no-U, 73 JIA-U). At E there were no significant differences in biomarker 
levels between JIA-U and JIA-no-U. During follow-up of JIA-U, monocyte 
chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) levels increased longitudinally from E to FU1 
and FU2 (1.63±0.31 to 2.46±0.31, p=0.005; and 2.89±0.32, p<0.0001), similar in 
Chemokine (C-X-C motif) Ligand (CXCL)-10 from E to FU1 and FU2 (4.39±0.41 to 
5.26±0.41, p = 0.030; and 6.51±0.43, p < 0.0001) and in IL-8 levels from E to 
FU1 and FU2 (3.09±0.30 to 4.25±0.30, p = 0.006; and 4.65±0.32, p ≤ 0.001). In 
both groups, S100A12 and S100A8/A9 increased from E to FU.
CONCLUSION: Longitudinal changes in MCP-1, CXCL10 and IL-8 levels in tear fluid 
in JIA-U may reflect inflammatory ocular processes and support the role of 
monocytes and interferon related pathways in uveitis. Lack of differences in 
S100 proteins may reflect systemic inflammation from arthritis. Tear-based 
biomarkers may support clinical factors for identifying children with JIA who 
develop uveitis.

Sema4A neutralization reduces fibrosis and inflammation in a mouse model of

﻿OBJECTIVE: We previously showed that Semaphorin4A (Sema4A) is elevated in 
patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc) and promotes inflammation and fibrosis in 
vitro. Here, we examined the effect of Sema4A neutralization in vivo and in 3D 
fibrosis models.
METHODS: Sema4A plasma levels were measured by ELISA in healthy controls (n=31) 
and patients with SSc (n=30). In the bleomycin SSc-model, mice were treated with 
an anti-Sema4A neutralizing antibody or its respective isotype control (n=6-7). 
The 3D fibrosis models, consisting of collagen hydrogel, dermal fibroblasts, and 
peripheral blood mononuclear cells, were stimulated with recombinant Sema4A, 
rapamycin, or antibodies neutralizing Sema4A, PlexinD1, PlexinB2, Neuropilin-1 
or their respective isotype controls (n=6-10). Collagen content was determined 
by trichrome staining and hydroxyproline assay. Gene expression was determined 
by RT-qPCR and obtained from GEO-NCBI expression arrays, while protein 
expression by immunohistochemistry, immunoblotting and flow cytometry.
RESULTS: Circulating Sema4A was elevated in patients with SSc (p<0.0001), while 
Sema4A receptors were elevated in SSc skin and lung (p ranged from <0.05 to 
0.0001). Anti-Sema4A administration significantly reduced skin and lung collagen 
content in bleomycin-treated mice (p<0.01), as well as the expression of 
extracellular matrix components, fibrotic and inflammatory mediators, and immune 
cell infiltration. In the 3D models, SSc serum and SSc PBMCs induced cell 
contraction, which was drastically abrogated by blocking Sema4A (p<0.01). This 
effect was associated with reduced expression of fibrotic mediators and 
attenuated mTORC1 pathway activation.
CONCLUSIONS: We confirmed the pro-fibrotic and pro-inflammatory role of Sema4A, 
postulating Sema4A neutralization as a novel approach for the treatment of SSc.

BACKGROUND: The efficacy of middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAE) for 
chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH) has heightened interest in imaging biomarkers 
that may reflect neomembrane activity, predict recurrence, and identify patients 
most likely to benefit from treatment. Characterization of hematoma internal 
architecture, referred to as the imaging phenotype, may provide indirect 
information regarding the biological activity and maturation of the neomembrane. 
However, imaging phenotype has not been incorporated into randomized trials or 
validated treatment-selection algorithms, and standardized definitions and 
reporting remain lacking.
METHODS: The American Society of Functional Neuroradiology Clinical Practice 
Committee developed this State of Practice statement through expert consensus 
and review of the available literature.
KEY MESSAGE: Noncontrast CT (NCCT) remains the primary imaging modality for cSDH 
assessment. Hematoma burden should be characterized by maximum thickness 
measured perpendicular to the inner table, midline shift, and, when appropriate, 
volume. Volume may be estimated using the ABC/2 formula, whereas segmentation is 
more accurate for irregular, crescentic, or multiloculated collections when 
available. Internal architecture should be described using the Nakaguchi 
framework of homogeneous, laminar, separated, and trabecular phenotypes, with 
mixed or transitional features explicitly reported. Advanced techniques, 
including dual-energy CT, photon-counting CT, MRI, and arterial spin labeling, 
may provide information regarding membrane activity but are supported by 
limited, largely single-center evidence and currently have a problem-solving 
rather than routine role. Standardized reporting and prospective validation are 
needed before imaging phenotype or advanced-imaging biomarkers can guide 
treatment selection.

Harnessing a Light-Activated Ruthenium(II) Complex Self-Delivery Nanoplatform 
for Tumor-Organelle Cascade-Targeted Immunotherapy via Type II Immunogenic Cell 
Death.

Wang J(1), Kuang T(1), Hu B(1), Yin J(1), Zhou Z(1), Qin G(1), He S(1), Yu 
CY(1)(2), Wei H(1).

Author information:
(1)Hunan Province Cooperative Innovation Center for Molecular Target New Drug 
Study, School of Pharmaceutical Science, Hengyang Medical School, University of 
South China, Hengyang421001, China.
(2)Affiliated Hospital of Hunan Academy of Chinese Medicine, Hunan Academy of 
Chinese Medicine, Changsha410013, China.

Immunogenic cell death (ICD) converts immunosuppressive "cold" tumors into 
immunogenic "hot" ones, yet ICD inducers with precise tumor-organelle cascade 
targeting and spatiotemporal controllability remain largely unexplored. Herein, 
we report a self-delivery nanoplatform (ER-Ru NPs) constructed via the 
self-assembly of well-defined tumor-endoplasmic reticulum (ER) cascade-targeting 
ruthenium(II) complexes. The intrinsic amphiphilicity enables self-assembly of 
the ruthenium(II) complexes into stabilized nanoparticles with efficient tumor 
accumulation properties via biotin-mediated active targeting, without any 
exogenous carriers. Following cellular internalization, the released 
ruthenium(II) complex monomer specifically accumulates in the ER to generate a 
cleaved Ru-H2O anticancer agent and in situ reactive oxygen species (ROS) upon 
red-light irradiation. The robust ROS burst triggers severe ER stress via 
activation of the PERK/eIF2α pathway, leading to the release of 
damage-associated molecular patterns and the type II ICD induction. Notably, 
this cascade-targeted ICD activation strategy enhances not only tumor 
specificity but also the immunogenicity of dying tumor cells, achieving 
effective primary tumor ablation in the 4T1 models and simultaneously 
suppressing distant tumors through dendritic cell maturation, cytotoxic T-cell 
infiltration, and memory T-cell generation. This study offers a paradigm for 
photoactivatable, self-delivery ICD inducers with cascade targeting, holding 
substantial promise for clinical translation in precision cancer immunotherapy.

The aryloxyalkylamine motif is a privileged pharmacophore found in bioactive 
molecules. However, achieving its direct and chemoselective construction via 
O-arylation of amino alcohols remains a significant challenge in synthetic 
chemistry. Herein, we report a mild and efficient nickel-catalyzed C-O

highlighting its potential for practical applications.

Sandwich SERS Chip with Raman‑Silent Reporters for Ultrasensitive Serum Cortisol 
Detection and Depression Differentiation.

Tong K(1)(2)(3), Liang H(3), Yu L(3), Song L(3), Gong E(3), Liu X(3), Lou 
Z(1)(2), Mi Y(1)(2), Ruan L(1)(2), Huang Y(3).

Author information:
(1)Health Science Center, Ningbo University, Ningbo, Zhejiang315211, China.
(2)Department of Psychosomatic Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital of Ningbo 
University, Ningbo, Zhejiang315010, China.
(3)Key Laboratory of Organosilicon Chemistry and Material Technology, Ministry 
of Education, Zhejiang Key Laboratory of Organosilicon Material Technology, 
College of Material, Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Department of 
Orthopedics, Hangzhou Normal University affiliated Hospital, Hangzhou Normal 
University, Hangzhou, Zhejiang311121, P. R. China.

Cortisol is a critical stress hormone, and its abnormal levels are closely 
linked to diseases such as depression and Cushing's syndrome. Cortisol has only 
a single binding site, which precludes conventional sandwich immunoassays, and 
the large antibody size often masks its SERS signal. Existing silent-region SERS 
strategies are limited by low signal intensity and poor reproducibility, arising 
from small-molecule reporters with low scattering cross-sections and randomly 
distributed hot spots. To address these challenges, we develop a silent-region 
SERS platform based on plasmonic superlattice enhancement combined with a 
top-bottom nanogap cavity. The bottom layer is a superlattice film of gold 
octahedral nanoparticles that generate uniform hot spots and is functionalized 
with anticortisol antibodies. The top layer uses Prussian blue@Ag core-shell 
nanoparticles as integrated reporters that exhibit characteristic Raman signals 
in the 1800-2400 cm-1 silent region and are functionalized with 
anticortisol-binding globulin antibodies. Because serum cortisol predominantly 
exists as a complex with cortisol-binding globulin, we designed a SERS chip with 
a dual-antibody sandwich configuration. This configuration enables efficient 
target capture and signal transduction within the three-dimensional nanogap hot 
spots. This sensing chip achieves a detection limit of 17.43 pM in serum samples 
from 93 patients with depression, with a linear range of 10 pM-10 μM and high 
reproducibility. It also exhibits excellent selectivity toward common serum 
interferents and distinguishes depressed patients from healthy controls. This 
work provides a robust approach for highly sensitive and specific SERS detection 
of single-binding-site small-molecule hormones and holds promise for objective 
molecular assessment of depression.

Current State of Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation for Still's 
Disease: A Collaborative Perspective from Attendees of the Systemic Juvenile 
Idiopathic Arthritis Foundation NextGen Conference.

Chandra S(1), Marsh RA(1), Silva JMF(2), Wobma H(3), Prockop S(4), Slatter M(5), 
Henderson LA(3), Schulert GS(6), Grom A(6), Sinha R(7), Connelly JA(8).

Author information:
(1)Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center, University of Cincinnati 
College of Medicine, Cincinnati, Ohio, USA.
(2)Department of BMT, Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children, London, UK.
(3)Boston Children's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA.
(4)Dana Farber Cancer Institute/Boston Children's Hospital Center for Cancer and 
Blood Disorders, Boston, MA, USA.
(5)Department of Paediatric Immunology and Haematopoietic Stem Cell 
Transplantation, Great North Children's Hospital, Newcastle Upon Tyne, UK.
(6)Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center, University of Cincinnati 
College of Medicine, Cincinnati, OH, USA.
(7)Systemic JIA Foundation, Cincinnati, OH, USA.
(8)Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, Tenn., USA.

OBJECTIVE: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) and adult-onset Still's 
disease (AOSD) represent a spectrum of Still's disease (SD) characterized by 
dysregulated innate immunity, severe systemic inflammation, and risk of 
life-threatening complications including macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) 
and associated lung disease (LD). Although IL-1 and IL-6 pathway inhibitors have 
improved outcomes, a subset of patients develop severe, refractory disease. This 
article summarizes the current evidence and multidisciplinary expert 
perspectives on the role of allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) 
in refractory Still's disease.
METHODS: This Special Article is a conference summary based on presentations and 
multidisciplinary discussion at the 2024 Systemic JIA Foundation NextGen 
Conference, which convened an international, multidisciplinary group of 
rheumatologists, transplant physicians, immunologists, pulmonologists, and 
patient advocates.
RESULTS: Recurrent MAS, progressive LD, persistent systemic inflammation despite 
IL-1/IL-6/JAK inhibition, and glucocorticoid dependence were identified as 
clinical features that may warrant consideration of allogeneic HCT in SD. 
Available data, mainly from small pediatric cohorts, suggest that allogeneic HCT 
can achieve clinical remission and improve pulmonary outcomes in select 
patients. However, transplant-related mortality remains substantial, 
particularly in patients with LD, and inflammatory disease may recur after HCT. 
HCT data in adults remain limited.
CONCLUSION: Allogeneic HCT may be considered for select patients with severe, 
refractory SD, particularly those with recurrent MAS and/or progressive LD. 
Early multidisciplinary evaluation, shared decision-making, and careful patient 
selection are essential. Prospective multicenter studies and closer 
collaboration between pediatric and adult providers are needed to refine patient 
selection and improve outcomes.

468. Vox Sang. 2026 Oct 20. doi: 10.1111/vox.70400. Online ahead of print.

Maternal immunoglobulin G anti-A and anti-B antibody titres for predicting 
neonatal immune sensitisation in ABO-incompatible pregnancies: The Maternal 
Anti-A and Anti-B Antibody Titres in ABO-Incompatible Pregnancies study.

Bansal R(1), Saini N(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Transfusion Medicine, FMHS, SGT University, Gurugram, Haryana, 
India.
(2)Department of Pathology, FMHS, SGT University, Gurugram, Haryana, India.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Maternal immunoglobulin G (IgG) anti-A and anti-B 
antibodies can cross the placenta and cause ABO haemolytic disease of the foetus 
and newborn (ABO-HDFN). We aimed to evaluate whether maternal IgG anti-A and 
anti-B titres predict neonatal direct antiglobulin test (DAT) positivity in 
ABO-incompatible pregnancies.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this prospective observational cohort study, 889 
consecutive ABO-incompatible mother-newborn pairs were enrolled between November 
2025 and June 2026. Maternal IgG anti-A and anti-B titres were measured after 
0.01 M dithiothreitol treatment using the conventional tube antiglobulin 
titration method. Neonatal ABO grouping and DAT were performed by column 
agglutination technology. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis 
and multivariable logistic regression assessed the predictive performance of 
maternal antibody titres.
RESULTS: Overall, 112/889 (12.6%) neonates were DAT positive. Maternal IgG 
anti-A and anti-B titres were significantly higher in mothers of DAT-positive 
neonates (both p < 0.001). Maternal IgG anti-A (area under the curve [AUC] 
0.778) and anti-B (AUC 0.803) showed acceptable diagnostic performance. Higher 
thresholds (anti-A ≥32; anti-B ≥16) achieved 100% specificity, whereas lower 
thresholds (anti-A ≥8; anti-B ≥4) provided high sensitivity for excluding 
neonatal DAT positivity. Increasing maternal IgG anti-A (adjusted odds ratio 
[aOR] 1.12, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.06-1.18) and anti-B titres (aOR 
1.18, 95% CI: 1.09-1.28) independently predicted DAT positivity (both 
p < 0.001). Most DAT-positive neonates required phototherapy (94.6%) but none 
required exchange transfusion.
CONCLUSION: Standardised maternal IgG anti-A and anti-B titres independently 
could predict neonatal DAT positivity. A dual-threshold approach may complement 
existing antenatal assessment by identifying high-risk pregnancies and guiding 
individualised postnatal surveillance.

Red cells stored in non-DEHP containers: The effect of washing, irradiation or 
storage as paediatric units on in vitro quality parameters.

Lagerberg JW(1), Vlaar R(1), Klei TRL(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Product and Process Development, Sanquin Blood Supply, 
Amsterdam, the Netherlands.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: In accordance with European Union (EU) regulations, 
the use of the polyvinyl chloride (PVC) plasticiser diethylhexyl phthalate 
(DEHP) in medical devices must be phased out by 2030 in the EU. We recently 
evaluated the in vitro quality of red cell concentrates (RCCs) in 
phosphate-adenine-glucose-guanosine-saline-mannitol (PAGGSM) drawn in 
di(isononyl) cyclohexane-1,2-dicarboxylate (DINCH) and stored in 
BTHC-plasticised PVC. Here we aimed to evaluate the effects of washing, gamma 
irradiation, X-ray irradiation and aliquoting into paediatric RCC units in the 
DINCH/BTHC hybrid system on in vitro quality during storage.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: RCCs in PAGGSM were made from whole blood collected in 
DINCH/BTHC hybrid systems. The study consisted of three independent and separate 
parts investigating (i) washing, (ii) irradiation of full units and (iii) 
irradiation of paediatric units. (i) On Day 30, RCCs (n = 12) were washed with 
PAGGSM and stored in BTHC-PVC containers until outdating. (ii) RCCs (n = 24) 
were pooled and split (Day 14), and were left untreated, gamma irradiated or 
X-ray irradiated and stored until outdating (n = 8). (iii) Eight RCCs were 
aliquoted into paediatric units, irradiated on Day 14 and stored until 
outdating.
RESULTS: Washing efficiently decreased potassium, lactate and protein 
concentrations in the supernatant. Irradiation led to increased haemolysis on 
Day 28 (0.18% ± 0.03% for controls vs. 0.35% ± 0.07% for gamma irradiation and 
0.39% ± 0.09% for X-ray irradiation). Splitting into paediatric units mostly 
resulted in comparable in vitro quality as obtained for adult-size RCCs.
CONCLUSION: Secondary processing of RCCs in DINCH/BTHC-PVC containers results in 
products that conform to requirements. Gamma or X-ray irradiation results in 
comparable in vitro quality.

Optical Fiber Needle Probes for In Situ-Distributed Biosensing Based on Optical 
Frequency Domain Reflectometry.

Guo H(1)(2)(3)(4), Zhu R(1)(2)(3)(4), Liu J(1)(2)(3)(4), Xu Q(5), Deng 
J(1)(2)(3)(4), Liu K(1)(2)(3)(4), Jiang J(1)(2)(3)(4), Liu T(1)(2)(3)(4), Ding 
Z(1)(2)(3)(4).

Author information:
(1)School of Precision Instruments and Opto-Electronics Engineering, Tianjin 
University, Tianjin300072, China.
(2)Tianjin Optical Fiber Sensing Engineering Center, Institute of Optical Fiber 
Sensing of Tianjin University, Tianjin300072, China.
(3)Key Laboratory of Opto-electronics Information Technology, Ministry of 
Education, Tianjin University, Tianjin300072, China.
(4)Key Laboratory of Optical Fiber Sensing Metrology and Measurement, State 
Administration for Market Regulation, Tianjin300072, China.

In situ detection is crucial for diagnosing lesions during surgery, endoscopy, 
or biopsy but has always been a challenge in medical diagnostics. Optical fiber 
biosensing needle probes, with their small size, can be nearly noninvasively 
guided to the lesion site for in situ detection. However, existing optical fiber 
biosensing probes are single-point sensors, unable to precisely locate lesions. 
We propose an optical fiber needle probe for in situ distributed sensing of 
hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) biomarker GPC3 in soft matter based on optical 
frequency domain reflectometry (OFDR). The needle type probe is fabricated by 
integrating a polydopamine (PDA)-assisted anti-GPC3 antibody-functionalized 
micro/nano fiber into a metal needle with a lateral opening near the distal tip. 
Through differential-phase demodulation, calibration experiments with varying 
GPC3 concentrations reveal that the needle probe exhibits an 8 mm sensing length 
with a sensitivity of 0.0031 rad/(ng/mL). More importantly, the proposed needle 
probe achieves the precise spatial localization of both independent and 
simultaneous multiple 250-μm mimic lesions loaded by GPC3 in an agarose-glycerol 
hydrogel soft matter phantom with a spatial resolution of 25 μm and a limit of 
detection (LOD) of 3.23 ng/mL, which offers unparalleled advantages compared 
with existing biosensors. The proposed method provides a potential for in situ 
detection and localization of HCC or other lesions.

Enhancing Proton Conductivity in the Ce0.9Gd0.1O2-δ Electrolyte for 
Low-Temperature SOFCs via Surface Doping with a Cobalt Oxide Redox Mediator.

Yu Y(1), Cheng X(1), Khalid MA(1), Shi R(1), Ji F(1), Chen H(1), Chen L(1), Zhao 
Y(1), Zhao Y(1), Huang J(1), Chen Y(1), Lu Y(1), Guo L(1).

Author information:
(1)State Key Laboratory of Multiphase Flow in Power Engineering, Xi'an Jiaotong 
University, Xi'an710049, P.R. China.

Developing oxide electrolytes with high ionic conductivity (∼0.1 S cm-1) at 
temperatures below 600 °C is essential for next-generation solid oxide fuel 
cells. However, current electrolyte materials rarely meet this benchmark, 
primarily because of limitations inherent in bulk doping and high-temperature 
sintering. To overcome this challenge, we demonstrate a surface engineering 
strategy that involves controlled cobalt doping onto the acid-etched surface of 
gadolinium-doped ceria (Ce0.9Gd0.1O2-δ, GDC), thereby constructing a Co3+/Co2+ 
redox mediator. The 3 mol% cobalt-surface-doped GDC (GDC-Co3) electrolyte 
exhibits optimal ionic transport behavior, achieving an ionic conductivity of 
0.153 S cm-1 at 500 °C and a 30% improvement over pristine GDC (0.118 S cm-1), 
while simultaneously reducing the activation energy from 0.64 eV to 0.36 eV. 
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and multi-wavelength Raman spectroscopy 
reveal that Co2+/Co3+ redox pairs are introduced onto the surfaces of GDC 
particles through doping with different Co(II)/GDC molar ratios. The formation 
of a Schottky junction, as evidenced by a rectifying effect, effectively 
prevents electron leakage across the electrolyte. Electrochemical impedance 
spectroscopy (EIS), combined with distribution of relaxation times (DRT) 
analysis, indicates that ionic conductivity is strongly correlated with 
electronic conductivity. These results collectively support a mechanism where 
surface-localized Co2+/Co3+ redox pairs act as mediators for the Ce4+/Ce3+ 
couples in GDC, establishing favorable surface pathways for proton transport via 
an alternating interstitial proton-hydrogen hopping process. The accompanying 
reduction in electrode polarization resistance suggests that accelerated 
interfacial reaction kinetics may also contribute to the improved cell 
performance, alongside enhanced proton transport. This work presents an 
innovative surface engineering approach that significantly enhances proton 
transport in fluorite oxide materials, with important implications for 
low-temperature solid oxide electrochemical devices.

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether providing authors with a manuscript template 
structured according to the Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for 
Interventional Trials (SPIRIT) 2025 reporting guideline for use during revision 
improves the completeness of reporting in randomised trial protocols.
DESIGN: Randomised controlled trial.
SETTING: BMJ Open.
POPULATION: 70 of 74 manuscripts screened between 29 April and 27 May 2025 that 
reported randomised controlled trial protocols with a decision of minor or major 
revision after the first round of peer review were randomly allocated (1:1) 
using an R generated sequence. Authors were not informed of the study.
INTERVENTIONS: Handling editors asked the intervention group authors to use a 
SPIRIT based manuscript template when preparing their first revision. The 
template included structured subheadings corresponding to SPIRIT 2025 items, 
along with guidance on reporting. Editorial decisions were not conditional on 
use of the template. Control group manuscripts underwent standard peer review.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome was completeness of reporting score 
in the revised manuscript (adjusted for baseline), calculated as the mean of 11 
SPIRIT items that are frequently inadequately reported (each scored 0, 0.5, or 
1) and linearly rescaled to a 0-10 score. After submission of their first 
revision, authors in the intervention group completed an online survey. The 
survey included both fixed response and open ended questions designed to capture 
the authors' perceptions of ease of use, helpfulness, and any challenges 
encountered when using the template. Secondary outcomes included mean 
completeness of reporting scores for each item, median time to submission of the 
revised manuscript, and authors' experiences of using the template. Outcome 
assessors, but not editors or investigators, were masked.
RESULTS: Of the 70 manuscripts randomised (35 in each group), all were analysed, 
with no loss to follow-up. In the intervention group, completeness of reporting 
in randomised trial protocols improved by 0.61 points (95% confidence interval 
0.20 to 1.01) compared with the control group, with mean (standard deviation) 
scores increasing from 5.42 (1.07) to 6.70 (1.23) and 5.77 (1.19) to 6.32 
(0.94), respectively. The largest improvements were observed for recruitment, 
data collection methods, and access to data. Median time to submission of the 
first revision was similar between the intervention and control groups (27.10 v 
29.86 days, respectively). Data on harms were not systematically collected. 
Among 14 of 35 survey respondents (40%), many (8/13, 62%) reported the template 
as time consuming and some (5/13, 39%) as burdensome. Most respondents, however, 
found it easy to use (10/13, 77%), helpful for improving the manuscript (9/13, 
69%), and reassuring for adherence to SPIRIT (13/13, 100%).
CONCLUSIONS: Providing authors of randomised controlled trials with a SPIRIT 
based template during manuscript revision modestly improved the completeness of 
reporting in the trial protocols without extending revision times.

Barriers and enablers to engagement with green social prescribing in primary 
care: a scoping review using the socio-ecological model.

Frost H(1), Mason B(2), Tooman TR(3), Bareham BR(4), Ng L(5), Haines H(6), 
Arakelyan S(3), Lewis S(3), Wolters MK(7)(8), Hawkins K(9), Ogden ME(10), Pain 
HG(10), Mercer SW(3).

Author information:
(1)Advanced Care Research Centre, Usher Institute, College of Medicine and 
Veterinary Medicine, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK h.frost@ed.ac.uk.
(2)Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, UK.
(3)Advanced Care Research Centre, Usher Institute, College of Medicine and 
Veterinary Medicine, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK.
(4)Advanced Care Research Centre, Newcastle University, Newcastle upon Tyne, UK.
(5)Usher Institute, College of Medicine and Veterinary Medicine, University of 
Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK.
(6)College of Medicine and Veterinary Medicine, University of Edinburgh, 
Edinburgh, UK.
(7)School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK.
(8)Department of Computer Science, Dortmund University of Applied Sciences and 
Arts, Dortmund, Germany.
(9)NHS Lothian, Scotland, UK.
(10)PPIE members of Advanced Care Research Centre, Usher Institute, University 
of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK.

BACKGROUND: Green social prescribing (GSP) connects individuals with 
nature-based interventions (NBIs) through healthcare providers, link workers, 
and social and community networks. While evidence supports the health benefits 
of NBIs, further research is needed to understand the factors that influence 
engagement.
AIM: To explore barriers and enablers to GSP and NBIs for prescribers, service 
users and community providers.
DESIGN & SETTING: A scoping review in primary care and community settings.
METHOD: We systematically searched Medline, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and 
SCOPUS from 2019. We assessed quality using the Critical Appraisal Skills 
Programme and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. We mapped data to the 
socioecological framework during synthesis.
RESULTS: Out of 4864 screened records, 45 studies from 11 countries were 
included. GSP and NBIs face micro-level barriers such as knowledge gaps, 
cultural and social issues, time and cost constraints and perceptions of adverse 
weather; meso-level and macro-level challenges include unequal access, 
underfunded NBIs, an emphasis on biomedical models, safety concerns, limited 
training, and insufficient policy support and leadership. Engagement was enabled 
by flexible, person-centred approaches, tailored NBIs with clear pathways, 
including link workers, strong cross-sector partnerships, community co-design, 
and public health campaigns.
CONCLUSION: Promoting engagement with GSP and NBIs requires a multi-level 
approach that addresses systemic barriers through collaboration between 
prescribers, third-sector organisations and policymakers. Investment in 
workforce training and sustainable funding models is critical to support 
long-term success in primary care and community settings. Addressing health 
inequalities by improving access for people in areas of high socioeconomic 
deprivation remains a priority.

Efficacy and Feasibility of Just-in-Time Nudging in Reducing Evening Snacking 
Measured by Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A 
Micro-Randomized Study.

Zhao L(1), Bidargaddi N(1), Vakulin A(2), Li W(1), Luscombe-Marsh N(3), Benton 
F(3), Adams R(2), Kemps E(4), Vincent AD(5)(6), Heilbronn LK(5)(6), Wittert 
GA(5)(6).

Author information:
(1)Flinders Health and Medical Research Institute, College of Medicine and 
Public Health, Flinders University, Adelaide, Australia.
(2)Flinders Health and Medical Research Institute-Sleep Health, College of 
Medicine and Public Health, Flinders University, Adelaide, Australia.
(3)Diabetes SA, Adelaide, Australia.
(4)Institute of Mental Health and Wellbeing, College of Human Sciences and 
Culture, Flinders University, Adelaide, Australia.
(5)School of Medicine, College of Health, Adelaide University, Adelaide, 
Australia.
(6)Lifelong Health Theme, South Australian Health and Medical Research 
Institute, Adelaide, Australia.

AIMS: This study aimed to determine whether in people with Type 2 diabetes 
mellitus (T2DM), a digital nudge delivered by a smartphone app soon after dinner 
reduces subsequent snacking events as measured by continuous glucose monitoring 
(CGM).
METHODS: Participants: Adults with T2DM, managed with diet or stable oral 
antidiabetic medication for at least 3 months, and who habitually snacked after 
dinner on ≥ 3 nights/week.
DESIGN: Pictographic nudges were co-designed with consumers. After-dinner 
snacking behaviours were confirmed during a 2-week Lead-In phase by CGM. 
Thereafter, eligible participants were micro-randomized daily (1:1, MRT phase) 
to either a pictographic nudge delivered-in-time (Intui Research) or no nudge 
for a second 2-week period. The primary outcome was the difference in 
incremental area under the CGM curve (net-iAUC) between nudging days and 
non-nudging days during the period 90-min post-dinner until 4 AM.
RESULTS: Sixty-six participants completed the Lead-In phase and 56 completed the 
MRT phase with available CGM data. CGM data were collected over 911 nights 
during the Lead-In phase and 780 nights during the MRT phase, with a total of 
410 digital nudges sent. Over the entire 2-week period there was no effect of 
nudging on the primary outcome (net-iAUC). However, secondary analyses showed 
that there was an initial nudge effect that faded over time. Similar results 
were observed for snacking behaviour and CGM time-in-range.
CONCLUSION: This study provides preliminary feasibility of delivering 
just-in-time nudges in adults with T2DM, with no overall glycaemic benefit. 
Exploratory early effects warrant confirmation and investigation of strategies 
to sustain efficacy.

Calcification patterns of a foundation species reveal resilience to 
environmental change in southern California over the twentieth century.

Vriesman VP(1)(2), Kennedy E(3)(4)(5), Van Ausdale G(2), Carlson S(4), Hill 
TM(4)(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Natural Sciences, Scripps College , Claremont, CA, USA.
(2)Department of Natural Sciences, Pitzer College , Claremont, CA, USA.
(3)Alaska Coastal Rainforest Center, University of Alaska Southeast , Juneau,

(4)Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California Davis , Davis, CA,

(5)Bodega Marine Laboratory, University of California , Davis, Bodega Bay, CA,

Oceanographic changes due to carbon dioxide emissions have complex and varied 
impacts on marine calcifying taxa. Changes in calcification can unfold over 
decades or longer, requiring a longer-term understanding of biomineralization 
patterns than laboratory-based studies can provide. Here, we investigate the 
calcification history of the marine mussel Mytilus californianus to determine 
how this ecologically critical foundation species has responded to past and 
ongoing environmental changes in the southern end of its range within the 
California Current System (CCS) between 27.72° N and 34.47° N. Calcification 
metrics based on shell morphology, growth banding, and mineralogical structure 
in 130 museum-archived M. californianus specimens collected decadally from 1913 
to 2010 revealed unexpected resilience in southern M. californianus shells after 
previous studies found calcification vulnerability in this species farther 
north. Shell growth data were paired with temperature datasets and regional pH 
records. Despite increasingly warmer and more variable conditions in the 
southern CCS, M. californianus shell features remained quantitatively unchanged 
in this region since 1913, although we present preliminary microstructural data 
that align with previous evidence of increased crystallographic disorder in this 
species. Based on overall consistencies in calcification metrics, M. 
californianus appears more resistant to environmental changes at the southern 
end of its range.

Consistent diversity loss but divergent functional responses of freshwater 
biofilms to salinity and nutrient enrichment across climatic regions.

Fuggle R(1), Mayer-Pinto M(2)(3), Matias MG(4), Marzinelli EM(1).

Author information:
(1)The University of Sydney , New South Wales, Australia.
(2)University of New South Wales , Sydney, New South Wales, Australia.
(3)Sydney Institute of Marine Science , Mosman, New South Wales, Australia.
(4)Museo Nacional de Ciencias Naturales Madrid, Community of Madrid, Spain.

Freshwater salinization and nutrient enrichment are intensifying globally. 
Despite their widespread co-occurrence, the generality of their combined effects 
across regions remains unclear, limiting identification of appropriate policy 
scales. Using outdoor freshwater ponds established >10 years ago, replicated 
across inland, coastal and mountain regions, we examined independent and 
interactive effects of elevated salinity (0, +5 and +15 g NaCl l⁻¹) and nutrient 
enrichment (10 : 1 N : P additions) on benthic biofilms. Salinity was the 
dominant driver of community structure and function. Nutrient enrichment 
increased green algae abundances after 30 days but did not affect biofilm 
function or bacterial structure. Across all regions, bacterial richness and 
Shannon's diversity index declined consistently with increasing salinity after 
30 days and bacterial community structures differed among all salinity levels by 
60 days. Responses of phototrophic groups and biofilm functions, however, were 
region-specific. In the inland region, high salinity increased biofilm biomass, 
gross primary productivity (GPP), net primary productivity (NPP) and abundances 
of diatoms and cyanobacteria; in the coastal region, GPP and NPP declined under 
high salinity with no change to phototroph abundances; while neither was 
affected in the mountain region. In sum, taxonomic changes in biofilm bacterial 
communities under salinization were consistent across regions, while functional 
changes varied.

Resource availability and predator cues shape within- and transgenerational 
reaction norms.

Dejeux L(1), Tariel-Adam J(2), Plénet S(1), Luquet E(1)(3).

Author information:
(1)Université Lyon 1, ENTPE, CNRS, LEHNA, UMR 5023 , Villeurbanne, France.
(2)School of Natural Sciences, Macquarie University , Sydney, New South Wales, 
Australia.
(3)Institut Universitaire de France (IUF) , Paris, France.

The main dilemma facing prey is how to reduce predation risk while acquiring 
resources. Phenotypic plasticity, by modulating traits for acquiring resources 
and for defences, is a key process driving this trade-off. While there is ample 
evidence that predator-induced within-generational plasticity depends on 
resources, the relationship between resources and predator-induced 
transgenerational plasticity (TGP) remains understudied. This study investigated 
how predator exposure and resource availability influence within-generational 
plasticity and TGP. We based our predictions on theories related to information- 
and state-based plasticity, two kinds of plasticity occurring in response to 
environmental information or alteration affecting somatic state, respectively. 
We conducted a two-generation laboratory experiment in the freshwater snail 
Physa acuta, manipulating predator cues and resource availability. Our results 
revealed that both types of plasticity participate in shaping the within- and 
transgenerational responses. Within a generation, the limited resource decreased 
the somatic state but did not constrain the defences. Across generations, the 
poor parental state decreased the offspring state even in high-resource 
conditions, which in turn decreased the absolute levels of their defences but 
increased their investment in reproduction. These results highlight the 
importance of integrating informational and state-based effects across 
generations to provide a more complete understanding of prey responses to 
predators.

The African Middle Stone Age (MSA) represents the cultural and technological 
context associated with the emergence of Homo sapiens and the development of 
complex cognition. In this setting, ochre use is considered a multifaceted proxy 
for modern behaviour, allowing inferences about technical and symbolic aspects 
of Homo sapiens. Powdered ochre is reported in multiple southern African 
ethnographic and archaeological contexts alongside various organic materials, 
some of which are protein-based. Yet, the recovery of proteinaceous residues is 
rare in the MSA. Since proteins can offer insights into their tissue and species 
of origin, identifying proteins in association with ochre may help to infer its 
function. At Klipdrift Shelter (South Africa), the 60 000-year-old Howiesons 
Poort layers contain a laterally continuous, ochre-rich sediment surface, 
possibly over 1 m long, 40 cm wide, and up to 1 cm thick. We used 
palaeoproteomics to identify proteinaceous traces from this feature. Our 
analysis identified type I collagen confidently matching common eland 
(Taurotragus oryx) in two samples. Together with the feature's highly complex 
nature, these findings suggest the deliberate mixing of eland-derived proteins 
with ochre powder. Our results confirm that palaeoproteomics can be a reliable 
tool for reconstructing the protein component of the early human material 
culture.

Caribbean Islands facilitated the colonization of Western Hemisphere barn owls, 
yet experienced rampant extinction.

Zhao M(1)(2), Steadman DW(1), LeFebvre MJ(1), Guralnick RP(1), Doby JR(1), Allen 
JM(2), Oswald JA(1)(3).

Author information:
(1)Florida Museum of Natural History, University of Florida , Gainesville, FL

(2)Department of Biological Sciences, Virginia Tech , Blacksburg, VA 24061, USA.

Island biodiversity reflects multiple evolutionary roles, encompassing lineages 
derived from nearby continents, relict taxa and, in limited cases, sources of 
continental diversity. Reconstructing the biogeographic history and 
island-mainland diversification dynamics requires an integrated understanding of 
speciation, extinction and dispersal processes to and from islands. Extensive 
Holocene extinctions may obscure patterns of diversity and connectivity. 
Tytonidae (barn and bay owls) is a bird group with a worldwide distribution and 
numerous Quaternary extinctions. Here, we use ultraconserved elements and 
mitogenomes extracted from tissues, historical museum specimens and fossils to 
reconstruct phylogenetic relationships and colonization pathways, with a focus 
on Western Hemisphere taxa. We also summarize extinct Tyto diversity to evaluate 
Quaternary diversity trends. Our results align with previous studies in 
supporting an Eastern origin for Western Hemisphere Tyto. We found that the 
Caribbean was, and still is, the centre of Tyto diversity in the Western 
Hemisphere, although nearly all Caribbean Tyto (and their mammalian prey) are 
now extinct. Unexpectedly, we identified two independent Tyto colonization 
events of the Galápagos. Our study provides strong evidence that islands can 
serve as sources of diversity for some continental lineages, as well as museums 
of diversity that harbour unique lineages prone to disturbance-driven 
extinction.

The role of genetic distance in modulating intraspecific plant-soil interactions 
among a diverse assemblage of tropical tree species seedlings.

Soria Penafiel RI(1)(2), Zambrano K(3), Aulestia C(3), Rivas-Torres G(4), 
Karubian J(1)(3)(4), Van Bael SA(1).

Author information:
(1)Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, Tulane University , New Orleans, LA, USA.
(2)Facultad de Ciencias Exactas, Naturales y Ambientales, Pontificia Universidad 
Católica del Ecuador , Quito, Pichincha, Ecuador.
(3)Fundación para la Conservación de los Andes Tropicales (FCAT) , Quinindé, 
Esmeraldas, Ecuador.
(4)Estación de Biodiversidad Tiputini, Colegio de Ciencias Biológicas y 
Ambientales, Universidad San Francisco de Quito , Quito, Pichincha, Ecuador.

Microbial specialization on host species can promote plant diversity through 
plant-soil interactions that affect seedling survival and performance. While 
these processes are typically studied at the interspecific level, emerging 
evidence suggests that plant-soil interactions can be genotype-specific, 
contributing to intraspecific density dependence (iDD). However, iDD remains 
poorly understood in tropical tree species, particularly with respect to its 
strength and frequency. We hypothesized that genetic distance among conspecific 
trees should modulate the strength of iDD, and the direction of the 
effect-positive or negative seedling response-should reflect the net balance of 
plant-microbe antagonistic and mutualistic interactions. Using a reciprocal 
planting experiment across eight tropical tree species, we show that genetic 
distance between conspecific individuals significantly influences seedling 
responses, consistent with iDD. Yet, the direction of this effect was variable: 
Castilla tunu showed higher survival and Wettinia aequalis greater biomass in 
soils from more genetically distant conspecifics, consistent with negative iDD; 
Inga marginata exhibited positive iDD; five species exhibited no pattern. These 
findings demonstrate that genotype-specific plant-soil interactions can generate 
biologically relevant but variable impacts on seedling responses. This 
highlights the need to further investigate the drivers and ecological 
consequences of intraspecific genetic variation in plant-soil interactions and 
iDD in tropical forests.

Tobler M(1)(2), Greenway R(3), Kelley JL(4).

Convergent evolution is common and a testament to the repeatability of 
evolution. Still, non-convergence is also widespread, and a major question is 
whether idiosyncratic, lineage-specific changes are reflective of chance events 
inherent to evolutionary processes, or whether they are influenced by 
deterministic genetic or ecological factors. To address this question, we 
quantified the degree of convergence in gene expression across lineages of 
livebearing fishes (Poeciliidae) that span 40 million years of divergence and 
have colonized toxic, hydrogen-sulfide-rich springs. We asked whether the degree 
of convergence across lineage pairs was related to their phylogenetic 
relatedness and the ecological similarity of their habitats. Using phylogenetic 
comparative analyses, we showed that the degree of convergence in gene 
expression was variable across lineage pairs. While closely related lineages did 
not exhibit higher degrees of convergence than distantly related ones, we 
uncovered a strong relationship between degree of convergence and the ecological 
similarity among lineages. These results suggest that variation in environmental 
conditions that is often overlooked in simplified descriptions of habitat 
differences can play an important role in shaping adaptive evolution. Our study 
highlights the importance of multivariate approaches that capture the 
complexities of selective regimes and organismal responses when assessing the 
repeatability of evolution.

The present does not reflect the past: geographic mismatches between fossil and 
modern records are widespread across the tree of life.

Shipley BR(1), Saupe EE(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Earth Sciences, University of Oxford , Oxford, UK.

The distribution of organisms across Earth provides insight into the origin and 
maintenance of biodiversity. Abundant fossil evidence suggests taxa have 
undergone substantial range changes over time. However, biogeographic theory and 
models often tend to assume that clades originated in the regions where we 
observe them today. Understanding the prevalence of geographically dynamic 
clades across the tree of life provides a way to evaluate these assumptions, 
thereby refining key evolutionary hypotheses. We provide a review of such 
range-shifting clades using a two-pronged approach. First, literature searches 
uncovered examples across most major multicellular groups (comprising 129 clades 
with mismatches between fossil and modern ranges). Concurrently, we used the 
well-sampled mammalian fossil record as a case study, finding that more than 
half of its terrestrial families (51%) had substantial (>1000 km) geographic 
mismatches. Geographically dynamic lineages are both common and widespread, but 
despite their ubiquity, fossil-modern mismatches have only recently been 
integrated into phylogenetic and biogeographic methods and no comprehensive 
overview of their advantages and challenges exists. We therefore review the 
current state of the field and discuss case studies where fossil evidence 
reshaped prevailing biogeographic theory. Biogeographers must take advantage of 
these rich fossil histories to better elucidate evolutionary theory across space 
and time.

Evolution of neurometabolic frugality in harvester ants.

Perl CD(1), Coto ZN(2), Johnson R(1), Johnson M(3), Graber L(4), Haas J(1), 
Waters JS(5), Traniello J(2), Harrison JF(1).

Author information:
(1)School of Life Sciences, Arizona State University , Tempe, AZ, USA.
(2)Biology, Boston University , Boston, MA, USA.
(3)Arizona State University , Tempe, AZ, USA.
(4)Cornell University , Ithaca, NY, USA.

Despite the importance of neurometabolic cost in brain size evolution, 
quantitative data on brain metabolic rates (MRs) are lacking. We measured ex 
vivo brain MRs among species of the ant genus Pogonomyrmex to test three 
hypotheses: (i) more socially complex species have higher brain MRs; (ii) 
smaller-bodied species have higher brain mass-specific metabolic rates (MSMRs); 
and (iii) more recently derived species have evolved more metabolically 'frugal' 
brains. Worker body size and colony size, a proxy for social complexity vary 
significantly among Pogonomyrmex species and were positively correlated. Species 
with larger colonies did not have larger brains or higher brain MRs. Species 
with smaller workers had relatively larger brains and higher brain MSMR: 38% of 
resting MR was attributable to brain metabolism in species with the smallest 
workers, compared to 6% in species with the largest workers. We suggest that 
smaller worker body sizes may require higher brain mass-specific energetic costs 
to achieve comparable performance by absolutely smaller brains. More derived 
species had strikingly lower mass-specific brain metabolic costs, suggesting 
that increases in worker body size have selected for neurometabolic frugality 
through reductions in brain MSMR.

Dynamic facial movements shape how confident speakers appear.

Nölle J(1)(2), Wu Y(1), Arias-Sarah P(1)(3)(4), Garrod OGB(1), Schyns PG(1)(5), 
Jack RE(1)(5).

Author information:
(1)School of Psychology & Neuroscience, University of Glasgow , Glasgow, UK.
(2)Centre for Language Evolution Studies, Nicolaus Copernicus University in

(3)Department of Cognitive Science, Lund University , Lund, Skåne County,

(4)Psychology and Neurocognition Lab, CNRS Université Grenoble Alpes ,

Human communication is inherently multimodal, relying on signals conveyed 
through speech, vocal tone and facial movements. While gestures and vocal cues 
are known to influence how speech is understood, the role of facial movements 
remains poorly specified. Here, we test whether dynamic facial movements shape 
how spoken responses are interpreted by systematically modulating listener 
inferences of speaker confidence and doubt. Using a data-driven 
reverse-correlation approach and a generative model of facial behaviour, we 
manipulated speakers' upper-face movements while holding verbal content 
constant. On each trial, participants (n = 44; UK English and Mandarin Chinese 
speakers) rated the confidence of speakers responding to questions (e.g. 'Would 
they make a good leader?') on a five-point scale across 1800 trials. We find 
that opposing facial movements bias these inferences: eye closure and brow 
raising are associated with confidence, whereas brow lowering and eye tightening 
are associated with doubt. Signal amplitude further shapes these inferences, 
primarily by intensifying perceived doubt for doubt-associated movements. These 
mappings are largely shared between the two cultural groups, indicating common 
signal-inference relationships alongside differences in the weighting of 
specific cues. Together, these findings show that facial movements provide 
graded social signals that systematically shape how spoken responses are 
interpreted.

Contagion and escalation of rule violations.

Molleman L(1), Hoyer K(1), van Kleef GA(1), Scholz C(2), Hausfeld J(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Psychology, University of Amsterdam , Amsterdam, The 
Netherlands.
(2)Department of Communication Sciences, University of Amsterdam , Amsterdam, 
The Netherlands.
(3)Department of Microeconomics, University of Amsterdam , Amsterdam, The

Human societies rely on rules to coordinate behaviour, sustain cooperation and 
maintain social order. Yet compliance can be fragile when rules are weakly 
enforced and individuals observe others violating them. Prior research shows 
that rule violations and other antisocial behaviours can spread through social 
influence, but less is known about how the severity of violations shapes these 
dynamics. In many real-world settings, rule-breaking occurs in degrees, from 
minor infractions to major violations, and individuals may not only imitate 
others but sometimes exceed the violations they observe. Here, we combine 
simulations and a behavioural experiment (n = 750) to study how the magnitude of 
observed rule violations shapes subsequent violations, and how this can generate 
escalation dynamics. Our simulations show that when individuals occasionally 
escalate beyond observed violations, even rare escalation can trigger a rapid 
shift from widespread compliance to collective rule-breaking. In our 
pre-registered experiment, observing major violations strongly increased 
rule-breaking, especially when committed by socially close others. Observing 
minor violations prompted many participants to follow suit and a minority to 
escalate beyond the violations they observed. Parameterizing the simulations 
with these behavioural responses shows that such escalators can 
disproportionately undermine collective compliance. These results highlight how 
asymmetric responses to rule violations and rare escalatory behaviour can 
transform small deviations into large-scale breakdowns of rule compliance.

Mature sperm are widely considered as transcriptionally inactive cells owing to 
the tight compaction of their chromatin with protamine. However, sperm cells 
have been demonstrated to retain RNA polymerase subunits, chromatin remodellers, 
transcription factors, and parts of their chromatin remain in a less condensed, 
nucleosome-bound configuration. Consequently, some studies have suggested that

tested this possibility by exposing mature human sperm to follicular fluid (FF),

potentially preparing sperm for fertilization and early embryo development. 
Furthermore, we envisage that activated sperm genes can have novel implications 
for the deeper mechanistic understanding of sexual selection.

BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Occupational hand dermatitis (HD) comprises irritant and 
allergic contact dermatitis (ICD and ACD), which share clinical features, often 
overlap, and may coexist with atopic dermatitis (AD), complicating diagnosis. 
The objective of this study is to explore whether stratum corneum (SC) 
biomarkers discriminate ICD from ACD.
PATIENTS: We recruited 126 patients from the Occupational Dermato-allergology 
Clinics of the Amsterdam UMC.
METHODS: SC samples were collected from lesional HD skin and patch test 
reactions to nickel, chromium, methylisothiazolinone, sodium lauryl sulfate 
(irritant), and control sites. Thirty-three biomarkers were analyzed. Random 
forest and penalized regression models were trained on the patch test dataset 
and validated in HD; an additional model was trained and validated in HD.

between AD, ICD and ACD.

BACKGROUND: There is growing evidence of ableism in pediatric health care, but

Prolonged lake use in Atlantic salmon juveniles prior to seaward migration is 
associated with higher apparent mortality and faster estimated growth.

Reed TE(1)(2), Finlay R(1)(3), Kaufmann J(1)(2)(3), Phillips KP(4)(5), McGinnity 
P(1)(2)(3), Poole R(3).

Author information:
(1)School of Biological, Earth and Environmental Sciences, University College 
Cork, Cork, Ireland.
(2)Sustainability Institute, University College Cork, Cork, Ireland.
(3)Marine Institute, Furnace, Newport, Ireland.
(4)Canadian Rivers Institute, University of New Brunswick, Fredericton, New 
Brunswick, Canada.
(5)Atlantic Salmon Federation, Chamcook, New Brunswick, Canada.

Lakes can present both risks and opportunities for migratory fishes, yet their 
role in the life histories of anadromous salmonids remains understudied. Here, 
we used Passive Integrated Transponder (PIT) telemetry to examine lake-use 
patterns and their associations with survival and growth in juvenile Atlantic 
salmon Salmo salar L. over 3 years in the Burrishoole catchment, western 
Ireland. A fixed antenna positioned at the transition between river and lake 
habitats allowed us to estimate the timing of lake entry into Lough Feeagh - the 
largest freshwater lake in the system through which the fish must migrate on 
their way to the sea. Fish entering the lake earlier took longer to reach 
downstream sea-entry traps, a pattern consistent across years. Earlier entry was 
associated with a lower probability of detection at the downstream traps, which 
may reflect seasonal timing itself (e.g., seasonal variation in food 
availability or predation), cumulative mortality associated with prolonged lake 
residence (e.g., increased exposure to predators or other lake-specific risks) 
or intrinsic differences among early- and late-migrating fish (e.g., 
physiological attributes). Fish also exhibited substantially greater growth 
between upstream river exit and downstream recapture than inferred growth rates 
prior to lake entry, indicating that the lake can provide important feeding and 
growth opportunities during downstream migration. These findings are consistent 
with a potential trade-off between growth benefits and survival costs during 
lake passage, although this trade-off remains to be demonstrated directly. 
Overall, our results show that Lough Feeagh is more than a migration corridor 
for Atlantic salmon smolts and highlight the need to understand how seasonal 
timing, lake residence and individual characteristics jointly shape the costs 
and benefits of lacustrine habitat during anadromous migration.

suffers from significant reporting gaps, as current data relies predominantly on

assess the incidence of all surgical adverse events at a specialized paediatric

METHODS: A retrospective review of prospectively collected data from January

Evaluation of the Clinical Usefulness of a Bioartificial Urethral Substitute 
Generated by Tissue Engineering in Laboratory Rabbits: Protocol for an In Vivo 
Study.

Sánchez-Porras D(1)(2), Campos F(#)(1)(2), Chato-Astrain J(#)(1)(2), Alaminos 
M(1)(2), Sánchez-Quevedo MC(1)(2), Fernández-Valadés R(2)(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Histology, Tissue Engineering Group, School of Medicine, 
Universidad de Granada, Granada, Spain.
(2)Instituto de Investigación Biosanitaria ibs.GRANADA, Granada, Spain.
(3)Division of Pediatric Surgery, Hospital Universitario Virgen de las Nieves, 
Granada, Spain.
(#)Contributed equally

BACKGROUND: Surgical management of diseases compromising the integrity of the 
human urethra remains a major clinical challenge, and congenital conditions, 
such as hypospadias and epispadias, and acquired diseases, such as trauma, 
tumors, and strictures, are difficult to treat, highlighting the need for novel 
regenerative approaches capable of restoring urethral architecture and function. 
Recent advances in tissue engineering have allowed the generation of 
bioartificial tissues, including several models of artificial urethra generated 
with different types of cells and biomaterials. Although potentially useful, 
these models cannot reproduce the multilayered native human urethra structure. 
One biomaterial showing excellent biocompatibility for use in tissue engineering 
is fibrin-agarose hydrogel, which has been used with promising results in 
patients with severe alterations of the cornea, skin, and oral mucosa, 
suggesting its potential use for multilayered urethral substitutes.
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to evaluate the biosafety and efficacy of a 
multilayered artificial urethra generated by tissue engineering using 
fibrin-agarose biomaterials in laboratory rabbits to determine its clinical 
potential as an advanced therapy medicinal product.
METHODS: Five study groups will be established, including a positive control 
group of rabbits with a native (ie, normal) urethra, a negative control group of 
rabbits in which the ventral side of the urethra will be surgically sectioned 
and left unrepaired, a gold standard group in which the ventral side of the 
urethra will be surgically sectioned and repaired with an oral mucosa autograft, 
an acellular group in which the urethral defect will be repaired using an 
acellular multilayered fibrin-agarose biomaterial, and a cellular group of 
rabbits in which a multilayered cellular bioartificial urethra will be used to 
repair the urethral defect. The cellular group will allow us to assess the 
usefulness of a biomimetic urethral substitute generated by tissue engineering, 
as demonstrated in previously published models of bioartificial tissues, whereas 
the acellular group will allow us to determine whether the effects observed for 
the artificial urethra are attributable to the biomaterial itself, which could 
act as a physical barrier, or to the action of the cells. In all cases, animals 
will be observed for 3 months, and variables related to biosafety, 
functionality, and the histological structure of the urethral grafts will be 
determined.
RESULTS: This study was approved by the ethics committee for animal research 
(Junta de Andalucía; 17/12/2024/178) on December 20, 2024. The in vivo study 
began in February 2025 and is expected to be completed by December 2026. The 
study was funded in January 2023, and data collection is expected to be 
completed by December 2026. The results are expected to be published in 2026 and 
2027.
CONCLUSIONS: The present preclinical study will contribute to determining the 
potential usefulness of these bioartificial tissues as novel advanced therapy 
medicinal products for clinical use.

Patient Use of a Comment Function in Electronic Health Records: Mixed Methods 
Case Study.

Hagström J(1)(2), Kharko A(1)(2), Hägglund M(1)(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Women's and Children's Health, Uppsala University, Uppsala, 
Sweden.
(2)Centre for Primary Care and Health Services Research, University of 
Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom.
(3)MedTech Science & Innovation Centre, Uppsala University Hospital, Uppsala, 
Sweden.

BACKGROUND: Patient access to their electronic health records (EHRs) could 
improve care and reduce errors by enabling patient contribution to 
documentation. However, interactive functions that support such engagement 
remain underresearched.
OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this study was to analyze patients' use of the 
free-text comment function in the Swedish national patient-accessible EHR.
METHODS: Comments made by patients between 2015 and 2021 for health care 
professionals to view were retrieved from the patient-accessible EHR 
administration service in Sweden. The number and length of comments were 
analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests, while the content 
was examined qualitatively using inductive content analysis. In addition, 
comments were coded for sentiment (positive, neutral, or negative) and note 
content, and users were classified according to whether they had submitted at 
least 1 comment referring to mental health care.
RESULTS: A total of 1670 comments were left by 659 patients, of which 15 had 
irrelevant content (15/1670, 0.9%; 95% CI 0.4%-1.4%), leaving 1655 comments for 
analysis. Most comments (948/1655, 57.3%; 95% CI 54.9%-59.7%) were related to 
matters other than note content, and nearly all had a neutral (920/1655, 55.6%; 
95% CI 53.2%-58.0%) or negative (702/1655, 42.4%; 95% CI 40.0%-44.8%) sentiment. 
Patients who submitted a comment referencing mental health care tended to leave 
more comments overall (median 7 vs 2 comments per patient), and their comments 
were more frequently negative than comments written by other patients (313/495, 
63.2% vs 389/1160, 33.5%; P<.001). The most prevalent categories were care 
engagement, perceived inaccuracies, complaints, and requests.
CONCLUSIONS: Patient engagement with clinical notes has the potential to enhance 
documentation accuracy and strengthen patient-clinician communication. To 
realize these benefits safely, such features must be deliberately designed and 
clearly explained to users to avoid patient safety risks and unnecessary burdens 
on health care professionals.

Effect of Sleep Hygiene on Metabolic Syndrome in an Adult Rural Population in 
India: Protocol for a Cross-Sectional Study.

Kothari R(1), Choudhari S(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Community Medicine, Jawaharlal Nehru Medical College, Datta 
Meghe Institute of Higher Education and Research, Wardha, Maharashtra, India.

BACKGROUND: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) refers to a group of conditions including 
high blood pressure, excess weight, high blood glucose, and abnormal cholesterol 
and triglyceride levels that together substantially increase the risk of heart 
disease and diabetes. Poor sleep hygiene is associated with a higher likelihood 
of type 2 diabetes, while sleep duration can affect the development of various 
MetS components. Approximately 25% of adults worldwide currently have MetS, and 
this prevalence is projected to increase to 50% by 2035. However, there is a 
distinct lack of evidence about the specific impact of sleep hygiene on 
cardiometabolic health within the rural Indian population. This study will focus 
on addressing this literature gap by evaluating these risk factor associations 
by using validated tools to help develop targeted community interventions.
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to estimate the prevalence of poor sleep quality and 
cardiometabolic risk factors in a rural Indian population and to determine the 
association between sleep hygiene and cardiometabolic risk factors.
METHODS: This study will be a community-based, cross-sectional, analytical 
study, and data collection will be carried out by trained personnel using 
validated tools during house-to-house visits. In this cross-sectional study of 
281 rural Indian adults aged ≥40 years, sleep quality will be assessed via the 
Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (a score >5 indicates poor sleep), alongside 
direct measurements of blood pressure, fasting plasma glucose, BMI (≥25 kg/m² 
for obesity), waist circumference, and the Madras Diabetes Research 
Foundation-Indian Diabetes Risk Score for diabetes risk. Data will be collected 
through a door-to-door approach, with informed consent entered into Google 
Forms, and quality checked via training and regular reviews. Using R software, 
analyses will include prevalence estimates with 95% CIs; chi-square or t tests 
for associations between poor sleep and cardiometabolic risks; and logistic 
regression (P<.05) adjusted for confounders such as diet, stress, and physical 
activity.
RESULTS: This study began in January 2025 with conceptualization and ethics 
approval obtained in June 2025. Data collection commenced in August 2025 
following Clinical Trial Registry-India registration, with 53 participants 
enrolled as of May 5, 2026. Standardized tools (GAD-7, PHQ-9, and GPAQ) were 
incorporated to assess key confounding variables. Data collection is projected 
to finish by January 2027, with final analysis and study conclusion expected by 
March 2027.
CONCLUSIONS: The relationship between MetS and sleep hygiene warrants greater 
attention, particularly as poor sleep habits become increasingly prevalent 
alongside MetS. This study will deepen the understanding of their connection, 
paving the way for targeted interventions and prevention strategies.

Adoption Strategies and Workarounds in the Evolution of Information 
Infrastructures Integrating Health and Social Care Providers in Scotland: 
Multimethod Qualitative Case Study of the Key Information Summary.

Sai V(1), Williams R(2), Cresswell K(1).

Author information:
(1)Usher Institute, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, Scotland, United 
Kingdom.
(2)Institute for the Study of Science, Technology and Innovation, University of 
Edinburgh, Edinburgh, Scotland, United Kingdom.

BACKGROUND: care records are digital technologies designed to support 
information sharing and care coordination across fragmented health and social 
care systems. However, adoption and use of these technologies can vary across 
diverse health and care settings, with users using workarounds and other 
strategies to meet their specific information needs. In Scotland, the Key 
Information Summary (KIS) has been in use for over 13 years, sharing key patient 
information from general practitioners (GPs) with other health and care 
providers for future care planning.
OBJECTIVE: Using the KIS as a case study, this study examines how various 
adoption strategies and workarounds have shaped the evolution of regional 
information infrastructures integrating health and social care in Scotland over 
time.
METHODS: This multimethod qualitative study examined the various contextual 
factors influencing adoption and use of the KIS across diverse health and care 
settings. Data collection included interviews with KIS users from health and 
care settings, implementers, and vendors; documentary analysis of user guides, 
websites, reports, and policies; and observation of multidisciplinary team 
meetings and technology use. Data analysis involved a hybrid approach. The 
technology-people-organization-macroenvironment framework was applied to code 
interview, documentary, and observational data, followed by an inductive 
analysis informed by science and technology studies theories of information 
infrastructures, domestication, and workarounds to examine strategies and 
workarounds for adapting the KIS to local contexts and evolving needs.
RESULTS: Data comprised 54 qualitative interviews, 59 documents, 2 websites, and 
20 hours of observational field notes collected between April 2024 and March 
2025. Findings indicate that adoption of the KIS varied across settings and over 
time due to misalignment between system design, evolving expectations of 
integrated care, and national initiatives during the COVID-19 pandemic that 
repurposed its use. Professional roles and associated information needs shaped 
differing expectations of what constituted useful information, generating 
tensions between users who relied on the KIS and GPs responsible for maintaining 
it. Formal workarounds enabled the extension of the health care-centric 
infrastructure into nonclinical settings to facilitate information sharing with 
GPs and, in some cases, supported clinician access to the KIS during system 
outages. Across settings, informal user-driven repair practices enabled diverse 
professionals to adopt and realign the KIS with its intended use.
CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates how regional information infrastructures 
integrating health and care evolve incrementally as they become embedded within 
local routines, practices, and existing systems. Adoption was shaped by 
professional roles, information needs, and users' capabilities, with formal 
workarounds extending infrastructures into new settings and informal, 
user-driven repair practices supporting ongoing use and maintenance. 
Policymakers and vendors must recognize that workarounds and user-driven repair 
practices are central to infrastructural growth and sustainability, and 
understanding these strategies can inform future technology development and 
innovation.

Agentic artificial intelligence for code status extraction from clinical notes: 
a cross-model comparison of single agent, reflective agent, and multiagent 
extractor-reviewer system.

Sun Y(1), Ang G(2)(3), Yap CW(1), Kannapiran P(1), Abisheganaden J(1)(4)(5).

Author information:
(1)Health Services and Outcomes Research (HSOR), NHG Health Group Office, 
308205, Singapore.
(2)National Healthcare Group Polyclinics, 738579, Singapore.
(3)Newcastle Australia Institute of Higher Education, 188064, Singapore.
(4)Department of Respiratory Medicine, Tan Tock Seng Hospital, NHG Health, 
308433, Singapore.
(5)Lee Kong Chien School of Medicine, Nanyang Technological University, 308232, 
Singapore.

OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether increasing agentic architectural complexity via 
self-reflection or multiagent design improves clinical code status extraction 
(Do Not Resuscitate [DNR], Do Not Intubate [DNI], Comfort Measures Only [CMO]) 
across open-source large language models (LLMs) of varying capabilities.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a controlled cross-model comparison 
evaluating 3 architectures: (1) single extractor agent, (2) single agent with 
self-reflection, and (3) sequential multiagent extractor-reviewer system. Four 
open-source LLMs (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, MedGemma-27B-IT, 
Qwen3.5-27B) were evaluated on 1000 Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care 
IV-Note discharge summaries. Ground truth labels were established through a 
physician-AI dual review with adjudication (Cohen's κ = 0.98-0.99). Models were 
evaluated on accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Cohen's κ, token 
consumption, and processing latency. McNemar's test was used for paired 
comparisons.
RESULTS: For capable larger models (GPT-OSS-20B, MedGemma-27B-IT, Qwen3.5-27B), 
single-agent architectures achieved comparable or superior performance for 
explicit code status (DNR, DNI) relative to complex systems, whereas multiagent 
review doubled token consumption and latency without accuracy gains. Reflective 
self-review significantly impaired MedGemma-27B-IT on DNI extraction (P = .047). 
For the smaller DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, multiagent review provided 
statistically significant corrective benefits for DNR (P = .017) and CMO 
(P < .001), demonstrating a capability-threshold effect, though performance 
remained below clinically acceptable levels.
DISCUSSION: Architectural complexity does not enhance extraction performance for 
capable LLMs, and reflective self-review may cause conservative overcorrection. 
Multiagent verification value is inversely related to model capability.
CONCLUSION: Single-agent LLMs provide optimal accuracy and efficiency for 
explicit clinical extraction in capable models. Agentic complexity must be 
matched to both task characteristics and model capability rather than adopted by 
default.
