Along-tract statistical mapping of white matter abnormalities in children with 
SeLECTS.

Xu G(1), Zhang Y(2), Huang K(2), Liu J(2), Song G(2), Chen X(2), Zeng L(3), 
Zhang Y(4), Liu H(2), Zhang T(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Radiology, The Affiliated Hospital of Zunyi Medical University, 
149th, The Dalian Road, Zunyi City, Guizhou Province, China. Electronic address: 
343470038@qq.com.
(2)Department of Radiology, The Affiliated Hospital of Zunyi Medical University, 
149th, The Dalian Road, Zunyi City, Guizhou Province, China.
(3)School of Medical Imaging, The Zunyi Medical University, 6(th), West Xuefu 
Road, Xinpu District, Zunyi City, Guizhou Province, China.
(4)The Public Experimental Center of Medicine, The Affiliated Hospital of Zunyi 
Medical University, 149th, The Dalian Road, Zunyi City, Guizhou Province, China.
(5)Department of Medical Technology, Bijie Medical College, Bijie, Guizhou,

BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Emerging evidence suggests that self-limited epilepsy 
with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS) may reflect atypical neurodevelopment. As 
WM maturation extends from the second trimester through adolescence, this study 
aimed to identify regions of delayed or aberrant white matter (WM) development 
in children with SeLECTS using along-tract statistical mapping for precise 
localization of microstructural alterations.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: 38 children with SeLECTS and 31 healthy controls 
underwent diffusion-weighted MRI scan. Fractional anisotropy (FA), mean 
diffusivity (MD), and radial diffusivity (RD) were derived from the diffusion 
tensor model. Whole-brain tractography was performed using deterministic EuDX 
tracking and registered to a standardized bundle atlas in MNI space. Thirty WM 
tracts per subject were extracted. Linear mixed models within the BUAN 
tractometry framework were used to assess segment wise group differences, while 
partial correlations were performed to evaluate associations between diffusion 
metrics and cognitive performance. FDR correction was applied per bundle for all 
comparisons.
RESULTS: After FDR correction, children with SeLECTS showed increased MD in the 
forceps minor, midbody of the corpus callosum, right corticospinal tract, right 
extreme capsule, and bilateral uncinate fasciculi. MD values in the affected WM 
segments showed negative correlations with performance and full-scale IQ, and 
the segments showing significant correlations overlapped with those showing 
significant group differences.
CONCLUSIONS: SeLECTS is associated with MD-based microstructural alterations in 
superficial frontal, temporal, and parietal pathways, potentially indicating 
delayed white matter maturation.

Mobile EEG Reveals Age-Dependent Cognitive-Motor Interference with Increasing 
Motor Task Complexity- a cross-sectional study.

Wollesen B(1), Winter L(2), Gramann K(3), Protzak J(4).

Author information:
(1)German Sports University Cologne, Cologne, Germany. Electronic address: 
b.wollesen@dshs-koeln.de.
(2)Medical School, Department of Neurology, University of Minnesota, 
Minneapolis, USA; Center for Clinical Movement Science, University of Minnesota, 
Minneapolis, USA.
(3)Biological Psychology and Neuroergonomics, TU Berlin, Berlin, Germany.
(4)The Wallace H. Coulter Department of Biomedical Engineering, Emory University 
and Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia, USA.

This study examined age-related differences in behavior and brain dynamics 
underlying cognitive-motor interference (CMI) during motor dual-tasks (DT) with 
increasing motor task complexity. Behavioral performance and electrocortical 
activity were assessed in 19 younger adults (11 males, 8 females; 25.5 ± 2.3 
years) and 11 older adults (6 males, 5 females; 72.6 ± 4.6 years) using mobile 
electroencephalography (EEG). Participants performed an oddball choice-reaction 
task under three conditions: sitting, standing, and treadmill walking. 
Event-related potential (ERPs; P1, N1, P3) amplitudes and latencies, response 
times, postural sway, and gait parameters were recorded to evaluate CMI. Data 
were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVAs with within-subject factors of 
motor condition and stimulus type and age group as a between-subject factor. 
Older adults exhibited reduced step length compared to younger adults, but no 
DT-related changes in gait or postural sway were observed. Response times were 
generally slower in older adults and increased from sitting to standing and 
walking whereas younger adults showed slowing only from sitting to standing. 
Early sensory ERP components (P1, N1) demonstrated increased amplitudes with 
higher motor demands. The P3 component was reduced in amplitude in both groups 
during walking, with delayed latencies in older adults. For both groups, P3 
latencies were associated with prolonged response times. Our findings suggest 
that this slowing during walking reflects altered cognitive resource allocation, 
characterized by delayed central information processing and enhanced early 
visual processing, rather than impaired peripheral motor coordination.

Long-Term Treadmill Exercise Improves Spatial Memory and Increases SOX2-Positive 
Cells in the Hippocampus of Middle-Aged Male Mice.

Yi R(1), Zhao Q(2), Zhang WM(3), Zhang XD(4), Chen Q(5), Liu JG(6).

Author information:
(1)Department of Neurosurgery, Shenzhen Hospital, Southern Medical University, 
Shenzhen 518000, China; School of Interpreting and Translation Studies, 
Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, Guangzhou 510080, China. Electronic 
address: yrong349@gmail.com.
(2)Department of Neurology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical

(3)Brain Hospital of Hunan, Changsha, Hunan Province 410007, China. Electronic 
address: weiminzhang093@126.com.
(4)College of Physical Education, Hainan Normal University, Haikou 570100,

Age-related cognitive decline is closely associated with hippocampal 
deterioration, yet the cellular and molecular adaptations underlying 
exercise-induced cognitive improvement remain incompletely understood. In the 
present study, nine-month-old male C57BL/6J mice were randomly assigned to a 
treadmill exercise group or a sedentary control group and trained for four 
months, reaching approximately 13 months of age at outcome assessment. Cognitive 
functions were assessed using the Morris water maze, and hippocampal tissue was 
examined by Nissl staining and immunofluorescence for SOX2 and GFAP. 
Database-based network analysis was performed to identify candidate targets 
shared between exercise-associated and hippocampus-associated gene sets, and the 
corresponding mouse genes were assessed by RT-qPCR. As a result, long-term 
treadmill exercise shortened escape latency, reduced swimming distance on the 
fifth acquisition day, and increased platform crossings during the probe trial. 
Exercised mice also exhibited fewer hippocampal neurons with condensed nuclei 
and more SOX2-positive cells than controls. The molecular network analysis 
identified 48 overlapping human targets, with TNF, IL6, IL1B, PTGS2, TP53, MMP9, 
TLR4, HMOX1, IGF1, and NFE2L2 ranked as the top hub targets. RT-qPCR confirmed 
altered hippocampal expression of eight of the ten corresponding mouse genes. 
Collectively, these findings link improved spatial memory in long-term treadmill 
exercise with changes in hippocampal neuronal morphology, SOX2-positive cells, 
and genes related to inflammation, oxidative stress, and cellular stress 
responses in middle-aged male mice.

NAT10-mediated ac4C modification of BMP6 regulates osteogenic differentiation of 
bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells in the pathogenesis of Adolescent 
idiopathic scoliosis.

Li Y(1), Yang S(2), Zhang J(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Spine Surgery, Weifang People's Hospital, Weifang City, 
Shandong 261000, China. Electronic address: liyuezhong@126.com.
(2)Department of Spine Surgery, Weifang People's Hospital, Weifang City, 
Shandong 261000, China.

BACKGROUND: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a three-dimensional spinal 
deformity. Bone morphogenetic protein 6 (BMP6) drives osteogenesis; this study 
probes BMP6 mechanism and its potential role in the impaired osteogenic 
differentiation of AIS-BMSCs.
METHODS: AIS-BMSCs were isolated and their surface markers (CD34, CD45, CD90, 
and CD105) were analyzed by flow cytometry. Osteogenic differentiation was 
assessed through alizarin red S staining quantification and ALP activity assays, 
while the expression of osteogenic markers osteocalcin (OCN), runt-related 
transcription factor 2 (RUNX2), BMP6, N-acetyltransferase 10 (NAT10), and 
Smad1/5/9 signaling pathway was detected by Western blot. The transcriptional 
and protein levels of BMP6 and NAT10, as well as knockdown and overexpression 
efficiencies, were measured by qPCR and Western blot. Cell viability was 
determined using the CCK-8 assay. Potential N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) 
modification sites in BMP6 were predicted using the PACES webserver. The 
interaction between NAT10 and BMP6 was examined by RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) 
and luciferase reporter assays. Rescue assays confirmed NAT10 pro-osteo effect 
requires BMP6.
RESULTS: AIS-BMSCs showed reduced ALP activity, mineralization capacity, and 
RUNX2/OCN expression, along with downregulated BMP6 expression; BMP6 
re-expression rescued these deficits in vitro. NAT10 mediates ac4C acetylation 
of BMP6 mRNA, extending its half-life and boosting osteogenesis, whereas 
inhibition of NAT10 or ac4C modification reversed these effects. BMP6 knockdown 
abolished NAT10-enhanced mineralization and p-Smad1/5/9, indicating that NAT10 
acts via BMP6-Smad1/5/9.
CONCLUSION: NAT10-mediated ac4C modification stabilizes BMP6 mRNA, activates 
Smad1/5/9, and ameliorates the impaired osteogenic differentiation of AIS-BMSCs 
in vitro. These findings suggest a potential mechanism by which NAT10-BMP6 
signaling may influence osteogenesis in AIS, but they are based solely on in 
vitro experiments.

Systems pharmacology reveals the molecular mechanisms of nerolidol against 
polycystic ovary syndrome through integrated transcriptomic, network 
pharmacology and experimental validation.

Kumar GS(1), Soni A(2), Pattanayak N(3), Morie F(3), Baldaniya LH(3).

Author information:
(1)Faculty of Pharmacy, Marwadi University, Rajkot-Morbi Road, Rajkot 360003, 
Gujarat, India. Electronic address: gsanthanakumar15@gmail.com.
(2)Ramanbhai Patel College of Pharmacy, Charotar University of Science and 
Technology, CHARUSAT Campus, Changa, Anand, Gujarat, India.
(3)Faculty of Pharmacy, Marwadi University, Rajkot-Morbi Road, Rajkot 360003, 
Gujarat, India.

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a heterogeneous endocrine and metabolic 
disorder marked by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, insulin resistance, 
chronic inflammation and oxidative stress, arising from dysregulation across 
several interconnected molecular pathways. Because its pathogenesis is 
multifactorial, therapies targeting diverse biological processes at once remain 
scarce. Nerolidol, a naturally occurring sesquiterpene alcohol with antioxidant, 
anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective properties, has an action against PCOS 
whose molecular basis remains unresolved. Transcriptomic differences associated 
with PCOS were examined using the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset 
GSE34526. Exploratory differential-expression screening identified nominally 
altered probes using an unadjusted P < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1; however, no 
individual probe remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction at 
FDR < 0.05. Functional enrichment analysis was subsequently used to investigate 
biological processes and pathways represented by these exploratory 
transcriptional signals. Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG enrichment were applied to 
pinpoint dysregulated biological processes and signalling pathways. 
Computational findings were tested in a letrozole-induced PCOS rat model treated 
with nerolidol, with efficacy judged from oestrous cyclicity, ovarian 
histopathology, reproductive hormone profiles, oxidative stress biomarkers, 
inflammatory mediators and metabolic parameters. Transcriptomic analysis showed 
marked enrichment of processes related to kinase regulation, insulin secretion, 
intrinsic apoptotic signalling, receptor-mediated signalling and the DNA damage 
response, while KEGG analysis pointed to pathways governing endocrine 
regulation, cell signalling and metabolic homeostasis. In animal experiments, 
nerolidol restored oestrous cyclicity, improved ovarian morphology, corrected 
endocrine disturbances, and reduced oxidative stress and PCOS-related pathology. 
These phenotypic effects were functionally concordant with several biological 
processes highlighted by the computational analyses. However, because the 
predicted signalling molecules and pathways were not directly measured in 
ovarian tissue following nerolidol treatment, the proposed molecular mechanisms 
remain hypotheses requiring targeted experimental validation.

Hyperoxia-induced acute lung injury (HALI) represents a serious consequence of 
prolonged oxygen exposure, characterized by oxidative stress, inflammatory 
responses, and impaired pulmonary function, whereas its underlying molecular 
mechanisms remain incompletely elucidated. The present work sought to delineate 
candidate genes and associated signaling pathways involved in HALI through 
integrated transcriptomic analysis and experimental validation. The microarray 
dataset GSE237260, including six control and six hyperoxia-exposed mouse lung 
samples, was analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). A total 
of 981 DEGs were identified, and random forest analysis identified 20 
characteristic genes, among which Sult1a1, Fibin, Ednrb, Tcim, and Ptpru were 
significantly overexpressed. Functional enrichment analysis indicated 
associations with hypoxia, inflammatory responses, mTORC1 signaling, p53 
signaling, and TNF-α signaling via NF-κB. Hyperoxia-induced mouse and cellular 
models using A549 cells and human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells 
(HPMECs) were established for experimental validation. Hyperoxia exposure 
induced inflammatory infiltration, pulmonary edema, impaired gas exchange, 
reduced cell viability, increased apoptosis, and elevated reactive oxygen 
species levels. Sult1a1, Fibin, and Ednrb were consistently upregulated in vivo 
and in vitro. Hyperoxia also increased the phosphorylation of mTOR, NF-κB p65, 
and S6K, whereas pharmacological inhibition of mTORC1 or NF-κB-related signaling 
and Ednrb knockdown attenuated cellular injury and reduced the phosphorylation 
of these signaling proteins. Conversely, Ednrb overexpression aggravated 
hyperoxia-induced cellular injury and increased the phosphorylation of mTOR, 
NF-κB p65, and S6K. Collectively, these findings identify candidate key genes 
and signaling pathways associated with HALI and provide experimental evidence 
supporting a potential involvement of Ednrb in hyperoxia-related cellular injury 
and mTORC1/NF-κB-related signaling.

BACKGROUND: Strategies to recruit the left ventricle in borderline left heart 
(BLH), whether utilizing primary or staged recruitment strategy, are challenged 
by lack of consensus regarding optimal substrate, timing, and technique.
METHODS: A panel of experienced congenital cardiac surgeons, cardiologists and 
imaging experts were convened to develop key questions related to BLH 
management, excluding unbalanced atrioventricular septal defect, from neonatal 
period through 1 year, using the PICO (Patients/Population, Intervention, 
Comparison/Control, Outcome) framework. Literature searches were performed for 
each question. Using a modified Delphi method, consensus statements were 
developed.
RESULTS: For neonates with BLH, primary biventricular repair should be adopted 
cautiously, and only with favorable anatomic and physiologic criteria determined 
by echocardiography and/or magnetic resonance imaging. Neonates in the 
'grey-zone', with smaller mitral and aortic valve sizes, endocardial 
fibroelastosis, indexed left ventricular diastolic volume < 25 ml/m2 and 
ascending aortic flow < 2.0 L/min/m2, should undergo staged recruitment to 
potentially facilitate growth of left-sided structures and more durable surgical 
rehabilitation of left ventricular inflow and outflow. Timing and type of 
subsequent procedures should be guided by interval cardiac catheterization and 
magnetic resonance imaging data. Initial palliation of grey-zone neonates can be 
accomplished with either surgical Norwood or hybrid stage 1 with possible atrial 
level restriction, and subsequent endocardial fibroelastosis resection along 
with aortic and mitral valve repair as components of successful complete 
biventricular conversion.
CONCLUSIONS: Biventricular approaches in BLH should be guided by integration of 
anatomic and physiologic criteria, with most neonates recommended for staged 
recruitment rather than primary repair.

The N-terminal protease (Npro) of bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) possesses 
two major biological functions, namely autoprotease activity and antagonism of 
interferon (IFN) synthesis, both of which are important for viral replication 
and immune evasion. Given the high mutation rate of the BVDV genome, whether 
mutations in Npro affect these functions remains largely unknown. Because 
cysteine and histidine residues are critical determinants of Npro activity, we 
systematically investigated the roles of all cysteine and histidine residues in 
regulating autoprotease activity and IFN antagonism. Synonymous codon 
substitutions involving cysteine or histidine residues did not affect the 
autoprotease activity of Npro. In contrast, analyses of nonsynonymous 
substitutions revealed that, in addition to the previously identified catalytic 
residues His49 and Cys69, His40, His99, and the zinc-binding residues Cys112, 
Cys134, and Cys138 were also essential for efficient autoprotease activity. By 
comparison, substitution of His148 had no detectable effect on either 
autoprotease activity or IFN antagonism. Functional dissociation analyses 
demonstrated that mutations at Glu22 and His49 enhanced IFN-β antagonism while 
abolishing autoprotease activity, whereas the Cys69 mutation abolished 
autocleavage but retained IFN suppression. In contrast, certain substitutions at 
His130 and Cys161 selectively impaired IFN antagonism without affecting 
autocleavage, indicating that these two functions are partially separable. 
Notably, mutations at His40, His99, Cys112, Cys134 and Cys138 markedly impaired 
both autoprotease activity and IFN antagonism, suggesting that these residues 
represent common functional determinants of the two activities. Sequence 
alignment of Npro proteins from different BVDV-1 strains identified naturally 
occurring non-conservative variations at positions 40, 130 and 148. Further 
analyses showed that the naturally occurring His40Arg and His130Pro 
substitutions significantly affected both autoprotease activity and IFN 
antagonism, supporting a functional association between Npro autocleavage and 
IFN suppression. In contrast, His148Arg, His148Asn, and His148Gln substitutions 
had no detectable effect on either activity. Collectively, these findings 
demonstrate that cysteine and histidine residues play critical roles in 
regulating both autoprotease activity and IFN antagonism of BVDV-1 Npro. 
Mutations at specific residues differentially affect these functions, 
highlighting the importance of conserved cysteine and histidine residues in 
maintaining the multifunctional properties of Npro.

In this study, the enzymatic hydrolysis process of steam explosion modified pea 
proteins was optimized through single-factor experiments and a Box-Behnken 
experimental design. The maximum degree of hydrolysis of 23.13% was achieved at 
7.38% substrate concentration (w/v), 5% enzyme-to-substrate ratio (w/w), pH 9.5, 
and 55 °C for 3 h. Steam explosion modified pea protein peptides (SE-PPP) 
exhibited strong antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus (S. 
aureus), with a minimum inhibitory concentration of 0.0244 mg/mL. Mechanistic 
studies revealed that SE-PPP disrupted the integrity of bacterial cell wall and 
membrane, as evidenced by increased alkaline phosphatase activity, decreased 
adenosine triphosphate levels, reactive oxygen species and malondialdehyde 
accumulation. These effects led to nucleic acid and protein leakage, thereby 
inhibiting bacterial proliferation. These findings confirmed that steam 
explosion pretreatment markedly enhanced the yield of low-molecular-weight 
peptides from pea protein. Moreover, the obtained SE-PPP had excellent 
antibacterial activity against S. aureus, supporting its potential as a natural 
food preservative for the high-value utilization of pea proteins.

The Evolution of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli Characterization and 
Risk Categorization Strategies.

Gill A(1), Romero-Barrios P(1), Jenkins C(2), Morabito S(3), Coulombe G(1), 
Lavoie MC(1), Feng P(4).

Author information:
(1)Health Canada, Bureau of Microbial and Toxicological Food Safety, Ottawa,

(2)UK Health Security Agency, Gastrointestinal Bacteria Reference Unit,

(4)Retired from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, College Park, MD. USA.

Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) are a group of E. coli that cause 
food and waterborne enteric illness. STEC are genotypically and phenotypically 
diverse as they do not have a single evolutionary origin, instead multiple STEC 
lineages have appeared independently following horizontal gene transfer events. 
The diversity of STEC is also reflected in an apparent variability in the 
potential of individual STEC strains to cause severe illness (bloody diarrhea or 
hemolytic uremic syndrome) or be involved in large foodborne outbreaks. In the 
context of food safety decision making, the variable characteristics of STEC 
strains and their potential health outcomes have resulted in an ongoing debate 
on how STEC should be categorized into risk groups. The aim of this review is to 
clarify that debate by examining how STEC characterization and risk 
categorization strategies have evolved over time in response to changes in 
analytical techniques, understanding of STEC epidemiology, and pathogenicity 
mechanisms. The origin of established perspectives and practices is explored, 
from the recognition of STEC O157:H7 as an emerging pathogen in the 1980s, 
through serotype-based identification and characterization of STEC, to 
contemporary approaches based on molecular markers for virulence. The evidence 
for the role of specific virulence factors in STEC pathogenicity is reviewed and 
their utility in STEC risk categorisation assessed. Finally, a binary 
categorization scheme is proposed, based on evidence for the correlation of 
hemolytic uremic syndrome, with the presence of Shiga toxin subtypes Stx2a, 
Stx2c, Stx2d, and colonisation factors including the Locus of Enterocyte 
Effacement (intimin/eae) and Enteroaggregative attachment (aggR/aaiC).

Salmonella is a major foodborne pathogen, and chicken meat is an important 
source of infection. This study investigated Salmonella prevalence, serovar 
distribution, antimicrobial resistance, and genomic characteristics in 150 
retail chicken meat samples collected in Japan in 2023. The predominant serovar 
was S. Schwarzengrund (42.7%), followed by S. Infantis (7.3%), which has long 
been the predominant serovar in Japan. The globally expanding S. Infantis 
sequence type (ST) 32 harboring pESI-like plasmids has declined in Japan. In 
contrast, S. Schwarzengrund ST241 was isolated more frequently in winter (66%) 
than in summer (31%, P < 0.001) and more often from chicken meat produced in 
eastern Japan (47.1%) than in western Japan (29.4%, P = 0.042). Antimicrobial 
resistance was most common to tetracycline (50.6%) and streptomycin (45.7%), 
whereas kanamycin resistance (33.3%) had declined compared with 2015 to 2019, 
consistent with reduced use of this antimicrobial in broiler production. 
Moreover, the proportion of S. Schwarzengrund isolates lacking antimicrobial 
resistance genes (ARGs) increased markedly from summer (19.4%) to winter 
(45.5%). cgMLST analysis revealed that antimicrobial-susceptible S. 
Schwarzengrund isolates formed the largest clade and, notably, retained 
pESI-like plasmids despite apparent loss of ARG-containing regions from these 
plasmids. These findings demonstrate ongoing genomic shifts in Salmonella 
populations in Japan and underscore the need for continuous genomic surveillance 
to mitigate their public health impact.

Tracking Illnesses Caused by Four Foodborne Pathogens Over Four Decades of the 
Healthy People Initiative.

Louis RP(1), Weller D(1), Shah HJ(1), Southern KJ(2), Noveroske D(2), Kadam 
P(3).

Author information:
(1)Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center for Emerging and 
Zoonotic Infectious Diseases, Atlanta, GA.
(2)United States Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service, 
Washington DC.
(3)U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 5001 Campus Drive (Room 3A-009), College

The Healthy People (HP) Initiative, a collaboration between the U.S. Department 
of Health and Human Services and various public and private organizations, aims 
to improve the health and well-being of all Americans. HP consists of national 
health objectives with 10-year targets to achieve by the end of the decade. 
Since HP2000, progress toward goals on four foodborne pathogens (Campylobacter, 
Listeria monocytogenes, Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli, and Salmonella) 
has been primarily tracked using data from the Centers for Disease Control and 
Prevention's Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network (FoodNet). The data 
used to inform the HP food safety goals spans nearly four decades from 1987 
(HP2000) to 2024 (the most recent HP2030 data point). Each decade, measuring 
foodborne pathogen objectives has become more rigorous and target-setting 
methods have evolved. HP2000 objectives aimed at a reduction in infections to no 
more than a set value and, most recently, HP2030 objectives were developed to 
align with key regulations or targeted a percent improvement in foodborne 
illness infections. Progress toward these targets has been monitored and 
categorized (getting worse, no detectable change, improving, or met target) for 
these pathogens. This article details the advancements made to more accurately 
establish targets, assess the data, and measure progress at the end or most 
recent data point of each decade. Each decade, measurement of objectives, 
baseline-setting methods, target-setting methods, and reporting progress methods 
have evolved. For this reason, caution must be taken when attempting to compare 
data across decades.

tuberculosis (TB), its frequency and species-specific antimicrobial

METHODS: We analyzed specimens from 2000 unique patients evaluated for suspected

OBJECTIVE: To develop quality assurance models for adverse procedural events 
after lung resection and esophagectomy for cancer.
METHODS: Using procedural outcomes after 16,430 lung resections and 3,068 
esophagectomies for cancer at 9 hospitals in 7 hospital systems, we developed 5

interaction structure among predictors. Risk-factor magnitude differed among

each focal hospital was excluded from the aggregate benchmark.

procedural events after lung resection and esophagectomy for cancer have been

initiatives in general thoracic surgery.

BACKGROUND: In locally advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (LA-ESCC), 
neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NCIT) plus high-quality surgery (R0 resection

value of adjuvant immunotherapy remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate

The role of the lymphatic micro-vasculature in malignant tissue fluid and drug 
transport.

Brown A(1), Penta R(2).

Author information:
(1)University of Glasgow, School of Mathematics and Statistics, University 
Place, Glasgow, G12 8QQ, Scotland, United Kingdom. Electronic address: 
Andrew.Brown.3@glasgow.ac.uk.
(2)University of Glasgow, School of Mathematics and Statistics, University 
Place, Glasgow, G12 8QQ, Scotland, United Kingdom. Electronic address: 
raimondo.penta@glasgow.ac.uk.

The contribution of lymphatic capillaries in the fluid and drug transport 
throughout vascularised malignant tissue is qualitatively and quantitatively 
discussed. Our starting point is the derivation of differential equations for 
coupled fluid and drug transport across three physical domains present in 
vascularised tissue: the interstitium, capillary vessels and lymphatic vessels. 
We begin from mass and momentum balance equations in each physical domain, which 
are geometrically characterised by the inter-capillary distance (microscale). 
The Kedem-Katchalsky equations are used to account for blood and drug exchange 
across the vessel walls. Employing asymptotic homogenisation, we can formulate a 
multiscale model which allows for a complex microstructure, under the regular 
assumptions such as local periodicity, accounting for spatial heterogeneity of 
the angiogenic nature of the capillary and lymphatic networks. At the 
macroscale, the fluid dynamics are governed by a triple-compartmental porous 
medium problem characterised by Darcy's law; whereas drug dynamics are 
characterised by a triple-compartmental advection-diffusion-reaction model. The 
microscopic properties of the malignant tissue are effectively encoded into a 
series of macroscopic coefficients, which enable the analysis of geometric 
changes at the microscale from a macroscopic perspective. Analysis of the 
models' isotropic case reveals the existence of a favourable permeability for 
lymphatic vessels, allowing for optimised fluid and drug transport. The purpose 
of this work is to create a robust theoretical platform that can account for the 
role of the networks of vessels that are to be considered to improve anti-cancer 
strategies.

BACKGROUND: Previous studies have reported gray matter volume (GMV) deficits in

METHODS: We conducted a quantitative voxel-wise meta-analysis of whole-brain 
voxel-based morphometry (VBM) studies in individuals with subthreshold 
depression (STD), first-episode drug-naïve depression (FEND), and long-term

were performed using the Seed-based d Mapping (SDM) toolbox. Meta-regression

from early to chronic depression. Meta-regression analyses revealed 
stage-specific associations between clinical characteristics and GMV changes.
CONCLUSIONS: This meta-analysis reveals stage-specific GMV abnormalities across 
depression. GMV changes shift from mixed alterations in early stages to purely 
atrophic reductions in chronic MDD, supporting a progressive model.

vulnerability markers, while GMV consolidation in long-term MDD underscores the 
importance of early intervention.

BACKGROUND: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading global cause of disease 
burden, and suboptimal medication adherence is a primary driver of treatment 
failure. Both depression stigma and antidepressant adverse drug reactions (ADRs)

temporal dynamics in MDD remain poorly characterized.

the Depression Cohort in China. Medication adherence, stigma, and ADRs were

Prospects for adiponectin-based therapeutics in myocardial ischemia reperfusion 
injury.

Bahit MC(1), Gibson CM(2), Lei Y(3), Hsu HH(4), Scherer PE(5), Sweeney G(6).

Author information:
(1)Baim Institute for Clinical Research, Boston, MA, USA; INECO Neurociencias

(2)Baim Institute for Clinical Research, Boston, MA, USA; Harvard Medical

(4)Allysta Pharmaceuticals, Bellevue, WA, USA. Electronic address:

(5)Touchstone Diabetes Center, The University of Texas Southwestern Medical

(6)Department of Biology, York University, Toronto, Canada. Electronic address:

Adiponectin is an adipocyte-derived hormone with broad cardiometabolic benefits, 
circulating at high levels in healthy individuals but reduced in obesity, 
diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Low adiponectin concentrations are 
strongly associated with coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, 
myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury (MIRI), and heart failure. MIRI remains a 
major unmet need in contemporary ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction 
(STEMI) care. Although reperfusion is essential in limiting ischemic myocardial 
necrosis, it causes deleterious effects such as impaired carbohydrate oxidation, 
excessive fatty-acid oxidation, intracellular acidosis, calcium (Ca2+) overload, 
oxidative/nitrative stress, and mitochondrial fragmentation, that expand infarct 
size, worsen microvascular obstruction, and fuel adverse ventricular remodeling. 
Activation of the adiponectin-adiponectin receptor (AdipoR) axis directly 
counteracts these processes by stimulating adenosine monophosphate-activated 
protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent metabolic rebalancing, restoring mitochondrial 
fusion-fission homeostasis, enhancing oxidative capacity, reducing inducible 
nitric oxide synthase (iNOS-) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate 
(NADPH) oxidase-mediated injury, improving endothelial nitric oxide (NO) 
bioavailability, and enhancing microvascular perfusion. In animal models, 
adiponectin or its mimetics consistently reduced infarct size, improved 
myocardial function, and attenuated apoptosis, inflammation, and no-reflow. A 
growing array of therapeutic strategies has emerged, each bringing its own 
pharmacologic nuances and implications for translation to the clinic. This 
review summarizes current strategies to enhance adiponectin action, highlights 
the progress in peptide and small-molecule mimetics, and discusses future 
directions for clinical translation in cardiometabolic diseases.

Tumor cells are the driving force of cancer progression, yet they also 
constitute a rich reservoir of tumor-associated and patient-specific antigens 
that can be harnessed for therapeutic vaccination. Whole tumor cell vaccines 
(WTCVs) exploit this unique duality by converting malignant cells into 
immunotherapeutic agents capable of eliciting broad antitumor immunity and 
overcoming tumor heterogeneity. However, their clinical translation remains 
constrained by the need to eliminate tumorigenic potential while preserving or 
enhancing immunogenicity. Here, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent 
advances in the engineering of WTCVs from the perspectives of safety assurance 
and therapeutic enhancement. We summarize current strategies for controlling

viability-preserving approaches, and discuss emerging immunopotentiation 
strategies that enhance antigen abundance and exposure, improve antigen 
presentation, activate innate and adaptive immune pathways, and integrate 
complementary therapeutic modalities. Collectively, these advances are 
transforming malignant cells into multifunctional therapeutic vaccines capable 
of eliciting potent and durable antitumor immunity. Finally, we discuss the key 
challenges and future opportunities for next-generation WTCVs and highlight 
design principles that may accelerate their clinical translation.

Isoniazid (INH) is a cornerstone antimicrobial for tuberculosis treatment, yet 
its potential immunomodulatory interactions with host innate immune effectors 
remain poorly characterized. Myeloperoxidase (MPO), an abundant neutrophil heme 
peroxidase involved in pathogen clearance, oxidizes INH into radical 
intermediates. This study investigated the biochemical and immunopharmacological 
effects of INH on MPO-dependent oxidative bacterial killing using Mycobacterium 
smegmatis mc2155 as a model. Using competitive kinetics with taurine, we 
demonstrated that INH reacts rapidly with hypochlorous acid (HOCl), with a 
second-order rate constant of 3.7 x 107 M-1 s-1. This reaction markedly impaired 
HOCl-mediated bactericidal activity, while INH retained most of its 
antimicrobial activity. In purified enzymatic assays, INH significantly reduced 
MPO/H2O2-mediated bacterial killing, restoring bacterial survival by up to 
approximately 70%. Furthermore, in human neutrophil-mediated killing assays, INH 
increased mycobacterial survival, with effects comparable to those observed with 
inhibitors of MPO and NADPH oxidase. INH did not significantly inhibit 
superoxide (O2•-) generation by activated neutrophils, indicating that its 
effects occur downstream of the primary NADPH oxidase-mediated oxidative burst. 
Together, these findings demonstrate that INH interferes with the MPO/HOCl 
antimicrobial pathway through both MPO inhibition and HOCl scavenging, revealing 
a previously underrecognized interaction between this first-line 
antimycobacterial drug and neutrophil oxidative antimicrobial mechanisms.

BACKGROUND: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a complex 
syndrome lacking effective targeted therapies, but its causal genes and 
mechanisms remain poorly defined.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the role of PLCB3 and its association with ferroptosis 
in HFpEF.
METHODS: We integrated transcriptomic data and genome-wide association studies 
(GWAS) data and employed differential expression analysis, mendelian 
randomization (MR), summary data-based mendelian randomization (SMR), and 
colocalization analysis to identify key genes associated with HFpEF. 
Furthermore, functional validation was performed using a HFpEF mouse model and 
siRNA mediated PLCB3 knockdown in AC16 cardiomyocytes. Cell viability, reactive 
oxygen species (ROS), lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis related protein 
expression were subsequently assessed to investigate the molecular mechanisms 
underlying PLCB3-mediated ferroptosis.

HFpEF and controls. Single-cell eQTL-based MR analysis further suggested that 
PLCB3 expression is associated with specific immune cell subsets, including B 
cells, CD4+ naïve T cells, and natural killer cells.
CONCLUSION: PLCB3 is a potential regulator of HFpEF and may contribute to 
disease progression by promoting ferroptosis and immune alterations. These 
findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms of HFpEF and suggest 
that targeting PLCB3 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy.

Author information:
(1)Neurobiology Research Unit, Copenhagen University Hospital Rigshospitalet,

Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is a network disorder extending beyond the 
structurally defined epileptogenic zone. Resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) 
may provide information on brain network alterations relevant to seizure outcome 
and cognitive risk after epilepsy surgery. We reviewed rsfMRI studies in TLE 
surgical cohorts to evaluate postoperative network changes, preoperative 
predictors of seizure outcome, and associations between functional connectivity 
and cognition. This systematic review followed PRISMA guidelines and was 
registered in PROSPERO. Fifteen studies were included, comprising 474 TLE 
patients who underwent resective epilepsy surgery and had at least 1 year of 
follow-up. Studies were reviewed for patient population, surgery, rsfMRI 
methodology, networks or regions, outcome definition, postoperative network 
changes, and cognitive assessments. Despite heterogeneity in patient selection, 
surgery, rsfMRI analysis, and outcome definition, studies consistently reported 
reduced DMN-related connectivity in TLE compared with healthy controls. 
Postoperative functional connectivity in seizure-free patients shifted toward 
healthy controls patterns in few studies. Preoperative rsfMRI-based prediction 
models showed promising accuracy for predicting seizure outcome but were 
generally developed in small cohorts and lacked external validation. Evidence 
relating rsfMRI to cognition was limited, but implicated thalamic, ascending 
reticular activating system, and thalamo-occipital connectivity in attention, 
language, and executive functions. RsfMRI is a promising research biomarker for 
network-level risk stratification in TLE surgery, particularly for seizure 
outcome prediction and postoperative network reorganization. Current evidence 
remains insufficient for clinical implementation. Future studies require larger 
homogeneous multicenter cohorts, standardized acquisition and preprocessing, 
consistent outcome definitions, systematic postoperative rsfMRI, 
neuropsychological assessment, and external validation of prediction models.

Interpersonal neural synchrony and parent-child behaviors during naturalistic 
interactions: A systematic review.

De Leener M(1), Sfeir M(2), Galdiolo S(2), Rossignol M(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Cognitive Psychology and Neuropsychology, Faculty of Psychology 
and Education, University of Mons, Mons, Belgium; Interdisciplinary Research 
Center in Psychophysiology and Cognitive Electrophysiology, Mons, Belgium; The 
Distress Lab, University of Mons, Mons, Belgium. Electronic address: 
Melanie.deleener@umons.ac.be.
(2)The Distress Lab, University of Mons, Mons, Belgium; Department of Clinical 
Psychology, Faculty of Psychology and Education, University of Mons, Mons, 
Belgium.
(3)Department of Cognitive Psychology and Neuropsychology, Faculty of Psychology 
and Education, University of Mons, Mons, Belgium; Interdisciplinary Research 
Center in Psychophysiology and Cognitive Electrophysiology, Mons, Belgium; The 
Distress Lab, University of Mons, Mons, Belgium.

Interpersonal neural synchrony (INS), defined as the temporal alignment of 
neural activity between socially interacting individuals, has been proposed as 
an index of parent-child interaction quality. However, its relationship with 
moment-to-moment adjustment of parent-child behavior remains insufficiently 
understood. This systematic review examined associations between INS and 
observable behavior during naturalistic parent-child interactions, the factors 
influencing these associations, and the methods used to investigate them. 
Following PRISMA guidelines, systematic searches of Scopus, PubMed, and 
ScienceDirect identified 15 peer-reviewed empirical studies involving children 
from preschool age to early adolescence. INS-behavior associations were 
heterogeneous across studies. Higher INS was most consistently associated with 
mutual engagement, shared positive affect, and supportive parenting, whereas 
findings concerning reciprocity, responsiveness, and child agency were more 
context-dependent. Time-resolved analyses further indicated that INS fluctuated 
in relation to specific behavioral events and revealed temporally asymmetric 
patterns in which parent or child neural activity preceded that of the 
interaction partner. However, these patterns do not establish causal 
directionality and may partly reflect shared exposure to task-related or 
interactional inputs. Task structure and the availability of direct social cues 
appeared to shape INS-behavior associations, while parental stress and child 
social functioning emerged as potential sources of variability in INS. 
Methodologically, the findings highlight the value of combining micro- and 
macro-level behavioral coding with time-resolved and directionality-sensitive 
analyses, alongside stronger controls for spurious synchrony and common inputs. 
Given the limited number and methodological heterogeneity of available studies, 
the findings should be regarded as preliminary and primarily 
hypothesis-generating.

In vitro inhibitory activity of recombinant olive flounder interferon-γ produced 
in Chlorella vulgaris against viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus infection.

Kim MJ(1), Kim SH(2), Choi TJ(3).

Author information:
(1)Ecological Risk Research Department, Korea Institute of Ocean Science &

(2)Department of Microbiology and School of Marine and Fisheries Sciences,

Viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus (VHSV) is a major viral pathogen that causes 
substantial and persistent economic losses in olive flounder aquaculture. In 
this study, recombinant olive flounder interferon-γ (IFN-γ) was produced in the 
eukaryotic green microalga Chlorella vulgaris PKVL7422, and its in vitro 
antiviral activity was evaluated in epithelioma papulosum cyprini (EPC) cells. A 
codon-optimized olive flounder IFN-γ gene was introduced into C. vulgaris, and 
Western blot analysis showed that the recombinant protein was detected mainly in 
the culture supernatant. Cytotoxicity assays showed no detectable cytotoxicity 
at the concentrations tested in the antiviral assays, and cell viability 
remained above 85.6% even at 10,000 ng/mL. Antiviral activity was evaluated 
using recombinant VHSV expressing enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP). 
Plaque assay showed that recombinant IFN-γ reduced VHSV infectivity in a 
dose-dependent manner, with an IC50 of 15.42 ng/mL and reduced infectivity to 
approximately 0% at concentrations of 100 ng/mL or higher. Fluorescence 
microscopy and flow cytometric analysis showed that recombinant IFN-γ reduced 
the VHSV-positive EPC cell population from 60.22% in the infected control group 
to 28.47%, 9.57%, and 4.92% at concentrations of 20, 50, and 100 ng/mL, 
respectively. In addition, recombinant IFN-γ induced the expression of antiviral 
immune-related genes, including STAT1 and ISG15, in EPC cells. These findings 
suggest that recombinant olive flounder IFN-γ produced in C. vulgaris retains 
biological activity after purification and exerts a dose-dependent antiviral

INTRODUCTION: The tumor suppressor TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in 
human cancer, and drugs targeting specific mutant p53 proteins have been 
developed. Rezatapopt, which reactivates the Y220C p53 protein, was recently 
evaluated in the Phase I PYNNACLE trial in patients with solid tumors, with 
promising results. The trial did not enrol any non-small cell lung cancer 
(NSCLC) cases, and little is known about the clinicopathological characteristics 
and genetic profile of the TP53 Y220C NSCLC patients.
METHODS: In this multicenter, European Thoracic Oncology Platform-sponsored 
study, we retrospectively collected data from NSCLC patients from several 
European institutions with Next Generation Sequencing data available.
RESULTS: The study included 28,244 NSCLC patients. We found that 195 (0.7%) 
harbored the TP53 Y220C mutation, a prevalence higher than the average in solid 
tumors (0.4%). Half of these TP53 Y220C NSCLC patients did not carry any known 
drivers. No significant association was observed between the TP53 Y220C and 
gender, smoking status, histology or stage. However, the mutation was 
significantly more prevalent in EGFR-mutant than EGFR-wild-type tumors (1.7% vs. 
0.7%; p=0.029). Finally, 17.0% of Y220C patients carried a second mutation in 
TP53.
CONCLUSIONS: The TP53 Y220C has a frequency similar to other low abundance, 
actionable alterations in NSCLC. Patients with NSCLC should be screened and 
included in future trials of Y220C reactivators. Co-mutations in TP53 should 
also be analyzed, since they might be associated with intrinsic resistance.

BACKGROUND: Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and isolated left 
ventricular dilatation (ILVD) are defined as left ventricular (LV) dilatation, 
with reduced or preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), 
respectively. We aimed to assess the prognostic value of late gadolinium 
enhancement (LGE) findings, including LGE extent, location, and number of areas 
to predict all-cause death in ILVD and DCM, separately.
METHODS: Between 2008 and 2021, we conducted a bicentric retrospective study 
including all consecutive ILVD and DCM patients referred for cardiovascular 
magnetic resonance (CMR). The primary outcome was all-cause death. A 
propensity-score matching was performed to balance characteristics between ILVD 
and DCM populations. Cox regressions were performed to determine the prognostic 
value of each LGE feature.
RESULTS: Of 2,752 patients (age 52±8 years, 56% males), 408 (15%) patients died 
after a median (interquartile range) follow-up of 9 (7-12) years, including 268 
(16%) of 1,668 DCM patients and 140 (13%) of 1,084 ILVD patients. Overall, 737 
(27%) patients had LGE, including 472 (28%) of 1,668 DCM patients and 265 (24%) 
of 1,084 ILVD patients. After propensity-score matching, in ILVD patients with 
LGE (N=265), the LGE extent (hazard ratio [HR] 1.38, 95% confidence interval 
[CI]: 1.06-1.78, p=0.015), multiple LGE areas (HR=3.39, 95% CI: 1.66-6.92, 
p<0.001), and its septal location (HR=2.68, 95% CI: 1.59-4.52, p<0.001) were 
strong prognosticators of death after adjustment. Similarly, after 
propensity-score matching, in DCM patients with LGE (N=277), the LGE extent 
(HR=1.39, 95% CI: 1.06-1.83, p=0.018), multiple LGE areas (HR=2.70, 95% CI: 
1.20-6.08, p=0.017), and its septal location (HR=2.82, 95% CI: 1.47-5.41, 
p=0.002) were strongly associated with death. The CMR LGE score performed well 
in participants with LGE (area under the curve [AUC] at 10 years, 0.79 [95% CI: 
0.69-0.89]).
CONCLUSIONS: LGE findings were strongly and independently associated with death 
in both ILVD and DCM patients, with each successive LGE characteristic providing 
significant incremental prognostic value beyond traditional prognosticators, 
including LVEF.

Multi-Modal Biometric Fusion for Athletic Performance Optimization: Clinical 
Validation of the Dynamic Multi-Sensor Fusion Classifier (DMSFC).

Tian W(1), Chen Y(2).

Author information:
(1)PhD. School of Physical Education, Baoshan University, Yunnan 678000, China.
(2)PhD. School of Physical Education, Baoshan University, Yunnan 678000, China. 
Electronic address: yafeichenn717sa@siteprofree.email.

Integrating real-time biometric monitoring into sports science is increasingly 
important for optimizing athletic performance and reducing injury risk. However, 
many existing systems have limited capacity to accurately combine data from 
multiple biometric sources. This study evaluated the Dynamic Multisensor Fusion 
(DMSFC) classifier for analyzing physiological and functional data collected 
from multiple biometric modalities, including electrocardiography (ECG), 
fingerprint measurements, and facial recognition. A multimodal biometric 
framework based on DMSFC was developed to monitor and classify key health and 
performance indicators in elite athletes. The variables evaluated included heart 
rate (HR), oxygen saturation (SpO₂), blood pressure (BP), flexibility, muscle 
strength, and endurance capacity. The performance of the classifier was 
evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver 
operating characteristic curve (AUC). After implementing the proposed monitoring 
framework, improvements were observed in the evaluated performance and health 
indicators. The mean heart rate decreased from 78 to 66 beats per minute, while 
oxygen saturation slightly increased from 98% to 99%. Blood pressure decreased 
from 120/80 mmHg to 110/70 mmHg. Flexibility improved from 32 to 36 cm, muscle 
strength increased from 105 to 122 pounds, and endurance capacity increased from 
20 to 24 minutes. Among the evaluated classifiers, DMSFC showed a strongest 
overall performance (i.e., accuracy of 0.94, sensitivity of 0.91, specificity of 
0.96, and AUC of 0.97). These findings suggest that DMSFC could be capable of 
providing an effective framework for multimodal biometric analysis in sports 
science. Its use may support athlete assessment, facilitate the development of 
individualized training programs, and contribute to injury prevention 
strategies. Because the reported physiological changes were observed after 
implementation of the framework, further controlled studies are needed to 
determine whether they were caused by the monitoring system, the associated 
exercise program, or other factors.

From Mesenchymal Roots to Pluripotent Reprogramming: Exosomal Crossroads in 
Regenerative Medicine.

Vardhan MH(1), Srivastava P(2).

Author information:
(1)Center for Nanobiotechnology, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, 
India.
(2)Center for Nanobiotechnology, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, 
India. Electronic address: priyanka@vit.ac.in.

Despite growing interest in exosome-based regenerative therapies, conventional 
mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) and somatic cell derived exosomes face persistent 
translational barriers, including donor heterogeneity, ethical constraints, 
limited scalability, and batch-to-batch variability. It remains unclear how far 
induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived exosomes can address these 
limitations, and how their advantages and remaining translational barriers 
compare with those of established MSC exosome platforms. This review synthesizes 
current evidence on the biology, therapeutic applications, and bioengineering of 
exosomes across cellular sources, with a focus on critically comparing MSC- and 
iPSC-derived exosomes rather than cataloguing individual sources in isolation. 
iPSC-derived exosomes are, on the evidence reviewed here, the more promising 
long-term platform; their unlimited, genetically homogeneous, and engineerable 
source material addresses the donor heterogeneity, ethical, and scalability 
limits that constrain MSC exosomes at their root, rather than merely working 
around them. This advantage remains largely theoretical in practice, however, 
since iPSC exosome production, GMP manufacturing, and clinical validation 
currently lag behind the more established MSC exosome pipeline. Closing that 
gap, rather than the underlying biological case for iPSCs, is therefore the 
critical bottleneck this review identifies. The first registered human trials of 
iPSC derived exosomes have now appeared, in stable vitiligo, atopic dermatitis, 
and Moyamoya disease, but these small, early phase, and dermatology or topical 
delivery led, underscoring that closing translational gaps, GMP compliant and AI 
assisted manufacturing, standardized potency and safety assays, exosome specific 
rather than cell inherited genomic risk assessment, and clearr regulatory 
pathways will determine whether either platform, or a combination of both, moves 
from this narrow clinical foothold to routine use.

A Cloud-Enabled LIMS-QMS Platform With Large Language Model-Assisted Standard 
Operating Procedure Generation for GLP/GMP-Aligned Theranostics Laboratory 
Operations.

Durmaz FA(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Biomedical Engineering, Istinye University, Istanbul, Türkiye; 
Biomedical Institute, Boğaziçi University, Istanbul, Türkiye. Electronic 
address: aytacd@gmail.com.

Theranostic development centers operate under stringent good laboratory practice 
(GLP) and good manufacturing practice (GMP) requirements that fragmented, 
paper-based workflows cannot adequately support. This paper presents the design, 
regulatory compliance mapping, and pilot deployment of the Laboratory Tracking 
Software (LTS) platform, a cloud-ready, web-based system that unifies laboratory 
information management system (LIMS) and quality management system (QMS) 
functions under a risk-based Computer Software Assurance (CSA) framework aligned 
with U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 21 CFR Part 11 and ISO/IEC 17025. 
The platform operationalizes a 6×6 deterministic request-and-service lifecycle 
across nine governance modules and embeds a large language model (LLM)-assisted 
module that, from a single service-name input, generates structured standard 
operating procedures (SOPs), identifies required consumables and instruments, 
performs operational risk assessment, and proposes an executable workflow. Pilot 
deployment across 187 laboratory requests is reported descriptively (23-day mean 
turnaround time, 1,456 quality-control checkpoints, and 43 deviation-handling 
episodes); because no comparable pre-deployment dataset could be reconstructed, 
these values are not interpreted as efficiency or error-reduction gains. A 21 
CFR Part 11-aligned control matrix and a CSA-based verification package document 
authenticated electronic approvals, activity records, two-factor authentication 
(2FA), and role-based access control (RBAC); a consolidated high-risk 
user-acceptance campaign executed 31 of 31 scripted scenarios successfully, with 
independent reviewer and approver sign-off still pending. Beyond the original 
single BRAF droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) illustrative case, a document-level 
evaluation was performed across a locked corpus of 20 laboratory services (10 
analysis and 10 synthesis workflows). All 280 mandatory template elements were 
present (100.0% template adherence), and none of the 80 predefined automated 
document-control checks was flagged (0.0%). Expert-adjudicated error rate, human 
edit distance, and time saving were not measured and are deferred to a 
prospective follow-up study. Comparative analysis against QT9 ERP/QMS, RAMS®, 
and SENAITE LIMS positions the platform as a governance-first, 
theranostic-specific informatics system with native LLM-assisted documentation 
generation, a capability absent from existing commercial and open-source 
alternatives. The results indicate that integrating LLM-assisted document 
generation into a regulated laboratory informatics platform is technically 
feasible; however, given the hallucination risk documented in the medical LLM 
literature, systematic human-in-the-loop validation of generated content remains 
a prerequisite for unsupervised deployment in GLP/GMP settings. The revised 
design description additionally specifies a template-constrained prompting 
strategy, a generation-record schema supporting prompt and output 
reconstruction, a model-change-control procedure, an explicit LLM data-privacy 
boundary, and alignment with the January 2026 FDA/EMA guiding principles of good 
artificial intelligence (AI) practice in drug development.

Improving Data Quality, Model Transparency and Performance in Lung 
Histopathology with Explainable AI.

Rashed SK(1), Nilsson M(2), Aits S(3).

Author information:
(1)Cell Death, Lysosomes and Artificial Intelligence Group, Department of 
Experimental Medical Science, Faculty of Medicine, Lund University, Lund, 
Sweden.
(2)Centre for Mathematical Sciences, Faculty of Engineering Lund University, 
Lund, Sweden.
(3)Cell Death, Lysosomes and Artificial Intelligence Group, Department of 
Experimental Medical Science, Faculty of Medicine, Lund University, Lund, 
Sweden. Electronic address: sonja.aits@med.lu.se.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have shown strong capabilities for image 
analysis. However, deploying these models in medical settings is complicated by 
their limited transparency. Over recent years, many approaches have been 
developed to overcome the so-called "black box" problem of deep neural networks. 
Here, we show how such explainable AI (XAI) approaches can be applied to not 
only improve transparency but also training data quality and model performance, 
with classification of lung damage in histopathology images as use case. First, 
we conducted a thorough exploratory data analysis and visually compared the 
compressed multi-dimensional representations of the histology images from the 
last CNN layers with labels given by pathologists to reveal flaws in the 
training data. Second, we used Gradient-based Class Activation Mapping 
(Grad-CAM) as well as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values to identify 
image regions that significantly contributed to the model decisions. To overcome 
identified shortcomings, we then finetuned additional top layers of the CNNs and 
introduced model architectures with attention which improved model performance. 
In summary, we developed a practical workflow that uses interpretability 
analyses to examine model perception, assess label consistency, and guide model 
refinement on the example of lung histopathology scoring, demonstrating how XAI 
approaches can increase both transparency and model performance. The code for 
this paper is shared at https://github.com/Aitslab/Histology_XAI.git.

NU-1025 Modulates Immunogenic Cell Death in Bladder Cancer: A Multi-omics 
Insight.

Li Y(1), Zuo L(2), Dong X(3), Sun R(3), Liu H(4).

Author information:
(1)Laboratory of Urology, Affiliated Hospital of Guangdong Medical University, 
Zhanjiang, Guangdong Province, 524001, P.R. China. Electronic address: 
liyutong@gdmu.edu.cn.
(2)Department of Traditional Chinese Medicine, The Second Affiliated Hospital of 
Guangdong Medical University, Zhanjiang, Guangdong Province 524003, P.R. China.
(3)Laboratory of Urology, Affiliated Hospital of Guangdong Medical University, 
Zhanjiang, Guangdong Province, 524001, P.R. China.
(4)Laboratory of Urology, Affiliated Hospital of Guangdong Medical University, 
Zhanjiang, Guangdong Province, 524001, P.R. China. Electronic address: 
lhwhongwei@gdmu.edu.cn.

Immune checkpoint blockade has shown limited efficacy in bladder cancer, 
underscoring the need for therapeutic strategies that enhance tumor 
immunogenicity. Immunogenic cell death (ICD) can stimulate adaptive immunity and 
remodel the tumor microenvironment, yet its comprehensive landscape and 
druggable potential in bladder cancer remain unexplored. Here, we performed 
integrative bioinformatics analysis of transcriptomic data from TCGA and GEO 
bladder cancer cohorts to characterize ICD-associated subtypes, construct a 
prognostic risk model, and analyze immune infiltration. Connectivity Map (CMap) 
database and the XSum algorithm were employed for computational drug screening. 
Molecular docking was used to predict interactions between candidate compounds 
and immune checkpoint proteins. In silico ADMET and toxicology profiles were 
evaluated. The clinical relevance was assessed through independent CT urography 
imaging and PD-L1 immunohistochemistry data. Two ICD molecular subtypes were 
identified with distinct prognostic and microenvironment features. An eight-gene 
ICD risk model was established and validated, effectively stratifying patients 
into high- and low-risk groups with differential survival, immune cell 
infiltration, and tumor mutational burden. Through computational screening, 
NU-1025 was nominated as a top candidate capable of reversing the high-risk gene 
expression pattern. In silico profiling indicated favorable drug-like properties 
and low toxicity risk. Clinical data analysis revealed that high-grade bladder 
tumors frequently exhibit low PD-L1 expression, aligning with the predicted need 
for ICD-inducing agents. Overall, this research decodes the ICD landscape in 
bladder cancer and, via a computational drug repurposing pipeline, nominates 
NU-1025 as a novel candidate with predicted ICD-inducing and/or immune 
checkpoint modulatory activity.

Engineering sticky microbes: A framework for appraisal of microbial cell-cell 
adhesion.

Schann K(1), Algar E(1), Haahr M(1), Miller CS(2), de Lorenzo V(1), 
Martínez-García E(3).

Author information:
(1)Centro Nacional de Biotecnología (CNB-CSIC), Systems Biology Department, 
28049 Madrid, Spain.
(2)Department of Integrative Biology, University of Colorado Denver CO 80204 
USA.
(3)Centro Nacional de Biotecnología (CNB-CSIC), Systems Biology Department, 
28049 Madrid, Spain. Electronic address: vdlorenzo@cnb.csic.es.

Engineering bacterial consortia is key in biotechnological applications where 
specific spatial interactions among their components determine system 
performance. Genetic tools for programming cell-cell binding such as the 
nanobody-antigen (Nb-Ag; relying on non-covalent binding) and SpyCatcher-SpyTag 
(Spy; based on covalent linkage) systems are increasingly adopted as assets for 
enabling specific interactions of interest among otherwise detached members of a 
given combination of strains or species. Yet, despite the potential of these 
technologies, a robust metrology to quantify and compare the efficacy, 
stability, and specificity of inter-cell binding in a consortium is lacking. 
This work introduces a conceptual and experimental framework to systematically 
evaluate synthetic binding systems by combining aggregation assays, flow 
cytometry, and microscopy. Together, these techniques provide detailed insights 
into the structure and composition of engineered bacterial aggregates. This 
methodology was benchmarked with two Escherichia coli strains tagged with 
different fluorescent markers and engineered to surface-display matching 
adhesins. Under the test conditions, results showed that the Spy system 
outperformed the Nb-Ag system in terms of aggregation speed and stability. We 
also applied the same metrics for assessing the efficacy of the Spy system to 
mediate synthetic consortia of the pathogenic bacterium Enterobacter cloacae. 
The robustness of the results suggests the proposed framework to become a 
valuable tool for quantitative studies on designer bacterial consortia.

Host physiological constraints limit microbial production of partially 
acetylated chitooligosaccharides.

Snoeck S(1), Malik H(1), Demeester W(1), Duchi D(1), Lips W(1), Guidi C(1), 
Moerschbacher BM(2), De Mey M(3).

Author information:
(1)Center for Synthetic Biology, Department of Biotechnology, University of 
Ghent, Belgium.
(2)Institute for Biology and Biotechnology of Plants, University of Münster, 
Germany.
(3)Center for Synthetic Biology, Department of Biotechnology, University of 
Ghent, Belgium. Electronic address: marjan.demey@ugent.be.

Chitooligosaccharides (COS) are versatile biomolecules with applications across 
food, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries. Expanding the COS portfolio, 
particularly with partially acetylated COS (paCOS) possessing defined structural 
characteristics, including degree of deacetylation and pattern of acetylation, 
is essential for advancing structure-function studies and enabling tailored 
applications. This study investigates the heterologous co-expression of chitin 
deacetylases (CDAs) with a chitin oligosaccharide synthase (oCS) RhNodC in 
Escherichia coli for the in vivo production of paCOS. Although this approach 
enables paCOS formation, co-expression of NodC and CDAs results in reduced COS 
yields and incomplete conversion of fully acetylated COS into paCOS. To identify 
potential cellular bottlenecks underlying these limitations, stress responses 
were monitored using a stress promoter-based fluorescent reporter system. CDA 
co-expression activated protein quality control and membrane-associated stress 
responses. Furthermore, confocal microscopy revealed altered intracellular 
localization of both RhNodC and CDAs compared to individual expression, with 
enzymes detected in the cytoplasm, membrane and inclusion bodies. Co-expression 
also resulted in pronounced cellular elongation, further indicating cellular 
stress during pathway implementation. Together, these findings reveal cellular 
bottlenecks associated with enzyme co-expression and highlight the need for 
deeper exploration of RhNodC-CDA co-expression and approaches to mitigate 
cellular stress to improve in vivo paCOS production.

Single-cell and spatial epitranscriptomics of m(6)A: Technologies, regulatory 
mechanisms, and biological insights.

Mukherjee O(1), Sarkar K(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Biotechnology, School of Bioengineering, SRM Institute of 
Science and Technology, Kattankulathur, Tamil Nadu, 603203, India.
(2)Department of Biotechnology, School of Bioengineering, SRM Institute of 
Science and Technology, Kattankulathur, Tamil Nadu, 603203, India. Electronic 
address: koustavsarkar@gmail.com.

Transcription serves as the primary mRNA blueprint for gene expression; however, 
transcription function is further regulated by co-transcriptional and 
post-transcriptional mechanisms, including N6-methyladenosine (m6A), the most 
widespread internal mRNA modification. The mammalian m6A landscape is primarily 
established by the METTL3-METTL14 writer complex, with METTL3 serving as its 
catalytic subunit, while accessory writer components, erasers, and readers 
contribute to the regulation and interpretation of m6A marks. Conventional bulk 
sequencing averages m6A profiles across large cell populations, masking cell- 
and tissue-specific heterogeneity in m6A deposition and interpretation. Studies 
show that the functional outcome of METTL3-mediated m6A deposition depends on 
the co-expression of the reader and eraser proteins in the same cell, and that 
these vary across cell types, developmental stages, and tissue compartments. 
Recent single-cell and spatial epitranscriptomic technologies are beginning to 
resolve this context-dependent regulation, revealing that m6A can promote mRNA 
decay, translation, stabilization, or altered splicing depending on cellular 
context. In this review, we discuss emerging technologies for single-cell and 
spatially resolved m6A profiling, using METTL3 as a conceptual framework for 
understanding how m6A deposition is linked to transcriptional state and 
subsequently decoded by cell-specific regulatory machinery. We further discuss 
their applications, technological challenges, multi-omics integration, and 
clinical potential in development, immunity, neuronal biology, and cancer.

Intrinsic and extrinsic connectivity of the seizure onset zone at rest and 
during stimulation.

LaRocque JJ(1), Ojemann WKS(2), Xu J(3), Lucas A(4), Sinha N(5), Cornblath 
EJ(3), Armstrong C(6), Tomlinson S(7), Marsh ED(8), Sinha SR(3), Litt B(3),

Author information:
(1)Department of Neurology, Perelman School of Medicine, University of

(2)Department of Bioengineering, University of Pennsylvania.
(3)Department of Neurology, Perelman School of Medicine, University of

(4)Department of Bioengineering, University of Pennsylvania; Perelman School of

(5)Department of Neurology, Perelman School of Medicine, University of

BACKGROUND: About half of patients who undergo epilepsy surgery for 
drug-resistant epilepsy have seizure recurrence, supporting the need for 
approaches that more accurately identify the epileptogenic zone, defined as the 
brain areas whose removal causes cessation of seizures. Altered network 
connectivity has emerged as a candidate biomarker of the epileptogenic zone, but 
how connectivity is altered in the epileptogenic zone remains uncertain, with 
prior studies reporting inconsistent results.
HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesized that a difference in intrinsic versus extrinsic 
connectivity of the epileptogenic zone may explain prior discrepant findings.
METHODS: We retrospectively studied a multicenter cohort of 37 adult and 42 
pediatric patients who underwent intracranial EEG recording and brain 
stimulation as part of epilepsy surgery planning. We measured spontaneous 
connectivity using Pearson correlation and perturbational connectivity using 
stimulation evoked potentials, modeling the connectivity according to the 
location of contacts in relation to the seizure onset zone while controlling for 
inter-electrode distance.
RESULTS: For both adult and pediatric patients, resting connectivity was higher 
within compared to outside the seizure onset zone. However, resting connectivity 
between channels within and outside seizure onset zone was reduced. Stimulation 
connectivity followed a similar pattern, with elevated connectivity within the 
seizure onset zone but reduced connectivity from within to outside seizure onset 
zone.
SIGNIFICANCE: These results support the hypothesis that the seizure onset zone 
is disconnected from the rest of the brain but intrinsically hyperconnected. 
This result helps reconcile prior inconsistencies across studies, aligns with 
basic science studies, and suggests an approach for future translational work 
aiming to localize the epileptogenic zone.

BACKGROUND: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is an ultra-rare 
genetic disorder caused by PHOX2B mutations. Patients lack central CO2 
chemosensitivity and require ventilatory support during sleep. Children with 
CCHS have been reported to lack CO2-induced air hunger, but respiratory 
sensations and dyspnea have not been characterized in adults.
RESEARCH QUESTION: Do genetically characterized adult CCHS patients experience 
respiratory sensations and dyspnea during unassisted resting breathing and CO2 
rebreathing, and along which dimensions?
STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: This was a prospective controlled observational study 
conducted on a convenience sample derived from a national cohort of an ultrarare 
disease. Thirteen adult CCHS patients carrying PHOX2B mutations underwent 
Multidimensional Dyspnea Profile (MDP) assessment during unassisted resting 
breathing and at the end of CO2 rebreathing. Healthy controls were studied under 
the same conditions.
RESULTS: Before the study, none of the patients had spontaneously reported 
dyspnea or bothersome respiratory sensations. When prompted with the MDP during 
resting breathing, 9/13 patients described breathing unpleasantness (non-zero 
MDP-A1) versus 0/18 controls (p < 0.0001), and 12/13 fulfilled criteria for 
dyspnea defined as breathing awareness associated with negative affect. During 
CO2 rebreathing, ventilatory responses remained profoundly blunted, yet 
breathing unpleasantness increased. Compared with controls, patients had lower 
sensory and affective ratings, with less frequent air hunger (p = 0.0108). MDP 
ratings did not correlate with ventilatory response to CO2 or genotype.
INTERPRETATION: Adult CCHS patients can experience conscious unpleasant 
breathing awareness at rest and retain a perceptual response to CO2 despite 
abolished or nearly abolished central chemosensitivity. These findings suggest 
respiratory interoceptive pathways beyond canonical brainstem chemosensitive 
circuits and support active multidimensional assessment of dyspnea in adult CCHS 
patients.

Sex differences in dietary leucine utilization revealed by (13)C tracing in the 
cockroach Blaptica dubia.

Pavlović R(1), Bouchebti S(2).

Author information:
(1)Mitrani Department of Desert Ecology, Blaustein Institutes for Desert 
Research, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Midreshet Ben-Gurion, 8499000, 
Israel.
(2)Mitrani Department of Desert Ecology, Blaustein Institutes for Desert 
Research, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Midreshet Ben-Gurion, 8499000, 
Israel. Electronic address: sofia.bouchebti@gmail.com.

Sex differences in amino acid acquisition and allocation are fundamental 
determinants of insect life-history strategies, yet the fate of assimilated 
amino acids after ingestion remains largely unknown. Here, we used 13C stable 
isotope tracing to investigate sex-specific patterns of dietary leucine 
utilization in the cockroach Blaptica dubia. Adult males and females were fed 
artificial diets containing either 13C-labeled or unlabeled leucine for 14 days, 
after which food consumption; body, gut, and fecal mass; gut length; fecal 
isotope enrichment; and tissue-specific 13C incorporation were measured. 13C 
enrichment of CO₂ was also measured. Females consumed less food than males but 
had substantially greater fresh and dry body mass, longer alimentary canals, and 
larger gut mass. Despite consuming more food and having significantly lower body 
mass (almost half that of females), males did not show greater 13C enrichment in 
somatic tissues; no significant sex differences were detected in the brain, fat 
body, muscle, or respired CO₂. In contrast, male reproductive tissues showed 
significantly higher isotope enrichment than female oothecae, suggesting 
differences in the timing and dynamics of nutrient allocation to reproduction. 
Male feces showed significantly greater 13C enrichment than female feces. In 
males, fecal 13C enrichment did not differ between days 7 and 14, whereas 
females showed greater enrichment on day 14, consistent with slower food 
transit. Together, the larger, longer alimentary canal and lower fecal 13C 
enrichment in females, combined with their lower food intake, are consistent 
with greater leucine retention and utilization and may indicate more efficient 
nutrient assimilation in females.

Choi CJ(1), Sung S(2), Kang Y(2), Kim YR(2), Hyun H(2), Kim EJ(2), Choi YH(2),

OBJECTIVES: We evaluated temporal trends in invasive pulmonary aspergillosis 
(IPA) incidence in relation to serum galactomannan (GM) testing intensity and 
compared outcomes by classical host-risk status.
METHODS: Adults with ICU stays ≥72 hours during 2017-2024 were retrospectively 
screened for proven/probable IPA. Consensus EORTC/MSGERC and FUNDICU definitions 
defined the primary cohort. Modified criteria were exploratory. Negative 
binomial and Cox regression assessed incidence and 30-day mortality.
RESULTS: Among 11,707 ICU stays, 135 patients met consensus definitions; 55 
(40.7%) lacked classical host risk factors, rising to 48.9% under modified 
criteria. IPA incidence increased over time (IRR/year 1.40; 95% CI 1.06-1.85). 
After adjustment for serum GM testing intensity, the calendar-year IRR was 0.73 
(95% CI 0.54-0.98), whereas testing intensity was strongly associated with 
measured incidence (IRR 6.15; 95% CI 2.81-13.43). Patients without classical 
host risk factors received antifungal therapy less often (12.7% vs 67.5%) and 
had higher crude 30-day mortality (58.2% vs 36.2%). The adjusted host-status 
association was attenuated (aHR 1.48; 95% CI 0.82-2.66).
CONCLUSIONS: The temporal rise in measured IPA incidence was associated with 
serum GM testing intensity, underscoring diagnostic ascertainment. Patients 
without classical host risk factors were treated less often and had higher 
mortality, although the adjusted association was attenuated.
