Fatigue, Anxiety and Depression 12 Months After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: 
A Population Based Cohort Study.

Okyere DO(1), Nehme E(2), Bray J(3), Dainty KN(4), Dantanarayana A(5), Nehme 
Z(6).

Author information:
(1)Centre for Research and Evaluation, Ambulance Victoria, Blackburn North, 
Victoria, Australia; School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, Monash 
University, Prahran, Victoria, Australia. Electronic address: 
daniel.okyere@ambulance.vic.gov.au.
(2)School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, Monash University, Prahran, 
Victoria, Australia.
(3)School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, Monash University, Prahran, 
Victoria, Australia; Prehospital, Resuscitation and Emergency Care Research 
Unit, Curtin University, Perth, Western Australia, Australia.
(4)North York General Hospital, Toronto, Ontario, Canada; Institute of Health 
Policy, Management and Evaluation, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, 
Canada.
(5)Centre for Research and Evaluation, Ambulance Victoria, Blackburn North,

(6)Centre for Research and Evaluation, Ambulance Victoria, Blackburn North,

AIM: To determine the prevalence and factors associated with fatigue, anxiety, 
and depression 12 months after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA); examine 
their associations with health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and functional 
recovery; and compare symptom burden with population norms.
METHODS: This prospective, population-based cohort study included adults (≥18 
years) who received EMS-attempted resuscitation and survived to hospital 
discharge following non-traumatic OHCA in Victoria, Australia, between July 2019 
and June 2022. Survivors were identified from a statewide OHCA registry and 
completed a 12-month telephone interview. Primary outcomes were fatigue 
(Modified Fatigue Impact Scale), anxiety and depression (Hospital Anxiety and 
Depression Scale). Secondary outcomes included HRQoL (EQ-5D, SF-12), functional 
recovery (GOSE), living arrangement, and return to work.
RESULTS: Of 1068 eligible 12-month survivors, 728 (68.2%) completed follow-up 
(median age 61 years; 555 [76.2%] male). Fatigue was reported by 35.8% 
(250/699), anxiety by 22.6% (162/716), and depression by 18.0% (129/716). Higher 
symptom burden was associated with lower EQ-5D and SF-12 scores, worse GOSE 
outcomes (all p<0.001) and reduced return-to-work rates. Compared with 
population norms, survivors reported greater fatigue (SMD 0.64; 95%CI, 
0.50-0.78;p<0.001), and depression (SMD, 0.12; 95%CI, 0.02,0.21;p=0.02) but 
lower anxiety (SMD, -0.27; 95%CI, -0.35 to -0.18;p<0.001). In adjusted models, 
younger age, preexisting anxiety or depression, diabetes and initial 
non-shockable arrest were associated with higher symptom burden, whereas 
EMS-witnessed arrests were associated with lower symptom burden.
CONCLUSIONS: Fatigue, anxiety, and depression were common at 12 months after 
OHCA and are associated with poorer recovery. Fatigue exceeded population norms 
and may be an under-recognised component of cardiac arrest survivorship.

BACKGROUND: The smart advanced life support (SALS) program was introduced to 
provide prehospital advanced life support under real-time video-assisted 
physician direction for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). This study 
evaluated the association between regional SALS implementation and OHCA 
outcomes.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used difference-in-differences and 
event-study analyses with data from the OHCA surveillance system in South Korea 
and included adult OHCA cases (aged ≥19 years) from 2 years before through 4 
years after SALS implementation in August 2015. The exposure was region-level 
implementation of SALS. Outcomes were the prehospital time interval, prehospital 
return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to discharge, and favorable 
neurological outcome. Pre- to post-implementation changes were compared between 
regions with and without SALS.
RESULTS: A total of 129,207 cases were included. SALS regions had greater 
increases in the prehospital time interval (4.12 minutes; 95% confidence 
interval [CI], 2.91 to 5.33) and prehospital ROSC (1.35 percentage points; 95% 
CI, 0.56 to 2.15) than regions without SALS. No significant additional 
improvements were observed in survival to discharge (-0.35 percentage points; 
95% CI, -1.31 to 0.62) or favorable neurological outcome (-0.35 percentage 
points; 95% CI, -1.08 to 0.37). Event-study analyses suggested differential 
pre-intervention trends for prehospital time, but not for the other outcomes.
CONCLUSION: SALS regions showed greater increases in prehospital time and 
prehospital ROSC without significant improvements in survival to discharge or 
favorable neurological outcome, but the finding for prehospital time should be 
interpreted cautiously because differential pre-intervention trends were 
observed.

AIM: To investigate the association between capnographic changes during pulse 
checks of different durations and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) outcomes.
METHODS: This multicenter, prospective, controlled, quasi-randomized study 
categorized patients according to pulse check duration: Group A (≤5 seconds) and 
Group B (>5 to ≤10 seconds). Five measurements were obtained during the first 
six CPR cycles. Four capnographic parameters were evaluated for each 
measurement: Post-CPR end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2), Pre-CPR ETCO2, loss rate 
(percentage decrease between Post- and Pre-CPR ETCO2), and recovery time (time 
required to regain the previous cycle's Post-CPR ETCO2).
RESULTS: The study included 252 cardiac arrest patients (Group A, n=124; Group 
B, n=128). In Group A, patients with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) 
had markedly lower loss rates and shorter recovery times than non-survivors, 
together with higher pre- and post-CPR ETCO2 values (all p<0.001). Group A also 
had a higher ROSC rate than Group B (36.3% vs. 19.5%; p=0.005). Logistic 
regression identified pulse check duration as an independent predictor of ROSC, 
with Group A having 2.39-fold higher odds of ROSC than Group B (odds ratio 
[OR]=2.39, 95% confidence interval [CI]=1.347-4.242; p=0.003). Pre-CPR ETCO2 was 
strongly negatively correlated with loss rate (ρ=-0.770), whereas Pre- and 
Post-CPR ETCO2 values (ρ=0.96) and loss rate and recovery time (ρ=0.89) were 
strongly positively correlated.
CONCLUSION: Pulse checks completed within 5 seconds were associated with more 
favorable capnographic dynamics and higher ROSC rates than those lasting 6-10 
seconds. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant prospective 
validation.

Identifying the Operational Bottleneck to Shock Delivery After Automated 
External Defibrillator Activation.

Nojima T(1), Yumoto T(2), Obara T(2), Tokioka K(2), Hongo T(2), Kosaki Y(2), 
Tsukahara K(2), Nakao A(2), Naito H(3).

Author information:
(1)Okayama University Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry, and Pharmaceutical 
Sciences, Department of Emergency, Critical Care, and Disaster Medicine, 2-5-1 
Shikatacho, Kita-ku, Okayama 700-8558, Japan. Electronic address: 
t.nojima1002@gmail.com.
(2)Okayama University Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry, and Pharmaceutical 
Sciences, Department of Emergency, Critical Care, and Disaster Medicine, 2-5-1 
Shikatacho, Kita-ku, Okayama 700-8558, Japan.
(3)Department of Emergency, Critical Care, and Disaster Medicine, Faculty of 
Life Sciences Kumamoto University, 1-1-1 Honjo, Chuo-ku, Kumamoto 860-8556, 
Japan.

INTRODUCTION: Cardiac arrest registries record automated external defibrillator 
(AED) use and shock delivery but not post-activation operational timing. We 
aimed to identify the largest measurable bottleneck and an exploratory 
pad-application target for shock delivery within 60 seconds of AED power-on.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed timestamps from remotely monitored Nihon 
Kohden AEDs between January 2018 and February 2026. After excluding inspection 
records, we grouped records into activation events and quantified intervals. 
Shock-timing and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were 
restricted to initially shock-advised events with recorded shock delivery.
RESULTS: We analyzed 8,115 activation events. Median times were 42 seconds 
(interquartile range [IQR], 30-56) from power-on to completion of pad 
application, nine seconds (IQR, 9-11) from pad application to the first 
analysis, and 52 seconds (IQR, 40-66) from power-on to the first analysis 
endpoint. The power-on-to-pad-application interval accounted for a median of 81% 
(IQR, 75-85) of the total power-on-to-first-analysis interval, increasing to 87% 
(IQR, 85-90) when first analysis occurred more than 60 seconds after power-on. 
Among 900 initially shock-advised events with recorded shock delivery, the 
median pad-application-to-shock interval was 15 seconds (IQR 13-17). Exploratory 
ROC analysis yielded a power-on to pad-application threshold of ≥ 51 seconds in 
relation to first recorded shock delivery occurring more than 60 seconds after 
AED power-on.
CONCLUSIONS: The interval from AED power-on to electronically detected 
completion of pad application, encompassing all intervening actions, was the 
largest measurable post-activation bottleneck. Completion within 50 seconds may 
serve as an exploratory process target for first recorded shock delivery within 
60 seconds among initially shock-advised events.

Association between burst-suppression with identical bursts and multimodal 
measures of cerebral oxygenation after cardiac arrest.

Faiver L(1), Tam J(2), Ratay CR(3), Elmer J(4), Coppler PJ(3); Pittsburgh Post 
Cardiac Arrest Service Investigators.

Collaborators: Callaway CW, Darby JM, Drumheller BC, Fong-Isariyawongse J, Okubo 
M.

Author information:
(1)Department of Critical Care Medicine, University of Pittsburgh School of 
Medicine. Electronic address: faiverlk@upmc.edu.
(2)Department of Critical Care Medicine, University of Pittsburgh School of 
Medicine; Department of Emergency Medicine, University of Pittsburgh School of

(3)Department of Emergency Medicine, University of Pittsburgh School of

(4)Department of Critical Care Medicine, University of Pittsburgh School of 
Medicine; Department of Emergency Medicine, University of Pittsburgh School of

OBJECTIVE: Burst-suppression with identical bursts (BSIB) is an 
electroencephalographic (EEG) pattern associated with severe post-cardiac arrest 
brain injury (PCABI). Whether modifiable mechanisms of brain injury underlie 
BSIB is unknown. We hypothesized BSIB is associated with impaired cerebral 
oxygen metabolism, reflected as pathologically elevated jugular bulb venous 
oxygen saturation (SjvO2), higher brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO2), normal 
jugular bulb venous-to-arterial carbon dioxide gradient (PbCO2 gap, and lower 
intracranial pressure (ICP) compared to other EEG patterns.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included patients resuscitated 
from cardiac arrest who underwent EEG and SjvO2 or PbtO2 monitoring. We 
categorized EEG patterns as BSIB, malignant without BSIB, and non-malignant. 
Using mixed effects linear regression, we examined associations between EEG and 
SjvO2, PbCO2 gap, PbtO2, and ICP.
RESULTS: The SjvO2 and PbtO2 cohorts included 109 and 33 patients, respectively. 
SjvO2 did not differ between BSIB and malignant EEGs (β=3; 95% CI, -0.6 to 7.0), 
butwas higher with BSIB compared to non-malignant patterns (β=12; 95% CI, 7.0 to 
16.0). BSIB was associated with lower PbCO2 gap compared to malignant (β=-1.4; 
95% CI, -2.6 to -0.3) and non-malignant (β=-2.6; 95% CI, -4.1 to -1.0) patterns. 
PbtO2 was highest with BSIB, but not significantly higher compared to malignant 
patterns in our adjusted model (β=4.0; 95% CI, -4.7 to 13.0). ICP was lower in 
those with BSIB compared to malignant patterns (β=-19.0; 95% CI, -32.5 to -5.6). 
Interpretation BSIB may represent a distinct subtype of PCABI characterized by 
impaired oxygen metabolism with preserved oxygen delivery and diffusion.

arrest: a before-and-after study (VEntilation during Cardiac Arrest 
Resuscitation Study, VECARS-2).

Jost D(1), Petermann A(2), Tassart B(2), Salome M(2), Lemoine F(2), Liscia J(2), 
Frattini B(2), Derkenne C(2), Lemaire M(2), Travers S(2); Paris Fire Brigade

Author information:

This study compared bag-valve-mask ventilation quality and adherence to the 
guideline-recommended ventilation volume range during 30:2 cardiopulmonary 
resuscitation for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest before and after the 
implementation of real-time feedback. We conducted a before-and-after 
observational study of two sequential adult cohorts with out-of-hospital cardiac 
arrest managed by basic life support teams from the Paris Fire Brigade. A 
bidirectional sensor measured insufflated volume (Vi) and expiratory tidal 
volume (Vt). The display was masked during Period-1 and provided real-time 
feedback during Period-2. We assessed adherence to the guideline-recommended 
range using mixed-effects regression; we analyzed Vt and leak volume using gamma 
log-link generalized linear mixed models. We analyzed 4,300 ventilations in 163 
patients, 96 without feedback and 67 with feedback. Median Vi was lower with 
feedback (471 mL) than without (513 mL, p=0.03 for the first ventilation of each 
cycle) but median Vt was unchanged (235 vs. 243 mL, p=0.84). Vi dispersion was 
reduced by 35% (mean within-patient IQR ratio 0.65 [95%-CI, 0.53-0.77]). Vi was 
400-600 mL in 68% of ventilations with feedback vs. 42% without feedback. In 
contrast, Vt was 400-600 mL in only 14% of ventilations with feedback vs. 15% 
without feedback. In multivariable analysis, leak volume was 12% lower with 
feedback (mean ratio, 0.88 [95%-CI, 0.77-0.99]). Real-time feedback was 
associated with improved adherence to the guideline-recommended range for Vi, 
less dispersed Vi,and lower leak volume. Causal inference, clinical 
significance, and generalizability warrant further evaluation.

Integrating New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) into Read-Across Evidence Streams 
for Short-Chain Nitroparaffins.

Kozal JS(1), Streifer M(2), Hofstetter E(2), Barutcu AR(3), Moreau M(3), Serfass 
P(4), Spencer PJ(4), Maier A(2).

Author information:
(1)Integral Consulting Inc., Boulder, CO, USA. Electronic address: 
jkozal@integral-corp.com.
(2)Integral Consulting Inc., Boulder, CO, USA.
(3)ScitoVation LLC, Durham, NC, USA.
(4)Advancion Corporation, Buffalo Grove, IL, USA.

Read-across is commonly used to fill data gaps for chemical registration and 
safety assessment. Current read-across guidelines recommend systematic 
approaches for evaluating suitability of analogue data for assessing target 
chemical data gaps. However, these frameworks still lack practical approaches 
for consistently integrating diverse evidence, such as data from new approach 
methodologies (NAMs), into final read-across determinations. Herein, we present 
a case study of integration of multiple lines of evidence, including NAMs, to 
assess the suitability of a read-across from nitromethane (NM) to nitroethane 
(NE) and 1-nitroproane (1NP). The three nitroparaffins are structurally similar, 
which historically was considered sufficient evidence for read-across. However, 
data from several other lines of evidence suggest that read-across is not 
appropriate. The nitroparaffins differ in terms of physicochemical, 
toxicokinetic, toxicological, and toxicodynamic properties, as well as the 
identity of aldehyde metabolites. Our analysis reaffirms current guidelines that 
grouping chemicals based on shared functional groups alone is not a sufficient 
read-across justification. Further, our analysis demonstrates how NAMs can serve 
as a critical component to the overall evidentiary basis for read-across 
arguments, which will be particularly impactful in cases where extant in vivo 
data is insufficient to make a read-across determination with high confidence.

Effects of calcium-based amendments on carbon and nitrogen emissions from soil 
and composting systems: a meta-analysis.

Ren X(1), Yang Q(2), Tang J(1), Sha Z(3).

Author information:
(1)Yunnan Key Laboratory of Efficient Utilization and Intelligent Control of 
Agricultural Water Resources, Yunnan Intelligent Water-Fertilizer-Pesticide 
Integration Technology and Equipment Innovation Team, Faculty of Modern 
Agricultural Engineering, Kunming University of Science and Technology, Kunming 
650500, China.
(2)Yunnan Key Laboratory of Efficient Utilization and Intelligent Control of 
Agricultural Water Resources, Yunnan Intelligent Water-Fertilizer-Pesticide 
Integration Technology and Equipment Innovation Team, Faculty of Modern 
Agricultural Engineering, Kunming University of Science and Technology, Kunming 
650500, China. Electronic address: yangqilianglovena@163.com.
(3)Yunnan Key Laboratory of Efficient Utilization and Intelligent Control of 
Agricultural Water Resources, Yunnan Intelligent Water-Fertilizer-Pesticide 
Integration Technology and Equipment Innovation Team, Faculty of Modern 
Agricultural Engineering, Kunming University of Science and Technology, Kunming 
650500, China. Electronic address: zp_sha@163.com.

Nitrogen (N) and carbon (C) losses from cropping and livestock systems 
contribute significantly to global warming and other ecological crises. 
Calcium-based materials, such as lime, gypsum, phosphogypsum (PG), and single 
superphosphate (SSP), are widely used in agriculture because of their 
affordability and multifunctional benefits; however, their overall efficacy in 
mitigating C and N losses across soil and compost systems remains insufficiently 
quantified. Therefore, this study conducted a comprehensive meta-analysis of 279 
published studies (200 on soil and 79 on compost) to evaluate the effects of 
Calcium-based amendments on C and N emissions. The results showed that liming 
significantly reduced N2O emissions by 27.9% in soil and 36.5% in composting 
systems. However, liming significantly increased soil NH3 emissions by 68.4% and 
CO2 emissions by 26%. Gypsum, SSP, and PG reduced NH3 emissions by 15.0%, 49.6%, 
and 64.6% in soil, and by 39.5%, 39.9%, and 54.8%, respectively, in compost. 
Gypsum and PG reduced CH4 emissions by 52.7% and 29.2% in soil, and by 23.2% and 
71.8%, respectively, in compost. PG reduced soil N2O and CO2 emissions by 17.9% 
and 20.5%, respectively, but increased N2O emissions from compost by 101.9%. SSP 
increased soil CO2 emissions by 5.4%, whereas it reduced N2O, CO2, and CH4 
emissions from compost by 25.2%, 14.1%, and 36.9%, respectively. Soil N2O 
emissions decreased with increasing liming rates, whereas C emissions showed the 
opposite trend. Increasing the N application rate stimulated both N2O and NH3 
emissions. In composting systems, the effects of SSP were governed by the 
application rate, C/N ratio, and initial pH. This study provides a comprehensive 
assessment of the effects of Calcium-based amendments and identifies key factors 
influencing their efficacy and differences in their effects across soil and 
compost systems. These findings provide a scientific basis for developing 
targeted strategies to mitigate greenhouse gas and NH3 emissions while 
delivering co-benefits for agriculture and the environment.

Next-Generation CRISPR-Based Molecular Diagnostics for Veterinary Parasitology: 
From Laboratory Innovation to One Health Surveillance.

Basit A(1), Hanif M(2).

Author information:
(1)College of Veterinary Medicine, Yangzhou University, Yangzhou 225009, China; 
Joint International Research Laboratory of Agriculture and Agri-Product Safety, 
Yangzhou 225009, China; Comparative Medicine Research Institute, Yangzhou 
University, Yangzhou 225009, China; Jiangsu Co-Innovation Center for Prevention 
and Control of Important Animal Infectious Diseases and Zoonosis, Yangzhou

Veterinary parasitic diseases remain a major threat to livestock production, 
companion animal health, wildlife conservation, and public health worldwide. 
Conventional diagnostic methods, including microscopy, serology, and 
culture-based techniques, often suffer from limited sensitivity, poor 
specificity, prolonged turnaround time, and dependence on specialized laboratory 
facilities. Recent advances in Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic 
Repeats (CRISPR)-based diagnostics have introduced highly sensitive, rapid, and 
field-deployable platforms for parasite detection. This review critically 
summarizes the principles and recent applications of CRISPR/Cas12, Cas13, and 
emerging Cas14-based diagnostic approaches in veterinary parasitology, covering 
protozoan, helminthic, and arthropod-borne parasites. It further compares CRISPR 
platforms and discusses their integration with isothermal amplification, lateral 
flow assays, fluorescence detection, and portable biosensors to improve 
diagnostic performance. Moreover, current challenges, including sample 
preparation, assay standardization, multiplex detection, regulatory approval, 
and commercialization, are highlighted. Finally, future perspectives on 
amplification-free CRISPR assays, artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostics, 
and point-of-care platforms are discussed. By providing a translational 
perspective from laboratory innovation to field application, this review 
highlights the potential of CRISPR-based diagnostics to transform veterinary 
parasite surveillance and disease control.

Composite polluted wastewater (CPW) containing ammonium nitrogen (NH4+-N) and 
Cu2+ discharged from industrial and agricultural activities poses severe threats 
to ecological environments and human health. Although nitrification and 
biomineralization technologies have been separately applied to the removal of 
NH4+-N and Cu2+, nitrate accumulation was a potential drawback of the former, 
while high toxicity of Cu2+ may triggered bacterial denaturation in the latter 
treatment system. In the present study, Bacillus megaterium was used to 
simultaneously remove NH4+-N and Cu2+ from CPW via heterotrophic 
nitrification-aerobic denitrification (HNAD) and microbially-induced phosphate 
precipitation (MIPP). Kinetic analyses revealed that the optimal cultivation 
conditions for Bacillus megaterium included an initial NH4+ concentration of 100 
mg/L, an initial Cu2+ concentration of 100 mg/L, and an initial pH of 7, with 
corresponding removal efficiencies of 99.7% for both NH4+ and Cu2+. Microscopic 
characterizations demonstrated that the bacteria converted NH4+ into N2 through 
the HNAD process and simultaneously generated alkalinity required for the MIPP 
process, thereby removing Cu2+ via adsorption and coprecipitation. Furthermore, 
the removal of NH4+ inhibited the formation of copper-ammonia complexes. This 
work provides a novel insight into the practical application of integrated HNAD 
and MIPP technologies for the simultaneous remediation of CPW co-contaminated 
with NH4+-N and Cu2+.

Machine learning based optimization of ultrasonic pretreatment and biogas

Çınar A(1), Akkaya EK(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Environmental Engineering, Yildiz Technical University, 
Istanbul, Türkiye; Carbon Management Technician Program, Dogus University,

Anaerobic digestion of livestock wastewater is frequently hindered by severe 
hydrolytic bottlenecks. This study integrates Response Surface Methodology (RSM) 
and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) to optimize ultrasonic pretreatment and 
predict biogas production dynamics. A Central Composite Design (CCD) optimized 
critical ultrasonic parameters (power, exposure time, and total solids 
concentration) to maximize cell disintegration and biogas yields. The CCD 
analysis identified exposure time as the most critical parameter, accounting for 
49% of the variance (R2 = 0.9879). Under RSM-optimized conditions (93.6% power, 
13 min exposure, 2.29% Total Solids), cell disintegration reached 12.4%. 
Concurrently, cumulative biogas production increased by 41% versus the untreated 
control, peaking at 568 ± 36 mL/g total chemical oxygen demand. To delineate the 
non-linear kinetics of biogas generation, a 9-neuron Multilayer Perceptron 
trained via the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno algorithm was constructed. 
Evaluated against an independent blind test set, the ANN yielded acceptable 
predictive accuracy (R2 = 0.9643; MSE = 9520), effectively bypassing the 
limitations of the Modified Gompertz equation in capturing multi-parametric 
dynamics. Sensitivity analysis revealed biogas measurement duration as the most 
influential factor, representing 48% of the model's relative importance. 
Ultimately, while RSM elucidated variable interactions and optimal conditions, 
the ANN reliably predicted complex digestion trajectories, yielding a 
comprehensive optimization-prediction framework for wastewater valorization.

Rapid urbanization has intensified the demand for compact, energy-efficient 
decentralized wastewater treatment technologies. This study investigated the 
long-term performance of a laboratory-scale primary settling tank-down-flow 
hanging sponge reactor (PST-DHS) system operated for over 500 days, benchmarked 
against a conventional trickling filter (TF) under progressively decreasing 
hydraulic retention times. The DHS reactor consistently outperformed the TF, 
achieving 91-95 % COD removal, >94 % TSS removal, and ∼95 % NH4+-N oxidation at 
an ammonia loading rate of 0.254 ± 0.060 kg-NH4+-N/m3·d. Although complete

enriched in the top and nitrifying taxa (Nitrospira and Nitrosomonas) 
predominating in the lower sponge media layers. This spatial organization was 
consistent with the proposed spatial coupling of nitrification and 
denitrification within a single reactor. Collectively, the hydraulic, 
biochemical, and microbial findings demonstrate that optimized effluent 
recirculation improves flow distribution and nitrogen transformation, 
establishing the DHS process as a robust and potentially energy-efficient 
solution for decentralized wastewater treatment.

Huang P(1), Pang X(1), Wang Z(1), Li X(1), Zhang T(1), Huang S(1), Zhang L(1),

Author information:
(1)The First School of Clinical Medicine, Lanzhou University, Lanzhou 730000,

Aging is intricately linked to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). 
Alveolar macrophages (AMs) senescence-induced impaired phagocytosis may 
contribute to persistent airway inflammation in COPD. The P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) 
is a crucial modulator of cellular senescence. However, its roles in AMs 
senescence and phagocytosis remain unclear. In this study, naturally aged mice, 
cigarette smoke (CS)-exposed mice, and MH-S cells stimulated by cigarette smoke 
extract (CSE) were used to compare the degree of AMs senescence and phagocytosis 
between CS-exposed and naturally aged mice, and to confirm the function and 
mechanism of P2X7R. Results showed that pulmonary function gradually declined, 
AMs senescence increased, and phagocytosis decreased with increasing age.

alleviates AMs senescence and impaired phagocytosis, and improves pulmonary 
dysfunction, histopathological damage, and airway inflammation in CS-exposed 
mice. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that the degree of AMs senescence 
and impaired phagocytosis is similar between CS-exposed and aged mice. 
Furthermore, CS may induce AMs senescence and impaired phagocytosis via the 
P2X7R-mediated ROS/p38 MAPK/SIRT1/NF-κB pathway, thereby driving airway 
inflammation.

High-throughput reevaluation of metal ion specificity in the Ca(2+)-binding 
photoprotein aequorin using automated quantitative imaging.

Inouye S(1), Nakatsu T(2), Hisada S(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Biochemistry, School of Dentistry, Aichi Gakuin University, 
1-100 Kusumoto-cho, Chikusa-ku, Nagoya 464-8650, Japan. Electronic address: 
sinouye@dpc.agu.ac.jp.
(2)Department of Biophysical Chemistry, Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences, 
Wakayama Medical University, Wakayama, Japan.
(3)Hamamatsu Photonics, K.K. Systems Division, Joko-cho, Hamamatsu, Shizuoka 
431-3196, Japan.

Aequorin is a Ca2+-binding photoprotein that emits blue light upon binding 
calcium ions and has been widely used as a calcium indicator. Although the metal 
ion specificity of aequorin was investigated in the early 1970s, discrepancies 
among previous studies have left its ion selectivity incompletely understood. In 
this study, we systematically reevaluated the metal ion specificity of 
recombinant aequorin using an FDSS-μCELL® v2 automated imaging system equipped 
with integrated dispensing and highly sensitive luminescence detection. 
Luminescence responses of recombinant aequorin to 29 metal ions (10-8-10-3 M) 
were characterized by measuring maximum luminescence intensity (Imax), 
integrated luminescence over 60 s (Int. 60s), and residual luminescence activity 
following the addition of excess Ca2+. Based on luminescence kinetics and 
recovery of aequorin activity, the responses to metal ions were classified into 
six categories. Ca2+ induced a concentration-dependent flash-type luminescence. 
Similar flash-type responses were observed with Sr2+, Y3+, Pb2+, and several 
lanthanide ions, whereas Ba2+, Ce3+, Ga3+, Mg2+, Nd3+, and V3+ induced weak 
glow-type luminescence without significant loss of aequorin activity. In 
contrast, Cd2+, Co2+, Cu2+, Fe2+, Ni2+, and Zn2+ induced glow-type luminescence 
accompanied by reduced residual activity, whereas Cr3+ and Zr4+ produced no 
luminescence but also decreased aequorin activity. These findings provide a 
comprehensive quantitative reevaluation of the metal ion selectivity of aequorin 
and indicate that flash- and glow-type luminescence arise from distinct modes of 
metal ion interaction with the EF-hand motifs and the resulting conformational 
changes in aequorin.

(2)Division of Surgical and Interventional Sciences, Department of Surgery,

Dysregulated macrophage responses to common surgical polymers contribute to 
implantable medical device failure. While biomaterial characteristics are known 
to influence macrophage behavior, the contribution of the local biological 
milieu and the adsorbed proteins remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate 
how biomaterial physicochemical properties and biofluid composition 
differentially modulate adsorbed proteomes and macrophage transcriptomes on 
common surgical polymers as well as explore the link between the latter two. We 
first quantify the stiffness, roughness, wettability and protein adsorption 
capacity of PDMS, PP, PTFE, HDPE and nylon, and characterize the protein 
composition of plasma, serum and surgical drain fluid obtained from breast 
reconstruction patients. Then, we expose these common surgical polymers to the 
three clinically-relevant biofluids and profile the resulting adsorbed proteomes 
with liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). In parallel, we 
culture THP-1 macrophages on the same preconditioned biomaterials and analyze 
their transcriptomes using RNA sequencing. We find that biofluid composition 
primarily establishes the adsorbed proteomes which the biomaterials subsequently 
refine into material-specific protein signatures. In contrast, biomaterial 
characteristics, except protein adsorption capacity, primarily determine 
macrophage transcriptomes, with stiffness, roughness and hydrophobicity being 
associated with inflammation, metabolic stress and tissue remodeling programs. 
Proteome-transcriptome integration reveals strong global concordance, alongside 
a subset of proteins - particularly lipoproteins and metabolism-associated 
proteins (e.g., zinc-alpha-2-macroglobulin and transthyretin) - that appears to 
disproportionally drive this relationship. Together, these findings support a 
model in which common surgical polymers regulate macrophage responses via both 
direct physicochemical cues and indirect protein-mediated mechanisms. STATEMENT 
OF SIGNIFICANCE: Implantable medical devices fail because protein adsorption 
onto their biomaterial surfaces initiates the foreign body response, culminating 
in inflammation and fibrotic encapsulation. How the composition of the adsorbed 
protein layer shapes macrophage behavior and subsequent inflammation remains 
largely unknown. Moreover, the relative contributions of biomaterial properties 
and the surrounding fluid has not been clearly defined. Integrating proteomics 
and transcriptomics, we demonstrate that biofluid composition establishes the 
structure of the adsorbed protein layer, whereas biomaterial properties refine 
it into protein signatures that are concordant with corresponding macrophage 
transcriptomes. Notably, lipid handling and metabolism-associated proteins 
emerge as potential predictors of inflammatory, metabolic stress and 
tissue-remodeling macrophage responses. These findings establish protein 
adsorption as a critical design consideration in engineering more biocompatible 
biomaterials.

Traumatic massive hemorrhage and surgical bleeding wounds remain major clinical 
challenges, driving the development of high-performance hemostatic materials for 
diverse wound microenvironments. Traditional hemostatic materials can control 
bleeding, but they generally provide limited functionality and are not well 
suited for complex injuries. As a result, multifunctional hemostatic materials 
tailored to specific clinical scenarios have emerged as an important research 
focus. This review summarizes recent advances in multifunctional hemostatic 
materials and the key strategies used in their design. Starting from a 
functional perspective, we systematically discuss the key functions of 
hemostatic materials, including antibacterial, anti-inflammatory/antioxidative 
capabilities, robust wet adhesion, and high mechanical strength, together with 
the major functional components and the common approaches used to construct 
these features. Furthermore, this work further analyzes, from the perspective of 
material form and structural design, how different types of hemostatic materials 
exhibit distinct physical characteristics, clinical advantages, and practical 
limitations, thereby affecting the integration of multiple functions and their 
suitability for specific applications. On this basis, representative 
multifunctional hemostatic materials are categorized by form, and the advanced 
functions and application scenarios of each category are systematically 
discussed. Finally, we summarize current challenges and outline future 
directions, including smart responsive systems, better function integration, and 
design that matches specific clinical scenarios. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: 
Controlling severe bleeding and treating non-healing wounds remain major 
clinical challenges that cannot be fully addressed by conventional hemostatic 
materials. Hemostatic materials with diverse functions have therefore been 
developed for complex bleeding conditions. However, existing reviews have mainly 
focused on individual components, specific functions, or particular material 
forms. Herein, we systematically review the multifunctionality of hemostatic 
materials from the perspectives of chemical composition and macroscopic 
architecture, with an emphasis on recent advances in functional optimization, 
component-structure-property relationships, and the mechanisms and outcomes of 
hemostatic and therapeutic functions.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a life-threatening vascular disease lacking 
effective pharmacological therapies. To identify potential therapeutic targets 
and candidate compounds, we performed integrative genetic analyses for drug 
repurposing by combining Mendelian randomization (MR), summary-data-based 
Mendelian randomization (SMR), and Bayesian colocalization. This framework 
prioritized multiple druggable candidates, among which STAT3 emerged as a key 
regulatory node. Subsequent functional studies demonstrated that emodin 
suppressed vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, migration, phenotypic 
switching, and inflammatory responses. These effects were accompanied by reduced 
STAT3 phosphorylation and nuclear localization. Molecular docking suggested a 
potential binding mode of emodin within the STAT3 SH2 domain, while cellular 
thermal shift assays demonstrated thermal stabilization of STAT3 by emodin in 
intact cells, consistent with target engagement. Notably, emodin and the 
selective STAT3 inhibitor STAT3-IN-13 produced comparable effects, and 
co-treatment did not yield additive efficacy, suggesting overlapping mechanisms. 
In vivo, emodin attenuated aneurysm development and reduced vascular 
inflammation in experimental models. Collectively, these findings identify 
emodin as a candidate modulator of AAA progression acting through suppression of 
STAT3-associated signaling pathways, and demonstrate the potential of genetic 
evidence-guided drug repurposing strategies in complex vascular diseases.

The development of cultured meat scaffolds requires a careful balance between 
mechanical properties and biological functionality to support muscle tissue 
formation. In this study, electrospun cellulose acetate (CA) scaffolds 
functionalized with galactomannan (CA/GM), L-alanine (CA/Ala), and their

modulation of early myogenic and extracellular matrix-related transcriptional 
responses. These findings demonstrate that scaffold composition influences early 
cell responses through combined biochemical and mechanical cues and provide a 
basis for further optimization of scaffold design for skeletal muscle 
engineering and cultured meat applications.

Chronic wounds are a major clinical challenge, commonly associated with 
diabetes, vascular diseases, and prolonged immobilization. Their varying depths 
and irregular geometries require wound dressings that can conform closely to 
complex wound surfaces while maintaining reliable adhesion. Although adhesive 
and dynamic hydrogels have been widely explored for wound management, 
integrating stable adhesion during application with controllable and gentle 
on-demand detachment, while retaining self-healing and injectability for

irregular wound surfaces and on-demand removal. These findings demonstrate a 
dual-dynamic-covalent hydrogel strategy that combines conformability, stable 
adhesion, and temperature-triggered atraumatic removal, providing a promising 
approach for the development of adaptive wound dressings for chronic wound 
management.

Non-equimolar stereocomplex polylactide fibers strengthen and toughen 
poly((L)-lactic acid) via interfacial stereocomplexation while retaining 
transparency.

Sun DX(1), Wang AY(1), Zhang ZX(1), Wang Y(2).

Author information:
(1)Key Laboratory of Advanced Technologies of Materials (Ministry of Education), 
School of Chemistry, Southwest Jiaotong University, Chengdu, 610031, China.
(2)Key Laboratory of Advanced Technologies of Materials (Ministry of Education), 
School of Chemistry, Southwest Jiaotong University, Chengdu, 610031, China. 
Electronic address: yongwang1976@swjtu.edu.cn.

In this work, stereocomplex PLA (SC-PLA) fibers with various PLLA/PDLA mass 
ratios were fabricated and subsequently incorporated into the poly(L-lactic 
acid) (PLLA) matrix to prepare all-PLA composites. By deviating from the 
stoichiometric ratio toward PDLA excess, in situ interfacial stereocomplexation 
was triggered, converting the initially weak fiber-matrix interface into a 
robust stereocomplex (SC)-mediated interface. Remarkably, although the PDLA-rich 
SC-PLA fibers (LD12) exhibited the lowest intrinsic SC crystallinity (35.1%), 
the corresponding composite showed the highest SC content and significantly 
enhanced birefringence under polarized light microscopy, together supporting the 
formation of additional SC crystallites preferentially associated with the 
fiber-matrix interphase. Dynamic mechanical analysis revealed that the glass 
transition temperature of the PLLA/LD12 composite was 4.4 °C higher than that of 
neat PLLA, representing the largest increase among the composites and indicating 
pronounced restriction of PLLA segmental mobility consistent with SC-mediated 
molecular anchoring. Consequently, the enhanced interfacial anchoring 
facilitated efficient stress transfer from the matrix to the fibers, promoting 
both crazing and shear yielding during tensile deformation. As a result, the 
PLLA/LD12 composite simultaneously achieved enhanced toughness and strength. 
Relative to neat PLLA, the elongation at break and fracture energy increased by 
285.7% and 418.5%, respectively, while the tensile strength increased by 23.1%. 
Moreover, because of the small refractive-index contrast between the SC-PLA 
fibers and the PLLA matrix, all composite films maintained high transparency 
(>88% transmittance at 750 nm). This work provides a new strategy for designing 
strong, tough, transparent, all-PLA composites through stereocomplex-mediated 
interfacial regulation.

Starch-polyphenol interactions in food systems: Molecular mechanisms, structural 
modulation and implications for nutrient delivery.

Zhao J(1), Zhang Y(1), Chen S(1), Wen X(1), Li J(2), Tang Y(3).

Author information:
(1)College of Food Science and Engineering, Changchun University, Changchun,

Starch-polyphenol complexes (SPCs), owing to their food compatibility and 
structural tunability, are promising materials for the development of food-grade 
nutrient delivery systems. However, the intrinsic relationships among 
starch-polyphenol interactions, multiscale structural evolution, and delivery 
functions remain insufficiently understood. From the perspective of food-grade 
nutrient delivery, this review examines how starch molecular structure, 
polyphenol chemical characteristics, and preparation methods govern SPC 
formation, structural organization, gastrointestinal behavior, and performance 
in food formulations. Current evidence indicates that starch chain architecture 
and polyphenol molecular characteristics jointly determine inclusion and 
non-inclusion complexation modes and, by modulating chain organization, 
crystalline structure, and particle and interfacial properties, further 
influence starch digestion, polyphenol retention and release, and system 
stability. Although existing studies demonstrate the potential of SPCs for 
modulating digestion, protecting bioactive compounds, and developing food 
formulations, the causal relationships between structural changes and functional 
outcomes require more rigorous validation. Moreover, their effectiveness in real 
food matrices and under in vivo conditions, long-term safety, and feasibility 
for large-scale production remain unclear. Future research should integrate 
multiscale structural characterization with dynamic gastrointestinal evaluation, 
establish comparable frameworks for assessing structure-function relationships, 
and develop rational design strategies that balance food compatibility, 
processing feasibility, and delivery performance, thereby facilitating the 
practical application of SPCs in food systems.

Enzyme immobilization can improve catalyst stability and reusability, but the 
relationship between support structure and enzyme performance is often not well 
defined. Here, cellulose beads (CBs) were oxidized with sodium periodate for 
different times to alter their mesoporous structure and introduce aldehyde 
groups for horseradish peroxidase (HRP) immobilization. The resulting dialdehyde 
cellulose beads (DACBs) were characterized using SEM-EDS, FT-IR, XRD, XPS, and 
N2 adsorption-desorption measurements. As oxidation time increased, the mean 
pore size first increased from 13.76 to 14.59 nm and then decreased to 9.45 nm. 
DACBs oxidized for 3 h provided the most favorable balance between HRP 
immobilization and preservation of accessible mesopores, yielding HRP-DACBs with 
an activity of 2.85 U g-1 wet support that retained 71.9% of their initial 
activity after 10 catalytic cycles. The immobilized enzyme achieved >83% 
apparent TC removal over a concentration range of 10-100 mg L-1 at a fixed 
H2O2/TC molar ratio of 6. LC-MS analysis suggested transformation pathways 
involving hydroxylation, demethylation, dehydration, decarbonylation, and 
ring-cleavage-related reactions. DFT calculations indicated high electronic 
susceptibility to oxidation in the conjugated keto/enol and adjacent 
hydroxyl/carbonyl regions of TC. Together, these results show that periodate 
oxidation can tune the pore structure and aldehyde content of the resulting 
DACBs for HRP immobilization, and that the resulting HRP-DACBs can be reused for 
TC transformation.

Structure-property insights of ZnO-embedded poly(acrylamide-co-itaconic acid) 
hybrid networks functionalized with carboxymethyl cellulose, collagen, 
L-arginine, or dextrin.

Akyol Z(1), Orakdogen N(2).

Author information:
(1)Graduate School, Chemistry, Istanbul Technical University, 34469, Istanbul,

(2)Faculty of Science and Letters, Department of Chemistry, Soft Materials 
Research Laboratory, Istanbul Technical University, 34469, Maslak, Istanbul,

Integration of various organic components systematically modulates the 
macroscopic properties of zinc oxide@poly(acrylamide-co-itaconic acid)-mace 
(ZnO@PAIM) anionic gels. The effects of structurally diverse auxiliary 
components; carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), collagen (COL), L-arginine (ARG), and 
dextrin (DEX) were investigated in terms of equilibrium swelling, 
polymer-solvent interaction parameter χ, and compressive modulus in the 
as-prepared G₀ and swollen G states. Due to cryoconcentration effect, 
freeze-polymerized cryogels formed at -18 °C exhibited restricted swelling and 
2- to 4-fold mechanical enhancement, reaching 1419.2 ± 162.9 Pa for 
ARG-integrated hybrid cryogels. Swelling ratios followed Blank > 
ARG > DEX > CMC > COL, consistent with increasing χ values toward theta 
threshold (χ ≈ 0.5). COL-integrated hybrids showed lowest swelling and highest χ 
value (0.4656 ± 0.0012), accompanied by a moderate effective cross-linking 
density (νe = 6.146 ± 0.917 mol/m3). Reflecting short-chain plasticization, 
ZnO@PAIM-DEX hybrids exhibited lowest cross-linking efficiency and highest 
network chain length (N = 22,456.1 ± 4651.7). CMC-integrated hydrogels retained

(G < G₀), with a restricted molecular weight between cross-links 
(Mc = 142.90 ± 23.73 kg/mol). Regarding responsive swelling behavior, increasing 
NaCl concentration from 10-5 to 1.0 M caused 9.1-, 5.7-, and 4.3-fold volume 
reductions in Blank, CMC-, and COL-integrated hybrids, respectively. Alternating 
pH between 2.1 and 11.2 produced highly reversible swelling/deswelling 
transitions associated with protonation/deprotonation of itaconic acid groups. 
These dynamic features highlight the reversible stimuli-responsive adaptability 
of anionic ZnO@PAIM gels, demonstrating their potential for advanced flexible 
hybrid platforms with tunable elasticity for emerging smart material 
applications.

Multi-scale characterization of calcium hydroxide mediated cell wall 
deconstruction during mild pretreatment.

Chen X(1), Liang S(1), Lu M(2), Zhang X(1), Zhou J(1), Wu B(1), Gao Z(1), Jin 
M(3).

Author information:
(1)College of Biotechnology and Pharmaceutical Engineering, Nanjing Tech 
University, No. 30 Pu Zhu Nan Road, Nanjing, 211816, China.
(2)School of Environmental and Biological Engineering, Nanjing University of 
Science and Technology, 200 Xiaolingwei Street, Nanjing, 210094, China.
(3)School of Environmental and Biological Engineering, Nanjing University of 
Science and Technology, 200 Xiaolingwei Street, Nanjing, 210094, China. 
Electronic address: jinmingjie@njust.edu.cn.

The ultrastructural and catalytic mechanisms underlying the efficient 
depolymerization of lignocellulosic biomass into high-quality sugar platforms 
under mild conditions remain poorly understood. A promising room temperature and 
high solid state pretreatment was called densifying lignocellulosic biomass with 
calcium hydroxide (ch) chemicals (DLC(ch)). It synergistically integrated 
mechanical densification and alkaline catalysis to overcome cell wall 
recalcitrance via compression-driven reagent penetration and expansion-induced 
structure loosening. Herein, we performed multi-modal visualization and 
characterization of corn stover (CS) cell walls to elucidate the underlying 
DLC(ch) mechanism. DLC pretreatment initially extruded chemical reagents into 
cell wall interior via mechanical compression. During post-treatment storage of 
DLC(ch)-CS, OH- sustainably catalyzed lignin and carbohydrate bond cleavage, 
while Ca2+ chelated with soluble intermediates to form "cotton-like" 
calcium-organic deposits (~50% reduction in phenolics). Subsequent mild steam 
treatment induced cell wall swelling and the calcium-organic deposits filled the 
nanoscale interstices between cellulose microfibrils, forming a "sandwich-like" 
interlayer structure. This unique structure greatly enhanced cellulases 
accessibility to the otherwise occluded cellulose domains. Calcium-based DLC-CS 
pellets achieved a total sugar conversion of over 90% at a solid loading of 35% 
(w/w) via enzymatic hydrolysis, and the corresponding ethanol concentration 
reached 82.6 g/L. This study provided fundamental insights for the development 
of low-cost and high-efficiency lignocellulosic biorefinery technologies.

Valorization of sunflower protein isolate in biodegradable poly(vinyl alcohol) 
composite films: Structure, properties, and end-of-life behavior.

Ugrinovic V(1), Barac N(2), Pajic JI(3), Katic K(4), Stajic-Trosic J(3), Perisic 
S(2), Grujic A(3).

Author information:
(1)Innovation Center of Faculty of Technology and Metallurgy, University of 
Belgrade, Karnegijeva 4, 11000, Belgrade, Serbia. Electronic address: 
vugrinovic@tmf.bg.ac.rs.
(2)Innovation Center of Faculty of Technology and Metallurgy, University of 
Belgrade, Karnegijeva 4, 11000, Belgrade, Serbia.
(3)Institute for Chemistry, Technology and Metallurgy, University of Belgrade, 
Njegoševa 12, 11000, Belgrade, Serbia.
(4)Faculty of Technology and Metallurgy, University of Belgrade, Karnegijeva 4,

Sunflower protein isolate (SP), a byproduct of oil extraction, was blended with 
polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) to develop degradable composite films for sustainable 
food packaging. SP/PVA films with varying mass ratios (0:100, 20:80, 50:50, 
80:20, and 100:0) and glycerol content (0-50 wt%) were prepared by solvent 
casting. Intermolecular hydrogen bonding between SP and PVA was confirmed by 
FTIR and XRD, which disrupted PVA crystallinity and enhanced compatibility. SP 
imparted excellent UV-blocking properties (transmittance <15% in UVC region) and 
remarkable antioxidant activity, with SP20GL20 achieving 99.4% ABTS radical 
scavenging inhibition. Mechanical properties were tunable by composition: 
increasing SP content reduced tensile strength from 45.2 MPa (SP0GL0) to 5.0 MPa 
(SP80GL0), while glycerol addition increased flexibility, with elongation at 
break reaching up to 200% for SP50GL20 and SP50GL50. Soil burial tests revealed 
composition-dependent degradation: pure PVA showed minimal mass loss (~4% after 
40 days), whereas SP80GL0 reached ~65% mass loss, and pure SP films degraded 
completely within 5-10 days. Physical observations confirmed progressive 
darkening with increasing SP content, consistent with microbial colonization and 
phenolic compound oxidation. These results demonstrate that sunflower protein 
can be successfully valorized into degradable films with tunable mechanical 
properties, intrinsic antioxidant functionality, and a clear end-of-life pathway 
for active food packaging applications.

Ultrasonication-induced modification of functional, structural and rheological 
properties of Rice bean (Vigna umbellata) protein isolate for 3D printable food 
ink applications.

Agarwal C(1), Mehta D(1), Jugran AK(2), Patel MK(3), Sharma L(4).

Author information:
(1)Amity Institute of Food Technology, Amity University Uttar Pradesh (AUUP), 
Noida, 201313, Uttar Pradesh, India.
(2)G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment, Garhwal Regional 
Centre, Srinagar, 246174, Uttarakhand, India.
(3)Advanced Engineering and Design (AED), CSIR-Central Scientific Instruments 
Organization (CSIR-CSIO), Chandigarh, 160030, India; Academy of Scientific and 
Innovative Research (AcSIR), Ghaziabad, 201002, Uttar Pradesh, India. Electronic 
address: manoj_patel.csio@csir.res.in.
(4)Amity Institute of Food Technology, Amity University Uttar Pradesh (AUUP),

The aim of this study was to analyze the effect of ultrasonication treatment on 
the functional, structural, and rheological properties of rice bean protein 
isolate (RBPI) and subsequently use the optimized RBPI to formulate the 
3D-printable food inks. Ultrasonication was applied at increasing treatment 
intensities (5-30 min), at a constant frequency of 40 kHz. FTIR, UV-Vis 
Spectroscopy, XRD, and SEM analysis confirmed that ultrasonication efficiently 
modified the secondary and tertiary structure of RBPI without altering its 
primary structure. These structural modifications resulted in significant 
(p < 0.05) improvements in solubility, water binding capacity, foaming and 
emulsifying capacity, and in-vitro protein digestibility. Particle size analysis 
further demonstrated enhanced uniformity and reduced aggregation, leading to 
improved dispersion behavior of ultrasonication-treated RBPI. Temperature sweep 
analysis demonstrated the formation of a robust protein network. Rheological 
characterization revealed improved non-Newtonian shear-thinning behavior and 
strain, frequency, and temperature-dependent viscoelastic properties of 
ultrasonication-treated RBPI. The developed RBPI-based 3D-printable food ink 
exhibited a higher storage modulus (G'). The results further confirmed the 
presence of a well-defined linear viscoelastic region in the inks and their 
controlled structural breakdown at higher deformation levels. Texture profile 
analysis revealed that the food ink exhibited good mechanical properties, 
maintaining shape fidelity and layer adhesion during printing. The combined 
structural, rheological, and textural results confirmed that ultrasonication 
significantly improved the functional characteristics of the RBPI. The 
functional, structural, and rheological properties demonstrate the potential of 
ultrasonication-modified RBPI for the development of a structured 3D-printable 
food ink.

Ultrasound-assisted proteolysis of pea protein: Structural and peptidomic

Zhao M(1), Sun H(1), Yan Q(2), Jiang Z(1), Chang C(3).

Author information:
(1)Key Laboratory of Food Bioengineering (China National Light Industry),

(3)Key Laboratory of Food Bioengineering (China National Light Industry),

With the increasing prevalence of diabetes mellitus, naturally derived 
α-glucosidase inhibitory peptides have garnered growing attention. Most studies 
have focused on preparation efficiency and bioactivity outcomes, while the 
structural mechanisms governing peptide release remain poorly understood. In 
this study, ultrasound-assisted proteolysis of pea protein was employed to 
elucidate how structural modifications regulate α-glucosidase inhibitory 
activity. Although ultrasonication reorganized protein conformations, subsequent 
pepsin hydrolysis promoted a more ordered and compact structure, resulting in a 
superior inhibition (IC50 = 2.17 mg/mL) than acidic protease hydrolysis. 
Medium-molecular-weight fractions (3-10 kDa) and α-helix-rich structures favored 
inhibitory expression, highlighting the importance of compact conformations. 
Peptidomic analysis combined with machine learning and molecular docking 
identified phenylalanine and glycine as key residues mediating inhibition via π 
interactions and hydrogen bonding. These findings emphasized the structural 
basis for the release of α-glucosidase inhibitory peptide and provided rational 
guidance for the targeted and efficient production of hypoglycemic ingredients 
and nutraceuticals.

Recent advances in cellulose-based dual-mode colorimetric and fluorescent 
sensors for anions sensing: A review.

Nawaz H(1), Wang Y(2), Shabbir I(3), He A(4), Wu Z(2), Xu F(5).

Author information:
(1)Jiangsu Key Laboratory for Biomass-Based Energy and Enzyme Technology, School 
of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Huaiyin Normal University, Changjiangxi 
Road, Huaian, 223300, Jiangsu, PR China. Electronic address: 
8202311006@hytc.edu.cn.
(2)Jiangsu Key Laboratory for Biomass-Based Energy and Enzyme Technology, School 
of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Huaiyin Normal University, Changjiangxi

(3)Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Science, Hong Kong Baptist University,

(4)Jiangsu Key Laboratory for Biomass-Based Energy and Enzyme Technology, School

(5)State Key Laboratory of Bio-based Fiber Materials, Zhejiang Sci-Tech

Anion contamination in aqueous and environmental systems poses severe threats to 
ecological balance and human health, necessitating the development of low-cost, 
eco-friendly, and high-performance sensing platforms for rapid and accurate 
anion detection. Dual-mode colorimetric and fluorescent sensors integrate the 
intuitive visual readout of colorimetric and fluorescent sensing. Among 
biopolymers, cellulose is an inexpensive/low cost raw material with many 
functional groups, which can be modified into wide range sensing materials. This 
review systematically summarizes the latest research progress of cellulose-based 
dual-mode colorimetric/fluorescent sensors targeting common harmful anions in 
recent years. It comprehensively discusses the mainstream fabrication strategies 
of functionalized cellulose sensing materials, including physical loading, 
chemical grafting and composite modification, and elaborates the dual sensing 
mechanisms for anions, based on photoinduced electron transfer, hydrogen bonding 
interactions and specific anion recognition reactions, focusing on key 
indicators such as detection limit, response time, selectivity and stability. 
Based on the structured literature search, and to the best of our knowledge, 
this is the first review devoted specifically to cellulose-derived colorimetric 
and fluorescent anion sensors and organized on anion-by-anion basis. This review 
aims to provide a comprehensive reference and insightful guidance for the 
rational design and engineering of high-performance, cellulose-based sensing 
materials for anion monitoring.

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) is the standard treatment for locally advanced 
rectal cancer (LARC), yet its molecular determinants of response remain unclear. 
We conducted longitudinal 4D-DIA proteomic profiling of pre- and post-treatment 
specimens from 156 patients, including 31 patients with matched pre- and 
post-treatment specimens, and integrated with bulk RNA sequencing, single-cell 
transcriptomics, and functional validation. At baseline, responders were 
enriched in innate and adaptive immune pathways, whereas non-responders showed 
proliferative and metabolic programs. Pre-treatment RAC2, elevated in 
responders, was positively associated with immune activation, oxaliplatin 
sensitivity, and survival, and was validated in GSE139255 and GSE35640 (all P < 
0.05). Moreover, RAC2 demonstrated strong predictive performance (training AUC = 
0.867; testing AUC = 0.857). During treatment, NAC induced fibrosis-related 
remodeling across all groups (all P < 0.05), while responders uniquely preserved 
CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration (P = 0.031). Responders and RAC2-high tumors exhibited 
concordant pathway dynamics during NAC. Single-cell analysis further revealed 
that pre-treatment tumor RAC2, higher in responders, transmitted signals to CD8⁺ 
T cells while receiving inputs from fibroblasts (P < 0.05). In vitro and in 
vivo, RAC2 knockdown reduced baseline tumor growth but promoted under 
oxaliplatin (all P < 0.05). Overall, this study offers proteomic insights into 
NAC in LARC, supports therapeutic decision-making, and identifies potential 
targets.

Renal fibrosis is a defining pathological feature of diabetic kidney disease 
(DKD) and a major contributor to progressive renal dysfunction. Although 
aberrant activation of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β)/SMAD3 signaling is a 
central driver of renal fibrogenesis, effective targeted therapies remain 
limited. Here, using an AI-guided target-prioritization strategy based on the 
deep learning platform Uni-Mol, we selected Celastrol for experimental 
investigation and subsequently characterized its molecular interaction with 
SMAD3. Activity-based protein profiling combined with a competitive 
iodoacetamide-based probe assay identified SMAD3 as a direct covalent target of 
Celastrol, which was further supported by molecular docking and site-directed 
mutagenesis. Mechanistically, Celastrol preferentially engages the 
non-phosphorylated form of SMAD3 and promotes KPNB1-dependent nuclear 
translocation, resulting in the premature nuclear accumulation of functionally 
inactive SMAD3 and reduced association of SMAD3 with TGFBR1. In parallel, 
Celastrol disrupts the interaction between SMAD3 and SMAD4, thereby limiting the 
formation of transcriptionally active SMAD complexes and attenuating profibrotic 
signaling. Collectively, our findings identify SMAD3 Cys421 as a functionally 
relevant covalent site for Celastrol engagement and reveal a previously 
uncharacterized mechanism by which Celastrol regulates the spatial and 
functional state of SMAD3. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the 
antifibrotic activity of Celastrol and may inform the future development and 
optimization of Celastrol-based therapeutic strategies for renal fibrosis in 
DKD.

Pharmacological TRPM8 blockade reprograms patient-derived intestinal fibroblasts 
and mitigates experimental fibrosis through modulation of myofibroblast 
activation.

Nanì MF(1), Rinaldi MM(1), Cerqua I(1), De Cicco P(2), Miraglia M(1), Pagano

(7)Department of Pharmacy, School of Medicine and Surgery, University of Naples

Intestinal fibrosis is a major long-term complication mostly prevalent in 
Crohn's disease (CD) and remains without approved antifibrotic therapies. 
Transient receptor potential melastatin 8 (TRPM8) is a pharmacologically 
targetable ion channel involved in inflammatory regulation, but its contribution 
to intestinal fibrotic remodeling is unknown. This study investigated TRPM8 
association with human stenotic CD and whether pharmacological TRPM8 modulation 
limits fibroblast activation and experimental intestinal fibrosis. TRPM8 
expression was increased in stenotic ileocolonic tissues from CD patients and in 
primary patient-derived intestinal fibroblasts. In these cells, the TRPM8 
antagonist AMTB reduced proliferation and migration at non-cytotoxic 
concentration and attenuated the expression of fibroblast activation, matrix and 
myofibroblast-associated markers. In mice with chronic 
2,4,6-trinitrobenzenesulfonic acid (TNBS)-induced intestinal fibrosis, AMTB 
reduced disease activity and endoscopic severity and attenuated stromal 
remodeling-associated gene expression. Histological analyses further showed 
reduced tissue injury and collagen remodeling, supported by Masson's Trichrome 
staining and quantitative analysis of Picrosirius Red. In contrast, 
pharmacological TRPM8 activation with WS12 did not significantly modify 
fibroblast proliferation in vitro or the evaluated clinical, endoscopic and 
molecular readouts in vivo. AMTB also reduced the TNBS-induced T helper 17 
response without reducing interleukin-23 production by colonic mononuclear 
phagocytes. Finally, fibroblasts isolated from AMTB-treated fibrotic mice 
displayed reduced expansion, lower collagenogenic gene expression, reduced 
contractile/activated fibroblast markers and decreased actin cytoskeletal 
remodeling ex vivo. Overall, these findings identify TRPM8 as a druggable 
regulator of fibroblast-driven intestinal remodeling and support TRPM8 
antagonism as a candidate antifibrotic strategy for stricturing CD.

From Blue Dye to Multimodal-Guided Surgery: The Evolution of Sentinel Lymph Node 
Mapping in Vulvar Cancer - A Narrative Review.

D'Angelo G(1), Ascione M(2), Palumbo M(2), Garganese G(3), Fragomeni SM(4), 
Bifulco G(2), Corte LD(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Public Health, University of Naples Federico II, Naples, Italy. 
Electronic address: giuseppe.dangelo3@unina.it.
(2)Department of Public Health, University of Naples Federico II, Naples, Italy.
(3)Surgery of the Female External Genital Organs, Gynecologic Oncology, 
Department of Women's and Children's Health, Fondazione Policlinico 
Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS, Rome, Italy; G-AURIG - Gemelli Advanced 
Ultrasound Research and Innovation Group, Fondazione Policlinico Universitario 
Agostino Gemelli IRCCS, Rome, Italy; Gemelli Women's Health Center for Digital 
and Personalized Medicine, Department of Life Sciences and Public Health, 
Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Rome, Italy.
(4)Division of Gynecologic Oncology, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, 
Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Largo Agostino Gemelli 8, 00168 Rome, 
Italy.
(5)Department of Neuroscience, Reproductive Sciences and Dentistry, School of 
Medicine, University of Naples Federico II, Naples, Italy.

The surgical management of inguinofemoral lymph nodes in early-stage vulvar 
cancer has progressively shifted from complete lymphadenectomy toward selective 
sentinel lymph node (SLN) biopsy, reducing treatment-related morbidity while 
preserving oncologic safety. This narrative review summarizes the historical, 
technical, and clinical evolution of SLN mapping, from vital blue dyes to 
radiotracer-based validation and contemporary multimodal image-guided 
approaches. A literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus was performed 
through May 2026, including landmark prospective studies, multicenter validation 
trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, guidelines, and studies evaluating 
indocyanine green (ICG) and hybrid radioactive-fluorescent tracers. Early blue 
dye studies established the feasibility of lymphatic mapping, whereas 
technetium-99m, lymphoscintigraphy, and gamma-probe guidance provided the 
reproducibility required for prospective validation. GROINSS-V I supported safe 
omission of complete inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy in carefully selected 
SLN-negative patients, complemented by diagnostic validation in GOG-173; 
subsequent evidence linked SLN tumor burden to prognosis and enabled 
risk-adapted management of positive nodes. ICG-based near-infrared fluorescence 
has emerged as a valuable tool for real-time visualization and may improve 
intraoperative guidance. However, most comparative studies have evaluated 
fluorescence after radiotracer-based localization or defined the SLN according 
to technetium uptake, limiting conclusions regarding stand-alone 
interchangeability. Current evidence therefore supports ICG primarily as an 
adjunct within multimodal mapping rather than as a validated replacement for 
technetium-99m. Future progress should focus on standardized fluorescence 
protocols, rigorously sequenced ICG-first validation, hybrid 
radioactive-fluorescent strategies, and integration of imaging-derived and 
artificial intelligence-based tools into individualized groin management.

Context Is Everything: Tumour-Type-Dependent Prioritisation of Tumour-Intrinsic, 
Microenvironmental and Host Determinants of Response to Immune-Checkpoint 
Blockade.

Wu Y(1), Fan W(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Oncology, The Cangshan District of the 900th Hospital, Fuzhou, 
Fujian 350000, China.
(2)Department of Oncology, The Cangshan District of the 900th Hospital, Fuzhou, 
Fujian 350000, China. Electronic address: 630790845@qq.com.

Predicting who benefits from immune-checkpoint blockade remains unsolved, and 
the search for a single universal biomarker has repeatedly failed: tumour 
mutational burden has no threshold that transfers across tumour types, PD-L1 
expression is inconsistent, and the determinants of response lie on three 
interacting axes - tumour, microenvironment and host - studied in isolation. We 
argue that the predictive weight of each determinant is not fixed but depends on 
tumour type, and we integrate the axes into a determinant-weight matrix: an 
evidence-graded, falsifiable synthesis ranking, for each histology, which factor 
most plausibly governs baseline response. It is a hypothesis-generating 
framework for prioritising which determinants to measure, not a validated 
decision algorithm. Four regimes recur: mutation-led tumours such as melanoma, 
non-small-cell lung, mismatch-repair-deficient and urothelial cancers; 
microenvironment-led tumours such as renal-cell carcinoma, where mutational 
burden is paradoxically misleading, together with sarcoma and head-and-neck 
cancer; host-sensitive contexts in which the gut microbiome and concomitant 
medications become rate-limiting; and cold tumours in which no single axis 
suffices. These weightings follow from the axes converging on one effector 
pathway, explaining why single-axis biomarkers are unstable and why integrative 
scores, though largely retrospective, outperform them. Each cell records the 
weight, evidence tier, context, predictive-versus-prognostic and validation 
status of the determinant, with an explicit rule where axes disagree. The 
framework covers baseline determinants at the point where first-line treatment 
is chosen, and sets immune-related toxicity aside. Presented as a scaffold 
rather than a decision rule, it reframes biomarker selection from a universal 
panel to a tumour-type-calibrated sequence.

The evolution of immunotherapy resistance in mismatch repair-deficient 
colorectal cancer: A spatiotemporal perspective.

Lv Y(1), Ding Y(2), Zhao Z(3), Song S(4), Zang D(3), Zhang J(5), Ji Y(6), Zhong

Author information:

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the therapeutic landscape 
for mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) colorectal cancer; however, primary and 
acquired resistance remain significant challenges in clinical practice. This 
review proposes a working hypothesis that resistance can be conceptualized as 
following an evolutionary trajectory from a dynamic spatiotemporal perspective: 
commencing with early immune evasion by tumor cells, progressing through an 
adaptive immunosuppression phase, and culminating in advanced metastatic 
resistance characterized by spatial heterogeneity. Within this framework, we 
critically evaluate combination therapeutic strategies targeting resistance 
signals at each stage, including dual immune checkpoint blockade, tumor 
microenvironment modulators, novel bispecific antibodies, and neoantigen 
vaccines. We further emphasize that future breakthroughs will depend on 
leveraging single-cell multi-omics and spatial transcriptomics technologies to 
unravel resistance heterogeneity. This will drive the development of dynamic, 
personalized sequential combination therapies, delivering sustained benefits for 
patients.

Tele-Based Ischemic Conditioning for Chronic Stroke: Safety, Feasibility, and 
Preliminary Neurophysiological and Motor Effects.

Madhavan S(1), Cummings M(2), Mathew D(2).

Author information:
(1)Brain Plasticity Laboratory, Department of Physical Therapy, University of 
Illinois Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA.. Electronic address: smadhava@uic.edu.
(2)Brain Plasticity Laboratory, Department of Physical Therapy, University of 
Illinois Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA.

To examine the safety and feasibility of a two-week (seven-session) tele-based 
ischemic conditioning (tele-IC) intervention in individuals with chronic stroke 
and to explore secondary neurophysiological and motor outcomes.
METHODS: Ten individuals with chronic stroke (8 males; age 61.7 ± 7.3 years; 
time since stroke 11.5 ± 7.5 years; Fugl-Meyer Lower Extremity score 20.5 ± 6.6) 
completed tele-IC. The primary outcomes were safety and feasibility. Safety was 
assessed through monitoring of IC-related adverse events and side effects across 
sessions; feasibility was evaluated through screening-to-enrollment, retention, 
intervention adherence, tolerability, and acceptability. Secondary exploratory 
outcomes included corticomotor excitability, transcallosal inhibition, 
lower-limb strength, paretic ankle motor control, and gait speed. Outcomes were 
assessed before and 24 hours after the intervention.
RESULTS: Across 70 tele-IC sessions, no serious adverse events occurred, and all 
10 participants completed all seven sessions. Acceptability was high, including 
ratings for safety (4.9/5), remote assistance (4.8/5), and overall satisfaction 
(4.8/5). Exploratory analyses showed increased transcallosal inhibition 
(d_z = 0.929, p = 0.017), changes in bilateral lower-limb strength 
(d_z = 0.873-1.756), and shorter paretic ankle reaction time (d_z = 0.844, 
p = 0.049). Corticomotor excitability and gait speed did not significantly 
change.
CONCLUSIONS: In this small, uncontrolled pilot study, synchronously supervised 
tele-IC was delivered with complete intervention adherence, no serious adverse 
events, and high participant acceptability. Exploratory secondary 
neurophysiological and motor findings require confirmation in larger controlled 
trials.

White Matter Hyperintensities of Presumed Vascular Origin: Current Understanding 
of Development and Progression.

Shang T(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Neurology, Peter O'Donnell Jr. Brain Institute, University of 
Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX. Electronic address: 
ty.shang@utsouthwestern.edu.

BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) of presumed vascular 
origin are among the most common MRI manifestations of cerebral small vessel 
disease and are a major contributor to vascular contributions to cognitive 
impairment and dementia. Although WMH have traditionally been attributed to 
chronic ischemia resulting from small vessel pathology, the biological 
mechanisms underlying their development and, more importantly, their progression 
remain incompletely understood. Recent advances in longitudinal neuroimaging, 
quantitative MRI, pathology, genetics, and physiological imaging have 
substantially expanded our understanding of WMH progression, making this an 
appropriate time to evaluate current concepts and synthesize emerging evidence.
OBSERVATIONS: We review contemporary evidence regarding the biological processes 
implicated in WMH development and progression, including hypertension and 
vascular risk factors, acute ischemic injury, chronic hypoperfusion, blood-brain 
barrier (BBB) dysfunction, endothelial activation and vascular inflammation, 
arterial stiffness, intracranial artery dolichoectasia (IADE), altered cerebral 
fluid dynamics and genetic susceptibility. Longitudinal studies demonstrate that 
WMH exhibit dynamic trajectories characterized by progression, stability, and 
partial regression, indicating that lesion evolution is not uniformly 
irreversible. Pathological and advanced neuroimaging studies show that WMH 
represent heterogeneous tissue injury involving demyelination, axonal loss, 
gliosis, interstitial fluid accumulation, and microvascular abnormalities. 
Hypertension and blood pressure variability are consistently associated with 
greater WMH burden and progression, whereas baseline WMH burden is the strongest 
predictor of future lesion expansion. Acute ischemic lesions detected by 
diffusion-weighted imaging contribute to, but account for only a minority of WMH 
progression. Longitudinal studies evaluating cerebral perfusion, BBB 
permeability, inflammation, arterial stiffness, IADE and cerebral fluid dynamics 
have yielded variable findings but, together with genetic evidence, support 
roles of BBB leakage, vascular inflammation, chronic hypoperfusion, arterial and 
extracellular-matrix remodeling, and impaired interstitial fluid clearance in 
WMH progression.
CONCLUSIONS: Emerging evidence supports a paradigm in which WMH are viewed as a 
dynamic manifestation of progressive neurovascular dysfunction rather than the 
consequence of chronic ischemia alone. Current data suggest that early 
neurovascular injury evolves into a potentially self-reinforcing process 
characterized by persistent BBB disruption, vascular inflammation, chronic 
hypoperfusion, altered fluid dynamics, and recurrent ischemic injury, 
collectively contributes to WMH progression. Future multimodal longitudinal 
studies integrating cerebral hemodynamics, neurovascular function and 
intracranial arterial remodeling will be essential to understand WMH 
progression.
