CFD-DEM simulation of capsule vibration facilitated powder discharge and 
dispersion in Breezhaler.

Yang Q(1), Li G(1), Xue R(1), Hall P(1), Shi K(2), Dong J(2), Wang Z(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Chemical and Environmental Engineering, Faculty of Science and 
Engineering, University of Nottingham, Ningbo 315100, PR China; Nottingham 
Ningbo China Beacons of Excellence Research and Innovation Institute, Ningbo 
315100, PR China.
(2)Suzhou Inhal Pharma Co., Ltd., Building B12, BioBAY, No. 218 Xinghu Street, 
Suzhou Industrial Park, Suzhou 215125, PR China.
(3)Department of Chemical and Environmental Engineering, Faculty of Science and 
Engineering, University of Nottingham, Ningbo 315100, PR China; Nottingham 
Ningbo China Beacons of Excellence Research and Innovation Institute, Ningbo 
315100, PR China. Electronic address: Zheng.Wang@nottingham.edu.cn.

This study presents a computational fluid dynamics-discrete element method 
(CFD-DEM) investigation on drug discharge and dispersion processes driven by 
capsule rotation and capsule-device collisions in Ultibro® Breezhaler®, where a 
layering dynamic mesh method is employed to characterize the capsule's complex 
rotational and vibrational motions, and a multi-scale model is adopted to 
evaluate the powder dispersion performance by predicting the fine particle 
fraction (FPF) based on carrier particle-wall collisions. The capsule vibration, 
either in continuous or intermittent regime, is found to effectively shake 
cohesive particles off the capsule wall, break particle clusters, and promote 
uniform particle distribution, facilitating complete drug discharge. Whereas, 
neglecting capsule vibration significantly underestimates the actual drug 
discharge efficiency. The particles inside the capsule and the rotation chamber 
are subjected to the strongest mechanical contact forces and aerodynamic forces 
with the former at least one order of magnitude greater than the latter. The 
capsule vibration is found to enhance both types of forces, particularly within 
the capsule. More importantly, capsule vibrations significantly increase the 
total number of particle-particle and particle-wall collisions in the inhaler, 
boosting the overall collision intensity relative to the none capsule vibration 
case. The predicted FPFemitted values for cases incorporating either continuous 
or intermittent capsule vibration regimes show good agreement with the 
experimental data, while the value for the none capsule vibration case is 
markedly lower. This highlights the necessity of incorporating the capsule 
vibration into the CFD-DEM model and validates the applicability of multi-scale 
model for predicting powder dispersion performance in the Breezhaler®.

Mechanisms underlying the promotion of intestinal absorption of baohuoside I by 
Dipsacus asperoides saponin fractions and their synergistic anti‑osteoporosis 
efficacy in combination.

Li M(1), Guo N(1), Zhong Q(1), Qi Z(1), Xia M(1), Feng L(2), Yang Y(3), Jia 
X(4).

Author information:
(1)School of Traditional Chinese Pharmacy, China Pharmaceutical University, 
Nanjing 211198, China.
(2)School of Traditional Chinese Pharmacy, China Pharmaceutical University, 
Nanjing 211198, China. Electronic address: wenmoxiushi@163.com.
(3)School of Traditional Chinese Pharmacy, China Pharmaceutical University, 
Nanjing 211198, China. Electronic address: 1570037600@163.com.
(4)School of Traditional Chinese Pharmacy, China Pharmaceutical University, 
Nanjing 211198, China. Electronic address: jiaxiaobin2015@163.com.

Baohuoside I (BA) is the key active ingredient in the compound anti-osteoporosis 
preparation Xianlinggubao; however, its poor solubility and permeability result 
in low oral bioavailability. This study systematically investigated, from both 
pharmaceutical and pharmacological perspectives, the role of Dipsacus asperoides 
saponins fractions (DAS) in enhancing BA absorption and their synergistic 
anti-osteoporosis effects. From a pharmaceutical perspective, DAS significantly 
improves BA's solubility, membrane permeability, and gastrointestinal stability, 
and forms nanocomposites with BA through noncovalent interactions (as verified 
by DSC, TEM, FT-IR, and molecular dynamics simulations). In vivo intestinal 
perfusion experiments in rats confirmed that DAS enhances BA absorption in all 
intestinal segments; in a Caco-2 monolayer cell model, DAS inhibited MRP2/BCRP 
efflux and reversibly opened tight junctions, increasing the apparent 
permeability coefficient of BA from (1.62 ± 0.21) × 10⁻⁶ to (4.25 ± 0.45) × 10⁻⁶ 
cm/s; Oral pharmacokinetic studies in rats further confirmed that the AUC0-∞ was 
significantly higher in the BA-DAS combination group. Pharmacologically, in an 
ovariectomized mouse model, the combination of BA and DAS significantly improved 
bone microstructure and serum bone metabolism markers compared to BA alone. 
Urinary non-targeted metabolomics results further revealed that this synergistic 
effect is associated with the regulation of Ascorbate and aldarate metabolism, 
Glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism, and Tryptophan metabolism pathways. 
In summary, DAS promotes BA absorption through a dual mechanism of inhibiting 
efflux and opening tight junctions, and the combination of BA and DAS produces a 
synergistic anti-osteoporotic effect, providing a mechanistic explanation for 
the formulation of traditional Chinese medicine.

Traditional ophthalmic solutions and viscous gels are limited by insufficient 
precorneal residence time, inaccurate dosing administration, and inconvenient 
sterile filtration. Pilocarpine, originally a classic muscarinic acetylcholine 
receptor agonist for glaucoma management, has been recently repurposed for 
presbyopia treatment; however, its clinical application is greatly restricted by 
frequent severe ocular adverse reactions, including xerophthalmia and 
conjunctival hyperemia. Herein, trehalose was adopted to modify poloxamer 407 
thermosensitive hydrogel, on the basis of its dual functions of tuning gel 
physicochemical properties and enhancing cellular desiccation resistance. The 
incorporation of trehalose lowered the critical gelation threshold concentration 
of poloxamer 407 without impairing the intrinsic physicochemical properties of 
the hydrogel. The optimized formulation exists as a low-viscosity aqueous 
solution (approximately 50 mPa·s) at ambient temperature, which allows 
convenient sterilization via 0.22 μm filtration, and rapidly undergoes in-situ 
sol-gel transition on the ocular surface to form isotonic hydrogel. This 
hydrogel protects loaded pilocarpine against hydrolytic degradation and improves 
corneal hydration. In vivo rabbit ocular irritation tests verified that the 
formulation effectively alleviates pilocarpine-induced ocular irritation. 
Benefiting from excellent thermal stability and industrial processability, this 
delivery system exhibits promising translational prospects and lays a solid 
foundation for follow-up clinical research on presbyopia treatment.

Impurities of impurities! Investigation of drug-related nitrosated impurities of 
omeprazole using optimized forced nitrosation conditions.

Shivashankar P(1), Kumari M(1), Dikundwar AG(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Pharmaceutical Analysis, National Institute of Pharmaceutical 
Education and Research (NIPER), Hyderabad, India.
(2)Department of Pharmaceutical Analysis, National Institute of Pharmaceutical 
Education and Research (NIPER), Hyderabad, India. Electronic address: 
amol.dikundwar@niperhyd.ac.in.

Omeprazole (OMP) is-one of the most commonly prescribed proton pump inhibitors 
for treating acidity, heartburn, and gastric/duodenal ulcers. The present work 
investigates nitrosation susceptibility of OMP to form drug-related nitroso 
impurities using optimized protocols employing forced nitrosation workflow in 
alignment with nitrosation assay procedure (NAP) and modified NAP. This approach 
allows evaluation of nitrosation propensity of OMP as well as its degradation 
products. A series of 10 distinct N-nitrosation products (NPs) were successfully 
identified and separated via gradient elution liquid chromatography on a C18 
stationary phase (250 mm × 4.6 mm, 5 µm) using 10 mM ammonium acetate and 
acetonitrile as mobile phases. Chemical structures of all the NPs were 
characterized using LC-QTOF-MS/MS analysis. The in-silico toxicity predictions 
indicated carcinogenic and mutagenic potential of the observed N-nitrosated 
impurities alongside qualitative risks such as hepatotoxicity, immunotoxicity, 
and respiratory toxicity in several cases. These findings underscore elevated 
risks from nitroso-impurities of API degradation products, beyond conventional 
API-focused assessments, urging expanded monitoring in pharmaceutical 
manufacturing and stability studies to minimize the patient exposure and enhance 
consumer safety.

Peritoneal dialysis induces hepatic metabolic stress as an instigator for 
systemic inflammation.

Eibensteiner F(1), Herzog R(2), Trauner M(3), Philippe C(4), Patronas EM(4),

christoph.aufricht@meduniwien.ac.at.
(14)Division of Paediatric Nephrology and Gastroenterology, Department of 
Paediatrics and Adolescent Medicine, Comprehensive Center for Paediatrics, 
Medical University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria. Electronic address: 
christoph.aufricht@meduniwien.ac.at.

INTRODUCTION: Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is a lifesaving therapy in patients with 
kidney failure, but results in daily intraperitoneal glucose administration 
corresponding to 50% of the recommended energy intake, most of which enters the 
portal circulation. As the impact of this glucose exposure on liver and 
metabolic health remains unclear, we explored hepatic and systemic metabolic 
effects of PD.
METHODS: Healthy mice and mice with chronic kidney disease (5/6 nephrectomy 
C57BL/6 aged 12-14 weeks) underwent seven weeks of PD. Combining morphologic 
studies, untargeted tissue proteomics, targeted plasma metabolomics and spatial 
transcriptomics, we assessed hepatic molecular and metabolic effects of PD. Gut- 
and gut-vascular barriers, systemic and hepatic lipopolysaccharide abundance and 
zonal transcriptional changes were assessed with multiplexed spatial single-cell 
analysis and transcriptomics.
RESULTS: Intraperitoneally administered glucose during PD was rapidly taken up 
by the liver and induced hepatic metabolic inflammation. Portal-venous glucose 
overload bypassing the gastrointestinal tract resulted in increased 
glucose-to-cholesterol shunting with elevated plasma cholesterol levels, despite 
the absence of hepatic steatosis or glycogen storage. Increased oxidative stress 
and endotoxin load were associated with reduced hepatic Kupffer cell numbers 
without increased gut permeability.
CONCLUSIONS: Ours study found chronic hepatic metabolic stress induced by PD. 
Evidence of hepatic glucotoxicity and oxidative stress as instigators for 
systemic metabolic inflammation induced by PD suggests that similar pathologic

INTRODUCTION: People with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) 
often experience medication intolerance and side effects that worsen with lower 
estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). This prespecified secondary 
analysis assessed the safety of semaglutide by baseline eGFR.
METHODS: FLOW (NCT03819153) was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled 
trial testing the efficacy of subcutaneous semaglutide 1.0 mg once-weekly on a 
primary kidney outcome (50% or more eGFR reduction, kidney failure, or death due 
to kidney or cardiovascular causes) in participants with T2D and CKD. Safety 
data were collected selectively and included serious adverse events (SAEs), AEs 
leading to treatment discontinuation, and prespecified AEs of special interest 
(AESIs). In this descriptive assessment, systematically collected safety data 
were reported numerically by baseline eGFR.
RESULTS: Of 3533 participants, 1767 received semaglutide and 1766 received 
placebo. Fewer SAEs were reported with semaglutide than placebo across baseline 
eGFR subgroups (45.1% versus 50.4% in the 60 or more ml/min per 1.73 m2 
subgroup, and 56.4% versus 60.4% in the under 30 ml/min per 1.73 m2 subgroup). 
SAEs related to infections and infestations; cardiac disorders; respiratory, 
thoracic and mediastinal disorders; and metabolism and nutrition disorders were 
generally less frequent with semaglutide than placebo, regardless of baseline 
eGFR. Treatment discontinuations due to AEs were higher with lower baseline eGFR 
across treatment groups (60 or more ml/min per 1.73 m2: semaglutide 11.2%, 
placebo 11.3%; under30 ml/min per 66 1.73 m2: semaglutide 18.8%, placebo 18.7%). 
Discontinuations specifically due to gastrointestinal AEs were reported more 
frequently with semaglutide (4.5%) than placebo (1.1%), regardless of baseline 
eGFR. Frequencies of AESI were similar between treatment groups across baseline 
eGFR subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS: In this safety assessment, SAEs were reported less frequently with 
semaglutide than placebo, with corresponding patterns observed for treatment 
discontinuations and AESIs. No unexpected safety concerns were identified across 
the spectrum of eGFR represented in the FLOW trial.

INTRODUCTION: While statins are effective for cardiovascular prevention in the 
general population, their benefit in patients with CKD G5D (kidney failure 
treated by dialysis) remains uncertain. Previous randomized controlled trials 
included mixed populations for primary and secondary prevention while excluding 
patients with recent cardiovascular events, leaving a knowledge gap regarding 
statin effectiveness for secondary prevention immediately following an 
atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) event. Here, we address this gap 
by providing real-world evidence.
METHODS: We conducted a landmark-based observational study, informed by the 
target trial framework using the French Renal Epidemiology and Information 
Network (REIN) registry and merged with data from the French national healthcare 
system database from 2010 to 2023. We included adults with CKD G5D who 
experienced an ASCVD event. We used inverse probability of treatment weighting 
to balance baseline characteristics between statin initiators and 
non-initiators, thereby estimating the average causal effect on all-cause 
mortality. Results focus on the relative and absolute risk difference and the 
life expectancy gain using delta restricted mean survival time (dRMST).
RESULTS: The study cohort included 5534 patients (median age: 75 years; 67% 
male). During the ten years of follow-up, statin use was associated with a 
reduced risk of mortality. The survival curves reached a maximum absolute 
difference at year four (risk difference -6.2% (95% CI: -10.2; -2.2); relative 
risk 0.88 [95% CI: 0.81; 0.96]). Life expectancy extended significantly over 
time with a mean survival gain of 69 days at five years (95% CI: 14-125) and 
reaching 135 days at ten years (95% CI: 31-239). No difference was identified 
between groups regarding hospitalizations for rhabdomyolysis or toxic hepatitis.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients receiving dialysis, statin initiation following an 
ASCVD event is safe and associated with a modest-to-moderate ten-year cumulative 
survival benefit. While interpreted within observational limitations, this 
real-world evidence supports their use in this secondary prevention setting.

INTRODUCTION: Abnormal iron homeostasis plays a critical role in 
extra-hematopoietic disorders. The relationship of hepcidin, the master iron 
regulator, to clinical outcomes, has not been characterized in a large cohort of 
chronic kidney disease (CKD).
METHODS: To determine if plasma hepcidin level predicts cardiovascular (CV), 
kidney, and metabolic outcomes in patients with CKD, we studied 3826 patients 
enrolled in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study. Hazard ratios 
for hepcidin tertiles were estimated from Cox Proportional Hazards regression 
for primary outcomes of incident heart failure (HF), end stage kidney disease 
(kidney failure) or halving of the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), 
and new onset diabetes or prediabetes. Secondary outcomes included 
atherosclerotic events and all-cause and CV mortality.
RESULTS: The median and interquartile range of plasma hepcidin level was 43 (22, 
77) ng/mL. Higher plasma hepcidin levels were associated with older age, male 
sex, non-Hispanic Black race, diabetes, lower eGFR, higher albuminuria, 
increased plasma levels of iron indices, C-terminal fibroblast growth factor 23, 
and markers of inflammation (high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and 
interleukin-6). We found no association between plasma hepcidin level and the 
risk for incident HF or prediabetes/diabetes. However, compared to the middle 
tertile, the highest hepcidin tertile was independently associated with 
increased risk for kidney outcomes (hazard ratio 1.19; 95% confidence interval 
1.09, 1.30) and atherosclerotic events (hazard ratio 1.34; 95% confidence 
interval 1.09, 1.64), while the lowest hepcidin tertile was associated with 
increased risk for all-cause and CV mortality in fully adjusted multivariable 
models including iron indices and inflammation.
CONCLUSION: Both low and high plasma levels of hepcidin are associated with 
adverse clinical outcomes.

INTRODUCTION: Apolipoprotein L1 (APOL1) risk variants (G1 and G2) confer 
immunity against Trypanosoma infection but markedly increase susceptibility to 
progressive kidney disease. However, only a subset of biallelic risk-variant 
carriers develops disease progression, distinct from murine models. Here, we 
evaluated molecular drivers of progressive kidney disease using a model that 
reflected the low human disease penetrance.
METHODS: To investigate the heterogeneity of APOL1-mediated kidney disease, we 
generated novel APOL1 bacterial artificial chromosome transgenic mice with 
doxycycline-inducible systemic interferon-γ expression (G0- or G1-IFNγ mice). 
Podocyte-specific transcriptomics using translating ribosome affinity 
purification (TRAP-seq) and single-cell spatial transcriptomics via 10x Genomics 
Xenium In Situ platform was performed. Mechanistic validation and analysis of 
factors regulating APOL1 upregulation were conducted in primary podocytes and 
subsequently validated in mouse kidney and in human kidney biopsy specimens via 
immunofluorescence.
RESULTS: A subset of G1-IFNγ mice developed severe albuminuria and focal 
segmental glomerulosclerosis, which strongly correlated with the magnitude of 
APOL1 upregulation. By pairing TRAP-seq with single-cell spatial transcriptomic 
data, we identified mitochondrial dysfunction and JAK-STAT signaling as a 
central mediator of podocyte injury. In primary podocytes, APOL1 risk variants 
triggered mitochondrial-derived oxidative stress, establishing a self-amplifying 
STAT1-APOL1 feedforward loop that further enhances APOL1 expression and APOL1 
oligomerization. This pathogenic loop was consistently enriched in podocytes 
from both G1-IFNγ mice and in kidney biopsy specimens from patients with 
APOL1-mediated focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, demonstrating translational 
relevance.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that biallelic risk variants initiate an 
oxidative stress-induced positive feedforward loop which promotes and sustains 
APOL1 upregulation and STAT1 phosphorylation, thereby contributing to disease 
susceptibility, severity and outcome.

OBJECTIVE: To compare programming visits and time to stable stimulation and 
medication management after staged versus simultaneous bilateral subthalamic

Convergent Ferroptosis and Pyroptosis in MASLD-Associated Cardiac Remodeling.

Gui H(1), Yuan X(1), Zhang Y(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Gastroenterology, Heilongjiang Academy of Traditional Chinese 
Medicine, No. 33 Xidazhi Street, Nangang District, Harbin, Heilongjiang 150006, 
P.R. China.
(2)Department of Gastroenterology, Heilongjiang Academy of Traditional Chinese 
Medicine, No. 33 Xidazhi Street, Nangang District, Harbin, Heilongjiang 150006,

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects ∼30% of 
the global population and is associated with increased risks of heart failure 
(particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction), atrial 
fibrillation, and cardiovascular mortality. Despite well-established 
epidemiological links between MASLD and cardiovascular disease, the molecular 
pathways driving MASLD-related cardiac remodeling remain incompletely 
understood. This state-of-the-art mini review examines ferroptosis and 
pyroptosis as potentially convergent regulated cell-death pathways relevant to 
both the steatotic liver and the remodeling heart. Ferroptosis is an 
iron-dependent, lipid peroxidation-driven cell death that mediates hepatocyte 
injury in experimental MASLD and contributes to cardiomyocyte injury under 
cardiac stress. Pyroptosis is an inflammasome-mediated pro-inflammatory cell 
death executed by gasdermin D, which amplifies tissue inflammation in hepatic 
and cardiac disease. Direct preclinical evidence from a pressure-overload 
heart-failure model demonstrates ferroptosis-to-pyroptosis signaling through the 
ACSL4/ALOX12/12-HETE/NLRP3 axis; however, this cascade has not yet been directly 
validated in MASLD models or in patients with MASLD-associated cardiac 
remodeling. We therefore distinguish experimentally established within-organ 
mechanisms from hypothesized interorgan liver-heart links, highlight shared 
regulators including reactive oxygen species, the cGAS/STING pathway, and the 
NRF2 hub, and discuss translational strategies and evidence gaps that should 
guide future validation.

topology, and de novo three-dimensional models were evaluated using PEPTIDE 2.0,

Historically, the main operation for cataract was couching, and the interior of 
the living eye could not be examined until Hermann von Helmholtz introduced the 
ophthalmoscope in 1851. Since the mid-twentieth century, seven advances have 
reshaped ophthalmic care. Harold Ridley implanted the first intraocular lens in 
1949, and the ophthalmologist Charles Kelman and the engineer Anton Banko 
developed phacoemulsification, reported in 1967. Robert Machemer performed the 
first pars plana vitrectomy in 1970, while David Huang and colleagues described 
optical coherence tomography in 1991. Endothelial keratoplasty, developed by 
Gerrit Melles and others between 1998 and 2006, replaced only the failing 
corneal endothelium instead of the full thickness of the cornea. Anti-VEGF 
therapy followed the purification of VEGF by Napoleone Ferrara and colleagues in 
1989 and the approval of ranibizumab in 2006. Minimally invasive glaucoma 
surgery has spread since 2012, and in 2017 voretigene neparvovec became the 
first approved gene therapy for an inherited retinal disease. Five of these 
advances enabled a new type of intervention, whereas endothelial keratoplasty 
and minimally invasive glaucoma surgery made existing operations safer. For each 
advance we summarize the best available evidence of benefit to patients and its 
certainty, which is high for some, such as anti-VEGF therapy, and low for 
others, such as the effect of imaging on patient outcomes. Each advance created 
new burdens, from chronic injections to dependence on donor tissue, and routine 
adoption depended on manufacturing, regulation, cost, reimbursement, and 
health-system capacity.

Repeated ketamine administration induces cross-tolerance to sodium salicylate 
but not to morphine in male rats.

Moghimian M(1), Fathi A(2), Ebadi A(2), Mansouri S(2), Shafaei-Bajestani N(3), 
Abtahi-Evari SH(4), Gholami M(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Physiology, Faculty of Medicine, Gonabad University of Medical 
Sciences, Gonabad, Iran.
(2)Student Research Committee, Gonabad University of Medical Sciences, Gonabad, 
Iran.
(3)Department of Pharmacology, Faculty of Medicine, Gonabad University of 
Medical Sciences, Gonabad, Iran.
(4)Department of Biochemistry and Nutrition, Faculty of Medicine, Gonabad 
University of Medical Sciences, Gonabad, Iran.
(5)Department of Physiology, School of Medicine, Arak University of Medical 
Sciences, Arak, Iran. Electronic address: ma.gholami@arakmu.ac.ir.

Cross-tolerance profiles provide critical insights into shared neurobiological 
substrates among analgesics. This study evaluated whether repeated 
sub-anesthetic ketamine administration induces cross-tolerance to morphine or 
sodium salicylate. Thirty-six adults male Wistar rats (180-200 g, n = 6/group) 
received either normal saline or ketamine (10 mg/kg, i.p.) once daily for 8 
consecutive days. Antinociceptive thresholds were assessed daily using the 
hot-plate test (52 ± 0.5 °C) at 45 min post-injection and expressed as the 
percentage of maximum possible effect (MPE%). On day 9, acute cross-tolerance 
challenges were conducted using morphine (10 mg/kg, i.p.) or sodium salicylate 
(300 mg/kg, i.p.). Serum malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and superoxide dismutase 
(SOD) activity was measured on day 8 to evaluate systemic oxidative status. 
Repeated ketamine administration produced a progressive decline in MPE%, 
demonstrating marked antinociceptive tolerance by day 8. On day 9, morphine 
maintained full antinociceptive efficacy in ketamine-pretreated rats, indicating 
no cross-tolerance. Conversely, sodium salicylate-induced antinociception was 
significantly blunted, confirming cross-tolerance. Biochemically, ketamine 
pre-treatment did not elevate serum MDA and preserved SOD activity substantially 
better than morphine. In conclusion, repeated sub-anesthetic ketamine 
administration induces antinociceptive tolerance and selective cross-tolerance 
to sodium salicylate, while sparing morphine responsiveness. These behavioral 
adaptations parallel a favorable redox balance, highlighting distinct 
pharmacodynamic mechanisms governing ketamine interactions with opioid versus 
non-opioid regimens.

Xiong M(1), Chen J(2), Su C(1), Wei X(2), Yang X(3), Geekiyanage S(3), Petrillo

Pre-mRNA splicing is essential for eukaryotic gene expression, and alternative 
splicing contributes substantially to plant development and stress adaptation. 
Splicing factor 3B subunit 3 (SF3B3), a core component of the U2 snRNP complex, 
is required for spliceosome assembly, but its evolutionary and functional 
features in plants remain poorly understood. Here, we performed a comprehensive 
analysis of plant SF3B3 genes using comparative genomics, phylogenetics, gene 
structure and motif analysis, alternative splicing profiling, promoter analysis, 
expression assays, subcellular localization, and protein interaction validation. 
We identified 105 SF3B3 genes from 71 plant species and found that SF3B3 is 
highly conserved in plants, especially in land plants, with most genes showing a 
typical three-exon/two-intron structure and conserved MMS1_N and CPSF_A domains. 
Intron retention was the major alternative splicing event detected. Moreover, 
SF3B3 was predominantly localized in the nucleus and interacted with SF3B5 and 
SF3B14, supporting its conserved role in processes associated with the 
spliceosome. These results provide a framework for understanding the 
conservation and functional diversification of SF3B3 in plants.

Kumatakenin alleviates cadmium-induced testicular toxicity by restoring 
steroidogenesis and suppressing oxido-inflammatory responses.

Umar Ijaz M(1), Salar MZ(2), Batool M(3), Pang S(4), Wang Y(4), Zhu G(5).

Author information:
(1)Anhui Provincial Key Laboratory of Molecular Enzymology and Mechanisms of

Cadmium (Cd) is a highly toxic compound that induces deleterious effects on 
living organisms and causes multi-organ toxicity, including testicular damage. 
Kumatakenin (KMK) is a flavonoid with potential antioxidant and 
anti-inflammatory properties. The present study was designed to assess the 
protective effects of KMK against Cd prompted testicular injury in rats. 24 
albino rats were divided into four groups including control, Cd (5 mg/kg), 
Cd + KMK (5 mg/kg + 25 mg/kg) and KMK (25 mg/kg). Following a 56-day trial, the 
rats were anesthetized, dissected and further analyses were performed. The 
results showed that Cd caused significant oxidative damage in the testes via 
increasing ROS and MDA levels and lowering Nrf-2 & HO-1 mRNA expressions and 
antioxidant enzymes activities. Moreover, Cd increased the expressions of TLR4, 
MyD88, TRAF6 and NF-κB, which further increased the levels of inflammatory 
markers (TNF-α, COX-2, IL-1β & IL-6). Moreover, Cd exposure also resulted in 
significant upregulation in the mRNA expressions of pro-apoptotic markers (Bax 
and Caspase-3), while reducing the expressions of anti-apoptotic marker (Bcl-2) 
as well as steroidogenic markers (StAR, 3β-HSD, & 17β-HSD). Additionally, Cd 
lowered the levels of plasma testosterone which further caused a reduction in 
sperm count, and motility while increasing sperm abnormalities. Cd also induced 
histological disruptions in the testicular tissues. However, KMK treatment 
mitigated Cd induced disruptions in the testicular tissues. These outcomes 
demonstrate that KMK has the ability to modulate the mRNA expression of genes 
associated with the TLR4/NF-κB and Bax/Bcl-2/Caspase-3 pathways, thereby 
mitigating testicular injury.

Deep phylogeny, a candidate ancestral whole-genome duplication, and gene-family 
evolution in Delphinieae.

Li WH(1), Luo YX(1), Chen JJ(1), Xiao JM(1), Wu HY(1), Puchałka R(2), He J(3), 
Xie L(4).

Author information:
(1)School of Ecology and Nature Conservation, Beijing Forestry University, 
Beijing 100083, China.
(2)Department of Ecology and Biogeography, Centre for Climate Change Research, 
Faculty of Biological and Veterinary Sciences, Nicolaus Copernicus University, 
Lwowska 1, 87-100 Toruń, Poland.
(3)School of Ecology and Nature Conservation, Beijing Forestry University,

(4)School of Ecology and Nature Conservation, Beijing Forestry University,

Delphinieae is a species-rich group in the buttercup family (Ranunculaceae) and 
its only lineage with complex, bilaterally symmetrical flowers, yet its early 
evolutionary relationships remain unresolved. To address this, we analyzed 
nuclear gene sequences from 54 transcriptomes, representing 40 species and two 
infraspecific taxa that cover all four genera of Delphinieae. Coalescent 
analyses consistently recovered Staphisagria as the earliest-diverging genus, 
followed by Gymnaconitum, with Delphinium and Aconitum as sister genera. These 
main intergeneric divergences occurred rapidly between 29.6 and 27.5 million 
years ago. Deep gene-tree conflict was concentrated around these early 
divergences and was best explained by incomplete lineage sorting; no clear 
signal of ancient hybridization was detected. Furthermore, analyses of 
duplicated genes and their chromosomal positions jointly supported a candidate 
whole-genome duplication on the Delphinieae stem lineage, with duplication ages 
concentrated near 52 million years ago. Two gene families involved in floral 
development also duplicated near this interval. For one family, corresponding 
copies occur in duplicated chromosome segments, and two related copies are 
adjacent, a pattern consistent with a large-scale duplication followed by a 
later local duplication. For the second family, one copy is incompletely 
represented in the chromosome-scale assembly, preventing a conclusive structural 
comparison. The candidate whole-genome duplication predates crown 
diversification of the living genera by more than 20 million years, indicating a 
prolonged interval between genome duplication and subsequent radiation.

Melanoma is a highly immunogenic malignancy in which T cell recognition of 
HLA-presented peptides plays a central role in tumour control. While 
immunopeptidomics has enabled detailed characterisation of melanoma antigen 
repertoires, its clinical application is limited by restricted access to tumour 
tissue. Soluble HLA (sHLA) complexes in circulation present a potential 
minimally invasive alternative. However, the extent to which circulating HLA 
repertoires reflect tumour-derived antigen presentation remains unclear. Here, 
we applied an optimised SAPrIm workflow coupled with Orbitrap Astral mass 
spectrometry to analyse the immunopeptidome of matched tumour tissue and plasma 
samples from five melanoma patients collected at the time of tumour resection. 
We identified 6,590-17,690 non-redundant HLA-I peptides from tumour tissue (5-25 
mg input) and 5,213-10,089 non-redundant HLA peptides from plasma-derived sHLA 
complexes (200-571 μL input within the volume of a routine biobank aliquot). 
Plasma-derived sHLA ligandomes retained key features of membrane-bound tumour 
HLA-I presentation, including dominant 9-mer peptide length distributions and 
conserved HLA-binding characteristics. Peptide recovery was strongly concordant 
between compartments following normalisation (Pearson r = 0.92), indicating that 
ligandome depth and recovery were primarily driven by intrinsic biological 
variation rather than sample input. Tumour-associated antigens were consistently 
detected in circulating sHLA peptides. Cryptic peptides derived from 
"peptideins" were preserved in circulation and comprised approximately 1% of the 
total repertoire. Somatic patient-specific variant calling revealed a candidate 
neo-peptide is also preserved and presented in sHLA. To assess tumour 
specificity and biomarker potential, identified HLA peptides were mapped to 
their corresponding source proteins and compared against healthy sHLA and benign 
tissue reference datasets. This analysis identified 247 candidate 
melanoma-associated source proteins not detected in healthy plasma or benign 
tissue reference datasets. Among these, 9 source proteins were recurrently 
detected across at least 4 of 5 patients, representing priority candidates for 
further biomarker validation. In this proof-of-concept study of five matched 
patients, these findings indicate that circulating sHLA ligandomes preserve core 
features of tumour antigen presentation and provide proof-of-concept support for 
plasma immunopeptidomics as a minimally invasive approach for antigen discovery 
and biomarker hypothesis generation.

Lignocellulosic biomass conversion is still limited by pretreatment strategies 
that are energy-intensive, chemically harsh, and difficult to scale. In 
contrast, termites and their symbiotic microbiota represent one of the most 
efficient natural systems for lignocellulose deconstruction, achieving rapid 
biomass conversion under mild physicochemical conditions. This review 
synthesizes current knowledge on termite-bacteria symbiosis and interprets it 
from a bioprocess engineering perspective, positioning it as a model for the 
design of engineered lignocellulosic biorefineries. By integrating gut 
compartmentalization, microbial community organization, enzymatic repertoires, 
and interaction networks, we develop a systems-level view of how spatial 
organization, physicochemical gradients, and cooperative metabolism jointly 
enable efficient biomass processing. Comparative analysis with conventional 
microbial platforms and industrial pretreatment technologies highlights the 
process advantages of termite-inspired systems in energy demand, process 
integration, and scalability. Rather than providing a purely descriptive 
synthesis, this review translates biological organization into engineering 
logic, outlining practical design principles for reactor architecture, 
consortium assembly, and enzyme deployment. We further identify key bottlenecks 
that constrain industrial translation, including transport limitations, gradient 
control, and community stability. Together, these insights provide a structured 
foundation for the rational development of robust, scalable, and sustainable 
termite-inspired lignocellulosic bioprocesses.

Biomanufacturing is increasingly transitioning toward sustainable non-grain 
carbon feedstocks, including gaseous C1 compounds, liquid C1 substrates, and 
solid non-grain biomass. However, the efficient utilization of these feedstocks 
remains hindered by mass-transfer limitations, thermodynamic constraints, 
substrate and intermediate cytotoxicity, and the inherent physical limitations 
of macromolecular catalysts. Intracellular multienzyme cascade catalysis offers 
a promising solution by organizing highly coordinated catalytic networks within 
living cells, thereby enhancing metabolic efficiency and overcoming multiple 
bioconversion barriers. In this review, we systematically analyze the mechanisms 
and engineering strategies underlying whole-cell cascade systems from the 
integrated perspectives of material, energy, and information flows. Based on 
these principles, we propose a universal diagnostic and design framework for the 
bioconversion of non-grain carbon feedstocks. We further illustrate how these 
general design rules can be tailored and implemented at the systems level for 
the efficient conversion of specific substrate classes. In addition, we 
highlight the emerging role of artificial intelligence in enabling predictive 
system reconstruction through generative design, global pathway optimization, 
and automated design-build-test-learn (DBTL) cycles. Collectively, this review 
establishes a unified theoretical and practical framework for the rational 
design of next-generation biomanufacturing platforms based on intracellular 
multienzyme cascade catalysis.

Shock Index-Creatinine as a Predictor of In-Hospital Clinical Outcomes in 
Patients with Anterior Wall ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction 
Undergoing Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention.

Venkadesan K(1), Nath RK(1), Aggarwal P(2), Sinha SK(3), Kuber D(1), Rao S(1),

Author information:
(1)Department of Cardiology, Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Medical Sciences 
(ABVIMS) and Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, New Delhi, India.
(2)Department of Cardiology, Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Medical Sciences 
(ABVIMS) and Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, New Delhi, India. Electronic

BACKGROUND: Early risk stratification in ST-segment elevation myocardial 
infarction (STEMI) is essential but established scores such as TIMI and GRACE 
require multivariable computation. The Shock Index-Creatinine (SIC) is a simpler 
bedside alternative, yet Indian data are sparse.
OBJECTIVE: To assess whether admission SIC predicts in-hospital adverse events 
in anterior wall STEMI patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary 
intervention (PCI).
METHODS: Two hundred consecutive patients with anterior wall STEMI undergoing 
primary PCI at a tertiary care centre in northern India were prospectively 
enrolled over 12 months. SIC was computed at admission as (Shock Index × 100) - 
Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance. The primary outcome was in-hospital death; 
secondary outcomes were heart failure, cardiogenic shock, contrast-induced acute 
kidney injury (CI-AKI), and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia. 
Discrimination was assessed by the area under the receiver operating 
characteristic curve (AUC).
RESULTS: The cohort was 73.0% male with a mean age of 54.5 years; in-hospital 
mortality was 10.0% (n = 20). Admission SIC was markedly higher in non-survivors 
than survivors (82.0 ± 42.4 versus -20.1 ± 19.4; p < 0.001). AUCs were 0.992 for 
mortality and cardiogenic shock, 0.971 for CI-AKI, 0.909 for ventricular 
arrhythmia, and 0.907 for heart failure (all p < 0.001). A SIC ≥ 20 predicted 
death with 95.0% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity.
CONCLUSIONS: In this Indian cohort, admission SIC was a powerful bedside 
predictor of adverse in-hospital events after primary PCI for anterior wall 
STEMI. The unusually high discriminative performance requires external 
validation in larger multicentre populations before routine clinical adoption.

Preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by

receptor phosphorylation.

Liu Q(1), Dong Q(1), Xu T(1), Jiao Y(1), Yu J(1), Zhang W(1), Gu X(1), Huang 
Y(2), Xu R(3), Ma Z(4).

Author information:
(1)Department of Anesthesiology, Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, The Affiliated 
Hospital of Medical School, Nanjing University, 210008, Nanjing, China.
(2)Department of Anesthesiology, Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, The Affiliated 
Hospital of Medical School, Nanjing University, 210008, Nanjing, China. 
Electronic address: hyl199006@126.com.
(3)Department of Anesthesiology, Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, The Affiliated

Electronic address: salt0226@163.com.
(4)Department of Anesthesiology, Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, The Affiliated

Preoperative sleep deprivation (SD) is known to exacerbate postoperative pain, 
but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a male mouse model of 
48-hour continuous SD followed by incisional surgery, we found that SD alone 
induced transient mechanical hyperalgesia, and when combined with surgery (SI 
group) it significantly aggravated and prolonged postoperative pain recovery 
until day 10. On postoperative day 7, SI mice showed marked downregulation of 
spinal dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression and decreased spinal dopamine 
concentration. D2R was predominantly expressed on spinal glutamatergic neurons. 
Overexpression of D2R on these neurons via intrathecal AAV injection effectively 
alleviated the prolonged hyperalgesia, normalizing pain sensitivity by day 7. 
Mechanistically, D2R downregulation led to increased phosphorylation of NMDA 
receptor subunits (p-NR1 and p-NR2B) without altering total NMDA receptor 
levels. Co-immunoprecipitation revealed an interaction between D2R and protein 
phosphatase 2A (PP2A). SI mice exhibited decreased PP2A expression but increased 
p-AKT, p-GSK3β, and β-catenin, indicating activation of the PP2A/AKT signaling 
pathway, which were reversed by D2R overexpression. Furthermore, pharmacological 
activation of PP2A with DT-061 not only downregulated p-AKT, p-GSK3β, β-catenin, 
p-NR1 and p-NR2B, but also produced significant analgesia in SI mice. 
Collectively, these results demonstrate that preoperative sleep deprivation 
prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal D2R on 
glutamatergic neurons, which disinhibits the PP2A/AKT pathway and enhances NMDA 
receptor phosphorylation. Targeting D2R or its downstream PP2A/AKT signaling may 
represent a novel therapeutic strategy for managing persistent postoperative 
pain caused by preoperative sleep deprivation in male mice.

This study focused on the relation between larval southern flounder 
(Paralichthys lethostigma) growth, cardiac performance, and metabolic physiology 
(metabolic rate, hormones). Two-way ANOVAs were performed among larvae groups 
that successfully survived through metamorphosis (n = 1) vs. those that 
succumbed to mass mortality early in development (n = 2). Larvae were monitored 
from 5 to 50 days post hatch (dph). The comparison of morphological and 
physiological parameters for the three batches for equivalent life-stages from 5 
to 12 dph (n = 8-10/dph), showed specific growth rate (SGR) in the surviving

oxygen consumption rate (AMO2) was ~5-fold higher in the surviving batch vs. the

the two failed batches. This mismatch for the surviving batch (a high SGR 
contrasted with low MO2 and HR), suggested a reduced cost of growth and likely 
bioenergetic conservation prior to metamorphosis-an energetically demanding 
process. The subsequent monitoring of the surviving batch through metamorphosis 
(~30-40 dph), showed a ~ 10-fold increase in AMO2 and ~ 2-fold increase in 
thyroid and corticoid hormones. Lastly, a strong negative correlation of HR vs. 
MO2 during early development putatively suggested future batch failure.

Hjemsæter T(1), Johansen IB(2), Fjelldal PG(3), Macqueen DJ(4), Nørstebø SF(5),

Author information:
(1)Unit of Anatomy, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Norwegian University of Life

(2)Unit of Physiology and Biochemistry, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine,

(3)Reproduction and Developmental Biology, Institute of Marine Research, Matre

(4)The Roslin Institute and Royal (Dick) School of Veterinary Studies, The

(5)The Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Ås, Norway.
(6)Unit of Anatomy, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Norwegian University of Life

Erythropoietin (EPO) is the main hormonal regulator of erythropoiesis in 
vertebrates and also mediates non-hematopoietic functions. Despite extensive 
characterization in mammals, the cellular sources and targets of EPO signaling 
remain poorly defined in non-mammalian vertebrates. The Atlantic salmon provides 
a valuable model to investigate paralog-specific organization of EPO signaling 
due to a recent whole genome duplication (WGD). Here, we characterize the 
tissue- and cell-specific expression of paralogs encoding EPO and the 
erythropoietin receptor (EPOR) in Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar). Phylogenetic 
analysis revealed four EPO encoding paralogs retained from the teleost-specific 
(Ts3R) and salmonid-specific WGD (Ss4R) events, designated epoa1, epoa2, epob1 
and epob2, and two Ss4R paralogs encoding EPOR, designated epora1 and epora2. In 
situ hybridization analysis targeting mRNA revealed that epoa2 was the 
predominantly expressed paralog in the heart, with cardiomyocytes as the 
principal source, while epob1 was the most abundant paralog in the kidney with 
expression mainly in tubular epithelial cells of the trunk kidney. mRNA from the 
epora genes was most highly expressed in erythropoietic tissues and cells but 
also detected in non-erythropoietic cell types. Temperature was shown to affect 
epoa2 mRNA expression in the heart. Collectively, these results identify the 
cellular sources of epo mRNA in the heart, head kidney and trunk kidney, and 
demonstrate paralog-specific partitioning of epo expression following the Ss4R 
WGD in Atlantic salmon. In addition, mRNA for epora genes was detected across a 
range of hematopoietic and non-hematopoietic cell types. Together, these 
findings provide a cell-resolved framework for understanding vertebrate EPO 
signaling, suggesting roles of EPO and EPOR in regulating both erythropoietic 
and non-hematopoietic processes.

Ohl F(1), Koch M(2), Lupše ŠK(2), Gutow L(2), Saborowski R(3).

Blue mussels (Mytilus edulis) from the southern North Sea are exposed to 
multiple natural and anthropogenic stressors, including parasite infestation and 
microplastic pollution. For example, the intestinal copepods Mytilicola 
intestinalis and Mytilicola orientalis are common endoparasites of blue mussels 
in the coastal areas. We investigated the prevalence and composition of 
Mytilicola species in mussels from the Wadden Sea. The infestation rate of M. 
edulis by Mytilicola spp. was 78%. One third of infested mussels harboured both 
parasite species. These parasites may feed on intestinal tissue, detached cells, 
or the gut content of the host which also may contain natural and anthropogenic 
microparticles that were ingested by the mussel. In a 5-day laboratory 
experiment, mussels either received no food, were fed with microalgae, or were 
exposed to microplastics. Activities of selected digestive enzymes were measured 
in the midgut gland of the mussels and in whole parasites. Digestive enzyme 
profiles revealed significant functional differences between the host and either 
parasite. Mussels showed high esterase and β-glucosidase activities, reflecting 
the utilization of algal food. In contrast, both Mytilicola species showed low 
β-glucosidase activities. Elevated α-glucosidase and 
N-acetyl-β-D-glucosaminidase activities in M. orientalis suggest the utilization 
of glycogen and mucus from the host. Treatments involving starvation, feeding, 
and microplastics had no significant effects on the enzyme profiles of the host, 
and there was no correlation between the enzyme activities of the host and its 
parasites. Enzyme profiles proved useful for interpreting trophodynamic 
interactions between mussels and their Mytilicola endoparasites, but there were 
limited responses to exposure conditions for all species.

Aflatoxin, a potent hepatocarcinogenic mycotoxin, remains a major public health 
concern in sub-Saharan Africa. Due to its severe health and socio-economic 
impact, aflatoxin exposure needs to be monitored and mitigated. This 
cross-sectional study assessed serum aflatoxin-albumin adducts (AF-ALB), an 
objective biomarker of systemic aflatoxin exposure, among gastroenterology 
patients in southwestern Nigeria using ELISA. AF-ALB levels were categorized 
into high and low groups based on interquartile ranges. Multivariate logistic 
regression was used to identify socio-demographic, dietary, and temporal 
predictors. Of the 573 participants, 405 (70.7%) were male, and 168 (29.3%) were

gastroenteric diseases (p < 0.001, Cramer's V = 0.478). Age, sex, education, 
occupation, marital status, and aflatoxin awareness status were not 
significantly associated with AF-ALB levels. These findings indicate that 
dietary practices, particularly frequent groundnut consumption, are important

RATIONALE & OBJECTIVE: Glomerulopathy with striated deposits (GSD) is a rare 
entity defined by ultrastructural deposits with striated substructure. Prior 
data were limited to case reports. This case series characterizes GSD's 
clinicopathologic spectrum and prognosis.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series.
SETTING & PARTICIPANTS: Eighteen GSD cases identified from the nephropathology 
archives of Mayo Clinic and Columbia University, 2011-2025.
FINDINGS: Fifty percent of the patients were male, 78% were Caucasian, and their 
median age was 73 years. Most patients presented with CKD (median creatinine, 
2.6 mg/dl), proteinuria (median, 3.8 g/day), and hematuria (80%), a minority 
(29%) with hypocomplementemia, and none with extrarenal manifestations. Fifteen 
(88%) patients had hematologic conditions, primarily (56%) monoclonal gammopathy 
of renal significance (MGRS). Histologically, most cases (67%) had a 
membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis pattern on biopsy. All exhibited 
striated ultrastructural deposits of regularly stacked straight electron-dense 
bands (13 nm in mean diameter) with distinctive periodicity (mean 20 nm), which 
were present mostly in subendothelial and mesangial regions. Ten (56%) cases 
exhibited monotypic Ig glomerular deposits (IgGκ in 7) on immunofluorescence 
(IF), which were masked in 6 (60%), requiring IF evaluation using 
pronase-digested paraffin tissue for unmasking. Six of these 10 patients (60%) 
had a circulating MIg whose isotype matched the deposited Igs. The remaining 
cases exhibited polytypic Ig glomerular deposits (4 cases) or had no detectable 
Ig (4 cases) identified histologically. After follow-up (median 14 months) in 15 
patients, 6 (40%) progressed to kidney failure within a median of 11 months, 
including 1 with recurrence in a kidney allograft. Kidney response to 
clone-directed therapy was observed in all 4 evaluable patients.
LIMITATIONS: Retrospective design, small sample size.
CONCLUSIONS: GSD is a rare heterogeneous glomerulopathy presenting in older 
patients with CKD and proteinuria, and frequently associated with hematologic 
conditions, particularly MGRS. We propose adding GSD with monotypic Ig deposits 
to the spectrum of MGRS lesions. Further studies are needed to elucidate precise 
deposit composition(s) and effective therapeutic approaches.

1.60 [95% CI 1.16-2.22], 1.64 [1.17-2.31], 1.47 [1.10-1.97] and 1.97 [1.43-2.71] 
fold higher risk of CKD progression, respectively, after adjustment for known 
clinical risk factors. These associations were more pronounced in participants 
with prevalent CKD (eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2) compared to those with preserved 
eGFR. Each one SD increase in urinary tryptophan and kynurenine concentrations 
was independently associated with 1.60 [1.24-2.06] and 1.35 [1.05-1.73] fold 
higher risk of CKD progression, respectively, in CRIC participants with 
diabetes.
LIMITATIONS: Observational study with unmeasured confounding.
CONCLUSIONS: Higher concentrations of urinary metabolites in the 
tryptophan-kynurenine pathway were associated with higher risk of CKD 
progression in patients with type 2 diabetes. Future studies are warranted to 
elucidate the biological mechanisms linking the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway 
and progression of kidney disease.

Reliability of Spot Urine Protein-to-Creatinine and Urine Albumin-to-Creatinine

RATIONALE & OBJECTIVE: Spot urine protein-to-creatinine (UPCR) and 
albumin-to-creatinine (UACR) ratios are common surrogates for 24-hour excretion, 
but their validity during acute kidney injury (AKI) is uncertain because kidney 
function is not at steady state. This study assessed the validity of these spot 
ratios during active AKI compared to after its resolution.
STUDY DESIGN: A prospective paired cohort study.
SETTING & PARTICIPANTS: One hundred hospitalized adult patients with AKI at a 
single center in Thailand.
EXPOSURE: Active phase of AKI was the period between diagnosis and resolution, 
which was defined as the return of serum creatinine to baseline or a value ≥50% 
below the peak value, sustained for ≥48 hours.
OUTCOMES: The agreement and reliability between protein-to-creatine and 
albumin-to-creatinine ratios in spot urine samples versus in 24-hour urine 
collections.
ANALYTICAL APPROACH: Agreement was evaluated using Lin's Concordance Correlation 
Coefficient (CCC) and Bland-Altman analysis to quantify systematic bias and 
random error. Limits of Agreement (LoA) were defined as the range within which 
95% of the differences between the two measurement methods were expected to 
fall.
RESULTS: Spot ratios differed from 24-hour collections during AKI (CCC: UACR 
0.81; UPCR 0.68) and became more reliable after recovery, (CCC: UACR 0.89; UPCR 
0.83) (p=0.001). Limits of agreement were wide during AKI (UACR 0.22 to 8.37; 
UPCR 0.31 to 7.99) and narrowed significantly upon resolution (UACR 0.40 to 
5.48; UPCR 0.47 to 4.91). Spot ratios systematically overestimated the 24-hour 
collections by 36% to 56% both during and after resolution of AKI. The 
unreliability of the spot urine values was most pronounced in patients with 
preserved baseline kidney function, severe AKI, and hemodynamic etiologies.
LIMITATIONS: Defining resolution via serum creatinine may not reflect complete 
resolution of AKI. The exclusively hospitalized cohort may limit 
generalizability to milder AKI occurring in the outpatient setting.
CONCLUSIONS: Spot urine ratios exhibit significant imprecision during active AKI 
compared to following its resolution. Clinicians should exercise caution when 
using these data to establish baseline proteinuria or monitor treatment response 
during AKI.

BACKGROUND: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic immune-mediated disease 
characterized by esophageal dysfunction and eosinophilic inflammation. 
Comparative efficacy and safety of therapies remain uncertain.
OBJECTIVE: To compare efficacy and safety of treatments for EoE in children and 
adults.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) of 
randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing pharmacologic, dietary, and 
mechanical interventions. We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CENTRAL to March 17, 
2026. Reviewers screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. We 
conducted random-effects NMA; assessed certainty using GRADE.
RESULTS: We included 48 RCTs (3,963 participants). High-frequency dupilumab 
[mean difference (MD) -11.08, 95% confidence interval (CI) -15.14 to -7.03; high 
certainty] and swallowed topical corticosteroids (STCs) (MD -6.86, 95%CI -9.17 
to -4.56; moderate certainty) are likely among the most effective for symptoms. 
Similarly, high-frequency dupilumab (MD 6.57, 95%CI 3.42 to 9.71; moderate 
certainty) and STCs (MD 7.20, 95%CI 1.01 to 13.39; moderate certainty) are among 
the most effective for quality-of-life. Certain biologics and epicutaneous 
immunotherapy are likely not different from placebo for symptoms (moderate 
certainty). Multiple interventions reduce peak eosinophil counts (high 
certainty) and likely do not increase harms versus placebo (moderate or high 
certainty). Four- and six-food elimination diets (FEDs) may be better than 1FED 
for symptoms (low certainty), but not other outcomes, with greater burden.
CONCLUSIONS: High-frequency dupilumab and STCs are among the most effective 
therapies across patient-important and inflammatory outcomes. Histologic 
improvements do not guarantee patient-important outcome improvement. FED 
benefits are modest and low certainty, and traded off by burdens.

BACKGROUND: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis/mycosis (ABPA/M) is 
characterized by systemic eosinophilia and eosinophil-rich mucus plugs, but 
mechanisms programming eosinophil pathogenicity remain unclear.
OBJECTIVE: We aim to define eosinophil activation programs and upstream signals 
that promote extracellular trap formation in ABPA/M.
METHODS: We performed multi-omics analyses (RNA sequencing and proteomics) of 
blood eosinophils from healthy participants, patients with eosinophilic asthma, 
and patients with ABPA/M. Surface-marker profiles were compared between blood 
and airway eosinophils from patients with ABPA/M. In vitro stimulation assays 
using IFN-γ, IL-5, and a nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing 2 
(NOD2) ligand were combined with multi-omics readouts and functional evaluation 
of IgG cross-linking-induced eosinophil extracellular trap formation.
RESULTS: Multi-omics profiling identified activation patterns consistent with 
IFN-γ and IL-5 signaling in ABPA/M blood eosinophils. ICAM-1 was upregulated on 
both blood and airway eosinophils, whereas PD-L1 upregulation was specific to 
airway eosinophils. PD-L1 induction required combined stimulation with IFN-γ and 
a NOD2 ligand, but not IL-5. Under IFN-γ plus NOD2 ligand stimulation, 
eosinophils exhibited inflammatory remodeling, including increased Fc gamma 
receptor expression. Functionally, pretreatment with IFN-γ and a NOD2 ligand 
enhanced IgG cross-linking-induced extracellular trap formation in an NADPH 
oxidase-dependent manner and required lymphocyte function-associated antigen 1 
interactions with ICAM-1. Combined stimulation with IFN-γ and IL-5 similarly 
augmented extracellular trap formation.
CONCLUSION: ABPA/M eosinophils are shaped by mixed inflammatory cues, in which 
IFN-γ cooperates with fungal-sensing signals or IL-5 to enhance Fc gamma 
receptor-linked, IgG-triggered extracellular trap formation, potentially 
contributing to mucus plugging.

Insulin availability and affordability have long limited access in low- and 
middle-income countries (LMICs), and recent shortages and product withdrawals in 
higher-income settings underscore the need for reliable supply worldwide. While 
documented disruptions do not establish an aggregate global manufacturing 
deficit, commercial decisions, regulatory barriers, procurement, financing, and 
distribution can restrict access even where production capacity exists. 
Nevertheless, product prioritization and investment decisions can constrain the 
capacity allocated to insulin and reduce the ability to respond to changing 
demand. This narrative review examines global insulin demand, supply insecurity, 
market structure, affordability, and health-system barriers, distinguishing the 
circumstances of the United States, other high-income countries, and LMICs. We 
consider the potential effects of incretin therapies on insulin requirements and 
industrial investment and assess manufacturing modernization, including 
continuous production, as one component of a broader response. Proposed 
technological benefits require insulin-specific validation of quality, 
productivity, cost, and commercial feasibility. Priorities include stronger 
shortage surveillance, diversified qualified suppliers, regulatory cooperation, 
sustainable procurement, reduced waste, and dependable distribution. Supply 
security must extend through safe storage, administration, education, and 
glucose monitoring. Coordinated action across manufacturing and health systems 
is needed to maintain uninterrupted, affordable access to appropriate insulin 
treatment.

Clinical and dermatological findings associated with Leishmania spp. 
test-positivity in shelter dogs of Kastamonu, Black Sea region of Türkiye: an 
exploratory cross-sectional study.

Civek E(1), Özkan Ö(2).

Author information:
(1)Kastamonu Municipality Temporary Stray Animal Shelter, Kastamonu, Türkiye.
(2)Department of Veterinary Parasitology, Institute of Health Sciences, Çankırı 
Karatekin University, Çankırı, Türkiye. Electronic address: 
ozcanozkan@karatekin.edu.tr.

Canine leishmaniosis (CanL) has a broad clinical spectrum, with cutaneous 
abnormalities among its most frequent manifestations. We characterised clinical 
and dermatological findings in 200 stray dogs admitted to the municipal shelter 
of Kastamonu, Türkiye, and explored associations with Leishmania test 
positivity, lymphadenopathy, age, sex, sampling month and geographic origin. 
Blood samples were examined by thin blood-smear microscopy and a lateral-flow 
serological rapid test. Nine dogs (4.5%) met the study's combined definition of 
test positivity. Above-normal body temperature, lymph-node abnormalities and 
skin abnormalities were recorded in 33.5%, 16% and 15% of dogs, respectively. 
Abnormal skin status was significantly associated with test positivity 
(microscopy p<0.001; combined positivity p=0.031, OR 5.08, 95% CI 1.28-20.15; 
Fisher exact tests), consistent with a rank-correlation analysis. All four 
microscopy-positive dogs had abnormal skin (4/30), whereas rapid/combined 
positivity occurred in 4/30 dogs with abnormal skin and 5/170 with healthy skin. 
Lymph-node status differed by sex in an exploratory Mann-Whitney analysis 
(U=4363.50; p=0.026). Skin-health ranks differed across recorded ages 
(Kruskal-Wallis χ²=31.797; df=10; p<0.001) and sampling months (χ²=13.541; df=5; 
p=0.019), but sparse older-age strata, uneven monthly sampling and an 
association between month and age limited inference. The data did not support a 
bimodal age distribution or an autumn-winter increase in skin abnormalities. 
Because diagnostic and lesion-specific confirmation were limited, these findings 
are interpreted as exploratory clinical associations and provide a baseline for 
molecularly confirmed prospective surveillance in the Black Sea region.

Clinical and Laboratory Predictors for Differentiating Visceral Leishmaniasis 
from Hematological Malignancies in Adults with Pancytopenia.

Savk ISK(1), Seyman D(2), Cuvalci NO(3), Karadogan E(4).

Author information:
(1)Health Sciences University Antalya Training and Research Hospital, Muratpasa, 
Antalya, Türkiye. Electronic address: sena253@hotmail.com.
(2)Health Sciences University Antalya Training and Research Hospital, Muratpasa, 
Antalya, Türkiye. Electronic address: seymander@gmail.com.
(3)Health Sciences University Antalya Training and Research Hospital, Muratpasa, 
Antalya, Türkiye. Electronic address: nefiseoztoprak@yahoo.com.
(4)Antalya Provincial Health Directorate, Public Health Department, Infectious 
Diseases and Early Warning Response Unit, Muratpaşa, Antalya, Türkiye. 
Electronic address: edakaradogan2016@gmail.com.

Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is a systemic, life-threatening zoonotic disease. VL 
and hematological malignancies (HMs) may present with overlapping clinical and 
laboratory features. The primary endpoint of our study was to identify the 
clinical and laboratory parameters for differentiating VL from HMs in adult 
patients with pancytopenia. The secondary endpoint was to evaluate the clinical 
and laboratory findings in patients with VL. In this 15.5-year retrospective 
case-control study, adult patients with pancytopenia who were diagnosed with VL 
or HMs at a tertiary referral hospital in Antalya were included. A total of 53 
patients were included (VL, n = 24; HMs, n = 29). The VL group was younger and 
presented with a significantly longer duration from symptom onset to hospital 
admission compared to the HMs group (each, p < 0.001). Fever, anorexia, left 
upper quadrant pain, and hepatosplenomegaly were more frequent in the VL group 
(each, p < 0.001). The VL group exhibited significantly elevated C-reactive 
protein (CRP), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyl transferase 
(GGT) and total protein levels, and lower albumin levels. A reversed 
albumin-globulin ratio was present in 79% of patients with VL. The splenic long 
axis was independently associated with VL diagnosis (OR: 2.45, 95% CI: 
1.31-4.59, p = 0.005). The highest discriminatory performance was achieved with 
a splenic long axis cut-off of >13.75 cm (AUC: 0.945, sensitivity: 92%, 
specificity: 93%), followed by CRP >33.5 mg/L (AUC: 0.817, sensitivity: 83%, 
specificity: 83%) and symptom duration >52.5 days (AUC: 0.799, sensitivity: 67%, 
specificity: 86%). VL should be considered in the differential diagnosis of 
adults with pancytopenia, particularly in endemic regions. We believe that our 
findings may contribute to earlier and more accurate diagnosis of VL. Prolonged 
symptom duration, hepatosplenomegaly, elevated AST, elevated CRP, 
hyperproteinemia, hypoalbuminemia, and reversed albumin-globulin ratio 
necessitate a high index of clinical suspicion for VL compared to HMs.

Malaria remains a major parasitic disease caused mainly by Plasmodium falciparum 
and Plasmodium vivax, and drug-resistant parasites continue to challenge disease 
control. Drug repurposing may help identify compounds with antimalarial 
potential. Here, we evaluated gallopamil, an L-type calcium channel blocker, 
using in vitro, ex vivo, in vivo and in silico approaches. Gallopamil inhibited 
the chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum W2 strain in vitro (IC₅₀ = 3.65 µM) and 
showed ex vivo activity against clinical isolates of P. falciparum and P. vivax 
from CEPEM/RO, with median IC₅₀ values of 6.4 and 9.87 µM, respectively. 
Selectivity indices calculated using HepG2 cytotoxicity data ranged from >51 to 
>137, indicating in vitro selectivity relative to HepG2 cells. In a preliminary 
murine P. berghei suppressive assay, gallopamil at 5 mg/kg reduced parasitemia 
by more than 40% at the day-5 endpoint, as measured by light microscopy and flow 
cytometry. Stage-specific assays showed that gallopamil inhibited parasite 
development when treatment began at the ring stage (p < 0.000001), whereas no 
significant inhibition was observed when treatment started with predominantly 
schizont-stage parasites (p = 0.30). Molecular docking predicted interactions 
between gallopamil and residues of Plasmodium hexose transporters, including 
LYS-51, GLN-167, ASN-309 and ASN-339, with binding energies of -6.1 kcal/mol for 
PvHT1 and -7.8 kcal/mol for PfHT1. These findings support gallopamil as an early 
antiplasmodial hit compound and provide a transporter-related mechanistic 
hypothesis for future functional validation.

Maternal metformin (MT) treatment improves the metabolic phenotype of high-fat 
(HF) diet-exposed offspring, but its effect on offspring's palatable food 
preference remains unclear. We assessed HF diet and sucrose preferences in adult 
offspring from Sprague-Dawley rat dams fed a control diet, an HF diet with or 
without MT treatment. Additionally, we measured the mRNA expression of sweet 
taste perception-related genes in taste buds and dopamine- and opioid-related 
genes in the central reward system. In adult males, maternal HF diet increased

system. Furthermore, maternal MT treatment decreased low-concentration sucrose 
preference, and reduced opioid-related gene expression in the reward system.

females, neither maternal HF diet nor MT treatment affected HF food preference.

reduced the expression of sweet taste perception-related genes, while maternal 
MT treatment did not reverse it. At weaning, maternal MT treatment generally 
decreased dopamine- and opioid-related gene expression in the central reward 
system across both sexes. Notably, this early-life central reward 
transcriptional suppression persisted into adulthood in males but not in 
females. Our results indicate that maternal HF diet and MT treatment influence 
HF diet and low-concentration sucrose preferences in adult offspring in a 
sex-specific manner, which may be associated with altered gene expression in the 
central reward system and the peripheral taste perception pathways.

Osteopontin (OPN) is a secreted phosphoprotein that is abundant in the bone 
matrix and plays an important role in bone homeostasis. Cortical bone in OPNnull 
mice has a heterogenous mineral density and reduced fracture toughness 
indicative of a defect in bone homeostasis. Osteoclasts binding to bone appears 
to be mediated by OPN at the surface of bone matrix interacting with the 
integrin αvß3 receptor that is abundantly expressed on osteoclasts. Activation 
of integrin αvß3 leads to cytoskeletal reorganization in the osteoclast that 
promotes binding and bone resorption. OPN also interacts with CD44 on the 
osteoclast surface which appears to promote osteoclast motility. Both integrin 
αvß3 and CD44 dependent signaling can induce cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression 
in non-skeletal cells. Our lab also recently found that OPNnull mice showed 
reduced COX-2 expression in fracture callus osteoclasts. Therefore, we wished to 
determine whether OPN could induce COX-2 expression in osteoclasts. Here, we 
show OPN induces COX-2 expression in osteoclasts through not only integrin αvβ3, 
but also the CD44 receptor. The results suggest that autocrine or paracrine 
signaling by osteoclasts may be mediated by COX-2.

CXC chemokines as context-dependent regulators of immunity, homeostasis and 
cancer.

Miralles CM(1), Manousakis E(1), Moreta-Moraleda C(2), Wright RHG(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Biomedical Sciences, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, 
Universitat Internacional de Catalunya, Barcelona, Spain.
(2)Department of Biomedical Sciences, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, 
Universitat Internacional de Catalunya, Barcelona, Spain. Electronic address:

(3)Department of Biomedical Sciences, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences,

Chemokines are a large family of small secreted proteins that mainly orchestrate 
immune cell trafficking and tissue organization. Among them, the CXC chemokine 
family plays a central role in regulating immune surveillance, inflammation, 
angiogenesis and stem cell dynamics. Despite their relatively simple conserved 
fold - characterized by a β-sheet core and a C-terminal α-helix - CXC chemokines 
exhibit remarkable functional diversity. This diversity arises from structural 
plasticity, including concentration-dependent monomer-dimer equilibria and 
interactions with glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), which collectively shape chemokine 
gradients, protect against proteolytic degradation and fine-tune receptor 
activation and selectivity. Emerging evidence indicates that these structural 
and spatial determinants enable CXC chemokines to regulate not only leukocyte 
recruitment but also tissue homeostasis, haematopoietic stem cell quiescence, 
activation, and microenvironmental organization. Dysregulation of CXC chemokine 
signalling contributes to a broad spectrum of human diseases, including chronic 
inflammatory disorders, degenerative conditions and cancer, where altered 
gradient formation and receptor engagement reprogram tumour immunity and promote 
metastatic progression. Here, we examine the structural principles governing CXC 
chemokine function, discuss how monomer-dimer dynamics and coordinated 
interactions regulate signalling specificity, and explore how context-dependent 
chemokine activity shapes immunity in health and disease.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: There is an ever increasing interest in using clinical 
prediction models to improve diagnostic and prognostic accuracy. However, the 
literature often conflates distinct prediction approaches, resulting in 
ambiguous findings and slowing scientific progress. This commentary aims to 
clarify the various ways in which physicians use clinical prediction models and 
highlight the implications of these approaches for prediction accuracy by 
drawing on an existing framework from the judgment and decision-making 
literature.
METHODS: We promote a framework distinguishing between four distinct prediction 
approaches: clinical judgment, mechanical judgment, clinical synthesis, and 
mechanical synthesis. We apply this framework to recent studies and illustrate 
how it distinguishes between previously conflated approaches.
RESULTS: Our analysis demonstrates that current research often obscures 
meaningful differences between the prediction approaches, thereby impeding 
improvement in patient care. The framework provides conceptual clarity and 
highlights clinical synthesis, in which the physician incorporates the model 
output into their own judgment, as a practical yet under-researched approach.
CONCLUSIONS: The prediction accuracy achieved in practice depends on how 
physicians use clinical prediction models. Greater recognition and use of the 
proposed framework can improve future research by properly classifying 
prediction approaches, fostering more accurate research syntheses, and 
supporting the more effective and fair application of clinical prediction models 
in practice.

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a progressive stage of

Mitochondrial calcium uniporter (Mcu) is essential for mitochondrial calcium 
homeostasis, yet its function and upstream regulatory mechanism in myocardial 
infarction (MI) remain unclear. This study was designed to define the pivotal 
regulatory pathway controlling Mcu expression post-MI and verify whether Mcu can 
act as a therapeutic target for MI. Mendelian randomization was used to verify 
the genetic link between Mcu and MI. In vitro gain- and loss-of-function assays 
together with m6A-seq, MeRIP-qPCR, RIP-qPCR and dual-luciferase assays were 
applied to explore the m6A-dependent regulatory mechanism of Fto/Ythdf2 on Mcu, 
and the biological effects of this axis on mitochondrial homeostasis and 
cardiomyocyte injury were validated via cell-based gene interventions. In vivo 
MI mouse models with cardiomyocyte-specific Fto/Mcu overexpression or 
DS16570511-mediated pharmacological Mcu inhibition were constructed to detect 
cardiac function, infarct size, myocardial fibrosis and mitochondrial injury. 
Our results demonstrated that elevated Mcu is positively associated with MI 
risk; excess Mcu triggers mitochondrial calcium overload, ROS buildup, 
mitochondrial membrane potential loss and respiratory chain damage to facilitate 
cardiomyocyte damage, whereas Mcu knockdown alleviates these pathological 
alterations. Mechanistically, ischemic injury downregulates Fto to increase m6A 
modification of Mcu mRNA. Meanwhile, ischemia-suppressed Ythdf2 expression 
impairs its binding to Mcu mRNA, which enhances Mcu mRNA stability and 
translation efficiency and leads to Mcu upregulation. Both Fto and Ythdf2 
overexpression counteract Mcu-induced mitochondrial dysfunction and 
cardiomyocyte damage. In vivo experiments further confirmed that specific Mcu 
overexpression partially offsets Fto-mediated cardioprotection, and the Mcu 
inhibitor DS16570511 significantly ameliorates post-infarction cardiac 
dysfunction. In conclusion, Mcu aggravates ischemic myocardial damage by 
disturbing mitochondrial calcium balance, and we newly identify an 
Fto-Ythdf2-Mcu regulatory axis, providing a promising therapeutic target for MI.

BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder and 
oxidative stress (OS) is believed to play a role in disease pathogenesis. 
However, reliable OS markers are lacking. In this study we aim to assess OS in 
AD by evaluating free thiols, which serve as key indicators of the systemic 
redox status.
METHODS: SCD (subjective cognitive decline), MCI (mild cognitive impairment), 
AD, and other dementias (Non-AD) were recruited. Comorbidity data were collected 
and free thiols were measured in plasma. Additionally, phosphorylated-Tau 
(pTau217), amyloid-beta ratio (Aβ42/40), Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP), 
and neurofilament light (NfL) levels were used to investigate correlation with 
free thiols. Further, associations between free thiols and disease severity in 
AD were calculated.
RESULTS: Three hundred and ten patients were included (SCD 109, MCI 51, AD 125, 
Non-AD 25). Free thiols were significantly lower in AD compared to SCD and MCI 
(p<0.01). Free thiols correlated negatively with pTau217, NfL and GFAP, also
