Prostate cancer (PC) is one of the most common male cancers. Cancer cells are 
well known for their capacity to avoid programed cell death (PCD) via a variety 
of molecular pathways, allowing them to survive oncogenic stress and therapeutic 
challenges. Although oncogenic splicing factors are frequently dysregulated in 
tumors, their functional interplay with PCD regulatory networks in PC remains 
largely uncharacterized. Here, we demonstrate that WBP11 exerts a 
pro-tumorigenic effect by promoting PC cell proliferation, while its genetic 
silencing triggers concurrent induction of apoptosis, pyroptosis, and 
ferroptosis. Mechanistically, WBP11 directly binds to and stabilizes OPLAH mRNA, 
leading to elevated intracellular glutathione levels that facilitate efficient 
clearance of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Additionally, we demonstrate that 
USP13 deubiquitinates WBP11 by specifically eliminating K48-linked ubiquitin 
chains at lysine 626, which increases the stability of the WBP11 protein and 
prevents proteasomal destruction. Using a combination of in vitro functional 
assays, in vivo tumor models, and systematic rescue experiments, we define a 
previously unrecognized signaling axis, USP13-WBP11-OPLAH, that orchestrates 
glutathione metabolism and confers resistance to PCD, ultimately driving 
malignant progression of PC. Consistent with these functional findings, clinical 
validation reveals that USP13, WBP11, and OPLAH are significantly upregulated at 
the protein level in human PC tissues, and that USP13 expression positively 
correlates with both WBP11 and OPLAH protein abundance. Collectively, our study 
identifies the USP13-WBP11-OPLAH axis as a critical regulatory module linking 
glutathione metabolism to PCD resistance, offering promising therapeutic targets 
for the treatment of advanced PC.

BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease 
(MASLD) affects one-third of adults, and one in five progresses to metabolic 
dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), which can cause liver failure, 
burdening hepatology clinics and transplant waiting lists. NRF2-KEAP1 axis is 
the principal regulator of hepatic antioxidant defence, yet its status across 
the disease spectrum is unclear. We mapped NRF2-KEAP1 transcriptional signatures 
across control, steatosis and MASH livers.
METHODS: Eight GEO datasets (590 biopsies: 154 control, 134 steatosis, 302 MASH) 
were harmonised by log2 transformation, within-dataset Z-scoring and ComBat 
correction. The pre-specified panel comprised NFE2L2, KEAP1 and six NRF2 targets 
(GCLC, GCLM, HMOX1, NQO1, SRXN1, TXNRD1). Groups were compared by ANOVA with 
Tukey post-hoc tests.
RESULTS: NFE2L2 was highest in control and reduced in steatotic and MASH livers 
(both p < 0.001), with KEAP1 reciprocally elevated. Targets were induced 
selectively where NQO1 and TXNRD1 peaked in MASH while HMOX1 was highest in 
control. NFE2L2-to-target co-expression was preserved across stages. Across 
fibrosis stages, NFE2L2 and KEAP1 were unchanged while NQO1 and TXNRD1 rose. 
Thus NQO1 and TXNRD1 rise in MASH even as NFE2L2 transcription falls.
CONCLUSIONS: NFE2L2 transcription decreases once MASLD is established, yet its 
targets are induced selectively and co-expression is preserved, so the pathway 
stays coherent while its output shifts. These are mRNA findings. We propose 
control of NRF2 at the protein level as a hypothesis consistent with our data 
and the pattern supports assessing NRF2 protein status in marginal donor livers 
and therapies targeting KEAP1.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by airflow 
limitation, dynamic hyperinflation, and intrinsic positive end-expiratory 
pressure (iPEEP), which increase inspiratory threshold load and complicate 
ventilatory support. Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is the preferred initial 
ventilatory support for COPD exacerbations complicated by acute or 
acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis, while invasive mechanical ventilation 
(IMV) may be required when NIV fails. External PEEP may reduce the inspiratory 
threshold load in patients with expiratory flow limitation, although excessive 
levels can increase lung volume and compromise hemodynamics. During IMV, PEEP 
adjustment requires assessment of respiratory mechanics, expiratory flow, 
hyperinflation, and cardiovascular tolerance. During NIV, where iPEEP cannot 
usually be measured directly, expiratory positive airway pressure (EPAP) should 
be adjusted according to clinical response, patient-ventilator interaction, and 
signs of excessive lung inflation. Inappropriate ventilatory assistance may also 
contribute to diaphragm dysfunction. Diaphragm ultrasound allows bedside 
assessment of muscle thickness and inspiratory thickening fraction (DTF), 
although these measurements are influenced by ventilatory assistance, 
respiratory drive, and lung volume. This review examines the physiological 
basis, available evidence, and limitations of using diaphragm ultrasound to 
complement PEEP adjustment in patients with COPD and dynamic hyperinflation. No 
DTF target or clinical benefit of ultrasound-guided PEEP titration has been 
established in this population.

Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) is an effective therapy 
for selected hematologic diseases. However, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) 
limits broader application of allo-HCT. The catecholaminergic sympathetic 
nervous system modulates immune cells. Beta-2 adrenergic Receptor (β2AR) acts as 
an immune checkpoint, yet its role in CD8+ T cells remains poorly understood. We 
used an MHC-mismatched model of acute GVHD to study how β2AR activity on donor 
CD8+ T cells affects GVHD severity. Host mice receiving β2AR+/+ (WT) CD8+ T 
cells demonstrated less severe GVHD, lower inflammatory cytokines in peripheral 
circulation, decreased donor CD8+ T cell expansion, and reduced central memory 
formation compared to host mice receiving β2AR-/- (KO) CD8+ T cells. Single cell 
RNA-seq and flow cytometry analyses revealed that donor-derived KO CD8+ T cells 
had an increased Tc1/Tc17 signature (T-Bet, IFNγ, TNFα, RORγT, and IL23r), 
expressed lower levels of Eomes and Gata3, and expressed inhibitory PD1, Tim3, 
Lag3, and CTLA4 less frequently than β2AR WT counterparts. In addition, host 
mice receiving KO CD8+ T cells exhibit a stronger graft-versus-lymphoma effect 
than host mice receiving β2AR WT CD8+ T cells. Together, these results indicate 
that β2AR activity in donor CD8+ T cells inhibits GVHD through transcriptional 
modulation of T cell differentiation and exhaustion, including a T-Bet/Eomes and 
PD1 relevant process.

Nykaza I(1), Chen A(2), Gu S(3), Dusza S(2), Shaffer B(4), Papadopoulos E(5),

BACKGROUND: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is a major complication of 
allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) and commonly exhibits 
cutaneous involvement. Topical and systemic therapies are frequently utilized to 
treat cutaneous GVHD, however these treatments are often limited by toxicity, 
incomplete response, and poor tolerability. Phototherapy has shown potential 
benefit as an adjunct treatment for cutaneous GVHD, although prior research has 
been limited to small retrospective studies.
OBJECTIVE: Evaluate the efficacy and safety of ultraviolet (UV)-based 
phototherapy in the treatment of cutaneous acute GVHD (aGVHD) and chronic GVHD 
(cGVHD).
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study of allo-HCT recipients with cutaneous 
GVHD treated with phototherapy at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center from 
2009-2024. Patients received either narrow-band UVB or UVA1 and were followed 
for response to phototherapy based on NIH scoring criteria, body surface area 
involvement, and physician notes.
RESULTS: Forty-six patients were evaluated, including 25 (54%) with aGVHD and 21 
(46%) with cGVHD. Most patients received narrow-band UVB (94%). For aGVHD, 
complete response (CR) occurred in 48% and partial response (PR) in 44%, with an 
overall response rate (ORR) of 92%. For patients with cGVHD, CR occurred in 43% 
and PR in 48%, with an ORR of 91%. Median time to best response was 48 days for 
acute GVHD and 42 days for chronic GVHD. Systemic treatments, including 
corticosteroids and ruxolitinib, were commonly tapered during phototherapy. 
Adverse events occurred in 22% of patients, most commonly burning, with 9% 
discontinuing due to toxicity. Four patients developed skin cancer during 
follow-up, however three patients had a prior history of nonmelanoma skin 
cancer, and the remaining patient received concurrent extracorporeal 
photopheresis leading up to the diagnosis of melanoma in-situ.
CONCLUSIONS: Phototherapy is an effective and well-tolerated treatment for 
cutaneous GVHD, achieving high response rates and facilitating tapering of 
systemic immunosuppression. Given its favorable safety profile and rapid time to 
response, phototherapy should be considered as an adjunctive or steroid-sparing 
option for cutaneous GVHD, particularly in patients with extensive or 
treatment-refractory disease.

Recent advances in nutrient sensing and endocrine regulation of insect growth 
and development.

Koyama T(1), Texada MJ(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Biology, University of Copenhagen, Universitetsparken 15, 2100 
Copenhagen, Denmark. Electronic address: takashi.koyama@bio.ku.dk.
(2)Department of Biology, University of Copenhagen, Universitetsparken 15, 2100 
Copenhagen, Denmark.

Regulation of proper growth across the whole body and within individual organs 
is fundamental for animals to achieve species-specific body size and 
proportions, which are crucial for maximizing fitness. To accomplish this, 
animals continuously sense changes in both environmental and internal conditions 
through specific cells and organs and adjust their growth to maximize their 
final size while minimizing developmental time, normally via endocrine 
signaling. Among environmental factors, nutrition is one of the most critical 
determinants of development. Because macronutrients are essential for growth, 
insects monitor both food quality and internal nutrient concentrations to adjust 
their growth and developmental timing through multiple endocrine factors. In 
insects, growth rate is primarily regulated by insulin-like peptides, functional 
and structural homologs of vertebrate insulin-superfamily peptides, and their 
receptor, insulin-like receptor. In contrast, growth duration is mainly 
controlled by the steroid molting hormone ecdysone and its nuclear hormone 
receptor, Ecdysone receptor. In addition to ecdysone, juvenile hormone, a 
sesquiterpenoid hormone that acts through its own nuclear receptor, 
Methoprene-tolerant, modulates the action of ecdysone and thereby influences 
both growth rate and duration. Recent studies have revealed that several cells 
and organs monitor both nutrient quality and internal macronutrient levels and 
release a variety of hormones and cytokines that fine-tune the production and 
secretion of the central growth-regulating hormones. This review summarizes 
recent advances in our understanding of how macronutrient-sensitive endocrine 
pathways coordinate appropriate growth and development in insects.

AIMS: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) encompasses patients with an atypical 
clinical course, where GFR declines precedes albuminuria. This study 
investigated the characteristics, risk factors, and vascular outcomes of DKD 
subgroups among 2,733 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
METHODS: Using data from a Japan-wide patients registry (J-DOME), we classified 
patients by albuminuria and eGFR, analyzed annual trends in eGFR and evaluated 
the incidence of new vascular complications.
RESULTS: The prevalence of DKD was 45%, one-third of whom had low 
eGFR/normoalbuminuria. Although the low eGFR/normoalbuminuria group showed 
similar glycemic control to the no DKD group, the albuminuria/normal eGFR group 
had poorer control of lifestyle-related risk factors. Both DKD subgroups had a 
higher prevalence of microvascular and macrovascular disorders at baseline. 
During a mean follow-up of 2.5 years, compared with the no DKD group, the low 
eGFR/normoalbuminuria group showed a slower rate of renal function decline, 
while the albuminuria/normal eGFR group exhibited a faster rate of renal 
function decline. In contrast, the incidence of vascular diseases did not differ 
between either DKD subgroup and the no DKD group.
CONCLUSIONS: The albuminuria/normal eGFR group exhibited accelerated renal 
function decline compared with the no DKD group, highlighting albuminuria as a 
marker of active renal injury in type 2 diabetes. In contrast, the low 
eGFR/normoalbuminuria group showed short-term renal stability despite a high 
baseline prevalence of vascular complications, representing a distinct clinical 
phenotype.

BACKGROUND: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) treatment is increasingly viewed through a 
remission lens, reflecting a shift from chronic management to disease 
regression. This study examined pre-implementation conditions, including 
barriers and facilitators, to adopt, implement, and scale a T2D remission 
program in primary care using a scalability assessment.
METHODS: Using the Intervention Scalability Assessment Tool (ISAT), a 
descriptive qualitative case study was conducted and included semi-structured 
interviews with a purposeful sample of 11 multidisciplinary professionals within 
one Ontario (Canada) Family Health Team (FHT) (January-March 2025). Framework 
analysis was used to code, categorize and develop overarching themes related to 
scale-up elements and how to optimize program delivery and acceptance.
RESULTS: The thematic analysis generated 3 themes, outlining the primary 
conditions perceived to be needed for successful implementation and scale-up: 
(1) Effectively conceptualizing and positioning a health coach within primary 
care; (2) Site readiness to adopt T2D remission implementation; and (3) 
Perceived opportunities for fostering positive health outcomes. Participants 
supported integrating a T2D remission program into the existing FHT, citing 
broad benefits. Participants unanimously agreed that there was a strong demand 
for such a program, both from individuals living with T2D and healthcare 
providers, and was well-warranted in comparison to the lengthy treatments that 
can be accrued throughout a diagnosis of T2D.
DISCUSSION: Using a single site FHT to understand the potential to scale-up, a 
T2D remission program in primary care was acceptable and feasible if 
context-specific barriers and facilitators are addressed, with strategic 
planning around role integration, capacity, and sustained patient engagement.

Type 2 diabetes (T2D) increases the risk for diabetic cardiomyopathy (DbCM), 
which is often characterized by diastolic dysfunction. Pre-menopausal women have 
a reduced incidence of both T2D and DbCM, but this disappears following 
menopause. Our goal was to evaluate the potential role for ovarian hormones in 
mediating these differences. The effect of ovariectomy (OVX) was investigated in 
female mice with experimental T2D following high-fat diet feeding for 12-weeks 
in combination with a low-dose treatment of streptozotocin at week 4. Body 
weight and body composition, glucose homeostasis, cardiac structure/function via 
ultrasound echocardiography, and myocardial substrate metabolism via isolated 
working heart perfusions were assessed. Sham and OVX female mice with T2D 
exhibited increases in body weight and fat mass, as well as impaired glucose 
homeostasis, though these parameters were more prominent in OVX than sham 
females when compared to their lean counterparts. However, only OVX female mice 
with T2D developed diastolic dysfunction as reflected by a significant decrease 
in the mitral E/A and tissue Doppler e'/a' ratios, as well as an increase in the 
E/e' ratio. Isolated working hearts from both sham and OVX female mice with T2D 
exhibited a reduction in glucose oxidation, though this was more pronounced in 
the latter. Lastly, only OVX female mice with T2D demonstrated cardiomyocyte 
hypertrophy. Our data illustrate key roles for ovarian hormones in impacting how 
T2D impacts the progression of DbCM in females, which may have relevance to 
women living with T2D as they transition to menopause.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) of endogenous NAD(P)H enables 
the label-free assessment of cellular metabolic state. Although metabolic 
imaging is increasingly combined with fluorescent protein (FP) reporters to 
enhance biological specificity, the potential cross-talk between the intrinsic 
and extrinsic labels remain ill-defined. Here, we systematically evaluate 
cross-talk from FPs in metabolic FLIM using phasor analysis of two-photon 
fluorescence microscopy. The results clearly show that many widely used 
fluorescent proteins are excited under the conditions used for NADH imaging; 
they emit blue-shifted, short-lifetime fluorescence that can interfere with 
imaging NADH metabolic signatures. This overlap persists across excitation 
wavelengths and FP classes, posing a significant challenge for multiplexed 
metabolic imaging. This cautionary tale argues against unvalidated multiplexing 
strategies in metabolic FLIM studies. Our study aims to identify acceptable 
imaging partners, offer a pipeline for assaying potential cross-talk, and 
provide practical guidance for experimental design.

Stator pool size shapes the mechanosensitivity of the bacterial flagellar motor.

Wise BM(1), Sawant SA(2), Wadhwa N(3).

Author information:
(1)Biodesign Center for Mechanisms of Evolution, Arizona State University, 
Tempe, AZ 85287, USA; Center for Biological Physics, Arizona State University, 
Tempe, AZ 85287, USA; Department of Physics, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ

(2)Biodesign Center for Mechanisms of Evolution, Arizona State University,

(3)Biodesign Center for Mechanisms of Evolution, Arizona State University, 
Tempe, AZ 85287, USA; Center for Biological Physics, Arizona State University,

The bacterial flagellar motor adapts to mechanical load by adding or removing 
stator units, which can either be inactive in the inner membrane (the stator 
pool) or attached to the motor in a torque-generating configuration. This 
adaptation is well understood, but what sets the load range over which the motor 
responds remains unclear. Building on a previous two-state model of stator 
binding, we derive how the on-rate depends on the diffusing stator pool and find 
that it increases in proportion to pool size. The model predicts that pool size 
governs motor occupancy at low load but not at high load, where the motor 
saturates regardless of how many stators are available. We confirmed this 
prediction in Escherichia coli: increasing motAB induction increased swimming 
speed and single-motor rotation rate at low load. This dependence on induction 
weakened as load rose and was undetectable at high load. The model further 
predicts that larger pools make the motor mechanosensitive at lower loads, which 
our measurements of load-induced occupancy change support. Mechanosensitivity is 
therefore not fixed by motor architecture alone, but also determined by stator 
abundance, which cells can set through expression to position their 
mechanosensory range.

Urban expansion and environmental fragmentation have intensified contact among 
wildlife, domestic animals, and humans, reshaping infectious disease dynamics at 
the human-wildlife interface. Non-human primates (NHP), particularly the 
black-tufted marmoset (Callithrix penicillata), readily adapt to anthropogenic 
landscapes and may serve as sentinel hosts for zoonotic pathogens. This study 
investigated the occurrence of Leishmania spp., Plasmodium spp., Toxoplasma 
gondii, and Trypanosoma cruzi. in 232 free-ranging C. penicillata found dead in 
urban and peri-urban areas of the Federal District, central Brazil, between 2018 
and 2023. Liver samples were analyzed by quantitative PCR. Plasmodium spp. was 
not detected (0/232). In contrast, 39.7% (92/232) of marmosets were positive for 
T. gondii, 32.4% (69/213) for Leishmania spp., and 21.1% (47/223) for T. cruzi. 
Overall, 71.6% of the animals tested positive for at least one protozoan agent, 
and 21.2% had coinfections, most commonly Leishmania spp. plus T. gondii. 
Positive cases were widely distributed across administrative regions, with 
evidence of spatiotemporal clustering in some urbanized areas. Parasitic loads 
varied substantially, and most infected animals showed no lesions attributable 
to these infections. These findings demonstrate the widespread circulation of 
zoonotic protozoa in free-ranging marmosets inhabiting anthropized environments 
and reinforce their epidemiological relevance within a One Health framework. 
Surveillance of urban NHP populations can contribute to understanding 
transmission networks and environmental contamination, thereby supporting public 
health strategies for the prevention and control of zoonotic diseases in central 
Brazil.

Liu YH(1), Xu RS(1), Hu JQ(1), Tong X(1), He CC(2), Gao XH(3).

Tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 1 (TRAF1) is a unique member of 
the TRAF family, distinguished by its lack of an N-terminal RING domain. At the 
transcriptional level, TRAF1 expression is regulated by diverse mechanisms, 
including methylation, RNA-binding domain (RBD) proteins, and microRNAs. 
Post-translationally, TRAF1 undergoes modifications such as M1-linked 
ubiquitination and phosphorylation. In immune signaling pathways, TRAF1 usually 
displays functional duality: it activates the canonical NF-κB pathway by 
enhancing cIAP recruitment downstream of TNFR1, whereas at death domain-lacking 
TNFR superfamily members (NDDTNFRs), it drives the non-canonical NF-κB pathway 
through TRAF3 degradation. Conversely, TRAF1 often acts as a negative regulator 
in Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling. Within the MAPK pathway, TRAF1 
participates in modulating multiple cascades, including ASK1/B-Raf(BRAF)/ERK1. 
In immune-mediated diseases, TRAF1 contributes to disease pathogenesis by 
regulating inflammatory cytokines, matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) expression, 
synovial cell apoptosis and tissue destruction. In infectious diseases, the 
anti-apoptotic effect of TRAF1 downstream of the 4-1BB signaling pathway serves 
as a host strategy to combat viral infections by preserving CD8+ T cell 
survival. However, Helicobacter pylori exploits TRAF1 upregulation to inhibit 
apoptosis in gastric epithelial cells, facilitating its persistent colonization. 
This contrast highlights TRAF1's functional diversity across infections. This 
review summarizes the post-translational regulation of TRAF1, its dual roles in 
signaling pathways, and its contributions to immune-related and infectious 
diseases, aiming to clarify its mechanistic complexity within the existing 
biological framework.

Homocysteine and related B-vitamins throughout our International Conferences: a 
historical perspective.

Rosenberg I(1).

Author information:
(1)Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy, Tufts University, Boston, 
Massachusetts, United States. Electronic address: irwin.rosenberg@tufts.edu.

In this invited keynote review, I reflect on biochemical, clinical, and 
epidemiological evidence on the role of folate and vitamin B12 in one-carbon 
metabolism and their relationship with homocysteine, integrating over five 
decades of research. One-carbon metabolism represents a central biochemical 
network linking folate-dependent one-carbon transfer reactions with vitamin 
B12-dependent remethylation of homocysteine to methionine. Disruptions in this 
pathway result in elevated homocysteine concentrations and impaired methylation 
capacity, providing a mechanistic link between micronutrient status and chronic 
disease. Early work demonstrated that folate is a major determinant of plasma 
homocysteine levels, supporting folic acid fortification policies that 
significantly reduced neural tube defects worldwide. Research in my laboratory 
in older adults shifted the paradigm of deficiency from inadequate intake to 
impaired bioavailability. Elevated homocysteine has been associated with 
cardiovascular disease, stroke, and cognitive decline, although intervention 
trials have yielded mixed results, suggesting that homocysteine is best 
interpreted as a marker of metabolic dysfunction, but when elevated, a potential 
target for mitigating cognitive decline. Recent advances in epigenetics and 
gene-nutrient interactions have expanded the relevance of one-carbon metabolism, 
highlighting its role in DNA methylation and gene regulation. Future research in 
precision nutrition may refine strategies for preventing chronic disease and 
promoting healthy aging.

Trichomonas vaginalis is the protozoan that causes trichomoniasis, the most 
common non-viral sexually transmitted infection in the world. Recently, studies 
have highlighted the possible association between T. vaginalis and the 
development of cervical cancer, as well as co-infection with human 
papillomavirus (HPV), suggesting a role of the protozoan in oncogenesis. In the 
cervical cancer context, the purinergic signaling influences immunosuppression 
and angiogenesis, while high concentrations of adenosine can induce cell death. 
T. vaginalis uptakes adenosine for survival as well it takes advantage in its 
immunomodulatory effects. Thus, the presence of T. vaginalis could influence 
cell survival, modulating the tumor microenvironment. Our study demonstrated 
that, in ex vivo models, T. vaginalis increased cell proliferation, immune 
infiltrate, and vascularization. Meanwhile, in in vitro 2D cell culture models, 
T. vaginalis combined with purinergic signaling differentially affects the 
viability of HPV-positive (SiHa) and HPV-negative (C33A) cervical cancer cell 
lines, with significant impact in the cell line without HPV. The ATP and 
adenosine signaling did not affect the cytotoxicity exerted by conditioned 
medium against both cell lines. T. vaginalis reduced the IL-6 production and E6 
oncogene expression by SiHa cells. the Ki-67 gene expression was modulated by 
the parasite and ATP/adenosine metabolism, highlighting the plasticity of the 
purinergic signaling combined with the parasite. These findings indicate that T. 
vaginalis exerts cytotoxicity and modulation of pathways relevant to the tumor 
microenvironment, influencing cell death, inflammation, and tissue remodeling 
processes, and shed light to further studies on the interactions between T. 
vaginalis and host cells.

OBJECTIVES: To address the focus question: in adults with peri-implantitis, does 
air polishing, used as an adjunct to or a replacement for non-surgical 
instrumentation, improve disease resolution and probing pocket depth (PPD) 
compared with instrumentation alone?
DATA AND SOURCES: MEDLINE (PubMed), Web of Science, Scopus, EMBASE and the 
Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) were searched from 
inception to 15 July 2026.
METHODS: Randomized and non-randomized comparative studies were eligible if the 
case definition required bleeding and/or suppuration on probing and radiographic 
bone loss. PPD and bleeding on probing (BOP) were pooled in a random-effects 
model with therapeutic role as a pre-specified subgroup, using 
Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman intervals and adjustment for clustering of implants 
within patients. Other outcomes were synthesized without meta-analysis (SWiM), 
and certainty was rated with GRADE.
RESULTS: Fourteen studies were included, ten in the meta-analysis. At six 
months, the mean difference in PPD change was -0.03 mm (95% CI -0.38 to 0.31) 
for adjunctive and +0.04 mm (95% CI -0.52 to 0.59) for replacement use, with no 
subgroup difference (p = 0.78) and negligible heterogeneity (I² = 3.4%). No 
significant differences were found at other timepoints or for BOP. Certainty was 
low for adjunctive PPD change and very low for all other outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: Low to very low certainty evidence does not show a clinically 
meaningful PPD benefit when air polishing is added to conventional 
instrumentation. For its use as a replacement, the evidence is too imprecise to 
establish superiority, equivalence or inferiority.
CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Adding air polishing to non-surgical peri-implantitis 
therapy has not been shown to improve outcomes beyond conventional 
instrumentation, and evidence on its use as a replacement is inconclusive. Given 
the low certainty of the evidence, well-designed trials with standardized 
endpoints are needed before firm recommendations can be made. PROSPERO 
Registration: CRD42023447967.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is associated with hippocampal mitochondrial 
dysfunction, including impaired mitophagy, biogenesis, dynamics, bioenergetics, 
and redox homeostasis, which may contribute to amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation, tau 
pathology, and cognitive decline. This systematic review examined whether 
exercise training is associated with changes in hippocampal mitochondrial 
regulation and cognitive function in transgenic AD rodent models. Following 
PRISMA 2020 guidelines, PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science were searched up to 
July 2, 2026. Twenty-one studies met inclusion criteria. Exercise modalities 
included treadmill running, voluntary wheel running, and swimming, with 
durations from 4 weeks to 8 months. Risk of bias was assessed using the SYRCLE 
tool. Due to heterogeneity, meta-analysis was not appropriate; a narrative 
synthesis was performed. Exercise training was associated with changes in 
markers of mitophagy, biogenesis, dynamics, and function, as well as reduced 
oxidative stress, decreased Aβ and tau pathology, and improved spatial learning 
and memory. However, most studies assessed static markers rather than functional 
flux, and risk of bias was unclear in several domains. The evidence suggests 
that exercise training may be associated with hippocampal mitochondrial 
modulation and cognitive benefits in AD models, but conclusions are limited by 
heterogeneity and incomplete reporting. Further studies with functional 
mitochondrial assays and clear reporting of methods and results are needed.

Chronic cerebral hypoperfusion is the leading risk factor for the development of 
vascular dementia and is associated with white matter damage and cognitive 
impairment. Here, we assessed sex differences in vascular and neural pathology 
and cognitive impairment in the asymmetric carotid arterial stenosis (ACAS)

neuropathology and sex differences in spatial memory and miRNA profiles.

Bone strength is a major determinant of osteoporotic fracture risk. Current 
clinical assessments, however, rely primarily on imaging-based surrogates such 
as bone mineral density, offering limited insight into the integrated mechanical 
behavior of vertebral bone. Inspired by engineered composite structures, in 
which interfacial interactions substantially enhance mechanical properties, this 
study introduces the concept of the cortical-trabecular interlocking effect to 
characterize the mechanical integration between these two compartments and 
investigate its contribution to vertebral bone strength. Micro-finite element 
models of mouse L4 vertebrae (control, mild, and severe osteoporosis) and 
idealized vertebral models were employed to quantify the independent 
contributions of isolated cortical bone, isolated trabecular bone, and the 
cortical-trabecular interlocking effect to whole-bone mechanical properties 
under axial load. To better characterize the cortical-trabecular interlocking 
effect, we propose a novel microstructural parameter, Lr.BV/TV, defined as the 
bone volume fraction within the interlocking ring, an interface region where 
cortical and trabecular bone are structurally integrated. The 
cortical-trabecular interlocking effect contributed 12.2-26.1% (mean 19.5%) to 
vertebral yield strength and its magnitude varied systematically with 
osteoporosis severity. Notably, asynchronous deterioration of cortical and 
trabecular bone in osteoporosis constrained the effective utilization of the 
interlocking effect, whereas well-matched components maximized this effect. 
Lr.BV/TV was identified as the dominant predictor of vertebral strength and 
outperformed both cortical thickness and trabecular bone volume fraction, 
accounting for 45.83% of the total explained variance, with its predictive 
relevance varying across stages of osteoporosis. These findings advance our 
understanding of vertebral fragility.

Repetitive movements impose distinct loading regimens on long bones, potentially 
eliciting predictable osteogenic responses and morphological change. Cortical 
responses to such movements are seldom investigated along whole diaphyses as 
opposed to selected locations. Morphometric mapping is a technique that is 
well-suited for comprehensively examining whole diaphyses. To assess responses 
to different movement regimens, we evaluated humeri of thirty-five female 
C57BL/6J mice raised from weeks 4 to 20 post-birth in one of three scenarios: 
linear-dominated (n = 12), turning-dominated (n = 12), and open cage (n = 11)

thicknesses (Ct.Th), second moments of area (SMA), and deltoid crest angles

shaft regions. Individuals in the open cage group tended to exhibit overall 
greater SMAs than individuals in the other groups. Bayesian probabilities 
support mean DCA differences between the linear (25.0°) versus the open cage 
(20.9°) and turning (22.0°) groups. Ultimately, three different movement 
regimens elicited unique combinations of site- and direction-specific shaft 
reinforcements and muscle attachment orientations without any substantial 
differences in overall humeral bone mass. The generally overall greater SMAs of 
the open cage group suggest benefits to skeletal health (e.g., diversified shaft 
reinforcement) may be accrued in a non-pharmacological intervention strategy 
that would emphasize multidirectional rather than repetitive activities.

Photobiomodulation and the Wnt/β-Catenin Pathway in Apexogenesis: Rationale and 
Evidence Gaps.

Bahrami R(1), Kiyamehr Z(2), Pourhajibagher M(3), Bahador A(4).

Author information:
(1)Department of Orthodontics, School of Dentistry, Iran University of Medical 
Sciences, Tehran, Iran. Electronic address: bahramirashin@yahoo.com.
(2)Department of Pediatric Dentistry, School of Dentistry, Iran University of 
Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran. Electronic address: z.kiyamehr@gmail.com.
(3)Dental Research Center, Dentistry Research Institute, Tehran University of

m-pourhajibagher@sina.tums.ac.ir.
(4)Department of Microbiology, School of Medicine, Tehran University of Medical

Apexogenesis is a vital pulp therapy that preserves vascularized pulp in 
immature teeth and relies on dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs) and stem cells from 
the apical papilla (SCAPs) for continued root growth and apical closure. 
Wnt/β-catenin signaling has an established role in odontoblast differentiation, 
reparative dentinogenesis, and root development, although normal root 
development requires regulated rather than simply increased Wnt activity. 
Photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) is proposed to act through mitochondrial 
photoreception, and in vitro studies report increased expression of 
odontogenic/osteogenic markers and angiogenic factors (VEGF, TGF-β2) in DPSCs 
and SCAPs. Because these markers overlap with Wnt/β-catenin targets, a link 
between PBMT and this pathway has been hypothesized but not tested in these 
cells. This review addresses three questions: the role of Wnt/β-catenin 
signaling in root development and dentin repair; the mechanism that could link 
PBMT to this pathway; and the in vitro evidence for PBMT effects on DPSCs and 
SCAPs and its consistency. The evidence is heterogeneous and limited. Increased 
odontogenic/osteogenic differentiation was the most consistent finding. Reported 
effects on "proliferation" were inconsistent and were estimated mainly by MTT, a 
metabolic assay that does not measure cell division; no study used a clonogenic 
assay, and only one performed direct cell counts. No superior wavelength or 
fluence was identified. No study has examined PBMT-induced modulation of 
Wnt/β-catenin signaling in DPSCs or SCAPs, and the markers involved are not 
pathway-specific. Therapeutic benefit in apexogenesis therefore remains 
unproven; direct mechanistic studies, light-delivery studies through dentin, and 
animal models are priorities.

Persistent autoantibody production after conventional immunosuppression or 
B-cell depletion has focused attention on antibody-secreting cells that survive 
without ongoing proliferation. Long-lived plasma cells (LLPCs) are indispensable 
for durable protective immunity, but autoreactive members of this compartment 
may also maintain pathogenic antibodies in selected autoimmune diseases. 
Interpretation is complicated because longevity is usually inferred from 
population kinetics, anatomical persistence, transcriptional state, or treatment 
resistance rather than demonstrated by lineage tracing in humans; neither CD19 
loss nor any single surface phenotype is a definitive identifier. We conducted a 
structured narrative review focused on rheumatic diseases and selected 
antibody-mediated disorders. We integrate developmental routes, CXCR4-dependent 
homing, adhesion, BAFF/APRIL receptor biology, stromal contact, proteostatic and 
metabolic adaptation, and single-cell heterogeneity. Systemic lupus 
erythematosus and lupus nephritis receive dedicated consideration because renal 
antibody-secreting-cell signatures distinguish active plasmablast-rich 
inflammation from LLPC-like persistence in refractory disease. Across diseases, 
the evidence ranges from direct kinetic or tissue studies to indirect 
serological observations and therapeutic inference. Plasma-cell-directed 
therapies-including proteasome inhibition, CD38 depletion, BCMA-directed T-cell 
engagers or cellular therapy, and immune reconstitution-have produced clinically 
important signals, but most autoimmune data remain uncontrolled, early-phase, or 
disease-specific. Niche disruption, apoptosis or autophagy inhibition, and 
antigen-specific deletion remain preclinical or conceptual. A useful 
translational framework is therefore not that LLPCs are universal master 
drivers, but that persistent autoreactive plasma cells may constitute one 
treatment-relevant disease module whose importance should be demonstrated with 
tissue, clonal, and longitudinal evidence before intervention.

The adaptive immune receptor repertoire (AIRR), composed of T-cell receptors 
(TCRs) and B-cell receptors (BCRs), underpins antigen-specific immunity through 
extensive diversity generated by V(D)J recombination and junctional 
modification. Advances in high-throughput AIRR sequencing have enabled 
comprehensive characterization of clonal diversity, gene usage patterns, and 
antigen-driven selection at unprecedented resolution. In autoimmune diseases, 
breakdown of immune tolerance permits the persistence and expansion of 
autoreactive lymphocyte clones, and is associated with characteristic repertoire 
remodeling. Reported alterations include changes in repertoire diversity, 
oligoclonal expansion, biased V(D)J gene usage, and convergent CDR3 motifs. 
Notably, repertoire changes exhibit spatial and temporal heterogeneity across 
peripheral blood and target tissues, highlighting the compartmentalized nature 
of adaptive immune responses. This review synthesizes current evidence on TCR 
and BCR repertoire alterations across major autoimmune diseases, including 
rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren's disease, type 1 
diabetes, and ankylosing spondylitis. We summarize emerging computational 
frameworks for AIRR analysis and highlight machine learning approaches for 
clonotype classification and antigen specificity prediction. Furthermore, we 
discuss the diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic implications of AIRR 
profiling, particularly the potential for identifying disease-associated 
clonotypes and guiding antigen-specific immunotherapies. Despite ongoing 
technical and biological challenges, continued advances in sequencing 
technologies and computational modeling are strengthening the role of AIRR 
analysis as a valuable framework for elucidating autoimmune pathogenesis and 
advancing precision immunology.

BACKGROUND: Endometriosis has traditionally been defined as a disease localized 
to the pelvis. However, its clinical presentation is often accompanied by 
systemic comorbidities that extend far beyond the pelvic cavity, a phenomenon 
that challenges the traditional disease paradigm.
OBJECTIVE AND RATIONALE: This study aimed to comprehensively assess the 
associations between endometriosis and autoimmune diseases, allergic conditions, 
chronic pain syndromes, and endocrine disorders through a systematic review and 
meta-analysis, thereby providing evidence for redefining endometriosis as a 
systemic immuno-inflammatory disorder.
SEARCH METHODS: To conduct this study, a comprehensive search strategy was 
employed to identify relevant published studies. Electronic databases, including 
Web of Science and Medline, were searched from their inception up to December 
31, 2025. We additionally examined the reference lists of all identified papers 
to capture any additional articles that were not identified through the 
electronic database searches. Eligible studies were observational in design 
(cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional) and reported quantitative data on 
the association between endometriosis and predefined comorbidities in women. 
Exclusion criteria included non-human studies, non-English publications, 
secondary literature types (e.g., reviews, case reports), and studies lacking 
sufficient data for effect size calculation. Quality assessment was conducted 
based on the GRADE criteria.
OUTCOMES: The final analysis included 55 studies that met the predefined 
inclusion criteria and were incorporated into the comprehensive analysis. Of 
these, 48 studies provided sufficient data for quantitative synthesis 
(meta-analysis). Specifically, 32 studies investigated the association between 
endometriosis and autoimmune diseases: 14 on systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), 
8 on Sjögren's syndrome (SS), 10 on rheumatoid arthritis (RA), 5 on multiple 
sclerosis (MS), 5 on celiac disease (CLD), and 4 on inflammatory bowel disease 
(IBD). Additionally, 17 studies examined associations with allergic diseases, 13 
focused on pain syndromes, and 6 explored associations with endocrine disorders. 
Meta-analysis showed that women with endometriosis had a significantly higher 
risk of certain autoimmune diseases in cohort studies, including SLE (RR: 1.81, 
95% CI: 1.50-2.18), SS (RR: 1.54, 95% CI: 1.40-1.71), and RA (RR: 1.71, 95% CI: 
1.40-2.09), as well as significantly higher odds in case-control and 
cross-sectional studies for SLE (OR: 3.93, 95% CI: 2.59-5.98), SS (OR: 3.13, 95% 
CI: 1.10-8.90), RA (OR: 2.27, 95% CI: 1.75-2.95), MS (OR: 2.30, 95% CI: 
1.57-3.37), CLD (OR: 4.50, 95% CI: 1.94-10.42), and IBD (OR: 2.82, 95% CI: 
0.58-13.61). Significant associations were also observed for allergic 
conditions-such as asthma (RR: 1.27, 95% CI: 1.14-1.40) and eczema (OR: 1.58, 
95% CI: 1.34-1.87)-and for pain syndromes including fibromyalgia (RR: 1.65, 95% 
CI: 1.42-1.92), chronic fatigue syndrome (RR: 1.41, 95% CI: 1.31-1.51), and 
irritable bowel syndrome (RR: 2.51, 95% CI: 1.55-4.07; OR: 3.49, 95% CI: 
3.21-3.80). In contrast, no statistically significant increase was observed in 
the odds of endocrine disorders such as hypothyroidism (OR: 1.89, 95% CI: 
0.61-5.90) and hyperthyroidism (OR: 0.95, 95% CI: 0.60-1.52) among women with 
endometriosis compared with women without endometriosis. However, the overall 
quality of evidence was generally low or very low according to the GRADE 
approach, largely due to a high risk of bias in most of the included study 
designs and statistical analyses.
WIDER IMPLICATIONS: The body of evidence provided by this study supports the 
reconceptualization of endometriosis as a systemic immuno-inflammatory disease. 
The associations with various comorbidities are underpinned by shared mechanisms 
of immune dysregulation and central sensitization. This paradigm shift 
necessitates a move in clinical practice from a purely gynecological 
intervention model toward a patient-centered, comprehensive multidisciplinary 
management approach. It also provides a theoretical foundation for developing 
novel treatment strategies targeting shared pathological pathways.

The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has established a tolerable daily 
intake (TDI) of 1mg/kg bw/d for the plasticizer DINCH 
(Cyclohexane-1,2-dicarboxylic acid diisononyl ester). To characterize the 
maximum internal doses resulting from a single dosing and to assess species 
differences relevant for extrapolating rat toxicokinetics to humans, 
concentration-time profiles of DINCH and its metabolites (specific monoesters: 
MINCH, OH-MINCH, oxo-MINCH, cx-MINCH; non-specific metabolite: CHDA) were 
quantified in the blood of male Wistar rats and male human volunteers. Urinary 
excretion of metabolites was additionally evaluated for humans. Single oral 
doses of ring-deuterated DINCH were administered (rats: 1 or 40mg/kg bw; humans: 
1mg/kg bw). In rats, gastrointestinal absorption exhibited saturation, as a 
40-fold increase in administered dose resulted in only ~25-fold increases in 
Cmax and AUC. Across species, the hierarchy of Cmax in blood was consistent: 
DINCH > CHDA > cx-MINCH > MINCH > OH-MINCH > oxo-MINCH. Notably, Cmax values for 
DINCH and MINCH in blood after a 1mg/kg bw (1.74µM and 0.10µM) dose in humans 
were like those observed in rats following a 40-fold higher dose (4.4µM and 
0.11µM). Corresponding AUC∞ values showed the same pattern, indicating greater 
systemic availability of DINCH in humans, although this is partly counter 
balanced by plasma protein binding. In humans, approximately 50% of MINCH and 
70-80% of the other monoester metabolites were glucuronidated, whereas these 
metabolites remained unconjugated in rats. CHDA was unconjugated in both 
species. Overall, the data highlight both shared and species-specific features 
of DINCH metabolism in rats and humans.

BACKGROUND: Type II endoleak (T2EL) is frequent after endovascular abdominal 
aortic aneurysm repair (EVAR) and may require reintervention in selected 
patients. However, the optimal treatment strategy for durable resolution remains 
uncertain. The aim of this study is to retrospectively analyze perioperative and 
long-term results of T2Els' reinterventions, both endovascular and open 
surgical, in a large patient cohort from twenty high-volume academic centers.
METHODS: A retrospective analysis of consecutive patients undergoing first 
reintervention for T2ELs was conducted across 20 centers over a 10-year period. 
Patients requiring concomitant treatment for other endoleak types were excluded. 
A total of 403 patients were included. Primary outcomes included technical 
success, 30-day AAA-related mortality and reintervention-free survival during 
follow-up. Secondary outcomes were perioperative complications, early 
reintervention, overall survival, freedom from aneurysm-related death and 
rupture, freedom from recurrent endoleaks, freedom from open conversion or 
semi-conversion in patients previously treated endovascularly and sac behavior 
during follow-up. Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox regression analyses were performed 
to analyze follow-up results.
RESULTS: Patients were predominantly male (90%) with a mean age of 77 years. 
Reintervention was indicated for sac enlargement in 94.5% of cases; 4% presented 
with rupture. Median time from EVAR to reintervention was 4.3 years. Lumbar 
arteries (55%) and the inferior mesenteric artery (35%) were the main sources. 
Endovascular treatment was performed in 86% and open conversion/semi-conversion 
in 14%. Technical success was 96%, with 1% mortality and 4% major complications. 
Overall survival was 80.5% and rupture-free survival 79.2% at 5 years. Recurrent 
T2EL occurred in 64.2%, and reintervention-free survival was 48.3%. Endovascular 
group showed significantly lower freedom from reintervention rates when compared 
to open conversion/semi conversion group (42.4% vs 86.8%, SE 0.04 vs SE 0.05, 
p<0.001, log-rank 15.9). Conversion/semi-conversion after endovascular treatment 
occurred in 14%. No differences were recorded comparing different fabric 
materials of the endograft in terms of freedom for reintervention and freedom 
from open surgery. A sac diameter ≥7 cm at the time of reintervention predicted 
further reinterventions, while primary open treatment improved durability.
CONCLUSIONS: Reinterventions for T2ELs are safe, with satisfactory immediate 
technical success and low perioperative mortality. During follow-up, risks of 
rupture and AAA-related death remain low. However, the endoleak recurrence rate 
exceeds 60% at five years, necessitating reintervention in over 40% of patients. 
Early intervention for patients with a sac diameter approaching 7 cm can be 
suggested, while a primary open approach may be considered in low-risk patients.

Motor planning in Colombian spider monkeys (Ateles fusciceps rufiventris).

Nelson EL(1), Weiss DJ(2), Shoukry CV(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Psychology, Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA. 
Electronic address: elnelson@fiu.edu.
(2)Harborview Medical Center, Seattle, WA, USA.
(3)Department of Psychology, Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA.

The morphological constraint hypothesis suggests that primates with less 
dexterity show more consistent motor planning because there is less flexibility 
to compensate for inefficient actions. Spiders monkeys offer a unique 
opportunity to test this hypothesis because they do not have a functional thumb. 
Colombian spider monkeys (Ateles fusciceps rufiventris, n=8) housed at a 
wildlife park were tested on a standard motor planning task. A trial began when 
a dowel baited on one end was placed on an elevated apparatus and ended when a 
monkey grasped the dowel with the hands. Grip use was coded from video as radial 
(pronated overhand grip with the radius bone towards food) or non-radial. The 
percentage of radial grips was used in analyses for comparison to other 
platyrrhines. As a group, spider monkeys used a radial grip significantly more 
than chance (M ± SD=73.38% ± 18.91), indicating spider monkeys engage in 
second-order motor planning. Spider monkeys differed in radial grip use from 
captive cotton-top tamarins (Saguinus oedipus) but not captive (Sapajus spp) or 
wild capuchins (Sapajus libidinosus) tested on the elevated dowel task in prior 
work by other investigators. Together, these findings have mixed implications 
for the morphological constraint hypothesis that merit further study.

PURPOSE: Isavuconazole (ISCZ) has demonstrated therapeutic efficacy for invasive 
fungal infections (IFIs); however, evidence supporting its prophylactic use 
remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the real-world effectiveness and 
safety of ISCZ prophylaxis in patients with hematological malignancies at high 
risk for IFIs.
METHODS: This retrospective study evaluated patients at high risk for IFI who 
received ISCZ as prophylaxis at our institution from June 2023 to June 2025. The 
primary outcome measure was the incidence of breakthrough IFI (bIFI) within 100 
days after ISCZ initiation. The secondary outcome measures were the treatment 
continuation rate, mortality rate, adverse events, and changes in liver and 
kidney function.
RESULTS: Overall, 38 patients (median age, 67 years; median body weight, 54.1 
kg) were evaluated. Most patients (97.4%) were treated in the 
hematology-oncology department. The median duration of ISCZ administration was 
119 days. Treatment continuation/completion was achieved in 44.7% of the 
patients. No deaths attributable to IFI were observed during the study period. 
No breakthrough IFIs were identified within 100 days after ISCZ initiation, and 
no Grade ≥3 adverse events were definitively attributed to ISCZ.

ISCZ prophylaxis initiation. Although Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred, 
their causal relationship with ISCZ could not be definitively established in 
this retrospective study. These findings provide real-world data on ISCZ 
prophylaxis in patients at high risk for IFIs. Further validation in multicenter 
prospective studies is needed.

Appropriate administration of tazobactam/piperacillin for urinary and genital

Hishikawa Y(1), Hiyama Y(2), Nishiyama N(1), Nagaoka K(3), Yamamoto Y(3),

Author information:

OBJECTIVE: Tazobactam/piperacillin (TAZ/PIPC) is a broad-spectrum antimicrobial 
agent. However, improper administration may contribute to antimicrobial 
resistance (AMR). The objectives of this study were to evaluate the 
appropriateness of TAZ/PIPC administration for UGTI based on antibiotic 
susceptibility testing and to elucidate the patients for whom alternative 
antibiotics can be utilized as the initial empiric therapy.
METHODS: Patients diagnosed with UGTI at the University of Toyama Hospital

antimicrobial susceptibility results.

Li W(1), Huang Y(2), Guan C(3), Fu Z(4), Zeng X(5).

(1)Hainan Medical University, Haikou, Hainan, China.
(2)Hainan Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention, Haikou, Hainan,

(3)Sanya Municipal Center for Disease Control and Prevention, Sanya, Hainan,

(4)Hainan Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention, Haikou, Hainan,

OBJECTIVE: To analyze the epidemiological characteristics of pertussis in Hainan 
Province from 2023 to 2025, describe the outbreak trajectory and patterns of 
population susceptibility, and provide evidence for optimizing pertussis 
prevention and control strategies.
METHODS: Clinically diagnosed and confirmed pertussis cases reported in Hainan 
Province between January 1, 2023, and December 31, 2025, were retrieved from the 
China Information System for Disease Control and Prevention; suspected cases 
were excluded, yielding a total of 2,927 eligible cases.Descriptive 
epidemiological methods were used to analyze the temporal, geographic, and 
population distributions of the cases; piecewise linear regression was employed 
to characterize monthly trends in case counts; and multivariable logistic 
regression was performed to identify risk factors for hospitalization.
RESULTS: The incidence of pertussis in Hainan Province exhibited an 
outbreak-and-decline pattern from 2023 to 2025, increasing from 4.29 per 100,000 
population in 2023 to 22.26 per 100,000 in 2024 before declining to 1.37 per 
100,000 in 2025, with a statistically significant difference across the three 
years (χ2 = 2,888.2, P < 0.001).Piecewise linear regression showed that the 
monthly number of cases increased significantly during the ascending phase (β = 
21.82, P < 0.001) and decreased significantly during the descending phase (β = 
-11.41, P < 0.001).The age distribution shifted significantly toward older 
children: the proportion of infants aged <1 year decreased from 43.1% to 27.3%, 
whereas that of individuals aged ≥1 year increased from 56.9% to 72.7%.Among 
cases with complete severity records after July 2024, infants aged 0-2 months 
had the highest risk of hospitalization and accounted for 90.0% of intensive 
care unit admissions.
CONCLUSION: This study shows that the 2024 pertussis outbreak in Hainan was 
followed by a rapid decline in 2025, with a shift toward older children and a 
persistently high hospitalization risk in infants aged 0-2 months. These 
findings support strengthening surveillance in schools and childcare 
institutions and evaluating the effectiveness of the 6-year DTaP booster policy, 
while maintaining maternal and infant protection strategies.

Dose-Response Profiles in Incretin and Multi-Agonist Obesity Pharmacotherapy.

Yousefian M(1), Baharmast M(2).

Author information:
(1)Tehran Medical Sciences, Islamic Azad University, Tehran, Iran. Electronic 
address: Mahdi2004@gmail.com.
(2)Tehran Medical Sciences, Islamic Azad University, Tehran, Iran. Electronic 
address: baharmastmaryam@gmail.com.

Incretin and multi-agonist therapies have transformed obesity pharmacotherapy, 
but dose selection remains less mature than efficacy assessment. This critical 
narrative review examines nonlinear relationships among administered dose, 
systemic exposure, weight and cardiometabolic benefit, gastrointestinal 
tolerability, treatment persistence, and maintenance. Across established and 
newer programs, average efficacy generally increases with dose, yet incremental 
gains may narrow at higher exposure while adverse-event burden and 
discontinuation can increase. The maturity of evidence is heterogeneous, and 
later-stage programs should not be interpreted as clinically equivalent to 
agents supported mainly by earlier-phase dose-ranging data. Moreover, an 
"optimal dose" is not an endpoint-independent quantity: the exposure most 
appropriate for weight loss may differ from that relevant to glycemic control, 
cardiovascular benefit, body composition, tolerability, or maintenance. We 
therefore distinguish nominal dose from exposure and present response-guided 
titration as a hypothesis-generating framework for prospective testing, not as 
an evidence-based dosing algorithm. Existing continuation and withdrawal studies 
support the importance of ongoing pharmacological treatment after successful 
weight loss but do not establish a minimum or optimal de-intensified maintenance 
dose. Future trials should jointly model efficacy, safety, body composition, 
patient-reported outcomes, pharmacokinetics, and discontinuation to test 
objective-specific, patient-level dosing strategies.

supervision after each session. The control group received usual medical care. 
Data were collected using the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ), Cognitive 
Flexibility Inventory (CFI), and Functional Bowel Disorder Symptom Severity 
Scale (FS-BSS) at pretest, posttest, and three-month follow-up, and analyzed 
using repeated-measures ANOVA in SPSS 26.
RESULTS: The intervention significantly increased cognitive reappraisal and 
cognitive flexibility and decreased expressive suppression and symptom severity 
at posttest and follow-up compared with the control group (p < .05).
CONCLUSIONS: Emotion regulation-based therapy appears to be an effective 
adjunctive intervention for improving emotional and cognitive processes and 
reducing symptom severity in patients with irritable bowel syndrome.

Epidemiological comparison of cirrhosis to other long-term health conditions in 
the United Kingdom.

Innes H(1), Morling J(2), Buch S(3), Kendall TJ(4), Fallowfield JA(5), Guha 
IN(6).

Author information:
(1)School of Health and Life Sciences, Glasgow Caledonian University, Glasgow, 
UK; Public Health Scotland, Glasgow, UK; Lifespan and Population Health, 
University of Nottingham, Nottingham, UK. Electronic address: 
Hamish.Innes@gcu.ac.uk.
(2)Lifespan and Population Health, University of Nottingham, Nottingham, UK.
(3)Department of Gastroenterology and Rheumatology, 4th Medical Clinic, Medical 
University of Lausitz - Carl Thiem, Cottbus, Germany.
(4)Centre for Inflammation Research, Institute for Regeneration and Repair, 
University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK; Edinburgh Pathology, University of 
Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK.
(5)Centre for Inflammation Research, Institute for Regeneration and Repair, 
University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK.
(6)NIHR Nottingham Biomedical Research Centre, Nottingham University Hospitals 
NHS Trust and the University of Nottingham, Nottingham, UK; Nottingham Digestive 
Diseases Centre, School of Medicine, University of Nottingham, UK.

BACKGROUND: Although cirrhosis is a serious long-term health condition (LTC), it 
tends to receive little attention from healthcare policymakers. Here, we sought 
to describe how cirrhosis compares to other LTCs to inform priority-setting 
discussions.
METHODS: We analysed data from the Our Future Health (OFH) study, a cohort of 
∼1.7 million individuals from England, United Kingdom. Self-reported diagnosis 
status for cirrhosis and 15 benchmark LTCs (including type 1 diabetes, type 2 
diabetes, Parkinson's disease, chronic kidney disease, schizophrenia, and stage 
4 cancer) were ascertained from the enrolment questionnaire. Each LTC was 
profiled with respect to: sociodemographic characteristics; mortality; 
comorbidity burden; and late diagnosis. Furthermore, information on each LTC's 
trajectory (i.e., increasing, stable, or decreasing over time) was determined 
from background mortality data over the last decade.
RESULTS: The study cohort included 1,613,777 participants, of whom 2,606 (0.2%) 
reported a diagnosis of cirrhosis. Mortality elevation for participants with 
cirrhosis versus without was substantial (HR: 7.46; P<0.001, with adjustment for 
age/sex) and comparable to dementia (HR:7.60), stage 4 cancer (HR:7.06), whilst 
higher than schizophrenia (HR:4.46) and heart failure (HR:4.01). People with 
cirrhosis had more co-existing health conditions/diseases than other LTCs (i.e., 
elevated prevalence for 58/145 distinct health conditions; second only to stage 
4 cancer). Area-based deprivation score was third highest for cirrhosis, behind 
COPD and schizophrenia. Late diagnosis of cirrhosis was commonplace, with <15% 
of new-onset liver failure reporting cirrhosis at enrolment. Cirrhosis also 
exhibited an upward trajectory, with mortality increasing by ∼20% in the last 
decade.
CONCLUSION: Cirrhosis is an anomaly LTC with respect to its deprivation, 
comorbidity, mortality, upward trajectory, and late diagnosis profile. Our data 
provide comparative evidence to inform priority-setting discussions with 
policymakers.
IMPACT AND IMPLICATIONS: Various levers are available to policy makers for 
reducing incidence of liver cirrhosis. However, other health conditions are 
often prioritised by policy makers ahead of cirrhosis; the decision-making 
process around this is not always transparent nor grounded in evidence. This 
study explores the characteristics of cirrhosis relative to other long-term 
conditions through a public-health lens. Our findings may guide priority-setting 
discussions between policy makers, advocates and other stakeholders and may 
shift current discourse onto a more empirical footing.

The incidence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) continues to rise annually, 
which severely threatens public health. While estimates indicate that current 
therapies cause a 30% IBD clinical treatment failure, the precise pathogenesis 
remains unclear. Here, we found that a key embryonic development regulator, 
KCTD10, is correlated with the severity of IBD. We observed enhanced KCTD10 
expression during enterocolitis. Intestinal epithelial cell (IEC)-specific

undescribed function of KCTD10 in modulating ulcerative colitis by regulating 
intestinal stem cell function.

We addressed the question: can the SARS-CoV2 spike protein persist in ACE2+ 
endothelia in the CNS/other sites and induce a prolonged microvasculature injury 
syndrome? People who died from COVID-19, with age-matched controls, and people 
with long COVID with symptoms persisting from 1-5 years, with controls of people 
who had recovered from COVID-19, were studied. Also compared were WT mice 
injected with the spike protein sacrificed at day 5 versus 1.5 months. The ACE2+

COVID-19 (0.9/0.3) (each p < 0.001). Microvasculature collagen 1 deposition was 
only evident in fatal COVID, long COVID, and in the mice exposed to S1 for 1.5 
mo. Thus, SARS-CoV2 spike (S1) protein can persist for months/years with an 
associated microvasculature pro-inflammatory state and a restrictive fibrosing 
microangiopathy; and exposure to high dose S1 markedly increases ACE2 
endothelial density.

Piezo-surgical pterygoid plate horizontal osteotomy (PS-PPHO): a novel 
alternative to the classic vertical pterygomaxillary split in LeFort I osteotomy 
- clinical experience in a tertiary center.

Vitkos EN(1), Bonitz L(2), Bicsak A(2), Hassfeld S(2), Soemmer C(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Oral- and Maxillofacial Surgery, Plastic Surgery, Dortmund 
General Hospital, Muensterstrasse 240, D-44145, Dortmund, Germany; Department of 
Health, University Witten/ Herdecke, Alfred-Herrhausen-Strasse 45, D-58453, 
Witten, Germany. Electronic address: envitkos@gmail.com.
(2)Department of Oral- and Maxillofacial Surgery, Plastic Surgery, Dortmund 
General Hospital, Muensterstrasse 240, D-44145, Dortmund, Germany; Department of 
Health, University Witten/ Herdecke, Alfred-Herrhausen-Strasse 45, D-58453,

BACKGROUND: The pterygomaxillary disjunction remains one of the most technically 
demanding and risk-prone steps in Le Fort I osteotomy, with potential for 
uncontrolled pterygoid fractures and severe hemorrhage. To enhance safety and 
control, we introduced the piezo-surgical pterygoid plate horizontal osteotomy 
(PS-PPHO), a novel alternative to the conventional blind vertical 
pterygo-maxillary split.
METHODS: A retrospective observational cohort study was conducted at a tertiary 
referral center between 2008 and 2020, including 243 consecutive patients who 
underwent Le Fort I osteotomy or surgically assisted rapid maxillary expansion 
(SARME) using PS-PPHO. Demographic, procedural, and postoperative data were 
collected from institutional records and analyzed descriptively. The study was 
conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and reported according 
to the STROBE guidelines.
RESULTS: All procedures were completed as planned without intraoperative 
conversion to conventional instruments. No major complications such as 
life-threatening hemorrhage, cranial base injury, or ophthalmic events occurred. 
Minor postoperative events were limited to mild epistaxis in 3.7% of patients 
and transient infraorbital numbness in 12.9%, both resolving spontaneously. 
Palatal sensory disturbance after SARME occurred in 5.3% of cases and resolved 
during follow-up.
CONCLUSION: PS-PPHO provides a controlled and direct approach to the 
pterygomaxillary junction. In this large single-center retrospective series, the 
technique was feasible and was associated with a low incidence of reported 
complications. In the absence of a conventional control group, no conclusions 
regarding comparative safety or superiority can be drawn. Further comparative 
studies are required to evaluate its relative safety and clinical outcomes.

Use of patient-specific instrumentation for hip resurfacing arthroplasty: 
Measurement of accuracy using pre and postoperative CT-scan.

Hormi-Menard M(1), Faure PA(2), Bauters M(2), Shaker R(2), Girard J(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Roger Salengro Hospital, University 
Hospital of Lille and University of Lille, Place de Verdun, 59037 Lille, France. 
Electronic address: mehdihormi@gmail.com.
(2)Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Roger Salengro Hospital, University 
Hospital of Lille and University of Lille, Place de Verdun, 59037 Lille, France.

BACKGROUND: Hip resurfacing arthroplasty (HRA) is a valuable option for the 
treatment of primary osteoarthritis in young patients. However, the learning 
curve for femoral component implantation remains long. Few data are dedicated to 
patient-specific instrumentation (PSI) in this indication, and merely applied to 
limited study groups using X-rays as tool to assess accuracy of the method. 
Therefore, we conducted a prospective study assessing the results of PSI for HRA 
using pre- and postoperative CT scans based aiming to: 1) assess the accuracy of 
the planned axis in the axial and coronal planes, 2) evaluate if 3D planning 
could reproduce the native head diameter by a maximum deviation of one implant 
size (2 mm) from the component ultimately implanted.
HYPOTHESIS: Our hypothesis was that PSI-assisted femoral component implantation 
would achieve an average accuracy within 5 ° of the planned axis in the axial 
and coronal planes.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective study analyzed 49 patients (51 HRA) with 
complete data from an initial cohort of 50 patients. On pre- and post-operative 
CT scans, the native caput-collum-diaphyseal (CCD) angle, stem-shaft angle 
(SSA), femoral anteversion and head diameter were measured. The objectives for 
the PSI jig were to restore head diameter, femoral anteversion and to implant 
the femoral component with a planned +5 ° valgus alignment in the coronal plane.
RESULTS: During the surgery, the calcar-guided PSI (inferior jig) was used in 39 
cases (76.4%), and the posterior neck-guided PSI (posterior jig) was used in 12 
cases (23.6%). No jig failures were observed. Native femoral anteversion 
averaged 20 ° (range, 15-24) compared to 18.5 ° (range, 10-27 °) postoperatively 
(p = 0,3). The mean preoperative CCD was 132.5 ° (range, 126-137). The planned 
SSA was 138 ° (range, 132-143) while the postoperative SSA was 136.5 ° (range, 
129-143) (p = 0,1). With accurate positioning being defined as placement within 
5 ° of the planned anteversion and SSA, 48 cases (94.1%) achieved the desired 
femoral component positioning. The mean acetabular cup and femoral head 
diameters were respectively 58 mm (range, 54-64) and 52 mm (range, 48-58). The 
native head diameter averaged 51.5 mm (range, 47-57) (p = 0,2).
DISCUSSION: The accuracy of the HRA position was excellent, with more than 94% 
of cases achieving desired positioning. The maximum difference between the 
planned and implanted head sizes was 2 mm (1 size), confirming our hypothesis. 
These findings support the use of this type of PSI for the HRA procedure.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: IV; prospective case series.

BACKGROUND: Early reocclusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) for acute 
ischemic stroke is underrecognized; its determinants and impact remain poorly 
defined.
METHODS: Random-effects meta-analysis of early reocclusion after successful EVT 
(PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library through January 2026). Crude odds ratios (ORs) 
were pooled and certainty rated with GRADE. Post hoc sensitivity analyses 
included only same-site reocclusion definitions.
RESULTS: Ten studies (3,381 patients) were included; 244 (7.2%) reoccluded. 
Reocclusion was associated with lower 90-day functional independence (OR 0.25, 
95% CI 0.17-0.38) and higher mortality (OR 1.86, 1.29-2.68), both moderate 
certainty. Reocclusion was more frequent with large-artery atherosclerosis (OR 
2.24, 1.41-3.55; same-site 3.04, 1.73-5.33) and less frequent with 
cardioembolism (OR 0.40, 0.28-0.57) and atrial fibrillation (OR 0.39, 
0.26-0.59), mutually confounded associations reflecting one 
embolic-versus-atherothrombotic axis. Prestroke antiplatelet therapy (OR 0.43, 
0.28-0.67) lost significance under the same-site definition (0.60, 0.31-1.16). 
Exploratory data (two cohorts) linked eTICI 2c-3 reperfusion with less 
reocclusion (OR 0.44, 0.28-0.69). No study reported when etiology was 
adjudicated; the atherosclerosis association may be partly outcome-induced.
CONCLUSIONS: Early reocclusion is uncommon but carries a substantial prognostic 
penalty. Its determinants appear to lie in the vascular substrate rather than 
thrombectomy technique; prospective studies with uniform same-site definitions 
and systematic follow-up imaging are needed.

44.8% female participants). Most reported symptoms were increased energy (79%, 
95% confidence interval (CI)=61-93%), irritability (77%, 95%CI=64-88%), and mood 
lability (76%, 95%CI=55-92%). Psychiatric comorbidities were common, with 
attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder being most frequent (53%, 
95%CI=36-70%). Treatment delay was longer in children and adolescents than in 
adults with BSD (SMD=0.39, 95%CI=0.15-0.64). 26.2% (95%CI=24.4-28.0) of children 
and adolescents with BSD attempted suicide at least once, with higher risk vs. 
children and adolescents with depression (OR=1.59; 95%CI=1.24-2.05) and

adolescents with BSD vs. HCs, children and adolescents with depression and

stabilizers (SMD=0.61, 95%CI=0.40-0.82) were superior for mania vs. placebo.

CONCLUSION: BSD in children and adolescents is linked to illness severity,

Development and Validation of the Shoulder Arthroplasty Risk of Non-Home 
Discharge (SHORD) Score: A Risk Stratification Model for Non-Home Discharge 
Following Primary Total Shoulder Arthroplasty.

Phadke RA(1), Salman SG(2), Khawaja SR(3), Fiedler B(3), Rana A(4), Hussain 
ZB(5), Garrigues GE(6), Edwards TB(7).

Author information:
(1)School of Medicine, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, TX, USA. Electronic 
address: rohan.phadke@bcm.edu.
(2)School of Medicine, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, TX, USA.
(3)Joseph Barnhart Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Baylor College of Medicine, 
Houston, TX, USA.
(4)Michael E. DeBakey Department of Surgery, Baylor College of Medicine, 
Houston, TX, USA.
(5)Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Florida College of Medicine, 
Gainesville, FL, USA.
(6)Midwest Orthopaedics at Rush, Rush University School of Medicine, Chicago,

(7)Fondren Orthopedic Group, Texas Orthopedic Hospital, Houston, TX, USA.

BACKGROUND: Non-home discharge (NHD) after total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA) 
increases cost, complications, and readmission, yet most existing risk tools 
depend on postoperative data or are not built to directly estimate the risk of 
this outcome. We developed and validated the Shoulder Arthroplasty Risk of 
Non-home Discharge (SHORD) Score, a purely preoperative bedside tool.
METHODS: We carried out a retrospective prognostic model development and 
validation study of 29,382 patients undergoing primary TSA in the American 
College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS-NSQIP, 
2016 to 2021). Patients were split into a derivation (two-thirds) and a held-out 
validation (one-third) cohort. Preoperative candidate predictors were screened 
by univariate logistic regression, assessed for collinearity, and entered into 
multivariable logistic regression; independent predictors were converted to 
integer points to form the SHORD Score. Discrimination (area under the receiver 
operating characteristic curve [AUROC]), calibration, and classification were 
assessed in validation and compared with the 5-item modified frailty index 
(mFI-5), American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) class, age, the Risk 
Analysis Index (RAI), and the NSQIP morbidity probability using the DeLong test. 
Sensitivity analyses addressed acute proximal humerus fracture, baseline 
non-home residence, missing albumin, and dyspnea.
RESULTS: NHD occurred in 2,057 patients (7.0%). 16 independent predictors formed 
the score, the strongest being age 85 years or older, transfer from acute care, 
ASA class 4, dependent functional status, and preoperative non-home residence. 
In validation, the SHORD Score achieved an AUROC of 0.816 (95% confidence 
interval 0.802 to 0.830) with excellent calibration (calibration slope 0.96; 
Brier score 0.057). It significantly outperformed every comparator (all DeLong P 
< .001) and produced a marked gradient exceeding 20-fold, from 0.4% in the 
lowest risk group to 20.3% in the highest. Discrimination was similar across 
subgroups and sensitivity analyses, including after excluding the 5.7% of 
patients with acute proximal humerus fracture (AUROC 0.811).
CONCLUSION: The SHORD Score is an internally validated, preoperative tool whose 
score is associated with non-home discharge after shoulder arthroplasty and uses 
only admission-day variables, which may support early discharge planning and 
resource allocation. External and prospective validation are warranted.

Chow AK(1), Sribhashyam S(2), Velichala SR(2), Smith MS(2), Cassidy BP(2),
