Thermal conversion of waste cigarette butts: Feedstock heterogeneity, process 
control, valorization pathways, and environmental safety: A critical review.

Zhang H(1), Fu J(2), Wang B(3), Hu H(4), Zhang L(5).

Author information:
(1)School of Chemical Engineering, Guangdong University of Petrochemical 
Technology, Maoming, 525000, China; School of Energy and Environmental 
Engineering, University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing, 100083, 
China.
(2)School of Control and Computer Engineering, North China Electric Power 
University, Baoding, 071003, Hebei, China.
(3)Guangdong Country Garden School, Foshan, 528314, China.
(4)Beijing Chaobai Environmental Technology Co., Ltd, Beijing, 101399, China. 
Electronic address: hhj200812091@163.com.
(5)School of Chemical Engineering, Guangdong University of Petrochemical 
Technology, Maoming, 525000, China. Electronic address: zhanglibo@gdupt.edu.cn.

Waste cigarette butts are abundant and widely dispersed composite solid wastes 
worldwide. They consist of cellulose acetate filters, residual tobacco, 
cigarette paper, ash, and carry nicotine, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons 
(PAHs), and heavy metals. During weathering, cellulose acetate filters release 
microfibers and contribute to microplastic pollution, while toxic components 
migrate into aquatic and soil environments. Conventional landfilling, 
incineration, and recycling fail to achieve pollution control and resource 
recovery. This review focuses on the thermal conversion of waste cigarette 
butts. It compares feedstock heterogeneity, reaction mechanisms, and the effects 
of different processes on product formation and toxic-component migration, with 
the aim of assessing resource-recovery feasibility and environmental safety. 
During thermal conversion, additives such as triacetin first undergo thermal 
desorption. Cellulose acetate then undergoes deacetylation and backbone 
cleavage, producing acetic acid and oxygenated volatiles. Cigarette paper 
releases phenols and aromatic compounds, while residual tobacco releases 
nicotine, pyridine, and other nitrogen-containing compounds. Volatiles may 
condense into pyrolysis oil or undergo cracking, reforming, or gasification into 
syngas at higher temperatures and under controlled atmospheres or catalytic 
conditions. The remaining carbon framework forms solid char through 
condensation, aromatization, and structural rearrangement. Different routes are 
oriented toward different products, but thermal conversion does not necessarily 
eliminate toxic components. Complete mass-balance data on their distribution 
among gas, oil, char, ash, and wastewater remain unavailable. Future studies 
should strengthen feedstock standardization, validation under realistic and 
continuous operating conditions, and life-cycle and techno-economic assessments, 
so that the environmental constraints and engineering requirements of waste 
cigarette butt thermal conversion can be defined more clearly.

Author information:
(1)Department of Water and Environmental Engineering, Faculty of Civil

(2)Department of Water and Environmental Engineering, Faculty of Civil 
Engineering, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia, 81310, Skudai, Johor, Malaysia. 
Electronic address: hazlamibasri@gmail.com.
(3)Department of Environment and Green Technology, Malaysia-Japan International 
Institute of Technology (MJIIT), Universiti Teknologi Malaysia, Jalan Sultan 
Yahya Petra, 54100, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.
(4)Department of Environmental Engineering, Gebze Technical University, 
Cumhuriyet, 2254. Sk. No:2, 41400, Gebze, Türkiye.
(5)Research Center for Applied Microbiology, National Research and Innovation 
Agency (BRIN), Jalan Raya Bogor KM 46, Cibinong, 16911, West Java, Indonesia.

Aerobic granular sludge (AGS) has emerged as a promising biological wastewater 
treatment technology due to its compact reactor footprint, excellent 
settleability, and ability to simultaneously remove carbon, nitrogen, and 
phosphorus within a single sequencing batch reactor (SBR). However, its 
practical application remains limited by the prolonged granulation period during 
reactor start-up and the instability of mature granules under continuous 
operation. This study investigated the use of indigenous extracellular polymeric 
substance (EPS)-producing bacteria as a bioaugmentation strategy to accelerate 
granule formation and improve reactor performance. Two laboratory-scale SBRs 
with a working volume of 2.5 L were operated using real domestic wastewater 
collected from the Bunus Sewage Treatment Plant, Malaysia, under 3-h operating 
cycles. Indigenous bacterial isolates obtained from activated sludge were 
screened based on biofilm formation, fluorescence spectroscopy, and aggregation 
ability. Two strains, Bacillus albus and Proteus mirabilis, were selected for 
co-inoculation because of their complementary functional characteristics, namely 
high surface adhesion and strong protein-like EPS fluorescence. The bioaugmented 
reactor achieved 50% granulation (dry mass >0.2 mm) within 10 days and complete 
conversion of flocs into granules by day 40, whereas the control reached only 5% 
and 80% granulation at the same time points. By day 10, the bioaugmented sludge 
reached a settling velocity of 2.24 m h-1 (vs. 1.37 m h-1 in the control), and 
its SVI5 decreased to 76 mL g-1 by day 40 (vs. 108 mL g-1). FE-SEM/EDS analysis 
revealed a dense EPS matrix with higher carbon and silicon contents than the 
control. The bioaugmented reactor consistently achieved higher pollutant removal 
efficiencies, reaching nearly 100% for COD, 75-90% for NH3-N, 70-83% for NO3--N, 
and about 60% for TP. 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing further showed 
enrichment of Nitrospira (0.95% to 9.94%), Candidatus Accumulibacter (0.13% to 
1.83%) and Chloroflexi, whereas the inoculated genera were not detected in the 
mature granules, suggesting that they acted mainly during early aggregation. 
Overall, the findings demonstrate that bioaugmentation with indigenous 
EPS-producing bacteria is an effective approach for accelerating AGS start-up 
and improving granule stability and treatment performance under tropical 
domestic wastewater conditions.

Pei Z(1), Guo S(2), Wang L(1), Liang Y(1), Liu X(1), Liu H(1), Zhang Y(1), Li

While the speciation and transport of uranium (U) in binary mineral-only or 
microbe-only systems have been well characterized, the coupled regulation of 
U(VI) retention and valence transformation at coexisting mineral-microbe 
interfaces remain poorly constrained. Therefore, this study investigated how 
Sphingomonas metalli (S. metalli), a prevalent bacterium in U mining areas, 
influences U(VI) sorption and redox behavior during its interaction with three 
representative silicate minerals with contrasting surface properties (chlorite, 
albite, and muscovite). Batch experiments conducted across a pH range of 5 - 10 
show that a slight decrease in U sorption (up to 22%) was observed in the 
presence of bacteria, except for the chlorite under near-neutral conditions, 
with this effect becoming less pronounced under alkaline conditions (pH 8 - 10). 
This decrease could be due to bacteria-induced modification of mineral surfaces, 
e.g., mineral surface charge screening and site-blocking effects driven by EPS, 
and possible sorption competition between U and bacterial extracellular 
metabolites. Infrared spectroscopy analyses support such surface modification, 
showing that bacterial attachment perturbs Si-O and Al-O functional groups on 
mineral surfaces. In addition to sorption processes, X-ray photoelectron 
spectroscopy suggests that a minor reduced U (as U(IV)) component may form in 
bacterial and mineral-bacteria systems even under aerobic conditions. 
Collectively, these results highlight that S. metalli acts as an interfacial 
regulator in microbe-mineral-U systems, suppressing mineral surface retention 
and inducing limited U(VI) reduction. These findings improve understanding of U 
partitioning in microbially active mining environments and provide a basis for 
more realistic assessment of uranium mobility and environmental risk.

Xiao S(1), Zhao D(2), Meng J(1), Li H(1), Yang R(1), Wu QL(3), Zeng J(4).

Author information:
(1)State Key Laboratory of Water Disaster Prevention, Hohai University, Nanjing, 
210098, China; State Key Laboratory of Lake and Watershed Science for Water

(2)State Key Laboratory of Water Disaster Prevention, Hohai University, Nanjing,

(3)State Key Laboratory of Lake and Watershed Science for Water Security, 
Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, 
Nanjing, 211135, China; Sino-Danish College, University of Chinese Academy of 
Sciences, Beijing, 101408, China; Center for Evolution and Conservation Biology,

Soil organic carbon (SOC) pool stability is fundamental to maintaining the 
long-term carbon sink function of coastal wetlands. Vegetation, topography and 
water-level changes can influence SOC accumulation and stability by modifying 
soil properties, carbon inputs, and microbial processes. However, how changes in 
these factors affect SOC stability and its underlying pathways over the short 
term remains unclear. Using the unchanged wetland (CK) as a seasonal reference, 
we investigated the effects of vegetation-topography changes (VT) and 
water-level changes (WL) on SOC stability across four time points over one year 
(pre-change, three months, six months, and nine months post-change), and 
identified the underlying pathways. Seasonal dynamics accounted for much of the 
variation in SOC and mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC), and VT and WL 
altered the magnitude of these changes. The magnitude of SOC change under WL 
(-16.44%) was smaller than that under CK (-34.41%) and VT (-35.34%), indicating 
that WL buffered seasonal SOC fluctuations. Concurrently, SOC stability (fMAOC, 
the ratio of MAOC to SOC) remained stable, with a non-significant decrease under 
VT and a non-significant increase under WL. Both VT and WL mitigated seasonal 
particulate organic carbon (POC) decline. VT and WL altered microbial community 
composition and life-history strategies, with microbial communities shifting 
toward K-strategy under VT and r-strategy under WL; these shifts were related to 
labile carbon availability. Structural equation modeling (SEM) further suggested 
that SOC stability under VT was associated with soil-property changes that were 
linked to carbon fraction allocation and microbial processes related to MAOC 
formation. Under WL, SOC stability was more closely associated with increased 
labile carbon availability and MAOC dynamics under altered water-level and soil 
conditions. These findings suggest that vegetation-topography and water-level 
changes can affect SOC fractions and stability through distinct pathways in the 
short term, while water-level changes may better buffer seasonal SOC 
fluctuations, providing targeted evidence for optimizing carbon-related 
management and protecting coastal blue carbon sinks.

Imran M(1), Xu N(2).

Author information:

China launched its clean-air action plans in 2013, which have played a crucial 
role in driving one of the world's most significant and rapid improvements in 
urban air quality. However, the relative roles of financial, governance, and 
structural determinants remain poorly understood. This study developed a 
national-scale, interpretable machine-learning framework to model and explain

The treatment of wastewater containing chelated copper (Cu), such as Cu-EDTA 
complexes, remains a persistent challenge owing to the high stability of the 
chelates and the generation of hazardous heavy metal-bearing sludge. This study 
proposes a selenium-enhanced anaerobic granular sludge (Se-GS) technology for

remains less studied than marine debris despite its role as a pathway to ocean

Not all sealed soils recover alike: Pedogenic and technogenic controls on 
post-de-sealing recovery.

Laudicina VA(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Agricultural, Food and Forest Sciences, University of Palermo, 
Viale delle Scienze, Building 4, Palermo, 90128, Italy. Electronic address: 
vitoarmando.laudicina@unipa.it.

Soil sealing is a major and often persistent form of soil degradation, yet 
removal of an impervious cover does not automatically restore the soil beneath 
it. Direct evidence of post-de-sealing trajectories remains sparse and 
heterogeneous, and a pedologically explicit framework linking residual soil-body 
properties and technogenic legacies to function-specific recovery expectations 
remains lacking. This review synthesises direct observations from de-sealed 
sites separately from mechanistic evidence on profile integrity, compaction, 
pore architecture, mineralogy, organic matter, exchange processes, phosphorus 
sorption, salinity, sodicity, hydromorphy and Technosols. The evidence supports 
a framework in which recovery reflects the interaction between residual 
pedogenic properties and technogenic alteration. Direct studies with explicit 
follow-up span only 2-36 months and show that structural, hydraulic, 
nutrient-related, organic-matter and biological recovery domains can follow 
different trajectories; rapid improvement in infiltration, for example, does not 
demonstrate recovery of water storage or multifunctionality. World Reference 
Base diagnostics and qualifiers can provide mechanistic context, but Reference 
Soil Groups are not resilience classes. Soil Recovery Potential (SRP) is defined 
as a conditional, reference-based, time-dependent and function-specific 
prospective assessment and distinguish de-sealing from subsequent soil 
development, realised recovery from prospective recovery potential, and in-situ 
recovery from soil reconstruction. The central conclusion is that the 
recoverable soil body, rather than surface opening alone, determines the 
attainable recovery of target functions. In practice, SRP should inform 
de-sealing prioritisation together with contamination risk, local functional 
needs, technical feasibility and cost. Long-term comparative experiments across 
contrasting pedological settings are needed to validate recovery predictions and 
derive transferable response functions.

groundwater coupling.

Gong Y(1), Liu Z(2), Niu L(1), Jia X(3), Turkeltaub T(4), Binley A(5), Shao 
M(1).

Author information:
(1)Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, Chinese 
Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100101, China; College of Resources and 
Environment, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China.
(2)College of Resources and Environmental Sciences, Nanjing Agricultural 
University, Nanjing, 210095, China.
(3)Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, Chinese 
Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100101, China; College of Resources and 
Environment, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China. 
Electronic address: jiaxx@igsnrr.ac.cn.
(4)Zuckerberg Institute for Water Research, Blaustein Institutes for Desert 
Research, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Sede Boqer Campus, 8499000, 
Israel.
(5)Lancaster Environment Centre, Lancaster University, Bailrigg, Lancaster, LA1 
4YQ, United Kingdom.

Intensive agriculture can transform the vadose zone into a long-term reservoir 
of legacy nitrate (NO3-). However, the magnitude, residence time, and release 
dynamics of this legacy remain poorly quantified in thick loess agricultural 
systems. Here, we developed a high-resolution, coupled modeling framework that 
integrates a multiple-column vadose-zone model with MODFLOW-MT3D to reconstruct 
41-year (1982-2022) NO3- dynamics across the Guanzhong Plain, where widespread 
cropland-to-orchard conversion has occurred since the 1990s. The model was 
constrained by extensive soil hydraulic measurements, profile NO3- observations, 
and groundwater records. Vadose-zone NO3- storage increased nearly 11-fold 
during agricultural intensification, from 670 kt N in 1982 to 7631 kt N in 2022. 
In 2022, annual NO3- leaching accounted for only 0.6% of the stored pool, 
revealing a strong storage-leaching imbalance and indicating that most 
accumulated NO3- remains retained within the deep loess profile. Simulated NO3- 
residence times ranged from 10 to >100 years and were governed primarily by 
vadose-zone thickness. Groundwater NO3- storage exhibited a delayed U-shaped 
response, declining to 3190 kt N in 1998 before increasing to 3328 kt N by 2022, 
even though fertilizer application had been substantially reduced after 2011. 
This delayed response demonstrates that the loess vadose zone regulates the 
timing and magnitude of groundwater contamination over multi-decadal to 
centennial timescales. These findings highlight the central role of soil profile 
properties and thickness in controlling NO3- legacy behavior, and suggest that 
effective NO3- mitigation in loess agricultural regions must account for 
vadose-zone storage and residence time as integral components of soil system 
management.

BACKGROUND: Intraoperative hypotension (IOH) is associated with myocardial 
injury, acute kidney injury, perioperative stroke, and 30-day mortality. Deep 
learning (DL) refers to a family of machine-learning methods that learn multiple 
levels of data representation through nonlinear transformations. In 
perioperative monitoring, DL models can learn patterns from time-varying 
physiological signals and combine them with clinical variables to estimate 
impending IOH risk. DL algorithms applied to continuous physiological waveforms 
therefore represent a rapidly expanding paradigm for early IOH prediction, but 
their pooled diagnostic accuracy has not been synthesised within a unified 
diagnostic-accuracy framework.
OBJECTIVE: To quantify the pooled diagnostic accuracy of DL-based IOH prediction 
models and to identify factors that modify their performance.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched 
through March 2026. Methodological quality was appraised with PROBAST+AI and 
certainty of evidence with GRADE. A bivariate random-effects model generated 
pooled sensitivity, specificity, and SROC-AUC; heterogeneity was quantified by 
τ2(Se), τ2(Sp), and ρ. Subgroup analyses (prediction window, DL architecture, 
modality, IOH reference, analysis unit) and random-effects meta-regression were 
performed.
RESULTS: Twelve studies were included; nine contributed 22 validation datasets. 
Pooled sensitivity was 0.78 (95% CI 0.73-0.81), specificity 0.88 (0.82-0.92), 
and SROC-AUC 0.87 (0.83-0.90); diagnostic odds ratio 24.7 (16.1-37.9), positive 
likelihood ratio 6.31, negative likelihood ratio 0.26. Heterogeneity was 
τ2(Se) = 0.25, τ2(Sp) = 1.04, ρ = -0.28. The 5-min window achieved the highest 
performance (sensitivity 0.81; specificity 0.91). Meta-regression identified DL 
architecture as the only significant moderator of specificity (P = 0.02), with 
hybrid CNN-RNN exceeding pure CNN (β = 1.77, 95% CI 0.45-3.09). Deeks' test was 
non-significant (P = 0.06). GRADE certainty was Low.
CONCLUSIONS: DL models for IOH prediction achieve moderate diagnostic accuracy, 
with hybrid CNN-RNN architectures and 5-min prediction windows showing the most 
favourable performance. Universal absence of formal calibration assessment, 
scarce external validation, and geographic concentration constrain immediate 
clinical translation.

Cervical cancer remains a major global health burden, and resistance limits the 
benefit of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Ubiquitin-specific proteases 
(USPs) regulate protein homeostasis and may connect human 
papillomavirus-associated oncogenesis with immune evasion. This narrative review 
evaluates USP-dependent mechanisms relevant to cervical cancer, distinguishing 
disease-specific findings from evidence in other tumor types and proposed 
pathways. Cervical cancer studies support USP7-associated immune-checkpoint 
regulation and USP14-dependent MCT4 stabilization and lactate export, although 
the immune consequences of the latter remain inferred. Evidence linking USPs to 
regulatory T-cell function, STING signaling, antigen presentation, and 
immunosuppressive metabolism derives largely from non-cervical experimental 
systems. The proposed E6-USP7 and E7-USP1 immune pathways therefore require 
direct validation. We discuss small-molecule inhibitors, targeted protein 
degradation and stabilization, combination strategies, and biomarker 
development. Compensatory USP Reprogramming (CUR) and a proposed USP-based tumor 
immune microenvironment (USP-TIME) framework are presented as hypotheses for 
investigating treatment-associated adaptation and the relationship between USP 
profiles and immune architecture, respectively. Therapeutic development must 
account for the possibility that USP inhibition also impairs antigen 
presentation or effector lymphocyte function. Although USP-directed approaches 
provide a rationale for further investigation, their clinical benefit in 
cervical cancer remains unproven. Progress requires cell-type-resolved 
mechanistic studies, immunocompetent models, validated pharmacodynamic assays, 
and compound-specific safety assessment.

INTRODUCTION: Patient education is essential for older adults with cancer and 
their caregivers to support understanding of diagnosis and treatment. However, 
the evidence describing patient education interventions has not been 
comprehensively mapped. Our objective was to characterize the features, delivery 
approaches, and outcomes of patient education interventions developed for older 
adults with cancer and/or their caregivers across any study design, and to 
identify gaps in the evidence.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A scoping review was conducted using the Arksey and 
O'Malley framework and reported according to the PRISMA-ScR guideline. MEDLINE, 
EMBASE, EMCARE, CENTRAL, PsycINFO, and Scopus were searched on January 23, 2025. 
Studies published from 2000 onward were included if they evaluated healthcare 
professional-delivered patient education.
RESULTS: From 26,898 records screened, 93 studies met inclusion criteria. Most 
interventions were delivered pre-treatment (n = 63), with surgery the most 
common context (n = 31). Common aims included side-effect prevention (n = 32) 
and supporting treatment decision-making (n = 26). Caregiver involvement was 
limited. Outcomes were clustered into 20 domains. Frequent reported domains were 
satisfaction/acceptability (52 occurrences) and knowledge/understanding (46 
occurrences), while caregiver outcomes and clinical endpoints were rarely 
assessed.
DISCUSSION: Patient education interventions generally improved knowledge and 
satisfaction, but evidence for clinical or system-level impacts remains limited. 
Key gaps include minimal integration of geriatric assessment, limited adaptation 
for cognitive impairment, sparse caregiver-specific outcomes, and inconsistent 
reporting of unintended effects. Future research should better integrate 
caregiver needs and geriatric principles into patient education design.

Dark energy: the cost of function in protein evolution.

Galpern EA(1), Caamaño F(2), Sánchez IE(2), Ferreiro DU(3).

The evolutionary fate of proteins is driven by both folding stability and 
biological function, dual constraints that often conflict, creating frustration 
and imposing functional costs beyond stability. These costs can be captured by a 
'dark energy': the difference between the evolutionary energy of protein 
sequences and their physical folding energy. Recent advances in deep mutational 
scanning, protein language models, and inverse-folding models have enabled the 
quantification of dark energy across the protein universe. We review the 
computational and experimental approaches that disentangle folding and function 
at scale, revealing a dark energy component and providing new insights into how 
biological information flows from sequence to structure to function and back to 
sequence.

Beyond structural cycles: computational mechanisms of biomolecular machines.

Cui Q(1).

Author information:
(1)Departments of Chemistry, Physics and Biomedical Engineering, Boston 
University, 590 Commonwealth Avenue, Boston, 02215, MA, USA. Electronic address: 
qiangcui@bu.edu.

Understanding biomolecular machines requires more than determining their 
structures; it requires identifying the dynamical principles that couple 
chemical or electrochemical free energy to function. Recent advances in cryo-EM, 
single-molecule spectroscopy, high-speed atomic force microscopy, and deep 
mutational scanning provide unprecedented experimental constraints for 
computational models, while developments in molecular simulation and kinetic 
modeling increasingly allow mechanistic interpretation of these observations. 
Here, we discuss recent computational advances that exemplify this transition 
from structural characterization toward predictive dynamical modeling, focusing 
on atomistic mechanisms of mechanochemical coupling, identification of slow 
collective variables and transition states, construction of branched kinetic 
networks, and emerging descriptions of memory effects arising from reduced 
dynamical representations. We conclude by discussing several pressing 
challenges, including the integration of physics-based simulations with machine 
learning, rigorous descriptions of nonequilibrium dynamics, and the 
computational design of dynamic proteins as an emerging test of our mechanistic 
understanding of biomolecular machines.

Velasquez J(1), Chalif J(1), Glassman D(1), Gonzalez A(1), O'Connor R(1), Abdeen

OBJECTIVE: This study examined both National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) 
guideline concordance and steroid taper duration with clinical outcomes in 
patients with gynecologic malignancies experiencing immune-related AEs.
METHODS: This single-institution retrospective cohort included patients with 
gynecologic malignancies treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) from 
August 2016 to September 2025 who developed grade 3 or 4 immune-related AEs 
requiring systemic steroids. Clinical and steroid treatment data were 
abstracted. NCCN guideline concordance and outcomes were assessed.
RESULTS: 63 patients contributing 73 steroid tapers were included. Most patients 
had endometrial (41.3%), cervical (27.0%), or ovarian cancer (23.8%), and 
pembrolizumab was the most used ICI (74.6%). 46 tapers (63.0%) were NCCN 
guideline concordant and 27 (37.0%) were NCCN guideline discordant, with 
discordance most often driven by taper length and premature initiation. 14 
(19.2%) were < 28 days, and 59 (80.8%) were ≥ 28 days. NCCN discordant tapers 
were more likely to require additional supportive medications for irAE 
management (e.g. secondary steroids) than concordant tapers (81.5% vs 56.2%, 
p = 0.0300). NCCN concordance was associated with longer time to ICI restart (56 
vs 21 days, p = 0.0241). Tapers <28 days were more likely to require additional 
supportive medications (100% vs 57.6%, p = 0.0027) and steroids (35.7% vs 8.4%, 
p = 0.0253) than tapers ≥28 days. Tapers ≥28 days were associated with higher 
rates of ICI discontinuation due to toxicity (59.3% vs 28.6%, p = 0.0381). Rates 
of hospitalization, ICU admission, and AE resolution did not differ by NCCN

Implementation and sustainability of surgical randomized trials in gynecologic 
oncology: Adoption beyond publication.

Agusti N(1), Bercow A(2), Ramirez PT(3), Plante M(4), Knisely A(2), Harter P(5), 
Fagotti A(6), Obermair A(7), Rauh-Hain JA(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Gynecologic Oncology and Reproductive Medicine, The University 
of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, TX, United States of America. 
Electronic address: nagustiga@gmail.com.
(2)Department of Gynecologic Oncology and Reproductive Medicine, The University 
of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, TX, United States of America.
(3)Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Houston Methodist Hospital, Houston, 
TX, United States of America.
(4)Division of Gynecologic Oncology, CHU de Québec-Université Laval, 
L'Hôtel-Dieu de Québec, Quebec City, QC, Canada.
(5)Department of Gynecology and Gynecologic Oncology, Ev. Kliniken Essen-Mitte, 
Essen, Germany.
(6)UOC Ginecologia Oncologica, Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli 
IRCCS, and Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Rome, Italy.
(7)Queensland Centre for Gynaecological Cancer Research, University of 
Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia.

Surgical randomized trials have transformed gynecologic oncology by redefining 
the extent and route of surgery, nodal assessment, and multimodality care. 
However, the effect of a surgical trial does not end at publication. Unlike 
medical therapies, surgical interventions depend on operator expertise, team 
coordination, pathology support and perioperative infrastructure. Beyond 
controlled trial settings, these conditions may change, creating technical 
drift, indication drift, and inequitable adoption. Implementation should 
therefore be considered a distinct, structured phase of surgical research. The 
period is particularly vulnerable because landmark trials often evaluate 
de-escalation or technically complex innovations. Expanding de-escalation beyond 
trial-tested eligibility can cause undertreatment, whereas diffusion of complex 
procedures without sufficient expertise or infrastructure can increase 
morbidity. Disparities in access to specialist surgeons, imaging, pathology, 
molecular testing, perioperative support, and long-term follow-up amplify these 
risks. Responsible translation requires trial reports to define the technical, 
institutional, and patient-selection conditions under which outcomes were 
achieved. Strategies may include credentialing expectations, operative 
standards, and risk-appropriate guidelines. Once findings sufficiently resolve 
equipoise, post-implementation surveillance should determine whether effective 
procedures are adopted-or ineffective ones abandoned-and whether appropriate 
use, technical fidelity, safety, equity, and outcomes are maintained as practice 
spreads. Secondary databases can evaluate utilization, perioperative safety, 
equity, practice-change attribution, and selected real-world outcomes at scale, 
but incompletely capture appropriateness, technical fidelity, granular 
complications, recurrence, and patient-reported quality of life. Surveillance 
should therefore use a multilevel approach that matches each objective to where 
information is generated and supplements broad databases with targeted clinical, 
procedural, and patient-reported data. Treated as an active research phase, 
surveillance can ensure that surgical innovation reaches the right patients and 
settings, with outcomes consistent with the supporting evidence.

INTRODUCTION: Perineural invasion (PNI) is a high-risk feature of pancreatic 
ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and is associated with aggressive behavior and poor 
outcomes. The biological programs associated with PNI in PDAC remain 
incompletely characterized.
METHODS: PDAC patients in The Cancer Genome Atlas were stratified by PNI status. 
Gene set enrichment analysis using Hallmark gene sets was performed to 
characterize transcriptomic differences between PNI-positive and PNI-negative 
tumors. Established immune, proliferative, and genomic annotations curated from 
prior The Cancer Genome Atlas analyses were used for downstream comparisons.
RESULTS: A total of 101 PNI-positive and 26 PNI-negative tumors were identified. 
PNI was associated with higher grade (P < 0.05). Gene set enrichment analysis

EMT-associated genes in PNI-positive tumors.
CONCLUSIONS: PNI-positive PDAC demonstrate enrichment of EMT-related 
transcriptional programs with concordant microenvironmental and gene-level 
support.

INTRODUCTION: Appendicitis diagnosis relies heavily on medical imaging procedure 
studies; however, a definite diagnosis is obtained through histological 
assessment. Understanding the imaging characteristics and their relation to 
various histological phases enhance the quality of treatment recommendations. 
This study analyzed imaging characteristics of acute appendicitis in relation to 
its histological severity.
METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted using data from a third-level 
hospital. Appendectomy specimens from patients with prior computed tomography 
(CT) scans or ultrasound (US) imaging were included. Histological stages were 
categorized into simple, suppurative, abscessed, and perforated phases, 
depending the presence of edema, vascular congestion, neutrophilic infiltrate 
into the muscular layer, microabscess formation, mucosal ulceration, purulent 
exudate, macroscopic pus, and perforation with transmural inflammation. Imaging 
features as fat stranding, presence of free fluid, contrast enhancement within 
the appendix, appendicolith detection, reactive lymph nodes in the vicinity, 
appendix diameter itself, increased echogenicity, and detecting heightened 
perfusion via Doppler imaging were compared across these stages.
RESULTS: Among 760 patients included (51.4% women, mean age 30.1 ± 5.3), 196 
(25.8%) had CT scans and 361 (47.5%) had US. CT confirmed appendicitis in 59.2% 
of cases, yielded a negative result in 19.4%, and provided an inconclusive 
diagnosis in 21.4% of cases, commonly identifying fat stranding, free liquid, 
and contrast enhancement. US diagnosed appendicitis in 67.6% of cases, whereas 
32.4% were reported as negative, with findings including increased echogenicity, 
Doppler perfusion, appendix identification, and free liquid in the right 
parietocolic gutter. All imaging characteristics were less prevalent in early 
stages compared to advanced stages, with a higher negativity rate in earlier 
stages.
CONCLUSIONS: Imaging findings are associated with the histopathological severity 
of appendicitis. Increased histopathological severity is associated with greater 
frequency of CT and US findings. These relations suggest the potential for 
managing appendicitis based on the histological phase suspected from imaging 
findings. Further research is warranted.

Psychiatrists' perceptions of mandatory treatment orders in Singapore: a 
qualitative study.

Yeo D(1), Poremski D(2), Chua J(3), Cheok C(3), Phang S(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Forensic Psychiatry, Institute of Mental Health, Singapore. 
Electronic address: derrick.yeo@nhghealth.com.sg.
(2)Data Science Office, Institute of Mental Health, Singapore.
(3)Department of Forensic Psychiatry, Institute of Mental Health, Singapore.

Mandatory Treatment Orders (MTOs) are used in Singapore to manage offenders 
whose culpability is diminished by mental illness, yet guidance on their optimal 
application remains limited. This qualitative study explored psychiatrists' 
perspectives on the use of MTOs and their role within the broader mental 
healthcare and justice system. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 21 
practicing psychiatrists at a tertiary mental health institution, and data were 
analyzed thematically. Participants described substantial variability in MTO 
practice, shaped by clinical experience and levels of forensic involvement. 
Three overarching themes emerged: determining appropriate MTO duration, 
distinguishing between criminal and civil use of MTOs, and balancing forensic 
assessor continuity with independence. Longer MTOs were generally favored for 
individuals with psychotic disorders and histories of non-adherence, while 
shorter MTOs were viewed as sufficient for milder conditions, minor offences, 
and individuals with established engagement and insight. Many participants 
expressed ethical concerns about extending MTOs to civil contexts, citing risks 
of coercion, weaker enforcement mechanisms, and prioritization of social control 
over therapeutic benefit. Although continuity of the forensic assessor was often 
preferred for clinical and practical reasons, concerns regarding impartiality 
were also raised. Overall, psychiatrists viewed MTOs as occupying a dual 
therapeutic-justice role, generating tensions that contribute to variability in 
practice. Clarifying policy objectives, strengthening training and operational 
supports, and defining assessor roles may help improve fairness, consistency, 
and treatment outcomes.

test to determine maximal oxygen consumption (V̇O2max) and maximal HR (HRmax), 
followed by 4 randomized, 20-minute HR-clamp trials at 86% HRmax using either a 
ramp (gradual increases in power output [PO]) or immediate (instantaneous 
application of target PO) protocol, each performed twice. Oxygen consumption 
(V̇O2), minute ventilation (V̇E), respiration rate (RR), rating of perceived 
exertion (RPE), PO, and time to target HR were assessed at HR attainment and 
averaged across the HR-clamp trials. Analyses included linear mixed models 
fitted with fixed effects and random intercepts, and one-way repeated measures 
ANOVAs with intraclass correlation coefficients to examine test-retest 
reliability (p < 0.05). Time to target HR did not differ between protocols (p = 
0.958). However, the ramp protocol elicited a greater V̇O2, RR, V̇E, and PO at 
HR attainment (p < 0.001-0.035) and a greater V̇O2 and PO across the HR-clamp 
trials (p = 0.008-0.017) compared with the immediate protocol, whereas RPE did 
not differ between protocols (p = 0.118-0.984). The ramp protocol demonstrated 
greater systematic error for metabolic and performance measures, whereas the 
immediate protocol showed less systematic error and comparable reliability. 
These findings indicated that the method used to attain a target HR 
significantly alters the physiological stimulus of HR-clamp exercise, and 
practitioners and researchers should carefully consider protocol selection when 
prescribing or interpreting HR-clamp exercise.

Controlled Edge-Mediated Photoelectrochemical Thinning and Patterning of 
Transition Metal Dichalcogenides.

Wörle S(1)(2), Wolz LM(2), Levashov S(2), Lim S(1)(2), Gröbmeyer F(3), Christis 
M(1)(2), Paulus C(1)(2), Cortés E(3), Finley JJ(1)(2), Eichhorn J(2), Robinson 
JT(4), Sharp ID(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Walter Schottky Institute, Technical University of Munich, Garching85748, 
Germany.
(2)Physics Department, TUM School of Natural Sciences, Technical University of 
Munich, Garching85748, Germany.
(3)Nanoinstitute Munich and Faculty of Physics, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität, 
München80539, Germany.
(4)U.S. Naval Research Laboratory , Washington, D.C.20375, United States.

Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are widely investigated for 
electrochemical and photoelectrochemical energy conversion applications, yet the 
oxidation processes that govern their stability in reactive electrolytes remain 
poorly understood. Here, we systematically compare dark electrochemical and 
illuminated photoelectrochemical anodic etching and thinning of mechanically 
exfoliated MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, and WSe2 flakes as a function of applied potential, 
electrolyte pH, irradiance, and oxidation time. In the dark, oxidation initiates 
at defect-rich flake edges and produces lateral etching without appreciable 
basal-plane thinning. The oxidation peak potentials exhibit significantly 
different pH dependences for sulfide- and selenide-based TMDs, revealing 
chalcogen-dependent oxidation chemistry and kinetics. Under illumination, an 
additional oxidation regime emerges at lower anodic potentials, in which 
multilayer n-type MoS2, WS2, and MoSe2 undergo vertical thinning with minimal 
lateral etching, whereas no thinning is observed for p-type WSe2. This 
observation, together with strong suppression of thinning by sacrificial hole 
acceptors, indicates that photogenerated holes accumulated in the upper layers 
of n-type TMDs drive a photoelectrochemical self-oxidation process. Tuning the 
bias, irradiance, and oxidation time enables controlled conversion of initially 
nonuniform multilayer flakes into homogeneous few-layer structures, while 
focused laser excitation yields spatially localized thinning and patterning. In 
addition to elucidating stability windows and oxidation mechanisms of TMD 
photoelectrodes, these results provide a versatile strategy for controllably 
tuning the thickness and morphology of layered semiconductors.

Milana FA(1)(2), Allegretto JA(3), Laucirica G(4), Marmisollé WA(5), Azzaroni 
O(5), Acosta RH(1)(2), Rafti M(5), Velasco MI(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Facultad de Matemática, Astronomía, Física y Computación, Universidad 
Nacional de Córdoba, Medina Allende s/n, CórdobaX5000HUA, Argentina.
(2)Instituto de Física Enrique Gaviola (IFEG), CONICET , Medina Allende s/n, 
CórdobaX5000HUA, Argentina.
(3)Laboratory for Life Sciences and Technology (LiST), Department of Medicine,

(4)GSI Helmholtzzentrum für Schwerionenforschung , Darmstadt64291, Germany.
(5)Instituto de Investigaciones Fisicoquímicas Teóricas y Aplicadas (INIFTA),

Transport in hierarchically porous membranes depends on pore organization at the 
mesoscale, yet how this organization shapes local dynamics remains poorly 
understood. Herein, we employ single-sided nuclear magnetic resonance (SS-NMR) 
to probe the in situ diffusion dynamics of water within solid-state nanochannels 
(SSNs) functionalized with UiO-66 metal-organic framework (MOF). We 
systematically compare two distinct synthetic protocols: a one-pot (OP) 
interfacial growth and a counter-diffusion (CD) method. By deconvoluting the NMR 
signal attenuation, we isolate a minor slow diffusion component corresponding to 
intraparticle micropores and a dominant fast diffusion component representing 
interparticle constructional porosity. Our results show that OP growth produces 
large particle agglomerates and poorly connected pores with narrow bottlenecks, 
forcing water along highly tortuous paths. Furthermore, leveraging the 
pH-responsive surface charge of UiO-66, we find that water mobility in the 
well-connected CD nanoarchitecture varies measurably with pH, consistent with a 
surface-charge effect, whereas OP membranes show a weaker, nonmonotonic 
variation, consistent with dominant geometric obstruction. These findings link 
nanochannel architecture directly to local water mobility and identify 
constructional porosity as a structural parameter to consider in MOF-based 
nanofluidic membranes.

Physiologic Stress During Walking and Cycling Early After Cardiac Surgery.

Dzikowicz DJ(1), Mummidi SK, Yu Y, Xia X, Couderc JP, Lachant DJ.

Author information:
(1)Author Affiliations: School of Nursing (Drs Dzikowicz and Mummidi) and 
Clinical Cardiovascular Research Center (Drs Dzikowicz, Xia, and Couderc), 
University of Rochester, Rochester, New York; Department of Nursing, University 
of Rochester Medical Center, Rochester, New York (Drs Dzikowicz and Lachant); 
Department of Computer Science, University of Rochester, Rochester, New York (Mr 
Yu); and Department of Pulmonology, University of Rochester Medical Center, 
Rochester, New York (Dr Lachant).

PURPOSE: To characterize cardiac effort and heart rate (HR) responses during the 
6-minute walk test (6MWT) early after cardiac surgery, compare HR patterns 
between walking and cycle ergometry, and evaluate differences by sex, frailty, 
and atrial fibrillation status.
METHODS: We analyzed a publicly available PhysioNet dataset of adults ≥65 years 
with pre-frailty/frailty undergoing cardiac surgery who completed a 6MWT and 
symptom-limited cycle ergometry with continuous single-lead electrocardiogram 
(ECG) monitoring (Polar H10). Cardiac effort was defined as total 6MWT 
heartbeats divided by distance walked (beats/m). Associations with 
cycle-ergometry performance were assessed using Spearman correlations with 
bootstrap CI; paired t tests compared HR responses between modalities; subgroup 
differences were evaluated using Welch t tests and multivariable linear 
regression.
RESULTS: Of 80 enrolled participants, 66 (83%) had analyzable 6MWT ECG 
recordings (mean age 73 ± 5 years; 67% male; 18 ± 8 days post-surgery). Mean 
6-minute walking distance (6MWD) was 300 ± 79 m, and mean cardiac effort was 
1.62 ± 0.52 beats/m. In 38 participants with paired cycle-ergometry data, HR 
responses were similar between walking and cycling. Greater 6MWD was associated 
with better cycle-ergometry performance, while higher cardiac effort was 
associated with lower cycle-ergometry performance. In multivariable analysis, 
female sex was independently associated with higher cardiac effort (β = .34 
beats/m; P = .042), atrial fibrillation with lower average and end-of-test HR (P 
≤ .035), and greater frailty with shorter 6MWD (P = .036).
CONCLUSIONS: Cardiac effort is a feasible ECG-derived metric that complements 
6MWD by integrating heart rate response with functional performance early after 
cardiac surgery. In this frail, predominantly beta-blocked cohort, HR responses 
during walking closely mirrored cycle ergometry.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: The rates and factors associated with complete 
recanalization after cervical artery dissection (CeAD) have not been 
comprehensively quantified in large cohorts. We sought to determine the 6-month 
rate of complete recanalization in CeAD, clinical and imaging factors associated 
with recanalization, and risk of recurrent ischemic stroke based on 
recanalization status.
METHODS: This was a planned subanalysis of the Antithrombotic Treatment for 
Stroke Prevention in Cervical Artery Dissection study, a multicenter 
retrospective cohort including patients with imaging-confirmed CeAD diagnosed 
between January 2015 and June 2022 at 63 sites worldwide. For this analysis, we 
included 1,095 patients with single-vessel CeAD causing stenosis at presentation 
who had available follow-up vascular imaging at 6 months after CeAD. The primary 
outcome was complete recanalization within 6 months after CeAD. Clinical and 
imaging variables, as well as recurrent stroke, were compared between patients 
with and those without complete recanalization. Factors independently associated 
with complete recanalization were identified using multivariable logistic 
regression. Time to complete recanalization was analyzed using an accelerated 
failure time Weibull model.
RESULTS: Among 1,095 included patients (median age 45 years; 46.7% female), 634 
(57.9%) achieved complete recanalization by 6 months. In multivariable analysis, 
each additional year of age was associated with lower odds of complete 
recanalization (odds ratio [OR] 0.97 per year; 95% CI 0.96-0.98; p < 0.001). 
Diabetes (OR 0.46; 95% CI 0.27-0.81; p = 0.006), active smoking (OR 0.69; 95% CI 
0.50-0.95; p = 0.025), and complete occlusion at presentation (OR 0.44; 95% CI 
0.32-0.59; p < 0.001) were independently associated with lower odds of complete 
recanalization. Complete occlusion at presentation was associated with both 
longer time to, and lower rates of, complete recanalization. We observed no 
effect of antithrombotic regimen (antiplatelet therapy vs anticoagulation) on 
complete recanalization. Incomplete recanalization was associated with a 
nonsignificant numerically higher proportion of recurrent stroke (5.4% vs 3.5%; 
p = 0.064).
DISCUSSION: Almost 60% of patients with CeAD achieved complete vessel 
recanalization by 6 months. Older age, diabetes, smoking, and complete occlusion 
at presentation were independently associated with incomplete recanalization. 
Further study is required to determine whether these findings may help guide 
tailored imaging surveillance and secondary prevention strategies.

La Doping Imparts Bifunctional Interfacial Catalysis for Dehydrolactonization of 
1,6-Hexanediol.

Wang Z(1), Wang W(1), Bao J(2), Yang M(2), Zhang X(1), Li Y(1), Zhu B(1), Zhang 
J(1), Wang X(1), Zhang Z(3), Wang T(1), Wang F(1)(4).

Author information:
(1)School of Chemical Engineering and Technology, Tianjin University, 
Tianjin300350, China.
(2)Zhengzhou Branch, China Nuclear Power Engineering Co., Ltd., Zhengzhou450000, 
China.
(3)State Key Laboratory of Petroleum Molecular & Process Engineering, Institute 
of Process Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing100190, China.
(4)Tianjin Key Laboratory of Applied Catalysis Science and Engineering, Tianjin 
University, Tianjin300350, P.R. China.

The dehydrolactonization of 1,6-hexanediol (1,6-HDO) to ε-caprolactone (ε-CL) 
requires a catalyst capable of cooperatively catalyzing two distinct 
half-reactions, namely dehydrogenation and cyclization. However, conventional 
catalysts lack the electronically asymmetric sites needed to drive both steps 
efficiently. Herein, a bifunctional Cu+-Ov-Ce3+ interfacial frustrated Lewis 
pair (FLP) is constructed by loading Cu onto La doping CeO2. La doping 
introduces additional oxygen vacancies (Ov) and Ce3+ species, thereby enriching 
the Ov-Ce3+ sites. Systematic characterizations (XPS, EPR, XAS, TPD, in situ 
FTIR) combined with DFT calculations reveal that Cu+ sites are responsible for 
α-H elimination to form 6-hydroxyhexanal (6-HA), whereas the cyclization 
reaction is driven by the FLP composed of Ov-Ce3+ and adjacent lattice oxygen. 
La incorporation lowers the energy barrier and enhances FLP formation. Under 
optimized conditions (3 wt % La, 280 °C, weight hourly space velocity of 1.5 
h-1), a ε-CL yield of 61.17% is achieved with good stability over 120 h. From 
these findings, the interfacial bifunctional mechanism is clearly elucidated, 
and a defect engineering strategy for decoupling interfacial components is 
demonstrated, providing a rational approach to the design of multifunctional 
catalysts for tandem reactions.

Potentiated Skin Permeation and Antitumor Efficacy of Fulvestrant-Loaded 
High-Permeation Vesicles for Localized Breast Cancer Treatment.

Akhtar J(1), Saren BN(1), Yadav V(1), Bhardwaj S(1), Jain S(1).

Author information:
(1)Centre for Pharmaceutical Nanotechnology, Department of Pharmaceutics, 
National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research (NIPER), Sector 67, 
S.A.S. Nagar, Mohali, Punjab160062, India.

Fulvestrant (FLV) is a selective estrogen receptor degrader used for hormone 
receptor-positive breast cancer. Nevertheless, its delivery is limited by low 
aqueous solubility and repeated intramuscular administration. Considering these 
drawbacks, a high-permeation vesicle-in-gel system (HPV-gel) was explored as a 
localized transdermal approach for FLV and evaluated for its physicochemical, 
permeation, cellular, pharmacokinetic, antitumor, and safety performance. 
Accordingly, FLV/HPVs were prepared using soya phosphatidylcholine and a ternary 
permeation-enhancer combination of sodium oleate (SO), diethylene glycol 
monoethyl ether (DEGEE), and propylene glycol (PG). Enhancer proportions were 
optimized using a D-optimal mixture design based on vesicle size, PDI, and 
entrapment efficiency. The optimized composition contained 80% phospholipid and 
20% of a permeation enhancer mixture, comprising SO, DEGEE, and PG in a ratio of 
6:1.5:2.5. FLV/HPVs showed a particle size of 94.02 ± 1.10 nm, a PDI of 0.241 ± 
0.029, a zeta potential of -38.6 ± 1.2 mV, an entrapment efficiency of 85.79 ± 
3.72%, a practical drug loading of 8.58 ± 0.16%, and a deformability index of 
1.62 ± 0.08. The optimized vesicles were incorporated into a 1.5% w/v Carbopol 
934P gel and compared with FLV-gel and FLV/Lipo-gel with the same gel base and 
an equivalent FLV amount. FLV/HPVs-gel showed sustained drug release and 
increased FLV permeation by nearly 8-fold and 3-fold compared with FLV-gel and 
FLV/Lipo-gel, respectively, with higher intradermal retention and deeper dermal 
distribution. Following topical administration, FLV/HPVs-gel increased Cmax by 
∼8.3- and ∼2-fold and AUC0-168 h by ∼8.1- and ∼2.6-fold compared with FLV-gel 
and FLV/Lipo-gel, respectively, while showing plasma concentration-time profile 
closer to FLV (i.m.). In 4T1 tumor-bearing mice, FLV/HPVs-gel showed the 
strongest tumor-suppressive effect, accompanied by greater intratumoral 
penetration, while biochemical parameters, major organ histology, TEWL, and skin 
histology indicated acceptable systemic and local safety. Overall, FLV/HPVs-gel 
improved skin permeation, drug exposure, and antitumor activity, suggesting its 
potential as a noninvasive transdermal approach for FLV in breast cancer 
therapy.

Engineering Subcutaneous Ectopic Tertiary Lymphoid Structures as Personalized 
Immune-Activation Niches for Cancer Immunotherapy.

Su JY(1), Wang TY(1), Zhuo SH(1), Feng GH(1), Li YM(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Key Laboratory of Bioorganic Phosphorus Chemistry and Chemical Biology 
(Ministry of Education), Department of Chemistry, Tsinghua University, 
Beijing100084, China.
(2)Center for Synthetic and Systems Biology, Tsinghua University, Beijing100084, 
China.

Tumor-associated tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) can promote anti-tumor 
immune responses and survival. However, intratumor TLS formation and maturation 
are limited in tumors with a "cold" immune phenotype, including reduced 
infiltration of immune cells and a suppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). 
Here, we present a personalized immunotherapy strategy utilizing a 
subcutaneously injected, bioengineered hydrogel (scTLS) that acts as an ectopic 
immune-activation center, effectively decoupled from the suppressive TME. Native 
immune cells and antigen-presenting cells (APCs) with autologous antigens are 
recruited through the release of chemokines. An agonist for CD40 is modified on 
the gel, enabling an immune-activated environment. We demonstrate that scTLSs 
promote robust dendritic cell (DC) activation and antigen presentation, driving 
the formation of organized T and B cell zones as confirmed by 3D imaging and 
transcriptomic analysis. This personalized, autologous vaccine-based approach 
elicited potent anti-tumor immune responses and effectively inhibited tumor 
progression across multiple murine models, with enhanced efficacy upon 
combination with doxorubicin-induced immunogenic cell death and immune 
checkpoint blockade. By overcoming the spatial and immunosuppressive limitations 
of the native TME, our scTLS platform offers a versatile, "off-the-shelf" 
engineering strategy for inducing functional TLSs to enhance therapeutic 
outcomes in a broad spectrum of malignancies.

Author information:

(4)University of Florida Cancer Institute, Gainesville, FL.

PURPOSE: Perioperative 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, and docetaxel 
(FLOT) is a guideline-recommended standard for patients with resectable gastric 
cancer or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma globally. Guidance is limited 
on patient selection, nutritional optimization, and toxicity management within 
existing guidelines. This study aimed to develop an international consensus to 
address these management gaps.
METHODS: A modified Delphi methodology, informed by the RAND/UCLA 
Appropriateness Method, was conducted virtually between March and August 2025. A 
multidisciplinary panel of 16 experts independently rated draft clinical 
statements across multiple domains. Responses were anonymized, with structured, 
iterative rounds of feedback and re-rating. Consensus was defined a priori as a 
median score of 7-9 (appropriate) or 1-3 (inappropriate) with a disagreement 
index ≤1.0.
RESULTS: Consensus was reached on 66.3% of the statements. Experts agreed that 
patients aged >70 years should not be routinely excluded from perioperative FLOT 
but require comprehensive assessment; inclusion of Eastern Cooperative Oncology 
Group performance status (ECOG PS) 0-1 is appropriate, and ECOG PS 0-2 may be 
considered on a case-by-case basis. Adequate organ function, correction of 
baseline conditions, hepatitis B screening, and dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase 
testing are appropriate before FLOT initiation. Universal baseline nutritional 
screening and support, proactive intervention for malnourished patients, and 
structured physical activity were endorsed. Surgical planning was supported 
through multidisciplinary input, with defined perioperative windows, 
individualized dosing, and flexibility in pre-/postoperative cycles. For 
toxicity management, the panel supported dose modification over drug omission, 
where possible.
CONCLUSION: This Delphi consensus provides expert-driven, practice-oriented 
advisories codifying fitness-based selection, nutrition-forward optimization, 
and pragmatic toxicity management. The resulting guidance builds on current 
standards and provides internationally applicable consensus statements to 
ultimately enhance patient care.

PURPOSE: Hormone receptor-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 
2-negative (HER2-) breast cancer, the most common subtype, lacks simple, 
noninvasive biomarkers for recurrence. We evaluated circulating eosinophil count 
as a clinically applicable biomarker for recurrence in this population.
METHODS: Associations between preoperative eosinophil count and patient outcomes 
were evaluated in a multimodal discovery cohort (N = 472) and validated via 
propensity score overlap weighting in an independent expanded cohort (N = 
23,170). We assessed the additive value of eosinophils in patients with 21-gene 
recurrence scores (RSs; n = 2,973) and their predictive role for adjuvant 
cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors in high-risk patients (n =

digital pathology, and in vivo preclinical models.

improved recurrence-free and distant metastasis-free survival in the discovery

from CDK4/6 inhibition.
CONCLUSION: Circulating eosinophil count serves as a potential clinically 
applicable, liquid biopsy biomarker that independently prognosticates recurrence 
risk and predicts CDK4/6 inhibitor benefit, reflecting systemic immune 
activation in hormone receptor-positive/HER2- breast cancer.

Family History of Eating Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

Rasmussen EB(1)(2), Sparvath SR(1)(2), Dissing JJ(1), Larsen MF(2), Nilsson

Author information:

OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesise the 
available literature on the prevalence of a family history of eating disorders 
(ED) among individuals with EDs.
METHOD: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, and APA 
PsycInfo. Studies were included if they reported prevalence estimates of a 
family history of EDs. PRISMA guidelines were followed. Study selection was 
conducted through independent, blinded screening by two reviewers. Risk of bias 
was assessed using the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist. Results were 
synthesised narratively and pooled using meta-analysis of prevalence estimates.
RESULTS: A total of 45 studies (N = 47,045) were included in the review, of 
which 32 were eligible for meta-analysis. The meta-analysis estimated that 18.1%

Considerable between-study heterogeneity was observed, although there was no 
evidence of publication bias.

aggregate within families, particularly among first-degree relatives, supporting 
familial liability to EDs. These findings underscore the importance of 
considering family history in both clinical assessment and future research. 
Further studies are needed to address evidence gaps and to place greater 
emphasis on underrepresented populations.

evaluations. We investigated whether low-cost visual and auditory psychophysical

trials was conducted in accordance with PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for 
Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses) 2020 guidelines and registered in PROSPERO 
(CRD420251236886). MEDLINE, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Scopus were searched 
through October 2025.
METHODS OF STUDY SELECTION: Eligible studies included randomized trials 
evaluating mifepristone for labor induction in singleton pregnancies at 37 weeks 
or more of gestation. Studies involving pregnancy termination, intrauterine 
fetal death, preterm induction, or concomitant cervical ripening interventions 
in which the effects of mifepristone could not be isolated were excluded. Two 
reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of 
bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. The primary outcome was cesarean 
delivery. Secondary outcomes included induction-to-delivery interval, time to 
labor onset, Bishop score, need for prostaglandin or oxytocin, postpartum 
hemorrhage, neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission, and 5-minute Apgar 
score less than 7. Data were pooled with a random-effects model.
TABULATION, INTEGRATION, AND RESULTS: The primary analysis included all 15 
eligible randomized controlled trials across mifepristone dosing regimens 
(n=1,063) and control conditions (n=811). Mifepristone was associated with 33% 
reduced odds of cesarean delivery (33.1% vs 41.9%, odds ratio 0.67, 95% CI, 
0.54-0.82) compared with the control method of induction. Mifepristone was 
associated with higher Bishop scores at 24 hours, shorter induction-to-delivery 
intervals, and less prostaglandin and oxytocin use compared with control 
methods. Findings were similar in sensitivity analysis limited to 
placebo-controlled and high-quality trials (cesarean delivery odds ratio 0.58, 
95% CI, 0.40-0.83). No differences were observed in postpartum hemorrhage, NICU 
admission, or low Apgar score, although most studies did not report these 
outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Use of mifepristone for labor induction was associated with reduced 
odds of cesarean delivery, as well as improved cervical ripening and labor 
induction efficiency. No evidence of short-term maternal or neonatal risk was 
found, although robust data were limited. Findings support the role of 
progesterone antagonists for labor induction.

Quorum-Sensing-Mediated Extracellular Electron Transfer Enables Hydrogel 
Morphogenesis.

Miniel Mahfoud IE(1), Damani VS(2), Partipilo G(2), Liu AY(2), Keitz BK(2).

Author information:
(1)Interdisciplinary Life Sciences Graduate Program, The University of Texas at 
Austin, Austin, Texas78712, United States.
(2)McKetta Department of Chemical Engineering, The University of Texas at 
Austin, Austin, Texas78712, United States.

Engineered living materials seek to capture the sensitivity, responsiveness, and 
programmable characteristics of biological systems. One emergent property of 
living systems is genetically driven spatial patterning, which controls cell 
differentiation and the development of complex multicellular organisms. Inspired 
by this capability, we use bacteria to spatially control material assembly. In 
our system, extracellular electron transfer (EET) flux from Shewanella 
oneidensis drives hydrogel synthesis via copper-catalyzed radical 
polymerization. We first construct a recombinant quorum-sensing system in S. 
oneidensis that allows for cell-cell communication between "sender" and 
"receiver" cells through an autoinducer. We then examine controlled gene 
expression and EET-driven chemical transformation in various synthetic 
consortia. Via diffusion through agarose, we examine 2D patterns of gene 
expression relative to localized sender cell populations and demonstrate 
controlled hydrogel crosslinking in predictable patterns. Finally, we apply 
computational methods and NOT logic in "receiver" cells toward more complex 
patterns of gene expression. Our results highlight the potential of bacteria to 
program material systems with life-like properties, including self-assembly, 
environmental responsiveness, and patterned differentiation.

Association Between Systemic Fluoroquinolones and Risk of Peripheral Neuropathy.

Brown JP(1)(2), Wing K(3), Mansfield KE(4), Evans SJW(5), Leyrat C(5), Smeeth 
L(1), Wong AYS(1), Galwey NW(6), Douglas IJ(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Non-Communicable Disease Epidemiology, London School of Hygiene 
and Tropical Medicine, UK.
(2)Faculty of Life Sciences and Medicine, King's College London, UK.
(3)Glasgow Lab for Health Data Science & AI, School of Health & Wellbeing, 
University of Glasgow, UK.
(4)School of Health and Care Sciences, University of Lincoln, UK.
(5)Department of Medical Statistics, London School of Hygiene and Tropical 
Medicine, UK; and.
(6)R&D, GSK Medicines Research Centre, GSK, UK.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Fluoroquinolone use has been associated with 
peripheral neuropathy in case reports, but there have been few noninterventional 
studies validating this association, and causality is unclear. The aim of this 
study was to estimate the association between systemic fluoroquinolone 
prescription and incident peripheral neuropathy relative to a comparator class 
of antibiotics, cephalosporins, using multiple databases to increase precision 
and assess the robustness of the results.
METHODS: Cohort studies were conducted using data from 2 databases of UK 
electronic primary care records, Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum and 
GOLD, from April 1, 1997, to December 31, 2019. Among adults (age ≥18 years) 
without diabetes mellitus or previously recorded peripheral neuropathy 
prescribed systemic fluoroquinolones or cephalosporins, hazard ratios were 
estimated between fluoroquinolone prescription and incident peripheral 
neuropathy within 60 days of prescription using stabilized inverse probability 
of treatment weighted Cox regression. Hazard ratios were similarly estimated for 
a positive control outcome of incident tendon rupture within 60 days of 
prescription. Risk differences for peripheral neuropathy were estimated using a 
weighted Aalen-Johansen estimator. Estimates were pooled across databases using 
fixed-effects meta-analysis.
RESULTS: In total, 2,933,982 individuals prescribed fluoroquinolones or 
cephalosporins in Aurum (63.7% [n = 1,868,793] female; median age 49.5 years 
[interquartile range (IQR) 34.1-67.5]) and 995,457 in GOLD (63.5% [n = 632,033] 
female, median age 51.5 years [IQR 35.6-68.0]) were included. Of these 
individuals, at first treatment episode, 1,002,004 (34.2%) in Aurum and 381,734 
(38.3%) in GOLD were prescribed fluoroquinolones. The estimated association 
between fluoroquinolones and peripheral neuropathy was close to the null at 
first treatment episode (pooled adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.96, 95% CI 
0.77-1.20) and over all treatment episodes (pooled aHR 1.05, 95% CI 0.92-1.20). 
Hazard ratios were elevated for a positive control outcome of tendon rupture at 
first treatment episode (pooled aHR 1.98, 95% CI 1.55-2.53) and over all 
treatment episodes (1.76, 95% CI 1.52-2.04).
DISCUSSION: Findings were not indicative of a substantive difference in risk of 
peripheral neuropathy between those prescribed fluoroquinolones and 
cephalosporins. Potential residual confounding is a study limitation. Study 
results provide some reassurance to clinicians regarding risk of peripheral 
neuropathy with fluoroquinolones relative to a comparator antibiotic.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Multiple sclerosis (MS), myelin oligodendrocyte 
glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), and aquaporin-4 
antibody-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (AQP4 + NMOSD) are 
inflammatory demyelinating disorders with distinct mechanisms of tissue injury. 
MS is characterized by diffuse neurodegeneration, whereas damage in 
antibody-mediated diseases is considered attack related. In MOGAD, the 
relationship between disease activity and brain atrophy remains unclear. We 
aimed to compare longitudinal trajectories of global and regional brain atrophy 
across MS, MOGAD, and AQP4 + NMOSD and investigate whether atrophy in MOGAD is 
associated with disease course and lesion dynamics.
METHODS: In this retrospective multicenter Magnetic Resonance Imaging in 
Multiple Sclerosis (MAGNIMS) study, patients fulfilling the following criteria 
were enrolled: (1) age 18 years or older, (2) MS/MOGAD/AQP4 + NMOSD diagnosis, 
(3) ≥2 same-scanner brain MRIs ≥6 months apart and ≥3 months postattack, (4) 
concurrent Expanded Disability Status Scale, and (5) disease course information. 
White matter lesions were segmented using the Lesion Segmentation Toolbox. 
Longitudinal brain volumes were quantified on lesion-filled T1-weighted images 
using Sequence Adaptive Multimodal SEGmentation (SAMSEG) with a within-subject 
template approach. In MOGAD, lesion dynamics were classified as stable/new 
lesions/lesion resolution. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, 
baseline volume, and center estimated atrophy rates.
RESULTS: Overall, 489 participants from 15 centers were included (98 MS [mean 
age 39.79 years, 68.37% female], 72 MOGAD [42.14 years, 66.67%], 41 AQP4 + NMOSD 
[51.25 years, 87.80%], and 278 healthy controls [42.94 years, 61.87%]). The mean 
follow-up was MS: 2.44 ± 1.55 years, MOGAD: 2.57 ± 1.85, and AQP4 + NMOSD: 3.22 
± 2.42. Compared with controls, MS showed accelerated global brain atrophy (β = 
-2.027 cm3 per year, 95% CI -3.430 to -0.623). MOGAD demonstrated white matter 
volume loss (β = -0.989, 95% CI -1.889 to -0.090) and ventricular enlargement 
(lateral: β = 0.219, 95% CI 0.089-0.350; third ventricle: β = 0.009, 95% CI 
0.003-0.015). AQP4 + NMOSD showed pallidal volume reduction (β = -0.008, 95% CI 
-0.014 to -0.001). Within MOGAD, relapsing patients (62.5%) exhibited greater 
third ventricular expansion than MS (β = 0.009, 95% CI 0.001-0.017). MOGAD with 
new lesions (22.22%) had greater ventricular enlargement than controls (lateral: 
β = 0.359, 95% CI 0.147-0.572; third ventricle: β = 0.016, 95% CI 0.006-0.025), 
MS, and AQP4 + NMOSD.

pattern of brain atrophy. In MOGAD, neuroaxonal loss seems associated with 
inflammatory activity and lesion accrual, supporting an event-driven pattern of 
tissue injury rather than diffuse neurodegeneration. Limitations include small 
NMOSD sample, heterogeneous follow-up, and potential scanner-related 
variability.

A novel strategy for the selective semi-reduction and exhaustive reduction of 
alkynyl phosphonates to (E)-vinyl phosphonates and alkyl phosphonates, 
respectively, has been developed using a Zn/NiCl2·6H2O system. The hydrogenation 
chemoselectivity is effectively tuned by simply switching the reaction solvent 
from acetonitrile to ethanol. Furthermore, the synthetic utility of this 
methodology is demonstrated through a late-stage tetradeuteration sequence

products. Notably, by using D2O as the deuterium source, a range of deuterated 
alkyl phosphonates were obtained in excellent yields.

PURPOSE: This work reports on the proof-of-concept testing for a suite of 
educational modules designed to improve oncology clinician sexual health (SH) 
communication with adolescent and young adult (AYA) patients.
METHODS: Pediatric oncology clinicians completed four interactive SH education 
modules. Intervention feasibility was evaluated through rates of intervention 
completion and study retention, with benchmarks of 60% and 70%, respectively. 
Acceptability and perceived usefulness were assessed through standardized 
self-report measures, using a benchmark of 70% of participants rating the 
intervention favorably. Pre- and postsurveys evaluated knowledge, attitudes and 
beliefs, SH communication practices, and perceived self-efficacy. Open-ended 
feedback and key takeaways from each module were analyzed qualitatively.
RESULTS: A total of 45 clinicians enrolled, with 39 completing the intervention 
and study surveys. Completion and retention rates (86.6% and 100%, respectively) 
exceeded the preset feasibility benchmarks. Positive endorsement of self-report 
measures demonstrated acceptability (100%) and perceived usefulness (94.9%). 
Pre- and postintervention surveys signaled increases in clinician knowledge, 
beliefs, and self-efficacy. Key qualitative insights from participants were 
received pertaining to AYA concerns, needs, and preferences and clinician 
responsibilities.
CONCLUSION: This innovative approach to clinician education on SH demonstrates 
potential to improve clinician knowledge and engagement in SH conversations with 
AYAs, a key first step in improving AYA SH during and after cancer. Next steps

Generative Artificial Intelligence in Midwifery Workforce Development: A Scoping 
Review Identifying an Evidence Gap.

Gibb F(1), Constantin A, Hill R.

Author information:
(1)Artificial Intelligence and its Applications Institute (AIAI), School of 
Informatics, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, Scotland, UK.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly explored across health 
care for clinical decision-making and education. Within digital health, 
workforce readiness and digital capability are recognized as critical to 
successful technology implementation. Midwifery faces persistent workforce 
challenges including limited protected learning time, restricted leadership 
development opportunities, and unclear career pathways, yet it is unclear 
whether generative AI has been examined as a tool to support midwifery workforce 
development. A scoping review was conducted following the framework of Arksey 
and O'Malley with PRISMA-ScR reporting. EBSCOhost (CINAHL, MEDLINE, ERIC), 
Google Scholar, and Elicit were searched for English-language studies published 
between 2015 and 2026 examining AI in midwifery in relation to at least one of 
the following: post-registration education, workforce, professional development, 
leadership, and career progression. Findings were synthesized using framework 
analysis. Eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Research focused 
predominantly on clinical decision-making, predictive models, and undergraduate 
education. No studies examined generative AI tools to support practicing 
midwives' professional development, leadership, or career progression. Attitudes 
towards AI varied with digital literacy, generational cohort, and ethical 
concerns. Generative AI in midwifery workforce development is unexamined in the 
empirical literature. Further research is required to understand acceptability, 
risks, and value within an ethically governed implementation framework.

Association Between Dynamic Changes in the Sling-Pubis Gap and Urinary Symptoms 
After Tension-Free Vaginal Tape Surgery: Protocol for a Prospective 
Observational Pilot Study.

Degirmenci Y(1), Efe Sayın C(2), Hasenburg A(1), Klamminger GG(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics, University Medical Center of the 
Johannes Gutenberg University, Langenbeck. Str. 1, Mainz, 55131, Germany, +49 
6131 17 ext. 1.
(2)Department of Biostatistics and Medical Informatics, Faculty of Medicine, 
Kahramanmaraş Sütçü İmam University, Kahramanmaraş, Türkiye.

BACKGROUND: Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is one of the most common pelvic 
floor disorders in women and is frequently treated surgically using midurethral 
sling procedures. Despite the high success rates of these procedures, 
postoperative voiding dysfunction remains a clinically relevant complication 
that may negatively affect patient satisfaction and quality of life. The 
underlying mechanisms are multifactorial and not completely understood. In 
particular, the interaction among sling position, urethral mobility, and pelvic 
floor dynamics during increases in intra-abdominal pressure may influence 
postoperative urinary function. Dynamic transperineal ultrasound has emerged as 
a valuable imaging modality for evaluating sling position and urethral mobility; 
however, the relationship between dynamic sonographic sling parameters and 
postoperative urinary symptoms has not yet been sufficiently clarified.
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to investigate the association between dynamic 
sonographic sling parameters and postoperative changes in patient-reported lower 
urinary tract symptoms following retropubic tension-free vaginal tape surgery.
METHODS: This prospective, noninterventional observational pilot study will be 
conducted at the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University Medical 
Center Mainz, Germany. Female patients scheduled for retropubic tension-free 
vaginal tape surgery for SUI will be recruited consecutively. Preoperative 
assessment will include clinical examination, completion of the International 
Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) questionnaire, and standardized transperineal 
ultrasound imaging at rest and during the Valsalva maneuver. Postoperative 
follow-up will be performed 3 months after surgery and will include repeat 
ultrasound examination and IPSS assessment. Sonographic parameters will include 
urethral mobility, sling-pubis gap, tape-urethra distance, and sling morphology. 
The primary outcome will be the correlation between changes in the sling-pubis 
gap during the Valsalva maneuver and changes in IPSS scores. Secondary outcomes 
will include associations among clinical variables, sonographic findings, and 
postoperative voiding symptoms.
RESULTS: Ethics approval for this study has been obtained from the Ethics 
Committee of the State Medical Association of Rhineland-Palatinate (reference 
number 2025-18448). At the time of manuscript submission, participant 
recruitment had not yet begun and was scheduled to begin in August 2026. The 
target sample size for this pilot study is 55 participants. Data collection is 
expected to take approximately 24 months, and the final study results are 
anticipated to be available in 2028.
CONCLUSIONS: This study will investigate dynamic sonographic parameters 
associated with postoperative urinary symptoms following midurethral sling 
surgery. A better understanding of sling-urethra interactions during increases 
in intra-abdominal pressure may improve the prediction of postoperative voiding 
dysfunction and contribute to more individualized surgical planning and patient 
counseling in women undergoing treatment for SUI.
