The Pallidothalamic Tract in Functional Neurosurgery: A Systematic Review.

Al-Smadi MW, Al-Khafaji YQ, Aslan S, Giampiccolo D, Xu SS, Akram H, Limousin P, 
Foltynie T, Zrinzo L, Krueger MT.

BACKGROUND: The pallidothalamic tract (PTT), formed by convergence of the ansa 
lenticularis and fasciculus lenticularis at Forel's field H1, is a major basal 
ganglia efferent pathway and an emerging functional neurosurgical target. No 
systematic review has previously synthesised outcomes across PTT-targeted 
interventions.
METHODS: This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review was registered on PROSPERO 
(CRD420251248260). PubMed, OVID, and Web of Science were searched for studies 
reporting functional neurosurgical outcomes targeting the PTT or Forel's fields. 
Prospective and retrospective studies, case series, and case reports were 
eligible. Methodological quality was assessed using design-appropriate 
risk-of-bias tools.
RESULTS: Forty studies encompassing 483 patients (1966-2025) were included 
across five modalities: MR-guided focused ultrasound (n=143), radiofrequency 
ablation (n=167), deep brain stimulation (n=40), cryogenic lesioning (n=82), and 
oil-wax injection (n=52). Mean follow-up was 21 months. In Parkinson disease (11 
studies; n=135), mean UPDRS-III improvement was 39%, with reductions in 
dyskinesia (UDysRS 90%) and tremor (75%). In dystonia (12 studies; n=87), BFMDRS 
and TWSTRS improved by 57% and 47%, respectively. Dual-target strategies, 
particularly PTT-VIM combinations, showed additive effects, including greater 
tremor reduction (77%) and improved rigidity. In drug-resistant epilepsy (6 
studies; n=157), seizure reduction occurred in 71% and seizure freedom in 33%.
CONCLUSIONS: PTT-targeted interventions yield meaningful motor improvements in 
Parkinson disease and dystonia, with preliminary evidence supporting additive 
dual-target benefits. Seizure-reducing effects in refractory epilepsy have been 
reported. Evidence remains limited by small uncontrolled studies, heterogeneous 
outcomes, and inconsistent adverse-event reporting. Prospective trials will 
elucidate the efficacy, safety, and clinical role of the PTT in neurosurgery.

Evidence-based practice implementation and associated factors among nurses 
employed at public hospitals in Siltie Zone, South Central Ethiopia: A 
cross-sectional study.

Ahmed SS(1), Gebresillassie AM(1), Bekele TT(1), Mekonnen HA(1).

Author information:
(1)Saint Paul's Hospital Millennium Medical College School of Nursing Department 
of Medical-Surgical Nursing, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

BACKGROUND: The use of the best available research evidence in clinical 
decision-making through the incorporation of clinical experience and patient 
preferences into the delivery of professional patient care is known as 
evidence-based practice. The best way to provide high-quality care that is 
secure and has positive results is through evidence-based practice. To use 
evidence-based practice. Despite the anticipated advantages of evidence-based 
practice, nurses have found it challenging to implement.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the implementation of evidence-based practice and related 
factors among nurses working in public hospitals in the Siltie Zone in South 
Central Ethiopia in 2023.
METHODS: An institution-based cross-sectional study was conducted from March 6 
to April 5, 2023, to assess the implementation of evidence-based practice. A 
sample size was 337 nurses working in Siltie Zone public hospitals; a 
self-administered, semi-structured questionnaire was used for data collection. 
Data was cleaned, coded, and entered into EpiData version 4.6 before being 
exported and analyzed in SPSS (version 26). To ascertain the relationship 
between the outcome variable and the predictors, binary logistic regression was 
performed, and those with a p-value of < 0.25 were entered into multivariate 
analysis. In multivariate analysis, a p-value < 0.05 was considered 
statistically significant. The Adjusted Odds Ratio (AOR) was calculated to 
determine the association between the dependent and independent variables at a 
95% confidence interval (CI).
RESULT: According to this study, 147 (45.5%) of nurses have good evidence-based 
practice implementation, and 176 (54.5%) of nurses were found to have poor 
evidence-based practice implementation. Factors significantly associated with 
implementation of evidence-based practice were age between 26 and 30 
(AOR = 5.247, 95% CI: 1.249, 22.047); educational level, BSc (AOR = 1.956, 95% 
CI: 1.035, 3.698) and masters (AOR = 4.149, 95% CI: 1.088, 15.817); working unit 
like emergency (AOR = 3.935, 95% CI: 1.300, 11.914) and inpatient (AOR = 4.684, 
95% CI: 1.633, 13.435); ability to formulate a question (AOR = 1.844, 95% CI: 
1.062, 3.201); and not relevant to the nursing profession (AOR = 0.459, 95% 
CI:  .236,  .878).
CONCLUSION: This study showed that the majority of nurses implement 
evidence-based practice ineffectively. Age, educational level, working unit, 
question formulation, and the applicability of evidence-based practice to 
nursing professions were the main causes of inadequate implementation of 
evidence-based practice. Therefore, multi-stakeholder approaches are required to 
address the main contributing variables and promote the implementation of 
evidence-based practice.

Modification of locomotion-respiration coupling in patients with obstructive 
sleep apnea syndrome.

Valentin R, Sandoz B, Niérat MC, Similowski T, Attali V, Pillet H.

INTRODUCTION: Locomotion is a complex motor task integrating sensory-motor and 
cognitive inputs through central pattern generator control. 
Locomotion-respiration coupling (LRC), defined as the synchronization between 
gait and breathing events, has been described during running and walking. 
Patients with obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS) exhibit altered gait 
patterns during wakefulness, which appear to be partially independent of 
nocturnal symptomatic treatment. While intermittent hypoxia may induce long-term 
("fixed") central nervous system alterations, OSAS patients also display 
"reversible" adaptive mechanisms during wakefulness aimed at preventing upper 
airway (UA) collapse, involving changes in respiratory control and posture. 
Whether these adaptive mechanisms affect LRC and contribute to gait alterations 
remains unknown.
METHODS: Ten awake patients with controlled OSAS treated with a mandibular 
advancement device (MAD) and ten matched healthy controls performed a one-minute 
walking trial on an instrumented treadmill with motion capture. Ventilation was 
assessed via thoracic expansion, and spatiotemporal gait parameters were 
extracted from kinematic and force platform data. LRC was quantified using 
phase-locking values (PLV) between ventilatory events and sagittal-plane joint 
kinematics. OSAS patients were assessed both with and without their MAD.
RESULTS: Compared with controls, OSAS patients exhibited a longer double-stance 
phase and a shorter swing phase. Expiratory events occurred preferentially 
during double stance in OSAS patients, whereas controls showed a higher 
occurrence during swing. PLV analysis revealed increased synchronization between 
inspiratory events and hip and knee motion, as well as between expiratory events 
and trunk and hip motion in OSAS patients. These significative differences were 
no longer observed when patients wore their MAD. Logistic regression 
demonstrated that PLV metrics of inspiratory-hip and expiratory-trunk coupling 
effectively discriminated OSAS patients from controls, but not when UA 
stabilization was applied.
CONCLUSION: Awake patients with controlled OSAS exhibit altered gait patterns 
characterized by increased locomotion-respiration coupling. This heightened 
synchronization likely reflects adaptive, reversible strategies aimed at 
limiting UA collapsibility during wakefulness rather than fixed hypoxia-related 
impairments alone. LRC may represent a functional marker of daytime motor

Neural drive and respiratory muscle effort in emphysema following lung volume 
reduction.

Ter Haar EAMD, Slebos DJ, Duiverman ML, Dijkstra LJ, Hartman JE.

Introduction Respiratory muscle impairment is common in patients with severe 
emphysema, primarily driven by lung hyperinflation. Endobronchial valve (EBV) 
treatment reduces hyperinflation and may restore respiratory mechanics in this 
patient population. Our aim was to investigate changes in neural drive and 
respiratory muscle recruitment following EBV treatment. Methods EBV-eligible 
emphysema patients from our prior study on diaphragm function were prospectively 
enrolled (NCT04735731). Respiratory muscle activation and timing were assessed 
using surface electromyography at baseline and 6 weeks following EBV treatment. 
Additionally, an age-matched control group without respiratory symptoms was 
included for comparison. Results We included 25 patients who underwent EBV

Activity of the diaphragm (4.7 vs 0.9 µV; p<0.001) and intercostal muscles (1.2 
vs 0.4 µV; p<0.001) during tidal breathing was significantly higher in patients. 
Furthermore, tonic (end-expiratory) activity of the diaphragm (1.4 vs 0.6 µV; 
p=0.012) and intercostal muscles (1.4 vs 0.6 µV; p=0.003) was significantly 
higher as well. Following EBV treatment, all measured outcomes improved 
significantly, approaching the values observed in the control group. Conclusion 
These findings indicate that neural drive and respiratory muscle effort are 
significantly elevated in severe emphysema patients. By reducing lung 
hyperinflation, endobronchial valve treatment reduces this load, resulting in

contributor to dyspnoea severity.

Applying normalized p-control charts for early detection of local COVID-19 
outbreaks.

Foox Y(1), Yamin D(1), Chalutz-BenGal H(2), Ben-Gal I(1).

Author information:
(1)School of Industrial & Intelligent Systems Engineering, The Iby and Aladar 
Fleischman Faculty of Engineering, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv, Israel.
(2)Department of Industrial & Information Systems Engineering, Faculty of 
Engineering, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat Gan, Israel.

The COVID-19 pandemic underscored the urgent need for early detection of local 
outbreaks to enable better resource allocation and effective mitigation. 
Outbreak identification largely depended on local infection rates, which were 
highly variable and influenced by daily testing volumes. Effective pandemic 
management requires accurate, adaptive methods that reflect the dynamic and 
localized nature of these rates, ensuring timely and appropriate interventions. 
This study seeks to improve the early detection and localization of COVID-19 
outbreaks through Statistical Process Control (SPC) and health data analytics. 
We propose an adaptive outbreak-detection framework that combines a normalized 
p-control chart with an Amplitude-based labeler (ABL). For each area and day, 
the monitored statistic is a standardized positivity-rate score, computed from 
the observed daily positivity rate, the number of tests performed that day, and 
an area-specific baseline positivity estimate derived from recent historical 
observations. This calibration is followed by Phase II sequential monitoring 
using fixed three-sigma limits on the normalized scale and Western Electric 
decision rules. The framework accommodates varying daily sample sizes, captures 
regional interconnectedness, and supports parameter tuning using a temporally 
ordered train/test design. Accounting for daily testing fluctuations and spatial 
variability, it enhances the accuracy of local outbreak detection. Compared with 
the benchmark outbreak-detection methods considered in this study, the proposed 
framework was evaluated on its ability to predict outbreak onset within the 
following three days, achieving overall accuracy of 0.81 and averaged precision 
and recall of 0.83 and 0.79, respectively. Performance was further evaluated 
using the Fβ-measure, enabling a flexible trade-off between precision and recall 
depending on the relative cost of errors. SPC-based methods like ours can 
significantly improve early outbreak detection and localization. In the 
post-vaccination era, when targeted responses are key to controlling localized 
spread while avoiding widespread restrictions, health data analytics offer a 
valuable tool for informed decision-making.

Efficacy of cetirizine, tamsulosin and their combination as medical expulsive 
therapy for distal ureteral stones: a prospective randomized study.

Hasan AM, Ahmed AA, Sayed RF, AbdelRazek M.

Background The management of ureteral stones, particularly those measuring less 
than 10 mm, has garnered considerable attention in urological research, with the 
goal of enhancing non-invasive treatment methods. Medical expulsive therapy is 
notable for its low invasiveness and cost.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the efficacy and safety of tamsulosin alone, cetirizine 
alone, as well as their combination in treating distal ureteric stones sized 
5-10 mm.
METHODS: Between March 2021 and March 2024, patients presented with lower 
ureteral stones 5-10 mm were randomly assigned to four groups: group A (121 
patients) took tamsulosin 0.4 mg; group B (120 patients) took cetirizine 5 mg; 
group C (119 patients) took a combination of tamsulosin 0.4 mg and cetirizine 5 
mg; and group D (120 patients) received analgesics on demand as a control group. 
We evaluated stone passage rates, time required for stone expulsion, total 
analgesic dosage, and any recorded side effects. All outcomes were recorded and 
analyzed accordingly.
RESULTS: Group C exhibited the highest rate of stone expulsion among all groups 
(85.8% vs. 67%, 55%, and 25% in groups A, B, and D respectively, p = 0.0001). 
Group C had a substantially shorter time required for stone expulsion in 
comparison with groups A, B, and D (13.15 ± 5.3 days vs. 14.95 ± 6.95, 17.57 ± 
6.21, and 20.94 ± 5.58 days respectively, p < 0.0001). A statistically 
significant reduction in the total analgesic requirements was demonstrated in 
group C (p < 0.0001). Except for retrograde ejaculation which was evident in 
groups A and C (40 %, 37.7 % respectively versus 0% in the other groups, p < 
0.0001), no substantial variations regarding the side effects were observed 
among the groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Combined therapy with tamsulosin and cetirizine significantly 
improves stone expulsion rate, shortens expulsion time, and reduces analgesic 
requirements compared with either therapy alone.

When Insulin Must Wait: The Role of Renal Replacement Therapy in Refractory 
Hypokalemia During Severe Diabetic Ketoacidosis.

Al-Lababidi S(1), Umer M(1), Herrera-Gonzalez MB(1), Alkhlaifat R(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Internal Medicine, New York Medical College at Saint Michael's 
Medical Center, Newark, NJ, USA.

BACKGROUND Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a common life-threatening metabolic 
emergency characterized by hyperglycemia, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and 
ketosis. Severe hypokalemia before insulin therapy is uncommon but may 
complicate management and delay treatment. CASE REPORT A 37-year-old man 
presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of generalized 
abdominal pain and progressive shortness of breath. He was drowsy and 
tachypneic, with Kussmaul respirations. Laboratory evaluation revealed severe 
DKA, acute kidney injury, and severe hypokalemia. Insulin therapy was initially 
withheld according to the DKA protocol. Intravenous potassium supplementation 
failed to achieve sustained correction, resulting in repeated interruptions of 
insulin therapy. Due to refractory hypokalemia, an emergency 2-hour session of 
intermittent hemodialysis was performed, followed by continuous renal 
replacement therapy (CRRT). During CRRT, serum potassium increased, serum 
creatinine decreased, metabolic acidosis improved, and the anion gap closed. 
Insulin therapy was resumed without further interruption. However, the clinical 
course was complicated by severe septic shock, disseminated intravascular 
coagulation, and catastrophic intracerebral hemorrhage, ultimately resulting in 
death. CONCLUSIONS Severe hypokalemia at presentation in DKA poses a critical 
therapeutic challenge because insulin therapy must be withheld until the 
electrolyte abnormality is corrected. In rare cases of refractory hypokalemia, 
CRRT may serve as an adjunctive strategy to facilitate metabolic stabilization 
and safe DKA management. This case adds to the limited literature and highlights 
the need for further studies to clarify the role and effectiveness of this 
approach. Biochemical resolution of DKA may not correspond to clinical recovery, 
and critically ill patients warrant continuous monitoring.

Type 1 diabetes in the youngest: from distinct needs to new frontiers in care.

Ingrosso D, Polle OG, Perge K, Pelicand J, Vermillac G, Godot C, Besancon A, 
Chiarelli F, Beltrand J.

Type 1 diabetes (T1D) in very young children poses unique clinical and 
psychosocial challenges due to distinct physiological, developmental, and 
behavioural characteristics of this age group. Advances in diabetes technology, 
particularly hybrid closed-loop (HCL) systems, are transforming T1D management 
in young children by integrating continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) with 
automated insulin delivery (AID). Evidence from randomized controlled trials and 
real-world studies consistently demonstrates that HCL systems improve time in 
range, lower HbA1c, and reduce glycaemic variability without increasing the risk 
of severe hypoglycaemia or diabetic ketoacidosis. Benefits are especially 
evident overnight, when glycaemic control is more stable, although daytime 
management remains more complex, due to unpredictable behaviours typical of 
preschoolers and marked circadian variability in insulin needs. Accordingly, the 
use of HCL fail to decrease hypoglycaemia in this population. Additional 
strategies, such as insulin dilution, may facilitate safer delivery of small 
doses, reducing the risk of nocturnal hypoglycaemia and improving time in range 
(TIR). Beyond metabolic outcomes, HCL systems substantially improve quality of 
life for both children and caregivers, reducing fear of hypoglycaemia, easing 
parental burden, and improving sleep and emotional well-being. Overall, current 
evidence supports HCL as a safe and effective therapeutic option for very young 
children with T1D, offering significant metabolic and psychosocial benefits, 
without completely eliminating the risk of hypoglycaemia. These findings 
highlight the need for further refinement of age-specific algorithms capable of 
addressing the unique physiological variability of this population.

Complementary insurance and free-choice modality expenditure in Chile's public

Goyenechea M(1), Aylwin A(1).

Author information:
(1)Fondo Nacional de Salud (Fonasa), Santiago, Chile.

INTRODUCTION: The Isapre system crisis, enrollee migration to the public

incentives in Fonasa's free-choice modality. Whether the higher spending of

LONGITUDINAL CLINICAL AND INTEGRATIVE MULTI-OMICS DATA REVEAL TRAJECTORY-DEFINED 
SUBGROUPS WITH DISTINCT KIDNEY FAILURE RISK IN DIABETIC KIDNEY DISEASE.

Jackson HR, Parton A, Gutheridge K, Marshall WR, Chinnadurai R, Rivero Viera Y, 
Baricevic-Jones I, Bhattacharjee A, Kuzmuk V, Díaz Novo N, Tugores A, Veluchamy 
A, Nkulikiyinka R, Palmer C, Boronat Cortés M, Sierra ML, Kalra PA, Cohain A.

Background Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is the leading cause of CKD globally. 
Despite marked heterogeneity in progression, risk stratification remains 
anchored to single-timepoint measures that fail to capture individual patient 
trajectories. We aimed to identify clinically meaningful DKD subgroups from 
real-world longitudinal data and characterise their molecular signatures using 
integrative multi-omics. Methods In this retrospective cohort study, 
unsupervised clustering of longitudinal creatinine and haematocrit trajectories 
was performed in the Salford Kidney Study (SKS; n=335 eligible for clustering, 
n=303 DKD) and validated in two independent cohorts: Scottish Health Research 
Register (SHARE; n=824) and CERCA-Diabetes (Spain; n=187). Prognostic 
performance was assessed by C-statistic, time-dependent area under the curve 
(AUC), IDI (integrated discrimination improvement), and decision curve analysis 
relative to the Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) and Kidney Disease Improving 
Global Outcomes (KDIGO) risk categorisation. Multi-omic characterisation 
(proteomics, metabolomics, DNA methylation) was performed in an 87-patient SKS 
subset using Data Integration Analysis for Biomarker Discovery using Latent 
Components (DIABLO). Results Two groups with markedly different progression 
rates were identified: high-risk (SKS-HR; n=173) and low-risk (SKS-LR; n=162). 
SKS-HR showed eGFR decline nearly four times faster and a higher rate of the 
composite kidney failure endpoint (HR 4.05 [95% CI 2.77-5.92] adjusted for age, 
sex, and eGFR; 2.95 [1.90-4.56] after further adjustment for haemoglobin, 
proteinuria, HbA1c, and cardiovascular burden; both p<0.0001). The signal was 
specific to renal progression (fully adjusted HR 5.98 [3.32-10.79], p<0.0001) 
and absent for cardiovascular or renal death (HR 1.00 [0.58-1.71], p=0.984). The 
subgroup-outcome association was independently replicated in SHARE 
(p=3.83×10⁻²⁷) and CERCA-Diabetes (p=1.72×10⁻⁴). The subgrouping added 
prognostic information complementary to the KFRE, raising the C-statistic from 
0.689 to 0.721 when added to static KFRE and 0.711 to 0.732 when added to 
longitudinal KFRE. KDIGO risk categories showed limited discriminatory capacity 
in this predominantly G3b-G4 cohort. Hypothesis-generating multi-omic profiling 
showed FDR-significant enrichment for lipid transport pathways and for an 
independent DKD progression proteomic signature; all multi-omic findings require 
independent validation. Conclusions Longitudinal creatinine and haematocrit 
trajectories, available from routine clinical records, identify DKD patients at 
high risk of kidney failure with prognostic information beyond current risk 
tools. The high-risk subgroup warrants prospective validation and evaluation of 
whether subgroup assignment can improve risk stratification beyond existing 
clinical tools.

Objective Maternal diabetes during pregnancy is associated with long-term

linked to metabolic comorbidities later in life, the impact of in utero exposure 
to maternal diabetes on psoriasis risk in offspring remains unknown. We 
investigated whether maternal diabetes during pregnancy is associated with the 
development of childhood psoriasis in offspring. Research Design and Methods We 
conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study using electronic health 
record data from Clalit Health Services, Israel's largest health maintenance 
organization. The cohort included 215,280 singleton live births between 2010 and 
2023, with follow-up through 2024. Maternal diabetes during pregnancy was 
identified using ICD-10 codes and categorized as gestational diabetes, type 1 
diabetes, or type 2 diabetes. The primary outcome was childhood psoriasis in 
offspring. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards analysis adjusted for 
maternal, pregnancy, and offspring characteristics were used to estimate 
associations. Results Overall, 5.4% of offspring were born to mothers with 
diabetes during pregnancy. During follow-up, 1,557 children (0.7%) were 
diagnosed with psoriasis. Psoriasis prevalence did not differ between offspring 
exposed and unexposed to maternal diabetes (0.7% vs. 0.7%). No associations were 
observed by diabetes subtype, treatment modality, or degree of glycemic control. 
In adjusted analyses, maternal diabetes was not associated with childhood 
psoriasis in offspring (HR 1.17, 95% CI 0.90-1.54; p = 0.246). Conclusions 
Maternal diabetes during pregnancy was not associated with increased childhood 
psoriasis risk in offspring. Our findings do not support a substantial role for 
prenatal metabolic dysregulation in childhood psoriasis development.

Endoscopic treatment strategies for gastric foveolar-type adenoma with a

Iwano T, Suzuki N, Ueyama H, Nakamura S, Uemura Y, Yamamoto M, Abe D, Oki S,

BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Endoscopic treatment strategies for gastric foveolar-type 
adenoma with a raspberry-like appearance (GFA-R) have not yet been established. 
We aimed to clarify the efficacy and safety of endoscopic procedures for GFA-R.
METHODS: We extracted GFA-Rs, which were pathologically diagnosed in accordance 
with WHO classification, at our hospital from January 2009 to December 2023 by

Spatial modulation enhances the effects of radiation on prostate cancer cells: a 
targeted mass spectrometry metabolomics study.

Chen B(1), Rogers LJ(2)(3)(4), Liu K(1)(5), Chen S(1), Deda R(1), Gotsbacher 
MP(6), Yang J(5), McKenzie DR(2)(3), Suchowerska N(3), Kwan AH(1)(7).

Author information:
(1)School of Life and Environmental Sciences, The University of Sydney, Sydney, 
NSW, Australia.
(2)Department of Radiation Oncology, Chris O'Brien Lifehouse, Camperdown, NSW,

(3)School of Physics, The University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW, Australia.
(4)Arto Hardy Family Biomedical Innovation Hub, Chris O'Brien Lifehouse,

(5)School of Mathematics and Statistics, The University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW, 
Australia.
(6)School of Medical Sciences, The University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW, Australia.
(7)Sydney Nano Institute, The University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW, Australia.

PURPOSE: Spatially modulated radiation fields, such as microbeam or grid 
therapy, have been shown to enhance tumor cell killing while sparing normal 
tissue compared to uniform fields of the same total dose. The biological 
mechanisms underlying this effect remain poorly understood. This study 
investigates metabolomic changes in prostate cancer and normal prostate cells 
following exposure to spatially modulated versus uniform irradiation.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Prostate cancer (LNCaP) and normal prostate (PNT1A) cells 
were irradiated using spatially modulated or uniform fields at equivalent, 
higher, or lower mean doses. Metabolites from cellular extracts were profiled 
using targeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) selected reaction 
monitoring (SRM). Multivariate analyses, including principal component analysis 
(PCA) with bootstrapping, were applied to identify dose- and field-dependent 
metabolic signatures.
RESULTS: PCA revealed a clear dose-response in uniformly irradiated LNCaP cells 
and distinct separation between non-irradiated and irradiated groups. Notably, 
cancer cells exposed to modulated fields clustered closer to those treated with 
a higher-dose uniform field than to those receiving the same mean dose, 
suggesting biological equivalence to dose escalation. Key metabolites driving 
this separation were associated with phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan 
biosynthesis pathways, indicating heightened metabolic stress under modulated 
irradiation. In contrast, PNT1A cells showed no significant metabolic 
distinction between modulated and uniform fields of the same mean dose.
CONCLUSION: Spatially modulated irradiation induces metabolic responses in 
prostate cancer cells comparable to those elicited by higher-dose uniform 
fields, while normal cells respond similarly to uniform fields of the same dose. 
These findings provide mechanistic insight into the therapeutic advantage of 
spatial modulation and support its potential role in improving tumor control 
without increasing normal tissue toxicity. Given that clinical radiotherapy 
sessions typically span 15-30 minutes, incorporating spatial modulation and 
temporal fractionation strategies into treatment workflows may offer a practical 
and effective means to improve therapeutic outcomes in prostate cancer.

Thin film beryllium oxide (BeO) is an emerging material that can potentially be 
used as a high thermal conductivity gate dielectric and/or passivation layer for 
high power electronic devices. This study presents the measurement of the 
thermal conductivity and thermal boundary conductance associated with 
plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PEALD)-grown polycrystalline BeO films 
on Si substrates with thicknesses ranging from 25 to 250 nm. The measured 
out-of-plane thermal conductivities of the 250, 113, 53, and 26 nm-thick BeO 
films are 13.45 ± 1.45, 8.7 ± 1.35, 7.2 ± 2.1, and 5 ± 2.2 W m-1 K-1,

dielectric materials such as SiN and SiO2. The measured thermal boundary 
conductance across the BeO/Si interface is ∼200 MW m-2 K-1 at room temperature,

helps reduce the channel temperature rise by an additional 5.2%.

Two Practices That Understate the Mental Health Risks Associated With Adolescent 
Social-Media Use.

Haidt J(1), Rausch Z(1).

Author information:
(1)Stern School of Business, New York University.

Why do researchers analyzing the same body of evidence reach different 
conclusions about whether social-media use poses risks to adolescent mental 
health? We offer a partial explanation: Two common practices can lead 
researchers to underestimate harm and reach divergent conclusions. First, 
studies often do not account for risk elevations, relying instead only on 
correlation coefficients, which are more prone to misinterpretation. Second, 
researchers often rely on highly blended analyses that combine heterogeneous 
exposures (e.g., multiple digital activities, including "TV watching"), outcomes 
(e.g., depression with life satisfaction), and populations (e.g., girls with 
boys), and then treat weak aggregate associations as evidence that specific 
risks are negligible. This is especially problematic when the central question 
is whether heavy social-media use is associated with internalizing symptoms 
among adolescent girls. We illustrate how sequential blending can transform a 
large and clinically relevant association into a negligible one, which helps 
explain the persistent disagreement in the literature. We conclude by urging 
researchers to present their findings in more practically interpretable terms, 
including elevated risks, and to investigate heterogeneity across platforms, 
usage levels, populations, and outcomes.

Multifunctional nanocomposite with stage-responsive behavior for wound healing.

Hou Y(1), Wu K(2), Zhang X(2), Duan W(2), Wang X(2), Zhu C(2), He Q(2)(3), Wang 
L(4).

Author information:
(1)College of Life Sciences, Qingdao Agricultural University, Qingdao, China.
(2)Medical Science and Technology Innovation Center, Shandong First Medical 
University & Shandong Academy of Medical Sciences, Jinan, China.
(3)School of Radiology, Shandong First Medical University & Shandong Academy of 
Medical Sciences, Taian, China.
(4)Department of Oncology, No. 1, Rushan People's Hospital, Rushan, China.

Chronic wounds, particularly refractory diabetic ulcers, typically fail to heal 
due to a self-perpetuating inflammatory state driven by persistent bacterial 
infection, severe oxidative stress, and impaired microvascular regeneration. 
Conventional static dressings cannot accommodate the spatiotemporal, multiphase 
complexity of tissue repair. Here, a stage-responsive hierarchical nanocomposite 
(SNF@GQDs@Arg) was engineered by covalently anchoring graphene quantum dots 
(GQDs) onto radially porous silica nanoflowers (SNF), followed by surface 
adsorption of L-arginine (L-Arg). The resulting platform coordinates wound 
repair through an integrated tripartite-physical, catalytic, and 
metabolic-cascade. In the initial hemostatic phase, the high-aspect-ratio 
topography of SNF enables rapid wound closure via a non-covalent nano-bridging 
effect. During the inflammatory phase, the immobilized GQDs act as 
peroxidase-mimicking nanozymes, converting pathological hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) 
into bactericidal hydroxyl radicals (·OH) to eradicate biofilms while 
simultaneously scavenging excess free radicals to resolve the reactive oxygen 
species (ROS) paradox. Concurrently, the sustained release of L-Arg replenishes 
the substrate pool for macrophage inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), 
restoring physiological nitric oxide (NO) bioavailability. This metabolic 
intervention drives pro-inflammatory M1-to-reparative M2 phenotype transition, 
upregulates CD31 and VEGF expression to stimulate angiogenesis, and promotes 
organized collagen deposition. In a murine infected full-thickness skin defect 
model, SNF@GQDs@Arg markedly accelerated wound closure, suppressed local 
inflammation, and enhanced tissue remodeling quality without inducing systemic 
toxicity. By synchronizing functional bioactivity with the endogenous repair 
rhythm, this platform provides a microenvironment-adaptive paradigm for 
refractory chronic wound therapy.

Is the use of Porous Threaded Titanium Implants Associated with Lower Rates of 
Implant Migration in Elderly Pelvic Ring Injuries?

Collins AP(1)(2), Caruso B(3), Rockov ZA(1)(2), Kleweno CP(1)(2), Firoozabadi 
R(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)University of Washington, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery and Sports 
Medicine, Seattle, WA, USA.
(2)Harborview Medical Center, Seattle, WA, USA.
(3)Washington State University Elson. S. Floyd College of Medicine, Spokane, WA,

OBJECTIVES: To determine if porous threaded titanium implant (PTTI) screws 
placed in the posterior pelvic ring as iliosacral (IS) or transiliac-transsacral 
(transsacral) were associated with implant positional changes, alterations in 
postoperative weightbearing restrictions, or the necessity of revision surgery 
in operatively managed geriatric pelvic ring injuries, compared to standard 
stainless steel screws.
DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.
SETTING: Academic Level I trauma center.
PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Patients with operatively managed pelvic ring 
injuries (AO/OTA61) from January 2017 to June 2025, aged ≥65 years with a 
minimum of 6-months of radiographic and clinical follow-up were included.Outcome 
Measures and Comparisons: The primary study outcome was the incidence of 
postoperative pelvic ring implant positional changes, ≥2mm from immediate 
postoperative radiographs compared among patients treated with PTTI versus 
standard stainless steel screws for IS and transsacral fixation. Secondary 
outcomes included subsequent revision surgery or alterations in postoperative 
weightbearing restrictions related to implant positional changes. A 
multivariable logistic regression was used to determine associations of 
demographic, injury, and treatment variables with implant positional changes, 
the necessity for revision surgery, or negative changes in postoperative 
weightbearing restrictions.
RESULTS: 271 patients were included; 215 (79.3%) were managed with standard 
screws, while PTTIs were used in 56 (20.7%). The standard screw cohort had a 
median follow-up of 8.9 months (interquartile range 6.2-11.3 months), while the 
PTTI cohort had a median follow-up of 9.1 months (interquartile range 6.3-10.9 
months). Compared with the standard screw cohort, the PTTI cohort had a higher 
proportion of female sex (57.2% versus 73.2%, respectively; p=0.029) and a 
higher average age (74.0 years versus 78.6 years, respectively; 
p<0.001).Radiographic migration ≥2mm for posterior implants was observed in 
18.1% of patients in the standard implant cohort versus 0.0% in the PTTI cohort 
(p<0.001). Implant migration >1cm was observed in 3.7% of patients in the 
standard implant cohort versus 0.0% in the PTTI group (p=0.231). The implant 
positional changes resulted in negative weightbearing restriction changes in 9 
of 215 (4.2%) patients in the standard implant cohort compared with 0 of 56 in 
the PTTI cohort (p=0.120). Of the patients with standard implants, 9 (4.2%) 
underwent revision for posterior implant loosening, compared with 0 (0.0%) in 
the PTTI cohort.On multivariate analysis, posterior implant positional changes 
were associated with a protective effect from PTTI and anterior ring fixation 
(OR 0.1, 95% CI 0.0-0.7, p=0.023 and OR 0.2, 95% CI 0.1-0.4, p<0.001, 
respectively). The necessity for revision surgery or negative change in 
postoperative weightbearing restrictions was not significantly associated with 
PTTI use (OR 0.3, 95% CI 0.1-1.3, p=0.106).
CONCLUSIONS: In geriatric pelvic ring injuries, PTTIs had no migration after 
placement and were associated with a lower incidence of any implant positional 
change and posterior implant positional changes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic Level III.

Structure-dependent removal of aromatic organophosphate flame retardants by 
combined adsorption and electrochemical oxidation.

Trzcinski AP(1), Harada KH(2).

Author information:
(1)School of Science, Engineering and Digital Technologies, University of 
Southern Queensland, Toowoomba, Australia.
(2)Laboratory of Food Hygiene and Environmental Health, Kyoto Prefectural 
University, Sakyo, Japan.

The removal of aromatic organophosphate flame retardants (OPFRs) from water 
remains a significant challenge due to their persistence, hydrophobicity, and 
resistance to conventional treatment processes. In this study, a combined 
adsorption-electrochemical oxidation system using graphite intercalation 
compound (GIC) was evaluated for the removal of five representative aromatic 
OPFRs: triphenyl phosphate (TPP), 2-ethylhexyl diphenyl phosphate (EHDPP), 
cresyl diphenyl phosphate (CDPP), tricresyl phosphate (TCP), and 
tris(4-tert-butylphenyl) phosphate (TTBP). Batch adsorption experiments showed 
rapid initial removal governed by pseudo-second-order kinetics, indicating that 
surface interactions dominate the adsorption process. Adsorption capacity and 
rate varied among compounds, with more hydrophobic OPFRs exhibiting faster 
removal and lower residual concentrations. Cyclic adsorption-regeneration 
experiments demonstrated that overall performance is strongly dependent on 
electrochemical conditions. At low current (0.5 A), regeneration was incomplete 
and partially governed by desorption, whereas increasing the current to 3 A 
resulted in higher Apparent Oxidative Removal (AOR) values, lower residual 
concentrations and more stable treatment performance over successive cycles. 
Under optimal conditions (3 A, 20 min regeneration), several OPFRs were reduced 
to concentrations below the GC-MS detection limits, and all compounds were 
reduced to concentrations below 5 µg L-1. Mechanistic analysis revealed that 
adsorption dominates initial removal, while electrochemical oxidation is 
essential for regenerating adsorption sites and preventing contaminant release. 
The combined GIC-electrochemical system offers a synergistic and effective 
approach for the treatment of aromatic OPFRs, with performance governed by 
compound structure, hydrophobicity, and operating conditions. These findings 
provide new insights into adsorption-electrochemical processes for the removal 
of persistent organic contaminants.

Enhanced Roughness-Matching Precision for Random Grating Textures at a 1.0-mm 
Mean Wavelength.

Kurita A, Okamoto S.

Natural surfaces contain local spatial irregularities, yet tactile texture 
perception has often been characterized in terms of mean geometric properties. 
It remains unclear whether information associated with such irregularities 
improves roughness-matching precision when the mean spatial scale of a texture 
is varied. We compared roughness-matching precision between physically 
fabricated periodic and random gratings with nominal mean wavelengths of 1.0 and 
2.0 mm. Participants selected, from a set of test gratings, the stimulus whose 
roughness they perceived as closest to that of a reference. Matching precision 
was quantified for each participant and condition using the standard deviation 
of the nominal wavelengths selected across repeated trials, with a smaller 
standard deviation indicating more precise roughness matching. At the nominal 
mean wavelength of 1.0 mm, the standard deviation was significantly smaller for 
the random gratings than for the periodic gratings. No significant difference 
was observed at 2.0 mm. These findings suggest that information contained in the 
1.0-mm random gratings beyond their mean wavelength may have contributed to 
roughness matching precision.

DIAN: Device Invariant Attention Network for Chest X-ray Classification.

Nguyen TK, Duy HK, Ngu HCV.

Deep learning has significantly advanced automated chest X-ray interpretation, 
yet models remain vulnerable to spurious correlations with visual confounders 
such as support devices. We propose the Device Invariant Attention Network 
(DIAN), which couples spatial self-attention with domain-adversarial learning to 
disentangle disease-relevant signals from device-induced artifacts. DIAN employs

Bhagat V, Yadav RK, Ghosh S, Muthukrishnan SP, Bo APL, Roy S, Dobbins C.

Understanding how brain activity varies during voluntary movement under

in both within-subject and subject-independent settings, providing preliminary

Transfer under Linear Haptic Simulation.

Liu Z, An L.

Passivity constraints bound the impedance range that force-feedback devices can 
stably display, so real-time haptic training defaults to linear 
physics-typically a mass-spring-damper (MSD) model-although materials worth 
training on are nonlinear and non-Newtonian. We define this discrepancy as the 
rheology gap and ask which motor-skill components survive a deliberately 
linearized rendering of an artisanal dough-stretching task. A within-instance

process efficiency ($-$45.6%), the most rheology-sensitive components, showed 
the largest deficits. Non-informative force feedback impaired learning, and 
gains persisted at 24 h. Because conditions covary on several factors, effects 
are reported as composite. Our central contribution is a reproducible, 
component-level benchmark-task protocol, objective metrics, characterized linear 
baseline, and published-rheometry reference-on which any future nonlinear engine 
(FEM, MPM, XPBD, neural physics) can be scored under identical conditions,

time-domain passivity control runs stably at 1 kHz and cuts force-fidelity error 
from 41.0% to 24.6% NRMSE. Pending closed-loop validation of the 
strain-stiffening hypothesis (offline $R^{2}=0.31$), current VR is best 
positioned as pre-apprenticeship scaffolding, not a substitute for physical 
practice.

Untangle Generalization Errors for Better Test-Time Adaptation in

Zhang S, Luo Y, Chen S, Shi Y, Chen X, Liu X, Li J.

Test-time adaptation (TTA) is a strategy that leverages unlabeled test data to 
adjust a pretrained model, improving robustness against distribution shifts. 
Recent advances in this research area are mostly driven by heuristic or 
empirical approaches with limited theoretical guidance. In particular, there is 
little theoretical analysis on what factors are important in TTA and how they 
impact the adaptation performance. We derive a closed form of expected 
generalization errors of overparameterized linear models in consideration of a 
general TTA setup involving sequentially different environments. As revealed by 
this theorem, well-trained models can be dynamically updated in response to test 
data shifts, demonstrating the advantages of TTA over the traditional

adaptation algorithms, influence the performance of TTA. Based on these

enhancement. TAP employs a memory bank to store probabilistic representations 
and label pairs during training and uses ready-made knowledge to gradually 
update the memory and prediction during inference. Extensive experiments on 
domain generalization benchmarks confirm that the proposed adapter is 
computationally lightweight and outperforms traditional TTA methods.

ParaDeco: Frame-Level Parallel Generative Decoding for Large-Scale Surveillance 
Video Analytics.

Wang X, Yan Y, Zhang S, Zhu A, Chen N, Chen Y, Meng L, Li X, Wang D, Liang Y, 
Qian Z, Wu J.

Video analytics pipelines (VAPs) have been a paradigm for large-scale video 
analytics. Due to temporal redundancy in video, frame filtering is widely used 
in VAPs to reduce analysis workload. While prior works have identified decoding 
as a significant overhead and proposed pre-decoding filtering to mitigate it, we 
find that codec reference dependencies still force decoders to process many 
unselected frames, manifesting an over-decoding trap that bounds end-to-end 
throughput. This limitation stems from the reference-based design in modern 
codecs, which requires decoding preceding frames to reconstruct any selected 
one. As a result, over-decoding has become the practical bottleneck in VAPs 
using modern decoders, highlighting a critical but under-explored problem. To 
address this issue, we propose ParaDeco, a high-throughput video analytics 
framework featuring a novel frame-level parallel generative decoder. Unlike 
traditional decoders, ParaDeco adopts a decode-what-matters approach with 
decoupled frame dependencies. To decode arbitrary frames independently, ParaDeco 
generates frame-wise features as standalone skeletons using compressed video 
metadata, then predicts pseudo frames maintaining semantic consistency with 
original frames. Moreover, ParaDeco identifies which frames truly matter for 
analysis via delicate contribution-based frame filtering. We implement ParaDeco 
on a cloud server and evaluate it on large-scale real-world surveillance video 
datasets. Our experimental results show that ParaDeco achieves a 2.76× speedup 
on averagparse e compared to state-of-the-art VAPs.

Evolutionary Dynamics of Reputation-Based Voluntary Prisoner's Dilemma Games.

Shen C, Song Z, Wang X, Shi L, Perc M, Wang Z, Tanimoto J.

Cooperation underlies many natural and artificial systems. While voluntary

Distributed Fixed-Time Command Recovery and Exact-Handover Cooperative Guidance 
With Impact Time and Angle Constraints.

Zheng H, Zhou B, Ding Y, Duan G.

This article investigates a layered cooperative guidance problem for multiple 
interceptors, where only a subset of interceptors has direct access to a common 
impact-time command, and all interceptors are required to satisfy terminal 
angular constraints. First, a distributed fixed-time observer is developed to 
recover the piecewise-constant impact-time commands available only to a subset 
of interceptors. Under the restart-amplitude condition and command-update timing 
conditions, rigorous analysis guarantees the recovery of each updated command

recovered common impact-time command together with its individual terminal-angle 
constraint. Finally, numerical simulations validate the effectiveness of the 
proposed framework.

Function-based Deep Learning Autoencoder for Passive Shimming in a Portable MRI 
Magnet with Enhanced Field Homogeneity.

Zhou J, Xiao X, Chen G, Zhao P, Pang Y, Wang Z.

High-field magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers excellent sensitivity and 
spatial resolution, yet its substantial cost and limited mobility restrict 
deployment in decentralized or resource-constrained environments. Portable MRI 
systems offer a complementary imaging modality to high-field MRI, but their 
performance depends critically on the uniformity of the main magnetic field 
(B0). Passive shimming, achieved by placing ferromagnetic materials within the 
magnet bore, is widely used to correct spatial field variations. Existing 
optimization strategies- including linear programming and evolutionary 
algorithms-can improve B homogeneity, but often struggle to achieve an effective 
trade-off among field strength, uniformity, and shim mass. To address this

optimize the spatial distribution of passive shims. The framework operates 
without a precompiled dataset and performs online self-supervised learning to 
iteratively refine the shim configuration. This approach improves B0 homogeneity 
from 4873 ppm to 547 ppm (parts per million) and increases the average field 
strength from 80.402 mT to 80.948 mT. Compared with linear programming (LP), it 
achieved lower inhomogeneity, reduced the shim mass by 0.29 kg, and shortened 
the optimization time from approximately 1.2 to 0.5 h. MRiLab simulations also 
showed a reduction in image NRMSE from 0.889 to 0.543. Relative to 
genetic-algorithm-based shimming, the resulting field uniformity is improved by 
nearly a factor of five. These results demonstrate that FDLAE may provide an 
efficient and comparatively robust passive-shimming approach for portable MRI 
magnets.

Making long-acting HIV PrEP routine in college health: durable systems, not 
dedicated heroes.

Broker P(1).

Author information:
(1)Student Health Services, Departments of Internal Medicine and Pediatrics, 
University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas, USA.

For many U.S. students, college health is the practical home of primary care and 
their most direct point of access to HIV prevention. In this commentary I argue 
that HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), including long-acting cabotegravir and 
lenacapavir, should be offered as routine preventive care in college health 
rather than as a specialty service. Nearly all responding student health 
services in national benchmarking data offer STI and HIV testing and 
contraception, while far fewer offer PrEP or prompt clinicians to educate 
patients on PrEP. That gap, the June 2025 approval of lenacapavir, and a quality 
improvement initiative that raised PrEP counseling from 3.0% to 97% point to a 
capacity-based framework of on-site, hybrid, and closed-loop referral models. 
The minimum standard is not identical infrastructure but a reliable pathway from 
routine offer to receipt of the chosen regimen. Clinics need durable systems 
rather than dedicated heroes.

Oxidative Stress in Female Reproductive Health and Infertility: Mechanisms, 
Biomarkers, Therapeutic Interventions.

Takalani NB(1), Lebelo SL(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Life and Consumer Sciences, University of South Africa, Cnr 
Christiaan de Wet and Pioneer Ave, Private Bag X6 , Florida, South Africa.

Infertility is defined by the World Health Organization as the inability to 
achieve pregnancy after one year of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse. 
Female infertility can result from problems with ovulation, hormone imbalances, 
endometriosis, blocked fallopian tubes, and poor egg quality. One factor linked 
to these conditions is oxidative stress, which occurs when harmful molecules in 
the body exceed its natural antioxidant defences. This imbalance may damage 
reproductive cells and tissues, affecting hormone function, embryo quality, 
implantation, and pregnancy outcomes. Oxidative stress has been associated with 
several reproductive disorders, including polyendocrine metabolic ovarian 
syndrome (PMOS), previously called polycystic ovary syndrome, and endometriosis. 
As a result, there is growing interest in natural approaches that may help 
protect reproductive health. Some medicinal plants contain natural antioxidants 
that may reduce oxidative stress and protect reproductive cells from damage. 
This review examines the impact of oxidative stress on female reproductive 
health and explores the potential role of medicinal plants in supporting 
fertility and reproductive well-being.

Testosterone as part of hormone replacement therapy in menopausal women - what 
do we know so far? A Narrative Review.

Mishra I(1)(2), Robinson L(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Birmingham Women's Hospital, Mindelsohn Way , Birmingham, UK.
(2)Department of Metabolism and Systems Science, Level 2, IBR Tower, College of 
Medicine and Health, University of Birmingham, Edgbaston , Birmingham, UK.

Testosterone, widely known as the male hormone, is also produced naturally in 
women and plays an important role throughout their lifespan. There has been a 
growing use of testosterone for a range of symptoms in menopausal women, 
including low sexual desire, low mood, fatigue, poor memory, and heart and bone 
health. This review brings together the current evidence and guidelines on 
testosterone as part of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in menopausal women, 
including its impact on reproductive and non-reproductive tissues; when it is 
indicated to be prescribed and in what forms; safety and gaps in existing 
evidence. We found that there is high-quality evidence to support the use of 
testosterone for low sexual desire where conventional HRT has not helped. 
Transdermal preparations are recommended with no serious side effects at 
testosterone levels normally found in women. There is insufficient evidence to 
support its use for brain, heart and bone health. This represents an area of 
focus for future research.

Soysal GG(1), Seyyar SA(2), Yılmaz İE(3), Doğan L(4), Mercanlı M(5), Güngör

Author information:
(1)Gaziantep City Hospital Ophthalmology Clinic, University of Health Sciences,

(2)Ophthalmology Department, Gaziantep University Hospital, Gaziantep, Turkey.

(7)Pediatric Clinic, Gaziantep City Hospital, Gaziantep, Turkey.

PURPOSE: To evaluate choroidal structural and vascular changes in children with 
Immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV) using optical coherence tomography (OCT).
METHODS: This prospective cross-sectional study included 90 eyes of 41 children 
diagnosed with IgAV and 49 age-matched healthy controls. All participants 
underwent comprehensive ophthalmic examination and OCT imaging. Subfoveal 
choroidal thickness (SFCT) and choroidal vascularity index (CVI) were measured.
RESULTS: Subfoveal choroidal thickness (SFCT) and choroidal vascularity index

CONCLUSION: Children with IgAV demonstrated significantly reduced SFCT and CVI 
compared with healthy controls. These findings indicate the presence of 
choroidal structural and vascular alterations in IgAV, even in the absence of 
clinically apparent ocular pathology.

The impact of racist events on post-trauma mental health symptoms among 
immigrants and refugees in Canada: the role of racial trauma.

Jin L(1), Nguyen T(1).

Author information:
(1)Werklund School of Education, University of Calgary, Calgary, Canada.

Background: Immigrants and refugees are at greater risk of mental health 
symptoms, including elevated symptoms of depression, anxiety, and posttraumatic 
stress disorder (PTSD). For racialized immigrants and refugees, frequent 
exposure to racist events is one of several predictors of mental health 
outcomes. According to race-based traumatic stress theory, repeated exposure to 
racist events can undermine safety, belonging, and dignity, and may lead to 
racial trauma, referring to the psychological and physiological stress responses 
arising from such experiences. However, it remains unknown whether racial trauma 
plays a mediating role in the relationship between racist events and mental 
health symptoms. To address this gap, the present study aimed to examine racial 
trauma as a mediator of this relationship among racialized immigrants and 
refugees in Canada.Methods: A sample of 182 immigrants and refugees in Canada 
(Mage = 30.76; 52.2% men; 52.7% of African descent) completed self-report 
measures. The mediating role of racial trauma in the relationship between racist 
events and mental health symptoms (PTSD, depression, anxiety) was examined using 
PROCESS Model 4.Results: Results indicated that racial trauma significantly 
explained the relationship between racist events and mental health outcomes, 
including PTSD (B = 0.35, CI [0.20, 0.56]), depression (B = 0.11, CI [0.06, 
0.18]), and anxiety (B = 0.12, CI [0.08, 0.17]). The model accounted for 34.02% 
to 46.21% of the variances in mental health outcomes.Conclusions: Among 
racialized immigrants and refugees, greater exposure to racist events was 
associated with elevated racial trauma, which contributed to higher PTSD, 
depression, and anxiety symptoms. Clinicians, community organizations, and 
policymakers should integrate anti-racism strategies and racial trauma 
frameworks to support the mental health of immigrants and refugees.

Plain Language Summary: Racialized immigrants and refugees in Canada with more 
exposure to racist events are more likely to show racial trauma, which may 
increase the risk of experiencing poor mental health.Findings highlight the need 
to target racial trauma to reduce mental health issues when working with 
immigrants and refugees.

Nutritional Supplements in the Treatment of Endometriosis-Associated Symptoms: A 
Systematic Review.

Seven M(1), Galla L(1), Gstoettner M(1), Wenzl R(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics, Medical University of Vienna, 
Waehringer Guertel 18-20 , Vienna, Austria.

Endometriosis is a condition where tissue similar to the lining of the uterus 
(endometrium) grows outside the uterus, which can cause severe chronic pelvic 
pain, limit quality of life, and lead to infertility. In addition to standard 
medical treatment (painkillers or hormones), many patients with endometriosis 
use additional supplements, such as vitamins or antioxidants, to alleviate 
symptoms, but it is unclear how well these approaches work. In this study, we 
reviewed 24 clinical trials involving 2,019 women with endometriosis to evaluate 
the effects of dietary supplements. Some trials reported improvements in pain 
and quality of life, particularly with specially formulated curcumin or 
selenium, alone or alongside dienogest. Studies on fertility found improvements 
in some fertility-related measures, but these did not lead to higher pregnancy 
rates. Evidence on progression was limited: some combination treatments reduced 
ovarian endometriosis, but supplements did not reduce recurrence after surgery. 
Supplements may therefore support standard treatment but should not replace it.

Soil amendments reduced potentially toxic elements (PTEs) in peanuts (Arachis 
hypogaea L.) grown in farmlands near Cu-Ni mine in Central Botswana.

Gaothobogwe K(1), Manyiwa T(1), Oleszek IS(2), Rzeznicka II(3), Ultra V Jr(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Sustainable Natural Resources, School of Earth Sciences and 
Engineering, Botswana International University of Science and Technology, 
Palapye, Botswana.
(2)Faculty of Science and Engineering, Waseda Research Institute for Science and 
Engineering, Tokyo, Japan.
(3)College of Engineering, Shibaura Institute of Technology, Saitama, Japan.

This study evaluated the effects of fly ash (FA), compost (COMP), lignite (LIG), 
and their combination (FA+COMP+LIG) on soil chemical properties, PTE total and 
available concentrations, PTE uptake by peanut (Arachis hypogaea L.) tissues, 
and associated human health risks in agricultural soils near BCL Cu-Ni mine. A 
field experiment was conducted in three farmlands located 2.6 km, 5 km, and 
10 km from the BCL Cu-Ni mine in Selibe-Phikwe, Botswana. The experiment 
consisted of five treatments arranged in a randomized complete block design 
(RCBD) with three replications: unamended control, FA at 20 t ha-1, COMP at 20 t 
ha-1, LIG at 10 t ha-1, and FA+COMP+LIG at 20 + 20 + 10 t ha-1. Amendment 
application increased soil pH and reduced both total and available PTE 
concentrations in soils across all farms. Additionally, all amendments improved 
peanut dry matter yield compared to the control treatment. The combined 
treatment showed the greatest reduction in PTE accumulation in peanut tissues, 
particularly in kernels, where the reduction exceeded 30% relative to the 
control. Estimated daily intake (EDI), hazard quotient (HQ), and hazard index 
(HI) values for both children and adults were significantly reduced following 
amendment application, indicating lower dietary exposure to PTEs. However, 
despite the observed reductions, the HQ and HI values for some PTEs remained 
above the threshold value of 1, suggesting potential health hazards. Overall, 
the combined application of FA, COMP, and LIG showed the greatest potential for 
reducing PTE uptake by peanuts and decreasing associated human health risks in 
mine-affected agricultural soils. Further long-term field studies are 
recommended to evaluate the sustainability of these remediation effects.

Biomechanical responses to incremental backpack loading during stair ascent in 
male adolescents.

Mao C(1), Lu Z(1), Zhang X(1), Sun Y(1).

Author information:
(1)School of Physical Education, Shaanxi Normal University, Xi'an, China.

Backpack carriage is common among adolescents, yet its biomechanical responses 
during stair ascent remain unclear. This study investigated the effects of 
incremental backpack loads (0, 10, 15, and 20% body weight) on stair-ascent 
biomechanics in 16 male adolescents. Three-dimensional motion analysis, 
kinetics, surface electromyography, and dynamic stability measures were assessed 
using SPM1D. Increasing loads significantly altered AP-MOS, COM-COP inclination 
angle, vertical GRF, lower-limb joint mechanics, and muscle activation, while 
traditional spatiotemporal parameters remained unchanged. Load-related 
adaptations occurred during single-support, double-support, and swing phases, 
involving altered activation of key lower-limb muscles. These findings suggest 
that adolescents maintain external stair-ascent performance through internal 
biomechanical adjustments under increased backpack loads.

Plain Language Summary: This study examined biomechanical responses to 
increasing backpack loads during stair ascent in male adolescents. Although 
conventional spatiotemporal gait measures remained relatively stable, increasing 
loads were accompanied by changes in dynamic stability, lower-limb mechanics, 
and muscle activation. Ergonomic evaluations should consider internal 
biomechanical responses beyond observable gait performance.

Digestate reuse as an intermittent bio-stimulant for municipal sludge anaerobic 
digestion: full-scale evidence, biochemical methane potential assessment, and 
semi-continuous validation.

Cheng KL(1)(2), Gao KQ(1), Zheng WX(1), Hsieh PH(1)(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Environmental Science and Engineering, National Pingtung 
University of Science and Technology, Pingtung, Taiwan.
(2)Forest Water Environmental Engineering Co., LTD., Taipei, Taiwan.
(3)Center for Sustainable Energy and Climate Change Research and Demonstration, 
National Pingtung University of Science and Technology, Neipu, Pingtung, Taiwan.

Digestate reuse has been proposed as a strategy for enhancing anaerobic 
digestion (AD) performance; however, full-scale validation remains limited. This 
study evaluated digestate reuse for municipal sludge treatment through 
full-scale monitoring, biochemical methane potential (BMP) assays, 
semi-continuous continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) experiments, and economic 
assessment. Operational data from two wastewater treatment plants revealed 
substantial differences in baseline digestion performance. BMP results showed 
that digestate reuse increased methane production by up to 28% and improved 
solids degradation in underperforming sludge, whereas limited benefits were 
observed in a well-performing system. Semi-continuous CSTR experiments 
demonstrated that intermittent digestate dosing at approximately 10% (v/v) 
improved total solids (TS) and volatile solids (VS) removal without compromising 
process stability. The enhancement effect persisted for 10-20 days following a 
single addition, suggesting that digestate acted primarily as a transient 
bio-stimulant rather than a conventional carbon source. Full-scale evaluation 
indicated that digestate reuse could reduce sludge disposal demand and generate 
net cost savings of approximately NT$100,000 (∼US$3,125) per month. These 
findings demonstrate that intermittent digestate reuse is a practical strategy 
for improving AD performance while supporting resource recovery and circular 
economy implementation.

OBJECTIVE: To assess a low-resource tracking workflow for improved documentation 
of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) treatment status and describe identified 
follow-up gaps in a Student Health clinic.
PARTICIPANTS: Students with confirmed LTBI before (2018-2023; n = 82) and after

METHODS: Retrospective before-after chart review. In 2024, the clinic added a

Distillation-based treatment of unsaturated polyester resin wastewater for 
propylene glycol recovery.

Do TX(1), Le TT(1), Nguyen TV(1), Nguyen HH(1), Dau CTH(1), Tran VTL(1), Dang 
TTN(1), Pham HH(2).

Author information:
(1)School of Chemistry and Life Science, Hanoi University of Science and 
Technology, Hanoi, Vietnam.
(2)Center for Environmental Intelligence and College of Engineering and Computer 
Science, VinUniversity, Hanoi, Vietnam.

This study evaluates distillation as an integrated treatment and resource 
recovery approach for wastewater generated from unsaturated polyester resin 
(UPR) production. An integrated experimental and modelling approach was 
developed to evaluate separation performance and support industrial process 
design. Laboratory experiments were conducted using a packed distillation column 
under different operating conditions, and a thermodynamic model based on 
vapour-liquid equilibrium data was developed and validated against experimental 
results. A continuous two-column distillation process was subsequently simulated 
and optimized using actual industrial UPR wastewater, with the total annualized 
cost as the optimization criterion. The system recovered water at 99.7% purity 
with a yield of 95%, while PG was obtained at 99.1% purity and 83.5% recovery 
efficiency at the lab scale. Recommended conditions for water separation were 
atmospheric pressure, 0.20 kW heat duty, and a reflux ratio of 0.25, whereas PG 
recovery achieved the highest performance under reduced pressure (<0.1 bar) with 
a reflux ratio of 1.8-2.0. The optimized industrial process achieved 86.63% 
overall valuable-chemical recovery using 9 and 22 theoretical stages for the 
water and phenol separation columns, respectively. The results demonstrate the 
feasibility of integrating validated process simulation with laboratory 
experiments for industrial wastewater treatment and resource recovery.

Wang X(1)(2), Bian X(1), Wen L(1), Zhang G(3), Cui B(1), Ma J(1).

Characterizing Features of Vulnerability in Narrative Production of 
Cantonese-Speaking School-Aged Children With Developmental Language Disorder.

Lai J(1)(2), Chan A(1)(2), Hui S(1), Lee MT(1), Kong NY(1), Wong S(1), Wong 
SW(1), Gagarina N(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Language Science and Technology, The Hong Kong Polytechnic 
University, Hong Kong SAR, China.
(2)Research Centre for Language, Cognition, and Neuroscience, The Hong Kong 
Polytechnic University, Hong Kong SAR, China.
(3)Research Area 2: Language Development and Multilingualism, Leibniz-Centre 
General Linguistics, Berlin, Germany.

PURPOSE: Narratives show vulnerability in children with developmental language 
disorder (DLD) cross-linguistically. However, certain narrative measures 
revealing significant deficits in English and European DLD literature have been 
studied primarily in preschoolers, with limited evidence in school-aged children 
and no data in Cantonese. We examine features of vulnerability in narrative 
production of school-aged children learning a major Chinese language, Cantonese.
METHOD: Twenty-five children with DLD (Mage = 9;7 [years;months]) and 
age-matched typically developing (TD) peers (Mage = 9;8) were assessed using the 
Cantonese Multilingual Assessment Instrument for Narratives (MAIN) in story 
retelling and storytelling. Their narrative competence across macrostructure, 
microstructure, and internal state term measures were analyzed at group and 
individual diagnostic accuracy levels.
RESULTS: Both expressive macrostructure and microstructure showed significant 
TD/DLD group differences, indicating story structure (SS), story complexity 
(SC), syntactic complexity, and grammaticality are vulnerable in monolingual 
Cantonese-speaking school-aged children with DLD. No significant TD/DLD group 
differences were registered in number of different words, mean length of 
utterance, productivity measures (total number of utterances, total number of 
words), or internal state terms. For diagnostic accuracies, SS and syntactic 
complexity reached acceptable sensitivity (91.7% and 83.3%, respectively) but 
limited specificity (41.7% and 70.8%, respectively); SC and grammaticality 
showed marginal sensitivity and specificity (both 70.8%).
CONCLUSIONS: This study confirms SS, SC, grammaticality, and syntactic 
complexity-but not productivity-as features of vulnerability in narrative 
production of Cantonese-speaking school-aged children with DLD. The exploratory 
diagnostic accuracy results support using narrative measures in combination with 
other assessments for diagnosis. Future studies should examine younger and 
larger samples to further document these vulnerability features and evaluate the 
clinical utility of narrative measures at earlier developmental stages.

PURPOSE: This study examined the mediating role of basic psychological needs 
(BPN) within the reciprocal associations between perceived social support (PSS) 
and physical activity (PA).
METHODS: This secondary analysis used Spring 2023 ACHA-NCHA data (N = 78,024).

PA→BPN→PSS.

associations with PSS through BPN, with effect sizes ranging from 0.008 to 
0.059.
CONCLUSION: BPN modestly mediated the reciprocal associations between PSS and

Spectrotemporal Processing Using the Spectral-Temporally Modulated Ripple Test 
and Its Relation to Cognition and Hearing Loss in Adults.

Papazian MR(1), Berg KA(2), DeFreese AJ(3), Tamati TN(4), Moberly AC(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Otolaryngology-Head & Neck Surgery, Vanderbilt University 
Medical Center, Nashville, TN.
(2)Department of Otolaryngology-Head & Neck Surgery, Washington University in 
St. Louis, Missouri.
(3)Department of Hearing and Speech Sciences, Vanderbilt University Medical 
Center, Nashville, TN.
(4)Department of Speech and Hearing Science, The Ohio State University, 
Columbus.

PURPOSE: The three-alternative forced-choice design of the spectral-temporally 
modulated ripple test (SMRT) may capture both auditory and neurocognitive 
functioning. The relationships between neurocognitive functions and SMRT 
performance remain unexplored in middle-aged and older adults, as does the 
degree to which hearing loss may affect these relationships. This study 
hypothesized that better neurocognitive functions and better hearing would 
predict better SMRT performance and that hearing loss and neurocognitive 
functions would interact in contributing to SMRT performance.
METHOD: Data were collected from 81 adults recruited from a single tertiary care 
medical center with hearing abilities ranging from normal hearing to profound 
hearing loss. Relationships were examined among SMRT performance; unaided 
pure-tone average (PTA) at 500, 1000, and 2000 Hz; age; nonverbal reasoning 
(Raven's Progressive Matrices [Raven's]); and short-term memory capacity (visual 
forward digit span).
RESULTS: Bivariate analyses revealed that PTA, digit span, and Raven's scores 
were significantly associated with SMRT performance, whereas age was not.

significant predictors; age again was not. Interaction terms of PTA × Digit Span 
and PTA × Raven's were not significant predictors of SMRT performance.

ongoing use of SMRT in middle-aged and older adults with hearing loss, although 
the independent effects of neurocognitive functions should be accounted for, or 
at least considered, when interpreting SMRT performance.

Searching for the Pattern: Understanding, Assessing, and Transforming Social 
Settings.

Seidman E(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Applied Psychology, New York University.

A historical analysis of systems theory ideas from the biological and physical 
sciences reveals their infusion into sociology and action-oriented subfields of 
psychology, including social, organizational, developmental, and community 
psychology. Constructs and processes are identified that are useful for creating 
a framework to understand, assess, and transform social settings. The central 
theoretical concept that surfaces is the emergent pattern of dynamic 
transactions that communicates critical information and meaning, referred to as 
"social regularity." This is followed by an examination of the varying 
definitions and frameworks of proximal social settings (e.g., classrooms, 
community-based organizations, workplaces) in which individuals derive the bulk 
of their experiences in forming their character, identity, learning, and 
well-being. Social regularity is at the core of an evolving social-setting model 
that communicates meaning through several channels-control and power, modes of 
expressing communication, and the flow of information-that result in 
corresponding distributional equity outcomes. From these communication channels, 
an action model for transforming social settings to create more equitable 
aggregate-level individual outcomes and improved setting outcomes is explicated. 
Corresponding methods of measurement are described. Various strategies and 
tactics are suggested to directly target social regularities. Relational-, 
norm-, and structural-focused examples are provided.

Measuring the spread of trust and distrust through influence in human-autonomy 
teams.

Zahmat Doost E(1), Gorman JC(1), Scalia MJ(1), Zhou S(1), Yin X(1), Hao R(1), 
McNeese NJ(2), Duan W(2), Freeman G(2), Funke GJ(3), Tolston MT(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Human System Engineering, Arizona State University, Mesa, AZ, 
USA.
(2)College of Engineering, Computing and Applied Sciences, Clemson University, 
Clemson, SC, USA.
(3)Air Force Research Lab, Dayton, OH, USA.

Trust in human-autonomy teams is dynamic and shaped by ongoing interaction, yet 
most measures rely on retrospective self-report, limiting detection of how trust 
and distrust propagate in real time. This study introduces and validates 
influence-an interaction-based metric computed as the average mutual information 
between joint and team-state time series-to track the spread of trust and 
distrust. Forty-five participants completed five simulated Remotely Piloted 
Aircraft System missions in three-member teams, with trust manipulated through 
communicative and behavioural spreading across congruent, mismatched, and 
human-versus-agent conditions. Influence predicted subjective team trust and 
objective performance during active spreading but not in a no-spreading control 
and showed strong reliability and construct validity. As validation checks, 
influence recovered known effects: credibility violations damaged trust most, 
and human sources outweighed agents. Critically, the influence-trust 
relationship reversed direction across contexts, revealing a context-dependent 
mechanism. Influence thus offers a real-time, unobtrusive measure linking 
interaction structure to team outcomes.

Plain Language Summary: This study examined whether trust and distrust in 
human–autonomy teams can be tracked in real time through interaction patterns 
instead of surveys alone. In a simulated RPAS task, an influence metric 
predicted team trust and performance during active trust/distrust spreading, 
especially when behaviour contradicted trust-related communication.

The m (6)A reader HNRNPC drives osteosarcoma metastasis and cisplatin resistance 
by stabilizing MTDH to coordinately regulate EMT and ferroptosis.

Zhang L(1), Zhou Y(2), Yan S(1), Zhang X(1), Xu T(1), Wang X(1), Zhang X(1), An 
W(3), Xing Y(1), Song Y(4).

Author information:
(1)The Fourth Department of Medical Oncology, Harbin Medical University Cancer 
Hospital, Harbin 150081, China.
(2)Departments of Critical Care Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital of 
Harbin Medical University, Harbin 150086, China.
(3)Institute of Cancer Prevention and Treatment, Harbin Medical University, 
Harbin 150081, China.
(4)Department of Orthopedics, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical 
University, Harbin 150001, China.

Osteosarcoma (OS) is a highly aggressive bone malignancy associated with a 
pronounced propensity for metastasis and the frequent development of therapeutic 
resistance. The epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) program is a 
well-established driver of metastasis, and dysregulation of ferroptosis 
contributes to chemotherapy resistance. In this study, a prognostic signature 
comprising four genes associated with EMT and ferroptosis is constructed. 
Notably, among the four signature genes, metadherin ( MTDH) is a robust, 
independent biomarker for predicting overall survival. Knockdown of MTDH 
significantly suppresses the EMT program and markedly impairs cell migration and 
invasion. Moreover, depletion of MTDH sensitizes OS cells to cisplatin and 
increases cellular ferroptosis levels. Interestingly, bioinformatic screening 
using online databases reveals that HNRNPC is a potential m 6A reader involved 
in the regulation of MTDH mRNA. This finding is experimentally validated by 
demonstrating that knockdown of HNRNPC significantly reduces both the mRNA and 
protein levels of MTDH. Furthermore, RIP assay results confirm a direct 
interaction between MTDH mRNA and HNRNPC protein. Mechanistically, 
downregulation of HNRNPC impairs the stability of MTDH mRNA. Silencing HNRNPC

Polycrystalline Er0.75Y0.25Fe1-xCoxO3 (x = 0.05, 0.15, 0.3, and 0.5) perovskites 
were synthesized via the solid-state reaction method, and their structural, 
magnetic, optical and photoelectrochemical properties were investigated.

perovskite phase (Pbnm) for all compositions. Magnetic studies demonstrated weak 
ferromagnetism governed by the interplay of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) and 
superexchange interactions. Spin reorientation transitions TSR exhibited as 
broad temperature intervals moved to higher temperatures relative to pure 
ErFeO3, ranging from 104-174 K (x = 0.05), 125-178 K (x = 0.15), 228-340 K (x =

Co3+/Co4+ states along with oxygen non-stoichiometry, consistent with Mössbauer 
evidence of weakened Fe-O-Fe exchange interactions. Mott-Schottky measurements 
indicated a decrease in valence band potential (from 3.51 to 3.07 eV) along with 
a transition from p-n to p-type semiconducting behaviour. These results 
highlight a tunable system with coupled spin, structural, and electronic 
functionalities, making it a promising candidate for spintronic and
