A rapid point-of-care detection system for OVA-specific IgG and IgE utilizing a 
rotational SlipChip.

Lu H(1), Jia Y(1), Wang J(1), Song Z(1), Wu D(1), Wang B(1), Zhang W(2), Yang 
F(1).

Author information:
(1)Key Laboratory for Molecular Enzymology and Engineering of Ministry of 
Education, School of Life Sciences, Jilin University, Changchun 130012, China. 
fangyang@jlu.edu.cn.
(2)Department of Pathology, The First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, 
130021, China. zhangwenxin@jlu.edu.cn.

Allergic diseases affect approximately 22% of the global population. Rapid and 
accurate identification of causative allergens is essential for enabling timely 
clinical intervention and preventing re-exposure. Current clinical approaches 
for in vivo allergen diagnosis often involve risks associated with direct 
allergen exposure, while many existing in vitro diagnostic methods remain 
labor-intensive, time-consuming, and technically demanding. For example, the 
basophil activation test requires sophisticated instrumentation and specialized 
operational expertise. Therefore, there is an urgent need for a convenient, 
rapid, sensitive, and easily assembled platform for reliable in vitro allergen 
diagnosis while reducing reliance on sample pretreatment, auxiliary 
instrumentation, and external control systems. In this study, a disc-shaped 
microfluidic device, termed the relative rotation SlipChip (rr-SlipChip), was 
developed. Unlike conventional SlipChip platforms that depend on precise 
microstructural alignment, the rr-SlipChip employs radial alignment and 
step-by-step rotation to enable convenient configuration of loading pathways for 
multiple immunoreagents. In addition, the reagent pathways are completely 
isolated from one another, thereby minimizing the risk of cross-contamination. 
Using a single rotary pneumatic control channel combined with a simple sliding 
operation, the proposed device enables immunoassays to be completed within 
approximately 25-37 min. The rr-SlipChip achieves favorable analytical 
sensitivity, with limits of detection of 0.614 ng mL-1 for sIgG and 0.689 ng 
mL-1 for sIgE. Therefore, the rr-SlipChip introduces a new rotational sliding 
microfluidic architecture distinct from conventional SlipChip designs, providing 
a novel platform for rapid, sensitive, continuous, and scalable in vitro 
allergen diagnosis with significant potential for point-of-care testing (POCT) 
and accessible precision allergy management.

Improving the design of AAC displays: preliminary study of the effects of

Sowers DJ(1)(2), Brittlebank S(1)(3), Panfil H(1), McAllister O(1), Semmler

Author information:
(1)Department of Communication Sciences and Disorders, The Pennsylvania State

(2)School of Communication Science and Disorders, Florida State University,

(3)Department of Speech and Hearing Science, University of Illinois

(4)Department of Communication Sciences and Disorders, Adelphi University,

This study investigates the effects of targeted motion (i.e., smooth movement of 
a selected AAC symbol from its location to the center of the display) and 
decluttering of the AAC display on visual fixation duration and accuracy of 
symbol identification by participants with Down syndrome across three sessions. 
In each session, participants were first asked to find a target symbol in a grid 
display with and without targeted motion of selected symbols; data on their 
visual fixation duration were collected using the Tobii Spectrum Pro. Then they 
were asked to identify target picture symbols from a unique grid in response to 
the spoken name of the symbol. Visual fixation duration to target symbols was 
significantly greater in the condition with targeted motion and decluttering of 
the display compared to the static display condition across all three sessions. 
It was difficult for many participants to identify symbols accurately in both of 
the display conditions; participants demonstrated continued improvements across 
the three sessions with targeted motion displays while their performance seemed 
to plateau with the static displays that mimic those used in current practice. 
Targeted motion may be a powerful tool to increase visual attention to key 
aspects of AAC displays, but further investigation is required to fully 
understand how to harness motion to support learning and use of AAC displays.

The emergence and rapid spread of multidrug resistance in Plasmodium parasites, 
particularly in the Greater Mekong region and increasingly in Sub-Saharan 
Africa. Resistance has led to an urgent need to develop novel anti-malaria 
therapies with an effective mechanism. Several non-classical targets, including 
Na++ pump PfATP4 (Plasmodium falciparum ATPase 4), PI4K (Phosphatidylinositol 
4-kinase) and PfNCR1(Plasmodium falciparum Niemann-Pick Type C1-Related

counterparts. Combating drug-resistant malaria parasites and strengthening the 
global antimalarial drug pipeline for long-term disease control can be achieved 
by developing new ways to target parasites. This comprehensive review discusses 
the current status of novel antimalarial drug targets, recent discoveries and 
future of novel therapies in the following innovation areas: Protein synthesis

therapeutic targets, Kinase targets, Organelles and cell targets, and 
mitochondrial targets, which fill critical gaps in the existing therapeutic 
arsenal.

PURPOSE: Community-acquired Clostridioides difficile infection (CA-CDI) is 
increasingly recognized outside healthcare settings, yet the contribution of 
dental antibiotic prescribing remains poorly characterized. This study compared 
patients with CA-CDI following antibiotics prescribed by dental practitioners 
versus family physicians.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study at the University Hospital 
for Infectious Diseases "Dr. Fran Mihaljević", Zagreb, Croatia, including adults 
with a first episode of confirmed CA-CDI following outpatient antibiotic 
exposure between 2011 and 2019. Characteristics were compared by prescriber.
RESULTS: Among 666 patients with CA-CDI, 190 (28.5%) had received antibiotics 
from dental practitioners and 476 (71.5%) from family physicians. 
Dental-associated CA-CDI increased significantly over time (13.1% in 2011 to 
31.1% in 2019; p = 0.003). Dental patients had a lower comorbidity burden, with 
less frequent diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and proton pump 
inhibitor use. Amoxicillin-clavulanate was the most frequently prescribed 
antibiotic overall; clindamycin was more common among dental patients (39.9% vs. 
11.9%), 79.7% of whom had no penicillin allergy. Severity and treatment duration 
were similar between groups.
CONCLUSION: Dental antibiotic prescribing emerged as an increasingly important 
contributor to CA-CDI, associated with higher clindamycin use despite a lower 
burden of traditional risk factors, highlighting the need to strengthen 
antimicrobial stewardship in dental practice.

INTRODUCTION: Renal involvement is increasingly recognized in Systemic Sclerosis 
(SSc) and Sjögren's Disease (SjD). However, the association between hypertension 
and renal function decline in these conditions remains poorly understood.
AIM: to compare renal function changes over time in patients with SSc and SjD; 
identify factors associated with clinically relevant renal function decline; and 
to evaluate whether the association between hypertension and renal function 
differs between the two diseases.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed patients with SSc and SjD, followed for up 
to 3 years. Renal function was assessed using estimated glomerular filtration

analyses, hypertension was significantly associated with renal decline in SSc 
but not in SjD.
CONCLUSIONS: Hypertension was independently associated with renal function 
decline, with a stronger association in SSc than in SjD. These findings warrant 
confirmation in prospective studies. Systemic Sclerosis, Sjögren's disease,

CYP1B1 is a potential target of kaempferol in renal fibrosis: a multi‑omics and 
single‑cell transcriptomics study.

Huang C(1), Shi X(2), Yan Z(3).

Author information:
(1)School of Clinical Medicine, Jiangxi University of Chinese Medicine, 
Nanchang, Jiangxi Province, China.
(2)Zhuang Medicine College, Guangxi University of Chinese Medicine, Nanning, 
Guangxi Province, China.
(3)School of Clinical Medicine, Jiangxi University of Chinese Medicine, 
Nanchang, Jiangxi Province, China. 19950153@jxutcm.edu.cn.

BACKGROUND: Renal fibrosis (RF) is a progressive and irreversible pathological 
process for which effective treatments are limited. This study explores the 
molecular targets and mechanisms through which kaempferol (Kae) ameliorates RF, 
with particular emphasis on cytochrome P450 1B1 (CYP1B1).
METHODS: Using a combination of transcriptomic profiling, weighted gene 
co‑expression network analysis (WGCNA), multi‑algorithm machine learning [least 
absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), support vector 
machine‑recursive feature elimination (SVM‑RFE), and Random Forest], and 
single‑cell transcriptomics, we identified the core targets of Kae intervention 
in RF. shapley additive explanations (SHAP) analysis evaluated gene 
contributions to the predictive model, while cell‑type identification by 
estimating relative subsets of RNA transcripts (CIBERSORT) estimated the immune 
microenvironment. The cell type-specific distribution of core targets was 
further characterized through single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and the 
scTenifoldKnk (a machine learning-based virtual gene knockout tool) algorithm 
simulated the effects of CYP1B1 loss-of-function on fibroblast activation and 
extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. Finally, molecular docking was performed 
to predict the binding conformations of kaempferol with the proteins encoded by 
the six prioritized genes.
RESULTS: Six core genes (VCAM1, NFKBIA, SFN, CCL5, CYP1B1, and AXL) were 
identified from 25 Kae-RF-related genes, with CYP1B1 as an upstream regulatory 
hub. Immune infiltration analysis revealed increased plasma cells and 
eosinophils, alongside decreased M0/M1 macrophages and activated NK cells. 
Single-cell analysis localized CYP1B1 to smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts, 
with significant upregulation during late-stage fibroblast-to-myofibroblast 
differentiation. Virtual knockdown of CYP1B1 upregulated 46 genes associated 
with fibrosis-related biological processes, including cell adhesion, G 
protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling, ion transport, and cytoskeletal 
remodeling. The six-gene diagnostic model achieved area under the curves (AUCs) 
of 0.889 (training) and 0.759 (external validation). Molecular docking showed 
favorable Kae-CYP1B1 binding (- 6.5 kcal/mol).
CONCLUSION: CYP1B1 may serve as a potential functional target of Kae in RF, 
likely through modulation of fibroblast activation and ECM remodeling. These 
findings are hypothesis‑generating and provide a computational basis for future 
experimental validation of CYP1B1‑targeted strategies in RF.

Cinchonidine (CD), a metabolite derived from gut microbiota, shows promise in 
protecting against traumatic brain injury (TBI), where mitochondrial dysfunction 
is a key driver of secondary damage. Using a mouse model of controlled cortical 
impact (CCI) and an in vitro primary neuron injury model, CD administration 
resulted in improved physiological status (weight recovery, stabilized heart 
rate) and behavioral outcomes (increased travel distance and speed) in TBI mice. 
Histological analysis showed reduced hippocampal neuronal damage, decreased 
pro-inflammatory cytokines (interleukin‑1β, interleukin‑6, and tumor necrosis 
factor‑α), and upregulated blood-brain barrier tight-junction proteins 
(Claudin-5, Occludin, zonula occludens‑1). Mitochondrial function was improved, 
evidenced by increased mitochondrial DNA copy number, elevated expression of 
translocase of outer mitochondrial membrane 20 and cytochrome c oxidase subunit 
IV, and restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential. In addition, CD 
attenuated TBI-induced changes in mitochondrial dynamics and biogenesis, 
restoring the phosphorylated dynamin-related protein 1 (p-DRP1)/DRP1 ratio and 
the expression of mitofusin 1/2 (MFN-1/2) and peroxisome proliferator-activated 
receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), while reducing mitochondrial DRP1. 
Network pharmacology identified proto‑oncogene tyrosine‑protein kinase Src (SRC) 
as a key target, validated by stable binding in molecular docking and drug 
affinity responsive target stability assays. Furthermore, cellular thermal shift 
assays demonstrated a direct interaction between CD and SRC. CD treatment 
suppressed the activation of the SRC/RAF proto-oncogene serine/threonine-protein 
kinase (RAF1)/nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling axis, as evidenced by 
reduced phosphorylation of SRC and p65, along with decreased expression of RAF1 
and cleaved Caspase-3. Crucially, SRC knockdown mimicked CD's protection, while 
SRC overexpression abolished its benefits. These findings suggest that CD 
ameliorates post-TBI mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and neuronal 
damage by inhibiting SRC kinase activity and its downstream RAF1/NF-κB signaling 
pathway. Thus, CD may represent a promising SRC-targeted neuroprotective 
strategy for TBI.

Itaconic acid is an immunometabolite that regulates macrophage polarization 
within the tumor microenvironment and influences tumor progression and invasion. 
Although its anti-cancer and tumor-promoting effects remain controversial, its 
role in modulating macrophage-derived exosomes and their impact on breast cancer 
cells is not well understood. This study investigated the effects of exosomes 
derived from dimethyl itaconate (DMI)-treated macrophages on 
epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), apoptosis, migration, and EMT-related 
miRNAs in MCF7 breast cancer cells. U937 macrophages were treated with 250 µM 
DMI for 48 h. Exosomes (DMI-EXO) were subsequently isolated, characterized, and 
used to treat MCF7 cells. The expression of EMT-related proteins (E-cadherin, 
N-cadherin, ZEB1/2, Slug, and Vimentin) and EMT-associated miRNAs (miR200C-5p, 
miR30C-5p, miR-638, and miR-137) was evaluated by Western blotting and 
quantitative real-time PCR, respectively. Apoptosis, cell migration, and 
invasion were assessed using Annexin V/PI staining, the scratch wound-healing 
assay, and the Transwell invasion assay, respectively. DMI-EXO treatment 
significantly increased the expression of the mesenchymal markers N-cadherin, 
ZEB1/2, Slug, and Vimentin while reducing the epithelial marker E-cadherin. In 
addition, the expression of EMT-suppressive miRNAs, including miR200C-5p and 
miR30C-5p, was significantly decreased, whereas no significant change was 
observed in miR-137 expression following DMI-EXO treatment. DMI-EXO treatment 
did not significantly alter apoptosis in MCF-7 cells but enhanced cell migration 
and invasion, as demonstrated by accelerated wound closure in the scratch assay 
and increased invaded area in the Transwell invasion assay. These findings 
indicate that DMI-induced macrophage-derived exosomes promote EMT and migration 
in breast cancer cells by modulating EMT-related proteins and miRNAs. This study 
provides new evidence that itaconic acid may facilitate breast tumor progression 
through exosome-mediated communication between macrophages and cancer cells.

BACKGROUND: The mitochondrial phosphate carrier (PiC) is a key protein in 
maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis, and its dysfunction is closely associated 
with cell fate determination. Recent studies suggest that PiC may regulate 
mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP) opening. However, its precise 
role during radiotherapy and the mechanisms by which it regulates cell death 
remain elusive.
METHODS AND RESULTS: Focusing on the clinical challenge of radioresistance in 
glioma, this study reveals for the first time that radiation specifically 
suppresses PiC expression, thereby inducing mitochondrial energy metabolism 
failure, collapse of membrane potential, dysregulation of mtDNA replication, and 
significantly promoting sustained MPTP opening. Further mechanistic 
investigations demonstrated that this cascade of mitochondrial damage activates 
the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway involving Bax/Bcl-2, cytochrome c, and 
caspase-3, ultimately driving apoptosis in glioma cells. Consistently, 
concordant alterations in apoptotic markers were observed in murine tumor 
models, further validating these findings in vivo.
CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies PiC as a critical regulator of the 
radiotherapy response in glioma, demonstrating for the first time that 
radiation-induced PiC suppression drives apoptosis via mitochondrial dysfunction 
and MPTP opening. Targeting the PiC-MPTP axis represents a novel potential 
strategy for overcoming radioresistance and enhancing radiosensitivity in 
glioma.

Deoxynivalenol (DON) is a prevalent trichothecene mycotoxin that threatens 
intestinal health, yet its effects on gut microbiota remain poorly understood. 
Here, Lactobacillus amylovorus isolated from Ningxiang pigs showed strong acid 
and bile tolerance but significantly impaired growth under DON exposure. 
Transcriptomic analysis revealed that DON disrupted amino acid metabolism in L. 
amylovorus, particularly glutamate metabolism. Among the amino acids tested, 
only glutamate supplementation restored bacterial growth under DON exposure. 
Futhermore, co-supplementation with glutamate and L. amylovorus alleviated 
DON-induced intestinal injury by improving intestinal barrier integrity and 
serum amino acid homeostasis in mice. Intestinal transcriptomics showed that 
differentially expressed genes were mainly enriched in the nuclear factor-κB 
(NF-κB) signaling pathway. Co-supplementation modulated NF-κB signaling, 
restored glutamate metabolism, reduced IL-1β and IL-6 levels, and increased 
Bcl2, Btk, and Cd40 expression. Correlation and protein-protein interaction 
analyses further suggested a potential association between B-cell lymphoma 2 
(BCL2) and glutamic-pyruvic transaminase 2 (GPT2), a key enzyme in glutamate 
metabolism. Overall, glutamate cooperates with L. amylovorus to alleviate 
DON-induced intestinal injury, potentially through coordinated regulation of 
glutamate metabolism and NF-κB signaling.

Magnus V(1)(2), Schäfer S(1)(2), Tyyger M(3), Iyizoba-Ebozue Z(4)(5), Unger

(2)Comprehensive Cancer Center Central Germany, Partner Site Leipzig, Leipzig,

(3)Medical Physics and Engineering, Leeds Cancer Centre, Leeds, UK.
(4)Leeds Institute of Medical Research, University of Leeds, Leeds, UK.
(5)Department of Clinical Oncology, Leeds Cancer Centre, Leeds, UK.
(6)Department of Medical Psychology and Medical Sociology, University Medical

(7)Department of Radiation Oncology, University Medical Center Leipzig, Leipzig,

(8)Comprehensive Cancer Center Central Germany, Partner Site Leipzig, Leipzig,

PURPOSE: To determine the prevalence of fatigue in head and neck cancer 
survivors and identify associated factors, including potential associations with 
radiation dose to cerebral organs at risk (OAR).
METHODS: This cross-sectional observational study included survivors treated 
with curative radiotherapy between 2005 and 2023 at a tertiary cancer center. 
Fatigue and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) were assessed with the EORTC 
QLQ-C30. Dosimetric analyses evaluated associations between fatigue and 
radiation dose to intracranial OAR (brainstem, cerebellum, posterior fossa, 
medulla, pituitary gland, basal ganglia, hippocampus), including voxel-based 
analysis (VBA).
RESULTS: One hundred fifty-eight patients were included. The most common tumor 
site was the oropharynx (38.6%). Median time from radiotherapy completion to 
study participation was 41 (IQR, 22-61) months. The mean fatigue score was 44.7 
(SD, 28.0), exceeding the fatigue levels in the age- and sex-adjusted German 
general population (29.7); 51.3% of patients showed clinically relevant fatigue 
(≥ 39 points). Fatigue was inversely associated with HRQoL (ρ = - 0.59, 
p < 0.001), and positively with distress (ρ = 0.54, p < 0.001) and fear of 
cancer recurrence (ρ = 0.41, p < 0.001). Higher fatigue was found in patients 
with impaired performance status and in those with laryngeal and hypopharyngeal 
cancers. Neither cerebral OAR radiation doses nor skeletal muscle mass index was 
associated with fatigue, and VBA revealed no relevant subregions.
CONCLUSIONS: Clinically relevant fatigue affects about half of head and neck 
cancer survivors.
IMPLICATIONS FOR CANCER SURVIVORS: The absence of a correlation with cerebral 
OAR doses suggests that other, probably multifactorial somatic, psychological 
and lifestyle-related factors play a more central role in the genesis of fatigue 
than the radiation-related brain exposures investigated.

Although papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) usually follows an indolent course, 
lymph node metastasis and locally advanced disease remain clinically important 
challenges. This study evaluated interleukin-1 receptor accessory protein 
(IL1RAP) in PTC using pan-cancer datasets, TCGA/GEO thyroid cancer cohorts, and

Dynamic risk assessment by landmark modeling of the restricted residual mean 
survival time.

Zhang Y(1), Schaubel DE(2).

Author information:
(1)Division of Biostatistics, Department of Preventive Medicine, University of 
Tennessee Health Science Center, Memphis, TN, USA.
(2)Department of Biostatistics, Epidemiology and Informatics, University of 
Pennsylvania, Perelman School of Medicine, Philadelphia, PA, USA. 
douglas.schaubel@pennmedicine.upenn.edu.

Dynamic risk assessment is an important tool for healthcare providers to inform 
treatment selection and optimize patient outcomes. Frequent evaluation of 
clinical status provides invaluable information on adverse event risk and/or 
treatment urgency, based on the changes in predictive biomarkers. Landmark 
analysis is a useful approach for dynamic risk assessment that obviates the 
complexity of jointly modeling longitudinal covariates and time-to-event 
outcome. Traditional landmark methods often rely on the proportional hazards 
assumption and assume independent censoring. We propose novel methods to broaden 
the scope of landmark analysis by directly modeling the restricted residual mean 
survival time (RRMST) at each landmark date while accommodating dependent 
censoring. Advantages of RMST models include removing the assumption that the 
(hazard) model is correct at every time point; RMST models instead consider a 
single capped survival time. Moreover, investigators may prefer the area under 
the survival curve to the hazard function as a metric in terms of 
interpretability. We derive the asymptotic properties of our proposed estimators 
and validate their performance in finite samples through extensive simulations. 
We apply the proposed methods to analyze outcomes under natural end-stage liver 
disease (ESLD) history (i.e., in the absence of liver transplantation).

Gohar M(1), Mumtaz A(2), Asim U(3), Shahzadi K(4), Majeed S(2), Ismail M(5),

Author information:

(4)Department of Chemistry, University of Southern Punjab, Multan, 60750,

(5)Energy Lab, Green Technologies and Advanced Matter (GREAT) Research Group,

Green synthesis provides an alternative to traditional chemical processes of 
nanomaterials preparation, which is cost-effective and environmentally benign. 
This paper has demonstrated synthesis of bismuth oxide nanoparticles (Bi2O3 NPs) 
using Cuminum cyminum seed extract as a natural reducing and stabilizing agent 
of bismuth nitrate precursor. The formation of nanoparticles was first signaled 
by a change of color of reaction mixture to be visible and subsequent analysis 
by physicochemical characterization. The UV-Visible spectroscopy displayed 
absorbance at 300 nm, and FTIR gave results that showed Bi-O-related absorption 
and phytochemical functional groups, which indicated the formation of bismuth 
oxide nanoparticles stabilized by plant-derived biomolecules. The crystalline 
character of the nanoparticles produced was verified by X-ray diffraction 
analysis with estimated crystallite size of approximately 136.9 nm. SEM analysis 
revealed irregular and strongly agglomerated structures. Image analysis of 
clearly distinguishable agglomerates indicated apparent dimensions of 
approximately 0.20-2.00 μm, with highest frequency in the 0.60-0.80 μm interval; 
however, individual primary particles could not be resolved reliably. The Bi₂O3 
nanoparticles biosynthesized had antimicrobial and antifungal effects against 
Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, Candida albicans, and Aspergillus niger 
with Candida albicans being the most sensitive. Furthermore, cytotoxicity 
studies revealed that HeLa and MCF-7 cell proliferation were greatly inhibited 
by synthesized nanoparticles, which indicates the possibility of biomedical 
applications of the synthesized nanoparticles. All in all, this work shows an 
easy and environmentally friendly path to green synthesis of Bi2O3 nanoparticles 
using Cuminum cyminum seed extract and reflects on their potential to have 
antimicrobial and cytotoxic capabilities.

Twelve-month tracking of metabolomic changes in ex vivo bloodstains: the 
analytical validity window of bloodstain metabolites.

Lee YR(1), Kwon S(2), Lee J(3)(4), Kang HG(5)(6)(7).

Author information:
(1)Department of Biomedical Laboratory Science, College of Health Science, Eulji 
University, Uijeongbu, 11759, Republic of Korea.
(2)Department of Biomedical Laboratory Science, Graduate School, Eulji 
University, Uijeongbu, 11759, Republic of Korea.
(3)Department of Biomedical Laboratory Science, College of Health Science, Eulji 
University, Uijeongbu, 11759, Republic of Korea. leejiyeong@eulji.ac.kr.
(4)Department of Biomedical Laboratory Science, Graduate School, Eulji 
University, Uijeongbu, 11759, Republic of Korea. leejiyeong@eulji.ac.kr.
(5)Department of Biomedical Laboratory Science, College of Health Science, Eulji 
University, Uijeongbu, 11759, Republic of Korea. kanghg@eulji.ac.kr.
(6)Department of Biomedical Laboratory Science, Graduate School, Eulji 
University, Uijeongbu, 11759, Republic of Korea. kanghg@eulji.ac.kr.
(7)Department of Biomedical Laboratory Science, College of Health Sciences, 
Eulji University, Seongnam, 13135, Republic of Korea. kanghg@eulji.ac.kr.

A comprehensive understanding of chemical changes in blood and bloodstains 
exposed to ex vivo environments remain limited. In this study, we evaluated the 
analytical validity window of metabolite analysis in ex vivo bloodstains by 
tracking chemical changes over 12 months. Bloodstains from a discovery set of 14 
participants were analyzed at monthly intervals from Month 0 to Month 12 using 
LC-MS/MS nontargeted analysis. A total of 2,210 molecular features (MFs) were 
filtered, of which 270 MFs persisted continuously throughout the 12-month 
period. Principal component analysis, hierarchical clustering, and correlation 
analysis showed that the most pronounced changes to MF-levels occurred within 
the first two months, with the majority of baseline-derived MFs disappearing 
between Month 0 and Month 2. Five identified metabolites (choline, 5'-AMP, 
pyroglutamic acid, aspartic acid, and ornithine) were then quantified by 
targeted analysis in an independent validation set of 40 participants, with 
concentrations expressed as median [IQR]. Choline increased significantly from 
Month 0 and remained elevated throughout the 12 months, supporting its potential 
utility as a candidate long-term marker for distinguishing fresh blood from aged 
bloodstains. 5'-AMP changed significantly only within the first four months; the 
remaining three metabolites showed only minor fluctuations with no significant 
pairwise differences. These findings indicate that MF-level changes primarily 
reflect loss of baseline-derived MFs and were most pronounced within the initial 
two months. Individual targeted metabolites follow distinct trajectories and 
more gradual, irregular changes continue thereafter. This study provides 
foundational insights for the application of metabolomics to forensic bloodstain 
analysis.

MicroRNAs and polymorphisms influencing MICA immune modulation.

Nicoletti MB(1), Ferraz IM(1)(2), Moço AC(1)(2), da Cruz Castelli E(1)(3), 
Castro CFB(4)(5).

Author information:
(1)Medical School, Botucatu Campus, School of Medicine, Molecular Genetics and 
Bioinformatics Laboratory, São Paulo State University (UNESP), Botucatu, State 
of São Paulo, Brazil.
(2)General and Applied Biology Graduate Program, São Paulo State University 
(UNESP), Institute of Biosciences, Botucatu, SP, Brazil.
(3)Pathology Graduate Program, São Paulo State University (UNESP), Institute of 
Biosciences, Botucatu, SP, Brazil.
(4)Medical School, Botucatu Campus, School of Medicine, Molecular Genetics and 
Bioinformatics Laboratory, São Paulo State University (UNESP), Botucatu, State 
of São Paulo, Brazil. camila.f.castro@unesp.br.
(5)Molecular Genetics and Bioinformatics Laboratory, Experimental Research Unity 
UNIPEX - Av. Prof. Mário Rubens Guimarães Montenegro, s/n UNESP , Botucatu, SP, 
18618687, Brazil. camila.f.castro@unesp.br.

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that play a central role in 
post-transcriptional gene regulation. They act mainly by interacting with 
sequences located in the 3' untranslated regions (3'UTRs) of messenger RNAs 
(mRNAs), thereby influencing mRNA stability and translation. Through these 
mechanisms, miRNAs contribute to the fine-tuning of multiple biological 
pathways, including immune activation, inflammatory signaling, and cellular 
stress responses. Among the genes involved in immune surveillance, the major 
histocompatibility complex class I polypeptide-related sequence A (MICA) has 
emerged as an important target for post-transcriptional regulation due to its 
role as a ligand for the activating receptor NKG2D (natural killer cell group 
2-D), which is expressed in natural killer (NK) cells and cytotoxic T 
lymphocytes. MICA is highly polymorphic, and several allelic variants differ in 
sequence composition, structural organization, and expression patterns, 
potentially influencing miRNA-mRNA interactions. Growing evidence suggests that 
miRNA-mediated regulation of MICA contributes to immune modulation in cancer, 
viral infections, and autoimmune disorders, particularly through mechanisms 
associated with immune evasion and altered NKG2D signaling. In addition, genetic 
polymorphisms and structural variations within regulatory regions, especially 
within the 3'UTR, can alter miRNA binding affinity by creating, disrupting, or 
modifying target sites. This mini review discusses the current understanding of 
miRNA-mediated regulation of MICA, emphasizing the impact of allelic diversity 
and regulatory polymorphisms on post-transcriptional control. Furthermore, it 
highlights current knowledge gaps and future perspectives regarding 
allele-specific regulation.

Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), the rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine (DA) synthesis, 
is conserved across most animal phyla. DA regulates motor activity, sensory 
processing motivation, neural homeostasis, and protection against oxidative 
stress. TH and DA have been described in vertebrates and in some invertebrates, 
including arthropods. This study investigated the anatomical location of TH and 
DA and characterized the biochemical and molecular structure of TH in the brain 
of the mangrove crab Ucides cordatus. This species is a useful environmental 
model for neurodegeneration studies, due to its occurrence in metal-contaminated 
mangrove ecosystems, and as prey of other species, including humans. Using 
immunohistochemistry, immunoblotting, and structural modeling, we mapped TH 
presence and distribution in the crustacean brain and analyzed its molecular and 
evolutionary characteristics. Our results revealed a TH fragment structurally 
similar to fragments found in 21 other species and in a complex dopaminergic 
network in U. cordatus, characterized by diverse neuronal morphologies, 
widespread projections, and sensitivity to dopaminergic neurotoxins. These 
findings may support further studies on catecholaminergic neurobiology.

Comparison of the safety and 24-36-month efficacy of medial unicompartmental 
knee arthroplasty versus total knee arthroplasty in elderly patients (≥ 75 
years) with isolated medial-compartment knee osteoarthritis.

Wang S(#)(1), Fu Y(#)(2), Guo Z(1), Zhang J(1), Lin C(1), Wang H(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Orthopaedics, Taicang Loujiang New City Hospital (Ruijin 
Hospital, Taicang), Suzhou, China.
(2)Department of Orthopaedics, Shanghai Key Laboratory for Prevention and 
Treatment of Bone and Joint Diseases, Shanghai Institute of Traumatology and 
Orthopaedics, Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, 
197 Ruijin 2nd Road, Shanghai, 200025, PR China.
(3)Department of Orthopaedics, Shanghai Key Laboratory for Prevention and 
Treatment of Bone and Joint Diseases, Shanghai Institute of Traumatology and 
Orthopaedics, Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, 
197 Ruijin 2nd Road, Shanghai, 200025, PR China. Drwanghongyi@hotmail.com.

The number of very elderly patients presenting with end-stage knee 
osteoarthritis (OA) is rising rapidly, yet the comparative merits of medial 
unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) in 
this group remain insufficiently characterised. We compared the perioperative 
safety and short-term clinical and patient-reported efficacy of the two 
procedures in patients aged 75 years and older with isolated medial-compartment 
OA. This single-centre retrospective cohort study compared patients aged ≥ 75 
years undergoing primary medial UKA or TKA for isolated medial-compartment OA 
between January 2018 and December 2022. Among 268 eligible patients (68 UKA and 
200 TKA), 1:2 nearest-neighbour propensity-score matching, incorporating 
operating surgeon together with demographic, comorbidity, radiographic and 
baseline functional covariates, yielded 60 UKA and 120 TKA patients. 
Perioperative outcomes, KSS, OKS, pain VAS, ROM, postoperative FJS-12, 
complications, readmission, reoperation and satisfaction were compared over 
24-36 months. Standardised mean differences assessed baseline balance; 
treatment-effect estimates, risk differences and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) 
were reported. Matching yielded 180 patients, with all post-match absolute 
SMDs < 0.10 (maximum 0.087). UKA was associated with shorter operative time 
(64.3 vs. 84.2 min), lower estimated blood loss (99.9 vs. 183.6 mL), smaller 
haemoglobin decline (1.5 vs. 2.6 g/dL), shorter stay (3.0 vs. 5.2 days) and 
earlier independent walking (18.3 vs. 29.6 h). Final KSS components were 
similar; UKA showed higher OKS and FJS-12, greater knee flexion and lower pain 
VAS. Complications occurred in 3/60 UKA (5.0%) and 19/120 TKA (15.8%; risk 
difference - 10.8% points, 95% CI - 19.4 to - 2.3; sensitivity-analysis adjusted 
OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.09-0.92). Transfusion was infrequent (1.7% vs. 3.3%); 
readmission and reoperation showed no clear difference. Final satisfaction was 
98.3% versus 86.7% (risk difference + 11.7% points, 95% CI 4.8-18.6). In 
carefully selected patients aged ≥ 75 years with isolated medial-compartment OA, 
medial UKA was associated with lower measured perioperative burden and more 
favourable patient-reported outcomes than TKA over 24-36 months. The observed 
difference in complications should be interpreted cautiously because event 
counts were small and findings were sensitive to the choice of statistical test. 
Retrospective allocation, surgeon and implant heterogeneity, potential residual 
confounding and limited follow-up preclude causal or long-term durability 
conclusions.

Bioethanol is a promising renewable fuel that mitigates dependence on fossil 
resources. As a potential candidate for bioethanol production, the homoacetogen 
Clostridium autoethanogenum is capable of metabolizing diverse carbon 
substrates, such as syngas components (CO and/or CO2/H2) and xylose. Since 
acetate formation is energetically favored over ethanol synthesis in acetogens, 
reassimilation of acetate through the aldehyde:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (AOR) 
pathway offers a feasible approach to enhance ethanol production. To improve AOR 
activity, two endogenous aor genes (CAETHG_0092 and CAETHG_0102) were 
individually overexpressed in C. autoethanogenum under the control of two 
separate constitutive promoters, Pthl and Ppta, generating four engineered 
strains: Ca(pta92), Ca(pta102), Ca(thl92), and Ca(thl102). Fermentation 
performance of the engineered strains was evaluated with xylose as the 
substrate. Compared to the wild-type strain, all engineered strains showed less 
acetate accumulation and higher ethanol yield. Moreover, the highest ethanol 
yield, specific productivity, and ethanol-to-acetate molar ratio were achieved 
in strain Ca(pta102), reaching 3.19-fold, 2.86-fold, and 11-fold of those in the 
wild-type strain, respectively. Engineered strains also exhibited elevated AOR 
activity in crude extracts, ranging from 2.52 to 4.74 times that of the 
wild-type strain. Results demonstrated that overexpressing either of the 
endogenous aor genes shifted product distribution toward ethanol in C. 
autoethanogenum, which provides a promising metabolic engineering strategy to 
boost ethanol biosynthesis.

Small waterways in boreal forests: How artificial waterways influence benthic 
macroinvertebrate communities.

Zivec P(1), Sponseller R(2), Kuglerová L(3), Laudon H(3), Trail A(4), 
Hasselquist EM(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Forest Ecology and Management, Swedish University of 
Agricultural Sciences, Umeå, Sweden. peta.l.zivec@gmail.com.
(2)Department of Ecology and Environmental Science, Umeå University, Umeå, 
Sweden.
(3)Department of Forest Ecology and Management, Swedish University of 
Agricultural Sciences, Umeå, Sweden.
(4)Department of Wildlife, Fish and Environmental Studies, Swedish University of 
Agricultural Sciences, Umeå, Sweden.

Across the boreal biome, extensive ditching and stream modification have created 
widespread networks of artificial waterways. These channels now form a major 
part of Sweden's aquatic landscape but remain poorly studied despite their 
potential ecological role. We surveyed 32 reaches representing natural streams, 
modified waterways, and ditches on peat and till soils to assess how habitat 
conditions and benthic macroinvertebrate communities vary across this gradient 
of naturalness. Natural streams supported higher taxa richness than ditches, 
while overall diversity and abundance were similar across waterway types. Peat 
ditches were distinguished by low pH and high organic substrates, whereas till 
ditches and modified waterways closely resembled natural streams, suggesting 
ecological convergence over time. Similar to studies done in purely natural 
systems, catchment area and pH were key predictors of taxa richness in our 
gradient of naturalness. Our results indicate that modified waterways contain 
similar biodiversity to natural streams and that soil type is more important for 
biodiversity than waterway origin, providing a baseline for conservation and 
restoration planning in managed forest landscapes.

Spinorphin Attenuates Acute Experimental Seizures and Associated Neurochemical 
Alterations: Possible Involvement of Opioid Receptors.

Torun IE(1), Baranoglu Kilinc Y(2), Kilinc E(3), Ankarali S(4).

Author information:
(1)Department of Physiology, Faculty of Medicine, Bolu Abant İzzet Baysal 
University, Bolu, Turkey.
(2)Department of Pediatrics, Gaziosmanpasa SUAM, University of Health Sciences, 
Istanbul, Turkey.
(3)Department of Physiology, Cerrahpasa Faculty of Medicine, İstanbul 
University-Cerrahpaşa, Istanbul, Turkey.
(4)Department of Physiology, Faculty of Medicine, Istanbul Medeniyet University, 
34700, Istanbul, Turkey. seyit.ankarali@medeniyet.edu.tr.

Spinorphin, an endogenous enkephalinase inhibitor, enhances physiological opioid 
signaling by preventing the degradation of endogenous enkephalins, however, its 
anticonvulsant potential has not previously been investigated. This study 
evaluated the effects of spinorphin on seizure activity and associated 
neurochemical alterations in two complementary acute experimental seizure 
models. The effects of spinorphin on seizure activity were investigated in 
pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)- and penicillin-induced acute seizure rat models. 
Behavioral seizure parameters, passive avoidance memory, electrocorticographic 
activity, cortical and hippocampal glutamate, GABA, c-Fos, calcitonin 
gene-related peptide (CGRP), inflammatory cytokines, and oxidative stress 
biomarkers were evaluated. Nalmefene was used to determine the contribution of 
opioid receptor signaling. Spinorphin significantly attenuated behavioral 
seizures, reduced cortical epileptiform spike frequency, and improved passive 
avoidance retention performance. It attenuated PTZ-induced alterations in 
cortical and hippocampal glutamate and GABA concentrations and reduced tissue 
levels of c-Fos and CGRP, together with changes in inflammatory and oxidative 
stress-related biomarkers in both the cortex and hippocampus. These effects were 
substantially attenuated by nalmefene, suggesting a possible contribution of 
endogenous opioid signaling, although the incomplete reversal indicates that 
additional opioid-independent mechanisms may also be involved. Spinorphin 
attenuates seizure activity and associated biochemical alterations in 
experimental seizure models. By enhancing the regional availability of 
endogenous enkephalins rather than directly activating opioid receptors, 
spinorphin may exert its anticonvulsant effects partly through endogenous opioid 
signaling, while additional opioid-independent mechanisms may also contribute. 
These findings provide a basis for further investigation of enkephalinase 
inhibition in experimental seizure models.

Impact of Fixed-Dose Combination Therapies on Cardiovascular Mortality and Major 
Cardiovascular Events.

Chia JE(1)(2), Lee E(3)(4), Iglesias J(5), Ang SP(6)(7).

Author information:
(1)Department of Medicine, Division of Endocrinology, University of Arizona,

(2)Department of Medicine, Texas Tech University Health Science Center, El Paso,

(3)Department of Medicine, Rutgers Health Community Medical Center, Toms River,

(4)Rutgers The State University of New Jersey, New Brunswick, NJ, 08901, USA. 
El989@rutgers.edu.
(5)Department of Medicine, Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine, Nutley, NJ,

(6)Department of Medicine, Division of Cardiology, University of Arizona,

PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Fixed-dose combination therapy (the polypill) was developed 
to reduce treatment complexity and improve adherence to evidence-based 
cardiovascular therapies. This review evaluates contemporary evidence for its 
effects on major cardiovascular events and cardiovascular mortality across 
primary prevention, secondary prevention, and emerging heart failure 
applications, while addressing implementation barriers and remaining evidence 
gaps.
RECENT FINDINGS: Early pharmacodynamic and adherence trials established that 
co-formulation preserves the effects of individual components and improves 
medication adherence. Event-powered trials subsequently demonstrated clinical 
benefit: PolyIran and TIPS-3 reduced major cardiovascular events in 
predominantly primary prevention population, whereas SECURE reduced recurrent 
events after myocardial infarction. Individual-participant and aggregate-data 
meta-analyses showed relative reductions of approximately 20% to 40% in 
composite cardiovascular outcomes and a reduction in cardiovascular mortality, 
with larger benefits among patients with greater adherence and in 
aspirin-containing strategies. POLY-HF extended the approach to heart failure 
with reduced ejection fraction, improving left ventricular ejection fraction and 
uptake of guideline-directed therapy; reductions in heart failure events were 
secondary findings that require confirmation in larger outcome trials. These 
findings supports fixed-dose combination therapy as an effective strategy for 
improving adherence and reducing cardiovascular events, with a cardiovascular 
mortality benefit supported by pooled analyses. Its greatest potential may be in 
high-risk populations and resource-limited settings, where treatment complexity 
impedes implementation. Broader adoption will require formulation 
standardization, sufficient dosing flexibility, longer-term safety data, and 
effective integration into clinical guidelines and health systems.

Adolescent M-CSF Administration Provides Durable Protection Against 
Trauma-Induced PTSD-Like Phenotypes in Male Mice Through Microglia-Dependent 
Mechanisms.

Li F(#)(1), Ye M(#)(2), Tong L(#)(3), Huang C(#)(3), Xu X(#)(4), Peng J(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Pharmacy, Changzhou No. 7 People's Hospital, Changzhou 
Geriatric Hospital Affiliated to Soochow University, Changzhou, 213000, Jiangsu, 
China.
(2)Department of Pharmacy, Kunshan Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine, 
Suzhou, 215300, Jiangsu, China.
(3)Department of Pharmacology, School of Pharmacy, Nantong University, #9 Seyuan 
Road, Nantong, 226019, Jiangsu, China.
(4)Department of Pharmacotherapeutics, School of Pharmacy, Jiangsu Medical 
College, Yancheng, 224005, Jiangsu, China.
(5)Department of Pharmacy, Yancheng No. 1 People's Hospital, Affiliated Hospital 
of Medical School, Nanjing University, #66 Renmin South Road, Yancheng, 224006,

Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a severe psychiatric condition for 
which effective preventive strategies are lacking. Innate immune preconditioning 
has shown promise for the prevention of PTSD, yet the transient nature of such 
protection when induced in adulthood poses a substantial limitation. Using male 
C57BL/6J mice, we tested whether administration of macrophage colony-stimulating 
factor (M-CSF, 100 µg/kg, intraperitoneally) during adolescence, a developmental 
period characterized by heightened microglial plasticity, could establish 
enduring resilience against trauma-induced PTSD-like behaviors. Mice received a 
single M-CSF injection at postnatal day 28 (PND28) and were subsequently 
subjected to single prolonged stress (SPS/FS) at 4, 16, or 32 weeks thereafter, 
with behavioral and molecular assessments conducted at PND70, PND154, and 
PND266, respectively. Our results showed that adolescent M-CSF exposure 
substantially prevented SPS/FS-induced anxiety-like behaviors assessed by the 
elevated plus maze and open field test, and SPS/FS-induced fear-like behaviors 
evaluated by contextual and cued fear conditioning tests, at all three 
post-administration intervals. Concurrently, M-CSF pretreatment prevented 
SPS/FS-induced interleukin-1β (Il-1β), Il-6, and tumor necrosis factor-α (Tnf-α) 
mRNA expression within the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex across all 
time points examined. These protective phenotypes were eliminated when 
microglial function was pharmacologically inhibited or when microglia were 
depleted before M-CSF administration, establishing that microglial integrity at 
the time of adolescent immune challenge is required for the establishment of 
long-term resilience. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that a single 
developmental immune intervention confers lifelong protection against 
SPS/FS-induced PTSD-like behaviors through microglia-dependent mechanisms, 
introducing a vaccine-like paradigm for the prevention of PTSD.

Revisiting Ehrlich carcinoma in the era of precision oncology: bridging 
classical models with modern systems biology.

Manjunath V(1), Nayak RR(1), Bhujanga AK(1), Ramesh AM(1), Santhekadur PK(2).

Author information:
(1)Centre of Excellence in Molecular Biology and Regenerative Medicine, 
Department of Biochemistry, JSS Medical College, JSS Academy of Higher Education 
and Research, Sri Shivarathreeshwara Nagar, Mysore, Karnataka, 570015, India.
(2)Centre of Excellence in Molecular Biology and Regenerative Medicine, 
Department of Biochemistry, JSS Medical College, JSS Academy of Higher Education 
and Research, Sri Shivarathreeshwara Nagar, Mysore, Karnataka, 570015, India. 
prasannakumars@jssuni.edu.in.

Ehrlich carcinoma (EC) and its ascitic form, Ehrlich ascites carcinoma (EAC), 
are among the oldest and most widely used experimental tumor models in cancer 
research. Although they have traditionally been used for anticancer drug 
screening, their potential to address broader aspects of aggressive tumor 
biology has received comparatively less attention. EC/EAC exhibits several 
characteristics associated with advanced malignancy, including rapid tumor 
growth, angiogenesis, immune dysregulation, metabolic changes, therapeutic 
resistance, and complex interactions between the tumor and host. These features 
make EC/EAC a useful complementary model for studying different aspects of tumor 
progression. However, research using these models has largely focused on 
transcriptional changes and individual signalling pathways, while 
post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms remain less explored. In particular, 
the role of the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), a major component of 
microRNA-mediated gene regulation, is still poorly understood in EC/EAC. In this 
review, we discuss the major limitations of current EC/EAC research, including 
the limited use of multi-omics approaches, single-cell and spatial analyses, 
functional genomics, immune checkpoint profiling, and integrated systems-level 
studies. We further discuss how incorporating RISC-centered regulatory networks 
with emerging approaches such as CRISPR-based studies, spatial transcriptomics, 
and metabolic profiling could provide deeper mechanistic insights and improve 
the translational value of these models. Bringing together the strengths of this 
established tumor model with contemporary approaches in cancer biology could 
help reposition EC/EAC as a relevant and versatile platform for studying tumor 
progression and therapeutic responses.

Numerical and neural-network analysis of Casson hybrid nanofluid flow and heat 
transfer in a sinusoidally stenosed artery.

Zeshan M(1), Ali K(2), Ahmad S(1), Gull H(3), Jawad M(4), Al-Mdallal QM(5).

Author information:
(1)Centre for Advanced Studies in Pure and Applied Mathematics, Bahauddin 
Zakariya University, Multan, 60000, Pakistan.
(2)Department of Basic Sciences and Humanities, MNS University of Engineering 
and Technology, Multan, 60000, Pakistan.
(3)Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Southern Punjab, 
Multan, 60000, Pakistan.
(4)Department of Mathematics, Physics and Statistics, The University of 
Faisalabad, Faisalabad, Pakistan.
(5)Department of Mathematical Sciences, United Arab Emirates University, P.O. 
Box 15551, Al Ain, United Arab Emirates. q.almdallal@uaeu.ac.ae.

We investigate unsteady flow and heat transfer in a blood-based Casson hybrid 
nanofluid containing Al2O3 and Fe3O4 nanoparticles as it passes through a rigid 
artery with a mild sinusoidal stenosis. The formulation includes a transverse 
magnetic field, Hall-current effects, viscous dissipation, and Joule heating. 
Under the long-wavelength approximation, the governing equations reduce to local 
radial initial-boundary-value problems. These problems are mapped onto a fixed 
domain and solved with a forward-time central-space (FTCS) scheme that uses a 
separate stencil at the centreline. Particular attention is given to the effects 
of the Casson, magnetic, Hall, Reynolds, Prandtl, and Eckert parameters, as well 
as the two nanoparticle volume fractions, on the velocity, temperature, wall 
shear stress, and local Nusselt number. We interpret the observed trends through 
the balance among viscous resistance, Lorentz damping, radial diffusion, 
internal heating, and the effective properties of the suspension. 
Parameter-specific Levenberg-Marquardt backpropagation neural networks are also 
trained to interpolate the FTCS data. In most of the sampled cases, the network 
follows the numerical profiles closely. However, a small number of negative 
centreline-temperature predictions make clear that a low overall error does not 
always imply physically acceptable behaviour at every point. The neural-network 
results should therefore be viewed as interpolation within the sampled ranges, 
while the physical conclusions remain tied to the assumptions of the idealized 
single-phase arterial model. Clinical trial registration: Not applicable.

Development, implementation and evaluation of a sustainable medication-use 
process in the intensive care unit: a lean-based quality improvement study.

Chen RQ(#)(1), Xie S(#)(1), Frenzel T(2), Percic-van Doorne S(2), van den Bemt 
B(1)(3), Natsch S(1), Bekker C(4).

Author information:
(1)Department of Pharmacy, Pharmacology and Toxicology, Radboud Institute for 
Health Sciences, Radboud University Medical Centre, Nijmegen, The Netherlands.
(2)Department of Intensive Care, Radboud Institute for Health Sciences, Radboud 
University Medical Centre, Nijmegen, The Netherlands.
(3)Department of Pharmacy, Sint Maartenskliniek, Nijmegen, The Netherlands.
(4)Department of Pharmacy, Pharmacology and Toxicology, Radboud Institute for 
Health Sciences, Radboud University Medical Centre, Nijmegen, The Netherlands. 
Charlotte.Bekker@radboudumc.nl.
(#)Contributed equally

BACKGROUND: In the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), substantial quantities of 
medication are wasted, negatively affecting ecological and economic 
sustainability.
AIM: This study aimed to develop, implement, and evaluate an ecologically and 
economically sustainable medication-use process to reduce medication waste in 
the ICU of a Dutch academic hospital.
METHOD: This lean-based quality improvement study comprised three phases: (I) 
Three-week baseline medication waste assessment in terms of quantity (i.e., 
disposed medication units) and economic value per 100 ICU beds per day. (II) 
Development and implementation of a sustainable medication-use process using 
lean principles. Causes of medication waste were identified among hospital staff 
using qualitative methods, and targeted interventions were identified and 
implemented accordingly. (III) Post-implementation effect evaluation of the 
sustainable medication-use process on medication waste.
RESULTS: At baseline, a mean total of 113 units, worth €1037, were wasted daily 
per 100 ICU beds. Causes for medication waste were: insufficient knowledge among 
hospital staff about quantities and impacts of medication waste; suboptimal 
medication ordering, supplying and preparing, resulting in unnecessary 
medication waste; and patient's therapy changes/discontinuation. Interventions 
implemented were: awareness campaigns on medication waste; adjustment of 
protocols and work processes to prevent excess order, supply and preparation of 
medication; and dispensing individually labelled medication to the patient 
following transfer or discharge. Implementing these interventions reduced 
medication waste by 31.8% to 77 units per 100 ICU beds per day, and economic 
losses decreased by 18.4% to €846.
CONCLUSION: Implementation of a sustainable medication-use process targeting 
staff's knowledge and work processes, reduced the extent of wasted medications 
in the ICU and associated costs.

Community pharmacists' views on the factors influencing prescription medication 
side effect counselling: a qualitative interview study.

Evrard P(1), Crowley M(1), Otway T(1), Dalton K(2).

Author information:
(1)Pharmaceutical Care Research Group, School of Pharmacy, University College 
Cork, Pharmacy Building, College Road, Cork, Ireland.
(2)Pharmaceutical Care Research Group, School of Pharmacy, University College 
Cork, Pharmacy Building, College Road, Cork, Ireland. kieran.dalton@ucc.ie.

INTRODUCTION: Community pharmacists play a crucial role in medication 
counselling, which includes side effect counselling (SEC), helping support 
informed decision-making, patients' adherence, and medication safety. Despite 
its recognised importance, deficiencies in SEC provision have been reported, and 
limited research has investigated the behavioural determinants underpinning 
pharmacists' SEC practices.
AIM: This qualitative study aimed to explore community pharmacists' views on the 
factors influencing prescription medication SEC.
METHOD: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with community pharmacists in 
Ireland. Transcripts were analysed using conventional content analysis and 
directed content analysis by using the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF). 
Predominant domains were determined based on the frequency of the beliefs, 
presence of conflicting beliefs, and perceived strengths of those beliefs.
RESULTS: From eleven interviews, six predominant TDF domains were identified in 
influencing SEC provision: environmental context and resources, social 
professional role and identity, memory, attention and decision-making, skills, 
beliefs about consequences, and social influences. While SEC was considered a 
core professional responsibility, time pressures and workload were dominant 
environmental barriers. Pharmacists employ cognitive heuristics to prioritise 
SEC for new and high-risk medications and tailor their language and information 
quantity based on patients' health literacy and emotional state to balance the 
need to inform against the risk of hindering adherence by overwhelming 
patients-skills which they believed they refined with experience.
CONCLUSION: This study provides unique insights into the behavioural 
determinants influencing pharmacist SEC. The findings offer a foundation for 
developing targeted interventions to enhance SEC in community pharmacy, 
ultimately helping to improve patient safety and therapeutic outcomes.

Integrative transcriptomic and network analysis elucidates the multi-target 
molecular mechanisms of carboplatin in melanoma.

Shahriarizade M(1), Ahmadi SM(2), Firouzjaei AA(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Biology, Science and Research Branch, Islamic Azad University, 
Tehran, Iran.
(2)Department of Medical Biotechnology and Nanotechnology, Faculty of Medicine, 
Mashhad University of Medical Sciences, Mashhad, Iran.
(3)Bioinformatics Research Center, Basic Sciences Research Institute, Mashhad 
University of Medical Sciences, Mashhad, Iran. ahmadizadf@yahoo.com.

Melanoma is an aggressive malignancy with high metastatic potential and frequent 
resistance to standard therapies, highlighting the need for robust biomarkers 
and improved mechanistic understanding of effective treatments. This study 
integrates transcriptomic profiling and network-based analyses to identify key 
regulatory genes and clarify how clinically used agents may counteract 
melanoma-specific molecular dysregulation. Comparative evaluation of three 
independent gene expression datasets yielded 194 overlapping differentially 
expressed genes (DEGs) enriched in pathways central to tumor progression. A 
protein-protein interaction network was constructed, and hub genes were 
prioritized using the Maximal Clique Centrality algorithm, revealing critical 
nodes involved in melanoma biology. Drug-gene interaction analysis via DGIdb 
identified carboplatin as a multi-target compound interacting with CDKN1A, 
BRCA1, PTEN, and AKT1. Although carboplatin, often combined with paclitaxel, is 
already utilized clinically for advanced or treatment-refractory melanoma, its 
multi-target molecular effects in relation to melanoma transcriptomic 
alterations remain insufficiently defined. Experimental validation in B16F0 
melanoma cells demonstrated dose- and time-dependent cytotoxicity, with an IC₅₀ 
of approximately 17 µM at 48 h. RT-qPCR analysis showed increased expression of 
CDKN1A, BRCA1, and PTEN, alongside reduced AKT1 expression, indicating 
activation of DNA damage response pathways and reinforcement of 
tumor-suppressive signaling. Overall, this study identifies key molecular 
determinants of melanoma progression and provides mechanistic evidence 
explaining carboplatin's therapeutic activity through modulation of dysregulated 
transcriptomic hubs. The combined computational and experimental framework 
offers a valuable strategy for biomarker discovery and mechanistic evaluation of 
clinically used agents in melanoma research.

A Foundation for Today's Healthcare Chaplaincy in Western Societies: The 
Liminality Model.

Schuhmann C(1), Varner-Perez SE(2), Lasair S(3), Bradford KL(4), Peng-Keller 
S(5), Nuzum D(6), Tuffnell J(7).

Author information:
(1)University of Humanistic Studies, Utrecht, The Netherlands. 
c.schuhmann@uvh.nl.
(2)Indiana University Health, Indianapolis, Indiana, USA.
(3)Canadian Association for Spiritual Care, Newmarket, Canada.
(4)Westmead Hospital, Westmead, Australia.
(5)University of Zurich, Faculty of Theology and the Study of Religion, Zurich, 
Switzerland.
(6)Cork University Hospital, Cork, Ireland.
(7)Department of Theology and Religion, University of Otago, Dunedin, New 
Zealand.

Given changes in the religious landscape and in health care in contemporary 
Western societies, healthcare chaplains are in need of a new shared and 
communicable understanding of their specific position and role in healthcare 
institutions. Developing such an understanding not only calls for more empirical 
studies into healthcare chaplaincy, but also for theoretical models which help 
interpret and integrate empirical findings. This paper describes the 'liminality 
model' of contemporary healthcare chaplaincy, which was developed on the basis 
of structured discussions of an international expert panel. This conceptual 
model characterizes healthcare chaplaincy as a practice of 'engaging with 
liminality'. 'Liminality' here refers both to individuals' liminal experiences 
in relation to health transitions and to liminal moments, spaces, and positions 
in healthcare organizations. At the experiential level, engaging with liminality 
involves offering compassionate presence, and addressing existential concerns of 
patients, family members, and staff. At the organizational level, engaging with 
liminality involves educating healthcare professionals about spirituality and 
spiritual care, supporting medical decision-making, and advocating for 
marginalized voices. The model thus explains how the different roles that 
chaplains fulfill in health care can be understood as different facets of 
engaging with liminality.

Opioid and Gabapentinoid Prescribing in Older Adults with Dementia Before and 
After the 2016 CDC Opioid Prescribing Guideline.

Veschio T(1)(2), McKendrick K(3), Li L(3)(4), Harrison K(5)(6), Hunt LJ(6), 
Muench U(6)(7), Smith CB(8), Aldridge M(3)(9), Sean Morrison R(10)(11), Rodin 
R(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Medical Education, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New 
York, NY, USA.
(2)The University of Arizona College of Medicine, Tucson, AZ, USA.
(3)Brookdale Department of Geriatrics and Palliative Medicine, Icahn School of 
Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, USA.
(4)Department of Population Health Science and Policy, Icahn School of Medicine 
at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, USA.
(5)Division of Geriatrics, Department of Medicine, University of California, San 
Francisco, USA.
(6)Philip R. Lee Institute for Health Policy Studies, University of California, 
San Francisco, USA.
(7)Department of Social and Behavioral Sciences, School of Nursing, University 
of California, San Francisco, USA.
(8)Department of Medicine, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY, 
USA.
(9)James J. Peters Department of Veterans Affairs Medical Center, Bronx, NY, 
USA.
(10)Brookdale Department of Geriatrics and Palliative Medicine, Icahn School of 
Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, USA. sean.morrison@mssm.edu.
(11)James J. Peters Department of Veterans Affairs Medical Center, Bronx, NY, 
USA. sean.morrison@mssm.edu.

BACKGROUND: In March 2016, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) 
issued guidelines advising against opioid use for most chronic pain because of 
their associated risks. Evaluating how this guideline affected subsequent opioid 
and non-opioid analgesic prescribing in older adults with dementia is critical, 
as this population is at heightened risk for both pain undertreatment and 
adverse medication effects.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether the 2016 CDC opioid prescribing guideline was 
associated with changes in opioid and gabapentinoid prescribing in older adults 
with dementia.
DESIGN: Interrupted time series analysis of a longitudinal cohort from 2010 to 
2022.
PARTICIPANTS: Community-dwelling older adults (≥ 65 years) with dementia 
enrolled in the Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS), a nationally 
representative survey linked to Medicare claims.
MAIN MEASURES: Quarterly prescribing rates of opioids (typical opioids, 
tramadol, buprenorphine) and gabapentinoids (gabapentin, pregabalin) before and 
after CDC guideline release. Interrupted time series models estimated level 
(immediate) and trend (slope) changes associated with the guideline.
KEY RESULTS: We identified 3246 older adults with dementia (median age [IQR] 
80.7 [73.8-86.2] years; 61.4% female). Typical opioid prescribing declined by 
26.5% over the study period, but the guideline was not associated with this 
decline (trend change: 0.09 [95% CI -0.1, 0.3] percentage points [ppts]/quarter; 
level change -1.5 [95% CI -4.1, 1.0] ppt). The guideline was associated with the 
27.1% decrease in tramadol prescribing (trend change: -0.2 ppts/quarter [95% CI, 
-0.3, -0.1]; level change: -1.8 [95% CI, -3.1, -0.6] ppts). Gabapentinoid 
prescribing increased from 9.5% to 11.5%, with no change in trend (0.0 
ppts/quarter [95% CI, -0.01 to 0.02]) after the guideline release. Buprenorphine 
prescribing remained near zero.
CONCLUSIONS: We identified analgesic selection shifts rather than uniform opioid 
reductions following the CDC guideline release, but the impact of these shifts 
on symptom control remains unknown. More nuanced, evidence-based analgesic 
prescribing guidance is needed for older adults with dementia.

OBJECTIVES: To investigate the performance of 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT for diagnosing 
tumor thrombus (TT) and predicting response to pembrolizumab and axitinib in 
renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with TT.
METHODS: We reviewed RCC patients who underwent contrast-enhanced CT, mpMRI, and 
68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT. Diagnostic performance for detecting TT was analyzed, with 
TT confirmed by experienced pathologists. We further analyzed clear cell RCC 
(ccRCC) patients with TT who received pembrolizumab and axitinib and evaluated 
imaging features for predicting therapeutic efficacy by using receiver operating 
characteristic analysis. Internal validation was performed using bootstrap 
resampling (1000 iterations). Model calibration was assessed with the 
Hosmer-Lemeshow test.
RESULTS: A total of 166 RCC patients were initially included, of whom 56 had TT. 
68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT showed higher overall diagnostic performance for TT than 
contrast-enhanced CT and mpMRI, with incremental detection primarily observed 
for Mayo level 0-I TT. The sensitivity and specificity of PET/CT in diagnosing 
TT were 0.96 (95% CI 0.88-0.99) and 0.97 (95% CI 0.92-0.99), respectively. Then, 
35 ccRCC patients with TT underwent an average of 5 cycles of pembrolizumab and 
axitinib, followed by surgery. Following neoadjuvant therapy, 21 patients 
exhibited a partial response, while 14 showed nonresponse. TT SUVmax 
demonstrated significant predictive value for response to neoadjuvant therapy, 
with an AUC of 0.80 (95% CI 0.63-0.92; bootstrap-corrected, 0.79). The 
Hosmer-Lemeshow test indicated adequate calibration (P > 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT may provide incremental value for detecting 
low-level TT and shows potential for predicting response to pembrolizumab plus 
axitinib in RCC. However, the clinical significance of detecting early TT 
remains uncertain.

Factors Associated with Delays in Breast Cancer Surgery Among Patients From 
Neighboring Hawaiian Islands Treated on O'ahu.

Yang D(1), Abdul-Ghani S(1), Miyagi M(1), Yamauchi H(2), Marumoto A(3).

Author information:
(1)John A. Burns School of Medicine, Honolulu, HI, USA.
(2)University of Hawaii Cancer Center, Honolulu, HI, USA.
(3)University of Hawaii Cancer Center, Honolulu, HI, USA. 
ashley.marumoto@gmail.com.

BACKGROUND: Breast cancer patients from neighboring Hawaiian Islands face 
challenges including limited access to specialists and geographic isolation. 
Surgical delays longer than 8 weeks from diagnosis can negatively impact 
survival. Time from diagnosis to surgery (TTS) and predictors of delay are 
unknown for this population.
METHODS: Retrospective chart review was performed on breast cancer patients from 
neighboring Hawaiian Islands who underwent upfront surgery on O'ahu categorized 
as TTS of 8 weeks or longer. Demographic and clinical characteristics were 
evaluated. Chi-square and Fisher's exact tests were used for categorical 
analyses. Binary logistic regression adjusted for confounding variables.
RESULTS: The study reviewed 221 breast cancer patients (2014-2024) from 
neighboring Hawaiian Islands. The mean TTS was 9.4 weeks. In the univariate 
analysis, TTS longer than 8 weeks was associated with post-pandemic diagnosis 
versus during and before the pandemic (41.8 vs. 16.3 vs. 418%), preoperative 
diagnostic testing compared with no testing (79.6 vs. 20.4%), plastic surgery 
consultation compared with no consultation (51.0 vs. 49.0%,), and mastectomy 
compared with breast-conserving surgery (61.2 vs. 37.8%) (all p < 0.005). 
Multivariate analysis showed post-pandemic diagnosis (odds ratio [OR], 2.84; 95% 
CI, 1.15-7.00; p = 0.023), time from biopsy to consultation (OR, 1.32; 95% CI, 
1.13-1.56; p < 0.001), and preoperative diagnostic testing (OR, 3.22; 95% CI, 
1.27-8.16; p = 0.014) as significant predictors of TTS longer than 8 weeks.
CONCLUSION: Nearly half of neighboring Hawaiian Islands breast cancer patients 
experienced delay in surgery. Streamlining preoperative management could 
meaningfully shorten the time from biopsy to surgery and improve access to care 
and outcomes for this population.

Effect of Extended-Duration Venous Thromboprophylaxis After Cancer Surgery.

Wang X(1)(2), Chen W(1), Ma L(1), You C(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Neurosurgery, West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, 
Sichuan, China.
(2)Trauma Center, West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, Sichuan, 
China.
(3)Department of Neurosurgery, West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, 
Sichuan, China. dr.chaoyou@outlook.com.

BACKGROUND: Cancer patients undergoing surgery are at significantly increased 
risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). Although extended thromboprophylaxis is 
recommended, the optimal anticoagulant type and duration remain unclear. This 
study aimed to evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of different 
extended thromboprophylaxis in this population.
METHODS: A Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) 
was performed to evaluate various thromboprophylaxis strategies for patients 
undergoing cancer-related surgery. We conducted both three-node and five-node 
network analyses to evaluate extended-duration versus standard-duration 
thromboprophylaxis strategies. Outcomes included venous thromboembolism, major 
bleeding, and all-cause mortality. Net clinical benefit and risk-benefit 
assessments were additionally performed to determine the overall impact of 
prolonged anticoagulant therapy. Treatment effects were summarized as risk 
ratios (RRs) with corresponding 95% credible intervals (CrIs).
RESULTS: A total of 14 randomized controlled trials involving 4,331 participants 
were included. Compared with placebo, extended-duration prophylaxis with direct 
oral anticoagulants (DOACs) (RR 0.12, 95% CrI 0.05-0.27) and 
low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) (RR 0.17, 95% CrI 0.05-0.55) significantly 
reduced the incidence of venous thromboembolism without a corresponding increase 
in major bleeding. In net clinical benefit analyses, both prolonged DOAC therapy 
(RR 0.27, 95% CrI 0.14-0.49) and LMWH (RR 0.36, 95% CrI 0.17-0.76) demonstrated 
favorable overall outcomes. Risk-benefit evaluation suggested that prolonged 
DOACs provided a more advantageous balance than LMWH, with an NNH/NNT ratio of 
4.17.
CONCLUSIONS: Extended thromboprophylaxis is effective and safe for cancer

BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have limited efficacy in 
estrogen receptor-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative 
(ER+/HER2-) breast cancer, and the mechanisms underlying immune resistance 
remain unclear. The androgen receptor gene (AR), expressed in a substantial 
proportion of ER-positive tumors, has been implicated in tumor biology; however, 
its role in the tumor immune microenvironment and immunotherapy response is not 
well understood.
METHODS: We investigated the association between AR expression, 
transcriptome-derived immune cell-associated signatures, and response to ICIs in 
4046 patients with breast cancer across five cohorts with bulk transcriptomic 
data and two cohorts with single-cell transcriptomic data.
RESULTS: High AR expression was consistently associated with reduced 
transcriptome-derived tumor-infiltrating leukocyte scores across multiple 
ER+/HER2- cohorts. Specifically, signatures associated with cluster of

Emerging Role of the Tumor Microenvironment in the Development of Metastasis, 
Drug Resistance, and Molecular Targeted Strategies A Commentary.

Mir R(1), Waza AA(2), Khan S(3).

Author information:
(1)Prince Fahd Bin Sultan Research Chair for Biomedical Research, Department of 
Medical Lab Technology, Faculty of Applied Medical Sciences, University of 
Tabuk, Tabuk, 71491, Saudi Arabia. rashid@ut.edu.sa.
(2)Multidisciplinary Research Unit (MRU), Government Medical College (GMC), 
Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, India.
(3)Zamzam Cancer Research Institute, Zamzam Medical Institute, Arampora,

It is gradually becoming clear that cancer development represents a 
systems-level process that is controlled by dynamic and reciprocal interactions 
between the tumor microenvironment (TME) and malignant cells. The TME does not 
act as a passive scaffold but active regulation of tumor initiation, growth, 
metastatic dissemination, immune evasion and therapeutic resistance in terms of 
coordinated metabolic, signaling and immunological networks. Adaptive metabolic 
reprogramming and phenotypic plasticity in both cancer and stromal compartments 
were found in microenvironmental stressors like hypoxia, nutrient deprivation, 
and extracellular acidosis. The adaptations maintain invasive, cancer stem cell 
persistence, immune suppression and survival upon therapeutic pressure. 
Crosstalk between cells metabolism, exosome-based communication, and 
extracellular matrix reorganization all determine ecosystem-level resilience 
disrupting traditional cancer therapies. Within the framework of this 
commentary, we generalize emerging evidence that places the TME at a hub of 
metastasis and drug resistance, and we focus on metabolic plasticity, stromal 
re-programming and immune-metabolic competition. Based on the integrative 
multi-omics framework by Mir et al., we expand on the way genomics, 
transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and spatial profiling are redefining 
precision oncology by solving intratumoral heterogeneity and determining 
ecosystem-wide vulnerabilities. Lastly, we emphasize the possibilities of 
translational multi-omics-informed targeting of metabolic and stromal 
dependencies to break tumor ecosystem resilience and resulting clinical 
responses to be more durable. Importantly, such therapeutic concepts should be 
interpreted within the context of the intrinsic biological complexity of the 
tumor ecosystem, in which metabolic interventions may have divergent and 
cell-type-specific effects on malignant, stromal, and immune compartments, 
necessitating careful translational consideration.

Neural stem cells (NSCs) reside in anatomically confined niches, where 
three-dimensional (3D) geometry and interstitial fluid (ISF) flow collectively 
regulate NSC behavior. However, in vitro platforms that simultaneously 
recapitulate size-controlled 3D architecture, ISF-like dynamics, and nanoscale 
therapeutic delivery remain limited. Here, we present a 3D printing-based 
platform with multi-sized microwells, termed the Neural-Inspired Culture for a 
Hydrodynamic Environment (NICHE)-chip, which incorporates an osmosis-driven flow 
system to generate ISF-like flow. The NICHE-chip enabled stable formation of 
uniform human neural stem cell (hNSC) neurospheres across defined microwell 
sizes. Under ISF-like flow, hNSC neurospheres showed enhanced viability, reduced 
apoptosis, and increased self-renewal and differentiation marker expression, 
particularly in 100 μm microwells. ISF-like flow also promoted laminin-rich 
extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition and cell-cell interactions, suggesting 
niche-like remodeling of the 3D microenvironment. In the ISF-integrated 100 μm 
neurosphere model, amyloid-β (Aβ) was introduced to establish an Alzheimer's 
disease (AD)-like neurotoxicity model, which was then used to evaluate 
nanoparticle-mediated neurotrophic factor delivery using brain-derived 
neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-loaded poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) 
nanoparticles. BDNF-loaded PLGA nanoparticles (BDNF-NPs) enabled sustained BDNF 
delivery, attenuated Aβ-induced neuronal marker loss, and counter-regulated a 
subset of Aβ-induced transcriptional alterations associated with 
neuroprotection. Overall, the NICHE-chip provides an ISF-integrated 3D 
neurosphere culture platform for NSC niche modeling, AD-like neurotoxicity 
assessment, and nanoscale neurotrophic factor delivery.
