This study assessed the effects of different final irrigation solutions and 
apical repair materials on apical microleakage in simulated immature teeth using 
confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM). Ninety-six extracted human permanent 
maxillary incisors were used to create a model of immature teeth with open 
apices. The teeth were randomly allocated into three groups according to the 
final irrigation solution: distilled water, 17% EDTA, and 0.2% chitosan. Each 
group was divided into four subgroups according to apical repair material: 
Biodentine, MTA Repair HP, TotalFill BC RRM Fast Set Putty (TotalFill FSP), and 
Endocem MTA Premixed Regular (EMPR). After material placement, the specimens 
were immersed in 0.2% rhodamine B dye, then sectioned longitudinally and 
analyzed using CLSM. Microleakage was quantified with ImageJ. Data were analyzed 
using aligned rank transform (ART) ANOVA followed by ART-based pairwise 
contrasts using the art.con() function with Tukey-adjusted p-values (p < .05). 
Final irrigation solutions, apical repair materials, and their interaction 
significantly affected apical microleakage (p < .05). Chitosan showed the lowest 
microleakage, followed by EDTA and distilled water (p < .05). Microleakage 
differed significantly among apical repair materials (p < .05), with increased 
values in the TotalFill FSP, Biodentine, MTA Repair HP, and EMPR groups. The 
chitosan-TotalFill FSP combination demonstrated the lowest microleakage values 
(1.24 ± 0.02 mm; p < .05), whereas the distilled water-EMPR combination showed 
the highest microleakage values (3.35 ± 0.03 mm; p < .05). Within the 
limitations of this in vitro study, final irrigation with chitosan and the use 
of TotalFill FSP improved the apical sealing in immature teeth with open apices.

Does clinical improvement indicate biological resolution after periodontal

Author information:
(1)Department of Periodontology, Faculty of Dentistry, Çankırı Karatekin 
University, Çankırı, Turkey. ata.bicakcioglu@icloud.com.

Periodontal therapy reduces the subgingival microbial burden and improves 
clinical parameters, yet residual pockets and recurrent inflammation persist in 
some patients and sites. This evidence-informed narrative review examines 
whether clinical improvement reflects restoration of periodontal tissue

were searched from inception to 1 August 2026, supplemented by the Cochrane 
Library and citation screening. Forty publications were included in the core 
synthesis, while 23 additional publications provided biological or mechanistic 
context. Evidence was classified by proximity to the treated periodontal 
setting, and design-specific methodological appraisal was undertaken. Human 
post-treatment studies indicate that residual disease sites may retain dysbiotic 
microbial features, altered inflammatory mediator profiles, or activated 
stromal-cell populations. Evidence from active periodontitis, periodontal 
experimental systems, and inflammatory models supports the plausibility of 
impaired resolution pathways, trained immunity-like and epigenetic 
reprogramming, fibroblast activation, cytokine feedback, macrophage-fibroblast 
crosstalk, inflammatory cell death and DAMP amplification, and extracellular 
matrix regulation. However, these mechanisms have not been shown to persist 
simultaneously in clinically stable treated sites or predict recurrence 
independently of clinical and microbial factors. Plaque control, anatomical 
conditions, and supportive periodontal care remain central to stability. 
Residual immune activity may reflect physiological surveillance, persistent or 
recurrent dysbiosis, or altered host responsiveness and should not be 
interpreted in isolation. The proposed self-reinforcing lesion-susceptibility 
framework is hypothesis-generating and does not imply microbial independence. 
Longitudinal human studies integrating clinical, microbial, cellular, and 
molecular measurements are needed to determine whether resolution-associated 
pathways provide information beyond established periodontal indicators.

Agricultural and forestry waste is rich in renewable lignin, which holds natural 
potential for the production of fine chemicals and functional materials. 
However, lignin is tightly cross-linked with cellulose and hemicellulose. 
Traditional extraction processes using strong acids and bases can easily cause 
lignin molecular condensation and damage to the molecular framework. At the same 
time, there are problems such as high energy consumption and heavy environmental 
burden, which seriously restrict its resource utilization. Due to their 
advantages of simple synthesis, high tunability, and environmental friendliness, 
deep eutectic solvents (DES) have become a research hotspot for the green and 
efficient extraction of lignin. This paper systematically reviews the latest 
research findings on DES-based extraction of lignin from agricultural and 
forestry waste, summarizes the characteristics of different types of DES 
components, investigates the effects of process parameters on lignin extraction 
efficiency and structural retention, and provides an in-depth analysis of the 
lignin's characteristic bonds, functional group composition, and other 
microstructural features. The study confirms that DES can achieve selective 
dissolution of lignin and effectively cleave ether bonds such as β-O-4; the 
resulting lignin has a low molecular weight, a narrow distribution, and a high 
content of phenolic hydroxyl groups, laying an excellent structural foundation 
for subsequent chemical modification and deep processing. The paper also further 
summarizes the high-value application potential of this type of lignin in fields 
such as the preparation of phenolic compounds and the synthesis of functional 
materials. At the same time, it objectively analyzes the practical challenges 
currently faced by DES technology in process optimization, solvent recycling, 
and industrial-scale upscaling, and makes targeted predictions regarding future 
key development directions. The aim is to provide a theoretical basis and 
practical reference for the iteration of green lignin separation technologies 
and the construction of high-value conversion systems for waste biomass.

Author information:
(1)Laboratory of Gastrointestinal Tumor Epigenetics and Genomics, State Key

(3)Colorectal Cancer Center, West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu,

(4)Laboratory of Gastrointestinal Tumor Epigenetics and Genomics, State Key

FLLL32 is a curcumin analogue with reported anti-tumor activity, mainly through 
inhibition of signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) 
signaling and induction of apoptosis. However, whether FLLL32 regulates 
ferroptosis in colorectal cancer (CRC) and the underlying mechanism remain 
unclear. Here, using a patient-derived CRC organoid screening platform, we 
identified FLLL32 as a potent anti-CRC compound. FLLL32 suppressed CRC organoid 
growth, inhibited CRC cell proliferation and migration in vitro, and inhibited 
xenograft tumor growth in vivo. In parallel, FLLL32 induced 
ferroptosis-associated iron accumulation, reactive oxygen species (ROS) 
production, lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial morphological and functional 
abnormalities. The ferroptosis inhibitor Ferrostatin-1 markedly restored 
FLLL32-impaired cell viability and reduced ROS, whereas the apoptosis inhibitor 
Z-VAD-FMK showed weaker protection. These findings suggest that ferroptosis is a 
major contributor to FLLL32-induced cell death, although apoptotic features are 
also present. Mechanistically, FLLL32 interacted with STAT3, and Glu638 and 
Met726 contributed to the FLLL32-STAT3 interaction. FLLL32 also suppressed STAT3 
Tyr705 phosphorylation and nuclear signaling, thereby disrupting pSTAT3-mediated 
transcriptional regulation of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and solute carrier 
family 40 member 1 (SLC40A1), weakening lipid peroxide detoxification and 
cellular iron efflux, promoting intracellular iron accumulation, and enhancing 
ferroptosis in CRC cells. These findings define a STAT3-GPX4/SLC40A1-dependent 
mechanism underlying the anti-CRC activity of FLLL32 and support further 
investigation of STAT3-associated ferroptosis regulation as a potential 
therapeutic vulnerability in CRC.

Cuproptosis and N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA methylation have been identified as 
significant factors in cancer. Consequently, we seek to uncover m6A RNA 
methylation-related prognostic genes that are correlated with 
cuproptosis-related genes (CRGs) in colorectal cancer (CRC) and develop an 
effective prognostic model. Based on public datasets, differential expression 
analysis, correlation analysis, and machine learning were conducted to identify 
prognostic genes. Subsequently, a prognostic model was constructed and 
validated. Furthermore, independent predictive markers were found through the 
use of clinical characteristics and risk score, to establish a prognostic 
nomogram. Prognostic gene expression in CRC and normal samples was evaluated 
using reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). According to the 
prognostic genes, potential drugs for CRC were predicted using artificial 
intelligence drug design (AIDD) and computer-aided drug design (CADD). A 
prognostic model was developed utilizing 7 m6A RNA methylation-related

SNAI1, CDC25C, XRN2, COX5A, and FBXL5) in CRC. Survival analysis uncovered a 
notable contrast in survival outcomes between the high- and low-risk groups. The 
nomogram constructed based on age, stage, T stage, and risk scores demonstrated 
good predictive ability. RT-qPCR results showed that MMP1, TIMP1, SNAI1, and 
CDC25C were upregulated in CRC samples, while COX5A was downregulated, 
consistent with the bioinformatics analysis results. Furthermore, 186 candidate 
drugs targeting COX5A were identified, 153 of which showed better predicted 
binding affinity than the positive-control ligand 3,5‑diiodo‑L‑thyronine. Our 
analysis sets the groundwork for a more comprehensive comprehension of the 
fundamental molecular pathways involved in CRC.

OBJECTIVE: Selective IgM deficiency (sIgMD) is an uncommon immunological 
phenotype characterized by persistently reduced serum IgM, but its 
characteristics within autoimmune rheumatic diseases (ARDs) remain poorly 
defined, particularly in Chinese populations. This study aimed to characterize a 
persistent isolated low IgM phenotype compatible with sIgMD from an ARD-centered 
perspective, focusing on its clinical features, and infection spectrum in a 
cohort of 257 patients.
METHODS: A retrospective study of adult inpatients diagnosed with both ARDs and 
persistent isolated low IgM was conducted. Data on demographics, ARD types, 
infections, treatments, and laboratory parameters were collected and analyzed.
RESULTS: A total of 257 adult patients with ARDs and coexisting persistent 
isolated low IgM were included. The median age was 48 (35-60) years, with a 
female predominance (203/257, 79.0%). Systemic lupus erythematosus was the most 
common underlying ARD (138/257, 53.7%), followed by primary Sjögren's syndrome 
(51/257, 19.8%) and rheumatoid arthritis (16/257, 6.2%). Pneumonia was the most 
frequently observed infection type (125/257, 48.6%). Among the 257 patients, 39 
(15.2%) had persistent isolated low IgM identified before exposure to 
immunosuppressive therapy (treatment-naïve patients), whereas 218 (84.8%) had 
received immunosuppressive treatment before low IgM was first documented. 
Overall, 40 of the 257 patients (15.6%) had documented use of intravenous 
immunoglobulin. Compared with treated patients, treatment-naïve patients had 
shorter disease duration (72 months vs. 108 months, P = 0.006) and higher IgG 
(15.0 vs. 12.0 g/L) and IgA (3.0 g/L vs. 2.1 g/L) levels (both P < 0.001). 
Multivariate analysis demonstrated that older age was associated with a higher 
likelihood of documented infection (OR = 1.049, P = 0.002).
CONCLUSION: This study provided a comprehensive characterization of persistent 
isolated low IgM in Chinese adults with ARDs. Our findings suggest that this 
phenotype may not be solely attributable to immunosuppressive treatment and 
highlight the need for further studies to clarify its underlying mechanisms and 
clinical significance, particularly in relation to infection. Key Points • This 
is the first ARD-centered study to systematically characterize persistent 
isolated low IgM and represents the largest clinical cohort reported to date. • 
Persistent isolated low IgM was observed across multiple autoimmune rheumatic 
diseases and was identified before immunosuppressive therapy in a subset of 
patients. • Older age was independently associated with documented infection in 
patients with ARDs and persistent isolated low IgM.

Pentalinonsterol at the Host-Parasite Interface: Antileishmanial Activity, Host 
Immunomodulation, and Unresolved Mechanisms.

Amin A(1), Nawaz T(2), Ullah N(3), Niaz SI(4).

Author information:
(1)Department of Life Sciences, Yeungnam University, Gyeongsan, 38541, Republic 
of Korea. adnan.amin@yu.ac.kr.
(2)Department of Pharmacy, Qurtuba University of Science and Information 
Technology, Peshawar, Pakistan.
(3)Department of Pharmaceutics, Faculty of Pharmacy, Gomal University, D. I. 
Khan, KPK, 29050, Pakistan.
(4)Institute of Chemical Sciences (ICS), Faculty of Science, Gomal University, 
D.I. Khan, KPK, 29050, Pakistan.

Leishmaniasis remains difficult to treat because available therapies are 
constrained by toxicity, administration burden, variable efficacy, cost, and 
drug resistance. This critical narrative review evaluates the preclinical 
evidence for pentalinonsterol (PEN), a plant-derived cholestane-type steroidal 
ketone originally isolated from the Mayan medicinal plant Pentalinon andrieuxii. 
Experimental studies demonstrate PEN activity against Leishmania promastigotes 
and intracellular amastigotes, together with marked parasite ultrastructural 
injury; however, no parasite molecular target has been validated. PEN also 
modulates host-cell responses involving NF-κB/AP-1 signalling, antigen 
presentation and co-stimulatory markers, dendritic-cell IL-12 production, T-cell 
IFN-γ responses, MAPK-cPLA₂ signalling, and Nrf2-associated transcriptional and 
redox responses. These findings establish host-active pharmacology but do not 
demonstrate that any PEN-responsive host pathway is required for parasite 
clearance. Liposomal PEN reduced parasite burdens in experimental visceral 
leishmaniasis, although its pharmacokinetic, tissue-delivery, safety, or 
efficacy advantage over free PEN has not been established. Overall, the 
available evidence remains preclinical: parasite-directed activity and host-cell 
modulation have each been demonstrated, but their molecular targets, causal 
interdependence, relative contribution to parasite clearance, and temporal 
relationship remain unresolved. PEN is therefore most appropriately regarded as 
a putative dual-action antileishmanial natural product for which the proposed 
dual mechanism requires direct experimental validation.

Pancreatic stone protein versus conventional biomarkers for prognostic 
discrimination in sepsis: a meta-analysis of paired AUC comparisons.

Melegari G(1), Valente V(2), Arturi F(2), Pacini I(3), Pilia E(4), Belletti 
A(5), Tognù A(6), Bertellini E(7), Barbieri A(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Azienda 
Ospedaliero-Universitaria Policlinico di Modena, Via del Pozzo 71, Modena, 
41124, Italy. melegari.gabriele@gmail.com.
(2)School of Anesthesia and Intensive Care, University of Modena and Reggio 
Emilia, Modena, Italy.
(3)Department of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico 
Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy.
(4)Department of Medical Science and Public Health, University of Cagliari, 
Cagliari, Italy.
(5)Department of Cardio-Thoracic Anaesthesia and Intensive Care IRCCS San 
Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milan, Italy.
(6)Department of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, ASST Gaetano Pini-CTO, Milan, 
Italy.
(7)School of Medcine, University of Modena and Reggio Emilia, Modena, Italy.

BACKGROUND: Pancreatic stone protein (PSP) has been proposed as a prognostic 
biomarker in sepsis, but its comparative performance versus C-reactive protein 
(CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT) remains uncertain.
METHODS: We performed a meta-analysis of direct within-study paired AUC 
comparisons between PSP and CRP and/or PCT in critically ill adults with sepsis, 
septic shock, or acute infection-related conditions in whom sepsis development 
or clinically relevant adverse outcomes were prospectively evaluated. 
Differences in AUC (ΔAUC) were pooled using random-effects models. The principal 
conservative analysis included one comparison per independent cohort and 
comparator.
RESULTS: Seven studies comprising 803 unique participants contributed 21 paired 
comparisons. In the principal conservative analysis, PSP showed a higher 
prognostic AUC than CRP, with a pooled ΔAUC of 0.179 (95% CI 0.095-0.262; 
p < 0.001), although between-cohort heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 81.65%). 
Compared with PCT, the pooled ΔAUC was 0.153 (95% CI 0.114-0.193; p < 0.001), 
with no observed heterogeneity (I² = 0.00%). The mortality-only sensitivity 
analysis showed a similar pooled effect for PSP versus CRP (ΔAUC 0.17, 95% CI 
0.08-0.26), with substantial heterogeneity persisting, and for PSP versus PCT 
(ΔAUC 0.153, 95% CI 0.114-0.193), with no observed heterogeneity. Exclusion of 
the clinically distinct intra-abdominal infection cohort (Michailides et al.) 
likewise did not materially change the PSP-versus CRP estimate (ΔAUC 0.166, 95% 
CI 0.077-0.256). The direction and approximate magnitude of the pooled effects 
were also preserved across alternative assumptions for the within-study 
correlation.
CONCLUSIONS: Available comparative evidence suggests that PSP may have greater 
prognostic discrimination than CRP and PCT. The findings were broadly maintained 
across sensitivity analyses, but the limited number of independent cohorts and 
substantial heterogeneity in the CRP comparison warrant caution. Further 
prospective studies are required to confirm these findings and establish their 
clinical relevance.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: This systematic review was prospectively registered in the 
International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; 
CRD420261340301).

Bladder preservation is still feasible in the rare aggressive small cell 
carcinoma subtype.

Ismail Y(1), Kamal A(2), Aboulkassem H(2), Ashour MG(3), AbouGabal AA(3), Allam 
RM(4), Gad M(5), Mostafa ME(1), Taher M(6).

Author information:
(1)Medical Oncology Department, National Cancer Institute - Cairo University,

(6)Surgical Oncology Department, National Cancer Institute - Cairo University,

PURPOSE: Primary urinary bladder small cell carcinoma (UBSCC) is a rare 
aggressive malignant neoplasm with no established treatment guidelines. Radical 
cystectomy (RC) alone is suboptimal in localized disease; therefore, 
chemotherapy and radiotherapy are required. We aimed to report our outcomes of 
UBSCC.
METHODS: UBSCC patients who presented to our institute between 2012 and 2021 
were retrospectively evaluated for their clinicopathologic features, management 
modalities, event-free (EFS) and overall survival (OS).
RESULTS: Sixty patients included. Metastatic disease was present at diagnosis in 
12 (20%). For localized disease patients, upfront RC was done in 9(19%); 
meanwhile, neoadjuvant chemotherapy was employed in the rest. In the latter 
group,18 patients (46%) achieved complete response (CR), and those proceeded to 
further concurrent chemoradiation as a bladder preservation management. 
Platinum-etoposide (PE) regimen was more frequently used than 
platinum-gemcitabine (PG) in the neoadjuvant/adjuvant and metastatic settings 
(57%). The latter combination was independent factor associated with less 
likelihood achievement of CR about 7 times that of PE 
(OR:7.27;95%CI:1.33-39.86;p = 0.02). The median EFS & OS were 42.4 & 52.7 
months, respectively, with cumulative 5-year EFS & OS of 46.9 & 49.5%, 
respectively. On multivariate analysis, PG protocol was independent factor 
associated with worse EFS compared to PE, while initially metastatic disease was 
independent factor linked with poor OS compared to localized disease.
CONCLUSIONS: Despite its hostile behavior, the high CR rate in our study 
confirms the remarkable sensitivity of localized UBSCC to chemotherapy 
especially PE. Bladder preservation is feasible in those achieved CR, and is 
associated with favorable outcomes. These findings, however, should be 
interpreted cautiously and warrant further prospective evaluation.

Kyei S(1)(2), Asiamah R(3)(4), Amoako PT(5), Afake H(6).

Author information:

College of Health and Allied Sciences, University of Cape Coast, Cape Coast,

(2)Biomedical and Clinical Research Centre, College of Health and Allied

(3)Biomedical and Clinical Research Centre, College of Health and Allied 
Sciences, University of Cape Coast, Cape Coast, Ghana. randyasiamah@gmail.com.
(4)Department of Clinical Optometry, School of Optometry and Vision Science,

PURPOSE: To synthesise the population-based prevalence of myopia, hyperopia and 
astigmatism in Ghana and evaluate the methodological drivers of heterogeneity 
within the existing epidemiological literature.
RECENT FINDINGS: A systematic review and meta-analysis of nine eligible 
population-based cross-sectional studies (n = 7153 participants, age range 5-70 
years) was conducted. Due to substantial inter-study heterogeneity, pooled 
estimates should be interpreted as weighted averages rather than definitive 
national prevalences. The pooled prevalence was approximately 3.1% (95% CI: 1.9% 
to 5.0%) for myopia, 2.2% (95% CI: 1.1% to 4.4%) for hyperopia and 1.7% (95% CI: 
0.7% to 3.9%) for astigmatism. Prediction intervals were wide, reflecting 
extreme between-study variance. Subgroup analyses revealed that myopia 
prevalence was significantly higher in urban (3.1%) and mixed settings (4.7%) 
compared with rural areas (0.8%; 95% CI: 0.4% to 1.6%). Furthermore, studies 
omitting cycloplegia severely underestimated hyperopia prevalence (1.3%) 
compared to the single cohort utilising cycloplegic refraction (4.6%). 
Continuous meta-regression indicated a positive correlation between hyperopia 
and advancing age, while apparent temporal declines in hyperopia and astigmatism 
may reflect methodological shifts rather than true epidemiological trends. The 
findings suggest higher myopia prevalence in urban and mixed settings and 
indicate that cycloplegic use may influence reported hyperopia prevalence 
estimates. Future epidemiological studies would benefit from standardised 
cycloplegic protocols and harmonised refractive error definitions to improve 
comparability of prevalence estimates.

Antibody-Drug Conjugates in Biliary Tract Cancer: Current Evidence, Emerging 
Targets, and Future Directions.

Liu H(1), Guo Y(1), Xue H(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Surgical Oncology, Shanghai Mengchao Cancer Hospital, Shanghai 
University, Shanghai, 201805, China.
(2)Department of Medical Oncology, Shanghai Mengchao Cancer Hospital, Shanghai 
University, Shanghai, 201805, China. xuehui2010@126.com.

PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Biliary tract cancer (BTC) is a heterogeneous group of 
malignancies with limited systemic treatment options and poor prognosis. While 
immunochemotherapy has become the first-line standard, second-line therapy 
remains inadequate. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have emerged as a promising 
therapeutic modality leveraging antigen-specific targeting to deliver potent 
cytotoxic payloads. This review provides a comprehensive, multi-target appraisal 
of the ADC landscape in BTC.
RECENT FINDINGS: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd), supported by DESTINY-PanTumor02 
(ORR 22%) and HERB (ORR 36.4%) trials, received 2024 FDA tumor-agnostic approval 
for HER2-positive solid tumors including BTC. Zanidatamab achieved 41.3% ORR in 
HERIZON-BTC-01, securing BTC-specific regulatory approval. BL-B01D1, an 
EGFR×HER3 bispecific ADC, demonstrated preliminary BTC activity (ORR 28.6%) 
without reported interstitial lung disease in the BTC cohort, though sample size 
and follow-up remain limited, while its phase III nasopharyngeal carcinoma trial 
established proof of concept for bispecific ADCs. BL-M05D1 phase I results (ASCO 
2026) provided the first clinical evidence for Claudin18.2 ADCs in BTC (ORR 
42.5%). Trop2-directed ADCs show theoretical applicability across solid tumors 
given 69.5% high-expression prevalence, but BTC-specific clinical data are 
absent. B7-H3 and CD44v5 represent emerging targets with early clinical or 
preclinical validation. This review provides a unified framework for navigating 
the rapidly evolving multi-target ADC landscape in BTC. Critical challenges 
remain, including the absence of phase III randomized trials, tumor 
heterogeneity, optimal biomarker-guided patient selection, and rational 
combination strategies with immunotherapy. Standardization of HER2 testing and 
broader molecular profiling will be essential to realize the clinical potential 
of ADCs in this historically treatment-refractory disease. Biliary obstruction 
and hepatic impairment, common in BTC, require ADC-specific pharmacokinetic 
vigilance and graded toxicity monitoring.

This retrospective study involving 225 centers assessed TP53 and IGHV molecular 
status and stereotyped BcR IG subsets in a large cohort of patients with CLL in 
Spain using data from the RED53 project. Three analytical reference centers 
determined the mutational status of treatment-naïve CLL patients requiring

with the most frequent being CLL#1 (23.2%), CLL#2 (24.0%), and CLL#6 (10.7%). 
The frequencies of TP53 and IGHV mutations were similar to those reported in 
other international series. The RED53 project enabled molecular testing to be 
incorporated into routine practice to guide treatment decisions.

Later-line Treatment Selection in Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: 
Trifluridine/Tipiracil Plus Bevacizumab, Regorafenib, and Fruquintinib.

Sagawa T(1), Hirakawa M(2), Nagashima H(3), Fujikawa K(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Gastroenterology, National Hospital Organization Hokkaido 
Cancer Center, 3-54 Kikusui 4-jo 2-chome, Shiroishi-ku, Sapporo, Hokkaido, 
003-0804, Japan. stamotsu@jk9.so-net.ne.jp.
(2)Division of Medical Oncology, Department of Internal Medicine, Sapporo 
Medical University School of Medicine, Sapporo, Japan.
(3)Department of Gastroenterology, National Hospital Organization Hokkaido 
Cancer Center, 3-54 Kikusui 4-jo 2-chome, Shiroishi-ku, Sapporo, Hokkaido, 
003-0804, Japan.

Later-line therapy for metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) increasingly requires 
selection among treatments with different mechanisms, toxicity profiles, and 
sequencing evidence. Trifluridine/tipiracil plus bevacizumab has robust 
randomized evidence from SUNLIGHT, but objective response remains uncommon and 
hematologic toxicity can limit treatment delivery in heavily pretreated 
patients. Regorafenib and fruquintinib are minimally myelosuppressive oral 
alternatives, yet they differ in dose strategy, hepatotoxicity, hand-foot skin 
reaction, hypertension, and proteinuria. This narrative review updates pivotal 
and recent evidence and proposes an evidence-informed framework that treats 
hematologic reserve as a clinical fitness construct rather than a fixed 
laboratory threshold. We additionally examine the clinical implications of low 
response rates, prior anti-angiogenic exposure, emerging molecular predictors 
including KRAS G12, evidence in older or vulnerable patients, and recent phase 
III developments. Current data do not support a validated molecular biomarker 
for choosing among these three options, and no randomized head-to-head 
comparison of regorafenib and fruquintinib exists. Accordingly, treatment 
selection should be individualized according to prior therapies, toxicity 
vulnerability, organ function, tumor tempo, and patient goals. Hypertension and 
proteinuria are important selection factors but may also be modifiable 
treatment-delivery factors. The proposed algorithms and adverse-event radar 
chart are intended as practical visual syntheses rather than validated 
guidelines or formal cross-trial comparisons.

Nanotechnology has a significant role in cosmetics and cosmeceuticals for 
epidermal care. In this review, mechanisms of nanomaterial penetration into the 
skin and penetration pathways, key physicochemical factors, as well as the 
various models, namely in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo, used to investigate 
nanoparticle behavior with the epidermis, have been discussed. The roles of 
nanocarriers and active ingredients have been discussed in the design and 
development of nanoformulations to address limitations of conventional topical 
formulations, including poor solubility, instability, and limited skin 
penetration of active ingredients. Furthermore, they improve skin hydration, 
promote skin repair, and support anti-aging and antioxidant functions, 
influencing their effectiveness, along with safety, environmental 
sustainability, and global regulatory frameworks for nanomaterials in skin care 
products. Future research should focus on sustainable nanomaterials and advanced 
toxicological assessment methods to ensure consumer safety without compromising 
product efficacy. The details of analysis and characterization of active 
ingredients and nanomaterials-based formulations in epidermal care have been 
provided. Furthermore, the guidelines from India, the EU, and the USA are 
briefly provided to support stakeholders. Finally, future research directions 
are highlighted, with particular emphasis on integrative design strategies that 
combine experimental evaluation with theoretical and in silico toxicity 
prediction models to ensure consumer safety while maintaining product 
efficacy.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

Dysregulated eating in obesity and eating disorders (ED) is associated with 
complex relationships between peripheral hormonal signals and neurobehavioral 
characteristics. Ghrelin and its endogenous antagonist liver-expressed 
antimicrobial peptide-2 (LEAP2) have been implicated in the regulation of energy 
homeostasis and food intake, while trait impulsivity has been proposed as a 
transdiagnostic characteristic associated with dysregulated eating. This study 
aimed to integrate narrative evidence with exploratory empirical data to examine 
associations between ghrelin, LEAP2, and trait impulsivity in women with 
obesity, with and without ED, and to explore their associations with food 
addiction (FA) and eating psychopathology. A total of 164 adult women (67 with 
obesity, 35 with obesity + ED, 62 healthy controls) completed anthropometric 
assessments, fasting ghrelin and LEAP2 determinations, and psychometric measures 
of trait impulsivity, FA, and eating psychopathology. Group comparisons and 
exploratory structural equation modeling (SEM) were used to explore associations 
between endocrine and behavioral variables. Women with obesity (with or without 
ED) showed significantly lower ghrelin levels than controls, while LEAP2 
concentrations did not differ between groups. Trait impulsivity and FA scores 
were higher in the obesity + ED group. Within this subgroup, SEM analyses 
identified positive associations of trait impulsivity and FA with eating 
psychopathology, while LEAP2 was positively associated with trait impulsivity 
and FA scores. Previous research has pointed to potential associations of 
ghrelin and LEAP2 with obesity and ED, as well as with behavioral 
characteristics related to dysregulated eating, although the available evidence 
remains limited and heterogeneous. In our study, ghrelin was lower in women with 
obesity, whereas LEAP2 did not differ between groups. The observed associations 
involving LEAP2 emerged only in the exploratory SEM analysis and should 
therefore be interpreted cautiously. These findings are hypothesis-generating 
and do not provide evidence of mechanistic or causal relationships. Further 
research in larger and longitudinal samples is needed to replicate these 
findings and clarify the relationships among endocrine and behavioral factors.

Tranexamic acid (TXA) is widely used to reduce bleeding in surgical, trauma,

TXA-associated thrombotic adverse events, and their phenotypic heterogeneity and 
clinical severity have not been comprehensively characterized. This study 
investigated TXA-associated thrombotic events using the Food and Drug 
Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) from 2004Q1 to 2026Q1. 
Thrombotic adverse events were identified using the Standardized MedDRA Query 
(SMQ) "Embolic and thrombotic events" and evaluated by disproportionality 
analysis based on reporting odds ratios (RORs). Qualifying thrombotic events 
were assigned to the SMQ vessel-type subgroups-arterial, vessel-type 
unspecified/mixed, and venous-and demographic characteristics, indications, 
clinical outcomes and time-to-onset were compared across subgroups; signal 
strength was further related to clinical severity. In all, 515 thrombotic cases 
associated with TXA and 26 selected thrombotic terms were found (arterial, 157; 
mixed, 168; venous, 190). Venous thromboembolism-pulmonary embolism (n = 128, 
ROR 13.94) and deep vein thrombosis (n = 58, ROR 9.09)-is the most frequent type 
and brings about the most severe and fatal consequences (death reported in 16.8% 
of venous versus 2.5% of arterial reports), whereas the strongest 
disproportionality signals were observed for rare site-specific events such as 
ovarian vein thrombosis (ROR 352.95) and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (ROR 
118.35). The three subgroups differed markedly in demographic and clinical 
characteristics: venous events occurred predominantly in women (73.7%) treated 
for menorrhagia (35.3%), whereas arterial events arose mainly in surgical or 
procedural settings (intravenous route 36.3%; surgery/prophylaxis 19.1%) and 
presented earliest after exposure [median time-to-onset (TTO) 0 versus 7 days]. 
Signal strength was not concordant with clinical severity across the thrombotic 
spectrum. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the thrombotic safety 
of TXA, indicate that the clinical background may influence the phenotypic 
differences among the different thrombotic types, and emphasize the necessity of 
enhanced attention and risk stratification in high-risk groups.

Automated quantification of RETeval™ sensor electrode position from infrared eye 
images: a preliminary technical report.

Constable PA(1)(2), Loh L(3), Posada-Quintero H(4), Zhdanov A(5), Sokolov G(5), 
Kulyabin M(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Optometry and Visual Science, University of Canberra, Canberra, 
Australia. paul.constable@canberra.edu.au.
(2)College of Health and Enablement, Flinders University, Bedford Park, 
Australia. paul.constable@canberra.edu.au.
(3)College of Health and Enablement, Flinders University, Bedford Park, 
Australia.
(4)Department of Biomedical Engineering, University of Connecticut, Storrs, USA.
(5)VisioMed.AI, Moscow, Russia.

PURPOSE: To present an automated method for computing the position of the 
RETeval skin sensor electrode and the iris color ratio (ICratio) from infrared 
eye images extracted from RETeval recording files.
METHODS: Infrared eye images were extracted from .RFF binary files recorded in 
19 healthy young participants (mean age 10.6 years, range 5.0-15.8; 7 male, 12 
female) using the RETeval 6-step Light First Troland ISCEV protocol. A 
multilabel deep learning segmentation model (SegFormer) was trained to delineate 
six ocular structures: pupil, iris/limbus, corneal reflex, visible white bulbar 
area, electrode, and inner lens ring. Electrode position was quantified as the 
signed displacement vector from the corneal reflex centroid to the electrode 
arc-contact point (Pₑ), decomposed into horizontal (dx) and vertical (dy) 
components in millimeters. The iris color ratio (ICratio) was derived from the 
segmentation masks as the mean gray level of the iris annular ring divided by 
the median gray level of the dark pupil, with corneal reflex pixels excluded.
RESULTS: The segmentation model achieved a mean validation Dice coefficient of 
0.971 across the six classes on a held-out recording session. Infrared images 
(n = 271) were extracted from 19 participants (38 eyes); 67 (24.7%) satisfied 
all three quality-control criteria, and an electrode measurement was obtained 
for all 38 eyes. Vertical electrode displacement (dy) was 8.57 ± 1.81 mm (right 
eye) and 9.14 ± 1.89 mm (left eye; p = 0.13 between eyes); horizontal 
displacement (dx) was - 3.11 ± 2.42 mm and - 3.70 ± 4.74 mm, respectively 
(p = 0.67). Euclidean displacement (|d|) differed significantly between eyes 
(9.45 ± 1.63 vs 10.74 ± 2.59 mm; p = 0.004), while angular displacement did not 
(p = 0.81). Mask-based ICratio was 1.128 ± 0.036 (right) and 1.121 ± 0.039 
(left), with a significant interocular correlation (r = 0.811, p = 0.008); the 
device-derived ratio was 1.134 ± 0.024 and 1.149 ± 0.038 (interocular r = 0.561, 
p = 0.12). The two methods differed by - 0.016 on average (95% limits of 
agreement - 0.108 to + 0.077; p = 0.14).
CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary study provides an automated method for determining 
the position of the RETeval sensor electrode from the infrared images recorded 
by the device. A measure of iris darkness derived from the same segmentation is 
reported as a secondary technical output.

Investigation of the most suitable 3D printing method and tissue equivalent 
materials for mimicking glandular-adipose tissues for production of breast 
phantom.

Safi̇ A(1)(2), Yücel H(3).

Author information:
(1)Institute of Nuclear Sciences, Ankara University, Besevler 10. Yıl Campus, 
06560, Yenimahalle, Ankara, Turkey.
(2)Gedik Vocational School, Istanbul Gedik University, Pendik Campus, 34913, 
Pendik, Istanbul, Turkey.
(3)Institute of Nuclear Sciences, Ankara University, Besevler 10. Yıl Campus, 
06560, Yenimahalle, Ankara, Turkey. hyucel@ankara.edu.tr.

In this study, the usability of masked stereolithography (MSLA) and fused 
filament fabrication (FFF) type printers to produce breast phantom is 
investigated. ABS, PET, PLA+, PVA and TPU-95 A filaments are used on FFF type 
printer with infill ratios between 70 and 100%; ABS-like, PLA and PMMA-like 
resins are used on SLA type printer with infill ratio 100% to tissue equivalent 
materials. The materials' CT scans are taken at 80, 100 and 120 kVp and the 
Hounsfield Units (HU) dependency on the infill ratio for each filament and resin 
is investigated. The materials' physical densities are measured; electron 
densities and effective atomic numbers are calculated. The suitability of the 
materials for mimicking adipose, glandular and skin tissue investigated in terms 
of HU value, physical density, electron density and effective atomic number. It 
is found that MSLA type printer is not eligible for printing breast tissue 
equivalent materials as the common resins have higher physical density and it is 
not possible to lower physical density by infill ratio. However, FFF type 
printer technology is more eligible for mimicking breast tissue. While ABS is 
suitable only for mimicking adipose tissue, PET, PLA+, PVA and TPU-95 A 
filaments can be used to produce adipose, glandular and skin tissues by just 
changing infill ratio. For production of a breast phantom via FFF printing, PET 
and PVA among the tested filament materials are preferable over the properties 
of PLA + and TPU-95 A due to their proper hydrogen(H) and carbon contents (C), 
and other physical and radiological properties.

Neoadjuvant Therapy for Gastric Adenocarcinoma with Signet Ring Cells: A 
Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

Mela E(1), Frountzas M(2), Apostolidou Kiouti F(3), Nikolakopoulou A(3), Haidich 
AB(3), Schizas D(4), Triantafyllou T(5).

Author information:
(1)First Propaedeutic Department of Surgery, National and Kapodistrian 
University of Athens, Hippocration General Hospital, Vasilissis Sofias 114, 
Athens, 11527, Greece. evmela@med.uoa.gr.
(2)Department of Colorectal Surgery, The Royal Marsden Hospital NHS Foundation 
Trust, London, United Kingdom.
(3)Department of Hygiene, Social-Preventive Medicine & Medical Statistics, 
School of Medicine, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Thessaloniki, Greece.
(4)First Department of Surgery, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, 
Laiko General Hospital, Athens, Greece.
(5)First Propaedeutic Department of Surgery, National and Kapodistrian 
University of Athens, Hippocration General Hospital, Vasilissis Sofias 114, 
Athens, 11527, Greece.

BACKGROUND: Signet ring cell-containing gastric cancer constitutes an 
increasingly recognized subtype. Although perioperative chemotherapy is the 
standard of treatment for locally advanced gastric cancer, its efficacy in 
signet ring cell-containing gastric adenocarcinomas remains controversial. This 
systematic review and meta-analysis aims to assess the impact of neoadjuvant 
chemotherapy compared to upfront surgery on overall survival.
METHODS: A systematic search of MEDLINE, Scopus, and Cochrane was conducted up 
to January 2026. Eligible studies included adult patients with signet ring 
cell-containing gastric cancer undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by 
surgery compared to upfront gastrectomy. A random-effects meta-analysis was 
performed to pool hazard ratios for overall survival.
RESULTS: Six studies, including seven cohorts and 5.388 patients, were included. 
The pooled analysis demonstrated no significant difference in overall survival 
between neoadjuvant chemotherapy and upfront surgery (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.68-1.34, 
I2 = 83.2%). Subgroup analyses by studies' geographic origin and design revealed 
consistent results with no significant differences in overall survival among 
Western (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.53-1.38, I² = 86.9%) or Eastern studies (HR 1.12, 95% 
CI 0.63-1.97, I² = 83%), and among different study designs (randomized 
controlled trial: HR 1.16, 95% CI 0.81-1.67; observational: HR 0.92, 95% CI 
0.62-1.38, I² = 85.5%).
CONCLUSIONS: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was not associated with a significant 
improvement in overall survival compared with upfront surgery in signet-ring 
cell-containing gastric cancer. While perioperative chemotherapy remains the 
recommended therapeutic approach, further studies employing contemporary 
chemotherapy regimens are warranted to define its role in this distinct 
histological subtype.

The Effects of Extreme Climate Events on Healthcare Access, Mental Health, and 
Economic Stability Among PLHIV in Brazil.

Brandelli Costa A(1)(2)(3), Graeff Bins-Ely I(4), Chaves LW(5), Freeman K(6), 
Lekveishvili L(6), Welter Wendt G(7), de Almeida-Segundo DS(8), Dos Santos 
Boeira L(8).

Author information:
(1)Graduate Program in Psychology, Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande 
do Sul, Porto Alegre, Brazil. angelo.costa@pucrs.br.
(2)Department of Psychological and Social Sciences, John Cabot University, Rome,

Climate change and HIV are intersecting crises, yet their combined impact on 
Latin America's HIV care continuum remains understudied. Using a descriptive 
cross-sectional design with data from the 2024 Brazilian HIV Stigma Index, we 
examined the consequences of extreme climate events-primarily the May 2024 
floods in Porto Alegre-on healthcare access, mental health, and socioeconomic 
stability among 156 people living with HIV. These events were associated with 
substantial care disruptions, with many participants reporting rescheduled or 
canceled medical appointments and laboratory monitoring. Furthermore, 60.5% 
reported negative mental health impacts and 37.3% suffered household income 
reductions. Institutional support reached a minority, leaving many reliant on 
civil society for survival needs. These findings highlight an urgent need for 
climate-resilient HIV policies integrating mental health care and social 
protection to sustain treatment adherence during public calamities.

"I think community is what keeps us all healthy": Findings from online 
interviews exploring health priorities and research engagement preferences with 
Métis youth in Ontario.

Sayanthan J(1), Simms AJ(2)(3), Sehar H(4), Koprich S(4), Garner J(2), Cripps 
S(2), Tsui N(2)(3), Edwards SA(4)(2)(3); Métis Nation of Ontario Youth Council.

Author information:
(1)Dalla Lana School of Public Health, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, 
Canada. psayanthan@uwaterloo.ca.
(2)Healing and Wellness Branch, Métis Nation of Ontario, Ottawa, ON, Canada.
(3)Data and Analytics Services, ICES (Formerly the Institute for Clinical 
Evaluative Sciences), Toronto, ON, Canada.
(4)Dalla Lana School of Public Health, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, 
Canada.

OBJECTIVES: There is limited research on the health priorities and research 
engagement preferences of Métis youth, a vital population for promoting 
Métis-specific health outcomes. Together with the Métis Nation of Ontario (MNO) 
and the Métis Nation of Ontario Youth Council (MNOYC), we explored this topic.
METHODS: This study (April 2022-August 2025) used an Etuaptmumk/Two-Eyed Seeing 
framework to weave Western and Métis worldviews. Community- and land-based 
engagements, an online survey, and online semi-structured interviews were used 
to explore the health priorities of MNO youth citizens. This paper reports on 
the findings of the online interviews, which were the only method that explored 
research engagement preferences. MNO citizen youth participants (16-29 years) 
were recruited through the MNO's pre-existing social media channels, website, 
the MNOYC's email listserv, and kin-based recruitment. Data from the interviews 
were transcribed, anonymized, thematically analyzed, and presented back to youth 
for verification.
RESULTS: An inductive thematic analysis generated the following themes: Cost of 
Living, Métis Ways of Living, Connecting/Sense of Community, Wholistic Health, 
Healthcare Access, Métis Identity and Lateral Violence, Programming 
Considerations, and Research Preferences. Community, land, and culture are 
fundamental to the wholistic health of Métis youth. Métis youth identified 
impediments to health such as cost of living, barriers to traditional and 
Western medicine, and lateral violence. Importantly, Métis youth want to be 
active decision makers.
CONCLUSION: This project contributes important insights regarding Métis youth 
health. Métis youth know themselves best, should be empowered to self-determine, 
and be included in health research, policy, and program development at all 
levels of government.

Epidemiological Evolution of HIV in Pakistan (1987-2026): From High-risk 
Populations to Emerging Pediatric Cases.

John A(1)(2)(3), Faridi TA(4), Iqbal N(5).

PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This narrative review examines the evolving epidemiology of 
HIV in Pakistan from 1987 to 2026, focusing on temporal trends among key 
populations, geographic hotspots, emerging pediatric infections, and 
health-system gaps affecting epidemic control.
RECENT FINDINGS: Evidence indicates a persistent concentrated epidemic, with the 
highest burden among people who inject drugs and continuing transmission among 
sex workers, transgender populations, and prisoners. HIV transmission remains 
geographically heterogeneous, with major urban hotspots in Karachi and cities 
across Punjab. Recent pediatric outbreaks have introduced an important 
healthcare-associated dimension, with unsafe medical practices and weaknesses in 
infection prevention and control emerging as major concerns. Pakistan's HIV 
epidemic remains concentrated but is becoming increasingly complex. Persistent 
transmission among key populations, geographic expansion, pediatric infections, 
and substantial gaps in diagnosis, treatment, and viral suppression highlight 
the need for strengthened surveillance, prevention, infection control, and 
continuity of HIV care.

Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring during general anesthesia: a prospective 
clinical audit of adherence to international guidelines.

Dantas de Oliveira C(1), Vieito P(2), Ferreira A(2), M Fernandes AS(2), P 
Tavares E(2), Sousa Braga I(2), Silva J(2), Abreu-Pires M(2), Ribeiro Neto P(2), 
Moreira Z(2), Esteves S(2).

Author information:
(1)Clínica de Anestesiologia, Medicina Intensiva, Emergência e Urgência, Serviço 
de Anestesiologia, Centro Hospitalar Universitário de Santo António, Unidade 
Local de Saúde de Santo António, Porto, Portugal. dantasoliveira91@gmail.com.
(2)Clínica de Anestesiologia, Medicina Intensiva, Emergência e Urgência, Serviço 
de Anestesiologia, Centro Hospitalar Universitário de Santo António, Unidade 
Local de Saúde de Santo António, Porto, Portugal.

Quantitative neuromuscular (qNM) monitoring is recommended whenever 
neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) are administered, but adherence in routine 
clinical practice remains inconsistent. This audit evaluated adherence to 
recommended qNM monitoring standards in adult patients undergoing general 
anesthesia at a Portuguese tertiary hospital. This prospective clinical audit 
evaluated adherence to recommended qNM monitoring standards in adult patients 
undergoing general anesthesia at a major Portuguese tertiary hospital. Over five 
predefined weekdays between March and May 2025, all adult patients receiving 
general anesthesia across six operating or procedural areas were assessed. Of 
329 patients included, 308 (93.6%) received NMBAs. Quantitative neuromuscular 
monitoring was omitted in 13.0% despite universal device availability. 
Utilization was lower in ambulatory and obstetrical settings and in procedures 
lasting less than one hour. Increasing anesthesia duration was associated with 
greater monitoring use in univariable analysis, but this association was not 
independent of clinical location. Equipment-related limitations accounted for a 
small proportion of omissions. This audit demonstrates high but incomplete 
adherence to qNM monitoring standards. Non-adherence is clustered primarily in 
procedures lasting less than one hour and in ambulatory and obstetrical 
settings. Although equipment was universally available, factors beyond equipment 
availability appear to contribute to incomplete implementation. Additional 
research is required to better understand the reasons underlying monitoring 
omission. In the meantime, targeted educational strategies and reinforcement of 
evidence-based neuromuscular monitoring practices may further enhance 
perioperative patient safety.

A tablet-based augmented reality system to reduce preoperative anxiety in 
pediatric patients: a quasi-experimental pilot study.

Narisawa A(1), Hayasaka T(2), Sato K(3), Honda Y(3), Makino F(3), Komoriya Y(2), 
Kuroki M(2), Toyama H(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Anesthesiology, Yamagata University Hospital, 2-2-2 Iidanishi, 
Yamagata City, 990-9585, Yamagata, Japan. asakamoto-ygt@med.id.yamagata-u.ac.jp.
(2)Department of Anesthesiology, Yamagata University Hospital, 2-2-2 Iidanishi, 
Yamagata City, 990-9585, Yamagata, Japan.
(3)Department of Medicine, Yamagata University School of Medicine, Yamagata, 
Japan.

Preoperative anxiety in pediatric patients remains a significant clinical 
challenge, yet existing interventions are limited by resource requirements and 
inconsistent effectiveness. The aim of this pilot study was to evaluate the 
feasibility and preliminary effects of a tablet-based augmented reality (AR) 
system integrated into routine perioperative patient transfer on preoperative 
anxiety in pediatric patients. In this single-center, quasi-experimental pilot 
study, 27 pediatric patients aged 3-10 years were assigned to an AR (n = 13) or 
control (n = 14) group based on surgery month. The AR system, implemented on a 
standard tablet device, overlaid virtual characters onto real-world surroundings 
to guide patients from the surgical center entrance to the operating room. The 
primary outcome was preoperative anxiety assessed using the modified Yale 
Preoperative Anxiety Scale (mYPAS) at operating room entry. Secondary outcomes 
included guardian-rated comfort visual analog scale scores and postoperative 
agitation. The AR group was younger than the control group. Median mYPAS scores 
at operating room entry were lower in the AR group than in the control group 
(28.3 [23.3-36.7] vs. 40.0 [36.7-52.9]; median difference - 11.7; 95% CI, - 18.4 
to - 1.60; p = 0.01). No significant differences were observed in secondary 
outcomes. This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating a 
tablet-based AR system into perioperative workflows. Preliminary findings also 
indicate that this approach may help reduce preoperative anxiety in this 
population. Given the pilot nature of the study, non-randomized allocation, and 
baseline imbalances between groups, validation in larger, well-controlled, 
randomized trials is required.

R-estimation with right-censored data.

Satten GA(1), Li M(2), Zhao N(3), Strawderman RL(4).

Author information:
(1)Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics, School of Medicine, Emory 
University, Atlanta, GA, USA.
(2)Department of Mathematics, University of Louisiana at Lafayette, Lafayette, 
LA, USA.
(3)Department of Biostatistics, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA.
(4)Department of Biostatistics and Computational Biology, University of 
Rochester, Rochester, NY, USA. robert_strawderman@urmc.rochester.edu.

This paper considers the problem of directly generalizing the R-estimator under 
a linear model formulation with right-censored outcomes. We propose a natural 
generalization of the rank and corresponding estimating equation for the 
R-estimator in the case of the Wilcoxon (i.e., linear-in-ranks) score function, 
and show how it can respectively be exactly represented as members of the 
classes of estimating equations proposed in Ritov (1990) and Tsiatis (1990). We 
then establish analogous results for a large class of bounded nonlinear-in-ranks 
score functions. Asymptotics and variance estimation are obtained as 
straightforward consequences of these representation results. The 
self-consistent estimator of the residual distribution function, and the 
mid-cumulative distribution function (and, where needed, a generalization of 
it), play critical roles in these developments.

Staphylococcus chromogenes as a cause of sequential mastitis episodes in a camel 
(Camelus dromedarius).

Ranjan R(1), Kuniyal A(2), Singh M(3), Jatoliya P(3), Kumar R(4), Ranjan A(4), 
Singathia R(4), Choudhary RK(3), Puniya AK(3).

Author information:
(1)ICAR-National Research Centre on Camel, Bikaner, Rajasthan, India. 
ranjanpau@gmail.com.
(2)ICAR-National Research Centre on Camel, Bikaner, Rajasthan, India. 
aruna.kuniyal1995@gmail.com.
(3)ICAR-National Research Centre on Camel, Bikaner, Rajasthan, India.
(4)College of Veterinary and Animal Sciences, Rajasthan University of Veterinary

Staphylococcus chromogenes is a coagulase-negative Staphylococci, reported to 
cause mastitis in cows and other dairy animals. This report describes sequential 
mastitis episodes caused by S. chromogenes in a single-hump camel from 
Rajasthan, India. One six-year-old Mewari she camel in second lactation showed 
two episodes of mastitis. S. chromogenes was isolated during both episodes from 
affected udder quarters. The isolate from second episode was later evaluated 
which was catalase-positive, coagulase-negative, non-hemolytic, and positive for 
arginine dihydrolase 1, had ability of L-lactate alkalinisation and grow in 6.5% 
NaCl; but negative for phosphatase and urease test. The isolate was found 
sensitive to a range of antibiotics. Phylogenetic analysis using 16 S rDNA 
sequences revealed that the isolate had close genetic relationship with the 
isolates from bovine mastitis from South Africa and Turkey. However, S. borealis 
and S. haemolyticus isolated from earlier cases of subclinical mastitis from the 
same camel herd formed a separate cluster. These findings suggest that S. 
chromogenes may represent a potential causative agent of mastitis in dromedary 
camels, highlighting the need for further investigations involving a larger 
number of animals to confirm its role in the disease.

PURPOSE: Enterocytozoon bieneusi is a microsporidium, and Giardia duodenalis is 
an important intestinal pathogen, both infect a wide range of hosts, including 
cattle. This study investigated the seasonal distribution and genetic diversity 
of these pathogens in dairy cattle in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, China.
METHODS: A total of 505 fecal samples were collected from an intensive dairy 
farm during different seasonal sampling periods in 2024. Genomic DNA was 
extracted, and the internal transcribed spacer region of E. bieneusi and the 
small subunit (SSU) rRNA, beta-giardin (bg), glutamate dehydrogenase (gdh), and 
triosephosphate isomerase (tpi) genes of G. duodenalis were amplified by nested 
polymerase chain reaction and sequenced.
RESULTS: Overall prevalence of E. bieneusi and G. duodenalis was 26.53% and 
29.90%, respectively. E. bieneusi predominated in spring and winter, whereas G. 
duodenalis predominated in autumn and winter. The genotypes of E. bieneusi were 
BEB4, J, and Horse1 alongside the HHOT1-12, with genotype BEB4 being dominant. 
G. duodenalis assemblages were identified as A, B, and E, with assemblage E 
being dominant.
CONCLUSIONS: To the best of our knowledge, this study reports the first 
systematic investigation of the seasonal distribution of E. bieneusi and G. 
duodenalis in cattle in Inner Mongolia, providing important baseline data for 
understanding their epidemiology.

Metformin has received increasing attention for benefits beyond blood glucose 
lowering. The purpose of this study was to identify changes in whole blood 
transcriptome from a course of metformin in a randomized trial (NCT02684578) of 
nondiabetic older adults with age-related macular degeneration (AMD). We 
included patients who were ≥ 55 years of age, nondiabetic, and had geographic 
atrophy due to AMD. We excluded patients with metformin use for another reason, 
reduced renal or liver function, or other vitreoretinal diseases. Participants 
were randomized to metformin or control. The metformin group was prescribed

approached for consent to blood sample collection. We performed metagenomic 
sequencing on whole blood samples and conducted differential expression 
analysis. Fifteen patients underwent blood collection, with eight in the

statistical significance of difference between groups after correction for

score = -2.2). There was possible inhibition of upstream proinflammatory 
molecules and activation of anti-inflammatory molecules by metformin. In this 
small sub-study of a randomized trial, no gene was significantly changed after 
metformin exposure. Pathway enrichment analysis identified signals potentially 
consistent with metformin-associated modulation of "inflammaging" and other 
biological pathways which require validation in larger cohorts.

Colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) are a major cause of mortality in colorectal 
cancer and are characterised by a profoundly immunosuppressive tumour 
microenvironment in which tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) play a central 
role. However, the molecular mechanisms driving TAM plasticity and maintenance 
remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated macrophage heterogeneity in CRLM 
and examined the contribution of the epigenetic regulator lysine-specific 
demethylase 1 (LSD1) to TAM polarisation. Analysis of patient-derived specimens 
by flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry and transcriptional profiling identified 
a population of large TAMs (L-TAMs) enriched in the peritumoral niche that 
displayed an immunosuppressive, M2-like phenotype and was associated with poor 
clinical outcome. In contrast, smaller TAMs (S-TAMs) exhibited a more 
inflammatory transcriptional programme, including increased IL1β expression. 
Tumour-conditioned media reproduced these distinct macrophage phenotypes in 
vitro, indicating that tumour-derived factors actively shape TAM identity. 
Pharmacological inhibition of LSD1 using baicalin or INCB059872 reduced the 
expression of CD206 and the immune checkpoint molecule PD-L1, consistent with 
macrophage reprogramming away from a tumour-promoting state. Collectively, these 
findings identify LSD1 as an epigenetic regulator of macrophage plasticity in 
CRLM, implicated in the maintenance of immunosuppressive TAM phenotypes, and 
potentially able to induce phenotypic reversion. Our findings identify LSD1 as a 
regulator of TAM phenotype and support further investigation of LSD1 targeting 
as a strategy to remodel the metastatic tumour microenvironment and potentially 
enhance anti-tumour immunity.

Priya R(1), Ragul G(1), Ritika G(1), Kannan K(1)(2), Ganapathy D(3), Pitchiah 
S(4)(5).

Author information:
(1)Centre for Marine and Aquatic Research (CMAR), Saveetha Institute of Natural

(3)Department of Prosthodontics, Saveetha Dental College and Hospitals, Saveetha

(4)Centre for Marine and Aquatic Research (CMAR), Saveetha Institute of Natural

(5)Department of Marine Sciences, Saveetha Institute of Natural and Physical

Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) represents a significant clinical burden, 
with limited advancements in metabolic-targeted therapies. Arginase is a 
metalloenzyme that plays an essential role in the hydrolysis of L-arginine into 
urea and L-ornithine. In recent years, arginase enzyme also shows promising role 
in therapeutic especially in anti-cancer therapy through arginine deprivation 
therapy (ADT). Among many tumors that are arginine-auxotrophic due to 
downregulation of ASS1 are hepatocellular carcinoma, melanoma, and subsets of 
oral cancers, and are therefore susceptible to depletion of extracellular 
arginine. Although recombinant human arginase has advanced to preclinical and 
clinical trials, issues such as immunological reactions and limited stability 
have sparked interest in alternative sources. Marine microorganisms, especially 
from deep-sea environments, are known to produce unique and stable enzymes with 
high catalytic efficiency and are less prone to protein denaturation. As a 
result of their remarkable stability in harsh conditions and variety of 
structures, marine microbial arginases have emerged as the top candidates for 
investigation. In addition to remaining active at varying pH, salinity, and 
temperatures, these enzymes offer a versatile platform for protein engineering 
and therapeutic optimisation. This review focuses on the biochemical and 
structural properties of arginase, compares microbial and human forms, and 
explores the mechanisms of its antitumor action, including tumor cell growth 
inhibition, angiogenesis modulation, and immune suppression within the tumor 
microenvironment. Additionally, it identifies developments in marine 
bioprospecting, combination strategies with immunotherapy, and 
nanoparticle-based delivery as major trends influencing future research.

20-year analysis of protocol-driven quality improvement in cardiac homograft 
banking.

Baruji MA(1), Syed Nong SN(2), Abdul Aziz KA(2), Nordin MN(2), Md Taib ME(2), 
Gaaffar IF(2), Kepli AS(2), Sallehuddin A(2).

Author information:
(1)Institut Jantung Negara, 145 Jalan Tun Razak, 50400, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. 
ashraffbaruji@ijn.com.my.
(2)Institut Jantung Negara, 145 Jalan Tun Razak, 50400, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

Cardiac homografts are indispensable in complex cardiac surgery, particularly in 
the paediatric population. Optimising procurement and minimising discard rates 
are important for maintaining graft availability, especially in resource-limited 
settings. This study evaluated 20 years of cardiac homograft procurement at a 
tertiary cardiovascular centre, focusing on discard rates, causes of discard, 
microbiological profiles, and the impact of protocol refinements. A 
retrospective analysis was conducted using procurement records from the Cardiac 
Homograft Tissue Bank at the Institut Jantung Negara, Malaysia, between January 
2004 and December 2024. The data collected included annual procurement volume, 
reasons for discarding, and microbiological culture results. In 2015, a revised 
procurement protocol was introduced, which incorporated instrument and operative 
field segregation, aseptic redraping, and enhanced donor screening. A total of 
190 hearts were procured (mean 9.05 ± 4.18 hearts/year), with an overall discard 
rate of 13.7% (of 26/190). Prior to 2015, the discard rate was 17.2% (20/116), 
with environmental contamination accounting for the majority of the discards 
(75%; n=15). Fifteen microbial isolates were identified in the pre-revision 
period: Candida (n=6), Klebsiella (n=4), Acinetobacter (n=2), Streptococcus spp. 
(n=1), Streptococcus viridans (n=1), and Pseudomonas spp. (n=1). Following the 
2015 protocol revision, the overall discard rate decreased to 8.1% (6/74), 
representing a 53% reduction, although this difference was not statistically 
significant (p=0.074). Environmental contamination-related discards decreased 
significantly from 12.9% (15/116) to 1.4% (1/74) (89% reduction; p=0.005), with 
only one Candida isolate identified post-revision. Protocol refinement has 
therefore produced a statistically significant reduction in 
contamination-related discards and a shift in the microbiological spectrum.

Young adults' understanding of, and reaction to, those with uncertain genetic 
results.

Ulph F(1), Fifield K(2), Christie G(2), Horowitz E(2).

Author information:
(1)Manchester Centre for Health Psychology, Division of Psychology & Mental 
Health, School of Health Sciences, Faculty of Biology, Medicine and Health, 
Manchester Academic Health Science Centre, University of Manchester, Oxford 
Road, Manchester, M13 9PL, UK. fiona.ulph@manchester.ac.uk.
(2)Manchester Centre for Health Psychology, Division of Psychology & Mental 
Health, School of Health Sciences, Faculty of Biology, Medicine and Health,

BACKGROUND: Genetic advances increase the likelihood that children may receive 
uncertain diagnoses such as cystic fibrosis screen positive inconclusive 
diagnosis (CFSPID) from newborn screening. Research suggests a profound impact 
on parents. Research is needed to understand the impact on the child, especially 
at key developmental points such as young adulthood, when identity forms. As 
young adults (YA) are influenced by peer reactions, this novel study explored 
YAs' sensemaking of CFSPID, and their hypothetical reactions to peers or 
romantic partners with CFSPID.
METHODS: Four focus groups were conducted and analysed using thematic analysis 
across three sections: understanding, peer and romantic relationships.
RESULTS: Understanding: Without knowledge about CFSPID, participants used cystic 
fibrosis, genetic and contagious illness knowledge to form assumptions. Peer and 
romantic relationships: In both sections, YAs wanted to support their 
friend/partner; however, their responses revealed assumptions that a person with 
CFSPID would need more physical and psychological support and would be seen 
differently by some. Most wanted to learn more but were unsure whether it was 
appropriate to ask the person with CFPSID. Although rare, some reported they 
would avoid romantic relationships with YAs with CFSPID. All data suggesting 
people with CFPSID would be treated differently was based on erroneous 
assumptions due to a lack of CFSPID knowledge. Providing information about how 
CFPSID is different from CF did not appear sufficient to stop a reliance on CF 
knowledge when making sense of CFSPID.
CONCLUSION: Further research should explore whether it's possible to change 
assumptions when YAs disclose uncertain results.

Neonatal gastric perforation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical 
characteristics, risk factors, surgical management and outcomes.

Najar FA(1), Ganayee MA(2), Nabi U(3).

Author information:
(1)Government Medical College, Srinagar, India. fayazgmc91@gmail.com.
(2)Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences, Soura, Srinaga, India.
(3)Government Medical College, Srinagar, India.

BACKGROUND: Neonatal gastric perforation (NGP) is a rare but life-threatening 
surgical emergency of the newborn. We systematically reviewed its clinical 
characteristics, risk factors, surgical management and outcomes.
METHODS: Five databases were searched from inception to 31 December 2025 for 
observational studies reporting at least five neonates (≤ 28 days) with 
confirmed gastric perforation. Two reviewers independently screened records, 
extracted data and appraised quality. Proportions were pooled using 
random-effects models; predictors of mortality were summarised as odds ratios 
(OR). The review followed PRISMA 2020 and was registered in the International 
Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO).
RESULTS: Twenty studies (410 neonates) were included. Pooled prevalences were 
prematurity 58.3%, low birth weight 63.5% and male sex 59.0%; abdominal 
distension (90.5%) and pneumoperitoneum (80.9%) were the commonest features. 
Primary repair was performed in 78.4% of operated neonates. Pooled in-hospital 
mortality was 28.6% (95% CI 22.0-36.3%). Sepsis at presentation (OR 4.10) and 
delay to surgery beyond 24 h (OR 3.55) were the strongest predictors of death.
CONCLUSIONS: NGP mainly affects premature, low-birth-weight neonates, and still 
carries approximately 28% mortality. Early recognition, prompt treatment of 
sepsis and timely surgery offer the clearest route to improved survival.
PROSPERO ID: CRD420261436438.

Mechanistic Role of Layer 5-to-2/3 Recurrent Feedback in TMS-Evoked Motor 
Potentials.

Mahmouie S(1), Saviz M(1), Baghdadi G(2), Towhidkhah F(1).

Author information:
(1)Biomedical Engineering Department, Amirkabir University of Technology (Tehran 
Polytechnic), Tehran, Islamic Republic of Iran.
(2)Biomedical Engineering Department, Amirkabir University of Technology (Tehran 
Polytechnic), Tehran, Islamic Republic of Iran. baghdadi.golnaz@gmail.com.

Objective We aimed to develop and validate a personalized neural field theory 
(NFT) model of the motor cortex incorporating recurrent connections from layer 5 
to layers 2/3. Methods We extended the established feedforward model of Wilson 
et al. (2021) by adding recurrent feedback connections. Synaptic coupling 
coefficients were derived using a bottom-up approach from microanatomical data 
and calibrated via Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) against experimental 
input-output (IO) curves. The model was then personalized for individuals by 
optimizing three recurrent weighted gains ([Formula: see text]). We simulated 
single-pulse IO curves, paired-pulse protocols (SICI, ICF, LICI), and responses 
to intermittent and continuous theta-burst stimulation (iTBS/cTBS). Results The 
model revealed a sigmoidal, non-linear relationship between TMS intensity and 
neuronal input, in contrast to previous linear assumptions. Recurrent weighted 
inhibitory gain ([Formula: see text]) was critical for generating realistic 
short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI). Also, this parameter was the 
dominant parameter for personalization, successfully fitting 13/18 iTBS and 
15/18 cTBS individual response profiles. The model demonstrated that SICI/ICF 
and LICI emerge from protocol-specific tuning of the same recurrent 
microcircuit, with LICI requiring a greater suppression of recurrent excitation 
consistent with GABAB mediation. Our model showed superior generalizability, 
achieving robust fits on an independent cTBS dataset not used for initial 
calibration. Conclusion We present a unified, mechanistically interpretable NFT 
model identifying inhibitory feedback as a primary regulator of TMS dynamics and 
inter-individual variability. Significance This work advances the Wilson (2021) 
model by providing a biologically grounded framework that links clinical TMS 
metrics to specific cortical circuits, offering a powerful tool for optimizing 
personalized neuromodulation therapies.

Primary cardiac angiosarcoma: From pathogenesis to therapeutic strategies.

Gao H(1), Zhang H(1), Zhu D(1), Zhang Y(1), Guo M(2), Zhu M(1), Wang Y(#)(2), 
Yang M(#)(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Ultrasound, Shandong Provincial Hospital Affiliated to Shandong 
First Medical University, Jinan, 250021, China.
(2)Department of Neurology, Shandong Provincial Hospital Affiliated to Shandong 
First Medical University, Jinan, China.
(3)Department of Ultrasound, Shandong Provincial Hospital Affiliated to Shandong 
First Medical University, Jinan, 250021, China. yangmingys@163.com.
(#)Contributed equally

Primary cardiac angiosarcoma (PCAS) is a rare yet highly aggressive malignancy 
arising from cardiac vascular endothelial cells. This tumor predominantly 
affects young to middle-aged males and carries a dismal prognosis, typically 
characterized by a median survival of less than one year. Owing to its 
nonspecific manifestations and rapid infiltrative growth, most patients present 
at an advanced or metastatic stage. Recent genomic and transcriptomic studies 
have revealed molecular drivers in PCAS, including recurrent mutations in POT1, 
KDR/VEGFR2, and PLCG1, loss of CDKN2A, and aberrant angiogenic cascade 
activation. In parallel, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment dominated 
by exhausted T cells and tumor-associated macrophages may collectively 
contribute to tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. Multimodal imaging, 
integrating echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance, computed tomography, 
and PET/CT, plays a central role in detection, tissue characterization, and 
systemic staging. Histopathology with immunohistochemistry remains the 
diagnostic gold standard. Current treatment strategies rely on multimodal 
approaches, including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, with emerging 
targeted therapies and immunotherapies under active investigation. Despite 
recent advances, clinical outcomes remain poor, highlighting the urgent need for 
improved mechanistic understanding and more effective personalized therapeutic 
strategies.

Not everywhere, not always: 30 targeted PFAS in ambient surface waters of 
Queensland, Australia.

Baddiley B(1), Myburgh A(2), Vardy S(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation, Water Quality 
Monitoring and Investigations, Water Ecosystem Science, Ecosciences Precinct, 
Yuggera, Dutton Park, GPO Box 2454, Brisbane, QLD, 4001, Australia. 
brenda.baddiley@detsi.qld.gov.au.
(2)Department of Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation, Water Quality 
Monitoring and Investigations, Water Ecosystem Science, Ecosciences Precinct, 
Yuggera, Dutton Park, GPO Box 2454, Brisbane, QLD, 4001, Australia.

This study provides a summary of ambient concentrations of 30 commonly analysed 
perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) at 54 sites adjacent to various land use types 
across the east coast of Queensland, Australia. Sites were sampled for surface 
water every 2 months for a year (2019-2020). The results showed higher 
concentrations of PFAS in surface waters adjacent to major city areas (e.g. 
urban, industrial, residential land use types), and the lowest in surface waters 
adjacent to remote and regional areas (e.g. national parks, agriculture land use 
types). Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) was the most reported compound (in 
53% of samples), ranging from < 0.1 to 0.4 ng L-1 in remote areas, < 0.1 to 
0.6 ng L-1 in outer regional areas, < 0.1 to 4.7 ng L-1 in inner regional areas, 
and < 0.1 to 37.0 ng L-1 in major cities. No PFAS were reported at nine of the 
54 sites during the six monitoring rounds, and 16 out of 30 PFAS were not 
reported at any of the sites sampled over the year. Although PFAS (such as PFOS) 
are described as ubiquitous, the results from this ambient monitoring program 
indicate that this assumption does not necessarily apply to all ambient surface 
waters in Queensland.
