Integrating ultrasound teaching is associated with higher medical student 
assessment performance and positive perceptions of learning anatomy: A 
multi-site mixed-methods study.

Mathangasinghe Y(1), Keshav H(1), Reid C(1), Hernandez-Salazar B(1), Nathan 
V(1), Dunlop D(1), Rogik V(1), Tantisirivat P(1), Chan S(1), Foo M(1), Thomas 
A(1), Higgins A(1), Tay S(1), Mayhew J(1), Massey JS(1), Le N(2), Chen J(2), 
Pamidi N(3), Stephens GC(1), Gonsalvez DG(1)(4), Pereira I(5).

Author information:
(1)Centre for Human Anatomy Education, Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health 
Sciences, Monash University, Clayton, Victoria, Australia.
(2)Monash Imaging Ultrasound, Monash Health, Clayton, Victoria, Australia.
(3)Jeffrey Cheah School of Medicine and Health Sciences, Monash University, 
Subang Jaya, Malaysia.
(4)Department of Anatomy and Physiology, Melbourne University, Parkville, 
Victoria, Australia.
(5)Department of Medical Imaging and Radiation Sciences, Faculty of Medicine, 
Nursing and Health Sciences, Monash University, Clayton, Victoria, Australia.

The integration of ultrasound imaging into preclinical anatomy teaching is often 
questioned with respect to its objective impact on anatomical knowledge. This 
study aimed to (i) evaluate short-term knowledge gain following 
ultrasound-integrated anatomy teaching, (ii) characterize students' perceptions 
of the learning experience, and (iii) assess the feasibility of delivery across 
rural, metropolitan, and international settings. Integrated ultrasound sessions 
were delivered to preclinical medical students in four settings (rural 
Australian graduate-entry, metropolitan Australian direct-entry, and 
metropolitan and rural Malaysian direct-entry). Short-term knowledge gain was 
assessed in the Australian rural cohort using a pretest-posttest design with 
counterbalanced parallel forms, analyzed with linear mixed-effects models. 
Student feedback underwent content analysis and feasibility was summarized using 
key implementation descriptors. In the short-term knowledge gain study (103 
students; 193 observed assessments), posttest performance was significantly 
higher than pretest performance (adjusted mean difference 0.66 correct answers, 
95% confidence interval [CI] 0.23-1.08; p = 0.003). Students reported benefits 
for in situ visualization, spatial understanding, and clinical relevance. 
Delivery was feasible at all four sites, including by videoconference where no 
local ultrasound unit was available. In conclusion, integrated ultrasound was 
feasible across diverse settings and, in the Australian rural cohort, was 
associated with higher assessment performance immediately after teaching. As the 
design had no parallel comparator, this finding indicates short-term knowledge 
gain rather than a causal effect or long-term retention. Together, these 
findings support ultrasound as a complementary preclinical tool, rather than 
being reserved solely for post-curricular clinical skill acquisition.

Semantic distance metrics in anatomy education: Toward AI-assisted mapping of 
anatomy-to-clinical reasoning.

Kasirga UB(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Anatomy, Bahcesehir University School of Medicine, Istanbul, 
Turkey.

Anatomy education traditionally emphasizes structural knowledge acquisition, 
with the implicit assumption that clinical reasoning capabilities will naturally 
follow. However, the cognitive pathway from anatomical understanding to clinical 
application is rarely linear or uniform. This article proposes a conceptual 
framework in which semantic distance-the conceptual separation between 
anatomical knowledge and clinical endpoints-operates at three analytically 
distinct levels: (1) the learner's internal cognitive network, shaped by prior 
experience and schema formation; (2) the structural distance within curriculum 
maps, ontologies, or knowledge graphs; and (3) the distributional proximity 
within large language model (LLM) embedding spaces, which may serve as a 
scalable computational proxy indicator for the first two levels. These three 
levels must be explicitly distinguished if semantic distance is to function as a 
useful construct in anatomy education. To illustrate the framework's utility, 
three worked examples are developed-the femoral nerve, coronary circulation, and 
spinal cord anatomy-accompanied by a preliminary computational illustration of 
embedding distances rather than an empirically validated diagnostic instrument. 
A practical educator workflow is proposed through which computational signals 
may be translated into targeted curriculum decisions. The article positions 
semantic distance metrics as complementary to curriculum network analytics and 
highlights how cross-domain transitions (from anatomy through physiology and 
pathology to clinical presentation) represent qualitatively different 
educational problems requiring different interventions. Prospective validation 
studies, multimodal computational approaches, and longitudinal curriculum 
outcome analyses are needed before this framework can be applied systematically.

during mitosis.

Vaquero-Pelaz D(1), Rodriguez-Rodriguez JA(1)(2), Ilinca MC(1), Casas-Fernández 
E(1), Picard A(1), Del Caño-Ochoa F(3)(4), Vernia I(1), Gabaldón T(5)(6)(7)(8), 
Juanes MA(9)(10), Queralt E(1).

Author information:
(1)Instituto de Biomedicina de Valencia (IBV-CSIC) , Valencia, Spain.
(2)Molecular Biology Program, Sloan Kettering Institute, Memorial Sloan 
Kettering Cancer Center , New York, NY, USA.
(3)Structure of Macromolecular Targets Unit, Instituto de Biomedicina de 
Valencia (IBV), CSIC, Valencia, Spain.
(4)Valencia Biomedical Research Foundation, Centro de Investigación Príncipe 
Felipe (CIPF), Associated Unit to the Instituto de Biomedicina de Valencia (IBV) 
, Valencia, Spain.
(5)Life Sciences Department, Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC), Barcelona,

(6)Mechanisms of Disease Program, Institute for Research in Biomedicine (IRB), 
The Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology , Barcelona, Spain.
(7)ICREA, Pg. Lluis Companys 23 , Barcelona, Spain.

(9)National Horizons Centre, Teesside University , Darlington, UK.
(10)Centro de Investigacion Principe Felipe , Valencia, Spain.

Accurate chromosome segregation during mitosis requires the precise regulation 
of separase, a protease that cleaves cohesin to trigger the separation of sister 
chromatids. Here, we identify the AMPK-activating kinase Sak1 as a novel 
regulator of separase in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Using a suppressor screen, we 
discovered a hypermorphic SAK1-E50K allele that restored separase activity and 
nuclear localization in esp1-2 and pds1Δ mutants. We demonstrated that Sak1 
phosphorylates separase independently of Snf1 activation, enhancing its 
enzymatic function and promoting nuclear accumulation. Loss of Sak1 delays Cdc14 
activation and phenocopies FEAR pathway defects, establishing Sak1 as a mitotic 
regulator. Extending these findings to humans, we demonstrated that human 
separase and the tumor suppressor kinase LKB1, which is homologous to Sak1, 
physically associate. This finding reveals an evolutionarily conserved 
regulatory link between LKB1 and separase, highlighting the kinase-protease 
interplay as a critical mechanism for ensuring faithful mitotic progression.

Objective rest-activity rhythm amplitude and lung function in US adults: A 
cross-sectional analysis of the 2011-2012 National Health and Nutrition 
Examination Survey.

Wang HJ(1), Mo T(1).

Author information:
(1)Tuberculosis Department, Zhejiang Hospital of Integrated Traditional Chinese 
and Western Medicine, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China.

This cross-sectional analysis of 4,150 US adults from the 2011-2012 NHANES 
examined associations between wrist-accelerometry-derived rest-activity rhythm 
metrics and respiratory outcomes spanning spirometry, exhaled nitric oxide, and 
self-reported respiratory symptoms and diagnoses. Relative amplitude (RA), 
interdaily stability, intradaily variability, M10, L5, and cosinor parameters 
were derived from hourly monitor-independent movement summary (MIMS) values. The 
co-primary outcomes were FEV1 and FVC z-scores (GLI 2012); secondary outcomes 
included FEV1/FVC, FeNO, and latent-class-derived respiratory phenotypes. 
Survey-weighted linear regression with progressive adjustment for demographics, 
socioeconomic factors, BMI, smoking, depression, and wear time was employed, 
with activity volume (M10 and total daily activity) addressed in dedicated 
sensitivity models. Each 1-SD increase in RA was associated with a 0.108 higher 
FEV1 z-score (95% CI: 0.053-0.164; p < 0.001), with concordant signals for 
cosinor amplitude and M10. Each 1-SD increase in RA was also associated with a 
0.120 higher FVC z-score (95% CI: 0.073-0.166; p < 0.001), a magnitude 
comparable to that for FEV1. This association persisted in never-smokers, those 
without diagnosed respiratory disease, and after adjusting for total activity 
volume. No amplitude metric was associated with FEV1/FVC or FeNO. Rhythm metrics 
did not independently distinguish respiratory phenotypes after full covariate 
adjustment. In conclusion, a stronger day-night activity contrast was associated 
with higher FEV1 and FVC z-scores, but not with FEV1/FVC, FeNO or adjusted 
respiratory phenotype membership, and this association was not attenuated by 
adjustment for M10 or total daily activity volume. Prospective studies with 
repeated accelerometry and post-bronchodilator spirometry are required to 
determine whether the day-night activity contrast has predictive value for 
lung-function decline.

INTRODUCTION: Non-invasive tests (NITs) accurately detect fibrosis and may 
reduce the need for liver biopsy (LB). Detection of advanced fibrosis (≥F3) is 
clinically important for prognosis, but few studies have explored the use of 
NITs in patients with Wilson Disease (WD).
METHODS: In this multicentre observational study, adult and pediatric WD 
patients from seven international expert centers with histologic fibrosis 
staging were included. NITs (Transient elastography (TE), Fibrosis-4 index 
(FIB-4), AST to platelet-ratio (APRI), Steatosis-associated fibrosis estimator 
(SAFE), and NAFLD fibrosis score (NFS)) and clinical data were collected. NITs 
were compared with liver biopsy (LB) to detect advanced fibrosis (≥F3).
RESULTS: In total, 123 patients were included: median age was 30 years (IQR 
17.4, 43.1); time from WD diagnosis to LB was 6.7 months (0.7, 144.1); 30.9% had 
advanced fibrosis (≥F3), while concomitant metabolic risk factors (obesity and 
diabetes) were rare. Overall, 64 patients had NITs measured within 1 year of the 
LB and constituted the primary analysis group. All NITs, except FIB-4, were 
significantly elevated in patients with ≥F3. TE had the best overall accuracy 
(AUC=0.79), and performed well at an optimized cut-off of ≥8.35 kPa (sens=0.88, 
spec=0.85). APRI had lower accuracy, but effectively ruled out ≥F3 at the 
optimized cut-off of ≥1.3 (AUC=0.71, sens=0.38, spec=1.00). Combining those into 
a score (APRITE) achieved an AUC of 0.88.
DISCUSSION: TE demonstrated good diagnostic performance for identifying advanced 
fibrosis in WD. APRI showed high specificity, while the exploratory APRITE score 
showed encouraging performance.

Key agricultural pesticides responsible for acute pesticide poisoning in rural 
Sri Lanka - data to guide policy decisions.

Weerasinghe M(1)(2)(3), Karunarathne A(4), Eddleston M(2)(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Community Medicine, Faculty of Medicine & Allied Sciences, 
Rajarata University of Sri Lanka, Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka.
(2)Centre for Pesticide Suicide Prevention, and Pharmacology, Toxicology and 
Therapeutics, Centre for Cardiovascular Science, University of Edinburgh, 
Edinburgh, UK.
(3)South Asian Clinical Toxicology Research Collaboration, Faculty of Medicine, 
University of Peradeniya, Peradeniya, Sri Lanka.
(4)Medical Services, Ministry of Health, Colombo, Sri Lanka.

INTRODUCTION: Acute pesticide poisoning is a major public health problem among 
agricultural communities in low-and middle-income countries. Using recent 
surveillance data, this analysis identifies key pesticides responsible for acute 
poisoning in Sri Lanka to inform timely, evidence-based policy interventions, 
with relevance to similar agricultural settings.
METHODS: We analyzed interim data from two prospective studies in rural Sri 
Lanka: 1) a suicide surveillance system (Oct 2023-Apr 2025) and 2) a 
community-based cohort of 1,200 pesticide sprayers (Jan-Dec 2024). 
Self-poisoning deaths were identified through police, coroner, and household 
follow-up data, while occupational poisoning was monitored through bimonthly 
cohort follow-up. Descriptive analyses were identified the pesticides and active 
ingredients responsible for poisoning events.
RESULTS: Of 1,040 suicides identified, 236 (22.7%) involved pesticide ingestion; 
a single pesticide was confirmed in 184 (78.0%) of deaths. Insecticides 
accounted for 165/184 (89.7%) deaths, predominantly the carbamate carbosulfan 
(120/184, 65.2%; 95% Confidence Intervals (CI) 58.3-72.1) and organophosphorus 
profenofos (20/184, 10.9%; 95% CI 6.4-15.4), with a small proportion involving 
illegal pesticides (13/184, 7.1%) or herbicides (19/184, 10.3%). Pesticide 
sprayers reported 1,311 incidents of acute occupational pesticide poisoning, 
with 856 events occurring after use of a single identified pesticide. 
Insecticides were the most frequently implicated, led by profenofos (167/856, 
19.5%; 95% CI 16.9-22.1), followed by herbicides, including pretilachlor 
(125/856, 14.6%; 95% CI 12.2-17.0) and glyphosate (81/856, 9.5%; 95% CI 
7.5-11.5).
DISCUSSION: These findings show that most pesticide poisoning is concentrated in 
two insecticides: carbosulfan and profenofos. Their continued prominence despite 
earlier regulatory actions suggests ongoing pesticide substitution and 
highlights the need for strengthened surveillance and targeted regulation.
CONCLUSION: Carbosulfan and profenofos now account for most pesticide suicides 
in Sri Lanka, while profenofos is also the leading cause of acute occupational 
pesticide poisoning. These findings highlight the need for ongoing surveillance 
and timely regulatory review.

Sleep, Dietary Intake, and Physical Activity: Examining Bidirectionality Using 
Repeated-Measures Analyses.

Taylor RW(1), Haszard JJ(2), Wickham SR(3), Galland BC(4), Russell-Camp T(3), 
Jackson RF(3), Brosnan BJ(3), Meredith-Jones KA(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Medicine, University of Otago, Dunedin, New Zealand. Electronic 
address: Rachael.taylor@otago.ac.nz.
(2)Haszard Biostatistics, Balclutha, New Zealand.
(3)Department of Medicine, University of Otago, Dunedin, New Zealand.
(4)Department of Paediatrics and Child Health, University of Otago, Dunedin, New 
Zealand.

PURPOSE: Studies examining how sleep impacts diet and activity and vice versa 
have been limited by the use of aggregate data in cross-sectional designs. We 
examined how sleep might influence diet and physical activity the next day, and 
daytime diet and activity relate to sleep that night, using temporal 
repeated-measures analyses.
METHODS: Twenty-four-hour time use (sleep onset, wake after sleep onset, total 
sleep time, sedentary time, light physical activity [LPA], and moderate-vigorous 
physical activity [MVPA]) was measured (AX3 accelerometers) over 7 days in 
adolescents (11-14.9 years) in Dunedin, New Zealand (March-December 2021). 
Bedtime was reported in daily diaries. Multiple-pass 24-hour dietary recalls 
were collected on days 3, 5, and 7. Mixed-effects regression models were used 
with participants as a random effect, adjusted for weekend days.
RESULTS: In 75 youth (mean age 12.9 y, 36% indigenous Māori, 37.3% overweight or 
obese), going to bed 1 hour later was associated with less LPA (mean difference; 
95% confidence interval: -3.8 minutes; -6.1 to -1.6) and MVPA (-14.0 minutes; 
-22.6 to -5.3) the next day. By contrast, LPA and MVPA during the day were not 
related to sleep that night. On days when bedtime was later, youth were more 
sedentary (25 minutes; 11-39, for each hour later) and consumed significantly 
more energy from ultraprocessed (618 kJ; 248-988) and noncore (732 kJ; 350-1113) 
foods and less from core foods (-419 kJ; -781 to -57).
DISCUSSION: Sleep timing appears more strongly related to diet and physical 
activity than total sleep time in youth. Encouraging earlier bedtimes might be a 
practical target to reduce obesity risk.

Advancing Racial Equity for Black Youth Within Sexual Health Programming: A 
Targeted Literature Review.

Offiong A(1), Coles-Quander C(2), Wulah A(3), Guerra G(3), Gilbertsen J(4), Abdi 
F(3), Smith A(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Health Behavior & Health Equity, University of Michigan School 
of Public Health, Ann Arbor, Michigan; Child Trends, Incorporated, Rockville, 
Maryland.
(2)James Bell Associates, Arlington, Virginia.
(3)Child Trends, Incorporated, Rockville, Maryland.
(4)University of Michigan School of Social Work, Ann Arbor, Michigan.
(5)James Bell Associates, Arlington, Virginia. Electronic address: 
assare@umich.edu.

Black youth in the United States experience persistent sexual and reproductive 
health (SRH) disparities driven by systemic factors, including inequitable 
access to care, racism, discrimination, and deficit-based narratives within 
health programming. This targeted literature review synthesizes recent research 
to explore how programs can advance racial equity for Black youth to address SRH 
disparities. Incorporating perspectives from an expert panel and a rigorous 
review of studies from 2014 to 2024, the findings highlight three themes: (a) 
providing tailored, culturally responsive programs, (b) shifting from deficit 
frameworks to strengths-based approaches, and (c) amplifying and uplifting the 
voices of Black youth in program design and implementation. Evidence points to 
the need for SRH interventions that directly confront structural inequities and 
embrace frameworks such as reproductive justice, critical consciousness while 
acknowledging the diverse identities, and experiences of Black youth. The review 
underscores the importance of intersectionality, youth engagement, and 
community-driven solutions as foundations for promoting and advancing equity. 
These insights inform future research and practice to reduce disparities and 
foster well-being by centering the unique experiences of Black youth.

BACKGROUND: Hidradenitis suppurativa affects 0.7% to 1.5% of the global 
population and causes substantial disability and meaningfully impairs quality of 
life.
OBJECTIVE: To provide evidence-based recommendations for the management of 
hidradenitis suppurativa.
METHODS: A workgroup conducted a systematic review and applied the Grading of 
Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach to assess the 
certainty of evidence and to develop recommendations.
RESULTS: This guideline presents 37 evidence-based recommendations. Strong 
recommendations are made for adalimumab, bimekizumab, infliximab, secukinumab, 
and routine pain assessment. Conditional recommendations are made for topical 
clindamycin, resorcinol, and ruxolitinib; oral doxycycline, tetracycline, and

systemic corticosteroids; upadacitinib; specific procedural interventions; 
tobacco cessation; supportive pain management; and zinc supplementation and 
vitamin D repletion.
LIMITATIONS: Analysis is limited to best evidence available from systematic 
review.
CONCLUSIONS: These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for the 
management of hidradenitis suppurativa.

Dual-stage inhibition of Plasmodium falciparum by a Skeletocutis-derived fungal 
metabolite targeting pyruvate kinase II.

Hervé L(1), Amanzougaghene N(2), Amand S(3), Achache S(1), Blaud M(4), Coppée 
R(5)(6)(7), Fourati Z(4), Franetich J-F(2), Goor Q(1), Houzé S(1)(5), Lohezic 
M(1), Patat M(1), Sarrasin V(1)(5), Toure S(2), Zelie E(4), Soulard V(2), Mann 
S(3), Merckx A(1).

Author information:
(1)MERIT, Université Paris Cité, IRD, Inserm, Paris, France.
(2)Centre d'Immunologie et des Maladies Infectieuses, CIMI-Paris, Sorbonne 
Université, INSERM, CNRS, Paris, France.
(3)Molécules de Communication et Adaptation des Micro-Organismes UMR 7245, 
Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle, CNRS, Paris, France.
(4)CiTCoM, Université Paris Cité, CNRS, Paris, France.
(5)Centre National de Référence du Paludisme, AP-HP, Hôpital Bichat 
Claude-Bernard, Paris, France.
(6)Centre National de Référence Cryptosporidioses, Microsporidies et Autres 
Protozooses Digestives, Institut de Biologie Clinique, Centre Hospitalier 
Universitaire de Rouen, Rouen, France.
(7)Laboratoire de Parasitologie-Mycologie, UR ESCAPE, Université de Rouen 
Normandie, Rouen, France.

Plasmodium falciparum resistance to current first-line treatments is threatening 
at-risk populations and underscores the urgent need for novel therapeutic 
targets and drugs. P. falciparum pyruvate kinases I and II are two essential 
enzymes with distinct roles and subcellular localizations within the parasite. 
PfPyrKI is cytosolic, while PfPyrKII is found in the apicoplast, a specific 
organelle of Apicomplexa, where it is required for the production of (d)NTPs 
essential for apicoplast maintenance. We identify skeletocutin E, a 
basidiomycete-derived metabolite, as a specific inhibitor of PfPyrKII. 
Skeletocutin E inhibits in vitro the activity of PfPyrKII with an IC50 of 0.52 ± 
0.08 µM through a mixed inhibition mechanism and does not affect the activities 
of three human pyruvate kinases. Structure-activity relationship analyses using 
synthetic skeletocutin E analogs allowed us to identify the molecular 
determinants of this inhibition. Furthermore, determination of the quaternary 
structure of PfPyrKII by mass photometry showed that skeletocutin E does not 
alter the distribution of the complexes, indicating that it does not interact at 
the subunit interfaces. We addressed the expression of PfPyrKII in liver stages 
and confirmed its apicoplast localization. Importantly, skeletocutin E inhibits 
P. falciparum growth in both blood and liver stages, with IC₅₀ values of 3.56 ± 
0.50 µM in red blood cells and 3.70 ± 0.74 µM in primary human hepatocytes. 
Together, these findings establish PfPyrKII as a druggable antimalarial target 
and identify skeletocutin E as a promising lead compound for the rational 
development of dual-stage antimalarial therapies.

Birth and clinical outcomes of pregnant participants with advanced HIV disease.

Nalintya E(1), Poeschla A(2), Fieberg A(3), Nerima P(1), Ajilong E(1), Adzemovic 
T(1), Nakiganda F(1), Schwartz E(2), Dai B(3), Meya D(1), Boulware DR(4), 
Rajasingham R(4); ENCORE trial team.

Author information:
(1)Infectious Diseases Institute, Kampala, Uganda.
(2)University of Minnesota Medical School, Minneapolis, Minnesota 55455.
(3)University of Minnesota, Department of Biostatistics & Health Data Science, 
Minneapolis, Minnesota 55455.
(4)University of Minnesota, Department of Medicine, Minneapolis, Minnesota 
55455.

INTRODUCTION: Clinical trials for the evaluation of novel diagnostics and 
treatments for HIV-associated opportunistic infections have historically 
excluded pregnant persons. Little information is available regarding the 
clinical outcomes and pregnancy outcomes of pregnant persons with advanced HIV 
disease while taking opportunistic infection prophylaxis for tuberculosis (TB) 
and cryptococcosis. In this study, we describe characteristics at enrollment, 
clinical outcomes, and birth outcomes of pregnant people with advanced HIV in 
Uganda.
METHODS: We prospectively enrolled pregnant adults with advanced HIV disease 
within an on-going pragmatic cluster randomized clinical trial evaluating an 
enhanced screening and prophylaxis package for opportunistic infections 
(NCT05085171). The trial began enrollment in May 2022 and continues in 26 
outpatient HIV clinics in the Kampala and Wakiso districts of Uganda. We present 
an analysis of pregnant participants enrolled through April 30, 2025, including 
their characteristics at study enrollment, opportunistic infections, and birth 
outcomes.
RESULTS: Overall, 15% (114/766) of female participants with advanced HIV disease 
were pregnant. Median CD4 cell count was 124 cells/µL (IQR: 82-170). Median time 
since HIV diagnosis was 7 days, and 45% were ART-naive at enrollment. Compared 
with non-pregnant female participants, pregnant participants were less likely to 
have a positive cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) test (2% vs 7%, p=0.023), to have a 
positive Alere tuberculosis (TB) lipoarabinomannan (LAM) test (11% vs 28%, 
p<0.001), and to be receiving active TB treatment (14% vs 39%, p<0.001). 
Overall, 18% (21/114) experienced at least one opportunistic infection during 
the study, of which 71% (n=15) were attributed to TB. Eighty-six percent 
(98/114) of pregnancies were carried to term. Participants on TB preventive 
therapy (TPT) had 94% of deliveries at term (51/54), compared with 80% (36/45) 
among participants who did not receive TPT (OR = 4.25, 95%CI:1.07-16.80), and 
67% (8/12) among participants on active TB treatment (OR = 8.50, 95%CI: 
1.60-45.25).
CONCLUSIONS: Although the incidence of opportunistic infections is less commonly 
reported among pregnant women with advanced HIV disease, TB is the most frequent 
opportunistic infection. Participants on TPT had 4-fold higher odds of having a 
term delivery compared with those not on TPT and 8-fold higher odds compared 
with those with active TB.

Photoredox-catalyzed dehalogenation of aryl halides in an aerated supramolecular 
hydrogel enabled by triplet-triplet annihilation upconversion.

Domínguez PD(1)(2), Bonardd S(1)(2), Herrera-Luna JC(3), Jiménez MC(3), 
Pérez-Ruiz R(3), Díaz Díaz D(1)(2)(4).

Author information:
(1)AFM-NANO, Instituto Universitario de Bio-Orgánica Antonio González (IUBO-AG), 
Universidad de La Laguna, Avda. Astrofísico Francisco Sánchez 2, La Laguna 
38206, Spain. ddiazdiaz@ull.edu.es.
(2)Departamento de Química Orgánica, Universidad de La Laguna, Avda. Astrofísico 
Francisco Sánchez 3, La Laguna 38206, Spain.
(3)Departamento de Química, Universitat Politècnica de València, Camino de Vera

Triplet-triplet annihilation upconversion (TTA-UC) is a powerful strategy to 
access high-energy excited states under low-energy irradiation, yet its 
practical implementation simultaneously in aqueous and aerobic environments 
remains severely limited by dye insolubility and oxygen quenching. By 
integrating a sensitizer-emitter pair within a surfactant-assisted hydrogel 
matrix, TTA-UC emission is sustained in an EtOH/H2O (1 : 1 v/v) medium under 
ambient air, consistent with our previous photophysical characterization of this 
hydrogel platform. This work expands the applicability of intragel TTA-UC 
systems to the photoreduction of aryl and heteroaryl halides in aqueous media 
under aerobic conditions. Systematic optimization of key parameters, including 
base identity, surfactant concentration, gelator content, and irradiation 
protocol, affords reaction yields approaching 50% in aerated EtOH/H2O mixtures 
without prior deoxygenation. The results are consistent with the previously 
reported oxygen-tolerant behaviour of this hydrogel platform and further 
demonstrate that the system can be used as a reaction medium for aerobic 
photodehalogenation. Overall, this work establishes supramolecular hydrogels as 
soft photochemical reactors for oxygen-tolerant photocatalysis and expands the 
scope of TTA-UC-assisted photochemistry in predominantly aqueous media under 
aerobic conditions.

Involvement of general dental practitioners in epidemiologic data collection: 
insights from the Belgian Oral Health Dental Registration and Evaluation Survey.

Carvalho JC, Voortmans D, Bottenberg P, Lambert M, Declerck D.

OBJECTIVE: In 2023-2024, a national cross-sectional survey of the oral health of 
the Belgian population aged 5 years and older was conducted involving general 
dental practitioners. The objective of the present study was to critically 
reflect on the involvement of general dental practitioners in epidemiological 
oral health data collection.
METHOD AND MATERIALS: The Oral Health Data Registration and Evaluation Survey 
(OHDRES) 2023-2024 combines data from face-to-face interviews conducted within 
the national Health Interview Survey, oral health examinations, and selected 
health care utilization data from the Belgian Inter-Mutuality Agency registers. 
To standardize the oral health examination, an illustrated clinical guideline 
was developed. General dental practitioners collected oral health data after 
online training and calibration. Only dentists achieving ≥ 75% agreement with 
the benchmark were authorized to perform the oral examinations. Both 
participants and general dental practitioners received financial incentives to 
promote participation.
RESULTS: A total of 614 general dental practitioners were involved in data 
collection and performed 1,724 oral examinations. Completion of the training 
module took an average time of 50 min (± 5 min 58 s). The average time spent on 
calibration was 23 min 44 s (± 21 min 4 s). Most general dental practitioners 
succeeded in calibration on the first (81.6%) or second attempt (12.5%), while 
5.2% needed three or four attempts.
CONCLUSION: Involvement of general dental practitioners in oral health data 
collection is feasible yet challenging, requiring an investment of time, 
training and calibration, as well as the use of motivational incentives.

Minimally invasive implant-assisted removable partial dentures with surveyed 
crowns for atrophic edentulous arches: a retrospective case series with up to a 
67-month follow-up.

Lim NK, Lim JS, Kim SJ, Kim HY.

BACKGROUND: The rehabilitation of completely edentulous arches with fixed 
implant-supported prostheses is often precluded by systemic, anatomic, or 
financial constraints that necessitate invasive posterior bone grafting. While 
conventional implant overdentures offer a surgical compromise, they frequently 
present mechanical complications such as loss of attachment retention and 
gradual collapse of the vertical dimension of occlusion over the long term. To 
address these limitations, this clinical report introduces a versatile paradigm 
utilizing implant-supported surveyed crowns (ISSCs) to retain an 
implant-assisted removable partial denture (IARPD).
CASE PRESENTATION: This report details the rehabilitation of four completely 
edentulous patients utilizing this protocol for two distinct purposes. First, it 
served as a primary rehabilitation strategy to circumvent invasive posterior 
bone grafting in medically compromised patients. Second, it acted as a 
prosthodontic revision strategy that repurposed existing, well-integrated 
fixtures from failing conventional overdentures, resolving severe biological and 
mechanical complications caused by problematic attachments. By strategically 
utilizing anterior implants to support splinted ISSCs and a distal extension 
IARPD, this approach provided stable vertical occlusal support and mitigated 
destructive cantilever effects. Over a follow-up period of up to 67 months, 
clinical and radiographic evaluations demonstrated favorable peri-implant tissue 
health with minimal marginal bone resorption (mean 0.44 ± 0.24mm). Furthermore, 
mechanical complications were minor and readily manageable, and patients 
reported a high level of masticatory and esthetic satisfaction.
CONCLUSIONS: The ISSC-retained IARPD is a predictable and minimally invasive 
treatment option for completely edentulous patients. By successfully bridging 
the biomechanical gap between fixed prostheses and conventional overdentures, it 
serves as both a primary and revision treatment. The favorable clinical outcomes 
of this protocol requires strategic implant distribution, precise prosthodontic 
design, and regular monitoring to prevent biomechanical overload.

Global environmental and cardiometabolic correlates of periodontitis- ischemic 
heart disease co-burden: a spatiotemporal network analysis.

Wang L, Song J, Zhou X, Sun J, Yao Y.

BACKGROUND: Geographic co-occurrence patterns and shared risk factors between 
periodontitis and ischemic heart disease remain inadequately characterized 
globally. This study aimed to characterize country-level spatiotemporal 
co-burden patterns of periodontitis and ischemic heart disease, thereby helping 
identify regions and risk profiles in which integrated periodontal and 
cardiovascular prevention may be most relevant.
METHODS: An ecological analysis was conducted using Global Burden of Disease 
2021 data from 204 countries. Machine-learning-based feature selection was used 
to screen 68 risk factors. Countries were classified as concordant-burden, 
periodontitis-predominant, or IHD-predominant. Negative binomial regression and 
population attributable fractions (PAF) quantified risk contributions across 
6,528 country-year observations (1990-2021).
RESULTS: Periodontitis incidence (1,740.92/100,000) remained 2.2-fold higher 
than IHD. Analysis revealed 73 countries (35.96%) as IHD-dominant, 74 (36.45%) 
as periodontitis-dominant, and 56 (27.59%) with dual burdens. Elevated systolic 
blood pressure was the sole shared risk factor (RR 1.006-1.008). For IHD, 
insufficient whole grain intake showed the highest attributable fraction (PAF 
6.16%), followed by elevated BMI (4.17%) and high LDL cholesterol (3.87%); 
kidney dysfunction had the strongest per-unit association (RR 1.111) with a PAF 
of 2.98%. For periodontitis, lead exposure showed the largest model-derived PAF 
among the assessed factors (PAF 2.36%), followed by blood pressure (2.30%) and 
particulate matter (1.26%). Disease-specific factors accounted for 20.55% of IHD 
and 4.51% of periodontitis burden. Temporal analysis revealed strong 
synchronization in dual-burden regions (ρ=0.901, P<0.001).
CONCLUSION: Elevated blood pressure was the only shared population-level factor 
associated with both conditions. Kidney dysfunction and dietary factors were 
more strongly associated with IHD burden, whereas lead exposure and particulate 
matter were associated with periodontitis burden in ecological models. 
Geographically tailored interventions are essential: metabolic management in 
IHD-dominant regions and environmental remediation in periodontitis-predominant 
areas, particularly Eastern Europe, Central Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa. 
Clinically, the findings support greater attention to blood pressure and 
cardiometabolic risk assessment in patients with periodontitis, while 
emphasizing that causal links and intervention benefits require confirmation in 
individual-level studies.

Photobiomodulation therapy for the management of pain associated with 
temporomandibular disorders: a systematic review.

Vargas-Neri C, Benitez-Cárdenas O, Garrocho-Rangel A, Félix-Sicairos B, 
Noyola-Frías M, Martínez-Martínez R.

PURPOSE: To determine whether photobiomodulation (PBM; formerly low-level laser 
therapy) reduces temporomandibular disorder (TMD) pain relative to a concurrent 
comparator, to report the evidence by diagnostic stratum, and to appraise its 
certainty and dosimetric reporting.
STUDY SELECTION: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were 
searched from January 2016 to July 2026 for controlled clinical trials of PBM 
for TMD-related pain in participants diagnosed by RDC/TMD or DC/TMD criteria. 
The review followed PRISMA 2020 and was registered on the Open Science Framework 
(DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/YP8GW); screening, extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment 
were duplicated independently.
RESULTS: Nine reports representing eight independent cohorts were included. 
Protocols were markedly heterogeneous in wavelength (635-940 nm), energy density 
(5-300 J/cm²), number of sessions, and follow-up, precluding quantitative 
synthesis. Pain decreased from baseline in most PBM groups, but placebo groups 
often improved comparably and between-group superiority was less consistent: 
three of five myogenous cohorts favored PBM and two did not. Only one trial 
prespecified myalgia and arthralgia as separate strata, favoring PBM for 
arthralgia but not myalgia. No trial reported the complete World Association for 
Laser Therapy (WALT) parameter set. Certainty was low for myogenous and very low 
for arthrogenous TMD.
CONCLUSIONS: Photobiomodulation demonstrates pain reduction superior to sham 
controls in several myogenous TMD trials. However, due to low GRADE certainty 
and evidence inconsistency, it should be considered a complementary treatment 
option rather than a standalone therapy.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: TMD affects approximately 31% of adults and is a leading 
cause of chronic orofacial pain. PBM was safe, noninvasive, and free of reported 
adverse effects, and may be considered an adjunct within a conservative, 
multimodal plan for myogenous TMD. Clinicians should be aware that no preferred 
dosimetric protocol is established, that the joint-pain evidence rests on one 
small subgroup, and that placebo responses were substantial. PBM should not 
displace established conservative measures, and patients should be counseled 
that the expected benefit over placebo remains uncertain.

Yin-Yang: The Dual Role of Lactate as a Context-Dependent Immunometabolic 
Regulator in the Inflammatory Microenvironment.

Wang S(1)(2)(3), Gan P(1)(2)(3), Chen Y(1)(2)(3), Yang B(1)(3), Ding T(1)(3), Wu 
H(1)(2)(3).

Author information:
(1)College of Pharmacy, Anhui University of Chinese Medicine, Hefei, China.
(2)Key Laboratory of Xin'an Medicine, Ministry of Education, Anhui University of 
Chinese Medicine, Hefei, China.
(3)Anhui Provincial Key Laboratory of Chinese Medicinal Formula, Hefei, China.

Lactate, once regarded merely as the terminal product of glycolysis, is now 
recognised as a pivotal immunometabolic regulator that actively shapes 
inflammatory responses. However, accumulating evidence reveals an apparent 
paradox that lactate can either amplify immune activation or promote 
inflammation resolution depending on the biological context. The mechanisms 
underlying this functional duality remain incompletely understood, limiting the 
development of effective lactate-targeted therapies. In this review, we propose 
that lactate functions as a context-dependent immunometabolic rheostat whose 
Yin-Yang properties are determined by the integration of four key factors: 
lactate concentration, cellular identity, disease stage and inflammatory 
microenvironment. We summarise how lactate regulates immune responses through 
coordinated control of metabolic reprogramming, intercellular lactate shuttling, 
receptor-mediated signalling, intracellular sensing, and protein lactylation, 
thereby orchestrating the activation and resolution of inflammation. We further 
discuss the cell-specific actions of lactate across endothelial cells, 
macrophages, fibroblast-like synoviocytes, neutrophils, and lymphocytes, 
highlighting how these mechanisms collectively remodel the inflammatory 
microenvironment. Beyond mechanistic insights, we examine evidence from 
representative inflammatory disease models, including rheumatoid arthritis, 
sepsis, and atherosclerosis, and evaluate emerging therapeutic strategies 
targeting lactate production, transport, sensing and metabolism. Rather than 
advocating indiscriminate lactate inhibition, current evidence supports 
context-specific modulation of lactate signalling according to disease stage and 
immune landscape.

The missing metric in ecological studies: Land tenure system of territorial 
carnivores.

Kanishka(1)(2), Koley S(1)(2), Khan S(1), Hussain Z(1)(3), Sathyakumar S(1)(2), 
Habib B(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Animal Ecology and Conservation Biology, Wildlife Institute of 
India, Dehradun, India.
(2)Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), Ghaziabad, Uttar 
Pradesh, India.
(3)Department of Environmental Science and Technology, University of Maryland, 
College Park, Maryland, USA.

Land tenure is a fundamental ecological process in territorial animals; it 
reflects how individuals establish and maintain access to space and resources. 
First conceptualised by Hornocker in 1969, it provides an early understanding of 
population dynamics. However, this critical aspect for interpreting the 
stability, predictability and exclusivity of a population is rarely evaluated. 
To date, there has been no clear ecological definition of the land tenure 
system. To understand this concept, we review more than 50 years of research on 
territorial carnivores and synthesise how land tenure has been quantified across 
taxa. We examine how this aspect links population and demographic processes that 
lead to species conservation in various landscape scenarios. The goal is to 
develop a standardised approach across species and landscapes to evaluate land 
tenure by providing a framework and testable hypotheses. As land tenure provides 
critical insights into the spatial stability of populations and informs 
conservation planning, its limited integration into ecological studies remains 
concerning despite advances in population ecology and monitoring technologies. 
We attempted to build a foundation for future research that aims to measure 
population stability and species persistence.

Jeffrey's Insights: Next-generation sequencing for primary immunodeficiency 
diagnosis, 2019-2025.

Quinn J(1), Fernández-Tabanera E(#)(2), Perea-Romero I(#)(2), Leon-Otegui M(2), 
Moreno-Coca M(2), Palao B(2), Izquierdo L(2), Cirigliano V(2), Ting YL(3),

Author information:
(1)Jeffrey Modell Foundation , New York, NY, USA.
(2)Veritas Intercontinental , Madrid, Spain.

Primary immunodeficiencies (PI), or inborn errors of immunity (IEI), are a 
clinically heterogeneous group of more than 550 monogenic disorders for which 
early molecular diagnosis is essential to guide management and improve outcomes. 
To address global barriers to genetic testing, the Jeffrey Modell Foundation 
implemented Jeffrey's Insights, a no-cost next-generation sequencing (NGS) 
program delivered through the global Jeffrey Modell Centers Network. From 2019 
to 2025, 5,991 patients across 59 countries underwent NGS testing, resulting in 
a molecular diagnostic yield of 22.7%. Molecular diagnostic yields were highest 
in Australia and New Zealand (40.9%), Asia (31.6%), and the Middle East and 
Africa (31.3%). Among 1,482 patients with clinician-reported follow-up, NGS 
altered diagnosis (38.1%), management (37.0%), treatment (32.8%), and genetic 
counseling (50.6%), and improved clinical outcomes (31.3%). Physicians reported 
on healthcare utilization and barriers to care prior to testing. These findings 
underscore the value of NGS as an available first-tier test for suspected PI and 
highlight the need for broader global access to genomic diagnostics.

The ups and downs of human UNC93B1: Autoimmune and viral conditions.

Idiiatullina E(1), Casanova JL(1)(2)(3)(4)(5)(6)(7)(8)(9), Zhang

Author information:

Mouse Unc93b1 was identified in 2006 by forward genetics as an ER membrane 
protein essential for the activity of the endosomal nucleic acid-sensing 
receptors TLR3, TLR7, and TLR9. In vitro studies in mouse and human cells have 
revealed its cellular functions, including ER-based stabilization and 
trafficking of endosomal TLR proteins (TLR3, TLR7, TLR8, and TLR9) and 
regulation of signaling thresholds through competitive trafficking control (TLR7 
and TLR9). Human genetic studies have clarified the physiological role of 
UNC93B1 in natural conditions. Biallelic loss-of-function UNC93B1 mutations 
impair TLR3 signaling in central nervous system-resident cells, thereby 
conferring a predisposition to HSV-1 encephalitis. UNC93B1 deficiency may also 
predispose to other viral infections, as suggested by patients with inherited 
TLR3 or TLR7 deficiency. Conversely, monoallelic or biallelic UNC93B1 
gain-of-function variants enhancing TLR7 and/or TLR8 signaling predispose 
patients to autoimmunity and inflammation, including early-onset systemic lupus 
erythematosus and chilblain lupus. Thus, in humans, UNC93B1 maintains a delicate 
balance between host defense and tolerance to self.

Araújo Leite GA(1)(2), Simão VA(3), de Paiva Coimbra JL(4), Sanabria M(5).

Author information:
(1)Laboratório de Reprodução e Toxicologia (Laretox), Centro de Ciências

(2)Departamento de Biologia Celular, Embriologia e Genética, Centro de Ciências

(3)Departamento de Biologia Estrutural e Funcional, Instituto de Biociências,

(4)Instituto de Ciências Biomédicas, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, Rio

(5)Instituto de Biociências, Universidade Federal de Mato Grosso do Sul, Campo

Statins are the main medications prescribed to improve lipid profiles and avoid 
cardiovascular risks in humans. Preclinical studies have shown that statins may 
impair male reproduction; however, their effects on female reproduction remain 
unclear. This study conducted a systematic review of the literature regarding 
preclinical primary studies that assessed female reproductive outcomes in rodent 
models after exposure to statins. The studies were searched in the databases 
PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, LILACS, and SciELO, using distinct 
combinations of the search terms "statins", "ovary", "uterus", "female 
reproduction", "mice", "rats", followed by the Boolean operators AND or OR. 
Subsequently, duplicities and studies that did not meet the eligibility criteria 
were excluded from this review. Afterward, the risk of bias was evaluated 
through the 10 points of the SYRCLE's risk of bias tool. Extraction and 
qualitative analysis of the data were carried out, and whenever possible, a 
meta-analysis was applied to assess the data quantitatively. The results 
indicated that normocholesterolemic female rodents exposed to statins showed 
ovarian morphological changes, such as impaired follicular dynamics. 
Additionally, when rodents were induced with endometriosis or 
reproductive-related cancer, there was a reduction in the volume of 
endometriotic implants and a complementary action on the reduction of tumor 
proliferation, respectively. As a limitation, there were no studies assessing 
the effects of statins in hyperlipidemic rodents, which may make it difficult to 
translate the adverse effects of statins observed in normolipidemic rodents to 
humans.

in vitro and in vivo experimental findings to elucidate the mechanisms and 
consequences of B[a]P-induced histone modifications. In vitro studies 
demonstrate that B[a]P and its ultimate metabolite, BPDE, significantly alter 
key histone marks, including phosphorylation (γH2AX), acetylation 
(H3K9/14/18/27ac, H4K5/12/16ac), methylation (H3K4/9/27/36/79 me), lactylation 
(H4K12la), and ubiquitination (uH2A), in epithelial and connective cells. These 
changes are driven through multiple interconnected pathways: (1) Direct 
interference, where BPDE-dG adducts physically widen the DNA minor groove, 
entrapping histone tails and sterically blocking modifying enzymes; (2) 
Regulation of epigenetic enzymes, via modulating the expression/activity of 
HDACs, HATs, HMTs, and ubiquitin ligases; and (3) Oxidative stress and receptor 
signaling, primarily through AhR activation and ROS generation, altering 
metabolite pools and downstream kinase cascades. In vivo evidence from animal 
models and occupational human exposure confirms these alterations, linking 
specific histone code disruptions (e.g. decreased H3K36me3, H3K79me2; increased 
H3K9me2) to functional outcomes such as genomic instability, impaired DNA 
repair, aberrant gene expression, stemness promotion, and ultimately 
carcinogenicity in lung, liver, and reproductive tissues. Notably, B[a]P 
toxicity exhibits tissue, cell-type, and species specificity, and can be 
transgenerational. Emerging as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets, 
these B[a]P-driven epigenetic alterations represent a critical, non-mutational 
axis of its toxicity. This mechanistic understanding bridges genetic and 
epigenetic carcinogenesis, offering novel insights for its risk assessment and 
intervention strategies.

Environmental and human-related gradients shape the community structure of 
medium and large terrestrial mammals in a central Amazonian white-sand Forest.

de Castro RC(1)(2)(3), do Nascimento EM(1)(2), Castro RM(1)(2), Rabelo R(1)(4), 
Bobrowiec P(1), da Cruz SLR(1), Schietti J(1), Luther D(5), Rosa C(1)(2)(3).

Author information:
(1)Programa de Pós-Graduação em Ecologia, Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas da 
Amazônia, Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil.
(2)Centro de Estudos Integrados da Biodiversidade Amazônica, Instituto Nacional 
de Pesquisas da Amazônia, Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil.
(3)Coordenação de Dinâmica Ambiental, Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas da 
Amazônia, Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil.
(4)Department of Terrestrial Vertebrate Ecology, Mamirauá Institute for 
Sustainable Development, Tefé, Amazonas, Brazil.
(5)Department of Biology, College of Science, George Mason University, George 
Mason, Virginia, USA.

Medium- and large-sized terrestrial mammals play key ecological roles in 
tropical forests; however, the relative importance of environmental filters and 
anthropogenic disturbances in structuring their assemblages in Amazonian 
campinarana (white-sand) ecosystems remains poorly understood. In this study, we 
evaluated the influence of these factors on species composition and habitat use 
by medium- and large-sized terrestrial mammals, as well as by the 
frugivore-herbivore guild in Amazonian campinarana ecosystems. We used camera 
traps and structural equation modelling. We recorded 22 species over 4721 
camera-trap days, with assemblages dominated by frugivore-herbivores and by 
dietary and habitat generalists, such as the common opossum (Didelphis 
marsupialis). Habitat use by the overall mammal assemblage was higher in areas 
with lower vegetation height, whereas terrain elevation relative to the nearest 
drainage (HAND index) had an indirect effect mediated by vegetation structure. 
In contrast, frugivore-herbivore species showed more selective responses, with 
higher habitat-use intensity in areas farther from human influence. Mammal 
assemblages were predominantly influenced by distance to houses, whereas the 
composition of the frugivore-herbivore guild was associated with distance to 
houses and tree height. Our results demonstrate that even low levels of human 
presence are sufficient to structure mammal assemblages, reinforcing the need 
for spatially explicit management strategies aimed at conserving the functional 
integrity of these unique and highly sensitive ecosystems.

Tissue-Specific Insulin Resistance Pattern Underlies Heterogeneous Disease 
Severity and Complications in MASLD.

Teng L(1), Luo L(2), Shao C(1), Sun Y(3), Lai J(1), Cao X(4), Dong Z(5), Ye 
J(1), Zhong B(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Gastroenterology of the First Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen 
University, Guangzhou, China.
(2)Department of Infectious Diseases, The Fifth Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen 
University, Zhuhai, Guangdong Province, China.
(3)Department of Clinical Laboratory of the First Affiliated Hospital, Sun 
Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, China.
(4)Department of Endocrinology, The First Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen 
University, Guangzhou, China.
(5)Department of Radiology, The First Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen 
University, Guangzhou, China.

BACKGROUND: Insulin resistance (IR) plays a pathophysiological role in the 
development of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). 
However, it remains unclear whether the specific distribution of IR across 
muscle, adipose tissue, hepatic tissue, and the whole body is associated with 
the heterogeneous disease severity and its complications.
METHODS: Consecutive subjects (non-MASLD: 1239, MASLD: 1067) were 
retrospectively enrolled between June 2014 and June 2024, undergoing 
comprehensive evaluations that included anthropometric, laboratory, and imaging 
measurements. Tissue-specific IR indices (muscle IR, adipose IR, hepatic IR) and 
systemic IR were quantified using parameters derived from an oral glucose 
tolerance test.
RESULTS: Patients with MASLD exhibited lower muscle IR levels but higher adipose 
IR, hepatic IR, and systemic IR levels compared to those with non-MASLD (all 
p < 0.001). Multivariate analyses revealed distinct tissue-specific 
associations: hepatic IR was associated with the odds of moderate-severe 
steatosis (OR: 15.91, 95%CI 5.92-42.74, p < 0.001), systemic IR with liver 
injury (OR: 2.75, 95%CI: 1.89-4.00, p < 0.001), adipose IR with significant 
fibrosis (OR: 5.90, 95%CI: 3.31-10.53, p < 0.001), and muscle IR was inversely 
associated with CVD (OR: 2.87, 95%CI: 1.70-4.87, p < 0.001). Additionally, MASLD 
patients with co-occurring adipose-hepatic IR had a higher prevalence of liver 
injury compared to those with isolated muscle IR (64.0% vs. 28.8%, p < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Tissue-specific IR profiles may help characterize heterogeneous 
MASLD manifestations and CVD-associated phenotypes. Further studies are needed 
to assess whether timely identification of these profiles and initiation of 
appropriate interventions is beneficial.

Tumor-Microenvironment-Activated DOX@Cu2S@PDA@MnO2 Nanoplatform for 
MRI/PAI-Assisted Chemophotothermal Therapy of Osteosarcoma.

Wang T(1)(2), Liu C(3), Yang H(3), Li H(3), Liu H(4), Jia F(4).

Author information:
(1)Department of Clinical Laboratory, Shandong Provincial Hospital Affiliated to 
Shandong University, Jinan, Shandong250021, China.
(2)Department of Clinical Laboratory, Qilu Hospital of Shandong University, 
Jinan, Shandong250012, China.
(3)Department of Spine Surgery, Shandong Provincial Hospital Affiliated to 
Shandong University, Jinan, Shandong250021, China.
(4)Department of Spine Surgery, Shandong Provincial Hospital Affiliated to 
Shandong First Medical University, Jinan, Shandong250021, China.

Osteosarcoma remains difficult to treat because surgery and chemotherapy can 
provide incomplete tumor control, cause systemic toxicity, and lack reliable 
local monitoring. In this study, a tumor-microenvironment-activated 
DOX@Cu2S@PDA@MnO2 nanoplatform was prepared by converting Cu2O nanocubes into 
hollow Cu2S, coating polydopamine, growing a MnO2 shell, and loading

Megafaunal engineering in the tropical rainforest: African forest elephants 
(Loxodonta cyclotis) reduce avian species richness but elevate functional 
diversity.

Korejs K(1)(2), Hořák D(3), Chmel K(4), Sedláček O(3), Motombi FN(5), Ewome 
FL(5), Molua LL(5), Tache JIT(6), Kamga SM(6), Christopher JSC(1), Riegert J(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Zoology, Faculty of Science, University of South Bohemia, České 
Budějovice, Czech Republic.
(2)Institute of Entomology, Biology Centre, Czech Academy of Sciences, České 
Budějovice, Czech Republic.
(3)Department of Ecology, Faculty of Science, Charles University, Prague, Czech 
Republic.
(4)Czech Society for Ornithology, Prague, Czech Republic.
(5)Bokwango, Buea, Cameroon.
(6)Laboratory of Applied Biology & Ecology, Faculty of Science, University of 
Dschang, Dschang, Cameroon.

African forest elephants (Loxodonta cyclotis) are critically endangered 
ecosystem engineers of African tropical forests. Despite their rapidly declining 
population trend, little is known of how forest elephants interact with other 
vertebrate assemblages. To explore this, we studied avian communities within a 
continuous tropical rainforest on the slopes of Mt. Cameroon. The area's 
topography allowed us to survey birds in elephant-grazed primary forest and in 
adjacent portions that elephants avoid, isolating the effect of megafaunal 
grazing within an otherwise intact system. We additionally surveyed nearby 
secondary forests fragmented by human activity, contrasting the disappearance of 
a single ecosystem engineer against the reshaping of forest by anthropogenic 
disturbance. We assessed the taxonomic diversity (species richness, Shannon 
index), functional diversity (Rao's quadratic entropy), functional redundancy 
(species overlap in functional space), and composition of functional traits 
(abundance-weighted trait averages). Previous research suggested that loss of 
forest elephants would negatively impact avian assemblages through reduced 
habitat heterogeneity. In contrast, we show that elephant grazing itself 
significantly reduced species richness, to levels comparable with heavily 
disturbed secondary forests. Functional diversity nevertheless increased in both 
the grazed and secondary forest, but at the cost of functional redundancy: in 
both of these habitats, the avian assemblages were taxonomically impoverished, 
yet functionally more dispersed, with some foraging niches negatively affected. 
The elephant-grazed forest was dominated by understory and terrestrial 
invertivores, whereas the ungrazed forest supported frugivores and larger birds. 
The secondary forest, in turn, harboured a functionally distinct assemblage of 
open-habitat species with high dispersal ability and divergent foraging 
strategies. Together these patterns show that although elephant grazing reduces 
taxonomic diversity to a degree comparable with anthropogenic disturbance, it 
reshapes functional composition in fundamentally different ways. The presence of 
forest elephants facilitates stable populations of forest specialist birds, such 
as terrestrial invertivores. Conversely, the adverse effects of elephant grazing 
on frugivores and large birds could be minimized by establishing larger reserves 
of lightly grazed forest, possibly alongside ungrazed refuges. Overall, our 
results show that loss of keystone megaherbivores has widespread consequences 
for other rainforest vertebrates, potentially resulting in a cascading 
restructuring of key ecosystem functions.

Human hunters-still poorly understood-likely cannot mimic the roles of 
disappearing top predators.

Darimont CT(1)(2), Khan P(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Geography, University of Victoria, Victoria, British Columbia, 
Canada.
(2)Raincoast Conservation Foundation, Sidney, British Columbia, Canada.

Research Highlight: Geng, Y., Mammides, C., He, R.-C., Wang, L., Luo, K., Zhang, 
Z.-Y., Wang, B., & Quan, R.-C. (2026). Human hunters are no substitute for 
vanishing apex predators. Journal of Animal Ecology, 1-13. 
https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2656.70306. As large carnivores decline and humans 
rise to become the planet's most influential predator, scant consideration has 
been given to the functional roles of hunters (and fishers) in ecological 
communities. In novel, landscape-scale work, Geng et al. (2026) ask whether 
hunters can serve similar roles as the predators they are replacing. Camera-trap 
records from 400 sites characterized as apex predator-dominated, 
hunter-dominated and predator-absent were analysed across multiple ecological 
measures. Apex predator-dominated sites hosted ~30% more species and nearly 50% 
greater abundances of mammals. Network measures of prey populations were most 
robust at apex predator sites and weakest at hunter-dominated sites. Finally, 
prey showed up to 2.6 times longer avoidance times following hunter presence. 
These striking patterns suggest that hunters do not replicate the ecological 
influence of the area's vanishing predators. Work like this can benefit from 
much more data about human predators. Specifically, ecologists can confront in 
careful ways the conceptual, methodological and ethical constraints of studying 
our own species as predators. Outcomes could include greater knowledge about the 
ecological influence of the planet's 'super predator', the underlying 
mechanisms, and related insight to apply to mitigation.

Medication administration (MA) has significant implications for patient safety.

Cuproptosis-associated retinal degeneration in a mouse model of retinitis 
pigmentosa and neuroprotection by copper chelation.

Li ZY(1), Li Y, Yang D, Guo X, Liu Q, Xu Y.

Author information:
(1)Guangdong-Hongkong-Macau Institute of CNS Regeneration, Key Laboratory of CNS 
Regeneration (Jinan University)-Ministry of Education, Guangdong Key Laboratory 
of Non-human Primate Research, Jinan University, Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, 
China.

Cuproptosis is a recently described copper-dependent form of regulated cell 
death linked to mitochondrial metabolism, but its relevance to retinal 
degeneration in retinitis pigmentosa is unknown. Here, we investigated whether 
cuproptosis-associated changes occur in the retina of the rd10 mouse model of 
retinitis pigmentosa and whether copper chelation confers neuroprotection. 
Cuproptosis-associated changes were assessed by measuring retinal copper 
accumulation, dihydrolipoamide S-acetyltransferase oligomerization, and 
iron-sulfur cluster protein expression. The copper chelator D-penicillamine was 
delivered by intravitreal injection, and treatment effects were evaluated using 
retinal histology, electroretinography, and visually guided behavioral assays. 
Degenerating rd10 retinas exhibited increased copper accumulation, enhanced 
dihydrolipoamide S-acetyltransferase oligomerization, and reduced iron-sulfur 
cluster-associated proteins, consistent with activation of 
cuproptosis-associated pathways. D-penicillamine attenuated these molecular 
changes, improved mitochondrial protein markers, and significantly preserved 
photoreceptor structure. Functional benefit was detectable in light perception 
behavior, although electroretinographic and optomotor responses were not 
significantly restored. The copper exporter ATPase copper transporting β was 
upregulated at an early stage but reduced during peak degeneration, whereas the 
copper importer copper transporter 1 increased at the later stage, suggesting 
dynamic copper dyshomeostasis. These findings identify cuproptosis-associated 
molecular changes as a feature of photoreceptor degeneration in rd10 mice and 
demonstrate that copper chelation provides structural neuroprotection.

The use of technology to improve wound care practice.

Walsh A(1).

Author information:
(1)VNS Health, New York, New York.

BACKGROUND: As clinicians we may encounter patients with complicated wounds of 
varying etiologies.
LOCAL PROBLEM: Wound education is often lacking in nursing and medical 
curriculums. There is shortage of wound specialized clinicians to offer 
guidance. Furthermore, there is a shortage of palliative specialized clinicians 
to assist when the goals of wound care may need to shift to symptom management.
METHODS: The accredited Wound Care Pro app was developed as an educational 
resource for clinicians to meet this critical care need. It includes an overview 
of eight wound etiologies with descriptions, images, treatment options, case 
studies, and interventions to manage distressing symptoms, such as wound pain, 
odor, bleeding, and excessive exudate.
INTERVENTIONS: Technology was used to develop an educational tool for clinicians 
to have at their fingertips to help bridge the knowledge gap. The goals include 
empowering clinicians caring for patients with wounds to improve the healing 
potential when healing is the goal, to decrease the risk of complications, to 
improve symptom management, to decrease the wasteful use of costly wound 
supplies, and to decrease the risk of litigation from inappropriate wound care 
plans.
RESULTS: More than 11,000 clinicians have downloaded the application with 
positive feedback received, including how it has helped them get more 
appropriate, cost-effective wound care plans in place.
CONCLUSION: Although there is a shortage of wound and palliative specialized 
clinicians to meet complex patient wound care needs, technology can help empower 
clinicians whether wound healing or palliation is the goal.

Kingsberg SA(1), Ajmera M(2), Shiozawa A(2), Buessing M(3), Kim JS(2), Renteria

RESULTS: The survey was completed by 253 matched women and partner pairs. Mean 
age for women was 50.7 and partners 52.2 years. Similar numbers of women (40.7%,

58.5% (n=148) of partners reported high likelihood of seeking treatment.

women (48.6%, n=123) than partners (67.2%, n=170) reported that the partner 
encouraged the woman to understand their symptoms and pursue VMS treatment. More 
than half of women (59.3%; n=131) and partners (50.5%; n=113) reported a 
≥2-point decrease in sexual satisfaction when comparing before VMS to the 
present.

women and for their partners. Although women and partners were generally aligned

importance of enhancing communication between women experiencing VMS and their 
health care professionals.

Magnetic-field-guided programming of symmetry-defined anisotropy in hydrogels.

Kim C(1)(2), Kang D(2), Kim D(1), Kim DS(1)(3), Lee A(1), Jin L(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Mechanical Engineering, Pohang University of Science and 
Technology (POSTECH), Pohang 37673, Republic of Korea. annalee@postech.ac.kr.
(2)Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, University of California, 
Los Angeles, CA 90095, USA. lihuajin@seas.ucla.edu.
(3)School of Interdisciplinary Bioscience and Bioengineering, Pohang University 
of Science and Technology (POSTECH), Pohang 37673, Republic of Korea.

Hydrogels with anisotropic architectures can direct mechanical responses, guide 
mass transport, and enable programmable shape morphing. However, scalable 
strategies for encoding symmetry-defined anisotropy with strong modulation of 
bulk properties remain limited. Here, we present a simple single-step approach 
for programming hydrogel anisotropy, based on aligning micron-scale disk-shaped 
platelets under low-strength magnetic fields during photopolymerization. Rather 
than relying on the intrinsic magnetic properties of the platelets, we coat 
superparamagnetic nanoparticles on the surfaces of the platelets to impart 
sufficient magnetic susceptibility, which enables large magnetic torques and 
robust alignment. By tailoring the magnetic field configuration to be absent, 
static, or rotating, we have fabricated isotropic, transversely isotropic, and 
co-planarly anisotropic hydrogels, respectively. We employ confocal laser 
scanning microscopy to directly visualize the three-dimensional, 
magnetic-field-dependent alignment, compression tests to confirm anisotropic 
reinforcement, and thermal actuation to drive reversible, patterned shape 
morphing. As a result, the co-planarly anisotropic hydrogels exhibit pronounced 
mechanical stiffening and accelerated deswelling perpendicular to the platelet 
normals, which may reflect reduced transport tortuosity associated with platelet 
alignment. This strategy provides a scalable route to symmetry-defined 
anisotropic hydrogels with tunable mechanical and deswelling responses, with 
potential applications in soft robotics, responsive biointerfaces, and 
programmable fluidics.

brain function in affected regions, yet whether the neural mechanisms through 
which dopaminergic therapy exerts its effects are linked to this heterogeneity

therapeutic strategies.

Molecular Mechanism of Amino Acids for Stabilizing Protein Dispersions.

Fujii T(1), Harada R(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Degree Programs in Life and Earth Sciences, Graduate School of Science and 
Technology, University of Tsukuba, Tennodai 1-1-1, Tsukuba, Ibaraki305-8577,

(2)Center for Computational Sciences, University of Tsukuba, Tennodai 1-1-1,

In living cells, numerous biomolecules coexist in highly crowded environments 
while maintaining their biological functions. Under such conditions, 
biomolecules are constantly exposed to the risk of aggregation, leading to the 
loss of their biological function. To mitigate these risks, cells employ various 
strategies, such as the accumulation of small molecules in the cytosol. For 
example, free amino acids (AAs) are well-known to inhibit protein association 
and stabilize protein dispersions. A recent experimental study using a simple 
theoretical model suggested that the adsorption of AAs onto protein surfaces 
induces repulsive interactions between proteins. However, the molecular 
mechanism by which the adsorption of AAs inhibits protein association remains 
unclear. In this study, we conducted molecular dynamics simulations to 
investigate the molecular mechanisms by which AAs inhibit protein association. 
As a model system, insulin was simulated in the presence of a 1 M proline 
solution using both monomeric and dimeric models. For the monomeric system, the 
adsorption behavior of proline on the protein surface was characterized, 
revealing that proline molecules preferentially and uniformly adsorbed onto the 
protein surface. For the dimeric system, we examined how proline adsorption 
influences protein association by calculating the potential of mean force (PMF) 
and the osmotic second virial coefficient. These analyses demonstrate that 
proline induces net repulsive interactions among proteins, which are consistent 
with experimental observations. Furthermore, the number of proline molecules at 
the protein-protein interface reached a maximum around the intermediate state in 
the PMF prior to protein association. This accumulation of interfacial proline 
molecules increases the effective free energy required for further protein 
association. In conclusion, this study provides a direct molecular-level 
mechanism by which the adsorption of AAs stabilizes protein dispersions.

Interfacial Confinement Enables Dual Hosting of Sulfur Mustard and Mustard 
Sulfoxide in NU-1000.

McCormick FS(1), Huang L(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)School of Sustainable Chemical, Biological and Materials Engineering, 
University of Oklahoma, Norman, Oklahoma73019, United States.
(2)Materials Science and Engineering Program, University of Oklahoma, Norman, 
Oklahoma73019, United States.

Zirconium-based metal-organic frameworks have emerged as promising materials for 
the capture and detoxification of chemical warfare agents, but the molecular 
mechanism by which a hierarchical MOF differentiates a hydrophobic reactant from 
its oxidized product remains incompletely understood. Here, we use molecular 
dynamics simulations, grand-canonical Monte Carlo adsorption calculations, and 
periodic density functional theory to examine the dual-hosting behavior of 
NU-1000 toward sulfur mustard (HD) and mustard sulfoxide (HDO). Rather than 
treating NU-1000 only as an adsorbent or oxidation catalyst, we resolve how its 
internal micropore, mesopore, and c-pore interfaces impose distinct confinement 
environments on reactant and product species. Density functional theory (DFT) 
calculations show that HD binds most favorably in the c-pore region, with a 
binding energy of approximately -12.5 kcal/mol, and similarly favorable 
stabilization in confined micropore environments, whereas substantially weaker 
binding is observed in the mesopore. Molecular dynamics simulations also reveal 
sharply different pore residence patterns: HD localizes predominantly in 
micropores, occupying this region for ∼80% of the trajectory, while HDO samples 
larger pore environments more broadly, with ∼45% mesopore and ∼34% c-pore 
occupancy. This pore-selective behavior persists under mixed HD/HDO coadsorption 
conditions, demonstrating that reactant-product differentiation is intrinsic to 
the NU-1000 pore network rather than an artifact of isolated single-component 
simulations. Radial distribution functions further show that HD is stabilized by 
dispersion-dominated confinement and weak halogen-hydrogen contacts, whereas HDO 
is governed by more localized, orientation-dependent interactions with hydrated 
zirconium node sites. These interaction differences produce a pronounced 
transport asymmetry, with HDO exhibiting a self-diffusion coefficient of 10.6 ± 
2.11 × 10-10 m2/s compared with 0.5 ± 0.09 × 10-10 m2/s for HD at comparable 
loading. The results identify NU-1000 as a dual-function molecular host that 
couples reactant retention with product mobility, providing an interface-level 
mechanism relevant to selective CWA detoxification and confined transport in 
hierarchical porous catalysts.

Nanobubble-Driven Selective Oxidation of Toluene to Benzaldehyde.

Yin R(1), Long X(1), Zhang Q(1), Zhang N(1), Hou X(1), Xie M(1), Tian Y(1).

Author information:
(1)State Key Laboratory of Analytical Chemistry for Life Science, Key Laboratory 
of Mesoscopic Chemistry of MOE, School of Chemistry, Nanjing University, 
Nanjing210023, China.

Selective oxidation of C(sp3)-H bonds remains a longstanding challenge in 
organic synthesis, especially under environmentally friendly conditions. 
Conventional strategies typically rely on harsh oxidants or complex catalysts, 
limiting their sustainability and scalability. Nanobubbles can generate highly 
reactive species during collapse because of their unique physicochemical 
properties. In particular, the gas-liquid interface of nanobubbles has attracted 
increasing attention for its ability to concentrate reactants and facilitate 
radical-driven transformations. Herein, we report a light-assisted ultrasound 
strategy in which nanobubbles produce hydroxyl radicals as the primary reactive 
species for C(sp3)-H bond activation under ambient conditions, without requiring 
additional oxidants or catalysts. With toluene as a model substrate, the method 
afforded 24.3% conversion and 61.6% selectivity toward benzaldehyde within 4 h. 
Mechanistic investigations, including isotope-labeling, radical-quenching 
experiments, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations, revealed that 
hydroxyl radicals originate from both water and dissolved oxygen and selectively 
abstract benzylic hydrogen atoms. This study establishes an efficient and 
environmentally friendly route for C-H bond oxidation while offering new 
mechanistic insights into radical generation at gas-liquid interfaces. We 
anticipate that this nanobubble-driven strategy will advance the development of 
green chemical transformations and may provide opportunities for the development 
of sustainable oxidation processes.

Binary suspensions of beeswax and mineral pigment nanoparticles offer a 
promising route to highly stable, water-based formulations for coating and 
painting films. In this work, we systematically characterized the stability and 
structural organization of binary suspensions of beeswax and various mineral 
pigment particles, including Armenian bole, glauconite, ultramarine, cardinal 
purple, golden ochre, and shungite. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed 
that all investigated mineral pigments naturally occurred as accreted aggregates 
of nanometer-sized particles, with separate individual nanoparticles also 
identified in several samples. These individual pigment nanoparticles ranged 
from 50 to 100 nm, with ζ-potentials from -16 to -37 mV. Beeswax nanoparticles, 
produced by the phase-inversion temperature method, exhibited diameters of 20-25 
nm and a ζ-potential of -7.3 mV. Because the native surface charges of these 
constituent nanoparticles were insufficient to provide adequate electrostatic 
stabilization, macroscopic stability against gravitational separation was 
achieved by rheologically modifying the continuous phase. Highly stable, 
nonsedimenting suspensions were successfully formulated by gelling the aqueous 
phase with 1 mass % Carbopol 940, thereby immobilizing the phase-mismatched 
nanostructures via polymer-network confinement. Scanning transmission electron 
microscopy (STEM) coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) 
demonstrated that, upon drying, the mineral pigments were embedded within the 
wax agglomerates or surrounded by the beeswax nanoparticles. Finally, the 
film-forming behavior of these binary compositions was evaluated through a 
preliminary qualitative demonstration of their application in cold encaustic 
painting.

Guo F(1)(2)(3), Wang J(1), Song H(1), Lu G(4), Liu X(5), Rao J(1)(2)(3), Zhang

Smart responsive anticorrosion fillers have significantly advanced metal 
protection by enabling a shift from passive physical barriers to dynamic, 
adaptive defense systems. This review systematically elucidates the evolutionary 
trajectory from traditional passive barrier fillers and inhibitor-loaded active 
systems to state-of-the-art smart responsive platforms that sense and respond to 
corrosive microenvironments. The fundamental design principles and response 
mechanisms are discussed, focusing on pH, chloride, electrochemical potential, 
and temperature/humidity stimuli. The critical role of micro/nanostructural 
engineering-including core-shell architectures, hierarchical porosity, and

highlighted. Advanced strategies such as hierarchical release kinetics, 
synergistic inhibitor combinations, and multifunctional system-level integration 
are addressed. Finally, key challenges related to interfacial defects, long-term 
response decay, and extreme environment reliability are outlined. This work 
provides insights into the rational design of next-generation smart 
anticorrosion coatings for complex service environments. This review is expected 
to provide a theoretical foundation and design guidelines for the development of 
novel adaptive anticorrosion coatings tailored for extreme service conditions.

Inducing and stabilizing mesoscale structures in fully miscible molecular 
liquids remains challenging because local heterogeneity is usually transient and 
rapidly averaged out. Here, we show that periodic thermal oscillation drives a 
50% (v/v) ethanol-water mixture along a traceable nonequilibrium ordering 
pathway from transient ethanol-water clusters to kinetically stabilized soft 
aggregates. The system evolves from initial clusters to water-containing

progressive stabilization across the structural hierarchy. These findings 
demonstrate that periodic thermal forcing can amplify transient molecular 
heterogeneity into mesoscale soft structures in a fully miscible liquid, 
providing a kinetic perspective on nonequilibrium cluster amplification and 
microphase-separated aggregate formation in hydrogen-bonded molecular systems.
