Contrasting edaphic and land-use signatures of microbial phosphorus mobilisation 
and accumulation genes.

Du M(1), Xue P(1), Minasny B(1), Tang Y(1), Tran TKA(1), McBratney A(1).

Author information:
(1)School of Life and Environmental Sciences & Sydney Institute of Agriculture, 
The University of Sydney, NSW 2015, Australia.

Phosphorus (P) is an essential nutrient that constrains productivity across many 
terrestrial ecosystems. Soil microorganisms regulate P transformation through 
distinct functional strategies, yet how these strategies vary with land use and 
environmental conditions across chronically P-impoverished landscapes remains 
poorly understood. Here, we combined 268 soil metagenomes from natural, pasture, 
and cropland systems across Australia with genome-resolved analyses of 1,077 
metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Results revealed contrasting genomic 
distributions among P-cycling strategies. P accumulation genes were widely 
distributed across bacterial phylogeny, whereas mineralization gene and 
solubilisation gene were concentrated within specific lineages. 
Land-use-associated differences were most evident in the relative abundances of 
mineralisation and solubilisation genes, whereas accumulation genes showed 
comparatively little variation. Soil properties were stronger predictors of 
relative P-cycling gene abundance than climatic variables. Among these 
variables, soil pH was the strongest predictor of both the combined relative 
abundance of P-cycling genes and mineralisation genes, whereas accumulation 
genes were negatively associated with the mineral-associated organic carbon 
fraction. Continental predictions further suggested higher combined relative 
P-cycling gene abundance in wetter south-western and coastal eastern regions. 
These analyses reveal contrasting microbial P-cycling gene strategies across 
Australian soils and provide a genome-resolved framework for understanding their 
phylogenetic distributions and environmental associations at the continental 
scale.

Eco-friendly cryolite-type Cs(3)CeI(6) halide: DFT+U insights into 
optoelectronic properties and defect-modulated deep-blue emission.

Yin Y(1), Shen X(1), Cao Y(1)(2), Yang H(1), Wang Y(1), Sun Z(3).

Author information:
(1)School of Physics and Opto-Electronic Technology, Baoji University of Arts 
and Sciences, Baoji, 721016, Shaanxi, China. yinyuan8008@126.com.
(2)School of Intelligent Manufacturing and Non-Destructive Testing, Wuhan 
College of Arts and Sciences, Wuhan, 430345, Hubei, China.
(3)School of Materials Science and Engineering, Jiangsu University, Zhenjiang, 
212013, Jiangsu, China. ztsun@ujs.edu.cn.

Eco-friendly rare-earth halide luminescent materials have emerged as promising 
candidates for deep-blue light-emitting devices, yet severe intrinsic 
luminescence quenching induced by intrinsic point defects severely limits their 
photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY). In this work, we systematically 
investigate the optoelectronic properties, defect behavior, and carrier 
recombination mechanism of cryolite-type Cs3CeI6via first-principles 
calculations. The orbital composition of the valence band and conduction band of 
perfect Cs3CeI6 is analyzed, and the intrinsic radiative limitation originating 
from the low Γ-point transition probability and parity-forbidden I 5p → Ce 4f 
transitions is clarified, which inherently results in weak deep-blue emission. 
We further calculate the formation energies and charge transition energy levels 
of typical intrinsic point defects including VCs and VI. The results reveal that 
VCs defects act as detrimental deep acceptor traps within the bandgap, which can 
simultaneously capture photogenerated electrons and holes and may serve as a 
potential source of nonradiative recombination and PLQY degradation. The density 
of deep quenching traps can be precisely regulated by tuning precursor chemical 
potentials: I-rich/Cs-poor growth environments reduce the formation energy of 
VCs and promote trap aggregation, while Cs-rich conditions effectively suppress 
the generation of VCs defects. Experimentally observed PLQY enhancement after 
CsI passivation is consistent with the interpretation that passivation 
suppresses nonradiative channels associated with VCs defects, thereby allowing 
photogenerated carriers to recombine through the parity-permitted Ce 5d → Ce 4f 
channel and significantly boost deep-blue luminescence efficiency. This work 
establishes a complete atomic-scale structure-defect-luminescence correlation 
for Cs3CeI6 halides, providing fundamental theoretical guidance for optimizing 
precursor stoichiometry and developing efficient defect passivation strategies 
to fabricate high-performance, stable rare-earth halide deep-blue emitters.

Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) is one of the most widely used 
molecular diagnostic methods and is considered a promising tool for 
point-of-care testing (POCT). However, because LAMP requires multiple complex 
primers, false-positive and false-negative results can occur, thereby limiting 
its clinical applicability. Herein, we propose a novel chemically modified 
double-stranded probe (CDP) to reduce false-positive and false-negative LAMP

validation. In summary, a novel CDP-based strategy was established to enhance 
the performance of LAMP, thereby improving its applicability and offering a 
promising tool for POCT molecular diagnosis.

BACKGROUND: Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), caused by MERS coronavirus 
(MERS-CoV), is a severe zoonotic respiratory illness first identified in Saudi 
Arabia in 2012. Dromedary camels are the recognised reservoir, with human 
transmission occurring through animal exposure and, less commonly, 
person-to-person spread, particularly in healthcare settings.
OBJECTIVE: To characterise all laboratory-confirmed MERS-CoV cases reported in 
Saudi Arabia from September 2012 to August 2025, examine trends across four 
periods defined by suspected-case definitions, and identify factors 
independently associated with mortality.
METHODS: We analysed laboratory-confirmed cases in the national surveillance 
database by period and probable infection source. Case-fatality ratios (CFRs), 
95% confidence intervals (CIs), and unadjusted odds ratios were calculated. 
Multivariable logistic regression assessed independent mortality associations 
using a prespecified model including period, age, sex, and infection source, and 
a fuller model additionally considering nationality, comorbidities, and 
pregnancy. Seasonality of primary cases was assessed using an annual harmonic 
term.
RESULTS: Among 2,219 cases, 1,545 (70%) were male, 1,566 (71%) Saudi nationals, 
and 608 (27%) aged ≥65 years. Overall, 1,211 (55%) were primary cases, including 
172 (14%) reporting camel contact; 737 (33%) were healthcare-associated and 271 
(12%) household- or community-associated. There were 867 deaths (CFR, 39%; 95% 
CI, 37%-41%). CFR declined from 65% in the earliest period to 32% in the most 
recent, although changing testing eligibility and ascertainment limit temporal 
comparisons. Older adults had the highest crude CFR. In the prespecified model, 
healthcare-associated infection among patients was associated with higher odds 
of death (aOR, 1.74; 95% CI, 1.15-2.65), while odds were lower among healthcare 
workers (aOR, 0.09; 95% CI, 0.05-0.17) and household contacts (aOR, 0.29; 95% 
CI, 0.18-0.48). No consistent seasonality was observed.
CONCLUSIONS: MERS-CoV epidemiology in Saudi Arabia reflects persistent zoonotic 
spillover, episodic healthcare-associated transmission, and substantial 
mortality, particularly among older adults. Sustained One Health surveillance, 
rapid detection, and rigorous infection prevention and control remain essential.

BACKGROUND: Lactation provides an important source of nutrition for infants, and 
physician parents desire to provide human milk to their babies. There are 
established barriers to workplace lactation for other groups of physicians, but 
no existing literature for psychiatrists, psychologists, or other 
psychotherapists.
METHODS: We disseminated a survey of demographics, experiences with gestation 
and lactation, and exposure to a variety of categorical and specific external 
barriers to workplace lactation for mental health clinicians.
RESULTS: Of 235 survey completers who had lactated anywhere from under 6 months 
to over 5 years, 98.7% had experienced barriers to workplace lactation. The most 
common external barriers were insufficient time (85.1%), lack of dedicated space 
(59.4%), nowhere to store milk (51.9%), and inflexibility of schedule (48.6%).

hospital-grade pump (p = 0.013), medical, pregnancy, and parental leave problems 
(p = 0.001), parental leave insufficient to establish supply (p = 0.000), and 
problems with supply or mastitis (p = 0.017). Only parental leave and medical 
problems were significant on multivariable analysis (p = 0.002).

significant barriers to lactation at work. More research in this area is needed. 
We provisionally recommend thoughtful and well-equipped lactation suites to 
mitigate this issue, improving worker wellness and the ability of lactating 
parents to return to the clinical workforce.

Adolescent Chronic Sleep Restriction Induces a Mesolimbic Hypodopaminergic State 
Associated with Addiction Vulnerability.

Huang TM(1), Liu CS(1), Huang CC(2)(3)(4), Yeh JW(5), Lee LJ(5)(6)(7), Shih 
MC(8)(9)(10), Tuan LH(1)(8)(11).

Author information:
(1)Institute of Systems Neuroscience, National Tsing Hua University, Hsinchu, 
Taiwan.
(2)Ph.D. Program in Biomedical Artificial Intelligence, National Tsing Hua 
University, Hsinchu, Taiwan.
(3)Department of Orthopedics, Hsinchu MacKay Memorial Hospital, Hsinchu, Taiwan.
(4)Department of Orthopedics, Hsinchu Municipal MacKay Children's Hospital, 
Hsinchu, Taiwan.
(5)Graduate Institute of Anatomy and Cell Biology, College of Medicine, National 
Taiwan University, Taipei, Taiwan.
(6)Neurobiology and Cognitive Science Center, National Taiwan University, 
Taipei, Taiwan.
(7)Institute of Brain and Mind Sciences, College of Medicine, National Taiwan 
University, Taipei, Taiwan.
(8)School of Medicine, National Tsing Hua University, Hsinchu, Taiwan.
(9)Institute of Statistics and Data Science, National Tsing Hua University,

(10)Institute of Bioinformatics and Structural Biology, National Tsing Hua

(11)Department of Medical Science, National Tsing Hua University, Hsinchu,

Adolescent sleep insufficiency is increasingly prevalent, but whether repeated 
insufficient sleep during this developmental period promotes addiction 
vulnerability remains unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of chronic 
sleep restriction (CSR) imposed during adolescence, from 4 to 7 weeks of age, on 
the mesocorticolimbic dopamine (DA) system and addiction-related behaviors in 
mice. Behavioral and neuronal responses in the mesolimbic pathway to the 
psychostimulant Amphetamine (Amph) were examined. Also, DA-related molecular and 
structural components, including DA receptors, DA turnover, and developmental 
regulators such as Netrin-1/deleted in colorectal cancer (DCC), were assessed.

characterized by reduced neuronal activity in the core regions of the mesolimbic 
DA circuit at baseline and upon acute Amph stimulation, downregulated striatal 
DA receptors, and reduced DA axon innervation in the ventral striatum. Altered 
Netrin-1/DCC signaling and mesocortical DA synthesis further suggest that sleep 
loss during adolescence disrupts ongoing maturation of DA circuitry. 
Furthermore, these neurobiological profiles were accompanied by enhanced 
Amph-induced conditioned place preference (CPP). Together, these findings 
indicate that chronic adolescent sleep insufficiency induces a constellation of 
behavioral and neurobiological adaptations relevant to addiction susceptibility. 
In contrast to prior acute sleep-loss paradigms that mainly capture transient DA 
activation, our data support a model in which repeated sleep restriction imposes 
cumulative allostatic load and promotes longer-term maladaptive remodeling of 
reward circuitry. These results identify insufficient sleep during adolescence 
as a potential risk factor for addiction vulnerability.

Xue W(1)(2)(3), Gao Z(1)(2)(3), Shi Y(4), Zhang Y(4), Du W(1)(2)(3), Tao 
B(1)(2)(3), Zhu F(1)(2)(3), Wan Q(1), Zhang W(1), Lui S(1)(2)(3), Lu P(5), Tang 
X(4), Xiao Y(1)(2)(3)(6).

Author information:
(1)Department of Radiology, West China Hospital of Sichuan University, Chengdu 
610041, China.
(2)Psychoradiology Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, West China Hospital of 
Sichuan University, Chengdu 610041, China.
(3)Research Unit of Psychoradiology, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, 
Chengdu 610041, China.
(4)Sleep Medicine Center, Department of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, 
Mental Health Center, Translational Neuroscience Center, and State Key

610041, China.
(5)Department of Anesthesiology, National-Local Joint Engineering Research

Insomnia disorder (ID) has become a prevalent sleep disorder worldwide, yet its 
underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear due to heterogeneous neuroimaging 
findings and uncertain network localization. We identified brain structural and 
functional abnormality locations associated with ID from 63 published 
neuroimaging studies, including 3391 patients and 3433 healthy controls. Using 
coordinate network mapping combined with a normative connectome database, we 
mapped these abnormalities to large-scale brain networks of ID across imaging 
modalities and further decoded them by integrating microscale 
chemo-architectural, cellular, and cognitive maps. The structural network widely 
involved the ventral attention (VAN), sensorimotor (SMN), dorsal attention (DAN) 
and default mode network (DMN); the task-induced network showed a similar but 
less extensive pattern, predominantly implicating the VAN, DMN, SMN and 
subcortical network (SCN); in contrast, the resting-state network was largely 
confined to the left middle frontal gyrus and the bilateral mid-cingulate 
cortex. Molecular mapping revealed both shared and distinct neurotransmitter 
signatures across the three networks, involving cholinergic, histaminergic, 
glutamatergic, noradrenergic, and opioid systems. Cellular decoding showed 
relatively selective associations of the structural and task-based networks with 
glial cells and excitatory neurons, whereas the resting-state network exhibited 
broader associations with glial cells and multiple excitatory and inhibitory 
neuronal subtypes. Cognitive decoding linked structural and task-based networks 
to sensorimotor processing and the resting-state network to memory-related 
functions. Our findings reconcile heterogeneous neuroimaging results and reveal 
neurobiological substrates of ID from a network perspective, providing a 
promising biomarker and paving the way for circuit-based precision therapies of 
ID.

Sn/Cl Co-Doped ZnO Cathode Interfacial Layer for High-Performance Organic 
Photodetectors.

Miao Z(1)(2), Fu M(1)(2), Zhou R(1)(2), Zhu K(1)(2), Xu Y(1)(2), Yu Z(1)(2), 
Zhang K(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Institute of Polymer Optoelectronic Materials and Devices, State Key 
Laboratory of Luminescent Materials and Devices, School of Materials Science and 
Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou510640, P. R. China.
(2)Guangdong Basic Research Center of Excellence for Energy and Information 
Polymer Materials , Guangzhou510640, P. R. China.

Organic photodetectors (OPDs) hold significant promise for applications spanning 
medical monitoring, bioimaging and night vision due to their unique advantages, 
such as flexibility, light weight, and potential for large-area fabrication. 
Nevertheless, the dark current density (Jd) of OPDs exhibits a pronounced 
increase under applied reverse bias, which consequently degrades the specific 
detectivity (D*). To tackle this challenge, this work proposes an interface 
engineering strategy based on Sn/Cl co-doped ZnO (SCZO). The doping effectively 
reduces oxygen defects in ZnO, causing the valence band maximum (VBM) to shift 
downward, thereby suppressing hole injection under bias and reducing Jd. 
Experiments show that the SCZO-based device exhibits a Jd of 4.05 × 10-11 A cm-2 
at -0.1 V, nearly one order of magnitude lower than that of the control device 
(4.07 × 10-10 A cm-2). Notably, the SCZO-based OPD enables real-time and 
accurate monitoring of human heart rate, demonstrating its considerable 
potential for health-monitoring applications. Furthermore, OPDs incorporating 
the SCZO interface exhibit excellent imaging performance under 820 nm 
illumination. These findings underscore the significant potential of SCZO-based 
OPDs for flexible, wearable health monitoring and near-infrared imaging 
applications.

Newman C(1), Klein LD(1), Booth M(1), Grzeskowiak L(2)(3), Clifford 
V(1)(4)(5)(6).

Author information:
(1)Australian Red Cross Lifeblood, West Melbourne, Australia.
(2)College of Medicine and Public Health, Flinders University, Bedford Park, 
Australia.
(3)SA Pharmacy, Flinders Medical Centre, SA Health, Bedford Park, Australia.
(4)Royal Children's Hospital, Parkville, Australia.
(5)Murdoch Children's Research Institute, Parkville, Australia.
(6)University of Melbourne, Parkville, Australia.

BACKGROUND: Potential milk donors should be carefully screened to ensure that 
donated human milk is safe for vulnerable infant recipients. Some medications 
and supplements may result in donor deferral or make donation impossible. 
However, evidence about medication or supplement exposures among those 
considering donating excess breast milk in Australia remains limited.
AIM: To examine medication and supplement use among pre-eligibility donors to an 
Australian nonprofit milk bank.
METHODS: A retrospective cross-sectional study analyzed 1,480 high-level 
screening questionnaires completed at the Australian Red Cross Lifeblood milk 
bank between January 2023 and December 2024. All medications and supplements 
reportedly taken during the 10 weeks preceding the pre-eligibility donor 
screening interview were extracted, categorized, and summarized descriptively.
RESULTS: Screening occurred a median of 9.7 weeks postpartum. Overall, 90% of 
pre-eligibility donors reported using either medications (75.2%) or supplements 
(64.1%), with many using both. Analgesics were most common (taken by 61.9%),

(11%), and antihypertensives (7%). Overall, 46.5% reported using at least one

pre-eligibility donors).

care. Supplement use was prevalent, with multiple products taken. Given the 
limited safety data for many medications and supplements in the context of donor

support safe and inclusive donor eligibility decisions.

Temporal regulation of metabolic processes in the marine diazotroph Crocosphaera 
watsonii WH8501.

Gauglitz JM(1)(2), Inomura K(3), Bittremieux W(2), Moran DM(1), McIlvin MR(1),

(1)Marine Chemistry and Geochemistry Department, Woods Hole Oceanographic

(2)Department of Computer Science, University of Antwerp, Antwerp, Belgium.
(3)Graduate School of Oceanography, University of Rhode Island, Narragansett,

Marine diazotrophic cyanobacteria play a crucial role in oceanic nitrogen 
cycling, supporting primary production and ecosystem balance. Crocosphaera 
watsonii WH8501 exemplifies this capability by temporally separating 
photosynthesis and diazotrophy. To investigate the regulatory mechanisms 
underlying this process, we employed mass spectrometry-based proteomics in a 
high-resolution diel culturing experiment, revealing tightly coordinated protein 
abundance patterns. Unsupervised clustering of diel protein abundance profiles 
identified six groups of co-regulated proteins characterized by distinct

proteins that were most abundant during the night and day-night transition, 
supporting carbon consumption and energy production. Clusters 3 and 4 were 
enriched in proteins involved in photosynthesis, cell division, and lipid 
synthesis, with maximal abundance around midday. Cluster 5 comprised peptide 
biosynthesis proteins that peaked later in the day and may facilitate 
nitrogenase complex formation. Cluster 6, expressed during the day-night 
transition, revealed coordinated nitrogenase assembly, with Fe-S cluster 
proteins preceding peak nitrogenase iron protein abundance, suggesting a 
temporally ordered sequence of enzyme maturation. Distinct temporal patterns in 
iron trafficking to heme and Fe-S cluster biosynthetic systems further indicated 
tightly regulated allocation of iron to metalloproteins across the diel cycle. 
Together, these results reveal the intricate temporal coordination that enables 
Crocosphaera to balance nitrogen fixation and photosynthesis within a single 
cell and underscore the central role of diel regulation in sustaining these 
globally important processes.IMPORTANCEMarine diazotrophic cyanobacteria play an 
essential role in global nitrogen cycling and ocean productivity. In this study, 
we investigate the temporal regulation of Crocosphaera watsonii metabolism using 
high-resolution proteomics under diel culturing conditions. Our analysis 
resolves six distinct clusters of protein abundance patterns across the 
light/dark cycle, reflecting intricate coordination of nitrogen fixation, 
photosynthesis, carbon allocation, and iron homeostasis. Notably, we identify 
temporally ordered assembly of nitrogenase subunits, including precursory 
expression of Fe-S cluster proteins and indications of tightly controlled iron 
trafficking systems. These findings provide new mechanistic insight into how 
unicellular diazotrophs synchronize key metabolic processes under natural diel 
cycles.

diverse cell types. For pathogenic fungi, EVs play critical roles by modulating 
immune responses and influencing disease progression. Previously, we 
demonstrated that vaccination with EVs from Candida albicans promoted protection

vaccine strategies.

High-entropy carbides: structure, synthesis and catalytic applications.

Cao PY(1), Zhu CY(1), Han YC(1).

Author information:
(1)Innovation Laboratory for Sciences and Technologies of Energy Materials of 
Fujian Province, State Key Laboratory of Physical Chemistry of Solid Surfaces, 
College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Xiamen University, Xiamen 361005, 
China. ychan93@xmu.edu.cn.

High-entropy carbides (HECs) - multicomponent interstitial compounds with 
multiple transition metals distributed on a shared metal sublattice and carbon 
occupying interstitial sites - expand the catalytic design space beyond 
conventional unary and binary carbides, owing to their diverse local 
coordination environments, tunable metal-carbon bonding, and rich defect 
chemistry. Nevertheless, HECs, especially nanoscale HECs, remain far less 
developed than high-entropy alloys and conventional transition-metal carbides. 
Their vast compositional space is paired with tightly coupled challenges in 
phase formation, carbon stoichiometry, elemental mixing uniformity, surface 
chemistry and structure, all of which are difficult to regulate independently. 
This Review establishes a structure-synthesis-catalysis framework for the field. 
We examine the crystal chemistry, thermodynamic descriptors, and computational 
design strategies for navigating the extensive HEC composition space, and 
compare conventional thermal processing with emerging ultrafast synthetic 
routes. We further define the core structural evidence required to rigorously 
verify phase purity, intraparticle elemental distributions, carbon vacancies, 
and reaction-induced surface reconstruction. We then critically assess reported 
catalytic applications, distinguish well-substantiated findings from prospective 
opportunities, and identify key priorities for scalable synthesis, operando 
characterization, and predictive catalyst design. By bridging materials design 
principles with working-state structural verification, this Review provides a 
rigorous foundation for the rational development of HECs as functional catalytic 
materials.

Bueno Ormerod F(1), Ramalho R(1), Sharma V(1), Lyons A(1).

Author information:
(1)The University of Auckland, Auckland, New Zealand.

Migrant women's alcohol use has been understudied despite evidence that gender, 
culture, and migration shape drinking experiences. This review synthesizes 
qualitative research on how migrant women experience host-country drinking 
cultures, their gendered drinking experiences and factors influencing their 
alcohol use. The review was conducted across five databases (ProQuest, 
Dimensions, Scopus, PsycINFO and PubMed). Inclusion criteria were peer-reviewed 
qualitative studies published since 2000 examining migrant women's experiences 
with alcohol and drinking cultures. Twenty-two articles were included in the 
review and analyzed using narrative synthesis. Studies came from five Western 
countries. Five key themes were identified: (1) coping with emotional 
challenges; (2) acculturation and drinking cultures; (3) policing of femininity 
through gendered norms regulating women's drinking behaviors; (4) fear of 
violence: gendered outcomes of drinking alcohol and (5) Alcohol as a religious 
transgression. Findings showed that some migrant women drink to soothe 
loneliness; others abstain yet risk social exclusion. Gendered double standards 
persist; while drinking may offer fleeting belonging, it also invites judgment 
and vulnerability. Migrant women face a balancing act as drinking can 
simultaneously facilitate social inclusion and reinforce host-country exclusion. 
Findings highlight how alcohol use among migrant women is deeply intertwined 
with broader structures of gender, cultural adaptation, and belonging.

Weyer E(1), Wang Y(2), Tomita T(1), Madrid-Aliste C(3)(4), Nandigrami P(4),

Author information:
(1)Department of Pathology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, New York, New 
York, USA.
(2)Department of Pathogenic Biology, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Cheeloo 
College of Medicine, Shandong University, Jinan, Shandong, China.
(3)Department of Biochemistry, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, New York, 
New York, USA.
(4)Department of Systems & Computational Biology, Albert Einstein College of

(5)Department of Genetics, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, New York, New

(6)Department of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, New York, New

Microsporidia such as Encephalitozoon hellem are obligate intracellular human 
parasites that remain genetically intractable, limiting the functional 
characterization of their proteomes. Experimental structural studies are 
challenging, as many proteins in microsporidia comprise a large percentage of 
disordered regions. Computational structural studies based on homology-based 
modeling and the use of deep-learning algorithms for microsporidian proteins 
also remain limited because most have little to no sequence similarity to 
proteins with solved structures. To address these limitations, we developed an 
approach that incorporates cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) data into 
structure prediction. XL-MS data provide upper-bound distance constraints that 
can be incorporated into protein deep-learning-based modeling and subsequent 
docking. Using this approach, we generated a model of two interacting E. hellem 
spore wall proteins, spore wall protein 1B (Swp1b) and endospore protein 1 
(EnP1), which have no clear homologs outside of microsporidia and contain 
several disordered regions. These proteins are abundant spore wall proteins of 
microsporidia and previously were not known to interact with one another. The 
resulting model not only is consistent with the experimental cross-links used to 
generate the model but was also subsequently confirmed by independently 
generated XL-MS data. The described AlphaLink-Modeller framework for structure 
prediction is particularly well suited to proteins with limited homology and/or 
substantial flexible regions, given that they adopt a defined structural state 
within a biological context, thereby extending integrative modeling approaches 
to previously inaccessible targets.
IMPORTANCE: In this article, we demonstrate an improved method for the 
prediction of the structure of protein complexes with no clear homologs and a 
considerable number of disordered regions. This is significant because these 
types of proteins are critical to understanding the biology of organisms, yet 
model generation of these classes has been inaccessible. The method incorporates 
experimental data obtained from cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) into the 
modeling process, providing a method to integrate such experimental data into 
computational modeling of the structure of proteins and protein interactions. 
For this paper, we have used this method for predicting the structure of two 
highly abundant Encephalitozoon hellem proteins in the spore wall that are 
important for host cell infection due to this pathogen of humans and other 
vertebrates.

Author information:
(1)Medical Radiation Engineering, Shahid Beheshti University, Tehran, Iran,

Radiomics analysis in PET offers a high-dimensional representation of tissue 
characteristics, yet its reliability is limited by sensitivity to acquisition 
perturbations, particularly dose reduction. This study aims to introduce a 
nonlinear stability phenotyping framework to characterize dose-response behavior 
of multi-organ radiomics and evaluate their potential relevance for future 
digital twin-oriented applications.&#xD;Approach: A multi-center dataset of 550 
total-body PET scans was analyzed. Dose reduction was simulated using list-mode 
subsampling (dose reduction factor - DRF = 2-100). A total of 107 radiomics

Correlation Coefficient (ICC) and summarized as stability fractions. Nonlinear 
models were fitted to organ- and feature-level trajectories. Stability

nonlinear, organ-dependent behavior. Feature-level analysis identified frequent

underlying nonlinear feature dynamics.&#xD;Significance: Radiomics stability in

tipping points and organ-specific sensitivity. The proposed framework provides a 
behavior-based approach for evaluating radiomics robustness and supports the 
selection of reliable features and organs for robust quantitative imaging and 
may inform future digital twin-oriented applications.

Feng Q(1), Yu AH(1), Shi DC(1), Wang XL(1).

Author information:
(1)School of Electronics and Information, Guangdong Polytechnic Normal

Existing Broad Learning System (BLS)-based Electrocardiogram (ECG) arrhythmia 
classification methods still face limitations in multi-source feature 
representation, sample reliability modeling, and minority-class recognition. To 
address these issues, this study proposes a combinational improvement framework 
built upon BLS, integrating uncertainty aware gated fuzzy feature enhancement 
and a minority-class ensemble strategy for ECG arrhythmia classification. First, 
heartbeat waveform, QRS complex structural information, and RR rhythm features 
are integrated to construct a hybrid ECG representation that jointly captures 
morphological and rhythm characteristics. The BLS is then employed for 
high-dimensional nonlinear feature mapping, upon which an uncertainty-aware 
gated fuzzy enhancement mechanism evaluates sample reliability through robust 
class prototype estimation and fuzzy membership calculation. A confidence-based 
gating strategy is further introduced to achieve adaptive feature enhancement, 
strengthening discriminative information from reliable samples while reducing 
noise interference caused by ambiguous boundary samples. Finally, a 
minority-class-aware ensemble classification strategy is developed, which 
employs eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) as the primary classifier. 
One-versus-Rest(OvR) classifiers, a complementary Logistic Regression (LR) 
model, and class-wise probability calibration are incorporated to refine 
classification decisions and alleviate majority class bias caused by class 
imbalance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 
overall accuracies of 99.04% and 92.58% (Macro-F1 of 93.39% and 61.60%) under 
the intra-patient and inter-patient evaluation protocols, respectively. The 
framework trades a moderate training-time and memory footprint (an ensemble of 
tree models over ANOVA-selected BLS features) for these minority-class gains, 
while inference remains a CPU-friendly single forward pass through the frozen 
pipeline. It improves minority-class recognition relative to the compared 
methods under severe class imbalance, while the recognition of fusion beats 
under the inter-patient protocol remains challenging(five-seed mean F1 of 
6.72%±2.69%)and is explicitly discussed as a limitation.

Mangroves are important coastal blue carbon ecosystems, but future sediment GHG 
emissions remain uncertain because global projections have largely emphasized 
atmospheric climate drivers, with less attention to coastal hydrology, 
particularly sea-surface salinity and tidal range. Here, we compiled 810 
sediment GHG flux measurements from 294 mangrove sites worldwide and used 
machine learning to project emissions to 2050, distinguishing climate-driven 
changes from the additional effects of projected shifts in sea-surface salinity

in emission budgets, largely owing to its extensive mangrove area. These 
findings highlight the importance of incorporating sea-surface salinity and 
tidal range into future projections of mangrove sediment GHG emissions under 
global change.

Current Strengths and Limitations of Toxicokinetic-Toxicodynamic (TKTD) Models 
for Freshwater Microalgae.

Yenney E(1), Cedergreen N(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Plant and Environmental Sciences, University of Copenhagen, 
Thorvaldsensvej 40, 1871Frederiksberg C, Denmark.

Toxicokinetic-toxicodynamic (TKTD) models are increasingly used to enhance 
environmental risk assessment by linking laboratory toxicity data with dynamic 
exposure scenarios. For freshwater microalgae, which are crucial primary 
producers, TKTD approaches offer a framework to predict population growth 
inhibition and recovery under fluctuating chemical stress. A review of 12 
studies (2012-2023) applying TKTD models to freshwater planktonic microalgae was 
conducted to compare their structural assumptions, end points, and validation 
methods. These models mainly focus on green algae and herbicides that inhibit 
photosystem II, with limited exploration of other taxonomic groups or modes of 
action. The complexity of models varies significantly, from simple structures 
assuming rapid equilibrium between external and internal chemical concentrations 
to mechanistic models that explicitly incorporate TK components and damage 
progression. While simple models support regulatory use, omitting TK processes 
can reduce their effectiveness for chemicals with delayed effects or complex 
uptake behaviors. Expanding taxonomic coverage and enhancing external validation 
under realistic exposure conditions is crucial to increasing the ecological 
relevance of algal TKTD modeling.

connected aquatic systems. This review synthesizes global field and mechanistic 
evidence on the expansion of freshwater harmful cyanobacteria along the 
freshwater-to-marine continuum. Hydrodynamic processes facilitate downstream

Elucidating pH-Dependent Silica Removal Mechanisms in Aluminum-Based 
Coagulation.

Malkoske TA(1), Garcia-Segura S(1), Tong T(1).

Author information:
(1)School of Sustainable Engineering and the Built Environment, Arizona State 
University, Tempe, Arizona85287, United States.

Silica scaling is a major limiting factor to the treatment and valorization of 
saline brines as alternative water sources. While coagulation provides 
competitive silica removal capacity compared to ion exchange and adsorption, the 
incomplete knowledge of silica removal mechanisms hinders efforts to improve 
process efficiency. In this study, we employed experimental investigations and 
materials characterization to advance the molecular-level understanding of 
silica removal during electrocoagulation (EC) and chemical coagulation (CC). EC 
provided greater silica removal compared to CC for all coagulant types 
considered. For both EC and CC, silica removal capacity increased 2- to 5-fold 
with rising pH. Characterization of precipitates showed that the pH-dependent 
increase in silica removal capacity was driven by Al-O-Si bond formation and 
silicic acid polymerization. A novel titration method revealed that at pH ≤ 8.0, 
silica binding occurred via η-OH2+ activated sites on aluminum precipitate, 
whereas at pH 10.0, binding resulted from reactions among partially deprotonated 
η-OH sites, bound silica, and silanol groups. Silica removal mechanisms were 
validated using synthetic brackish groundwater, where synergistic interactions 
between aluminum and Ca2+/Mg2+ substantially increased silica removal. This work 
provides a mechanistic basis for the rational operation of aluminum-based 
coagulation to enhance silica removal from saline brines.

We estimate block-level emission intensities of nitrogen oxides (NOX) and fine 
particulate matter (PM2.5) from on-road vehicle traffic for every census block 
in the United States, combining MOVES-based emission factors with street level 
traffic data. We use this spatially refined, computationally efficient, and 
policy-sensitive metric to evaluate emissions burden. Despite comprising less

burdens. Statistically significant racial-ethnic or income disparities are 
present in 85-89% of US counties. Critically, these disparities are not confined 
to large metropolitan areas. They are widespread across both urban and rural 
counties nationwide. We also show that spatial aggregation substantially 
attenuates estimated disparities of burdened groups, underscoring the importance 
of spatially refined analysis.

priority for enhancing Fenton/Fenton-like processes to degrade emerging 
contaminants (ECs). In conventional iron-based catalysts (e.g., Fe2O3, FeOOH), 
the iron center is tightly locked inside a rigid cage of hexa-oxygen 
coordination ([FeO6] unit) that is resistant to geometric distortion and 
electron transfer. This phenomenon, termed "Rigid Locking Effect", hinders the 
Fe(III)-to-Fe(II) conversion. To break this, we propose a ligand-engineering

unique [O-FeCl4-O] motif in laminated reduced graphene oxide (rGO) nanochannels.

delocalization, and enhanced spin-orbit coupling (SOC). This tailored motif 
significantly promotes Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycling, resulting in a turnover frequency 
per iron site (TOFFe) of 43.66 h-1, which is a 1091-fold enhancement compared to 
that of the conventional [FeO6] motif in Fe2O3. This enhancement leads to a 
30.7-fold increase in HO• yield, enabling efficient removal of diverse ECs in 
complex water matrices and during long-term continuous operation. This study 
establishes a proof-of-concept paradigm for designing efficient heterogeneous 
catalysts and advances practical Fenton-based water decontamination.

We developed a bottom-up, data-driven approach for constructing a time-informed 
adverse outcome pathway (AOP) network for environmental chemical-induced 
cardiotoxicity. Mechanistic end points were systematically extracted from 339 in 
vitro and in vivo studies, yielding 1759 Key Event (KE) entries and 4938 Key

support thresholding, 62 unique KEs and 256 unique KERs were retained for

reduced left ventricular function. A central methodological finding was that

of KEs. The same KE could occur across multiple durations depending on the

resolved distinct acute, subacute, and chronic pathway patterns not apparent 
from KE timing alone. This framework provides an evidence-weighted synthesis of 
the most consistently supported cardiotoxicity mechanisms and introduces a 
temporal layer for the mechanistic interpretation of heterogeneous evidence.

releases of substances, yet they remain difficult to locate because records are 
incomplete and surface indicators are often absent. Unmanned aerial vehicle

Carboxylation and decarboxylation are among the most ubiquitous processes in 
chromophoric dissolved organic matter (CDOM) transformation, occurring during 
humification, photooxidation, and microbial activity. However, their impacts on 
the formation of excited triplet-state CDOM (3CDOM*) remain poorly constrained. 
Using more than 20 model compounds representing common CDOM chromophores, we 
demonstrate that carboxylation enhances triplet quantum yields (Φ) by 
1.1-69-fold relative to their parent compounds. Consistently, Φ values of CDOM 
isolates positively correlate with their carboxyl content. Theoretical 
calculations reveal that carboxylation shifts the lowest excited state from 
locally excited π-π* character toward mixed n-π*/charge-transfer states and 
increases spin-orbit coupling, thereby promoting intersystem crossing and 
triplet formation. Building on these insights, we developed quantitative models 
that predict Φ using thermodynamic and electronic descriptors and established 
empirical relationships between Φ and bulk CDOM properties, including molecular 
weight and total antioxidant capacity. Furthermore, solar irradiation of humic 
acid induced decarboxylation accompanied by a decline in Φ, whereas carboxyl 
introduction enhanced the overall photochemical reactivity of CDOM toward 
organic contaminant degradation. Together, these findings elucidate how 
carboxylation-decarboxylation modulates 3CDOM* formation, advancing mechanistic 
understanding of aquatic reactive species generation and natural attenuation of 
organic contaminants.

Effective sludge dewatering is essential for reducing sludge volume and 
associated transportation and disposal burdens. However, conventional approaches 
often require substantial chemical addition or energy input, increasing 
operating costs and potential secondary environmental impacts. Here, we present 
a CO2 hydrate crystallization-based dewatering approach that avoids conventional 
chemical sludge conditioners. Residual water in mechanically dewatered sludge is 
converted into separable solid hydrate structures, with water molecules

hydrate-dissociated water with reduced aqueous constituent levels following 
hydrate layer separation. These results highlight CO2 hydrate crystallization as 
a phase-transition-driven strategy for deep sludge dewatering, with energy 
integration and solid-liquid separation remaining key considerations for further 
process development.

N-(1,3-Dimethylbutyl)-N'-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine-quinone (6PPD-Q) has been 
widely detected in aquatic environments and exhibits extremely high toxicity to 
aquatic organisms, establishing it as the primary culprit behind urban runoff 
mortality syndrome. This review systematically examines its environmental 
migration, transformation pathways, and aquatic distribution, toxicity, and 
removal. The key findings are (1) 6PPD-Q originates mainly from tire wear and 
undergoes long-range transport via runoff and atmospheric circulation, with 
microbial processes dominating its condition-dependent biotransformation. (2) It 
is widely detected in surface water, groundwater, sediments, and wastewater, 
showing pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity driven by rainfall and snowmelt. 
(3) 6PPD-Q displays strong species-specific toxicity, particularly to salmonids, 
causing acute lethality and sublethal effects including oxidative stress, 
neurotoxicity, and developmental toxicity at environmentally relevant 
concentrations. (4) Removal technologies include advanced oxidation, adsorption, 
biodegradation, and coupled approaches. Light-driven oxidation shows promise, 
yet unrealistic experimental concentrations, unknown byproduct toxicity, and 
economic feasibility remain key barriers. Based on current findings and 
identified research gaps, we propose recommendations to deepen the understanding 
of the environmental implications of 6PPD-Q and guide the development of 
effective mitigation technologies.

Domestic waste generates volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and emits strong malodors 
that reduce environmental comfort. The generation of these odor-causing 
molecules usually occurs in relatively high-humidity conditions, which speed up 
the deterioration of adsorbents, creating secondary waste from frequent 
replacement. Herein, we report a lithium-doped manganese dioxide (Li-MnO2) 
photothermal system that sustainably degrades acetic acid (CH3COOH, a key VFA). 
Mechanistic studies reveal the ionic bond in Li-O localizes electrons at the 
oxygen atom, while the covalent bond in Mn-O establishes an efficient electron 
transport channel. This electron-rich oxygen can cleave the O-H bond in H2O with 
an ultra-low energy barrier of 0.01 eV, generating dihydroxy groups, which 
subsequently initiate a nucleophilic attack on the O-H and C-H bonds in CH3COOH 
molecules. The introduction of light not only efficiently converts the material 
surface into thermal energy, but it also triggers electron rearrangement. The 
engineered Li-MnO2 catalyst demonstrates complete CH3COOH degradation at 291 mW 
cm-2. A modular photothermal purification device demonstrates above 1000 h odor 
removal efficiency in municipal waste scenario. We anticipate this work will 
enable perpetual CH3COOH removal from domestic waste without external energy 
input, offering a sustainable solution for odor control in waste management.

Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) is an important flexibility management technology for 
lower-carbon transport and the electricity grid. However, its effectiveness 
relies on the temporal alignment between the price incentives and grid dynamics. 
To overcome the challenge of coordinating electricity pricing with V2G 
deployment, we integrated a Bayesian optimization framework into a unit 
commitment model of the 2030 Jing-Jin-Tang power grid. Results demonstrate that

pricing mechanisms is essential to ensure that widespread V2G deployment 
effectively supports decarbonization goals.

Temperature monitoring is critical for endoscopic laser surgery to prevent 
tissue damage. Thermal injuries of the urothelium have been reported as a known 
complication of laser lithotripsy, however, in most cases real time temperature 
measurement is not available due to the absence of sensors in conventional 
endoscopes. In this study, we present an all-optical fluorescein-based thermal 
sensing approach enabling temperature measurement via an optical fiber, 
independent of the endoscope model, using a biocompatible fluorescent probe. The 
temperature-dependent fluorescence response originates from the redistribution 
between the monoanionic and dianionic forms of fluorescein, which is influenced 
by albumin through different mechanisms depending on the solution environment. A 
comparative analysis in water and in saline solution, which is commonly used for 
irrigation during surgery, revealed distinct environmental contributions to the 
temperature response of fluorescein emission. In water, a stable 
fluorescein-albumin complex was formed, accompanied by a systematic shift in the 
monoanion-dianion equilibrium, leading to strong temperature-dependent spectral 
changes. In saline solution, which is more relevant to intraoperative 
irrigation, no stable complex was observed, as shown by time-resolved 
fluorescence techniques; nevertheless, a reproducible temperature response was 
retained and was attributed to weaker, non-specific microenvironmental effects, 
including local pH variations near the protein surface. These findings 
demonstrate a reproducible temperature-dependent fluorescence response under 
defined solution conditions and provide a proof of principle for further 
development of optical temperature-monitoring approaches relevant to minimally 
invasive procedures.

Magnetocardiography (MCG) measures the magnetic fields produced by the cardiac

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Range shifters (RS) are used to treat shallow targets 
in pencil beam scanning (PBS) proton therapy. This study aims to validate an 
in-house-fabricated epoxy resin RS through mechanical and dosimetric 
measurements, evaluate the Monte Carlo (MC) algorithm dose‑calculation accuracy 
of the treatment planning system (TPS) beam model incorporating this device, and 
assess its clinical feasibility for PBS proton therapy applications.
METHODS: The RS was fabricated using a silicone mould and machined to the 
required dimensions after curing. It was further evaluated through material 
characterization, mechanical testing, and dosimetric validation. Material 
characterization included determining the elemental composition, mass density, 
and mean excitation energy, which were incorporated into the beam modelling. 
Mechanical validation comprised dimensional verification, fitment testing, and 
assessment of material integrity and uniformity. Dosimetric validation was 
performed by measuring water-equivalent thickness (WET), range parameters, spot 
size, absolute dose, and fluence, and comparing them with TPS-MC calculations.
RESULTS: The cured epoxy resin exhibited normalized elemental composition of 
H:8.0%, C:65.0%, N:0.1%, and O:26.9%, with mass density 1.15 g/cm³ and mean 
excitation energy 72.5 eV. The fabricated RS matched the reference design within 
±1 mm and demonstrated satisfactory fitment, reproducibility, material integrity 
and uniformity. The measured WET agreed with TPS estimated values within 0.06 
g/cm², while differences in range parameters were <1 mm. Measured spot sizes and 
the 9-spot matrix showed excellent agreement with TPS estimates across different 
air-gap settings. Absolute dose measurements agreed with TPS-MC calculations 
within 3%, and patient-specific fluence measurements showed excellent agreement 
with TPS calculations under stringent gamma evaluation criteria.
CONCLUSION: This study presents the first comprehensive clinical validation and 
evaluation of cured solid epoxy resin as an RS material for PBS proton therapy 
applications. The in-house-fabricated, cured epoxy resin-based RS demonstrated 
excellent agreement with TPS-MC calculations and experimental measurements, 
establishing its clinical feasibility.

Pharmacotherapeutic management of chronic pain in joint hypermobility and 
Ehlers-Danlos syndromes: a clinical perspective.

Castori M(1).

Author information:
(1)Inborn Errors of Morphogenesis Research Unit and Division of Medical 
Genetics, Fondazione IRCCS-Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza, San Giovanni Rotondo, 
Italy.

INTRODUCTION: Joint hypermobility-related pain is an increasingly recognized 
musculoskeletal pain characterized by mixed pain mechanisms, frequent 
chronicity, and an incompletely defined natural history. Joint 
hypermobility-related pain may occur in monogenic Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, but 
it is more frequently encountered in people with hypermobility spectrum 
disorders and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, conditions that remain 
molecularly unresolved.
AREAS COVERED: This article places joint hypermobility-related pain in its 
historical and conceptual context, summarizes the mechanisms thought to 
contribute to its development, and critically reviews pharmacotherapeutic 
evidence identified in PubMed, Web of Science, EMBASE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and 
WHO ICTRP without date restrictions.
EXPERT OPINION: Current evidence is low-level and does not support the efficacy 
of any disease-specific, repurposed, or novel drug for joint 
hypermobility-related pain. Medication alone may be appropriate for occasional 
or recurrent pain and predominantly nociceptive flares. Chronicity, 
musculoskeletal disability, and overlapping nociceptive, neuropathic, and 
nociplastic mechanisms limit the effectiveness of drug-only strategies and 
envisage multimodal management. Pharmacological approach should stand on one 
drug at a time, usually at a low dose, and benefit and adverse burden should be 
reassessed after a predefined trial. Patients are best managed by keeping the 
diagnostic and therapeutic pathways separate.

Exhaled breath analysis is a non-invasive approach for assessing physiological 
alterations in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This study evaluated overnight 
changes in exhaled CO₂, O₂, and N₂O concentrations and their associations with 
OSA severity and polysomnographic parameters.&#xD;Methods: In this prospective

composition, particularly greater changes in exhaled O₂ and N₂O concentrations.

physiological alterations associated with OSA severity and warrant further

We found evidence of mutual recognition of chemical cues between fish lice 
(Argulus spp.) and three-spined sticklebacks (Gasterosteus aculeatus). Each 
manifested changes in movement in response to chemical cues from one another; 
Argulus increased speed while G. aculeatus decreased theirs. As Argulus use

searching activity. Conversely, G. aculeatus may slow down to augment visual

represents the first evidence that G. aculeatus may use chemical cues to 
mitigate the risk of parasitism from lice.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common brain disorder in 
children that can persist into adulthood, affecting social, academic, and career 
life. Early diagnosis is crucial for managing these impacts on patients and the 
healthcare system but is often labor-intensive and time-consuming. This paper 
presents a novel method to improve ADHD diagnosis precision and timeliness by 
leveraging Deep Learning (DL) approaches and electroencephalogram (EEG) signals. 
We introduce ADHDeepNet, a deep learning model that utilizes comprehensive 
temporal-spatial characterization, attention modules, and explainability 
techniques optimized for EEG signals. ADHDeepNet integrates feature extraction 
and refinement processes to enhance ADHD diagnosis. The model was trained and 
validated on a dataset of 121 participants (61 ADHD, 60 Healthy Controls), 
employing nested cross-validation for robust performance. The proposed two-stage

deviations and magnification levels is applied for data augmentation. ADHDeepNet 
achieved 100% sensitivity and 99.17% accuracy in classifying ADHD/HC subjects.

bands for ADHD diagnosis, we analyzed the learned weights and activation 
patterns of the model's primary layers. Additionally, t-distributed Stochastic

interpreting the model's decisions. This study highlights the potential of deep 
learning and EEG in enhancing ADHD diagnosis accuracy and efficiency.

The combination of stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy with 
fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) offers a powerful route to 
functional super-resolution imaging, but remains technically challenging for 
lifetime-based sensing because of the complex interplay between stimulated 
emission, photon budget, and accurate lifetime quantification. In this technical 
note, we evaluate and optimize STED-FLIM for nanoscale mapping of bacterial 
membrane mechanics using the mechanosensitive probe Flipper-TR. This probe is 
particularly demanding for STED-FLIM because it exhibits a biexponential

analysis workflow that combines optimized imaging conditions with tail fitting

resolution compared with confocal microscopy, while maintaining sufficient 
photon counts for robust lifetime estimation. Finally, we discuss the trade-offs 
between spatial resolution and photon budget and provide practical 
recommendations for implementing STED-FLIM with environmentally sensitive 
probes. These results extend the application of Flipper-TR to functional 
super-resolution microscopy and provide a framework for robust STED-FLIM 
measurements of membrane nanomechanics and other fluorescence lifetime-based 
sensing applications.

Brenig W(1).

Author information:
(1)Institute for Theoretical Physics, Technische Universität Braunschweig,

A study of the dynamical two-dimensional (2D) nonlinear response of the 
dimerized spin-1/2 chain to external electric fields is presented. The coupling 
of the spin system to light is set to arise from the inverse 
Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. In the XY-limit, we provide analytical 
expressions for the second-order nonlinear dynamical response function. Apart 
from multi spinon continua, this response displays a strong antidiagonal, i.e. 
galvanoelectric, feature in the 2D frequency plane. This allows to read off 
scattering rates of the fractional spinon excitations. For the XXZ-case, we

considering vertex corrections which are induced by the zz-exchange. We show 
this renormalization to modify the spinon joint density of states significantly, 
potentially allowing for the formation of in-gap bound states. As a result, the 
vertex corrected light-matter coupling can induce a dramatic spectral weight 
transfer to lower energies for the dynamical response function within the 2D 
frequency plane.

Prevention Before Therapy in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: The Clinical, 
Economic, and Human Case for Weighting Resources Upstream.

Eibl G(1), Hines OJ(1), Rozengurt E(1).

Author information:
(1)University of California, Los Angeles Los Angeles, California United States.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is projected to become the 
second-leading cause of US cancer death by 2030, and survival is dominated by 
stage at diagnosis: roughly 44% at five years for localized disease versus about 
3% with distant metastases. Only about 15% of cases are detected while 
localized, surgery reaches a minority of patients, and no validated screening 
test exists for average-risk adults. This topical review examines the biologic, 
clinical, economic, psychological, equity, and therapeutic evidence bearing on 
where scarce resources should be directed. The long interval between initiating 
mutation and invasive disease provides a mechanistic rationale for prevention 
and interception, and the modifiable exposures of obesity, tobacco, type 2 
diabetes, and alcohol act largely within that window. We consider innovations 
that extend prevention beyond lifestyle advice-incretin-based weight management, 
risk stratification anchored in new-onset diabetes and biomarkers, and 
immunoprevention-together with early-onset disease, implementation and policy, 
and the barriers and evidentiary limits that temper these arguments. We propose 
a three-tier framework of primary prevention, early detection in high-risk 
groups, and therapy, and argue that research, policy, and clinical investment 
should be weighted upstream, because every case prevented spares the cost, 
capacity, and suffering that the downstream tiers must otherwise absorb.

Azo dyes are widespread in the environment, and humans ingest a range of these 
dyes present in food and drugs. The human gut microbiome significantly impacts 
the fate of ingested azo dyes primarily through the reduction of the azo bond 
(R-N = N-R'). Flavin-dependent azoreductases have been considered the key 
enzymatic drivers of this process. To challenge this paradigm, we constructed a 
sequence similarity network of known azoreductases and focused on AzoA of 
Klebsiella pneumoniae, a central representative within the gut microbiome 
cluster. Unexpectedly, K. pneumoniae AzoA displayed relatively low in vitro 
activity against a range of azo compounds. While the physiological implications 
remain unclear, these findings are consistent with the possibility that 
nonenzymatic mechanisms contribute substantially to azo compound reduction in 
the gut. Furthermore, structural characterization of AzoA, as a holoenzyme and 
in its ligand-bound state, revealed a previously unrecognized ligand-coupled 
mechanism involving remodeling of the active site and oligomeric state.

A New Family of Electron-Bifurcating Enzymes Represented by Ferredoxin- and 
NAD-Dependent Glycerol-3-Phosphate Oxidoreductase.

Schut GJ(1), Poole FL(1), Adams MWW(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Biochemistry & Molecular Biology, University of Georgia, 
Athens, Georgia30602, United States.

Glycerol is abundant in natural environments and is utilized by many microbes. 
In aerobes, it is typically converted, via glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P), to 
dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) by a quinone-linked dehydrogenase thereby 
coupling glycolysis and respiration. Under anaerobic conditions, an 
NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase has been proposed to oxidize G3P to DHAP in several 
bacteria but this reaction is thermodynamically unfavorable. Herein, we have 
purified a heterotrimeric electron bifurcating enzyme from the archaeon 
Pyrococcus furiosus where the simultaneous oxidation of both G3P (Eo' -190 mV) 
and reduced ferredoxin (Em ∼ -450 mV) enables reduction of NAD+(Eo' -320 mV) and 
production of DHAP. Surprisingly, this ferredoxin-dependent NAD+G3P 
oxidoreductase (FngABC) is unrelated evolutionarily to the four known families 
of bifurcating enzyme. Analysis by UV-visible spectroscopy and of its predicted 
structure suggest FngABC has a nonclassical bifurcation mechanism. Phylogenetic 
and genome context analyses of 4,273 P. furiosus FngA homologues revealed they 
are widespread with ∼35% found mainly in Clostridia as FngABC and ∼10% found 
mainly in Actinomyces as FngAB, most of which utilize polyols in addition to 
glycerol. The remaining ∼40% are present in Gammaproteobacteria and halophilic 
archaea but here FngA is associated with homologues of E. coli GlpBC, which are 
unrelated to FngBC, and these enzymes typically only use glycerol. It is 
therefore proposed that P. furiosus FngABC and the previously characterized E. 
coli GlpABC are disparate members of a new electron bifurcating family 
widespread in the microbial world that are involved in the metabolism of a range 
of sugars as well as glycerol.

Cnidarians possess a large number of opsins in their genomes for their various 
photoreceptive functions. In particular, they uniquely possess Gs-coupled opsins 
that induce intracellular cAMP accumulation in a light-dependent manner. These 
Gs-coupled opsins, cnidopsins, are powerful optogenetic tools that manipulate 
cAMP-dependent cellular responses. In this study, we characterized a cnidopsin, 
named AtCnidop3a, from the coral Acropora tenuis as a Gs-coupled and

substitution. Our characterization and engineering of the cnidopsin revealed the 
functional diversity of cnidarian opsins and their potential utility as 
optogenetic tools regulating Gs-dependent physiological responses.

regulation of neurotransmitter release and in the integration of dendritic 
inputs in the central nervous system (CNS). However, their precise localization

Three Distinct Binding Modes Govern High-Affinity Ligand Interactions with 
Amyloid Fibrils.

Chisholm TS(1).

Author information:
(1)Yusuf Hamied Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge, CambridgeCB2 
1EW, U.K.

Fibrillar protein aggregates are a defining feature of neurodegenerative 
diseases and represent attractive biomarkers and therapeutic targets. However, 
the rational design of small-molecule ligands and probes targeting these 
aggregates is limited by a poor understanding of how ligands bind to amyloid 
fibrils. This work outlines an experimental approach to determine the binding 
mode of ligands to amyloid fibrils using previously overlooked information 
contained within standard binding assays. Using a mathematical framework to 
analyze binding behavior, three distinct high-affinity binding modes were 
identified: discrete, overlapping, and interacting binding. Reanalysis of 
published binding data indicates that these binding modes are widespread among 
common amyloid-binding ligand scaffolds. Two ligands were designed using 
principles informed by these binding modes, yielding improved binding affinities 
and characteristic fluorescence responses. These findings establish a practical 
framework for determining how small molecules bind amyloid fibrils using 
straightforward binding assays and for guiding the design of future 
fibril-binding ligands and probes.

N-Acetylglucosamine exists in various glycoforms and linkage patterns within 
organisms, playing a crucial role in numerous vital biological processes. The 
signal of β-1,2-N-acetylglucosamine is a key component within complex 
biantennary N-glycans on the cell surface, leaving related research in its early 
exploratory stages. Currently, there is a lack of efficient tools and methods 
capable of directly modifying terminal N-acetylglucosamine on living cells. In 
this study, we identified a novel β-N-acetylglucosaminidase from Elizabethkingia

β-1,2-N-acetylglucosamine, enabling direct removal from native glycoproteins

time the successful removal of β-1,2-N-acetylglucosamine from the living cell 
surface using this enzyme. Based on its isolation and newly characterized 
cell-surface glycan-editing activity, we designated it as EmNag, also termed 
cell-surface glycan-editing N-acetylglucosaminidase (csgeNag). It showed 
favorable enzymatic stability between pH 5-8 and from 4 to 37 °C. Sequence 
analysis and alanine-scanning mutagenesis identified a conserved active pocket 
containing the catalytic residue pair Asp317-Glu318, with Asp317 being essential 
for activity. In summary, our findings provide an effective and reliable method 
for the targeted removal of β-1,2-N-acetylglucosamine from the living cell 
surface, establishing a foundation for further functional studies and practical 
applications.

Many antiviral and anticancer drugs are based on the structure of pyrimidine 
nucleosides. Once phosphorylated, they function by interfering with either DNA 
or RNA replication or transcription. The antiviral enzyme, viperin, catalyzes 
the dehydration of CTP to produce 3'-deoxy-3',4'-didehydroCTP (ddhCTP), which 
functions as a natural antiviral nucleotide. Various drugs mimic the structure 
of CTP, and furthermore, viperin is upregulated in some cancers and autoimmune 
diseases. Therefore, we examined whether such drugs may be substrates for 
viperin. A panel of eight commercially available nucleosides, including several 
clinically used drugs, were enzymatically converted to their triphosphate forms 
and investigated as substrates for viperin. Five of the nucleotides were not 
substrates, indicating that viperin has generally high specificity for CTP. Two 
nucleotides, 3'-deoxy-3'-fluoroCTP and cytarabine triphosphate elicited 
reductive cleavage of SAM and were converted to their dehydrated products by 
viperin. The last compound, gemcitabine triphosphate, elicited reductive 
cleavage of SAM, but no dehydrated product was observed, implying that it 
activates SAM cleavage without undergoing hydrogen atom abstraction. The 
implications of these results are discussed.

mRNA Structure Regulates Translation at Every Step.

Khitun A(1), Weeks KM(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Chemistry, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, North 
Carolina27599-3290, United States.

Precise, context-sensitive control of protein synthesis is critical in 
eukaryotic cells, and mRNA structure has emerged as a central mechanism for 
achieving this control. mRNA structures influence every stage of translation. 
During initiation, structures within 5' untranslated regions modulate ribosome 
association with mRNA and the balance between translation of the main open 
reading frame and use of upstream or alternative start sites. During elongation, 
structures in the coding sequence govern ribosome pausing in ways that can 
either protect mRNA stability or trigger decay. During termination, structures 
downstream of primary stop codons promote readthrough to generate protein 
isoforms in a tissue-specific manner. mRNA structures are remodeled by helicase 
expression, post-transcriptional modifications, and translational programming to 
provide additional layers of regulation. We review recent advances illuminating 
diverse mechanisms by which RNA structure modulates translation.

Zawistowski RK(1)(2), Chauviré T(1)(2), Manna S(1), Ananth N(1), Crane BR(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Cornell University, Ithaca, New

(2)Weill Institute for Cell and Molecular Biology, Cornell University, Ithaca,

Long-range protein electron transfer (ET) often depends on tryptophan and 
tyrosine residues acting as radical relay sites. For example, cytochrome c 
peroxidase (CcP) generates a W191•+ radical to increase ET from cytochrome c 
(Cc) to the active center. W191 substitution to Tyr reduces ET rates, but 
introduction of an adjacent general base (as Glu or His) at position 232 
(Y191:E/H232 CcP) recovers activity. E232 fluorination lowers the pKa of the 
conjugate base and confirms that a hydrogen bond is critical to elevate the 
Y191• formal potential for effective ET. Photoinitiated ET between Zn-porphyrin 
(ZnP) CcP (ZnCcP) and Cc also depends on activating Y191 with a basic residue 
but through a different mechanism than for the peroxide-driven system. In ZnCcP, 
pH dependencies and solvent isotope effects indicate that proton-coupled 
electron transfer to the basic residue and ZnP•+, respectively, facilitates 
Y191• formation. Replacing Cc with the irreversible oxidant [Co(NH3)5Cl]2+ 
isolates distinct protein radicals for characterization by electron paramagnetic 
resonance (EPR) spectroscopy. Radical distributions and computation indicate 
that W191•+ lies close in potential to ZnP•+ and that the two radicals exchange 
on a slow time scale despite their close separation. Remarkably, Y191:E/H232 
ZnCcP variants propagate radicals differently to peripheral sites depending on 
the nature of the 232 residue. QM/MM calculations support radical exchange 
between ZnP•+/Trp•+ and the importance of a hydrogen bond to Y191• for 
maintaining a high potential to oxidize peripheral donors. These resolved 
reactivity patterns of CcP/ZnCcP have general relevance for engineering proton 
management to separate and migrate charge in proteins and potentially other 
molecular systems.

that AtGPPA/PPX possesses pppGpp dephosphorylation activity in vivo. 
Loss-of-function mutants of AtGPPA/PPX exhibited no overt growth defects under 
either standard or nitrogen-starvation conditions. However, chlorophyll

after actinic-light illumination without changes in the PSII quantum yield, 
suggesting faster electron transport and reduced need for thermal dissipation. 
Together, these results suggest that the cytosol-localized AtGPPA/PPX functions 
as a phosphatase with unknown physiological substrate(s) and plays a key role in 
photosynthetic acclimation to fluctuating light conditions.

Transient Directing Groups for Enhancing Affinity between Native Substrates and 
Transition Metal C-H Activation Catalysts.

Yirak JR(1), Wang Z(1), Tomanik M(1), Chen YQ(1), Wu K(1), Yu JQ(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Chemistry, The Scripps Research Institute, 10550 N. Torrey 
Pines Rd., La Jolla, California92037, United States.

In the past two decades, transition metal-catalyzed C-H activation has emerged 
as an attractive and valuable strategy for enabling novel disconnections in the 
synthesis of natural products and pharmaceuticals. Substrate-directed C-H 
activation, which employs pre-coordination of a substrate's functional group 
with the catalyst to recruit it for C-H metalation with high site-selectivity, 
is a particularly powerful approach. Early directed C-H activations relied on 
bespoke directing groups with separate installation and removal steps, reducing 
synthetic efficiency and practicality (limited functional group tolerance, 
substrate scope). The development of C-H activation methods which use functional 
groups native to common building blocks and synthetic intermediates would be 
highly valuable. In this account, we highlight the discovery and development of 
a transient directing group (TDG) platform for Pd-catalyzed C-H activation 
reactions of native aldehydes, ketones, and amines. This approach leverages the 
reversible imine formation event between the substrate and a complementary TDG 
motif to transiently generate the optimal L,X-type assembly capable of 
recruiting Pd catalysts for a diverse range of C-H activation reactions, 
including C-C, C-halogen, C-O, and C-N bond formations. We also describe the 
application of pyridone ligands in concert with the TDG approach to amplify the 
reactivity of the Pd catalysts and to activate previously inaccessible C-H 
bonds. Finally, we cover notable applications of Pd-catalyzed TDG C-H activation 
in complex molecule synthesis.

Editing Enzymes with Multiscale Metal-Based Components.

Li X(1)(2)(3), Zare RN(4), Ge J(5)(2).

Author information:
(1)College of Life Science and Technology, Beijing University of Chemical 
Technology, Beijing100029, China.
(2)State Key Laboratory of Green Biomanufacturing, Beijing100084, China.
(3)Beijing Synthetic Bio-Manufacturing Technology Innovation Center, 
Beijing102209, China.
(4)Department of Chemistry, Stanford University, Stanford, California94305, 
United States.
(5)Key Lab for Industrial Biocatalysis, Ministry of Education, Department of 
Chemical Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing100084, China.

Enzymes are powerful natural catalysts distinguished by high efficiency and 
selectivity. The use of enzymes in the chemical industry can theoretically 
enable numerous efficient and sustainable reaction pathways. Nevertheless, the 
application of enzymes is hindered by their narrow catalytic repertoire. Enzymes 
are readily deactivated under nonnatural environments, and their reaction types 
are limited. Developing enzymes with new catalytic functions has been a 
longstanding challenge in the field of biocatalysis. Strategies such as directed 
evolution and de novo protein design have been very successful in designing new 
enzymes. However, as both approaches rely on the engineering of amino acid 
sequences of proteins, they remain constrained and cannot fully meet the growing 
demand for non-natural biocatalysis. Incorporating abiotic components with 
enzymes is a powerful tool for editing enzymes to render new catalytic 
capabilities. Metal-based components possess a broad catalytic repertoire, 
structural stability, and multifunctionality, making them promising building 
blocks for enzyme editing. This Account summarizes our contributions over the 
past decade in editing enzyme catalysts with metal-based components as a 
scale-dependent evolution, from nanoscale environmental modulation to atom-scale 
active site redefinition, illustrating how enzyme editing with metal-based 
components can systematically address non-natural catalytic challenges. A 
conceptual framework in which enzymes are edited with metal-based components 
across scales from the nanometer to the atomic dimension is introduced, 
establishing a logical basis for integrating biocatalysis with abiotic 
reactivity. At the nanoscale, enzymes are encapsulated in metal-based frameworks 
to improve the configuration stability, enabling catalysis under non-native and 
harsh conditions. The robustness of enzymes under extreme pH, high temperature, 
and organic solvent can be largely enhanced through the regulation of 
metal-based frameworks. At the sub-nanoscale, metal clusters are embedded within 
enzyme scaffolds to construct enzyme-metal hybrid catalysts. By integration of 
enzymatic and chemical catalysis, new non-natural catalytic processes can be 
established. At the atomic scale, metal atoms are incorporated into the enzyme 
catalytic pocket, creating new hybrid active sites. The hybrid active site 
endows an enzyme with capabilities to drive new-to-nature reactions, unlocking 
an expanded enzyme catalytic space. This work provides a unifying conceptual 
framework that clarifies how metal-based components can be strategically 
employed to reprogram enzyme stability, functionality, and reactivity. We hope 
that the strategies and concepts discussed herein offer comprehensive design 
principles for biohybrid catalysts and establish a foundation for reprogramming 
enzymatic function beyond evolutionary limitations.
