The MBW complex regulates floral volatiles in petunia: transcriptional repressor 
EOBV is a MYB component of the complex.

Skaliter O(1), Cohen R(1), Leor-Librach E(1), Shor E(1), Rudich O(1), Edelbaum 
O(1), Shklarman E(1), Masci T(1), Vainstein A(1).

Author information:
(1)Institute of Plant Sciences and Genetics in Agriculture, The Robert H. Smith 
Faculty of Agriculture, Food and Environment, The Hebrew University of 
Jerusalem, Rehovot 7610001, Israel.

Anthocyanin biosynthesis in Petunia is regulated by the bHLH AN1 and the WDR 
protein AN11, which together with interchangeable MYBs form the MYB-bHLH-WDR 
(MBW) complex. As they share the same biosynthetic pathway, anthocyanins are 
interlinked with phenylalanine-derived volatiles. However, involvement of the 
MBW complex in regulating these floral volatiles has not been demonstrated. 
TRV-based suppression of either AN1 or AN11 led to an increase in volatile 
emission, indicating that they are involved in negative regulation of this 
trait. Yeast two-hybrid and in-planta pairwise and three-way protein-interaction 
assays revealed that EMISSION OF BENZENOIDS V (EOBV) is a component of the MBW 
complex. Headspace and internal pool analyses of flowers from eobv-knockout 
lines, generated using a viral-based CRISPR/Cas9 system, revealed that EOBV 
fine-tunes volatile production: phenylpropenes and vanillin levels increased 
while those of benzenoids and phenylpropanoid-related compounds decreased. 
Accordingly, transcript levels of C4H2, directing carbon flux to phenylpropenes 
and vanillin production, and ADT3 were significantly elevated in eobv-knockout 
flowers, along with decreases in PAAS and BSMT. Moreover, in-planta promoter 
activity assays in petunia flowers further demonstrated that C4H2 is negatively 
transcriptionally regulated by EOBV. In addition to its involvement in volatile 
production, EOBV is heat-responsive and affects flower development under 
high-temperature conditions by mitigating the reduction in flower size. EOBV's 
participation in the MBW complex that regulates volatiles and anthocyanins 
reveals an intriguing molecular link between these showy traits and flower 
development.

Deciphering the Mechanistic Origin of Divergent Radical Annulation Reactions of 
ortho-Cyanoaryl Acrylamides.

Fıstıkçı M(1), Zozik Y(2), Eşsiz S(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Medical Services and Techniques, Vocational School of Health 
Services, Hakkari University, Hakkari30000, Türkiye.
(2)Department of Property Protection and Security, Oltu Vocational School, 
Atatürk University, Oltu, Erzurum25400, Türkiye.

The divergent radical annulation reactions of ortho-cyanoaryl acrylamides 
involving cyanomethyl and α-oxyalkyl radicals were investigated using density 
functional theory (DFT) combined with DLPNO-CCSD(T) single-point computations. 
The calculations provide a detailed mechanistic comparison of the experimentally 
observed reaction pathways and reveal distinct downstream reactivity of the 
corresponding radical intermediates. Activation strain model (ASM) analyses show 
that the competing cyclization and C-C bond cleavage via β-scission pathways are 
characterized by different balances between structural distortion and 
interfragment interactions. For the cyanomethyl-radical-derived system, the 
cyclization pathway is associated with a substantially lower distortion energy, 
whereas for the α-oxyalkyl-radical-derived system, the cleavage pathway benefits 
from stronger stabilizing interfragment interactions that compensate for the 
larger distortion penalty. Noncovalent interaction (NCI) analyses provide 
qualitative structural support for these energetic trends. Overall, these 
computations provide a detailed mechanistic comparison of the competing 
downstream pathways of the cyanomethyl- and α-oxyalkyl-radical-derived 
intermediates.

A novel strategy for reconstruction of AORI type III proximal tibial defects : 
surface-type knee reconstruction following defect reconstruction with 3D-printed 
extension-stem augment.

Li X(1), Han Q(1), Zhao X(2), Zhang J(1), Wan Q(1), Gan Z(1), Wang X(1), Zhao 
X(1), Chen H(1), Zhang A(1), Wang J(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Orthopedics, The Second Hospital of Jilin University, 
Changchun, China.
(2)Department of Endocrinology and Metabolism, The First Hospital of Jilin 
University, Changchun, China.

AIMS: For cases of Anderson Orthopaedic Research Institute (AORI) type III 
proximal tibial defects with intact medial collateral ligaments (MCLs), knee 
reconstruction is conventionally performed using semi-constrained prostheses 
with stemmed tibial components in conjunction with cones or sleeves. This study 
aimed to reconstruct AORI type III tibial defects using a 3D-printed 
extension-stem augment, followed by surface-type knee reconstruction to achieve 
long-term stability and promising clinical outcomes.
METHODS: A patient-specific porous extension-stem augment was designed based on 
the defect morphology. The microporous structure allowed direct contact for 
osseointegration, the proximal portion supported tibial baseplate, while the 
distal stem achieved intramedullary fixation. Finite element analysis (FEA) 
assessed the biomechanical stability of the augment. A retrospective analysis 
was conducted between July 2021 and September 2023 on patients who underwent 
reconstruction of AORI type III proximal tibial defects with extension-stem 
augment and surface-type total knee prosthesis.
RESULTS: FEA demonstrated favourable stress and strain distribution and 
micromotion at the prosthesis-bone interface, although localized high-strain 
regions were observed under higher-demand loading conditions. Four patients (0 
male, 4 female) were included, with a minimum follow-up of 20.7 months (20.7 to 
30) and a median age at surgery of 63.0 years (IQR 60.3 to 66.3). The mean Knee 
Society Score (KSS) improved significantly to 85 (82 to 87), and the mean 
Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score 
decreased by 18 (16 to 20). One patient developed periprosthetic joint infection 
on the femoral side at 20.7 months postoperatively and underwent revision 
surgery. Intraoperatively, the augment was securely integrated and could not be 
extracted. Radiological evaluation demonstrated satisfactory alignment and joint 
stability, with no evidence of prosthesis loosening or migration at the latest 
follow-up.
CONCLUSION: The extension-stem augment achieved anatomical reconstruction of 
AORI type III proximal tibial defects and provided stable support for the 
surface-type prosthesis, ensuring reliable knee stability after reconstruction. 
This represents a feasible option for revision of AORI type III tibial defects.

A Novel CCMS Model Reveals a Critical Intronic Sequence in the Snrpb Gene that 
is Required for Normal Development.

Beauchamp MC(1), Alam S(1)(2), Moore J(1), White H(3), Jerome-Majewska 
LA(1)(2)(3)(4).

Author information:
(1)McGill University Health Centre at Glen Site, Montreal, H4A 3J1, Quebec,

(2)Department of Human Genetics, McGill University, Montreal, H3A 1Y2, Quebec,

(3)Department of Anatomy and Cell Biology, McGill University, Montreal, H3A 0C7,

(4)Department of Pediatrics, McGill University, Montreal, H4A 3J1 Quebec,

Pathogenic variants in SNRPB, a common core spliceosomal factor, cause 
Cerebrocostomandibular Syndrome (CCMS). Most CCMS-associated variants result in 
increased inclusion of a PTC-containing alternative exon 2 (AE2). Using 
CRISPR/Cas9 we generated two mutant mice that carried a 46bp or a 61bp deletion 
upstream of Snrpb AE2. Mice and embryos carrying the 46bp deletion are normal.

reduced levels of Snrpb. In addition, this deletion increased the penetrance and 
severity of defects in Snrpbncc and Snrpbmes mutant embryos. Our findings 
indicate that this intronic region is important for SNRPB regulation in mice and 
should be investigated in CCMS patients that do not carry mutations in SNRPB 
coding exons.

Second-Generation Synthesis of the Male Contraceptive YCT-529.

Gantasala N(1), Cheryala N(1), Georg GI(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Medicinal Chemistry and Institute for Therapeutics Discovery & 
Development, College of Pharmacy, University of Minnesota, 717 Delaware Street 
SE, Minneapolis, Minnesota55414, United States.

We report a practical synthesis of the nonhormonal male contraceptive YCT-529. 
The method features key transformations: Grignard-mediated acetylation, the 
α-methylenation of a methyl ketone, and pyrrole formation via the Stetter and 
Paal-Knorr reaction sequence. It avoids iridium and palladium catalysts, 
overcoming the major limitations of an earlier synthesis. The current scalable 
synthesis proceeds in 6 steps from bromochromene 4 in 51% overall yield and does 
not require chromatographic purification.

Development of a therapist-supervised flexibility and resistance exercise 
intervention for adults aged 50 years and over with a distal radius fracture in 
the Wrist Injury Strengthening Exercise (WISE) trial.

Sheehan W(1), Lamb SE(2), Forde CP(3), Srikesavan C(2)(4), Nicolson PJA(4), 
Tutton E(3), Gould J(3), Grant R(3), Achten J(3), Appelbe D(3), Costa ML(3), 
Keene DJ(3).

Author information:
(1)Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Oxford, UK.
(2)Public Health and Sport Sciences, University of Exeter, Exeter, UK.
(3)Kadoorie Institute of Trauma, Emergency and Critical Care, Nuffield 
Department of Orthopaedics, Rheumatology and Musculoskeletal Sciences, 
University of Oxford, Oxford, UK.
(4)Botnar Institute for Musculoskeletal Sciences, Nuffield Department of 
Orthopaedics, Rheumatology and Musculoskeletal Sciences, University of Oxford, 
Oxford, UK.

AIMS: The definitive Wrist Injury Strengthening Exercise (WISE) trial is a 
multicentre superiority randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluating usual care 
advice plus a therapist-supervised flexibility and resistance exercise 
intervention versus usual care advice alone for adults aged ≥ 50 years with a 
distal radius fracture (DRF). This paper describes the development and delivery 
of the therapist-supervised exercise intervention evaluated in the definitive 
WISE RCT.
METHODS: The intervention was developed iteratively in accordance with Medical 
Research Council (MRC) guidance for complex interventions. UK DRF clinical 
guidelines, published rehabilitation RCTs, UK NHS patient information leaflets, 
common post-injury impairments, and exercise and behavioural theory were 
reviewed to inform candidate intervention components. Feedback from UK 
therapists and patient and public involvement partners then informed the design 
of the initial intervention. Two methods of intervention delivery were then 
evaluated in a multicentre feasibility RCT and embedded qualitative study 
involving 117 participants aged ≥ 50 years with a distal radius fracture.
RESULTS: Review of guidelines and previous research highlighted uncertainty 
regarding the optimal rehabilitation after DRF and limited reporting of 
progressive exercise interventions. NHS patient information leaflets largely 
focused on flexibility exercises and self-management advice. Therapist and 
patient feedback informed the intervention content, progression, and participant 
materials. Findings from the feasibility RCT and embedded qualitative study 
supported a therapist-supervised delivery model with three sessions, rather than 
a single-session independent exercise approach. The final intervention comprised 
usual care advice plus up to three one-to-one sessions with a physiotherapist or 
occupational therapist over 12 weeks. Participants also received a workbook 
containing self-management advice, progressive flexibility and resistance 
exercises with resistance bands and therapeutic putty, and behaviour change 
strategies to support exercise adherence.
CONCLUSION: Using an iterative MRC-informed process, a therapist-supervised 
rehabilitation intervention was developed and refined prior to definitive 
evaluation. Transparent reporting of intervention development and content should 
support interpretation, replication, and implementation.

Half-Cycle-Selective Thermal Activation Decouples Oxide Quality from Interfacial 
Oxidation in Atomic Layer Deposition.

Kim J(1)(2), Jeon J(1)(2), Ye S(1)(2), Wang G(2)(3), Baek SH(1)(4), Kim 
SK(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Electronic and Hybrid Materials Research Center, Korea Institute of Science 
and Technology, Seoul02792, Republic of Korea.
(2)KU-KIST Graduate School of Converging Science and Technology, Korea 
University, Seoul02841, Republic of Korea.
(3)Department of Integrative Energy Engineering, Korea University, Seoul02841, 
Republic of Korea.
(4)Advanced Materials Science and Engineering, KIST School, Korea National 
University of Science and Technology, Seoul02792, Republic of Korea.

As semiconductor devices approach nanometer-scale dimensions, functional oxide 
integration increasingly requires the simultaneous improvement of oxide quality 
and preservation of chemically fragile interfaces. Conventional atomic layer 
deposition (ALD) imposes a single substrate temperature on all half-reactions, 
creating an intrinsic trade-off in which thermal conditions that densify and 
crystallize oxides also accelerate oxidant-driven interfacial oxidation. 
Temporal thermal-budget engineering is introduced as a route to break this 
coupling by selectively positioning intense pulsed light (IPL)-induced transient 
thermal activation within the ALD cycle. Placing IPL before the metal precursor 
pulse activates precursor-related surface reactions, while allowing the 
substrate to cool before the subsequent O3 pulse. This half-cycle-resolved 
thermal control reduces impurities, increases film density, and promotes 
tetragonal ZrO2 crystallization at 220 °C, while avoiding pronounced interfacial 
oxidation on oxidation-sensitive electrodes such as TiN, Mo, and W. The 
resulting ZrO2 films exhibit a dielectric constant of ∼33 with a small 
interfacial equivalent oxide thickness. This concept is extended to HfO2 ALD on 
Mo, and its applicability to high-aspect-ratio trenches is verified by 
crystalline ZrO2 formation with comparable crystallinity along sidewall and 
bottom regions. These results establish temporal thermal-budget engineering as a 
broadly applicable strategy for oxide integration on oxidation-sensitive 
electrodes and complex three-dimensional architectures.

Wang J(1)(2), Zheng Y(1)(2), Wang W(1)(2)(3), Hou J(1)(2)(3), Tang X(1)(2)(3),

Under prolonged cold stress, tetraploid plants displayed enhanced 
glucosinolate-associated transcriptional and metabolic responses, which may 
contribute to their improved stress adaptation. At the epigenetic level, diploid 
and tetraploid wucai showed distinct DNA methylation responses to short-term 
cold, with diploid plants tending toward greater CHH hypermethylation in 
promoter regions. This ploidy-specific increase in methylation correlates with 
transcriptional repression of multiple stress-responsive loci in diploids. 
Notably, expression of the glucosinolate biosynthesis gene METHYLTHIOALKYLMALATE 
SYNTHASE1 (BcMAM1) diverged between ploidies after cold treatment, inversely 
correlating with opposing CHH methylation (H = A, C, or T) trends in its 
promoter. Pharmacological demethylation using 5-azacytidine upregulated BcMAM1 
and improved cold tolerance. Through a combination of functional assays and 
promoter-binding analyses, we identify the upstream transcription factor 
C-REPEAT BINDING FACTOR4 (BcCBF4), which binds to differentially methylated 
regions within the BcMAM1 promoter in a methylation-sensitive manner, supporting 
an association between the epigenetic state and transcriptional output. 
Together, our findings support a mechanistic model for the distinct cold 
response observed in the autotetraploid wucai line, involving coordinated 
changes in transcriptional activation and DNA methylation dynamics. The 
epigenetic and transcriptional targets identified in this study may inform 
breeding strategies for cold-resilient crops.

Epidemiology of malaria in the Torres Strait Islands, Australia, 2000-2025 and 
the public health response to three recent outbreaks.

Bowers C(1), Pourmarzi D(2), Hanson J(3), Hempenstall A(4), Dugdale P(5), 
Cashman C(5), Fauid A(6), Ehlers G(6), Davis J(6), Peniyamina D(5), Stephens 
L(5), Taunton C(5).

Author information:
(1)Torres and Cape Hospital and Health Service, Cairns, Queensland, Australia; 
National Centre for Epidemiology and Population Health, Australian National 
University, Canberra, ACT, Australia. claire.bowers@health.qld.gov.au.
(2)National Centre for Epidemiology and Population Health, Australian National 
University, Canberra, ACT, Australia.
(3)Cairns and Hinterland Hospital and Health Service, Cairns, Queensland, 
Australia.; Kirby Institute, University of New South Wales, Sydney, NSW, 
Australia.
(4)Torres and Cape Hospital and Health Service, Cairns, Queensland, Australia.; 
College of Medicine and Dentistry, James Cook University, Cairns, Queensland,

(5)Torres and Cape Hospital and Health Service, Cairns, Queensland, Australia.
(6)Cairns and Hinterland Hospital and Health Service, Cairns, Queensland,

BACKGROUND: Australia was declared malaria free in 1981. However, the proximity 
of Australia's Torres Strait region to malaria-endemic Papua New Guinea (PNG), 
and the presence of the Anopheles mosquito across Northern Australia, means 
there is an ongoing risk of malaria for many Australian residents. This paper 
describes the epidemiology of malaria in the Torres Strait region between 2000 
and 2025 and reports the public health response to three malaria outbreaks 
between 2023 and 2025.
METHODS: Case data from 1 January 2000 to 31 December 2025 were extracted from 
the Queensland Notifiable Conditions System to describe the epidemiology of 
malaria in the Torres Strait. The public health responses to each of the three 
recent outbreaks were reported against the Queensland Health Public Health Unit 
Guidelines for Malaria.
RESULTS: During the period 2000-2013, there were 171 cases of malaria reported 
in the Torres Strait region. Of these, 89 (52%) were positive for Plasmodium 
falciparum and 82 (48%) for P. vivax. Of cases during this period, 130 (76%) 
were imported from PNG; 13 (8%) were acquired in Australia; and 28 (16%) had an 
unknown place of acquisition. After a nine-year period without any confirmed 
malaria cases in the region, eight cases were reported across three outbreaks 
between 2023 and 2025. In all six of the outbreak cases in which a species could 
be confirmed, P. vivax was identified. The three outbreaks were managed 
effectively in partnership with local leaders, and included active case finding 
and vector control activities.
DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION: The public health response successfully halted 
transmission of malaria during three separate outbreaks in the Torres Strait 
Islands. However, there is an ongoing local risk due to the high incidence of 
malaria in PNG and cross-border movement under the Torres Strait Treaty. Ongoing 
collaboration with PNG stakeholders and enhanced local surveillance are 
essential to minimise the future importation of malaria, and other potentially 
life-threatening pathogens, into mainland Australia.

Thomas S(1), Phang R(1), Bogdanovic-Sakran N(1), Atkepe T(1), Bines J(2), Donato

This report from the Australian Rotavirus Surveillance Program (ARSP) describes 
the circulating rotavirus genotypes identified in children and adults during the 
period 1 January to 31 December 2025. In 2025, the ARSP saw a continuation of a 
high burden of rotavirus disease in the Australian population. During this 
period, 2,419 faecal specimens were referred to the National Rotavirus Reference 
Centre (NRRC) for rotavirus G- and P-genotype analysis; of these samples, 2,288 
were confirmed as rotavirus positive. This represents the highest number of 
referred samples and the highest number of positive samples recorded in a single 
surveillance year in the NRRC's more than 20-year history. Of the 2,288 samples 
confirmed rotavirus positive, 2,071 (90.5%) were identified as wildtype 
rotavirus; 215 (9.4%) were identified as the Rotarix vaccine-like strain; and 
two G1P[8] samples could not be confirmed as wildtype or vaccine-like due to 
inadequate sequence quality. The equine-like G3P[8] variant was the dominant 
genotype nationally (87.7%; n = 1,816/2,071). Other genotypes were identified at 
low frequencies, including wildtype G1P[8] (0.3%; n = 6/2,071), G2P[4] (2.0%; n 
= 42/2,071), G3P[8] (2.4%; n = 50/2,071), G8P[8] (0.5%; n = 10/2,071), G9P[4] 
(0.3%; n = 6/2,071), G9P[8] (2.2%; n = 46/2,071) and G12P[8] (0.3%; n = 
6/2,071). Genotype distribution was consistent nationally, with equine-like 
G3P[8] the dominant genotype in all jurisdictions. Consistent with observations 
in recent years, a small number of samples with unusual genotypes were 
identified (3.7%; n = 77/2,071). Of these unusual genotypes, the most frequently 
detected was equine-like G3P[6] which accounted for 26.0% of unusual samples (n 
= 20/74) and 1.0% of all positive wildtype samples (n = 20/2,071). The high 
number of rotavirus positive samples received by the program reflected the 
notifications for rotavirus disease reported to the National Notifiable Diseases 
Surveillance Service (NNDSS). Across Australia, 9,520 notifications were 
recorded, which is the second highest annual total reported since rotavirus 
became nationally notifiable in 2018. Outbreaks were reported in the Northern 
Territory, Western Australia and Queensland. The ability to monitor the 
genotypes of rotavirus strains causing disease across ages and jurisdictions 
provides important data to aid in assessing the performance of the national 
rotavirus vaccination program and to inform public health interventions during 
outbreaks. The ARSP also provides important data to monitor annual variations in 
genotypes circulating in the population. Understanding the diversity of 
genotypes in circulation and the emergence of variants provides important 
context for any changes observed in disease epidemiology in the community. The 
ARSP provides diagnostic laboratories with valuable feedback on laboratory data 
quality by reporting incidences of wildtype, vaccine-like, and/or false positive 
rotavirus results.

Lahra M(1), Hogan T(2).

Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Programme Annual Report, 2025.

Hogan T(1), Lahra M(2).

Author information:
(1)Neisseria Reference Laboratory and World Health Organization Collaborating 
Centre for STI and AMR, Sydney. NSW Health Pathology, Microbiology, The Prince 
of Wales Hospital, Randwick, NSW, 2031, Australia.
(2)Neisseria Reference Laboratory and World Health Organization Collaborating 
Centre for STI and AMR, Sydney. NSW Health Pathology, Microbiology, The Prince 
of Wales Hospital, Randwick, NSW, 2031, Australia; School of Medical Sciences, 
Faculty of Medicine, The University of New South Wales, NSW, 2052, Australia . 
monica.lahra@health.nsw.gov.au.

The Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Programme (AGSP) has continuously 
monitored antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG) for more than 
45 years through the system of jurisdictional Neisseria reference laboratories, 
the National Neisseria Network (NNN). In 2025, a total of 10,204 isolates across 
Australia, from public and private sectors, were tested for in vitro 
antimicrobial susceptibility by standardised methods. In 2025, the AGSP captured 
antimicrobial susceptibility data for 23.9% of all gonococcal infection 
notifications nationally. The current treatment recommendation for gonorrhoea, 
for the majority of Australia, continues to be dual therapy with ceftriaxone and 
azithromycin. In 2025, of NG isolates tested, 0.73% (74/10,204) met the World 
Health Organization (WHO) criterion for decreased susceptibility (DS) to 
ceftriaxone, defined as a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) ≥ 0.125 mg/L. 
This proportion of isolates meeting the ceftriaxone DS criterion was greater 
than that reported in 2024 (0.51%), with the majority from New South Wales and 
Victoria. Genomic analysis indicated that 64.9% of these isolates (48/74) 
possessed the mosaic penA 60.001 allele, the key target associated with 
ceftriaxone resistance. Resistance to azithromycin was reported in 7.1% of NG 
isolates nationally, increasing from being proportionally stable (3.9% to 4.7%) 
since 2019. Of NG isolates tested, 0.20% (20/10,204) exhibited high-level 
resistance to azithromycin (MIC value ≥ 256 mg/L), with cases reported across 
Australia, predominantly in New South Wales, Victoria and non-remote Western 
Australia. There were ten isolates detected in 2025 that had an extensively 
drug-resistant (XDR) phenotype: i.e., displaying both high-level resistance to 
azithromycin and decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone (MIC ≥ 0.125 mg/L). 
When added to the 14 XDR isolates reported during 2022-2024, this brings the 
total to 24 XDR NG isolates reported in Australia since 2022. Genomic analyses 
of the ten XDR isolates reported in 2025 indicated all harboured the mosaic penA 
60.001 allele, with several differing sequence types (ST) identified. By 
contrast, during 2022 and 2024, XDR NG sequence types were limited to ST-16406, 
consistent with reports from Europe and England. Travel information, where 
available, indicates infections in 2025 were associated with travel to Southeast 
Asia but also arose where no travel was involved. In 2025, penicillin resistance 
was found in 23.4% of gonococcal isolates, and ciprofloxacin resistance in 59.3% 
of isolates where tested, although there was variation by jurisdiction 
particularly in remote settings, where acquisition of cultures for antimicrobial 
susceptibility testing is low. Tetracycline resistance has been included in 
surveillance in the AGSP in recent years, coincident with increasing use of 
doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis for syphilis and chlamydia. Nationally 
36.2% of NG isolates in 2025 were tetracycline resistant, with variation by 
jurisdiction. No isolates were resistant to spectinomycin; data for gentamicin, 
whilst no breakpoints are defined, are reported by the AGSP as these data are 
reportable to the WHO Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance 
System (GLASS). The emergence of antimicrobial resistant NG in Australia has 
largely occurred through importation, spread and local transmission. In 2025, in 
Australia and overseas, increased detection of drug-resistant NG isolates is of 
significant concern as the threat for the future of the current recommended 
therapeutic agents is increasingly evident, and no ideal alternate therapeutic 
agent has been identified. Disease prevention strategies under investigation for 
the future have included the MenB-4C vaccine, designed to protect against 
meningococcal disease. Despite early promise, recent results from a large 
Australian trial indicate the MenB-4C vaccine is not effective at preventing 
gonorrhoea in men who are at high risk of infection. The AGSP continues to 
monitor antimicrobial resistance and to identify emerging resistant clones by 
enhanced surveillance approaches, to inform strategies for disease management 
and treatment of gonorrhoea in Australia.

Nationwide survey of testing practices for respiratory viruses in Australia in 
the post COVID-19 pandemic era.

Tuckerman J(1), Daley A(2), Wurzel D(3), Barr I(4).

Author information:
(1)Murdoch Children's Research Institute, Victoria, Australia; Department of 
Paediatrics, University of Melbourne, Victoria, Australia. 
jane.tuckerman@mcri.edu.au.
(2)Department of Paediatrics, University of Melbourne, Victoria, Australia; 
Royal Children's Hospital, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia.
(3)Murdoch Children's Research Institute, Victoria, Australia; Department of 
Paediatrics, University of Melbourne, Victoria, Australia; Royal Children's 
Hospital, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia; Allergy and Lung Health Unit, School 
of Population and Global Health, The University of Melbourne, Victoria, 
Australia.
(4)World Health Organization (WHO) Collaborating Centre for Reference and 
Research on Influenza, The Peter Doherty Institute for Infection and Immunity, 
Melbourne, Victoria, Australia; Department of Microbiology and Immunology, The 
Peter Doherty Institute for Infection and Immunity, The University of Melbourne, 
Melbourne, Victoria, Australia.

BACKGROUND: In the wake of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, 
there have been dramatic changes in the testing protocols for respiratory 
illness. Laboratory identification of respiratory pathogens causing clinical 
symptoms has become more important in the post-COVID-19 era, both for 
epidemiological and clinical reasons. This is particularly the case for 
respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) where a number of preventatives are at the 
point of clinical translation. The laboratory diagnosis is one of the critical 
elements in understanding the disease burden of respiratory pathogens and the 
effectiveness of preventatives. The aims of this study were to understand 
current laboratory testing and reporting practices across Australia.
METHODS: We undertook a cross-sectional survey of Australian NATA (National 
Association of Testing Authorities) accredited laboratories to collect data on 
patterns of laboratory testing, the methods used and their reporting processes. 
The survey asked participants to report on testing of respiratory samples for 
2022 as well as current respiratory multiplex testing in 2023.
OUTCOMES: In total, 45 out of 193 eligible laboratories (23%) completed the 
online survey. The majority of laboratories were from Victoria and New South 
Wales (31% and 27%, respectively) and most were hospital-based clinical 
diagnostic laboratories. Overall, 40% of responding laboratories (18/44) 
reported that > 80% of all tests in the molecular laboratory in 2023 were 
respiratory multiplex. Influenza viruses, RSV and SARS-CoV-2 were tested most 
frequently on respiratory multiplex PCR panels. RSV typing (RSV A or RSV B) was 
included in under a quarter of panels (9/43; 21%), compared to almost two-thirds 
for influenza typing (influenza A or influenza B: 29/44; 66%). There was 
considerable variability in testing platforms used, with thirty-seven 
laboratories using 87 different platforms (18 unique platforms). GeneXpert® 
(Cepheid) was the most commonly used platform; with a higher concentration of 
this instrument in laboratories from the eastern states (New South Wales, 
Queensland, Victoria). Forty percent of laboratories reported changes to 
respiratory testing procedures/panels in 2023 compared to the previous year. 
Laboratories were most likely to report results directly to the referring doctor 
(96-100%) followed by notifying their jurisdictional Department of Health.

Bias-Switchable ZnO/AlScN Heterojunction for Self-Powered UV Photodetection and 
Neuromorphic Learning.

Huang J(1), Lu W(2), Lu C(2), Ma Y(3), Shi Z(2), Wang X(2), Xu C(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)School of Physics, Southeast University, Nanjing211189, China.
(2)School of Electronic Science and Engineering, Southeast University, 
Nanjing211189, China.
(3)School of Microelectronics and School of Integrated Circuit, Nantong 
University, Nantong226019, China.

The convergence of ultraviolet (UV) communication and neuromorphic computing 
demands multifunctional devices that integrate high-speed photodetection with 
synaptic learning, yet the intrinsic mismatch between fast photoresponse and 
slow memory retention poses a fundamental challenge for monolithic integration. 
Here, we report a dual-mode UV optoelectronic device based on a ZnO/AlScN 
heterojunction, in which flexible switching between a self-powered 
photodetection mode and a neuromorphic mode is achieved through bias modulation. 
In mode I, operating at zero bias, the device exploits the type-II band 
alignment and built-in electric field of the heterojunction to realize a rapid 
response to 365 nm UV illumination, exhibiting a pA-level dark current, an 
on/off ratio of ∼ 4.2 × 103, rise/decay times of 279/64 ms, a responsivity of 
101.06 mA/W, and a specific detectivity of 1.15 × 1012 Jones. It also 
demonstrates UV optical communication based on ASCII encoding. In mode II, 
operating under a 1 V bias, enhanced carrier separation together with 
oxygen-vacancy-induced persistent photoconductivity (PPC) in ZnO enables a 
series of neuromorphic behaviors, including excitatory postsynaptic current, 
paired-pulse facilitation, the transition from short-term to long-term memory, 
memory-forgetting characteristics, and Pavlovian associative learning. Our 
findings demonstrate the potential of the ZnO/AlScN heterojunction as a 
versatile two-terminal platform integrating self-powered UV detection and 
neuromorphic learning, enabled by interfacial band engineering and 
bias-controlled oxygen-vacancy dynamics for dual-mode switching. This strategy 
offers an approach for developing multifunctional optoelectronic devices for UV 
communication, biomimetic visual perception, and neuromorphic information 
processing.

Ortho N-H-Directed Divergent Post-Ugi Cascade Cyclization: Additive-Controlled 
Selective Access to Fused Indazoles and 2,5-Dihydrofurans.

Mao NQ(1), Yu HF(1), Chen JZ(1), Han MN(1), Lin YF(2), Xiong J(1), Zeng ZG(2).

Author information:
(1)School of Pharmacy, Xianning Medical College, Hubei University of Science and 
Technology, Xianning, Hubei437100, P. R. China.
(2)School of Nuclear Technology and Chemistry and Biology, Hubei University of 
Science and Technology, Xianning, Hubei437100, P. R. China.

A facile one-pot sequential Ugi/tunable cascade cyclization of 
indazole-3-carboxylic acid, amines, enynals, and isocyanides has been developed 
for the divergent construction of two distinct pharmaceutically relevant 
heterocyclic frameworks: fused polycyclic indazoles and 2,5-dihydrofurans. The 
ortho N-H moiety of indazole serves as an indispensable neighboring group 
switch, regulating two independent cyclization pathways. Under metal-free 
DBU-mediated conditions, intramolecular Michael addition followed by 5-exo-dig 
cyclization occurs, leading to the formation of dual C-N bonds and the 
generation of fused indazole polycycles. In contrast, cooperative AgNO3/K2CO3 
catalysis triggers a silver-activated alkyne cyclization/ring-opening cascade, 
selectively forming C-O bonds to afford 2,5-dihydrofuran derivatives. This 
transformation is characterized by simple additive-switchable selectivity, broad 
functional group compatibility, gram-scale synthetic practicability, and the 
simultaneous access to two classes of pharmaceutically relevant heterocycles 
from identical four-component starting materials.

Quadruple Boronic Acid-Functionalized Lanthanide MOFs Enable Deep and Unbiased 
Spatial Proteomics from Ultra-Trace Laser-Captured Microtissues.

Zhu Y(1)(2)(3)(4), Wu J(1)(2), Luo Q(1)(2), Zhang S(1)(2), Wang Q(1)(2), Jiang 
L(1)(2), Duan J(1)(2)(3), Chen AF(4), Ding X(1)(2)(5).

Author information:
(1)Department of Anesthesiology and Surgical Intensive Care Unit, Xinhua 
Hospital, School of Medicine and School of Biomedical Engineering, Shanghai Jiao 
Tong University, Shanghai200030, China.
(2)State Key Laboratory of Oncogenes and Related Genes, Institute for 
Personalized Medicine, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai200030, China.
(3)Department of Gerontology, Xinhua Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong 
University School of Medicine, Shanghai200011, China.
(4)Institute for Developmental and Regenerative Cardiovascular Medicine, Xinhua

(5)Department of Clinical Laboratory, The First Affiliated Hospital of Bengbu

Spatial proteomics of laser capture microdissection (LCM) specimens is 
fundamentally constrained by protein loss during processing of ultra-trace 
samples, limiting proteomic depth and biological insight. Here, we report the 
integration of a quadruple metal-organic framework (qMOF)-enhanced 
surfactant-assisted one-pot sample preparation (MSOP) workflow for deep 
proteomic profiling of micro-scale tissues. The qMOF composite, featuring 
high-density boronic acid functionalities, acts as a potent protein capture 
vehicle, drastically minimizing surface adsorption losses. Applied to 
LCM-isolated mouse myocardial sections as small as 100 × 100 μm (∼20 cells), the 
MSOP workflow approximately doubled the number of confidently identified 
proteins, compared to the conventional surfactant-assisted one-pot sample 
preparation (SOP) method (mean of 2238 vs. 1116), while exhibiting lower 
quantification variance and preserving unbiased coverage of the proteome's 
physicochemical landscape. We further demonstrate the workflow's utility by 
resolving spatially distinct proteomic signatures in perivascular regions of 
aged cardiac tissue, identifying molecular hallmarks of aging characterized by 
impaired cytoskeletal stability and dysregulated mitochondrial functions. 
Protein-protein interaction network analysis identified Rack1 as a potential key 
node in cardiac aging, which was further validated by immunohistochemistry. This 
MSOP-assisted platform provides a robust, cost-effective, and highly sensitive 
chemical strategy to significantly enhance the depth of discovery-driven spatial 
proteomics.

Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing 
Wisely Scenarios.

Ariel D(1), Endelman S(2), Laban G(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Family Medicine, Clalit Health Services, Tel Aviv; and Gray 
Faculty of Medical & Health Sciences, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv, Israel 
(D.A.).
(2)Gray Faculty of Medical & Health Sciences, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv; and 
Division of Dermatology, Rabin Medical Center-Beilinson Hospital, Petach Tikva, 
Israel (S.E.).
(3)Department of Industrial Engineering and Management, Ben-Gurion University of 
the Negev, Be'er-Sheva; The Azrieli National Center for Autism and 
Neurodevelopment Research, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Be'er-Sheva; and 
The School of Brain Sciences and Cognition, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, 
Be'er-Sheva, Israel (G.L.).

BACKGROUND: The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, 
testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. 
Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs).
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint 
or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations.
DESIGN: Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used 
to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was 
appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs 
each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the 
clinician perspective.
SETTING: Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and 
Google from February to March 2026.
PARTICIPANTS: No human participants were involved.
MEASUREMENTS: Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when 
restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an 
appropriate action).
RESULTS: The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); 
LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations 
accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental 
subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine 
electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM 
responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the 
remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), 
was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific 
antigen screening (3.3%).
LIMITATIONS: Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than 
real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. 
Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use.
CONCLUSION: The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was 
appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations.
PRIMARY FUNDING SOURCE: None.

Diagnosis and Treatment of Cardiovascular Conditions in Medicare Advantage 
In-Home Health Risk Assessments.

Oseran AS(1), Liu-Hass M(2), Shanab BM(3), Zheng Z(3), Lalani C(4), Yeh RW(4), 
Wadhera RK(1).

Author information:
(1)Center for Health Policy at the Richard A. and Susan F. Smith Institute for 
Evidence, Innovation and Policy and Division of Cardiology, Beth Israel 
Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts (A.S.O., R.K.W.).
(2)Center for Health Policy at the Richard A. and Susan F. Smith Institute for 
Evidence, Innovation and Policy and Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women's 
Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts (M.L.-H.).
(3)Center for Health Policy at the Richard A. and Susan F. Smith Institute for

(4)Center for Medical Device Evaluation at the Richard A. and Susan F. Smith

BACKGROUND: Medicare Advantage insurers conduct in-home health risk assessments 
(HRAs) to identify high-risk patients and facilitate appropriate care. Critics 
argue this practice increases risk-adjusted payments without improving quality. 
Comprehensive data on use of in-home HRAs and downstream treatment are lacking.
OBJECTIVE: To examine trends in cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during 
in-home HRAs, characteristics associated with HRA-based diagnoses, and treatment 
rates after diagnoses.
DESIGN: Cohort study.
SETTING: Population-based.
PARTICIPANTS: Medicare Advantage beneficiaries.
MEASUREMENTS: Using 100% Medicare claims, trends in the proportion of 
cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during in-home HRAs (vs. facility-based

estimate the association between beneficiary- and plan-level characteristics and 
HRA-based diagnoses and compare treatment rates across settings.
RESULTS: Among 21 496 506 Medicare Advantage beneficiaries diagnosed with a 
cardiovascular risk factor or disease, the proportion diagnosed during in-home

(30.0% to 36.0%), ischemic heart disease (37.2% to 41.6%), peripheral vascular 
disease (64.5% to 73.9%), and heart failure (34.7% to 42.6%). Racial and ethnic 
minority beneficiaries and those enrolled in lower-rated plans were more likely 
to receive HRA-based diagnoses. Treatment rates were substantially lower after 
HRA-based diagnoses across all conditions.
LIMITATIONS: Differences in the severity of conditions between groups could not 
be assessed. Prescription fills were used as a proxy for management. Observed 
differences in the diagnosis and treatment of conditions across encounter

CONCLUSION: Among Medicare Advantage beneficiaries, an increasingly large share 
of cardiovascular conditions are being diagnosed through in-home HRAs, but 
treatment rates after these diagnoses are consistently lower than after

We report a Sc(OTf)3/AgOAc relay-catalyzed multicomponent [4 + 1] cycloaddition 
cascade for the efficient synthesis of polysubstituted pyrazoles 5-6 from 
sulfoxonium ylides, vinyl diazo esters, and vinylene carbonates or maleimides. 
Although vinyl diazo esters have been widely used as C1 and three-atom synthons,

roles: Sc(III) promotes pyrazole ring assembly, whereas Ag(I) facilitates

studies support the proposed relay catalytic pathway. The reaction is readily 
scalable to gram scale, providing a modular and practical approach to the rapid 
synthesis and late-stage diversification of biologically valuable pyrazole 
derivatives.

Titanium-based metal-organic frameworks (Ti-MOFs) are widely investigated for 
their potential in photocatalytic applications owing to their unique structural 
and electronic properties. However, the local identity of long-lived 
photoinduced Ti(III) species remains unresolved. In this study, the nature of 
photogenerated Ti(III) species in the stable Ti-MOF MUV-10(Ca) was examined by 
electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy. The results of X- and Q-band 
(9/34 GHz) continuous wave (CW) EPR provided unequivocal evidence for the 
presence of two chemically distinct Ti(III) sites, with the selectivity of 
Ti(IV) photoreduction governed by the hydration state of the material and the 
wavelength of the incident light. Consolidation of CW EPR and 1H Davies 
electron-nuclear double resonance (ENDOR) data allowed us to clearly determine 
the structure of both centers: one associated with an ideal Ti2Ca2-cluster and 
another one assigned to the missing-linker defect of the MUV-10(Ca) structure. 
This first example of such hydration state and wavelength-controlled selectivity 
in photoactive Ti-MOFs contributes to a deeper understanding of the nature of 
photoactive centers in Ti-MOFs, highlighting the importance of defect 
engineering for advanced applications.

Ring-fused heteroarenes are essential building blocks found in a wide range of 
compounds, including pharmaceuticals, natural products, and organic materials. 
While the intramolecular dearomative didehydro-Diels-Alder (IMDDDA) reaction of 
heteroarenes is a powerful method for the synthesis of ring-fused heteroarenes,

forward stepwise selection, which highlights the critical role of vibrational 
frequencies and heteroarene type in predicting these complex reactivity trends.

Aqueous zinc metal batteries (AZMBs) are constrained by water-induced side

Radiation Vasculopathy of the Coronary Arteries: State-of-the Art Review.

Xia J(1)(2), Kim J(1)(3)(2), Sharma A(1)(2), Yang B(1)(2), Alluri PG(4)(3), 
Atkins K(5), Miller ED(6), Williams TM(7), Addison D(1)(3)(2), Arbune

Author information:
(1)Departments of Medicine (J.X., J.K., A.S., B.Y., D.A., A.A., A.C., K.W.Z., 
V.G.Z.), University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX.
(2)Parkland Health, Dallas, TX (J.X., J.K., A.S., B.Y., D.A., A.A., A.C.,

(3)Harold C. Simmons Comprehensive Cancer Center (J.K., P.G.A., D.A., A.A., 
A.C., K.W.Z., V.G.Z.), University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas,

(4)Radiation Oncology (P.G.A.), University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center,

(5)Departments of Radiation Oncology and Cardiology, Cedars-Sinai Medical 
Center, Los Angeles, CA (K.A.).
(6)Department of Radiation Oncology, The Ohio State University Comprehensive 
Cancer Center, Columbus, OH (E.D.M.).
(7)City of Hope National Medical Center, Los Angeles, CA (T.M.W.).
(8)Department of Cardiology, Division of Internal Medicine, The University of 
Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, TX (E.K.).

Radiation-associated coronary artery disease (RACAD) is a distinct form of 
coronary artery disease with several specific biological and clinical aspects as 
well as key knowledge gaps. RACAD is prevalent in patients with cardiac exposure 
to radiotherapy. As radiotherapy is integral to the effective treatment of many 
thoracic malignancies, improved long-term survivorship is coupled with increased 
risk for RACAD. Ionizing radiation induces free radical generation and 
activation of proinflammatory cascades, leading to endothelial dysfunction and 
accelerated atherosclerosis. Risks for RACAD are determined both by 
radiotherapy, including the radiation dose and the proximity of coronary 
arteries to the radiotherapy field, and by patient-specific factors, such as 
younger age, higher baseline cardiovascular risk, and concurrent cardiotoxic 
systemic therapies. Importantly, radiotherapy delivery is highly individualized 
on the basis of tumor location and treatment strategy, resulting in 
heterogeneous coronary exposure to radiation and patient-to-patient variability. 
Clinical presentation may occur early, within 1 to 2 years, especially in 
patients with higher cardiac radiation doses (eg, lung or esophageal cancer), or 
after a latency period of 5 to 20 years with lower cardiac dose radiation 
exposure (eg, left-sided breast cancer). Patients generally present with 
symptoms similar to conventional coronary artery disease. However, RACAD 
symptoms may be underrecognized in cancer survivors due to overlapping 
treatment-related fatigue, pulmonary disease, or competing oncologic symptoms. 
Diagnosis and management generally follow standard coronary artery disease 
guidelines while incorporating cancer-specific considerations, such as planned 
oncologic surgeries, bleeding risk, postradiotherapy complications such as 
atretic internal mammary arteries, and cardiotoxic effects of systemic cancer 
therapies. Primary prevention of RACAD is critical, emphasizing advances in 
precision radiotherapy, including delivery techniques with improved coronary 
dosimetry, and cardiac shielding. Key knowledge gaps include understanding 
long-term outcomes with contemporary 3-dimensional conformal radiotherapy 
techniques, validated cancer-specific risk prediction models on the basis of 
coronary dosimetry, optimal surveillance protocols, targeted molecular 
pharmacotherapies, and risk analysis of percutaneous versus surgical management 
of RACAD. Prospective studies are needed to develop cancer- and 
dosimetry-specific risk calculators, validating cardioprotective interventions, 
and improving multidisciplinary cardio-oncology collaboration to optimize early 
detection of RACAD and timely intervention in the growing population of cancer 
survivors.

Area Deprivation Index and Survival Outcomes for Patients With Metastatic Solid 
Tumors Treated With Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in the United States.

Rhinehart DP(1)(2), Feinaj A(1), Nair S(2), Zahaurak M(1), Mata J(1)(2), Lansey 
D(1), Elias R(1)(2), Hoffman-Censits J(1)(2), Lipson EJ(1)(2), Yarchoan M(1)(2), 
Warrier G(1)(2), Ged Y(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive 
Cancer Center, Baltimore, MD.
(2)Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD.

Due to increasing evidence that socioeconomic deprivation influences cancer 
outcomes through biological effects and care disparities, this 
single-institution retrospective study estimated associations between 
neighborhood-level socioeconomic deprivation, measured by the area deprivation 
index (ADI), and clinical outcomes among patients with metastatic solid tumors 
treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Eligible patients included 
adults with metastatic solid tumors who received ICI between 2013 and 2024 and 
had a response assessment. Exclusions included adjuvant ICI receipt and missing 
ADI. Survival outcomes were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and Cox 
regression models were used to measure associations between ADI and survival in 
the full cohort and stratified by tumor type. In a cohort of 691 patients with 
multiple solid tumor types and a median follow-up of 56.1 months, there was a 
trend toward shorter overall survival (OS) with increasing ADI quartile (HR=1.60

significant (P=0.143). There was no significant association between ADI and 
progression-free survival (P=0.215). Exploratory analyses of tumor type subsets 
also revealed no statistically significant association between ADI and OS. In 
conclusion, there was no significant association between survival and ADI in 
this cohort. Further study in larger and more diverse cohorts is needed to 
elucidate the relationship between neighborhood-level socioeconomic deprivation 
and survival among patients with metastatic solid tumors receiving ICI.

Latency after preterm prelabour rupture of membranes vs. gestational age: a 
maturation-growth trade-off.

Garg G(1), Sangwan N(1), Madan S(1), Singhal SR(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Pt. B.D. Sharma Postgraduate 
Institute of Medical Sciences (PGIMS), Rohtak, Haryana, India.

OBJECTIVES: In preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM), prolonging 
pregnancy for fetal maturity is traded against infection risk, yet latency is 
entangled with gestational age. We examined its determinants and, disentangled 
from gestational age, its impact on fetomaternal outcome.
METHODS: In a prospective tertiary-centre cohort, 96 singleton pregnancies with 
PPROM at 28-34 weeks, undelivered at 48 h, were followed to delivery. Admission 
and pre-delivery haematological and ultrasound measures were recorded. Analyses 
included Kaplan-Meier, restricted mean survival time, competing-risks and 
gestational-age-adjusted models.
RESULTS: Median latency was 5 days (IQR 3-11); 61 % delivered within a week. 
Gestational age at admission was the only predictor (rho -0.21, p=0.037); 
earlier-gestation women remained undelivered longer (restricted mean 10.5 vs. 
6.4 days, p=0.006); amniotic fluid volume did not predict latency 
(oligohydramnios p=0.700; 6.6 vs. 9.0 days, p=0.084). Longer latency was 
associated with neonatal complications (OR 10.9), NICU admission (OR 3.4) and 
caesarean (OR 5.5). The near-zero crude latency-birth-weight correlation 
reflected gestational-age suppression: at equal gestational age at admission, 
longer latency meant greater birth weight (+129 g per 10 days, p=0.004), yet at 
equal age at delivery a lower weight (p=0.033). The neonatal-morbidity 
association persisted after adjustment (OR 1.21 per day). The serial 
total-leucocyte-count rise tracked chorioamnionitis (AUC 0.77), the 
neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio did not.
CONCLUSIONS: Gestational age at admission, not amniotic fluid volume, governs 
latency. Prolonged latency is a genuine, double-edged trade-off, not a 
confounded marker of prematurity: at equal gestational age it yields 
maturational weight yet restrains growth-for-age and carries a 
gestational-age-independent morbidity and infection risk.

The development of a high-accuracy, low-cost, numerical tensor method for the P 
states of three-particle systems.

Kammegne Tcheugam B(1), Witek HA(2), Cox H(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Chemistry, University of Sussex, Brighton BN1 9QJ, United 
Kingdom.
(2)Department of Applied Chemistry, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, 
Hsinchu 300, Taiwan.

In this paper, we solve the non-relativistic many-body Schrödinger equation (SE) 
for the excited P states (L = 1) of three-particle systems with natural and 
unnatural parity. The exact separation of the rotational degrees of freedom from 
the internal degrees of freedom presented by Sadhukhan et al. [arXiv:2506.23962 
(2025)] is exploited. The angular matrix elements involve the product of two 
bipolar harmonics and are calculated using an explicit analytical expression 
containing the Wigner 3j- and 6j-symbols. Using a symmetry and parity adapted 
wavefunction for P states in perimetric coordinates, the variational form of the 
SE in canonical tensor format is derived. This consists of a sum of triple 
tensor products of factor matrices and is an exact representation. From this 
canonical format, the SE can be solved in full tensor format or used to derive 
an exact representation as a second-order tensor train. Two formulations are 
presented. In the first, scaled perimetric coordinates are used; it is assumed 
that the like-charged particles have the same asymptotic behavior so that the 
orthonormality of the Laguerre functions can be exploited and the matrices are 
sparse. In the second, the like-charged particles are not constrained to have 
the same asymptotic behavior and an analytical integral is used which results in 
dense matrices. It is shown that by optimizing either one or two non-linear 
variational parameters, it is possible to obtain excited P state energies that 
are accurate to the picohartree, for atomic and molecular systems in less than 
25 min on a standard desktop computer.

Variational block-correlated coupled-cluster Monte Carlo.

Brodie H(1)(2), Shilcusky A(2), Feiguin A(2).

Author information:
(1)Rudolf Peierls Centre for Theoretical Physics, University of Oxford, Oxford 
OX1 3NP, United Kingdom.
(2)Department of Physics, Northeastern University, Boston, Massachusetts 02115, 
USA.

Motivated by the recent success of quantum neural states, we present a 
variational implementation of the coupled-cluster method suitable for quantum 
Monte Carlo simulations. We introduce a Young tableaux representation of the 
wave-function coefficients and their derivatives that substantially reduces the 
computational complexity of the variational optimization. While the algorithm is 
generic, we illustrate its implementation with an application to the Heisenberg

Microscopic origin of polytype-dependent melting in SiC revealed by 
machine-learning molecular dynamics.

Stojanović L(1), Magorrian SJ(1), Kabalan L(1), White RN(2), Thiemann FL(3), 
Zólyomi V(1).

Author information:
(1)Hartree Centre, STFC Daresbury Laboratory, Warrington WA4 4AD, United 
Kingdom.
(2)Lucideon Limited, Stone Business Park, Brooms Road, Stone, Staffordshire ST15 
0SH, United Kingdom.
(3)IBM Research Europe, Daresbury WA4 4AD, United Kingdom.

Predicting how crystal structure influences high-temperature stability remains a 
key challenge in materials modeling and design. Silicon carbide (SiC), one of 
the most thermally and chemically stable materials known, provides an ideal 
system for studying this problem because its many polytypes preserve similar 
local tetrahedral bonding while differing in long-range stacking geometry. To 
determine the impact of polytype structure on the high-temperature stability of 
SiC, we combine phase-coexistence machine-learning molecular dynamics with 
finite-temperature phonon analysis, enabled by a fine-tuned MACE interatomic 
potential that accurately describes crystalline, high-temperature, and 
disordered configurations across multiple SiC polytypes. We identify a clear 
stability ordering, 3C > 2H > 9R, reflected consistently in structural 
disordering, interlayer sliding, and finite-temperature phonon spectra. Across 
all polytypes, melting initiates through the formation of short C-C contacts and 
carbon-rich local regions, followed by a progressive loss of tetrahedral Si-C 
connectivity. The reduced stability of the long-period 9R polytype is associated 
with a denser manifold of low-frequency transverse-acoustic modes arising from 
its stacking periodicity and associated zone folding, which broaden and soften 
further at high temperature. These modes can provide additional low-energy 
channels for thermally activated lateral bilayer motion, consistent with the 
larger sliding amplitudes observed in 9R and their positive correlation with 
local structural disorder.

The structure of molecules at surfaces and buried interfaces can be probed by 
second-order nonlinear optical techniques that derive their response from 
environments with broken centrosymmetry, thereby simultaneously enhancing the 
signal from the molecules of interest and suppressing the responses of the

Collective intermolecular Coulombic decay beyond Coulomb.

Falkowski AG(1)(2), Cederbaum LS(1).

Author information:
(1)Theoretische Chemie, Physikalisch-Chemisches Institut, Universität 
Heidelberg, Im Neuenheimer Feld 229, Heidelberg D-69120, Germany.
(2)Instituto de Física "Gleb Wataghin," Universidade Estadual de Campinas, 
13083-859 Campinas, São Paulo, Brazil.

Intermolecular Coulombic decay (ICD) is a widely spread phenomenon in nature and 
the laboratory in which the excess energy of a donor is utilized to ionize a 
nearby acceptor. If the excess energy is insufficiently large to enable ICD, two 
(or more) donors can collectively transfer their combined excess energy to 
ionize the acceptor. Experiments show that this collective ICD is, surprisingly, 
operative in gases. Recently, it has been demonstrated that standard ICD can 
take place efficiently at large distances between the donors and acceptors due 
to retardation. Here, we derive the theory of collective ICD including 
retardation. Quantum electrodynamics perturbation theory is used, and it is 
shown that the theory can be substantially simplified and the process made more 
amenable to interpretation by introducing two-body interaction potentials that 
include retardation. Explicit formulas for the rate of collective ICD are 
derived and interpreted by expressing the rate in terms of measurable quantities 
and geometric factors. It is demonstrated that the change in the permanent 
dipole moments of the species upon excitation is a relevant ingredient in 
collective ICD.

Revisiting the visible B̃2A2 ← X̃2B1 spectrum of the phenoxy radical: 
Multireference energetics and finite-temperature Franck-Condon simulations.

Suma K(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Science Education, Faculty of Education, Kagoshima University, 
1-20-6 Korimoto, Kagoshima 890-0065, Japan.

The visible B̃2A2 ← X̃2B1 absorption system of the phenoxy radical is 
characterized by a pronounced ∼500 cm-1 vibronic progression and broad, 
asymmetric band profiles. The assignment of the lowest-wavenumber component to 
the 0-0 band is supported by the 7 K Ar-matrix spectra, whereas the progression 
and room-temperature asymmetry have been assigned to the Wilson 6a vibration and 
sequence structure involving the low-frequency 10b vibration, respectively. 
Reference SA-CASSCF and TD-B3LYP Franck-Condon simulations show complementary 
limitations: CASSCF gives an overly compact 6a progression, whereas TD-B3LYP 
gives an overly extended cold-band envelope. The X̃2B1 and B̃2A2 states are 
therefore treated by second-order multireference Rayleigh-Schrödinger 
perturbation theory using a common state-averaged CASSCF reference. The 
resulting structures and harmonic force fields define a Duschinsky 
transformation involving all 30 normal coordinates. The finite-temperature 
vibrational basis was then expanded across all four C2v symmetry species and 
converged using mode-specific vibrational limits and state-energy cutoffs. The 
converged 30-mode model is compared directly with the room-temperature 
cavity-ringdown spectra of Araki et al. after one common wavenumber shift and an 
explicitly defined local normalization. It reproduces the principal 6a 
progression and parts of the asymmetric local envelopes qualitatively, but 
overestimates several wings and the high-wavenumber congestion. A calculation 
differing only in population temperature shows that this global high-wavenumber 
rise disappears at 7 K, identifying it as an accumulation of transitions from 
thermally populated lower states. The room-temperature spectrum is better 
described as a congested 6a progression with contributions from 10b and other 
modes than as a single 10b sequence.

Quantum simulation of ligand-like molecules through sample-based quantum

Patra AK(1), K S V A(1), P SS(1), Bhat R(1)(2), V R(3), Maitra R(4), G J(1).

Author information:
(1)Qclairvoyance Quantum Labs, Secunderabad, Telangana 500094, India.
(2)The University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona 85721, USA.
(3)Department of Computing Technologies, SRM Institute of Science and

The accurate treatment of electron correlation in extended molecular systems 
remains computationally challenging using classical electronic structure 
methods. Hybrid quantum-classical algorithms offer a potential route to overcome 
these limitations; however, their practical deployment on existing quantum 
computers requires strategies that both reduce problem size and mitigate 
hardware noise. In this work, we investigate ground-state energy calculations of 
ligand-like molecules using Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) within 
the Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) framework, focusing on low-symmetry 
systems with diverse bonding motifs that exhibit subsystem-dependent variations 
in fragment-environment entanglement. These entanglement-based variations 
directly influence bath orbital construction, impurity sizes, and the structure 
of the embedded Hamiltonians, posing nontrivial challenges for both embedding 
and quantum sampling. By combining DMET fragmentation with SQD-based 
construction of reduced configuration spaces through quantum sampling and 
iterative configuration recovery, we perform quantum simulations on IBM's Eagle 
R3 (ibm_sherbrooke) and IBM's Heron R3 (ibm_boston) superconducting quantum

subsystems plays a central role in determining the efficiency and accuracy of 
the simulations. Despite these complexities, we show that the DMET-SQD framework 
yields ground-state energies in strong agreement with DMET-full configuration 
interaction benchmarks, achieving chemical accuracy (1 kcal/mol) across all 
systems studied. These results demonstrate that SQD-based quantum simulations 
can be robustly extended to low-symmetry, chemically realistic, industry 
relevant molecules and highlight the importance of entanglement-aware embedding 
strategies for scalable quantum electronic structure calculations.

Interpreting peripheral immune phenotypes in Parkinson's disease: an 
immune-context framework for biomarker qualification.

Kahveci O(1)(2), Ay U(2)(3), Gürvit H(4).

Author information:
(1)Department of Physiology, Faculty of Medicine, Bezmialem Vakıf University, 
Topkapı Mahallesi, Adnan Menderes Bulvarı No: 113, 34093 Fatih, Istanbul, 
Türkiye.
(2)Department of Physiology, Istanbul Faculty of Medicine, Istanbul University, 
Topkapı Mahallesi, Turgut Özal Caddesi No: 118, 34093 Fatih, Istanbul, Türkiye.
(3)Neuroimaging Unit, Hulusi Behçet Life Sciences Research Laboratory, Istanbul 
University, Topkapı Mahallesi, Turgut Özal Caddesi No: 118, 34093 Fatih, 
Istanbul, Türkiye.
(4)Department of Neurology, Behavioral Neurology and Movement Disorders Unit, 
Istanbul Faculty of Medicine, Istanbul University, Topkapı Mahallesi, Turgut 
Özal Caddesi No: 118, 34093 Fatih, Istanbul, Türkiye.

Peripheral immune alterations are widely reported in Parkinson's disease (PD), 
but their biological meaning and clinical utility remain uncertain because 
circulating immune profiles are shaped by aging, latent infection, medication 
exposure, comorbidity, disease stage, and preanalytical conditions. This 
concept-driven narrative review examines how technically valid peripheral immune 
findings should be biologically interpreted and clinically qualified through an 
immune-context phenotyping framework. Available human evidence suggests 
alterations in neutrophil- and monocyte-related inflammatory indices and 
cellular states, α-synuclein-responsive T-cell pathways, cytotoxic and 
regulatory T-cell states, B-cell phenotypic alterations, and peripheral-central 
immune associations. Much of this evidence, however, derives from 
cross-sectional and cohort-dependent studies, and within the human evidence 
considered in this review, PD specificity remains insufficiently established for 
most candidate signals. An observed blood difference may reflect altered 
production, survival, differentiation, redistribution, denominator effects, 
systemic inflammatory context, or measurement-related distortion rather than a 
single disease mechanism. Immune-context phenotyping, therefore, integrates 
trait, state, disease-trajectory, measurement, and treatment contexts with 
biological identifiability, disease-control comparisons, cross-compartment 
corroboration, repeated sampling, and external validation. The framework adapts 
established biomarker concepts to distinguish diagnostic, prognostic, 
monitoring, predictive, pharmacodynamic/response, and treatment-selection claims 
without treating peripheral target engagement, CNS engagement, pathway 
modification, and clinical benefit as equivalent. Based on the human evidence 
considered in this review, no peripheral immune phenotype appears ready for 
stand-alone clinical implementation in PD. The proposed framework defines a 
testable path from descriptive peripheral immune associations toward 
biologically coherent, temporally informative, and clinically qualified 
phenotypes.

Investigating the relationship between age and gender of blood donors with

storage.

Nakhaei Moghaddam F(1), Samiee S(1), Teimourpour A(2), Deyhim MR(1).

Author information:
(1)Iranian Blood Transfusion Research Center.
(2)Biological Products and Blood Safety Research Center, High Institute for 
Research and Education in Transfusion Medicine, Tehran, Iran.

The variations in donor characteristics, may affect the progression of platelet 
storage lesion (PSL). Additionally, oxidative conditions and mitochondrial 
function play a role in these alterations. This study aims to investigate the 
impact of donor age and gender on oxidative stress and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) 
during the storage of platelet concentrates. In this study, 42 platelet-rich 
plasma platelet concentrates (PRP-PCs) were selected from male and female 
donors. We measured the research parameters, which include; platelet count, 
platelet metabolism, oxidative parameters, platelet viability and mtDNA during 
platelet concentrate storage. We found a significant increase in the levels of 
reactive oxygen species (ROS) and malondialdehyde (MDA), along with a decrease 
in pH, in platelet concentrates obtained from female in comparison to male blood 
donors (P < 0.05). Correlation analysis indicated a direct relationship between 
mtDNA and both ROS and MDA, as well as a negative correlation between mtDNA and 
pH. These alterations did not show significant differences among the groups. It 
seems that platelet concentrates prepared from female donors show oxidative 
stress earlier than those from male donors. It is suggested that these products 
be given priority for transfusion to prevent further deterioration of the 
quality of platelet concentrates during storage.

Successful systemic fibrinolysis in pulmonary embolism with a 
thrombus-in-transit.

Ivanova S(1), Irfan I(2), Radkova M(1), Stoyanova K(1), Karamfiloff K(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Cardiology, Aleksandrovska University Hospital, Medical 
University of Sofia.
(2)Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive care, Alexandrovska University 
Hospital, Sofia, Bulgaria.

Right heart thrombus-in-transit with acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is a rare but 
potentially lethal clinical finding. Optimal management remains controversial, 
particularly when major contraindications or risk factors coexist. We present a 
72-year-old male admitted to the emergency room with leading diagnosis acute 
coronary syndrome who was later diagnosed with acute PE and a massive, mobile 
right heart thrombus along with a concomitant ascending aortic aneurysm. Due to 
high surgical risk, systemic fibrinolysis was performed under close monitoring. 
Follow-up echocardiography demonstrated complete resolution of the intracardiac 
thrombus, rapid right ventricular recovery, and an intact thoracic aorta. This 
case highlights the importance of echocardiography in initial evaluation of 
patients with acute cardiovascular symptoms and also systemic thrombolysis as a 
viable, life-saving strategy for right heart thrombosis even in complex clinical 
scenarios.

A review of the monitoring of argatroban by anti-IIa methods, ecarin assays, 
point-of-care testing methods and specialized drug quantification methods for 
patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

Guy S(1), Horner K, Leeson K, Maclean R.

Author information:
(1)Sheffield Haemophilia and Thrombosis Centre, Royal Hallamshire Hospital, 
Sheffield, UK.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is caused by anti-PF4/heparin IgG 
antibodies stimulating platelet activation, causing thrombocytopenia and 
thrombosis. Classical HIT occurs due to exposure to heparin, whereas autoimmune 
HIT occurs via heparin-independent platelet activation (caused by 
anti-PF4/polyanion IgG) and relates to a platelet count fall that begins or 
persists without heparin. Treatment for HIT requires transitioning patients onto 
alternative anticoagulation. The direct thrombin inhibitor argatroban has been 
licensed for use in patients with HIT and was recommended to be monitored by the 
activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT). Recent European guidelines have 
suggested that monitoring drug concentrations is more suitable and will reduce 
the risk of under or over anticoagulating patients. This review will discuss 
anti-IIa and ecarin-based laboratory methods for determining plasma argatroban 
concentrations, the use of viscoelastography methods and other point-of-care 
testing (POCT) methods in whole blood. The use of more specialised tests based 
on high-performance liquid chromatography will also be discussed, comparing 
these methods with aPTT.

Clinical characteristics, risk factors, and outcomes of pediatric thrombosis: a 
prospective single-center study.

Fahmy EM(1), Youssef HA(1), Sharaf AAA(1), Abozaid YKA(1), Salama EH(2), Kassem 
MA(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Pediatrics.
(2)Department of Clinical Pathology, Faculty of Medicine, Sohag University, 
Sohag, Egypt.

The incidence of pediatric thrombosis is increasing due to multiple causes and 
risk factors, including genetic and acquired factors. This study aimed to 
evaluate clinical characteristics, risk factors, genetic mutations, and clinical 
outcomes of children with thrombosis. This prospective observational study 
included 40 children with thrombotic events. Detailed demographic, clinical, 
laboratory, and imaging data, as well as clinical outcomes, were collected. 
Thrombophilia gene testing included MTHFR C677T and A1298C, Factor XIII V34L, 
and factor V Leiden mutations. Statistical analyses included univariate 
comparisons and multivariate logistic regression to identify predictors of poor 
outcomes. Twenty percentage of the study population had genetic thrombophilia, 
while 80% had acquired risk factors. Acquired risk factors mainly included 
hematological (22.5%) and cardiac disorders (20%). Venous thrombosis was the 
most common site (80%), followed by arterial (10%) and cardiac (10%) thrombi. 
MTHFR C677T and factor XIII V34L mutations were detected with genetic 
thrombophilia only (P < 0.01), while factor V Leiden was present in both groups 
(P = 0.11). Overall, 67.5% of patients improved, 20% died, and 12.5% developed 
permanent disabilities. Multivariate analysis identified thrombocytopenia as an 
independent predictor of poor outcomes [odds ratio (OR) 18.44; 95% CI: 
1.76-192.49; P = 0.02]. Positive blood cultures were associated with a fourfold 
increased risk of adverse outcomes (OR 4.0; 95% CI: 0.75-21.23; P = 0.1). 
Pediatric thrombosis was predominantly caused by acquired risk factors, though 
genetic mutations were significantly evident in this study. Screening and early 
diagnosis are essential for high-risk profiles. Identifying and managing sepsis 
and thrombocytopenia are critical to improving outcomes.

Heavy menstrual bleeding with direct oral anticoagulants and vitamin K 
antagonists: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

Quon S(1), Ma LIJ(1), Tsang P(2).

Author information:
(1)Faculty of Medicine.
(2)Division of Hematology, Department of Medicine, University of British 
Columbia, Vancouver, BC, Canada.

Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is a clinically important but underrecognized 
complication of oral anticoagulation that can impair quality of life, cause of 
iron deficiency or anaemia, and lead to treatment interruption. We conducted a 
systematic review and meta-analysis to compare menstrual bleeding outcomes among 
direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) and vitamin K antagonists (VKAs). MEDLINE, 
Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception through 
February 2026. Random-effects meta-analyses pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% 
confidence intervals (CIs) for HMB, anticoagulant modification, treatment for 
menstrual bleeding, and hospitalization, transfusion, or procedural 
intervention. Twenty-five studies published from 2015 to 2025 were included; 
most were observational. Compared with apixaban, rivaroxaban was associated with 
higher odds of HMB [odds ratio (OR) 2.83, 95% confidence interval (CI) 
2.11-3.81; I2 = 0%] and anticoagulant modification because of menstrual bleeding 
(OR 6.05, 95% CI 1.91-19.19; I2 = 0%). Hospitalization, transfusion, or 
procedural intervention did not differ significantly (OR 1.04, 95% CI 
0.10-11.13). Compared with VKAs, rivaroxaban was associated with greater odds of 
requiring treatment for menstrual bleeding (OR 4.01, 95% CI 1.88-8.54), whereas 
estimates for HMB and anticoagulant modification were imprecise and 
nonsignificant. Pooled DOAC-VKA comparisons for HMB were inconclusive. Menstrual 
bleeding risk appears to vary by individual anticoagulant rather than uniformly 
across the DOAC class. Proactive assessment of menstrual symptoms and iron 
deficiency, and patient-centred anticoagulant selection, are warranted, 
particularly for patients with preexisting HMB or anaemia.
