There is substantial concern about the ability of advanced AI to influence 
people's behavior. A rapidly growing body of research has found that AI can 
produce large persuasive effects on people's attitudes, but whether AI can 
persuade people to take consequential real-world actions has remained unclear. 
In two large preregistered experiments ([Formula: see text] responses from 
14,779 people), we used conversational AI models to persuade participants on a 
range of attitudinal and behavioral outcomes, including signing real petitions 
and donating money to charity. We found sizable AI persuasion effects on these 
behavioral outcomes (e.g. [Formula: see text]19.7 percentage points on petition 
signing). However, we observed no evidence of a correlation between AI 
persuasion effects on attitudes and effects on behavior. Moreover, we replicated 
prior findings that information provision drove effects on attitudes, but found 
no such evidence for our behavioral outcomes. In a test of eight behavioral 
persuasion strategies, the strategy focused on information provision produced 
the smallest behavioral effect, though differences among the eight were small. 
Taken together, these results suggest that previous findings relying on 
attitudinal outcomes may generalize poorly to behavior, and therefore risk 
substantially mischaracterizing the real-world behavioral impact of AI 
persuasion.

Suryadevara P(#)(1), Casiulis M(#)(1)(2), Martiniani S(1)(2)(3)(4)(5).

Author information:

The energy landscape picture is a central tool to study many-body systems. In 
particular, the energy landscapes of glass-forming liquids, jammed packings, 
constraint satisfaction problems, or neural networks contain a plethora of 
minima corresponding to competing states. Due to their complexity, these 
landscapes resist analytical treatment and must be studied numerically. We focus 
on jammed soft spheres, a paradigmatic model of glasses and granulars, to expose 
the limitations of standard numerical methods in resolving the true structure of 
energy landscapes. We show that the C-language Variable-coefficients ordinary 
differential equation solver is the one with the best time-for-error trade-off 
for this problem, outperforming commonly used steepest-descent solvers by 
several orders of magnitude. Using this numerical approach, we provide 
unequivocal evidence that optimizers widely used in computational studies 
destroy all semblance of the true landscape geometry, even in moderately low 
dimensions. Employing a range of geometric indicators, both low- and 
high-dimensional, we show that earlier claims on the fractality of basins of 
attraction of minima originated from the use of inadequate mapping strategies. 
In reality, the basins of attraction of soft-sphere packings are smooth 
structures with well-defined length scales, a result that likely extends to a 
much broader family of problems.

Mesenchymal cell migration starts with the protrusion of the cell's leading 
edge, enabled by the branching growth of the actin network. Two crucial 
molecular players in protrusion are actin filaments and the Arp2/3 complex, the 
branching agent. Traditionally, protrusion models are intuited from several 
perturbative experiments. Recent multiplex microscopy imaging data promise to 
change this paradigm by providing measurements of naturally fluctuating 
densities of key proteins at the leading edge of unperturbed cells. We report an 
attempt to reconstruct the mechanistic protrusion model from such data. We 
analyze fluctuations of densities of actin filaments and Arp2/3 complex and cell 
edge velocity using phase space and regression analysis to reconstruct 
linearized dynamics of the coupled actin-Arp2/3-velocity system. We then build a

parsimony. The resulting models recover the rates of reactions and mechanical 
and transport processes in the lamellipodium from a single nonperturbative 
experiment. The models posit that the dominant nonlinear term in the

in the cell frame. The models suggest that the protrusion is dominated by a 
damped oscillatory cycle resulting from a combination of positive feedback from 
the Arp2/3 complex to protrusion velocity and negative feedback from actin 
density to the velocity.

Stepwise unknotting of complex polymer knots under nanochannel confinement.

Mao R(1)(2), Dorfman KD(2).

Author information:
(1)Innovation Institute of Carbon Neutrality, International Joint Laboratory of

We performed Langevin dynamics simulations to investigate the unknotting 
dynamics of knotted DNA molecules confined within nanochannels, specifically 
examining three different torus knot types: 31, 51, and 71 knots, and the 61 
twist knot. 51 and 71 knots typically undergo stepwise unknotting, in which 
knots are partially untied into a simpler knot topology when they first reach 
the chain end, subsequently requiring multiple rounds of topological 
simplification before being fully untied. In contrast, as would be expected, 
simple trefoil knots untie directly as they approach the chain ends, following a 
one-step process. We further examined the impact of nanochannel size on 
unknotting dynamics and topological changes across different knot types. For the 
complex 51 and 71 knots, stepwise unknotting is the prevalent mechanism, and 
increasing the spatial confinement prolongs the entire stepwise unknotting 
process. For the 61 knot, the primary mechanism of untying is also sequential, 
with ∼20% of the knots untying in a single step. In addition, the topological 
changes induced by both confinement and knot types are found to be correlated 
with the extended unknotting times; while the topology of the knot (twist vs 
torus) dictates the possible unknotting pathways, the rate of unknotting is 
modulated by the channel size.

A new approach for calculating activation energies, activation volumes, and

Minimum-energy paths and intrinsic reaction coordinates are central tools for 
analyzing chemical reactions. As one-dimensional objects, however, individual

Exact decomposition and approximate power-law scaling of truncation errors in

Liu J(1), Du J(2), Zhao L(1), Zhang J(1), Liu R(1), Jiang G(1).

Author information:
(1)Institute of Atomic and Molecular Physics, Sichuan University, Chengdu

Although truncation errors in multiconfigurational expansions are known 
empirically to correlate with the discarded weight, a rigorous, 
scheme-independent theoretical foundation for this relation is lacking. From an 
orthogonal decomposition of the full configuration interaction (FCI) wave 
function, we derive an exact expression ΔE = ω(Ed - EFCI)/(1 - ω) and validate 
it across 20 systems, four orbital representations, and four truncation schemes. 
In the weak-truncation regime (ω ≪ 1), the mean discarded excitation energy 
varies slowly, yielding an approximate power law ΔE ∝ ωα, where α depends 
systematically on the truncation strategy (0.86-0.91) and electronic structure, 
yet the error remains dominated by ω. Because ω requires the exact FCI wave 
function, it serves as an a posteriori diagnostic. This framework provides a 
unified theoretical basis for comparing truncation and orbital schemes and 
rationalizes the empirical success of coefficient-based selection methods.

Research and scholarship are shaped by article citations, which underpin the 
communication of ideas, assignment of credit, journal impact factors, and author 
career progression. Given their key influence on author and journal metrics, 
citations can be intentionally manipulated to inflate the reputation of journals 
and researchers. Paper mills, unethical organizations that produce and sell 
manuscripts and publishing services, may also be manipulating citations, but the 
extent of this manipulation is unknown. Here, we show that molecular cancer 
articles sharing features with retracted papers from paper mills display 
citation patterns that suggest systematic inflation. These articles were 
published in journals in the top decile of journal rankings. Suspected paper 
mill articles received 50 to 100% more citations than other papers 1 to 3 y 
after publication, while paradoxically attracting fewer readers and online 
accesses. Suspected paper mill articles also cited-and were cited by-other 
suspected paper mill articles, which frequently appeared in journals previously 
reported as paper mill targets. Citations from suspected paper mill articles 
measurably inflated journal citation metrics. These findings suggest that paper

Brain functional connectivity changes throughout development, and individuals 
with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may follow trajectories that differ from

attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder did not reveal comparable results.

alterations are developmentally heterogeneous and organized along the cortical 
hierarchy, providing a developmental perspective for understanding the

Author information:
(1)Department of Psychology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138.

From childhood to adulthood, individuals' learning and decision-making may be 
differentially impacted by two salient value signals for adolescents: emotions 
and rewards. This study superimposed these information sources to assess their 
independent and joint influences on learning and choice processes. Participants

incidental emotion cues, adults' shift toward prioritizing integral reward

(1)The Pathogen and Microbiome Institute, Northern Arizona University,

Laboratory production of botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) began more than 90 y ago 
for medical, military, and later pharmaceutical applications, creating one of 
the longest-running examples of microbial cultivation under sustained human 
control. A single Clostridium botulinum Group I lineage, Army Hall A (AHA), was 
established by the US military in 1942 and later gave rise to Hall A-hyper 
(HAH), the strain widely used for pharmaceutical BoNT production. We analyzed

infer the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) shared with its nearest lineage.

single-nucleotide substitutions, 44 small insertions or deletions, and several 
large deletions and structural variants that led to the loss of more than 80 
genes. A nonsense mutation in mutS generated a hypermutator phenotype that 
accelerated mutation rates and increased genetic diversity. This event is 
inferred to have occurred early in the lineage's domestication and appears to 
have facilitated laboratory-adaptive traits, including the lack of sporulation 
and increased BoNT yield. Competition experiments under standard growth 
conditions confirmed substantial laboratory adaptation, with AHA exhibiting a 
strong fitness advantage over a close relative. Together, these results 
reconstruct the genomic trajectory of a bacterium evolving under prolonged 
human-mediated selection and provide a genome-resolved example of microbial 
domestication. The findings show how laboratory conditions, industrial 
selection, and changing mutation rates can shape bacterial evolution, and they 
offer a general framework for understanding domestication and laboratory 
adaptation across microbial systems.

Mechanistic versus descriptive interpretation of brain activity pattern 
reconstruction.

Jung K(1)(2), Eickhoff SB(1)(2), Patil KR(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Institute of Neurosciences and Medicine, Brain and Behaviour (INM-7), 
Research Centre Jülich, 52425 Jülich, Germany.
(2)Institute of Systems Neuroscience, Medical Faculty, Heinrich Heine University 
Düsseldorf, Düsseldorf 40225, Germany.

The geometric eigenmodes, derived from the shape of the cortical surface, have 
been suggested as a better model for explaining brain function due to their high 
accuracy in reconstructing patterns of both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked 
brain activity patterns captured by functional MRI, when contrasted with 
alternative models including structural connectome derived bases. While a 
descriptive representation offers valuable utility for neuroimaging studies, it 
is necessary to examine the extent to which it supports a mechanistic 
explanation for human brain function. Although the observation that geometric 
eigenmodes accurately fit brain activity is intriguing, we argue that accepting 
them as a model of brain function risks conflating descriptive and mechanistic 
interpretations. While a representation that effectively describes the 
underlying geometry is inherently adept at fitting patterns within that 
geometric space; it does not necessarily shed light on mechanisms that give rise 
to the brain's functional attributes. To this end, we provide two lines of 
empirical results: a) geometric eigenmodes demonstrate a high flexibility when 
fit to a range of manipulated patterns, and b) localized parcel-based 
representations can reconstruct activity patterns as well. Based on those 
results, theoretical considerations, and previous data, we argue that more 
consideration is needed regarding the complementary roles of descriptive 
representation and mechanistic explanation in neuroimaging research. While we 
recognize the potential role of the brain's geometry in influencing its 
dynamics, assertions regarding its efficacy should be weighed against its 
inherent lack of specificity, biological interpretability, and anatomical 
evidence.

Microbial niche partitioning explains N(2)O distributions and cycling in marine 
oxygen minimum zones.

McCoy D(1), Sun X(1)(2), Buchanan PJ(1)(3), Zakem EJ(1).

Author information:
(1)Biosphere Sciences and Engineering, Carnegie Institution for Science, 
Pasadena, CA 91125.
(2)Department of Biology, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA 19104.
(3)Environment, Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisations, 
Hobart, TAS 7004, Australia.

Oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) are marine hotspots for cycling and emission of the 
powerful greenhouse gas nitrous oxide (N2O). Steep redox gradients host diverse 
microbial communities that produce and consume N2O, generating a characteristic 
vertical distribution, with low concentrations in anoxic cores and 
supersaturated accumulation in surrounding oxyclines. Although the accumulation 
is commonly attributed to stronger O2 inhibition of N2O consumption than 
production, this differential inhibition is not consistently observed, 
suggesting that interactions among nitrogen-cycling metabolisms may provide 
additional mechanisms. To evaluate the ecological controls on the N2O profile, 
we embed a trait-based ecosystem model into an eddy-resolving simulation of the 
Eastern Tropical South Pacific OMZ. In this framework, redox energetics, 
metabolite exchange, competition, and grazing structure microbial growth, 
setting emergent niches of microbial functional types, particularly aerobic 
ammonia oxidizers and diverse anaerobic denitrifiers that mediate N2O cycling. 
In the anoxic core, cross-feeding tightly couples denitrifiers that produce and 
consume N2O, maintaining low concentrations. As O2 increases in the oxycline, 
competition with aerobic metabolisms and intensified grazing gradually exclude 
denitrifiers. However, because they draw on more abundant substrates, 
N2O-producing denitrifiers persist to higher O2 than N2O consumers, reflecting 
the vulnerability of populations dependent on intermediate metabolites. This 
ecological decoupling drives N2O accumulation and captures the characteristic 
double-peaked vertical structure without imposing physiological O2 intolerance 
thresholds. More broadly, by revealing how niche partitioning and 
producer-consumer coupling shape other features of OMZ biogeochemistry, these 
results provide a basis for projecting future shifts in marine nitrogen loss and 
N2O emissions.

Superconductivity in the high-pressure tetragonal phase of UTe(2).

Deng Y(1), Mee G(1), Wannamaker T(1), Feng K(1), Xu M(2), Xie W(2), Maple MB(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Physics, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA 
92903.
(2)Department of Chemistry, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI 48824.

Electrical transport and magnetic measurements have been made on UTe2 under 
pressure P up to ~16 GPa to determine the superconducting transition temperature 
Tc vs. P phase diagram in the high-pressure tetragonal phase. Superconductivity 
emerges near ~5 GPa, coincident with the orthorhombic-tetragonal phase 
transition; in the tetragonal phase, Tc reaches a maximum value of ~4 K at 6 GPa 
and then decreases with P and appears to vanish near 18 GPa. Tetragonal UTe2 has 
a relatively small upper critical field Hc2(0) ≈ 1.2 T at 5.3 GPa, smaller than 
the Pauli paramagnetic limit, and is orbitally limited with a coherence length 
ξtetra ≈ 16.5 nm. This small value of Hc2(0) favors more conventional 
superconductivity; in contrast, the large values of Hc2(T) for orthorhombic UTe2 
exceed the Pauli paramagnetic limit in all three crystallographic directions and 
have been attributed to unconventional superconductivity, widely believed to 
involve spin-triplet pairing. The temperature-pressure phase diagram of UTe2 
shows a striking dichotomy: a narrow, fragile, unconventional superconducting 
region in the orthorhombic phase vs. a broad, robust, and more conventional 
superconducting dome in the tetragonal phase. This dichotomy is consistent with 
the proposal that U-dimers, present (absent) in the orthorhombic (tetragonal) 
phase, may play a role in spin-triplet superconductivity of orthorhombic UTe2. 
In the tetragonal phase, the normal-state electrical resistivity ρ(T) exhibits 
metallic behavior with a "knee" at 200 to 240 K that depends weakly on P and 
most likely marks the onset of a transition to a magnetically ordered phase that 
coexists with superconductivity.

Interpersonal contact is essential for cooperation and care, but it also 
provides a route for pathogen transmission between individuals. Hence, a key 
challenge for social organisms involves maintaining beneficial social contact 
while also limiting exposure to infection risks. Existing proposals suggest that 
this trade-off is guided by the interpersonal value of specific social targets. 
In addition, ecological and cultural factors, including historical pathogen 
prevalence, individualism-collectivism, tightness-looseness, and relational 
mobility, might also shape how people avoid pathogens. To test whether and how 
infection-risky social contact varies with individual-level interpersonal value 
and these societal-level factors, we collected data from 47,756 participants 
across 61 societies. Participants were randomly assigned to picture a social 
target - either a friend, acquaintance, stranger, or enemy. They then rated 
their comfort with infection-risky contact with that target (e.g., drinking from 
the same water bottle) and whether they would touch the target when greeting 
them. In all societies, participants were more comfortable with infection-risky 
contact and more likely to engage in physical contact during greetings with 
targets of higher interpersonal value. Such associations varied only modestly 
across societies. Notably, the associations between infection-risky contact and 
societal-level factors depended on target interpersonal value and were 
concentrated among high-value targets-contact was lower where historical 
pathogen prevalence and tightness were greater and higher where individualism 
and relational mobility were greater. These findings suggest that 
infection-risky contact is primarily guided by the value of social targets, with 
ecological and cultural factors playing a lesser role.

Synthetic reconstitution of planar polarity initiation reveals principles of 
symmetry breaking across scales.

Wallach LA(1)(2), Thomas C(1)(2), Li P(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 
02139.
(2)Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, Cambridge, MA 02142.

Development often relies on molecular prepatterning over large tissue scales, 
and how these patterns emerge is an essential question. Planar cell polarity 
(PCP), manifested as asymmetric distribution of junctional proteins within 
individual cells and coordinated across entire tissues, is a key module 
controlling tissue morphogenesis and organization. How tissues break symmetry to 
initiate PCP remains unknown. By reconstituting polarity initiation ex vivo 
using engineered epithelial cells, we found that collective migration acts as 
the symmetry-breaking cue, inducing front-back enrichment of CELSR junctions and 
establishing aligned multicellular CELSR polarity. Individual cells directly 
interpret the migration cue and remain sensitive to it. Strikingly, CELSR 
polarity arises without reciprocal VANGL-FZD interactions, identifying CELSR as 
the driver for polarity initiation. These findings reveal that collective 
migration initiates and coordinates PCP across molecular, cellular, and tissue 
scales, demonstrating that morphogenetic events act as a trigger for spatial 
pattern emergence.

Drivers of the likelihood of evolutionary rescue in response to novel infectious 
diseases.

Balstad LJ(1)(2), Baskett ML(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Environmental Science and Policy, University of California, 
Davis, CA 95616.
(2)Center for Population Biology, University of California, Davis, CA 95616.

The introduction of novel infectious diseases has caused significant declines in 
many species, and in some cases, local extinction. Simultaneously, hosts might 
adapt to these novel pathogens, allowing population recovery, an example of 
evolutionary rescue (ER). Novel infectious diseases differ from sudden, abiotic 
stressors in that disease only impacts a subset of individuals within the 
population and individuals might be affected for a finite period. Whether ER 
occurs in an infectious disease context, and how likely it is relative to 
abiotic stress, might depend on both host and pathogen characteristics such as 
the scale of transmission (e.g., local density-dependent transmission only or 
additional infection through an external reservoir), the degree of fatality or 
immunity, and the adaptive pathway in terms of whether adaptive alleles reduce 
mortality, reduce likelihood of infection, or enhance recovery. Here, we use a 
stochastic mathematical model of host-pathogen dynamics with evolution of a 
novel allele conferring disease robustness to quantify how population 
trajectories, including the probability of and time to ER, vary across adaptive 
pathways and disease characteristics. We find that ER is more likely to occur 
with dynamical disease transmission compared to a lasting stressor that affects 
the entire population, indicating that protecting a subset of the population 
from stress facilitates ER. Among cases with disease transmission, ER is 
generally more likely to occur with the adaptation of mortality-blocking alleles 
and sources of transmission that include an external reservoir.

Restructuring hydrogen-bonding networks via hydroxyl-functionalized covalent 
organic frameworks for efficient nitrate electroreduction.

Zhang R(#)(1), Zhang H(#)(1), Duan H(1), Han D(1), Li X(1), Wang Z(1), Mao R(1), 
Cai M(1), Zhu Y(2), Huang H(1), Qu W(3), Cortes E(4), Zhang D(1).

Author information:
(1)Innovation Institute of Carbon Neutrality, International Joint Laboratory of 
Catalytic Chemistry, Department of Chemistry, College of Sciences, Shanghai 
University, Shanghai 200444, China.
(2)Department of Chemical Engineering, School of Engineering, The University of 
Manchester, Manchester M13 9PL, United Kingdom.
(3)Department of Chemistry, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON M5S 3H6, Canada.
(4)Nanoinstitute Munich, Faculty of Physics, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität, 
Munich 80539, Germany.
(#)Contributed equally

Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) is a promising strategy for 
nitrate removal and ammonia synthesis, but its efficiency is largely limited by 
sluggish proton transfer kinetics and poor reaction selectivity. Herein, we 
rationally design a series of hydroxyl-functionalized copper 
phthalocyanine-based covalent organic frameworks (Cu-COF-nOH) to regulate 
interfacial proton transfer via restructuring hydrogen-bonding networks. The 
hydroxyl functional groups in Cu-COF-nOH enhance water adsorption and 
dissociation to enrich interfacial proton supply. Optimized hydroxyl loading 
further induces the formation of continuous hydrogen-bond chains, enabling 
oriented and accelerated proton shuttling toward Cu active centers instead of 
stochastic diffusion. Electrocatalytic tests in 0.5 M nitrate electrolyte show 
that the optimal Cu-COF-4OH catalyst achieves an ammonia Faradaic efficiency of 
93.20% and an NH3 yield rate of 65.84 mg·h-1, along with excellent long-term 
stability, outperforming most state-of-the-art NO3RR electrocatalysts. Combined 
with in situ characterizations and theoretical calculations, we clearly clarify 
that hydroxyl-mediated hydrogen-bonding restructuring plays a critical role in 
boosting proton transfer kinetics and reaction selectivity. This work provides a 
versatile interface engineering strategy for efficient 
multiproton/electron-coupled electrocatalytic reactions, offering insights into 
the design of high-performance NO3RR catalysts.

A GPRC5B-Fyn signaling axis regulates VRAC activity by targeting LRRC8A.

Kostritskaia Y(#)(1), Gaitán-Peñas H(#)(2)(3)(4), Bertelli S(#)(5)(6),

The mechanisms by which physiological signals gate the volume-regulated anion 
channel (VRAC) remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a GPRC5B-Fyn 
signaling axis that directly controls VRAC activation by targeting the essential 
subunit LRRC8A. We found that the orphan G protein-coupled receptor GPRC5B binds 
LRRC8A and recruits the Src family kinase Fyn, which in turn suppresses 
hypotonicity-evoked VRAC activation. Disrupting Fyn binding to GPRC5B or 
substituting a predicted phosphorylation site on LRRC8A (Y362) abolishes this 
inhibition. Across primary astrocytes and reconstituted systems, GPRC5B prevents 
the intersubunit conformational rearrangements associated with VRAC opening 
without altering basal channel expression. In astrocytes, the MLC protein MLC1

Starving bacteria must synthesize stress proteins to survive, but how protein 
synthesis persists in the absence of nutrient influx is unclear. We show that in 
Escherichia coli, carbon starvation triggers large-scale proteome remodeling, 
with global proteolysis supplying both the amino acids (AAs) and ATP for protein 
synthesis. This remodeling occurs in two phases, with a short preparatory phase 
relying on constitutive proteolytic machinery and fueled by residual carbon 
waste, and a more extended phase, relying on starvation-induced protein 
components synthesized during the preparatory phase and fueled by AA catabolism. 
The starvation-induced protein degradation (SPD) program dominating the extended 
phase depends on YeaG, a little-known, broadly conserved protein highly 
expressed in stationary phase under the control of the general stress sigma 
factor RpoS. SPD fuels the synthesis of stress proteins, including those in the 
RpoS regulon and AA catabolic enzymes, markedly enhancing survival and 
accounting for much of the viability benefit conferred by RpoS during carbon 
starvation. However, in mutants where an energy source can be supplemented 
without enabling biomass growth, SPD and the accompanying protein synthesis are 
largely dispensable for survival, indicating that a primary physiological 
function of the synthesized stress proteins is to conserve or recycle energy 
during carbon starvation. Because SPD targets biosynthetic enzymes 
nonspecifically, proteome remodeling via SPD imposes a fundamental trade-off 
between long-term survival and short-term metabolic activity, manifested as a 
lag before regrowth upon nutrient replenishment. Together, these findings 
establish SPD as a general physiological strategy shaping protein synthesis and 
survival in nongrowing bacteria.

the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to 
highly reactive states remain elusive. This stems from a fundamental 
computational bottleneck: Ab initio methods offer quantum-level fidelity but are

empirical force fields lack the reactive fidelity required for complex 
combustion environments. Here, we bridge this gap by employing a human-audited,

accuracy while exhibiting near-linear scalability. Strikingly, our simulations

Tipping point forecasting in nonstationary dynamics on function spaces.

Liu-Schiaffini M(1), Singer CE(2), Kovachki N(3), Leung SC(1), Bae HJ(1), 
Azizzadenesheli K(3), Anandkumar A(1).

Author information:
(1)Division of Engineering and Applied Science, California Institute of

(2)University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO 80309.

Tipping points are abrupt, drastic, and often irreversible changes in the 
evolution of nonstationary and chaotic dynamical systems. For instance, 
increased greenhouse gas concentrations are predicted to lead to drastic 
decreases in low cloud cover, referred to as a climatological tipping point. In 
this paper, we learn the evolution of such nonstationary dynamical systems using 
a recurrent neural operator (RNO), which learns mappings between function 
spaces. After training RNO on only the pre-tipping dynamics, we employ it to 
detect future tipping points using an uncertainty-based approach. In particular, 
we propose a conformal prediction framework to forecast tipping points by 
monitoring deviations from physics constraints (such as conserved quantities and 
partial differential equations), enabling forecasting of these abrupt changes 
along with a rigorous measure of uncertainty. We illustrate our proposed 
methodology on nonstationary ordinary and partial differential equations, such 
as the Lorenz-63 and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations. We also apply our methods 
to forecast a climate tipping point in stratocumulus cloud cover and airfoil 
wake and stall transitions using only limited knowledge of the governing 
equations. For the latter, we show that our proposed method zero-shot 
generalizes to forecasting multiple future tipping points under varying Reynolds 
numbers. In our experiments, we demonstrate that even partial or approximate 
physics constraints can be used to accurately forecast future tipping points.

Understanding the elementary processes that follow the interaction of ionizing 
radiation with biomolecules is of fundamental importance in radiation chemistry 
and radiation biology. Nucleobases are a class of biomolecules that are of 
particular interest in these fields due to their significance as the building 
blocks of DNA and the role of nucleobase radicals in DNA damage. Here,

photodetachment. Density functional theory calculations assign the observed 
vibrational modes and quantify the extent of structural rearrangement following 
photodetachment. This work provides insights into the ultrafast structural 
dynamics that accompany the ionization of biomolecules in an aqueous 
environment.

tetrafunctional silicon core, trifunctional =Si(CH3)- branching units, and 
terminal hydroxyl groups, adopt a characteristic "umbrella" conformation at low 
coverage, with hydrophilic termini anchored in water and the hydrophobic core 
aligned with the nonpolar phase. Interfacial chemistry fundamentally modulates 
this architecture: favorable toluene-core interactions promote core swelling and 
homogeneous lateral dispersion, whereas the sharp hydrophobic mismatch at the 
water-air interface drives dendrimer aggregation. Lateral compression induces a 
systematic transition from flattened, anisotropic conformations to more 
isotropic, near-spherical geometries, accompanied by redistribution of hydrogen 
bonds from dendrimer-water to intra- and interdendrimer contacts. Under strong 
confinement, steric crowding and transient interdendrimer hydrogen bonding lead 
to dynamic arrest, with lateral diffusion suppressed by orders of magnitude. 
These findings establish a unified molecular picture of how surface density and 
solvent compatibility jointly control conformation, interactions, and mobility 
in amphiphilic dendrimer monolayers, providing design principles for tunable 
interfacial materials with tailored mechanical and transport properties.

Electronic stopping power of protons in transition metals: Bragg peak.

Du JW(1), Han X(1), Li J(1), Qi Y(2), Gao CZ(1)(3), Fan Z(1)(3), Yan J(1)(3).

Author information:
(1)Institute of Applied Physics and Computational Mathematics, Beijing 100088, 
People's Republic of China.
(2)College of Mechanical Engineering, Jiaxing University, Jiaxing 314001, China.
(3)HEDPS, Center for Applied Physics and Technology (CAPT), Beijing 100871, 
China.

For the electronic stopping power of protons in period-6 transition metals, the 
Bragg peak positions measured in experiments are nearly independent of the 
element for lanthanides and suddenly show a linear growth for non-lanthanides, 
while the Bragg peak magnitudes monotonically decrease with increasing atomic 
number. These observations can be partially explained qualitatively by the 
velocity-matching criterion. In this study, we reproduce experimental results by 
using the dielectric response models. To interpret them, we develop approximate 
analytical models of the Bragg peak position and magnitude for specified shells, 
which are correlated to both the ionization energy and average electronic 
density. It is found that for inner shells, the element-independent Bragg peak 
position for lanthanides is due to a weak variation of ionization energies and 
average densities, and a strongly dependent relationship for non-lanthanides is 
attributed to a distinctly remarkable increment of ionization energies. In 
addition, it shows that the consideration of the electronic density, a factor 
neglected in the velocity-matching formula, is essential for reproducing the 
element-dependent peak positions for inner shells. For valence shells, a uniform 
density is the unique factor, which almost remains unchanged for lanthanides but 
can be increased by about an order of magnitude for non-lanthanides. An analytic 
simplification of the Bragg peak magnitude reveals that the maximal stopping 
cross section is inversely proportional to the Bragg peak position for inner 
shells, and it is determined by the atomic number density for valence shells, 
which well explains the experimental results in period 6.

The identification of novel mesophases is an important research theme in both 
simple and complex block copolymer systems. While self-consistent field theory 
(SCFT) is a standard tool for finding ordered structures, its predictions of the 
free energy local minima depend heavily on the initial seed fields and the 
initial cell parameters, complicating efforts to perform an exhaustive search.

evaluating a surrogate function trained using kernel ridge regression, which is 
both computationally inexpensive and generalizable to large formulation spaces.

Quaternion Dirac-Coulomb-Breit integral transformation for relativistic

Oele M(1), Majumder R(1), Upadhyay S(1), Zhang T(1), Beck RA(1), Shayit A(2), 
Visscher L(3), Li X(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Chemistry, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington 98195, 
USA.
(2)Department of Physics, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington 98195, 
USA.
(3)Department of Chemistry and Pharmaceutical Sciences, Vrije Universiteit

High-accuracy correlated four-component relativistic electronic structure 
methods are typically formulated in terms of integrals over molecular orbitals 
(MOs). Consequently, an efficient and scalable strategy is required to deal with 
the complexity of transforming relativistic two-electron integrals from the 
atomic orbital (AO) to the MO basis. The transformation bottleneck is 
particularly acute for approaches that include Breit interaction integrals, 
whose computational and memory demands further exacerbate the transformation 
cost. To overcome this challenge, we develop a quaternion-based, AO-driven 
direct integral transformation scheme. The method operates on scalar AO 
integrals and combines quaternion density-based contractions with direct 
Cauchy-Schwarz screening to systematically exploit integral locality. As a 
result, the proposed framework substantially lowers the practical computational 
scaling and provides an efficient, memory-conscious, and highly parallelizable 
pathway for the routine inclusion of relativistic Dirac-Coulomb-Breit integrals 
in large-scale four-component correlated calculations.

Author information:
(1)Department of Physics, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei

(3)Hefei National Research Center for Physical Sciences at Microscale,

Attributing a confined dielectric change to one constituent of a composite 
nanostructure requires each plasmon resonance to be tied to its mode identity 
and to the region dominating its shift. We establish this link using 
boundary-element calculations for silver particles of 40 nm fixed outer diameter

Hydrodynamic modulation of sequence-dependent compaction in active-passive 
copolymers.

Jangir M(1), Das S(1).

Author information:
(1)Center for Condensed Matter Theory, Department of Physics, Indian Institute 
of Science, Bengaluru, Karnataka 560012, India.

Sequence patterning has recently emerged as a route to control the conformations 
of active-passive copolymers, but most studies have used free-draining models in 
which the solvent acts only as a local dissipative bath. Here, we ask whether 
hydrodynamic interactions can alter the nonequilibrium conformation selected by 
an active-passive sequence. We simulate a self-avoiding polymer with a fixed 
fraction of active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck monomers arranged in different sequences 
and compare free-draining dynamics with simulations including 
Rotne-Prager-Yamakawa hydrodynamic interactions. Increasing sequence blockiness 
drives a non-monotonic conformational response from expansion to compaction and 
then re-expansion. Hydrodynamic interactions preserve this qualitative sequence 
dependence but shift the compact regime, alter the degree of compaction and 
mechanical size balance, and render center-of-mass transport sequence-dependent.

active contribution to radial swelling and develops an internally segregated 
structure with a passive-rich core and active peripheral protrusions. At larger 
blockiness, the polymer re-expands despite this suppression, with the increase 
in size arising instead from the growing spatial separation between the active 
and passive blocks. This block separation is reduced by hydrodynamic 
interactions, thereby modifying the high-blockiness conformations. Formation of 
the compact state proceeds through rapid global compaction followed by slower 
radial reorganization, leaving the active segments dynamically constrained in 
the compact state. These results show that hydrodynamic interactions do more 
than renormalize relaxation. They reshape the sequence-selected conformational 
landscape and couple internal organization to long-time transport in 
active-passive copolymers.

Warming up ground-state orbitals: A route to excitation energies?

Gould T(1), Pittalis S(2).

Author information:
(1)Quantum and Advanced Technology Research Institute, Griffith University, 
Nathan, Qld 4111, Australia.
(2)Istituto Nanoscienze - CNR, S3, Via G. Campi 213/A, 41125 Modena, Italy.

Linear-response time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) is the 
workhorse of spectral prediction, yet it can struggle to predict or even 
describe important low-lying excitation energies. An alternative is to use 
static formalisms to target excited-state energies directly from variational 
density functional theory (DFT). This may involve using custom excited-state 
functionals or feeding excited-state orbitals and densities into standard 
ground-state approximations, and can often be effective, even for describing 
states for which adiabatic TDDFT fails. However, this comes at the cost of 
requiring specialized algorithms to find stationary points. In this exploratory 
work, we demonstrate that finite-temperature DFT can provide an effective 
auxiliary framework for generating excited-state-like orbitals from ground-state 
orbitals for modern ensemble and state-specific functionals, such as the GX24 
ground-state (G) and excited-state (X) functional. Notably, the necessary 
fixed-point algorithms are already available and well optimized in many 
electronic-structure codes.

Long-lived sharp interfaces in fully miscible fluids exhibit a transient quartic 
excess free-energy landscape and a Fermi-Dirac logistic concentration profile, 
whose microscopic statistical-mechanical origin has remained unresolved. Here,

hematopoietic cell differentiation. Here, we have shown that MBD3 deficiency in 
the T cell compartment resulted in spontaneous development of T cell-mediated 
multiorgan autoimmune diseases including fatal autoimmune myocarditis. The 
MBD3-deficient mice notably showed a significant reduction of CD25+Foxp3+ 
regulatory T (Treg) cells in both the thymus and periphery without much 
affecting the development and function of conventional T (Tconv) cells. Mixed 
bone marrow (BM) chimeras reconstituted with wild-type and MBD3-deficient BM 
revealed a cell-intrinsic defect in thymic Treg cell lineage differentiation in 
MBD3-deficient cells. Transcriptional, phenotypic, and functional analyses of 
thymocyte subsets further revealed that MBD3 deficiency particularly affected 
the activation of a Treg-specific enhancer of the Il2ra gene encoding CD25, 
hence impaired CD25 expression in immature CD4 single-positive thymocytes 
(ImCD4SP) but not in peripheral T cells. The impairment markedly limited thymic 
Treg precursor cell generation and substantially reduced overall thymic Treg 
cell output. By contrast, MBD3 deficiency scarcely impacted the 
TGF-β/IL-2-dependent in vitro Treg cell generation from Tconv cells. Thus, 
Treg-specific developmental properties such as high IL-2/CD25 dependency of 
their thymic differentiation may render them more sensitive than Tconv cells to 
epigenetic changes of the whole T cell compartment. The results provide a 
mechanistic basis by which general epigenomic alterations in the T cell 
compartment can be causative of autoimmune and other immunological diseases 
through selectively affecting thymic Treg cell development.

While fivefold point symmetry is common in nature, fivefold spatial symmetry is 
seldom observed. Regular pentagons cannot tile a plane without leaving voids, 
and even the densest "ice-ray" packing is exceptionally rare. Fivefold helices 
are equally elusive. We report a small molecule that self-assembles into 
hydrogen-bonded pseudo-fivefold helices and adopts an ice-ray pentagonal packing 
motif over crystallographic length scales using peripheral disorder that 
partially occupies regions that would otherwise be void in an ideal pentagonal 
tessellation. The resulting structure exhibits weak and nondirectional 
interhelical interactions within the (bc) plane and comparatively strong and 
directional intrahelical hydrogen bonding along the a axis. This structural 
anisotropy gives rise to single crystals with large aspect ratios and distinct 
mechanical behavior. This realization of two rare structural motifs within a 
single crystal shows the capability of simple organic molecules to form complex 
structures and highlights an untapped potential for symmetry engineering in 
molecular solids through the interplay of intermolecular interactions with 
pronounced differences in strength and directionality.

Convergent genome streamlining accompanies independent miniaturization in the 
world's smallest fishes.

Sudasinghe H(1)(2), Matschiner M(3), Britz R(4), Conway KW(5), Tan HH(6), 
Salzburger W(7), Peichel CL(2), Rüber L(1)(8).

Author information:
(1)Natural History Museum Bern, Bern 3005, Switzerland.
(2)Division of Evolutionary Ecology, Institute of Ecology and Evolution, 
University of Bern, Bern 3012, Switzerland.
(3)Faculty of Biology, Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, Planegg 82152, 
Germany.
(4)Senckenberg Natural History Collections, Dresden 01109, Germany.
(5)Department of Ecology and Conservation Biology and Biodiversity Research and 
Teaching Collections, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX 77843.
(6)Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, National University of Singapore, 
Singapore 117377, Singapore.
(7)Department of Environmental Sciences, Zoological Institute, University of 
Basel, Basel 4051, Switzerland.
(8)Division of Aquatic Ecology and Evolution, Institute of Ecology and

Miniaturization, the reduction of adult body size to an extreme degree, has 
evolved repeatedly across vertebrates. Yet its genomic underpinnings remain 
poorly understood. Cypriniformes, the most species-rich order of freshwater 
fishes, contains multiple miniaturized lineages that have evolved via 
contrasting developmental processes. Proportioned dwarfs are tiny-bodied but 
otherwise morphologically similar to larger relatives, while progenetic 
miniatures exhibit developmental truncation and retain larval-like anatomical 
features into adulthood. Using a new time-calibrated phylogeny of 309 
cypriniform species and comparative genomic analyses of 33 high-quality genome 
assemblies, we investigated the evolutionary history and genomic correlates of 
miniaturization across this order. Ancestral state reconstruction revealed 
multiple independent origins of both miniature types, with reversals to the 
nonminiature state rarely recovered and miniature origins nonrandomly 
distributed across the phylogeny. The origins of the two types of miniatures 
differed in their timing. Progenetic miniatures arose predominantly in the 
Eocene whereas proportioned dwarfs arose mainly within the Miocene period. 
Genome size variation across Cypriniformes has been overwhelmingly driven by 
polyploidy. However, progenetic miniatures showed a directionally consistent, 
though nonsignificant, trend toward genome size reduction. Comparative genomic 
analyses revealed that all three independently evolved progenetic miniature 
lineages share convergent signatures of repeat loss alongside genome-wide intron 
shortening, patterns absent in proportioned dwarfs. Our study provides the 
broadest evidence to date that progenetic miniaturization, despite independent 
origins, is underpinned by predictable structural genomic changes, revealing a 
fundamental link between developmental truncation and genome architecture in 
vertebrates.

Trans-vatabnet: transcriptomic signatures for Parkinson's disease detection 
using deep learning.

Vishwakarma PP(1), Vishwakarma PP(2), Avanti S(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Computer Engineering, Shah & Anchor Kutchhi Engineering

(2)Department of Geriatrics, MGM Medical College and Hospital, Kamothe, Navi

Background: Early detection of Parkinson's disease (PD) is essential for timely 
clinical intervention. However, transcriptomic-based diagnosis faces challenges 
associated with high-dimensional gene expression data, redundant features, class 
imbalance, and limited interpretability. Objective: This study proposes 
TransVaTabNet, an integrated framework for PD detection and biomarker 
identification using transcriptomic analysis, deep learning, and explainable 
artificial intelligence. Methods: RNA-seq data were preprocessed using 
low-expression gene filtering, Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM) normalization, and 
voom transformation. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using 
limma-voom, followed by stage-specific gene analysis and functional enrichment 
to investigate disease-associated pathways. A Variational Autoencoder (VAE) 
generated compact latent representations, while the Synthetic Minority 
Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) addressed class imbalance. TabNet classified the 
derived features using sequential attention, and SHapley Additive exPlanations 
(SHAP) supported model interpretation and potential biomarker identification. 
Results: Evaluation on the GSE216281 RNA-seq dataset achieved an Area Under the 
Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) of 90.95%, outperforming the 
classical machine learning models evaluated in this study.Conclusion: 
TransVaTabNet combines dimensionality reduction, attention-based classification, 
and explainability to support PD detection and potential biomarker discovery. 
The framework offers an interpretable approach to identifying disease-associated 
transcriptomic patterns and may support future precision diagnostic research.

Heat and childhood respiratory health: exploring the evidence and raising the 
red flags.

Buthelezi MS(1), Jeena P(2), Naidoo RN(1).

Author information:
(1)Discipline of Occupational and Environmental Health, School of Medicine, 
College of Health Sciences, University of KwaZulu-Natal, Durban, South Africa.
(2)Discipline of Paediatric and Child Health, School of Medicine, College of 
Health Sciences, University of KwaZulu-Natal, Durban, South Africa.

INTRODUCTION: Climate change impacts on the health of vulnerable groups 
globally. Heat, as a specific component of climate change, affects the 
respiratory health of children, particularly those from marginalized communities 
and in low- and middle-income countries. Understanding the exposure pathways for 
these outcomes is critical for interventions and policy development.
AREAS COVERED: A synthesis of the evidence for key heat-related childhood 
respiratory outcomes (asthma, infections, rhinitis and lung function) is 
presented. The knowledge gaps are highlighted. Interpreting the evidence 
requires understanding the approaches to heat exposure characterization in 
epidemiological studies. These exposure-response complexities are explored.
EXPERT OPINION: While the evidence for heat-related adverse events among 
children with asthma and respiratory infections is strong, it is less so for 
other respiratory outcomes. Inconsistencies exist across studies. These 
inconsistencies may be a result of how exposure is characterized in studies. 
While acute outcomes have been investigated mostly from hospital records, 
sub-clinical effects among children in community-based studies are absent. 
Limited studies have been conducted in marginalized communities or in low- and 
middle-income countries. Understanding exposure-response relationships and 
addressing gaps in the evidence is necessary for the development of appropriate 
interventions to protect the respiratory health of children.

INTRODUCTION: Cervical cancer remains a significant global health challenge. 
This narrative review synthesizes evidence from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and 
ClinicalTrials.gov (January 2010 to August 2026), focusing on randomized 
prospective trials of systemic combination therapies.
AREAS COVERED: In locally advanced cervical cancer, pivotal phase 3 trials such 
as INTERLACE (induction chemotherapy) and KEYNOTE-A18 (pembrolizumab plus 
chemoradiation) have shown improved survival. For advanced, persistent, 
recurrent, or metastatic disease, adding pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-826) or 
atezolizumab (BEATcc) to chemotherapy, with or without bevacizumab, has 
increased median overall survival from 26 to over 37 months. In the second-line 
setting, tisotumab vedotin (innovaTV 301) has become a new Category 1 standard.

blockade (cadonilimab), TROP2-directed antibody-drug conjugates (sacituzumab 
tirumotecan), and therapeutic vaccines.
EXPERT OPINION: Immune checkpoint inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates have 
improved survival; however, high costs limit access, especially in low- and 
middle-income countries where disease burden is greatest. Key priorities include 
harmonizing predictive biomarkers, managing overlapping toxicities, and 
designing resource-conscious cooperative trials to evaluate shorter or 
lower-dose maintenance regimens. Addressing access disparities while refining 
patient selection is essential to achieving equitable global care.

A designathon to co-create strategies to increase uptake of sexual health 
services among older adults, including those with disabilities: findings from a 
UK-based participatory event.

Subba A(1), Conyers H(2), Tembo M(3), Babatunde Y(4), Wu D(2)(5), Tucker 
JD(2)(6), Kpokiri EE(2), Sakuma Y(2).

Author information:
(1)London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, London WC1E 7HT, UK.
(2)Department of Clinical Research, Faculty of Infectious and Tropical Diseases,

BACKGROUND: Sexual health services and research often neglect middle-aged and 
older adults, including those with disabilities. The Sexual Health in Older 
Adults Research (SHOAR) study addresses this gap through a designathon, engaging 
adults aged 45+ years to co-create inclusive, user-centred sexual health 
interventions in the UK.
METHODS: We used a participatory action research approach to co-develop sexual 
health interventions for middle-aged and older adults, including people with 
disabilities and sexual minorities. The 2.5-day event, supported by diverse 
stakeholders, produced five prototype interventions, with one selected to 
present at a national sexual health conference.
RESULTS: A total of 34 participants (41.2% males and 58.8% females) aged from 
under 25 years to 62 years participated in the designathon in London. Five teams 
developed proposed interventions that addressed assigned themes: (1) community 
theatre, knit and natter (knitting and social group), scripted peer-support 
stories, and street festivals with signposting; (2) use of self-care (e.g. 
barbers, hair salon) to promote discussion of sexual health; (3) inclusion of 
sexual health-related questions in routine National Health Service health checks 
performed by general practitioners; (4) information and advertisement campaign 
for older and women with disabilities with catchy slogans and buttons/stickers; 
and (5) peer champions providing training on inclusive services, peer-support in 
clinics in community settings.
CONCLUSIONS: We describe the process and outcomes of a sexual health-related 
designathon with middle-aged and older adults. The use of participatory 
activities to engage this population proved to be a valuable source of insights 
for improving sexual health research, practice, and policy. Further research is 
needed to evaluate their effectiveness and implementability.

Yin Z(1)(2), Zhang X(3), Li L(1), Fitzpatrick TS(4), Zhao P(5), Yuan J(1)(5)(6),

BACKGROUND: Bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs) disproportionately 
impact gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM) in China. 
Doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (DoxyPEP) can prevent syphilis and 
chlamydia among GBMSM; however, it has not yet been officially endorsed in 
China. This study aims to investigate the perceptions and use of DoxyPEP among 
GBMSM in a nationwide sample.
METHODS: We conducted a nationwide online cross-sectional survey in China 
between November 2024 and February 2025. Participants were recruited through 
community-based organizations and Centers for Disease Control offices using 
convenience and snowball sampling. Eligible participants were cisgender GBMSM 
aged ≥18 years living in China. The survey assessed sociodemographic 
characteristics, sexual behaviors, and DoxyPEP awareness, willingness and use. 
Modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimation was used to identify 
correlates of DoxyPEP awareness, willingness and use.
RESULTS: A total of 1022 GBMSM completed the survey (mean age 29 years); 96.9% 
identified as gay/bisexual. Most were unmarried (87.7%), had graduated college 
(87.8%) and had a monthly income >USD750 (68.3%). Overall, 55.1% had heard of 
DoxyPEP, 42.7% reported willingness to use it and 12.8% had previously used it. 
DoxyPEP awareness was associated with prior HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) 
use (aPR 1.47, 95% CI: 1.31-1.65) and recent sexual activity with female 
partners (aPR 1.42, 95% CI: 1.23-1.64). Willingness to use DoxyPEP was 
associated with multiple casual sexual partners (aPR 1.41, 95% CI: 1.15-1.73), 
commercial sex (aPR 1.31, 95% CI: 1.07-1.62), prior PrEP use (aPR 1.22, 95% CI: 
1.05-1.41) and DoxyPEP awareness (aPR 2.12, 95% CI: 1.78-2.53). The most 
reported barriers were insufficient information (72.7%), concerns about 
side-effects (35.5%) and doubts about effectiveness (30.6%). DoxyPEP use was 
associated with multiple casual partners (aPR 2.17, 95% CI: 1.22-3.85), 
commercial sex (aPR 1.63, 95% CI: 1.07-2.47), prior PrEP use (aPR 2.56, 95% CI: 
1.75-3.74) and DoxyPEP awareness (aPR 14.60, 95% CI: 6.12-34.80).
CONCLUSIONS: DoxyPEP awareness and willingness among GBMSM in China were 
moderate; however, actual uptake remained low. Having multiple sexual partners, 
commercial sex history, and prior HIV PrEP experience were associated with 
DoxyPEP willingness and use. Targeted health education and integration of 
DoxyPEP into existing HIV and STI prevention services may facilitate scaled 
uptake of DoxyPEP in practice.

often ascribed to evolutionary transitions in locomotion, including the origin 
of flight during the dinosaur-bird transition. However, the potential for 
transformations of braincase architecture to influence SCC shape independent of 
sensory-functional adaptation has generally been overlooked. We evaluate the

extinct crown birds, including taxa representing ~24 independent evolutionary 
losses of flight, together with Mesozoic stem avialans, nonavialan dinosaurs,

Poli F(1)(2), Oldham S(3)(4), Mousley A(1)(2), Bullmore ET(2)(5), Vértes PE(2),

Author information:
(1)Medical Research Council Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit, University of

(2)Department of Psychiatry, University of Cambridge, Cambridge CB2 0SZ, United 
Kingdom.
(3)Developmental Imaging, Murdoch Children's Research Institute, The Royal

(4)Turner Institute for Brain and Mental Health, School of Psychological

Brain network formation unfolds on a nonuniform developmental timetable, with 
different cortical regions generating connections at different developmental 
phases. Generative network models (GNMs) aim to uncover the principles 
underpinning the organization of connectomes by creating synthetic networks 
according to simple computational rules. These models capture the connectome's 
topology, operationalized here as the cumulative distributions of network 
metrics (e.g., modularity, small-worldness, rich-club structure). However, GNMs 
typically ignore the differential timing of connectivity formation, and by 
omitting this temporal programme they often misplace topological features in 
physical space. Here, we add a heterochronous growth term to GNMs and use a 
model fitness function that weighs topology and topography equally. Topography 
refers to the spatial embedding of the network-the actual anatomical positions 
of the axonal tracts. With these advances, we can generate synthetic networks 
that more faithfully reproduce the spatial layout of diffusion-MRI connectomes 
from two independent adult cohorts. Compared with classical, temporally agnostic 
models, heterochronous simulations improve model fit, accurately locate cortical 
hubs and modules across individuals, and converge on a single caudal-to-rostral 
gradient of brain maturation. Overall, integrating heterochronicity makes GNMs 
more faithful to brain development, and allows for better identification of 
individual differences in network formation.

Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are often found forming a peripheral 
stromal barrier around tumors. Here, this paradigm is challenged using 
microfabricated 3D cancer-CAF spheroid models combined with quantitative 
magnetic force tensiometry. A surface tension atlas is established for eight

Evolution shapes ecosystem resilience through spatial self-organization.

Dong X(1), Richardson AJ(2), Muneepeerakul R(3).

Author information:
(1)Department of Environmental Science and Policy, University of California, 
Davis, CA 95616.
(2)Department of Mathematics, University of California, Davis, CA 95616.
(3)Department of Agricultural and Biological Engineering, University of Florida,

Drylands are globally widespread and ecologically important but vulnerable to 
climate change. Many exhibit spatially self-organized vegetation patterns that 
enhance resilience by enabling vegetation to reorganize their patterns under 
drying, thereby optimizing water use and maintaining productivity. Plants can 
also undergo evolution in response to environmental change. Although both 
spatial self-organization and rapid evolution are fundamental mechanisms of 
resilience, their interaction remains largely unknown. Using a theoretical 
model, we examine how these mechanisms interact to shape vegetation 
transitions-abrupt or gradual-and ecosystem resilience under climatic drying. We 
find that pattern formation can suppress adaptation by maintaining soil moisture 
beneath vegetation patches despite rainfall decline, thereby limiting selection 
for increased drought tolerance. However, this suppression is largely alleviated 
under the variable rainfall typical of drylands. In turn, evolution feeds back 
on self-organization by increasing the spatial plasticity of vegetation patterns 
and their ability to reorganize under changing climate, although this positive 
effect weakens as evolutionary rate increases. Considering direct (adaptation) 
and indirect (pattern-mediated) effects, evolution enhances resilience, with 
indirect effects via pattern plasticity dominating. Within model scenarios 
spanning plausible rainfall variability and relative evolutionary-to-ecological 
rates, more than half of vegetation transitions are abrupt involving biomass 
losses exceeding 50%, highlighting a potential mechanism underlying recent 
global observations of widespread abrupt vegetation losses in drylands. These 
results demonstrate that evolution and spatial self-organization jointly 
determine dryland resilience under environmental change and highlight the 
unexpected role of evolution in patterned landscapes, calling for integrative 
approaches to predict ecosystem responses in a changing world.

Competing presynaptic protein assemblies coordinate basal neurotransmission with 
homeostatic plasticity.

Hsieh WC(#)(1), Han TH(#)(1), Vicidomini R(#)(1), Nguyen P(1), Serpe M(1).

Author information:
(1)Section on Cellular Communication, Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute 
of Child Health and Human Development, NIH, Bethesda, MD 20892.
(#)Contributed equally

Neural circuits establish a stable basal level of synaptic transmission that is 
maintained throughout life. When synaptic activity is perturbed, homeostatic 
mechanisms restore this set point, but how neurons reconcile long-term stability 
and rapid compensatory plasticity remains unclear. Here, we identify two 
competing presynaptic multimolecular complexes that control steady-state 
transmission and homeostatic potentiation and define the molecular switch that 
enables transitions between these functional states. At Drosophila neuromuscular 
junction, the transmembrane protein PlexinB (PlexB) and the auxiliary subunit 
Neto-α regulate both basal synaptic function and homeostatic plasticity. PlexB 
association with presynaptic KaiR1D/Neto-α receptor complexes modulates channel 
properties and fine-tunes neurotransmitter release, whereas PlexB signaling with 
Semaphorin2b (Sema2b) and Neto-α drives homeostatic potentiation. KaiR1D and 
Sema2b/PlexB compete for a limited pool of presynaptic Neto-α. Motor neurons 
switch from steady-state transmission to homeostatic potentiation by exchanging 
KaiR1D/Neto-α/PlexB complexes for Neto-α/PlexB/Sema2b. Critically, Neto-α must 
dissociate from KaiR1D-containing complexes to initiate the homeostatic 
response. Variants of Neto-α or KaiR1D that fail to dissociate support normal 
basal neurotransmission but abolish homeostatic plasticity. These findings 
demonstrate that dynamic reorganization of competing presynaptic protein 
assemblies enables neurons to preserve stable baseline transmission while 
mounting robust compensatory responses to perturbations. Given the widespread 
roles of presynaptic receptors and Semaphorin/Plexin signaling in synaptic 
regulation, this mechanism may represent a conserved strategy for balancing 
stability and plasticity in neural circuits.

Pagan N(1), Törnberg P(2), Bail CA(3), Barrie C(4)(5).

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to 
simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these 
applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments 
of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark 
for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack 
robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for 
calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, 
we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation 
framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic 
similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers 
and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a 
given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five 
calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context 
retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even 
after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, 
especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models 
generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve 
human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic 
fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from 
the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable 
framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while 
underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

Efficient immune cell migration requires physical interactions with surrounding 
tissues. While tissue matrix mechanics influence leukocyte motility, it is 
unknown how leukocytes exert pushing and pulling forces to traverse cell-dense

The origin and early radiation of winged insects (Pterygota) represent one of 
the most transformative events in terrestrial evolution, yet phylogenetic 
relationships among their basalmost lineages (Ephemeroptera, Odonata and 
Neoptera) continue to be a central debate within insect systematics. Here, we 
present the most taxonomically comprehensive phylogenomic analysis to date, 
leveraging genomic and transcriptomic data from 101 species, including 16 
sequenced ephemeropteran genomes. Employing 1,367 universal single-copy 
orthologs across two supermatrices, we used concatenation- and coalescent-based 
frameworks under homogeneous and heterogeneous, and multispecies coalescent 
models. Our analyses support Palaeoptera monophyly. Although coalescent-based 
methods initially suggested a Chiastomyaria (Ephemeroptera + Neoptera) topology, 
subsequent signal dissection and topology tests confirm that the preponderance

emerged in the Late Devonian. By reconciling molecular evidence with 
morphological synapomorphies, such as wing-base sclerite homologies, this study 
provides a coherent framework for the early evolution of winged insects, 
supports a single origin of wings, and identifies the neopteran wing-folding 
mechanism as a singular evolutionary innovation.

Learning dissipative chaotic dynamics with boundedness guarantees.

Tang S(1), Sapsis TP(1), Azizan N(1).

Author information:
(1)Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139.

Chaotic dynamics, commonly seen in weather systems and fluid turbulence, are 
characterized by their sensitivity to initial conditions, which makes accurate 
prediction challenging. Recent approaches have focused on developing data-driven 
models that attempt to preserve invariant statistics over long horizons since 
many chaotic systems exhibit dissipative behaviors and ergodicity. Despite the 
recent progress in such models, they are still often prone to generating 
unbounded trajectories, leading to invalid statistics evaluation. To address 
this fundamental challenge, we introduce a modular framework that provides 
formal guarantees of trajectory boundedness for neural network chaotic dynamics 
models. Our core contribution is a dissipative projection layer that leverages 
control-theoretic principles to ensure the learned system is dissipative. 
Specifically, our framework simultaneously learns a dynamics emulator and an 
energy-like function, where the latter is used to construct an algebraic 
dissipative constraint within the projection layer. Furthermore, the learned 
invariant level set provides an outer estimate for the system's strange 
attractor, which is known to be difficult to characterize due to its complex 
geometry. We demonstrate our model's ability to produce bounded long-horizon 
forecasts that preserve invariant statistics for chaotic dynamical systems, 
including Lorenz 96 and a reduced-order model of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky 
equation.

In mammals, a small population of spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) is 
established shortly after birth. These cells self-renew and produce sperm for 
the male's reproductive lifespan, passing the genome on to the next generation. 
Establishment of a population of SSCs with high genomic integrity is essential. 
SSCs are derived from a much larger precursor population of male germ cells 
(MGCs) that differentiate during fetal life. During the last third of gestation, 
MGCs undergo a prolonged period of G0 cell cycle arrest during which they 
sustain high levels of transcription and acquire epigenetic programming for SSC 
fate. Although these differentiation steps can cause cellular and genomic 
damage, it has been unclear whether selection for germ cell quality occurs 
during G0 arrest since no classic markers of cell death have been detected. In

Metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGlu5) is essential for synaptic plasticity 
and memory, making it a potential therapeutic target in Alzheimer's disease 
(AD). While hemispheric asymmetries in hippocampal function have been observed 
in AD patients, the lateralized contribution of mGlu5 signaling to cognitive 
decline remains unclear. Here, we show a physiological left-right asymmetry in 
hippocampal mGlu5 expression in wild-type mice, with higher levels in the left 
hemisphere, consistent with previous reports. This physiological asymmetry is

hyperphosphorylation, across both hemispheres, indicating a widespread impact of 
hemisphere-selective intervention. These findings establish a functional 
lateralization of hippocampal mGlu5 signaling and identify the left hippocampus 
as a critical site for mGlu5-dependent memory dysfunction in AD. They also 
highlight the therapeutic potential of region-specific photopharmacology for 
precise intervention in early AD pathology, providing a strategy for spatially 
targeted modulation of pathological synaptic signaling in neurodegenerative 
disease.

uncertainties both in sources and its role in atmospheric oxidation. Based on

contribution of CO from atmospheric oxidation in South Asia, calling for a 
reassessment of regional emission-oxidation coupling in models and of mitigation 
strategies.

A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation.

Han CT(1), Tsay K(2), Lobo S(3), Najafi S(2), Monahan K(1), Hong E(1), Shell 
MS(3), Shea JE(2)(4), Han S(1).

Author information:
(1)Department of Chemistry, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL 60208-3113.
(2)Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of California, Santa 
Barbara, CA 93106-9510.
(3)Department of Chemical Engineering, University of California, Santa Barbara, 
CA 93106-5080.
(4)Department of Physics, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA 
93106-9530.

Tau assembles into fibrillar aggregates that are pathological hallmarks of a 
group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively called tauopathies. Templated 
aggregation of naïve tau to seeding-competent fibrils that proceed from cell to 
cell is a key driver of prion-like progression of tauopathies. This study tests 
the hypothesis that tau, an intrinsically disordered protein, achieves 
in-register stacking to form seed-competent fibrils by a pinning action of tau 
to each other and/or the seed surface via a single dominant hotspot to avoid 
mismatch in tau stacking to fibrils. Structured solvation water has been 
proposed to be a signature of such hot spots at both the tau fibril-end surface 
and soluble tau monomers. Although jR2R3-P301L tau exhibits a heterogeneous 
hydration landscape in its intrinsically disordered state, with enhanced water 
structuring near the P301L mutation site, it is unclear whether a localized 
hotspot exists at the fibril end surface and surface water facilitates the 
initial contacts in templated aggregation. Using rapid 1H-15N SOFAST-HMQC NMR to 
track seed-induced aggregation of jR2R3-P301L in real time, complemented by 
molecular dynamics simulation of fibril surface hydration, we identify a 
residue-specific pinning hotspot that is prone to dewetting followed by 
sequential folding and incorporation of the remaining segment in a two-step 
dock-and-lock process. Site-specific spin labeling further demonstrates that 
blocking this pinning hotspot disrupts templated aggregation, leading to shorter 
fibrils. The identification of a dominant pinning site will facilitate the 
rational design of binders to effectively disrupt fibril extension or serve as 
diagnostic or therapeutic strategies.

Beyond stroke: atrial fibrillation and the broader burden of thromboembolic

Höiby P(1), Zarrouk M(2), Lind L(3), Basna R(1), Overton MC(1), Elmståhl S(1).

Author information:
(1)Division of Geriatric Medicine, Department of Clinical Sciences in Malmö,

(2)Division of Vascular Medicine, Department of Clinical Sciences in Malmö, Lund

(3)Department of Medical Sciences, Cardiovascular Epidemiology, Uppsala

OBJECTIVES: To investigate the distribution and risk of thromboembolic events 
(TEs) among adults with and without atrial fibrillation (AF), and to assess oral 
anticoagulant (OAC) use over time.
DESIGN: This population-based longitudinal cohort study included EpiHealth 
participants recruited between April 2011 and December 2016 and followed through 
linkage to Swedish health data registers from baseline until the first TE, 
death, or December 31, 2016.
RESULTS: At baseline, 873 of 22,616 participants (3.9%) had AF and 297 developed

An Analysis of Characteristics of Physician Assistant Programs by US News & 
World Report Ranking Tier.

Min E(1), MacLean M.

Author information:
(1)Northwestern University PA Program, Chicago, Illinois.

INTRODUCTION: The US News & World Report (USNWR) is the most widely recognized 
publication currently ranking PA programs. Concerns have been raised about the 
methodology particularly that the metrics are subjective, oversimplified, and do 
not reflect educational quality. Because rankings may influence PA program 
reputation and applicant decision making, examining characteristics of the 
top-ranked PA programs is important.
METHODS: This nonexperimental, descriptive study analyzed PA Programs ranked in 
the USNWR 2025 "Best Physician Assistant Programs" publication. Data were 
collected from individual PA program websites, the Accreditation Review 
Commission on Education for the Physician Assistant website, and the PA 
Education Association Centralized Application Service for Physician Assistants 
Directory. Programs were grouped into 4 tiers. Program, institutional, and 
outcome variables were compared using ANOVA, χ 2 testing, and correlation 
analysis.
RESULTS: Data from 206 programs were collected. Program age and academic health 
center affiliation differed significantly between higher and lower-tier 
programs. Public versus private institution and geographic region varied across 
tiers but were not statistically significant. Accreditation status, 5-year 
Physician Assistant National Certifying Examination pass rates, and student 
attrition rates were similar across all tiers.
DISCUSSION: Program age and academic health center affiliation were the only 
characteristics that significantly differed across ranking tiers. Outcomes data 
were similar across all tiers, reinforcing concerns that USNWR rankings may 
reflect visibility and reputation rather than educational quality.

Exploring the sexual risk-taking practices of bi+ femmes: a two-wave qualitative

Cooper SC(1), Memaj I(2), Kaywin E(1), Henderson SB(3), Tillewein H(4).

Author information:
(1)Community Health and Social Sciences, City University of New York School of 
Public Health and Health Policy, New York, NY, USA.
(2)Community Health and Health Policy, CUNY Graduate School of Public Health & 
Health Policy, New York, NY, USA.
(3)Planned Parenthood Federation of America Inc, New York, NY, USA.
(4)Department of Health and Human Performance, Austin Peay State University,
